(II)

INTRODUCTION 

This constructive study of the operations of the Internal Revenue Service was commissioned by the Administrative Conference of the United States. The Conference, a permanent independent Federal agency, was established by statute (5 U.S.C. §§571-576) to study the efficiency, adequacy and fairness of the administrative procedures used by Federal agencies and to recommend improvements to the President, the agencies, Congress and the courts. The project was undertaken at the request and with the continuing cooperation and encouragement of Senator Joseph M. 

Montoya of New Mexico, Chairman of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Treasury, Postal Service and General Government. 

The study was carried out by a team of tax experts headed by Professor Charles Davenport of the University of California Law School at Davis. Their work was performed under the oversight of a Steering 

Committee of specialists in tax law and public interest representation. The It must be noted that this is a report to the Administrative Conference of the United States and not a report of the Conference. report has been circulated to the membership of the Conference, together with a set of proposed recommendations based on the report and submitted by the Steering Committee for Conference consideration. However, neither the membership nor any other official body of the Conference will adopt or pass upon the report as such. The full texts of any recommendations adopted by the Conference at its Plenary Session appear in the Federal Register and will be published in future Conference documents. *See Appendix. 1371316 

(III)

IV 

In working on this report, Professor Davenport received the cooperation of the officials and staff of the Internal Revenue Service. 

While the report is critical of certain aspects of IRS' operations, it also recognizes significant efforts at improvements presently under way. 

It is hoped that through this report and the attention which it stimulates the IRS will be encouraged to make still greater efforts to achieve fairness and efficiency in its dealings with taxpayers.

(VI)

FOREWORD by CHARLES DAVENPORT 

The end product of this nearly year-long study of some procedures employed by the Internal Revenue Service is the work of many people. It is divided into three parts. The Reports are the lengthy documents in six chapters, describing various aspects of the procedures we studied. The Summaries are shorter statements of each Report chapter, with special emphasis on those matters addressed by Proposed Recommendations. 

The Proposed Recommendations are suggestions for improvements. Many of them can be effectuated by administrative action. Others will require statutory action or authorization.

Before the Project staff was assembled, the Administrative Conference of the United States had established a Steering Committee composed of devoted, helpful, and eminent authorities. They debated and chose the areas of study. They met, often at great personal inconvenience, many times and even in several cities to give guidance and make criticisms. More importantly they read drafts of the Reports, found weaknessess, suggested editorial improvements, and offered encouragement. The Reports are not, however, their documents. The best parts of the Reports may be tied directly to the Steering Committee. Weaker points are not their shortcomings. Rather their formal contribution lies in the developing and voting of Proposed Recommendations. 

(VII)

VIII 

The Reports are largely the work of the Project's staff and consultants. 

Those who worked part or full time for some or all of the 

Consultants had period of the study are here referred to as the staff. many different responsibilities, but the collection of data and writing was shared by the staff and consultants. 

The portion of Chapter 1 on the audit process is primarily the work of Laurence Wohl. Professor Gifford outlined the settlements discussion while Shirley Lane, Laurence Wohl, and other staff members collected and shaped most of the information. Chapter 2 on collection techniques is largely the work of John McGregor with much assistance from Pamela Pecarich and Dominick Franco. Professor Gustafson was consulted in some of the policy areas. Chapter 3 on penalties is largely the work of 

Professor Asimow with Laurence Wohl and William Anspach contributing from the staff. 

Theodore S. Lynn contributed the legal analysis of Chapter 4 on the summons, and the staff added a bit of practical information. Pamela Pecarich had virtually completed the Taxpayer Services portion of Chapter 5 when she departed for other pursuits. William Anspach picked up where she left off. Professor Marshall worked unstintingly in creating the part of Chapter 5 dealing with complaints. Professor 

Emory prepared Chapter 6 on confidentiality of tax returns and was editorially assisted by John McGregor.

Background of the Study 

No Federal agency so directly affects so many people as does the Internal

IX 

Revenue Service. More than eighty million individual income tax returns, representing a far greater number of taxpayers, are filed each year. Over two million of these returns are likely to be audited. The computer must remind nearly 5 million people that they failed to make proper payment of tax, and about one-half of those contacted by the computer will dally long enough to receive personal attention from Service employees. About 35 million people call, write, or walk into Service offices seeking assistance in understanding the tax law or the Service's operations. The Service issues about 30,000 rulings annually. It prints and mails over 100 million forms and instruction pamphlets. There are few backwaters of society that the Service does not reach.

For several years, there have been rumblings of complaint concerning abrasiveness or abuse in the conduct of some Service activities. At least as early as 1967, stories in the news media charged tyranny in the Service. While the Service responded to these charges, the questions posed were not put to rest. Similar charges received national attention in hearings before a Senate 

Subcommittee in February, 1973, where a number of witnesses appeared and complained that IRS treatment was abusive and arrogant.

Even so, probably few were prepared for the bombshell carried by John Dean into the Ervin Committee hearings. That testimony and later proceedings before the House Judiciary Committee suggested that the Internal Revenue Service had became responsive to political stimuli from the White House, to gather material on

dissident groups, to prefer political friends, to harass political enemies, and to obtain information which could be used for political extortion. While subsequent investigations resulted in somewhat mixed findings about these charges, public suspicion of the Service was exacerbated and has not yet subsided. More recent hearings have brought to light other instances of misuse of the Service's investigative powers, particularly in the Intelligence Division. 

At the same time, a number of litigated cases have suggested improper practices on the part of Service personnel. In increasing numbers of cases taxpayers have charged that the Service employs, almost with abandon, its nearly confiscatory powers conferred for use only in situations when collection of taxes would be jeopardized by delay. Also, allegations have been made that the Service's response to the Freedom of Information Act appeared contrary to both the spirit and the letter of the law. 

Against this background of public criticism of the Service, the Administrative Conference, with the support and encouragement of Senator Joseph Montoya, whose Appropriations Subcommittee has jurisdiction over both the Conference and the Service, commissioned this study. 

Despite the glamour and headline potential offered by the controversies surrounding the Service, we made an early decision to avoid the more sensational aspects of these charges. This decision was grounded in several considerations. First, the project staff, not disposed to investigation as

XI distinguished from study, thought that its contribution would be more general and have greater applicability by studying and analyzing systemic procedures rather than aiming to uncover specific abuses of them. There was no purpose to develop facts for the mere sake of reporting the sensational. 

Rather, interest lay in explaining the Service's operations and in developing facts for analysis and formulation of policy. 

Second, there were serious limitations on the ability to investigate. 

The Administrative Conference of the United States is not essentially an investigatory agency. While it has authority to receive any information which the Service is not specifically prohibited from disclosing to it, the Conference lacks the power of compulsory process. Furthermore, its access to tax return information is severely restricted. 

Moreover, both time and resources available for the study were limited. 

Topics of Study This study treats the following topics: 

1. 

The Audit and Settlement Processes 

2.

Collection of Delinquent Taxes 3. Civil Penalties 

4. 5.

Taxpayer Services and Complaints

Two additional topics (Availability of Information to the Public and Public Access to Rulings) are not discussed in the accompanying study. 

Comprehensive treatment of them was impossible within the constraints of time and resources.

XII In particular, the Steering Committee struggled at length with the problems raised by recent decisions of the Courts of Appeals requiring public access to private letter rulings under the Freedom of Information Act. The Committee concluded that this is an important subject, and has urged that the Conference commission a separate study, giving full consideration to the various alternative proposals for responding to these developments in the law.

Our study has led to an awareness of other topics that could profitably be examined, by the Administrative Conference or by others. One might examine the impact of IRS's computers upon both the operations of the Service and society at large. The question of proper oversight bears consideration; in recent sessions, at least twelve Congressional committees or subcommittees have devoted attention and hearing time to affairs of the Internal Revenue Service. Finally, the broad question of the place of criminal law in tax compliance merits review.

Limits of the Study 

The general thrust of the study was to ascertain facts sufficient to permit judgments on the more important policies in each of these areas. 

Revenue Service. 

Certainly, this study should not be seen as an investigation of the Internal Rather it is a look at only a few parts of the total operation, and is specifically aimed at those activities that most directly impact on relatively large segments of the taxpaying population. The reports should be viewed

XIII as exposition and conclusions, based on information requested and received from the agency, garnered from public documents, and gleaned from numerous interviews and the many letters received from interested citizens. 

We spoke with numerous Service employees in the national office, regional offices, and district offices. We also met with many former Service personnel and interested members of the professions having contact with the Service. All seemed eager to help us in our task. 

In a few instances, for reasons explained to us and mentioned in the Report, the Service did not respond affirmatively to requests for information. 

In some cases, there was doubt as to the appropriate paper to request. Sometimes requests were misunderstood. At other times, the reply noted that the information was not collected or compiled. In some cases even if information existed, Service personnel to whom the request was made did not know of it. Possibly, some requests were dealt with insincerely. These remarks are tendered not to question the Service's responsiveness, which we judged to be good, but only as limitations on the work.

Thus, though we had a high degree of cooperation, we cannot conclude that we obtained all the significant information on any issue. As a consequence, some of the assertions and conclusions in the Report remain tentative, and might be revised or reinforced by additional study and interviews. There is, however, a limit to personnel, time, and other resources. 

Where the objective data cited in the Reports do not entirely support a particular assertion, it is a conclusion based on papers, letters, and interviews too numerous to cite in

XIV 

detail and on the experience and judgment of the authors. Such conclusions seemed to us sufficiently accurate. Some will stand the test of time; others may not.

Thus, few sweeping generalizations or judgments should be made on the basis of our material. If more and broader conclusions and a more probing inquiry are desired, a much different operation with greater resources and legal powers would be necessary. Certainly, given the charges and denials that gave rise to this study, and have grown greater as the study progressed, the broader inquirty may well be justified. Since our study has not been an investigatory one, we do not verify or refute any of these charges, but we can report that the Service has and continues to develop improved procedural systems designed to be responsive to many of the complaints that have arisen. But whether Congress chooses or declines to endow such a venture, this study clearly was not that inquiry. Its scope is limited. It poses as many questions as it answers. 

Most of the data for this study were collected by May 1, 1975, and, generally speaking, the Report refers to procedures in effect on that date.

CHAPTER THE AUDIT AND SETTLEMENT PROCESSES I. INTRODUCTION 

A. 

Scope and Methodology. 

While many taxpayers have experienced an audit (the examination of returns and supporting books and records), there is much about the process which remains unknown or not understood even by those who have undergone it. This chapter first endeavors to describe in general terms the selection of returns for audit and the audit itself as these processes affect individual taxpayers. That description is followed by a discussion of the settlement of controversies arising in the course of an audit. Such controversies revolve around amounts of tax, interest, and penalties. As described in Chapter 3, there are penalties which may be assessed for filing returns showing too little tax if the understatement of the tax liability results from negligence or fraud (as defined for tax purposes). 

The procedures by which such penalties are imposed are in the usual case the same as the process for assessment of additional taxes. 

In addition to describing the audit and settlement process, this chapter has the purpose of examining possible deficiences or abuses in those processes. Limitations on resources and the inability to examine tax returns have to some degree required us to be selective as to the areas in which these resources should be expended. We arrived at such judgments after requesting and studying numerous documents, interviewing national office (7)

staff personnel, and interviewing regional and district personnel. interviews were held with examining officers and their immediate supervisors. 

Although the number might not be regarded as sufficient to present a valid national statistical profile, at least as to many factors the persons interviewed were substantially in agreement. As to other areas, disagreement ranged from little to sharp. Sometimes written documents conflicted with interviews, and the discrepancies could not always be explained. Thus, as is indicated at relevant points in this chapter, the information available to us for some aspects of this subject was less than ideally complete. 

In such areas, since our presentation inevitably reflects a measure of inference and judgment, recommendations are not offered. 1/ A few words about the emphasis given to return selection may be helpful. Congressional hearings, mail received by us, mail received by 2/ many others, and other events of recent years suggest an uncertainty among the public and Congress as to the integrity and impartiality of the process for selecting returns for audit. Though the Internal Revenue Service has increasingly relied on an anonymous, computerized scoring system as its major return selection technique, some of the public seemingly believes that other and less impersonal processes are utilized by it. Thus, the selection processes used by the Service and same procedures bearing on the possibility of abuse are discussed.

In addition, the process of return examination has been the subject of public attention and comment, not all of which is laudatory. 

While many such complaints reflect taxpayer ignorance of a complicated tax law and frustrations caused by dealing with a complicated and not always responsive administrative system, some also indicate that audits are not always conducted as they should be. Thus, we discuss the return examination process, the Service's attempts to make it less mysterious and frightening to the taxpayer, and some of the difficulties arising from it. 

No comment on the quality of the audits is expressed. Such comment would have required an intensive review of audit files which were not accessible. A lack of resources and the inability to obtain tax return information made such review impossible.

A. 

Introduction 

1. 

II. THE AUDIT PROCESS The Audit Process. 

Scope.

Execution of the audit process (dealt with in part II of this chapter) is left almost entirely in the hands of local offices (district offices or branches thereof), but most of the policy decisions are made at the national and regional offices of the Service. We have thus described the Audit 3/ Division at all levels, but the focus is on the structural and systemic pressures emanating from the national and regional offices. 2.

The Audit Process Summarized. 

The Internal Revenue Service has been empowered by Congress to ". . .proceed, from time to time, through each internal revenue district and inquire after. . .all persons. . .who may be liable to pay any. .tax. 5/ To accomplish this function, it has been given power to obtain for review the books and records pertinent to a taxpayer's tax return. 6/ These provisions are the statutory authority for the audit function. This function has never been extended to "all persons" who may be liable, but rather, it has been much more limited.

This limited program has as its goal, best stated by the Service itself, inducing the populace to comply voluntarily with the country's tax inducing laws.

Comments on the functioning of the audit process must, of course, be made with this goal in mind. While "voluntary compliance" 78" is easily stated, its meaning and the means of achieving it are not so 9/ easy.

At best the term creates a vague image. Thus, the development of strategies which might be adopted to achieve it have not been, and are not, immediately apparent. But, a strategy has been devised. It appears to be based on the assumption that the public will respond positively and become more compliant if (1) there is a possibility that any return may be audited, and (2) if there are sufficient audits to render the possibility credible. For reasons hereinafter discussed, one, and perhaps the most striking, consequence of this program appears to be the formation of pressures to (1) achieve audit coverage (large numbers of audits), (2) increase revenue as measured by audit results, and (3) eliminate from the audit process, by the use of computer-selection techniques, returns with little potential to yield additional revenue,

A low no-change rate (i.e., a rela-

tively low percentage of audits resulting in no recommended tax change) is considered a significant factor in measuring the adequacy of the selection process. 10/ Obviously, not all tax returns can be audited. Thus, the 

Service has adopted a policy of auditing a mix of returns consisting of those which, on their face, indicate the greatest potential for discovery of a tax increase or decrease (tax change) and those which allow the Service to maintain, as inducement to voluntary compliance, a visible presence at all income levels. 

For ease of administration, individual returns are separated into seven classes based on the level and kinds of income shown on the return. These classes are: 

Level of Adjusted Gross Income and Other Characteristics 

$0-$10,000 with only a standard deduction

This Report

Middle income non-business High income non-business Low income business Middle income business 

High income business

Any amount of business income causes the return to be classified as a business return. A return with no business income but with very high amounts of investment income, such as dividends and interest, will be classified as a non-business return. 

A mix of returns from these return classes is determined at the beginning of each fiscal year and is communicated to Service personnel as the Audit Plan. The Plan is a management projection of the numbers of returns in each of several income classes which are expected to be audited during the year. It is developed by the national office with substantial assistance from management personnel at the district and regional offices. It is the most important management tool used by the Service to plan and monitor the Service's audit activities.

Accomplishments toward examining the anticipated number of returns in each of these income classes are collected monthly, quarterly, and annually. 

The selection of returns for audit is accomplished by a number of techniques designed to achieve the objectives of coverage, additional revenue, and a low no-change rate. It is a highly sophisticated process employing both people and machines. It commences when a return is 11/ filed with the Service Center. Here every return is reviewed manually and by machine for math errors and Unallowable Items (prima facie legal errors), computer-scored for tax-change potential (DIF scored), and transcribed into computer-cognizable language for inclusion in the computer-stored Individual 

Master File. 

Once processed, a return is catalogued and stored at the 12/ 

Service Center. 13/ Upon request the return will be forwarded to a district office of the Audit Division for audit.

If errors (either in favor of or against the taxpayer) are detected, the taxpayer is notified by the Service Center, and the issues so raised are resolved with its personnel. On the other hand, an audit in which all aspects of a return may be subjected to review requires a major time commitment and concomitant expense. Thus, a number of different techniques have been developed to assist the staff of the Audit Division in efficient selection of returns for audit. These techniques have been grouped into two types of programs: (1) manual selection prograns and (2) computer selection. 

Manual selection programs are used to choose returns for audit on the basis of specific return characteristics. These characteristics have sometimes been pre-identified by Audit Division

executive personnel as requiring special attention. The focus of this special attention may change from year to year as different items require such consideration. Such characteristics might include, for example, exceptionally high adjusted gross income, certain types of deductions resulting from "tax shelters", and many other such particular factors. 

On the other hand, the computer selection program is based upon the measurement, by machine scoring, of the tax-change potential reflected in a return. Such scoring is done on the basis of the entire return and the relation to each other of various entries on the return. Such scoring does not depend on one specific characteristic. 

All returns, including those in which math errors or Unallowable Items have been detected, are so scored by application of a scientifically developed discriminant function (DIF). This process is known in Service parlance as DIF scoring.

Some audits are performed by Service Centers largely through correspondence. The vast majority are performed by one of the district offices, or their branches, scattered throughout the country. They are primarily responsible for conducting audits, making collections, and providing taxpayers with information and assistance when these activities require personal contact with the taxpayer.

When a local district office needs returns to audit, it will order returns from the Service Center servicing that particular office. 

Need is determined by the number and type of returns necessary to assure the accomplishment of the objectives prescribed by the annual Audit Plan. The Service Center sends those returns having the characteristics specified by the district as necessary for accomplishment of the annual Audit Plan. The number ordered and received by the district is always greater than the number needed for examination. Consequently, on arrival at the district office returns are further reviewed to ascertain those most suited for audit.

This further review is manually done by the district's Returns Program Manager (RPM) and his staff. As a result of this review, some returns are judged not to require audit and are returned to the Service Center. Those which seem to warrant audit are further divided between those necessitating field audit (the most complicated returns) and those which may be audited in the IRS office (simpler returns, in 14/ which category fall most individual returns).

Once so classified, the returns will be forwarded to the personnel who supervise the examining officers. These individuals are known as Group Managers. A Group Manager will screen each return he receives to determine whether he agrees with the RPM that the return is worthy of audit. If he does not, he will return it to the RPM who will then return it to the Service Center unaudited. If the Group 

Manager determines that a return should be audited, he will assign it to one of the examining officers on his staff who will then be responsible for conducting the audit of the return.

The nation is divided into seven regions. Each region has a Regional Commissioner and is, in turn, divided into districts. There are 58 districts, and each district is headed by a District Director. 

There are ten Service Centers, each under the supervision of a Director.

B.

The Planning Process. 

1. The Budget and Long Range Plan. 

The budget for any year is first considered five years prior to its implementation as a component of the Long Range Plan (LRP), sometimes referred to as the Five Year Plan. The LRP is an estimate 19/ of the operating budget for the succeeding five years. The Audit 

Division anticipates and allocates those resources anticipated neces- 20/ sary to reach planned audit coverage and levels of compliance. 

Annually in each of the next four years this projection will be modified to reflect new policies, improved techniques, methods, equipment, or facilities, and changes in organization and, perhaps, Congressional attitudes.

This document is the Commissioner's, but emanates from the Assistant Commissioner (Planning and Research) who has relied on his Research and Operations Analysis Division to coordinate its preparation. However, each operational unit (e.g., Audit, Collection, Intelligence) participates in this work. The Resources and Analysis 

Branch is the participating unit for the Audit Division, and it, in turn, draws upon national and field office staff and line personnel. 

While the Commissioner holding office at any time has responsibility for the Long Range Plan, the past record indicates that there is little, if any, likelihood that he will be in office through- 21/ out the period covered by any LRP prepared during his tenure. 

Because the program of the sitting Commissioner is reflected in present operations and because the LRP is largely a projection of these

present operations to the future, he is unlikely to protest, and can be expected to promote, the projection of present operations into the 22/ future by the LRP. Moreover, even if he insists on certain inclusions or exclusions, those items included at his will may be excised on his departure, and vice versa. Thus, the sitting Commissioner, though having personal and direct interest in the current year's Plan, may be unable to have much lasting influence on the Long Range Plan. 

The one force of continuity between Commissioners is the upper- They also have prepared the LRP echelon career managers of the Service. under the direction of various Commissioners. 

Such managers have accompanied each Commissioner to the annual budget and other hearings and must prepare each year to explain those matters left unresolved at the last hearings and to deal with those problems which have become of public concern since the last hearings. Thus, they are sensitive to the concerns and criticisms 23/ of members of Congress and the media. It seems likely, therefore, that the Long Range Plan is largely the bureaucracy's notion of good tax administration as shaped to respond to Congressional signals and public criticism. While sensitivity to such messages undoubtedly may be proper, such messages are likely to be reactions of a single influential Congressman or newspaper to an isolated situation of interest to him or it, and not his or its reactions to the Service as a whole, because the Service will rarely be viewed as a whole. The Service's reponsiveness to such

messages often may be without consideration of its overriding goals and objectives, which are, as later discussed, sufficiently malleable to encompass nearly any strategy. 

So far as Audit is concerned, the signals to which it appears to have responded are unmistakable: (1) audit coverage is desirable, 24/ i.e., greater compliance will result from a greater number of audits;

25/ (2) audits should increase revenue, i.e., should be cost-effective; and (3) the number of audits not resulting in a tax change should be 26/ low, i.e., the "no-change" rate should be low. Not surprisingly, these messages are built into the Long Range Plan and the budget projections, resulting in the Plan being largely an estimate of the number of audits necessary to maintain at least current levels of coverage and to utilize personnel efficiently in maintaining that coverage. 

Each year the Long Range Plan is updated to take into account current realities, largely Congressionally imposed budgetary limits. 

When the most recent edition of the LRP is approved, it becomes the basis for the Service's budget request for the following year and is sent to the Treasury Department for incorporation as a part of Treasury's budget request. Treasury's budget request is then sent to the Office of Management and Budget for review and final Administration action prior to submission to Congress as a part of the President's budget. 

Congressional hearings on the Service's budget are a part of Treasury's hearings, but separate attention is given to the Service, and its personnel must justify and discuss its requests. Congress then

passes on the Service's budget by making separate appropriations for 27/ all Compliance activities, for all activities related to the func- 28/ tions of Accounts, Collection and Taxpayer Service, and for other 29/ Service Salaries and Expenses. Though the Service is given discretionary powers over the expenditure of funds within these broad categories, appropriations are made in three parts to insure that funds 30/ appropriated for one purpose are not used for another. It is on the basis of these appropriations that personnel allocations are made, and these in turn establish the basis for determining the type and extent 31/ of audit coverage.

Since a large percentage of the budget is devoted to salaries and other personnel costs, budget ceilings have primary impact on deciding the number of personnel available to accomplish the results Congress is perceived as desiring. Because they are perceived as desiring audit coverage, the bureaucracy strives to deliver it while working within the strictures of the budget allocations. Thus, given limited funds, more audit coverage can be obtained by examining simpler returns which, by their nature, are less time consuming. Hence, there is motivation to audit relatively simple tax returns. And if, as seems apparent, the budget rarely results in authorization for sufficient 32/ new personnel to reach planned levels of coverage, there is a nearly irresistible attraction to maintaining current numbers by increasing the number of simple tax returns audited. 

The result is a commitment 33/

www to numbers, and more particularly, to audit coverage expressed in numbers of examinations. The effect of this kind of planning on operations will be discussed later. 

2. The Audit Plan. 

The LRP and the budget are translated into operations by the annual Audit Plan (the Plan). This Plan allocates available manpower among the various examination programs to achieve the desired coverage (penetration) of the various income classes. Though the schedule for completing this Plan will vary to some extent from year to year, the following is a fair generalization of the internal timetable adhered to 34/ by the Service.

The preparation of the Audit Plan for the upcoming year begins in the national office and appears at that level to be the product of two considerations: (1) what is being done in the current year, and (2) what changes may be effected more nearly to conform to the latest edition of the LRP. 

For example, the 1974 edition of the LRP for the fiscal year to end June 30, 1976, as amended for the last time, became, in effect, that year's budget request to the Office of Management and Budget, which modified and approved the request for submission to Congress in January 1975. Since, however, Congress may not approve the 1976 budget for several months from the date of submission and since increases over current operations may not be anticipated, the Audit Division in the national office assembles two plans. One is based on the assumption that

the 1976 budget submission will be approved. The other, the base plan, is a restatement of the current fiscal year operating budget with updated costs and assumes no increase in personnel or other resources. For the purpose of planning audit coverage, these plans deal with numbers of examinations. Both plans are prepared by the national office, which also allocates the plans to each of the seven regions. Both should be completed by March 15 and sent to the Regional Commissioners for their 35/ review and changes.

The regional office is not an operational office, and so, each region turns to its operating units, the districts, to prepare a response to the plans. The district response can be understood only by first explaining certain aspects of return classification and personnel manage- Theoretically, each return may be classified as a return to be audited by an individual working at a particular GS grade level from GS-7 through GS-13. 

Returns are classified for assignment largely by the reported level of income and the complexity of the issues that may be raised. Thus, if we assume a GS-7 can audit returns in the $0-$10,000 income category with issues of certain complexity, and if we know the number of returns we expect a GS-7 to examine in a year, multiplying the number of personnel at that grade level by the expected number of examinations will establish the number of returns to be examined. This calculation is very rough and must be adjusted to take account of the fact that personnel at each grade are expected to examine same returns classified as being appropriate for the next higher GS grade level. This serves as training to prepare for promotion.

Through this process, each local office estimates the number of returns in each income category which it can examine in the upcoming year. Such estimates are made on the basis of current personnel and also on the basis of projected increases in personnel and other resources. 

These estimates are forwarded to the district office which simply aggregates the estimates of all subordinate offices. The district will also prepare its comments indicating, for example, that it believes that certain kinds of returns should be given more attention or that certain examination programs be instituted, at least on the district level. 

After receiving a response from each of its districts, each region will establish its own program priorities, although largely within the confines of the national office's plans. By April 30 each region will have transmitted its recommendations and adjustments to the national office. While both the regional and district offices are thus consulted, their advice is largely geared to allocation of personnel or shaping of programs to attain the number of examinations forecast by the national office plans. 

June 1 is the target date for the national office to inform the regions whether the "April 30" transmittals to the national office have been approved, modified, or disapproved. Thereafter, the national office will make last-minute adjustments. By July 1 the final examination plan will have been approved and will have become operational. 

If by that date Congress has not passed on the budget, the effective examination plan is the base plan, i.e., the prior fiscal year's

operations. When the budget is finally approved, the national office distributes available man-years in excess of the base plan down to the 36/ regions. any time.

The national office retains the right to alter the Plan at A region may, however, change the amount of coverage of one or more of the various classes of returns or institute a new program, although only on approval of the national office. Within the region, however, the Regional Commissioner has full authority to allocate personnel among districts and programs. Thus, though a region's Audit 

Plan for each income class may not be changed without national office approval, allocation of the Plan among the region's districts may be changed significantly.

Thus, the Plan is established at the national office. It has the objective of coverage or penetration built into it by the process just described. But other objectives, such as increase in revenue and a low no-change rate, must also be achieved. A low no-change rate is achieved by selecting the proper returns for audit. Returns are selected for audit to a large extent based on their scoring by the so-called Discriminant Function (DIF) which, in turn, depends on the Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program (TCMP). We turn now to that program. 

3. Audit Programs and Return Selection. 

a. Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program and DIF. 

(1) The Program. 

The Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program is an audit program for the selection and examination of returns.

However,

unlike most other audit programs, TCMP selects returns for examination 37/ not because of their potential for tax change. Rather, TCMP audited returns are selected as a random sample of all returns filed in each of 38/ the income classes. The purpose is to obtain a statistically valid profile of the types and magnitude of errors in each income class. 

Random sampling as a test of taxpayer compliance and as a far back as 1947. 39/ technique for selecting returns for audit was originally considered as However, not until the early 1950's was the concept accepted, and not until 1963 was TCMP established as an ongoing program. Delay in originating the program seems to have resulted from (1) an unwillingness to accept statistical sampling as a basis for audit procedures, (2) an unwillingness to invest resources in a program which had only a distant pay-off, and (3) a lack of computer capacity until the late 1950's and early 1960's. 

As originally conceived, the program which later became the TCMP was mainly intended only to determine existing levels of and trends in compliance. Information so derived was to be used in planning and evaluating administrative efficiency in return selection and examination. 

However, the 1963 TCMP audit of individual tax returns provided for the first time data for the development of formulas that would permit computer-selection of returns for audit. Including the 1963 cycle, there have been four TCMP cycles examining returns of individual tax- 40/ payers. A fifth cycle is now in progress.

The costs of the Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program are substantially higher than the costs of audits under most other programs examining a comparable number of returns. As an example, while a routine audit of an individual reporting adjusted gross business income under $10,000 may require seven hours, a TCMP audit of the same return 41/ averages approximately fourteen hours.

The greater time required results from two factors. First, in a TCMP audit every item on the return must be scrutinized, whereas in an ordinary audit an item is not examined if the examining officer thinks it is reasonably accurate. Second, the degree of verification and documentation of items entered on the return is increased. Thus, in a TCMP audit the auditor must pursue each item until, in his professional judgment, it is determined to be accurate. This is a greater burden than in the ordinary audit wherein the auditor does not require such a high degree of verification. These higher standards are required to obtain some measure of the difference between reported tax and that which, in the auditor's "professional judgment", is believed to be the proper tax.

Time of the examining officer alone, however, is not the only factor influencing the cost differential. A routine audit is conducted by a competent auditor, but the TCMP audit usually is conducted by 42/ 43/ auditors with above average capabilities. Further, examining officers must undergo special orientation; the district Returns Program 44/ and Group Managers must monitor the progress and Manager must assume special supervisory tasks; each audit must be thoroughly reviewed; 45/

46/ All accuracy of such audits more carefully than ordinary audits. these factors combine to render the cost of TCMP audits substantially more than a routine audit.

Greater costs are also imposed on the taxpayer in terms of his time, money, and psychological well-being. From the taxpayer's point of view, these greater costs are particularly galling because a substantial portion of these randomly selected returns would ordinarily escape audit and even under this intensive examination result in no or de minimis tax change. Nevertheless, this audit, done primarily for research purposes and for the benefit of the taxpaying society in general, results in substantial costs in time, professional assistance, and frustration to be borne by the individual taxpayer. Costs which benefit the government and society are thus borne by the group selected for 

TCMP audits. 

One way of minimizing these costs would be to assure that only the most experienced and capable agents who presumably work quickly and exercise discretion appropriately be assigned to TCMP audits. While such a procedure might not increase efficiency greatly, it seems a small price to pay for a decrease in the demands on a taxpayer's patience and pocketbook. (2) 

The Discriminant Function (DIF). 

TCMP audits establish a data base of approximately 200 to 250 individual items of information taken from each return. 

These data are converted into a computer program for selecting returns for audit. This conversion is done through the development of six so-called 

DIF formulas for each of the seven income categories described earlier. 

Returns examined in the TCMP audits are first segregated into 47/ income categories based on the income reported without audit correction.

Each income category is then treated separately, and returns in each category are then further sorted by the magnitude of tax change recommended by the auditor (herein referred to as tax change). The 200 to 250 information variables on returns with relatively high, low, and no tax changes will then be fed into a computer to isolate those variables having differentiating capabilities. 

For example, large tax change in the $0-$10,000 adjusted gross income category may correlate highly with the reporting of dividend income of X or more dollars. If so, then this variable is deemed significant. However, large tax change may also be found to correlate well with the claiming of four or more exemptions. Further, those returns on which both four or more exemptions are claimed and also dividend income in excess of X dollars is reported may produce a higher average tax change than do returns with only one of the two variables. If so, then high tax change correlates with the combination of these variables, and the formula for scoring a return for potential tax change would place returns having this combination of variables higher than returns with only one of the variables. Obviously, the characteristics of returns showing little or no tax change would also be taken into account, and such returns would have lower scores. 

By performing this kind of exercise for each of the 200 to 250 variables, each variable or particular combination of variables may be weighted as a relative indicator of potential tax change. 

Returns may then be scored depending upon the weights given the combinations of variables as they appear on each return. The higher the score,

the greater the tax change potential; the lower the score, the lower the tax change potential.

By this process six (three developed by IRS and three by a non-governmental firm) formulas for each income class are developed. 

We believe that each formula is based on the appearance or combination of about 15 or so variables. The formula which will produce the most tax change is used unless technical or disclosure difficulties require 48/ a shift to another.

It should be noted that though DIF is a return selection method which enables the Service to segregate for possible audit those 49/ returns indicating the highest potential for tax change, it does not provide an error-free process of selecting erroneous returns. Returns selected by DIF may be no-change returns. Further, the DIF score does 50/ not tell the auditor where to look for errors by identifying specific items which have caused high scores. 

Because of the substantial costs which would be involved in data collection and formula preparation on a local basis, both TCMP and DIF reflect national, rather than local, characteristics. The result of using national data is that DIF scores returns with no attention to items which, though normally highly questionable, may be perfectly reasonable under specific local circumstances. The Service has responded to this situation by manually reviewing at local offices DIF-scored returns before commencing examination of the return. This process is 51/ hereinafter discussed. We note, however, that this review is performed only as the highest DIF-scored returns are sent to the district office for screening prior to audit.

Needless to say, the DIF formulas are well-guarded secrets. 

No judgment is passed on their biases or lack thereof as the formulas were not examined. Furthermore, the General Accounting Office is understood to be preparing a report on the Service's audit techniques, including the DIF formulas, for use by the Joint Committee on Internal 

Revenue Taxation. 

Whatever the problems with TCMP and DIF, the DIF formulas result in the selection of approximately 60 percent of all individual returns selected for audits. Such scoring and return selection is sometimes referred to as the Audit Division Classification Program. 52/ Those returns so selected are referred to as computer-selected. 

As is detailed later, a return selected by a DIF formula is not automatically audited. Rather, returns with high DIF scores (classified by income level) are held at readiness for delivery to a district office when the district needs returns in an income category. They are then sent to the district where further screening occurs before audit. 

b. Other Return Selection Techniques. 

In addition to the Audit Division Classification Program, there are a number of methods used to select returns for the audit pool, and nearly all rely on some sort of manual selection. The major manual categories are Claims and Requests for Refunds, Multi-Year Audits, Related Pick-Up Audits, so-called Audits Initiated by IRS and Others, and Miscellaneous. 

Claims and Requests for Refund is the review of a claim to ascertain whether to pay the claim or audit the return. Multi-Year 76

7347 Audits occur when the examining officer expands his audit to years not originally contemplated. Related Pick-Up's occur when an examining officer determines that the return of a party related to the taxpayer under audit should also be examined. Audits Initiated by IRS and Others is a title covering a wide range of selection techniques. The 

Miscellaneous category includes numerous selection techniques not falling under any of the above and includes TCMP audits and the Unallowable Items Program discussed below. In addition, returns missing certain schedules or returns showing income in excess of certain amounts may be automatically selected for the audit pool. 53/ The purpose of these techniques is to penetrate areas where compliance deficiencies are believed to exist and where more visible enforcement will encourage greater compliance. Some of these techniques may fairly be characterized as programs in that broad parameters have been set for qualification, but manual screening is performed for selection. For example, the TCMP, Audit Research, and the Joint 

Compliance Programs clearly seem to be programs, and they are, perhaps, the most important because they are or may be the font from which other special programs spring. TCMP has been discussed. 

The Audit Research Program is administered and directed by the Director of Audit. Ideas for it came from various sources within the Service. Its purpose is to identify areas of non-compliance worthy of further investigation and corrective action. These areas may result from the lack of specificity of the law, causing the implementation

of such projects as those which were undertaken to verify proper reporting of Medicare payments by doctors or income by door-to-door salesmen; or they may result from the Service's belief that there is an attempt to evade the effects of the tax law. 

The Joint Compliance Program is jointly operated by the Audit and Intelligence Divisions. The national office has limited the amount 54/ but permits the districts, with of manpower to be devoted to it, regional guidance, to pursue programs aimed at curbing particular types 55/ of abuses. "The purpose of the Joint Compliance Program is to conduct research to uncover tax compliance conditions not identified by 56/ established approaches." Frequently these locally-generated programs will prove so successful that they will be adopted as a national audit program, e.g., the Return Preparers Program which originated in 57/ the Joint Compliance Program in the Southeast Region in 1972.

There are numerous other programs which provide information for the manual selection of tax returns for audit. One such program is the Informers Program, whereby the Service receives "tips" from outside the Service which lead it to individuals in need of audit. Another is embodied in the referrals to Audit from the Intelligence Division. 

Other programs include the Unallowable Items Program, discussed in detail 58/ below; the Narcotics Traffickers Program; and the Strike Forces Program.

The latter two, however, have only tangential relationships to revenue collection or voluntary compliance.

In addition, returns sometimes may be put into the audit pool merely because the Organized Crime and Racketeering Section of the Department of Justice has expressed an interest in the return even though the taxpayer has not been identified as a Strike Force target. 

Other Federal agencies may express an interest in a taxpayer. An examining officer may develop information while auditing X that suggests Y should also be audited, sometimes called an independent pick-up. 59/ A taxpayer's return may be isolated on the basis of information submitted to the Service by other parties. 

Manual selection techniques, then, permit selection for the pool to be made under a wide range of conditions. 

Some programs involve decisions at the highest policy levels of the national, regional, or district office that the program be undertaken. Others seem to require only a decision by a Service employee and perhaps his supervisor that a return be selected, e.g., the independent or related pick-up's. Others allow Federal employees outside the Service to suggest names for audit. submitted anonymously or otherwise by informers. 

Finally, some audits result from information 60/ 

Nearly all of these techniques permit an exercise of discretion by Service personnel. 

Obviously, the opportunities for improper (whether intentional 61/ or not) exercise of this discretion occur most where there is the least guidance, or where the program outlines are the least well defined, or where there is the least supervision over the manner in which the discretion is exercised.

The latter point is discussed later in this chapter.

C. 

Conclusion. 

In recent years about 40 percent of the individual returns audited were selected from the pool created by manual selection techniques. They are thus an important source of returns for audit, although not as great as computer-scored returns. There is a great difference in the selection process. DIF scoring is impersonal, while manual selection seems to range from fairly impersonal to perhaps highly personal. As detailed below, more discretion is exercised when returns are reviewed at the district for audit. 

Despite this difference, taxpayers are generally not told which technique flushed their returns to the surface for inspection. 

Further, if manual selection is involved, they most likely will not be told anything about the selection technique. While many a taxpayer's educated guess will be correct, others will not be so wise or may suspect sinister motives when, in fact, none exist. While an explanation of the selection technique would impose a slight burden on the Service, the increased confidence in the selection system should be worth the cost. If such a statement were in writing, taxpayers should have a means of verifying the accuracy. Also, the requiring of a written statement with possible audit by the Service's Internal Audit Division or investigation initiated by the taxpayer would likely be an inhibiting agent on improper conduct by personnel who can cause selection for audit.

4. 

Plan vs. Accomplishment. 

Having established an annual Audit Plan to examine specified numbers and types of returns, the Service has also established a means of measuring accomplishments toward Plan goals. This monitor is the National System for Controlling Returns in Inventory and Production 62/ Data (SCRIP). 

SCRIP, however, has not proven adequate to perform the job for which it was intended, and thus, it will soon be replaced by the Audit Information Management System (AIMS). This system will be integrated with existing and soon-to-be-implemented computerized data retrieval systems 63/ and • • .will satisfy Audit Division's current needs for accurate timely inventory controls, better control of assessments, and up-to-date management reports. . . .Further, the system will trace examination results through final determination of tax "1 64/ a capability not liability including Appellate and Tax Court. existing in SCRIP. AIMS is to be implemented in an operational pilot system at the Atlanta Service Center by July 1, 1975, and in a fully operational national system by October 1976.

Though techniques of data input and output may change under AIMS, there is no intent to change the nature of the data accumulated, but rather, to accelerate their collection and translation into management reports and information tools. Thus, we will discuss here the types of data gathered and the methods of their accumulation under the current system.

65/ The purpose of SCRIP and eventually the aim of AIMS are to provide the Service with an inventory control mechanism and timely data to assure Plan attainment.

The former function will be discussed later in the report. As to the latter, the most important information comes from (1) the Audit Technical Time Reporting System, the backbone of which is the daily time report, the ATTR (Audit Technical Time Report), 66/ required of all district and Service Center technical personnel, and (2) the information provided by Form 1247. "The entire system is mechanically monitored through computer operations at the IRS Data Center.

After approval by the National Office, the regional man-year allocations. .are. .used as feeder reports for the Audit Technical Time 

Reporting System. Monthly comparisons of planned vs accomplished man-year allocations are submitted to district, regional and National Office management officers for monitoring purposes. 67/ "1 ATTR's are kept by each technical employee on a monthly basis. 

If properly kept, they show all cases in progress, cumulative time, and current month's time devoted to each one. On the last workday of each month the auditor gives the report to his Group Manager, although it is available for inspection at any time during the month. Among other things, it will reveal a larger-than-acceptable inventory of open cases, any case which by the Service's standards has been open too long or to which an unusual amount of time has been charged, and the neglect 68/ of difficult cases in favor of easier ones. This form, thus, is a tool for ascertaining whether personnel goals are being attained. 

Information pertaining to units, i.e., numbers of examinations, is derived from Form 1247. Form 1247 has six parts and is attached to

the return when the appropriate Service Center sends a return to the 69/ district office for audit. At least one of the six parts remains on the return at every stage of the audit and appellate processes. 

The Service Center is responsible for completion of items on the form which identify (1) the taxpayer and the attached return, (2) the tax 70/ period represented by the return, (3) the program under which the (4) the history of the taxpayer's return was selected for audit, 71/ prior audits,

Service Center. 

and (5) any pre-audit settlement actions taken by the 72/ When the Form 1247 reaches the district, it is the responsibility of that office to enter the date on which the return was assigned to the Group Manager; the name, grade, and group of the ex- 73/

The person responsible for disposition (for example, manager, returns classifier, or examining officer) indicates the disposition and reason therefor.

The indication that follow-up is necessary is normally accompanied by a full written statement (Form 4298) as to the reasons for such sug- 78/ gested action.

Such follow-up may or may not lead to an audit the following year. That decision is deferred until the return for the following year is filed and reviewed in light of Form 4298. 

There are two other types of information on Form 1247 of interest. At the completion of an audit each Group Manager must classify the return as is appropriate for an examining officer of a particular GS grade level and enter the proper classification code on the Form 1247. Further, office Audit Group Managers must indicate one of 13 79/ principal issues in the examination." The purpose is primarily to identify errors which might be prevented by a change in the tax forms and then to collect such data for the Service's Tax Form Committee. 

After the case is closed, the return is returned to the Service Center with Form 1247 attached. The return is ultimately re-stored on shelves, and the part of the Form 1247 maintained at the Service Center in lieu of the return, while the return was in the district office, is destroyed. The district maintains its own file of 

1247's, but forms on closed cases are removed from the files and destroyed from time to time after the return is transmitted to the 

Service Center. 

Apparently, procedures for verifying the accuracy of information on Form 1247 have been changed recently. When this study commenced, all available information indicated that except for manual

inspection of returns, there was no method by which an independent group of auditors, such as the Service's own Internal Audit Division, could review the accuracy of the entries made on Form 1247. For example, if these auditors had wanted to review the accuracy of the notation on Form 1247 indicating the method by which the return to which it related was selected, they would not have been able to do so. 

The record-keeping was said to be inadequate to list by name and/or geographical location returns the audits of which were initiated for any one particular reason. This capability apparently has been developed in 80/ the intervening period and is said to exist now. 

Information on "closed cases" 81/ is submitted monthly for compilation by the National Data Center into a series of tables from which management can discern the extent to which progress in units, i.e., 82/ closed cases, is being made.

Various reports result from this pro- 83/ cess, the most important of which are monthly and quarterly reports to each district on the district's accomplishments, i.e., number of closed cases. The monthly reports should be received by the districts by the third week of the following month. However, this goal is missed on an alarmingly regular basis, and often the reports are three or more 84/ weeks late. This delay may prevent timely "corrective" action. Also, this time lag is the major factor causing the introduction of AIMS. 

AIMS should provide district accomplishments within a few days or a week's time.

Though accomplishments are compiled by districts, the national office forbids the breakdown of case closure statistics by branches,

85/ groups, or agents.

However, branch chiefs and Group Managers are well aware of their responsibilities to make the Plan, and certainly district personnel believe that branch chiefs and Group Managers do have statistics concerning case closures for the branch, groups, and the individuals comprising them. 86/ Group Managers are well aware of the Plan and their group's part in accomplishing it. One manager, in fact, stated that he was well aware of management's expectations for his group, and he saw his primary function as assisting his group in "making the Plan." This view was shared, but not so bluntly stated, by most, if not all, managers. 

This attitude is shared, if not promoted, by national policy. In the soon-to-be-distributed revised Handbook for Audit Group Managers, the manager is informed that . . [Y]our branch chief and other managers in the district office have a responsibility to tell you of the type and quality of work needed to accomplish planned objectives. .As a first line manager, you must intelligently control the flow of work by directing the efforts of each employee in a manner which will convert objectives into achievements. 87/ 

The Handbook further states just three paragraphs later: "Your branch chief will monitor your group's accomplishments and your effectiveness in planning for and managing group actions. Your planning efficiency is reflected by: (a) your group's measurable results and the status of its work in process. [and] (b) your leadership and influence to guide the efforts of your employees toward mutually understood program objectives." [emphasis added] 88/ 

While a manager is appropriately encouraged to use, though 89/ judiciously, the statistical reports available, the Handbook does not

direct, and the manager should not understand, that statistics are to replace management by personal review and contact with subordinates. 

The Handbook, to the contrary, stresses throughout that statistics are an aid to good management, not a replacement for it. Nevertheless, there is a clear message: the manager's function is to make the Plan. 

This attitude affects the examining officer. We spoke with many who stated that they had no quotas or production goals. They also stated that the number of cases they close is closely watched. In addition, they thought that excessive time on cases would be a negative factor in rewards and promotions. Thus, there was no carrot for achieving the Plan, but examining officers certainly perceive a stick if individual contributions were not satisfactorily or adequately explained. 

5. Accomplishments of the Plan. 

In the fiscal year ended June 30, 1974, the Service closed 2.2 million examinations, a significant increase over 1973's total of 

1,771,000. The numbers for recent years have been: 1.696 million in 

1972, 1.646 million in 1971, 2.010 million in 1970, 2.544 million in 

1969, and 2.904 million in 1968.

These numbers were achieved to a large extent by greater audit penetration of the lower non-business AGI (adjusted gross income) classes wherein returns can be processed cheaply, rather than the higher ones which are likely to have larger deficiencies, but the audit of which requires more expensive manpower and more time. For example, in fiscal 

1974 approximately 92 percent of all returns audited were individual and fiduciary returns, and approximately 43 percent of all returns (or 47

percent of all individual and fiduciary returns) audited were low income 90/ non-business returns in the $0-$10,000 income class. In the low income class with itemized deductions 3.6 percent of the individual and fiduciary returns were audited, while only 2.4 percent of the returns 91/ reporting $10,000-$50,000 income were subject to examination. During this same period, the low income business returns, which TCMP data have 92/ indicated are, by far, the least compliant of any class of returns, were given less audit coverage. Only 2.4 percent of business returns reporting less than $10,000 income and only 2 percent of those businesses reporting from $10,000 to $30,000 income were subjected to audit in fiscal year 1974. 93/ In the same period Revenue Agents averaged between 9 hours for the simplest individual returns to 753 hours for the most complex corporate returns with an average additional assessment of $1,307 for the 94/ former and $924,967 for the latter. Revenue Agents recommended total additional assessments amounting to $4,784,788,386, while examining only 95/ 453,007 returns.

On the other hand, Tax Auditors averaged between 96/ 1.4 and 8.3 hours per individual return with an average additional assessment of $199. Their total additional assessments amounted to only $273,566,756, approximately 5.71 percent of the revenue produced by 

Revenue Agents, while they audited 1,375,649 returns, approximately 97/ three times as many as Revenue Agents. 

The no-change rate for 1040 returns claiming a standard deduction was 43.1 percent. These no-change returns represented almost 17 98/ percent of the returns audited by Tax Auditors.

The average no-change

rate for all returns reviewed by Tax Auditors was approximately 29 percent. On the other hand, the average no-change rate for returns audited by Revenue Agents was approximately 24 percent with a range from 7.7 percent for the very largest corporations to 34.4 percent for individual returns filed with a standard deduction. 99/ 6. Impact of the Plan on the Service, the Public, and the Congress. a. Effect on the Bureaucracy.

The figures discussed above are representative and suggest that the Service's search for numbers has led it to audit a relatively large number of returns of the lower income classes. To audit these returns, a staff has been built, and its bulk militates against the initiation of changes in the audit program. The difficulty arises 100/ because this staff cannot easily be transferred to other functions, and indeed, does create a great deal of the closed cases that are reported to Congress. Thus, there is little systemic incentive to break away from the Plan as a structure within which to work, and, its presence leads to future budgets which are stated in terms of those activities and structures which prior budgets have built. The past must then be defended as the most efficient method for achieving the agency's goals because history will happen again. It happens again because the structure is there and is ready, willing, and able to replicate last year, but is not so attuned to striking off in new directions. 

Since production was desired in the prior years, what better way is there to justify an increase in budget than to increase production?

For example, in a colloquy between the then Commissioner Dana Latham and Congressman Canfield (R.-N.J.), the Representative stated: 

..[n]ow, you tell us that fully trained men in the fiscal year 1961 will be able to produce $60 million of increased revenue for $4.8 million expended?. . .That is good, I think that that being true, it is only proper that we do what we can to get this increased intake." 101/ 

Similarly, in 1963 then Commissioner Caplin justified additional Audit personnel by maintaining that they would be necessary to audit 157,000 102/ 

Thus, a circle begins. more returns in 1964 than the previous year. 

The Service must attempt to do more returns or at least as many as it did last year to justify the current year's budget. More audits will, however, require more staff doing the same thing. The cycle begins again and is difficult, if not impossible, to break. b. Pressure for Goal Attainment.

Reliance on improved production, rather than a demonstration that production affects the attainment of the Service's ultimate goals, also has a pronounced effect on the way the Service accomplishes its audits. What message does its personnel glean from a national office news release stating that: ". . . [T]he past fiscal year. . .[was] 'a banner year for our Audit program.' The 2.4 percent of returns audited for the year represents the first major increase in audit coverage since 1963. . [R] ecommendations for additional tax resulting from all types of audit totaled $5.9 billion, the largest amount of tax ever proposed by Audit and an $800 million increase over the previous high achieved in 1973." 103/

Obviously, an increase in the number of audits and assessments is desired. When this desire combines with the belief that the current selection process is very effective in isolating the most productive returns, line personnel may conclude that they need only to worry about using their time effectively. If they do so, cases will be closed and revenue will be raised.

Examining officers do not have difficulty in finding cases which contain tax change. As is discussed more fully later, they believe that assignment of a return without tax change is unlikely. Tax Auditors are given a list of items already determined to be questionable by other Service personnel. Once the return is assigned for audit, many examiners believe they should find a deficiency and close the case to show an efficient use of time.

Numerous interviews with agents and management personnel This belief translates indicate that they believe that closing cases so as to "make the Audit 104/ Plan" is the most important part of their job. into a standard of work behavior for line personnel. Although official accumulation of individual performance data in terms of dollars and closed cases is not kept, most Group Managers seemed to have a good idea of these factors for each individual in his group. One would expect as much from any manager in private industry. While such information is not collected for the purpose of exerting production pressure, but rather as a device for monitoring behavior, pressure does result. 

These pressures, then, lead to the use of judgment to close cases as quickly as possible with some tax change. Of course, this type

of perceived pressure can cut both ways. As expressed in numerous letters written to us and others made available to us, agents may assert non-existent or questionable issues, or, as has been expressed to us by Service personnel, they may drop or trade viable issues, both actions for the purpose, we suspect, of closing cases or justifying time spent on a case. The Service's attempt to counteract this tendency has, in our opinion, been sincere, but the pressures on line personnel have been translated by the Plan into production requirements. C. 

Diversion from Goals. 

The Plan also seems at least partially responsible for the Service's failure to study the reasons for compliance, motivations about which little is known. The Service does not know why people comply with the tax law, and it has made few, if any, credible efforts to study the phenomenon of compliance. Significantly, neither Congress nor any member has shown interest in finding the causes of compliance. In the hearings previously mentioned there is much talk of audit coverage and cost effectiveness, but no mention is made of reasons for compliance. 

Instead, audit coverage seems to rely on an analogy to criminal law enforcement where enforcement presence is believed to control criminal activity. The same is said to be true for compliance with the tax law, and audits are considered enforcement activities. 

Assuming arguendo the conclusions of these criminal studies are correct, the analogy is questionable if for no other reason than the criminal law provides rights and wrongs discernable with relative ease. 

Normally, one knows when he is partaking of criminal activity not 77-842 O- 76-5

condoned by society. The same cannot be said of those "not complying" with the tax law, unless one assumes that the Service's interpretation of the law is always correct and known throughout the taxpaying public. 

It is reasonable to assume that even without specific knowledge of the law, a citizen knows that theft is not socially acceptable behavior. 

It is not reasonable to assume that many taxpayers even suspect that it is "illegal" (because Social Security payments provide 51 percent of her support) to claim as a dependent parents who live with them. Correction of their returns may prevent this recidivism, but it may not have any deterrent effect on others similarly situated.

There are other reasons to doubt that the criminal law enforcement analogy is proper. First, there is little evidence that the increased presence results in better compliance. For example, if a taxpayer's chances of audit are one in 30 or 40, and if his potential gain from non-compliant behavior are, say, 10 percent of his tax bill, a change in the odds to, say, one in 20 are not likely to change his behavior unless there is some penalty attaching to his deviant actions. 

And the imposition of a penalty is unlikely due to the difficulty of proof. Furthermore, much of the non-compliant behavior is judgmental and often results from professional advice. In other cases its deviant character is wholly unknown. Thus, with many of the non-compliers audit coverage appears unlikely to change behavior. The one study which was done on the subject of methods to promote better compliance is, at best, ambivalent and inconclusive and has been allowed to die without

105/ any subsequent attention. 

It may, of course, prevent widespread criminal evasion, but even that assumption is unproven. 

Furthermore, there is evidence that the Internal Revenue Service does not wholeheartedly believe the criminal law enforcement analogy. If it did, one would expect to find the incidence of audit greatest in the areas where compliance is least. But that is not the case. As we saw above, there is more coverage in the low income nongroup filing itemized returns than there is of low business business income reporters. Yet, compliance as measured by TCMP is much lower in the latter group. 106/ Finally, some have asserted that the real impact of the audit is the fear of the unknown. Once one goes through an audit and realizes that his mistakes and even his dishonesties, if detected, will only be corrected rather than punished, one may be even less inclined to comply voluntarily.

The impact of the Plan, then, is to divert the Service and others from a more difficult task of developing strategies to reach the goal of compliance. Instead, the Plan appears designed to register the attainment of objective measures which are translated into success. 

The strategy, i.e., the Plan, so far as is shown has little relation to the goal, may be less effective than other strategies, and may even hamper attainment of the goal. 

7. Conclusion. 

It is clear that the Internal Revenue Service has not devised the Audit Plan as some type of diabolical method for the subtle

application of production pressures on line personnel. Quite the contrary, the national office seemingly has made sincere efforts to abolish quotas, norms, and other such standards. Nevertheless, in an effort to direct its employees toward the accomplishment of its established objectives, it has developed a tool to measure and monitor progress towards their achievement. This tool is the Audit Plan, and whether it is effective as a management tool is not the question addressed here. 

Indeed, one may safely assume that the annual Audit Plan is highly effective in allocating personnel and other resources and that were it not available some similar technique would have to be devised. 

The concern here is with the inhibiting effects of the Plan. 

By focusing resources on it, the Service is less likely to question whether reliance almost solely on audit coverage is the best, most efficient and effective means of attaining the goal of voluntary compliance. The Plan is grounded as much in assumption as proven fact. 

It is built on the premise that auditing is the best method to achieve this goal, and the Plan's very existence forestalls the questioning of this assumption.

One other matter should also be made clear. Directives from 

Washington, D. C. will not abolish regional, district, branch, group, or individual quotas unofficially maintained below the district level, but officially collected there and above. Neither will the mere failure 107/ to discuss numbers at budget hearings be satisfactory. Commissioners will continue to be obligated to make speeches. Given public interest in numbers, these speeches will discuss audits and numbers. 

These will

be remembered by Service personnel and treated as important. importantly, such speeches adopt the premise which justifies the Plan that audit coverage causes compliance. Hence, it is an endorsement of the Plan which produces the pressure which produces the quotas. But, even if Commissioners should cease such speeches, the Plan would remain. 

As long as the Plan remains, the entire Audit Division knows that case closures are the name of the game. Certainly, the Plan will not be abandoned until other means of employing the present staff are devised. 

And, other uses of the staff require data about compliance which is not now available. Also, there appears to be little interest in obtaining such data.
