The Plan does serve several valid purposes, however, It satisfies Congress. It employs and manages a large staff in a cost-efficient and useful way.

It serves as a strategy. It permits (perhaps encourages?) the feeling of productivity apparently necessary to even government workers in a private, profit-and-growth-oriented society. It also permits objective, even if perhaps erroneous, measurement of abstract concepts and offers rocks to cling to in a sea of otherwise subjective quicksand. Similarly, it permits objective evaluation of subordinates, thereby avoiding subjective weighing of imponderables. Objective evaluation may not be bad, given the fact that in many, and perhaps an overwhelming majority of, cases the best subjective evaluation of an employee would reach the same conclusion as the objective evaluation. 

The Plan does serve many purposes.

The Plan thus is a force for both good and bad within the Service. In this respect, however, the Service is much like any other agency faced with the administration (and perhaps enforcement) of a law which has a substantial impact on those subject to it. Without enforcement effort, much of the public may suspect rampant evasion. 

On the other hand, any enforcement of a law having such sweeping coverage affects a substantial number of citizens who believe that enforcement against them is not necessary. There is, then, a mandate from the public and Congress that the law be enforced, but many object to having it enforced against them. The Service, thus, has tried to steer a path between these two imperatives. In doing so, it has built a large organization committed to its present program of enforcement which, in the overall, appears to work rather well. In this respect it is similar to nearly all enforcement agencies.

The Service now argues that there are no production pressures because there are no production goals. While this denial is sincere, some of the public perceives that such pressures do exist. The analysis above argues that this perception is accurate. The 

Service's denial in the face of apparently contrary facts harms the institution's credibility, and public mistrust of the Service's motivations grow much more readily in such an atmosphere. Frank, public recognition that the Plan exerts influence in the manner suggested might improve the Service's credibility. It might also open the path to a meaningful discussion of the problems and ways to handle the pressures which, to many, quite clearly do result from the Plan. Such discussion

could also result in both the public and the Congress's being willing to grant increased resources or force reallocation of present resources to consider the rationale for compliance.

C. The Audit Process. 

1. The Service Center. 

There are ten Service Centers serving the seven regions. Each 

Service Center is responsible to the Regional Commissioner for the region in which the Center is physically located. process, catalogue, and store tax returns. 108/ 109/ 

Primarily, Service Centers

When times were slower and less complicated, district offices were responsible for and capable of receiving, storing, and classifying all returns from their area of responsibility. Due to increased workload and the introduction of data processing equipment, the Service began centralizing these functions into regional Service Centers. In 1955 there was one such Center in Kansas City, Missouri, which processed 1.1 million 110/ income tax returns for the mid-western states. 

In 1956 the Lawrence, Massachusetts Center, servicing New England, New York, and New Jersey was 111/ added, and in that year the two Centers processed 11 million returns. 

In 1957 the Midwest Center added Michigan and Wisconsin to its area of coverage, as did the Northeast Center add the Cleveland, Ohio District to its coverage. Also, the Western Service Center, servicing the eight western states, was established. That year the three Centers processed 

22 million years. 112/ With the introduction of even better data processing and computer capability in 1962, the Service Centers took on their current form and functions. In 1974 they processed approximately 121 million 113/ returns of all kinds.

Returns received at the Service Centers are immediately sorted 114/ 

Receipts are by type of return and presence of a payment attached. segregated and deposited in banks as quickly as possible. Also, at this time every return receives a document locator number (DIN). This number, not the taxpayer's Social Security or other employer identification num- 115/ ber, is used by the Service to account for all returns.

116/ A return is next "coded" and "edited" by Tax Examiners who perform two functions on each return. First, the examiner edits the return by making more readable otherwise nearly illegible items and completing, if possible, any incomplete entries. The accuracy of these items is not verified at this point. "Coding" is the penciling on the return of numbered codes which translate certain items entered thereon into computer cognizable language. For example, the Unallowable Items Program (discussed below) often requires a determination that the taxpayer has deducted an 117/ item which is prima facie not deductible. 

Each such item has a numeric or letter coding which is placed on the return. This code is then transcribed to the computer tape, using the number or letter code. 

Upon completion of the code and edit process, the information on the return is then transcribed into the computer. Transcription is the typing of return information into the computer through a typewriter-like keyboard. The transcriber visually reviews the input on a cathode ray viewing screen attached to the transcribing machine. All information is entered twice, each time by different operators. If the two inputs do not agree, the computer rejects the information. A review of the return

118/ is then followed by a third transcription, which presumably will agree with one of the first two inputs. The agreed information will then be accepted and stored by the computer. 

The Service Center computers review the return information for math errors and Unallowable Items. If either exists, the computer automatically recomputes the tax, although both the recomputed and original return information and calculations are retained on the tapes. Tapes containing information from all returns are shipped in weekly cycles to the National Computer Center (NCC) in Martinsburg, West Virginia, for posting to the appropriate Master File. Also, at the NCC all returns are 

DIF scored and listed on a district-by-district basis in descending order 119/ of DIF score in each income class. This listing, along with a listing of taxpayer accounts which apparently will require taxpayer contact, are transferred to another tape and returned to the Service Center from which they originated. The tape returned to the Service Center is the heart of the Integrated Data Retrieval System (IDRS). 

a. Service Center Audit Operations. 

The Service Center Audit Division has primary or secon- 120/ dary responsibility for 12 separate programs relating to proper tax determination. The two which affect the greatest numbers of taxpayers are discussed here. They are the Unallowable Items and Math Error Programs. 

The Correspondence Audit Program is also discussed. It is the method by which the Service Centers conduct all their programs, including the Math 

Error and Unallowable Items Programs. In addition, the Information Document Matching Program (IDM) is described.

(1) The Math Error Program. 

The Math Error Program allows for the detection of 122/ mathematical miscalculations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, or division of figures) on the return, but not errors of judgment or description. It is a mere clerical recomputation performed by the Service Center 121/ computer of the entries computed by a taxpayer on his return. notice of the amount due or increased refund is sent to the taxpayer. 

Notably, this review and correction does not amount to an examination of books and records or an examination of the return. It is, then, not an "audit", although it is generally discussed with audit programs. 

Since it is not an audit, a notice of deficiency need not be sent prior to assess- 123/ ment of the tax, and administrative appeal is not allowed. Further, correction of a math error is not treated as a case closure and thus is 124/ not subject to the policy against re-opening closed cases.

The Math Error Program must be distinguished from the Unallowable 

Items Program which has the purpose of correcting clearly and unquestionably erroneous entries on the return. The line between the two is thin. For example, the failure to reduce casualty and theft losses by the $100 125/ floor is considered an Unallowable Item, rather than a math error.

As well as being thin, the line is also scrupulously maintained. 

Thus, an item becomes a part of the Unallowable Items Program only after careful deliberation by the Audit Division. Questionable items have at times been reviewed by the Office of Chief Counsel. The extreme care in differentiation apparently is taken because the Unallowable Items

Program is considered by the Service, for all practical purposes, to be an audit procedure. As such, a notice of deficiency must be sent prior to assessment; an administrative appeal is allowed; and the policy against re-opening closed cases applies. (2) 

The Unallowable Items Program. 

The Unallowable Items Program uses less expensive methods than the ordinary audit procedure and permits the collection of taxes due to errors of a type or magnitude which would not ordinarily 126/ prompt an audit. Before institution of the program, many of these items were undetected. For fiscal year 1974 it has been reported that 

51 percent of all Unallowables were found on returns reporting more than $10,000 of adjusted gross income and 49 percent in the under $10,000 income class. Additional assessments were made on approximately 450,000 returns 127/ filed in 1972.

Each item on the Unallowable Items Program is listed in a Handbook. Moreover, the entry of the item on the tax return must appear clearly improper. Frequently, these issues are no more complex than those which constitute math errors, but because they require some judgment, their correction is considered, for all practical purposes, an audit, albeit a simplified procedure. Thus, audit procedures are followed. 

Some Unallowable Items are manually identified when the return is coded and edited. Others are found by the computer after transcription. 

Manual review identifies items for which judgment or verbal description are important, such as the deduction of personal legal expenses. The

computer will reveal errors which result from incorrect calculations, but which are not considered math errors. Examples of these types of errors are the deductions of dividends in excess of the permissible dividend exclusion and the failure to reduce medical expenses by 3 percent of a taxpayer's adjusted gross income. All but one of the manually coded and all of the computer-identified Unallowables will generate, but will not cause to be mailed, computer letters adjusting the tax and explaining the 128/ adjustment. One manual code, used when the coder is not certain that the item is unallowable, identifies the return for further review by Audit personnel who make a determination to accept the return or to propose the tax change and notify the taxpayer.

All returns identified as having Unallowables are manually 129/ reviewed to verify the accuracy of the identification. 

If inaccurate, the return re-enters the processing channel, and the computer-generated letter is suppressed. If accurate and if the DIF score of the return is below a floor established on a regional rather than district basis, the computer-generated notice adjusting the tax will be sent to the taxpayer. 

If the DIF score exceeds the floor, the return is screened to determine whether there may be other errors with potential for significant tax change. If so, the return is sent to the district office for handling as explained below. 

(a) Cases Without Potential for Tax Change. 

If there is no apparent potential for tax change, the computer-generated letter will be mailed directly from the

Service Center. Upon mailing of a notice adjusting the tax, any refund which would result from allowance of the Unallowable is frozen, i.e., 130/ halted.

The letter is a request that the taxpayer agree to the pro- 131/ posed correction or explain the reason 132/ for disagreeing. Occasionally, a taxpayer's response indicates that the taxpayer made a correct entry, but merely mislabeled it. 133/ If so, the matter is settled in the taxpayer's favor. If the taxpayer's explanation is not convincing, the Service Center will either retain the matter for handling 134/ by its Correspondence Section or transfer the case to the proper district office.

The Correspondence Section of the Service Center retains the case if either one of two conditions exists: (1) the taxpayer has not requested a personal interview, or (2) Service personnel believe that the taxpayer is able to express himself adequately in writing and will not be disadvantaged by a correspondence audit. If, however, a personal interview is requested by the taxpayer or deemed necessary by Service personnel, the case is transferred to the taxpayer's district office, frozen funds are released, and a proposed deficiency notice is not sent. Such a case will then be resolved by the district office following its normal audit procedures.

In cases retained by the Service Center under the above standards, a notice of proposed deficiency is sent, but frozen refunds are not released. They are retained pending resolution of the matter. However, the amounts withheld are not considered by the IRS as a collection of the 135/ but rather, they are considered a mere pre-payment of a potential tax,

assessment, the only effect of which is to toll the accumulation of interest charges. 136/ If no resolution between the taxpayer and the IRS can be achieved, the Service Center Audit staff handling the matter will then issue a notice of deficiency. This, then, permits the taxpayer to 137/ petition the Tax Court for relief. If a petition is filed with the 

Tax Court, the frozen refund is released to the taxpayer. If the taxpayer has not petitioned the court at the expiration of the time within which he is permitted to do so, the Service retains the frozen refund and credits it to the taxpayer's account as a payment of tax. (b) 

Cases With Potential for Tax Change. 

In other cases review at the Service Center may indicate that there is potential for significant tax change in addition to the apparent Unallowable. Because there is a policy (explained below) of not re-opening closed cases, and Unallowables cases fall under this policy, a return with tax change potential must be identified for audit at this point or it will be closed with only the Unallowable having been questioned. Thus, when such a return is identified, no letter is sent to the taxpayer. Rather, the return and the computer-generated letter adjusting the tax are sent to the proper district office for further 138/ review, and the frozen refund, if any, is released. At the district office the Returns Program Manager will review the return and decide whether the return should be assigned to a group for audit. If he decides on assignment, both the Group Manager and the examining officer will also review the return for potential tax change. If they agree with the

Returns Program Manager, audit will follow in due course. In the ensuing audit the Unallowables will be merely issues in the audit. If, however, the Returns Program Manager, the Group Manager, or the examining officer decide against audit, the computer-generated letter correcting the tax will be sent. If the taxpayer agrees, the case is closed. If he does not agree, he will be permitted to appeal his case to District or Appellate Conference or the Tax Court. (c) 140/ 141/ 

Re-opening Closed Cases. 

The Service has a well-considered policy 139/ against re-opening closed cases unless there are strong reasons justifying the action. Furthermore, the discretion to re-open generally, 142/ but not always, requires approval of a District Director.

There is a reluctance to initiate such re-openings, and thus the Service has developed the foregoing procedure to prevent its personnel from closing a case containing an Unallowable without being certain that its potential for tax change has been thoroughly considered. 

(3) The Information Document Matching Program (IDM). 

Another program of public and Service interest which is administered from the Service Center is the Information Document Matching Program (IDM). For our discussion an "information document" can be defined as a form, e.g., a W-2 or 1099, completed and filed by a payor to inform the government of monies remitted to a payee which should be reported by such payee on his income tax return as income. It "...is a correction program for handling potential income under-reporters identified by matching information documents and other records with the 

Individual Masterfile. 143/

of income.

IDM is a program to disclose unreported or misreported items 144/ When an item is discovered, the return is corrected;

the 145/ 

At present, the tax is recomputed; and the taxpayer is billed. matching program is not 100 percent effective, and only certain types of 1099's are matched. 146/ One of the major difficulties is the careless completion of many information documents. For example, in isolated instances as many as 40 percent of the W-2 forms (wage information documents) have been found to have inaccurate Social Security numbers, though overall, less than 5 percent of the Form W-2's filed with the Service have inaccurate Social Security numbers. At present, the Service can do no more than 147/ penalize the negligent filer $5 for each transgression, and it does not do so with any regularity. 148/ To improve this matching process, the Service has embarked on a new program called Information Returns Processing (IRP). The purpose of the new program is to develop methods and techniques for more complete and efficient matching of documents. To this end, the Service has requested bids for optical scanning devices for implementation by 1976 at 149/ Although the Service expects to issue new regulations specifying minimum standards for the weight and format of information returns, it will continue its efforts to encourage transmission of such reports by magnetic tape, rather than paper document. the earliest. 

b. The Correspondence Audit Technique. 

As indicated earlier, the Service Center has primary One of importance is responsibility for various other audit programs. 77-842 O-76-6

the Correspondence Audit Program. This program has the aim of reducing cost and delay and increasing efficiency by handling by mail, from the 150/ Service Center, as many simple matters as possible. While a few supplementary telephone calls may be made, the case will be transferred to a district office if the taxpayer requests an interview or if issues 151/ become too involved for effective treatment by mail or telephone. 

Otherwise, the audit procedure is the same in all significant aspects as for an audit in which taxpayer presence is required. 

2. The District Office. 

a. 

Selection of Returns for Audit. 

(1) The Returns Program Manager and the Classification 

Program. 

An understanding of the return selection process at the district office begins with the district's Returns Program Manager (RPM): "[T]he primary objective in the selection of tax returns for examination will be the highest possible revenue yield from the examination man-hours expended, and the examination of as many returns of all classes as is feasible for the maintenance of a high degree of voluntary taxpayer compliance. "The Returns Program Manager (RPM). . . [is] responsible for developing a yearly classification plan to meet the requirements of the approved examination program. In addition, he will be responsible for monitoring and executing the plan. "I 152/ The position was established following a 1972 study of the district Audit Division structure. 

153/ 

The RPM replaces the former

Returns Classification Officer (RCO) and formalizes what had been his

154/ informal duties. than a division chief.

Under the new job classification, the RPM is limited to a three-year tenure and is approximately two GS grade levels lower 155/ It is considered an entry or mid-level management position, upon the conclusion of which its holder is likely to move into a job as Chief of an Examination Branch, Senior Regional Analyst, 156/ The RPM has no 

Chief of Review, or Chief of District Conference. line authority over the Audit staff and must rely on the Chief of Audit, to whom he is immediately responsible, to exert any necessary pressure. 

Though the RPM has numerous duties, his most important are to ensure that the proper returns are being audited and that the Audit Plan 157/ (the Plan) is being met. The first of these depends upon selection of the "returns most in need of examination." This process is termed "classifying".

Classification begins by requesting returns from a Service Center, generally in large quantities for specific examination programs and for each income class in each program where an income class is a relevant factor. These programs were discussed earlier and are generally dictated by the national office, but occasionally may be created by the region or district. They will show on the annual Audit Plan for the district. An order may estimate needs for, say, a four-month period. 

The order will not, however, be limited to the number of returns in each program expected to be examined in the four-month period. Since, as described below, many returns will not be sent into the audit stream, the order may be for a number equal to two or three times the number of expected examinations during that period.

Armed with this inventory of returns, the RPM's staff begins its review. The staff consists of a Returns Classification Specialist, the RPM's assistant, and a staff of classifiers, Revenue Agents and Tax Auditors temporarily detailed to the RPM. Only the best available 158/ examiners are to be assigned to the RPM, and interviews with Group Managers indicated that they attempted to comply appropriately. 159/ То assure the quality of work being performed by these agent-classifiers, the RPM is required to maintain an effective program for training and evaluating classifiers. 160/ The job of the classifier is to review income tax returns and to decide whether a return should be audited and, if so, in what manner. 

This evaluation is the first manual review at the district level of a return's potential for tax change. In performing this task, classifiers are to inspect the return in the manner they would if the return were 161/ assigned to them in their capacity as examining officers. Most of the returns which they will review will have been DIF scored, and except for returns selected for non-DIF programs or reasons, they will be the highest DIF-scored returns then remaining from the returns filed in the district. If the classifier determines there is sufficient likelihood of tax change, the return will find its way to a Group Manager who has ordered returns for his group. If, on the other hand, a return does not suggest audit potential, it will be surveyed, a procedure discussed below.

This post-DIF review is necessary because it permits the DIF measurement of tax-change potential to be tempered by circumstances and

filing habits unique to any particular district and the classifier's experience. "The DIF score is an indication of the audit potential of the return as a whole. The line items on the return have not necessarily been erroneously reported by the taxpayer. Therefore, the screener must scrutinize DIF returns both as to items and to the return as a whole. He must use his skills, technical expertise, local knowledge and experience, to single out hidden as well as obvious issues and determine the scope and type of examination for a return to be selected. 162/ The classifiers not only decide, in the first instance, which returns will be accepted as filed and which will be subjected to further scrutiny, but they also determine the kind of examination. In general, corporate and the most complicated individual returns will be assigned to 163/ Revenue Agents, and individual returns with simple issues will be assigned to Tax Auditors for office interview or correspondence audit from the district office.

Not only is there a difference in the type of returns assigned to Revenue Agents and Tax Auditors, but there is also a difference in processing by the classifiers. Returns classified for the attention of a Revenue Agent may, at district office discretion, include a checklist 164/ of items in need of examination. Our discussions with personnel from various districts did not uncover any district offices that follow this 165/ procedure.

However, for the less highly skilled Tax Auditor a check- 166/ list is required. 

Except in rare cases, the Tax Auditor is not expected to expand the examination beyond this checklist. 167/ Interviews with Tax Auditors and their supervisors confirmed that such expansion arises very infrequently.

Once classified, returns are inventoried at the district office (i.e., are in the district's inventory of unaudited returns) until the 

Group Managers order more returns for their group to examine. order returns by taxpayer name, but rather, by income class or by program specifications. They depend upon the RPM to supply the returns with the greatest potential for tax change. Though, as indicated earlier, the 

RPM has no authority over the Group Managers, it is his duty to monitor the Audit and Classification Plans and to ensure the required penetration into each income class of taxpayers under the DIF program and to see that other programs are carried out. As a part of this responsibility, the RPM may, for example, compare audit plans with audit accomplishments 168/ and analyze the survey and no-change rate. 

The Audit Plan was discussed in greater detail earlier in this report. It affects the districts. They audit the number and class of returns that have been laid out for them. The RPM's classification program and activities which have just been discussed are tailored to meet the guidelines set out by the Plan. Though the Plan itself is broken down only as far as the regions for national office purposes, it is broken down to its district components by the region. Thus, the RPM's primary job is to maintain an inventory of returns with high potential tax change. 

Survey of Returns.

Not all returns ordered from the Service Center and b. 169/ received by the district office are examined. 

Some are merely "surveyed", a term of art which means a review of the return resulting in a decision that the potential for significant tax change is too low to

justify examination and thus leading to the closing of the case, normally prior to contact with the taxpayer. If the taxpayer is contacted, examination usually follows.

Any one of a number of Service personnel may survey returns. 

The RPM's staff has the first opportunity to survey, and its judgment seemingly is made on the basis of a brief review of the return, not on an 170/ Returns which survive this procedure are sent to in-depth study. an examination group where the Group Manager is instructed to ". . .comply with procedures for survey before assignment to dispose of incoming 171/ returns which cannot or should not be examined.

11 

Apparently, it is a classifier. thought within the Service that the Group Manager brings to the decision judgments based on longer experience and greater maturity than that of The Group Manager may decide the return does not have sufficient potential for tax change and that it should not be examined. 

When this decision is made before assignment to an examining officer, the return has been "surveyed before assignment" (SBA). 

Presumably, screening by the Group Manager will ferret out most returns with low potential for tax change. Nevertheless, an examining officer may, with his supervisor's approval, also survey a return at any 172/ time prior to his initial contact with the taxpayer. Beyond the directive that examination should follow if taxpayer contact is made, there is no systemic impediment to the surveying of returns. However, interviews with numerous examining officers indicated that Revenue Agents are reluctant (and Tax Auditors more so) to survey returns. 173/

They seem to think that a return would not be assigned unless it contained errors which would result in same meaningful tax change. Nonetheless, they do have this authority, and they exercise it if the pre-audit 174/ analysis suggests insignificant tax changes. A return so closed after assignment to an examining officer is termed "surveyed after assignment" (SAA). 

(1) Repetitive Audits. 

A significant by-product of an examining officer's decision to audit rather than survey a return is the problem of repetitive audits. Simply stated, a repetitive audit is an audit of a taxpayer's Such sit- return raising issues which were raised previously but which resulted in little, if any, tax change in an examination or examinations for one or more tax years closely preceding the return for the year in question. uations generally arise when a taxpayer reports, from year to year, income or deductions of a type or magnitude which trigger high DIF scores, but which, upon examination, are found entirely or very nearly accurate. 

One such example is the case of traveling salesmen who deduct traveling expenses of such size every year so as to cause a high DIF score and thus repeated selection for audits. Examination may demonstrate that all, or nearly all, of such expenses were valid. 

The Service has recently addressed this issue and has made an effort to ameliorate this area of abrasion with the taxpayer. Along these lines it had planned to commence in 1975 a program to provide for a computer-applied method of removing returns from the audit stream of the type here discussed. Under this proposed program, if an individual

had a no-change audit on either one or both of his last two consecutive years' returns, the current year's return would have been given (assuming no substantial variation in the items' characteristics) neutral scores for the next two years on those items which were not changed (or only insignificantly changed) in the prior audits. This proposed policy became public knowledge. Thereafter, the Service decided that such knowledge would encourage tax evasion, and this procedure will not be implemented. 

In its place, however, the Service is implementing a different program. 

This new program is set out in the Service's Law Enforcement Manual, and the IRS has requested that we not make the details of its operation public. However, these procedures provide, in general terms, for a careful review of a return by the examining officer with a view toward survey of those returns which seem to raise the repetitive audit problem. 

No judgment can be passed on secret procedures. However, there are techniques which will reduce the incidence of unnecessary repetitive audits without hindering the Service's enforcement effort. 

If the prior year files were associated with the current year return and both were carefully reviewed by the Group Manager, a decision to audit again would be based on the combined mature judgment of both the examining officer and the Group Manager. They should not, of course, proceed with the examination unless the review suggests a likelihood of more than a de minimis tax change. 

Another inhibition on unnecessary repetitive audits might be created by requiring that the taxpayer receive an explanation of the reason for the examination. The taxpayer who is subjected to a repetitive audit should be informed in writing that he may inquire about the necessity for this audit.

Any resulting inquiry should be addressed to the Chief of Audit in the District, who should respond in writing to the taxpayer either explaining in some detail the reasons for his selection for audit, or advising that the case is to be closed without change. While the response to such inquiries would impose a slight additional burden on the Chief of Audit, it could easily be discharged. 

For example, if the prior examination resulted in substantial tax change and if the current return suggests no reason to believe a different result, the taxpayer could simply be so informed. Also most taxpayers who experienced substantial tax change in prior years probably would not bother to make such an inquiry. Most such inquiries probably would be made by those who experienced little prior tax change and who thus have the most apparent justification for objecting to a repetitive audit. It is just those cases where some reason should be available and provided the taxpayer. On balance the burden does not seem too great to pay for better administration. However, TCMP audits, even if resulting in repetitive audits, should not be subject to this procedure. Halting a TCMP audit would risk skewing the TCMP sample.

C. 

The Audit. 

The examination of a tax return is in fact, if not in intention, an adversary proceeding; as with most adversary situations, the better advocate is likely to fare better. (1) 

The Adversary Setting. 

175/ Interviews with examination personnel left no doubt on several points. Examining officers believe that nearly all returns assigned for examination contain errors in need of correction. They also believe that duty requires the assertion of the Service's position on issues. The examining officer also thinks that he must educate the

176/ taxpayer in the correct interpretation of the law. 

These beliefs help to produce the adversary atmosphere discussed below and may result in incorrect advice at least on occasion. 

Further, such beliefs are rarely altered, even by reversal of the officer's findings Such reversals are seen by at a District or Appellate Conference. examiners as necessitated by those bodies' concern over the control of their inventories and the need to prevent the next level of appeal from being inundated with cases. From an examiner's point of view, only infrequently do such reversals result from substantive legal or factual judgments.

Examining officers seemingly do not come to this state of mind without reason. The Service has recognized that many tax returns are either carelessly or intentionally incorrectly prepared. For example, as far back as 1953, the Commissioner stated: 

"While. [there] is an exceptionally high degree of voluntary and conscientious tax compliance. there remain substantial numbers of returns requiring corrections because of carelessness, ignorance, or willfulness on the part of taxpayers filing the returns. [emphasis added] 11 177/ More recently, the somewhat same view has been stated as "Although the underlying good faith of the public may be a principal strength of the selfassessment system, it would be folly to rely completely upon the combination of such good faith and the ability of taxpayers to understand and apply convoluted tax laws to themselves. . .innocent errors. [are] made, . .but bad faith may exhibit itself in an enforcement vacuum. .Universal honesty cannot be assumed.

"To the extent that. .[the taxpayer] does have room for maneuvering, there is evidence to suggest that many. .avail themselves of the opportunity. 

For example, 5 percent of tax returns filed contain mathematical errors and such errors are predominantly in the taxpayer's favor. Moreover, the size of the error favoring the taxpayer is about 1 1/2 times as large as the error favoring the Government. "Also, there is evidence tending to indicate that 2 out of every 5 individual returns filed contain tax errors (other than math errors) and that in 85 out of 

100 cases the error is in the taxpayer's favor." 178/

The institution thus believes that returns contain accidental, negligent, This view can hardly be concealed from examining 179/ and intentional errors. personnel or the public. 

Furthermore, the examining officer has been told that return selection has become increasingly scientific; that it is done by a computer (carrying the implicit suggestion that a mistake could not have been made); that DIF returns have a high potential for tax change; and that DIF is based on data collected in TCMP audits performed by his most 180/ skilled colleagues in their most careful manner.

He is aware that 181/ influential members of Congress and his supervisors in the bureau- 182/ cracy will be upset if his returns result in a high "no-change" rate.

The examining officer is also aware that returns have been screened by classifiers who have concurred in the likelihood of tax change and that his Group Manager is instructed not to ". . .assign a 183/ return to an employee if you are not convinced it should be examined. 

In addition, the examining officer knows that his failure to find a change in tax (i.e., an error on the return) will, if it occurs frequently, 11

result in a review of returns examined by him to ascertain whether he is being assigned the proper returns or whether his skills are deficient. 

Finally, both he and his employer believe his work is an "enforcement activity." It is continually so described in the 

Commissioner's Annual Reports. 

184/ It is most graphically demonstrated by the Report for fiscal year 1973 in which the title page to "Enforcement 185/ Activities" carries a large illustration of a policeman's badge;

186/ Audit statistics are contained in this section three pages later. 

Unfortunately, all this seems to carry with it the attitude that the examining officer must apprehend the intentionally and carelessly guilty and that his universe of returns is largely limited to those who have either carelessly or intentionally prepared returns inaccurately. 

All of this builds an expectancy of error in the mind of the examining officer and a knowledge that everyone in the organization expects him to find an error. This expectancy would seem to exert substantial pressure on the examining officer. He has been told that he would not get the return if errors were not likely, and if he finds none, he may have feelings of self-doubt and/or suspicions as to the veracity or intentions of the taxpayer. 187/ Further pressures causing an adversary attitude result from the natural human necessity of feeling that one's work is productive and meaningful. The value of such work has been defined by the hierarchy in terms of numbers of cases worked and a low no-change rate. These and other similar numbers are the objective indicators of acceptable achievement established by the Service against which an examining officer can

measure his work, and, to the extent work satisfaction is a factor in an individual's self-esteem, maintain his self-respect. 

Thus, the examining officer enters an audit with the expectation of finding errors and assessing a deficiency against a taxpayer whom he suspects as being dishonest, careless, or unknowledgeable, but probably not correct. Of course, the taxpayer does not enter the fray without his own well-entrenched attitudes about the process and the method by which the audit should proceed. 

Despite the Service's sincere and extensive attempts to convince the taxpayer otherwise, the public views the audit with the fear and indignation of an innocent person being mistakenly arrested for the com- 188/ mission of a crime. Exacerbating the taxpayer's attitude is the tendency of the public to blame the IRS for everything from abusive 189/ tactics to the perceived unfairness of the oil depletion allowance. 

From our mail and comments by Service personnel, it is clear that many taxpayers blame the Service for the complexities and vagaries of the substantive tax law, and they frequently bring this anger to the audit. 

Also, it should not be overlooked that an audit potentially involves an out-of-pocket expense to the taxpayer. He may have to pay additional tax, and he may have to undergo the expense of professional advice. He may also be inconvenienced by loss of work and sleep. These actual and potential losses are likely to make many taxpayers aggressive and adversary in their dealings.

Further, taxpayers may feel helpless, even if represented by competent advisors. They not only do not understand the law, they also

do not understand the confusing procedures involved in the audit. In addition, particularly for the unrepresented taxpayer, they may learn for the first time that they must maintain and provide records to substantiate any number of individually insignificant items. For many taxpayers recordkeeping is not a part of their daily lives, and they are confused by this sudden insistence on verification. They were not even informed by the 

Commissioner when they received their blank returns and instructions that such might be necessary. In many cases this insistence for documented verification is seen as merely a harassment tactic, even though in some cases it may be required by the statute itself. 

The potential for disputes and contention is naturally greater when a taxpayer who has knowingly cheated, even in a small way, is challenged. Petty chiseling is rarely treated as either civil or criminal fraud, but few petty chiselers act on that knowledge, and, unlike the honest taxpayers who mainly resent having to pay more money, this group may have some desperate feeling that an audit will result in incarceration and a fine. 

Given the inevitability of some degree of contentiousness, the Service would be wise to minimize it by more adequately advising taxpayers of the need to retain their records. This need should be brought home to taxpayers before the return is filed. Such a message could be sent to taxpayers and prominently displayed when the Commissioner sends his annual message with the tax forms and instructions. Those who read the instructions would not then be caught unaware. 

(2) Effects of Taxpayer Representation. 

While a study of the effect of taxpayer representation on ultimate assessments was not made, a few general comments seem obvious. 

Many taxpayers apparently are confused and intimidated by the audit process. Most Service personnel concurred with this perception. 

Many of the factors which make the proceeding adversary also result in

its being a frightening experience. Numerous complaints state or imply that fright is a part of the audit process. an error.

Further, the taxpayer, if unrepresented, is not capable of knowledgeable or forceful contradiction of an examining officer's assertions of law and little better able to contradict his assertions of fact. Given these circumstances, the represented taxpayer probably will emerge from an audit with, at least on the average, a more favorable result than will the unrepresented taxpayer. This conclusion persists despite sincere efforts by the Service to instruct examining officers not to take advantage of the unrepresented and to be fair. Since the officer is likely to think that error exists, he may be very fair and still find Furthermore, represented taxpayers seem more likely to appeal cases where the law is ambiguous or the facts questionable. Without doubt, appealed cases will on the average result in smaller settlements than agreed cases. For example, data for fiscal year ending 1974 show that the Appellate Division settled non-docketed cases involving individual taxpayers for approximately 41 cents on the dollar nationally, 190/ while docketed cases were settled for 57 cents on the dollar. 

A non-docketed case is one settled at Appellate level; a docketed case is one which has been appealed to the courts, although settled, at least as to some issues, prior to an actual judicial hearing. There appears to be many reasons for this phenomenon, and they are dealt with in the portion of this chapter dealing with the settlement process. 

The lack of representation may be even more serious when viewed in relation to criminal fraud investigations.

Service practice

in initiating potential criminal investigations requires a Special Agent from Intelligence to display his credentials and to explain his function 191/ Yet, a significant number of letters as a criminal investigator. were received from taxpayers undergoing criminal investigations who seemingly had no inkling of the criminal nature of the investigation. 

The lack of representation is, perhaps, the most serious difficulty in the audit process. The examination is clearly adversary, and the 

Service representative is far better trained to handle the issues. Given the environment and background of the audit, even an overly fair agent is unable to protect the taxpayer. 

(3) Who Is Performing the Audit. 

Agents or Tax Auditors. 

The examining officers can either be Revenue GS-5 or GS-7 is the entry-level grade, and GS-11 is the journeyman grade for Revenue Agents. GS-5 is the entry-level grade, and GS-9 the journeyman grade, for Tax Auditors. Revenue Agents can attain a grade of GS-13 and Tax Auditors a grade of GS-9. 

Educational requirements for the two positions also vary. 

Revenue Agents are required to have on entry a Bachelor's degree with at least 15 credit hours of accounting and 9 hours of other business-related 192/ subjects. 

Tax Auditors, on the other hand, must have only a Bachelor's degree; there are no accounting or business-course requirements, and all 193/ of their technical training is received at the Service. 

Both classes of examining officers undergo similar initial training; however, Tax Auditors do not receive the same in-depth instruction received by Revenue Agents. Their training is acquired during their

first six months on the job and is a mixture of classroom and on-thejob training with sessions of each being alternated. While it is not altogether clear, it appears that classroom training is devoted primarily to teaching the law, and on-the-job training is primarily devoted to the development of proper technique and procedure. The adequacy or quality of the Service's training program for examining officers was not reviewed, and no comment is made on it. 

Because of the varied background and expertise of the two classes of examiners, they examine different kinds of returns. Revenue

Agents are assigned most corporate and the more difficult and intricate 194/ individual and business returns, while Tax Auditors receive most individual returns and the less difficult business returns. 195/ 

In very broad terms a Revenue Agent takes cases in which a sophisticated capability in accounting and tax law is required for an adequate examination. 

On the other hand, a Tax Auditor will be asked to examine returns where an adequate audit can be accomplished by resolving simpler legal issues and where fact issues can be easily evaluated and verified by the use of simple clerical techniques such as checking receipts. 

(4) Examining Officers' Techniques. 

(a) Revenue Agents. 

After receiving a return from his Group Manager, a Revenue Agent performs a pre-audit analysis. This review consists of scrutinizing the return as a whole, a review of any available information on prior years, and a specific item-by-item analysis to 196/ uncover any unusual items raising a question as to correctness.

At

this point, the agent is instructed to research the law in areas in which 197/ he is unfamiliar.

Whether this is done adequately and whether an agent feels he has enough time for adequate research were not ascertained. 

Though apparently not required by the Audit Technique Handbook for Internal Revenue Agents, interviews indicated that most district offices require Revenue Agents to prepare a written plan prior to commencement of an audit. The process assists the agent in getting his thoughts together and the Group Manager in reviewing the planning and followthrough capabilities. These pre-audit plans, done in conjunction with an examining officer's preliminary review of a case, consist of estimations of time required on the case and the issues to be raised. However, many examining officers indicated that they do not complete these "pre-audit plans" until sometime near the completion of the audit. Pre-audit plans are not to be confused with work papers which are required and which "...should include summaries or transcripts of those accounts which were analyzed, schedules of the items specifically verified by the examiner, reconciliation of accounts on the books with items on the return, analyses of reserves, and all other pertinent notes of the work performed 198/ during the examination.

Some managers may look at the pre-audit plan prior to commencement of the examination to assist an examining officer in determining the direction he should take. In the usual case, however, if the manager looks at this plan at all, he will compare the audit's actual results against what was planned, looking to the deviations and explanation of them as a guide to difficulties encountered.

At the same time the pre-audit plan is supposed to be prepared by the examining officer, he should also determine as best he can those documents, books, and records the taxpayer will need to provide for an examination. The next step is likely to be the initial taxpayer contact to make an appointment. At that time, the examining officer should be in a position to tell the taxpayer what records he will need to see ini- 199/ tially. Additional records are likely to be needed as the audit progresses. 

In the main, the initial contact is with the taxpayer, not his represen- 200/ tative (even if a power of attorney has been filed), by telephone, followed by a letter of confirmation. For audits which will require substantial travel, the Service recommends that the initial contact be by mail with sufficient time for taxpayer response as to the proposed 202/ appointment time and date. 201/ Because of the size and/or business nature of most returns examined by Revenue Agents, they must generally go to the taxpayer to obtain complete access to the taxpayer's books and records. (b) Tax Auditors.

The initial steps in an audit performed by a Tax Auditor are not the same as those performed by a 

Revenue Agent. 

"Generally, the operating procedure in Office Audit does not provide for pre-examination planning. 

This is particularly true of correspondence and interview examinations initiated by mass audit techniques. 

In these instances, the case is not assigned to the technician until after replies are received to the correspondence, or the taxpayer comes into the office for a scheduled interview." 203/

Normally, an Auditor conducting a correspondence audit wi receive at the same time both the return and the taxpayer's response to an 204/ initial letter generated elsewhere.

Assignments of interviews are not made until the day of or the day before the taxpayer appears for examina- 205/ tion.

Working papers are not given the degree of importance that they are for Revenue Agents. 206/ The Auditor must, however, prepare work papers to verify and support his conclusion. 

A pre-audit analysis is not required of Tax Auditors, primarily because the issues are pre-selected (by the RPM or Group Manager) and are generally simpler. Another factor may be the expectation that the Tax 

Auditor is to close from two to four cases a day and thus is prevented by time constraints from preparing a pre-audit analysis. telephone. 207/ The Tax Auditor does not make his initial taxpayer contact by "In most correspondence and interview examinations, initial taxpayer contact is made by use of form letters and questionnaires prior to assignment of the return. The technician generally has little or no control over the content, preparation, or issuance of these letters. 208/ Interviews with Tax Auditors in various districts indicate that most appointments are made by a clerk attached to a particular group. Apparently, assignment of returns to Auditors is largely a district decision. 

In some districts as Auditors become available they are assigned to examine the return of the next person awaiting examination. In other districts managers assign specific returns to a specific Auditor the day before or the day the audit is to take place. However, no matter what

assignment method is used, there seems to be little preparation time available to the Auditor. 

d. Quality of Audits. 

No comment on the quality of the audits is expressed. Such comment would have required an intensive review of audit files which were not accessible. A lack of resources and the inability to obtain tax return information made such review impossible. 

e. Improper Return Selection and Examination. 

to be abused.

There are at least two opportunities for the audit system First, a return may be improperly selected or obtained for audit. 

Improper in this sense may have at least two meanings. Since there are usually many more returns fitting the parameters of an approved program than may be examined, selection of a particular return under that program may proceed from improper motives such as retribution or harassment. Another improper technique is the selection of a return for reasons unrelated to DIF scoring or to a program or other criterion for examination. Such selection may proceed from the most laudable of intentions to ferret out pockets of non-compliance suspected only by the examining officer, or it may proceed from vindictive motivations. However, the reason for selection in either case is unrelated to responsibilities assigned in accordance with the Plan.

Second, the examination itself may be performed in

a fashion which unduly prolongs or delays it or results in recommendations not justified by the facts. A number of people, including our correspondents, believe both improper selection and examinations occur, but the evidence in 

Procedures, however, one celebrated group of cases was found wanting. 209/ may be sufficiently loose to permit both improper selection and examination.

(1) 

Return Selection. 

Some returns may be selected for audit through requisitioning by line personnel. The requisition form may pinpoint returns for 

The form is Form 4298, the Audit Requisition and Information future audits. 210/ Report. "Form 4298. . .is a five-part assembly used by [a] district Audit Division. . .to requisition returns and secure Forms 1247. .for other than machine identified returns. It also serves as an Information 

Report." 211/ This form must be completed and signed by the individual initiating a request for a return, most often an examining officer, but potentially anyone involved in the audit process. Further, the request must be 212/ approved by the requester's first-line or immediate supervisor. 

The approval procedure is, however, apparently ministerial. 

In the usual case the requester is not required or meant to explain why he has requisitioned a return, other than by indicating with a two-digit numerical 213/ code the broad category in which the requested return falls.

Given a Group Manager's crushing load of paperwork, one can hardly expect him to interrogate every requester as to the necessity and reason for the request. Further, the breadth of numerical code categories can be exemplified by the description of one such item as "[a]ll pick-ups of returns that are not

214/ related to a taxpayer under examination.

It is difficult to imagine 215/ fortunately, are more specific. a less well-defined criterion. There are 75 other such codes, most of which, Thus, a return may be requisitioned and examined for reasons unrelated to the requisition code, or if the reasons are related, the code is sufficiently broad to allow improper return selection. 

At least some inhibition on such practices might result from a requirement that the reason for requesting specific returns be indicated in writing by the examining officer rather than by a mere number code. The need to have the file or return would then be expressed in such a way that the reviewing officer might more likely ask the requester questions about the written justification. After reviewing the written statement, the reviewer could then translate it into a letter code to facilitate the keeping of files for any later scrutiny of the return requisition process which proves necessary.

The Service at present has the capability of scrutinizing the 216/ propriety of return selection by its individual officers. The suggested procedures could help make this capability a practical reality.

Interviews with managers and line personnel suggested that they have little interest in possibly improper return selection. This disinterest seems founded on the notion that if such occurs, it does so very infrequently. 

While that premise may be true, the individual who has suffered from an improper selection process, though statistically insignificant, may have suffered financial or psychological costs. And, to make matters worse, he has no effective method of redressing the injustice even if it is discovered, though even discovery appears unlikely unless someone is willing to volunteer an explanation. Certainly, the likelihood of this kind of return selection would be less if the requisitioning party had to explain to the taxpayer the program under which the return was selected. 

Such a statement need not be lengthy or detailed. The program of selection should, however, be one which can be described simply and which will at least inform the taxpayer of the general reasons for selection. 

If return selection were so conditioned, there would be at least two constraints on the whim of the examining officer. By requiring a statement of reasons, a paper trail sufficient for internal audit would be created. 

Second is the possibility that, under the Freedom of Information Act, the Service would be required to disclose to a taxpayer so much of his file as may be necessary to verify that his return was in fact selected for the reasons he had been given. 217/ By The problem may extend beyond initial return selection. completing an Information Report, the examining officer may recommend at least a review of next year's return. Item 34 of Form 4298 solicits

remarks and information in the following manner: "Whenever an employee in Audit Division receives information of sufficient compliance value to warrant enforcement follow-up concerning a return filed or to be filed by a taxpayer, Form 4298. . .will be prepared and submitted to the employee's immediate supervisor for approval. .Form 4298 should not be prepared or approved unless the information provides substantive reason to conclude that enforcement effort will result in an additional or delinquent tax liability of material compliance consequence." 218/ At least theoretically, the originator of the Form 4298 for these purposes must convince his immediate supervisor that a taxpayer's next return should be audited. The approval form will then be sent to the district office's Service Branch which will perform some administrative activities 219/ 220/ on it and then send it to the district's Returns Program Manager. "[The] RPM. .will promptly screen Forms 4298 received from district Service Branch. Those that do not warrant selection for examination because of prior year returns, workload capacity, or other factors may be closed during the screening process. 221/ The 4298's for those returns which the RPM believes should be audited will 222/ then be forwarded to the Service Center where "[i]f the return has already been filed, it will be pulled and forwarded to the Service Center "If the return has not been filed, the appropriate 

Audit Division. 

223/ Masterfile will be posted so as to automatically identify the 224/ return when it is filed. ..

and forward it to the Service Center Audit 225/ Division."

When pulled by the Service Center, the return will be forwarded to the originating district office where "[o]n receipt of selected returns from the Service Center, Service Branch, the district office will assign them for examination in accordance with established 226/ procedures.

These procedures offer some assurance that a taxpayer will not be audited by the same agent in successive years. They do not, however, protect a taxpayer from successive audits generated for improper reasons.

Given the cursory review which managers have indicated to us is the best they can do in most cases, it is possible for an agent angered by some facet of the current audit or an agent acting out of other improper motivations to develop enough "good" reasons to pass the manager's inspection.

It must be reiterated that this discussion should not be read to indicate that these transgressions are rampant; no evidence is offered that they are. Mail and statements by Service personnel suggest that these possibilities are not, however, straw men. While the integrity of the system and the professionalism, integrity, and high character of the Service's employees are enough to protect most taxpayers, more may be necessary to prevent those few instances where procedures are improperly used. 

Yet, the taxpayers have no protection against them, for once a return enters the audit stream, there is little attention paid to how it got there.

The Service's present internal procedures probably are not adequate to insure that a taxpayer could be fully informed of why he was selected for audit. The coding used internally by Service personnel to indicate the reasons for audit selection are probably insufficient, when translated into words, to be very informative to a taxpayer. The

programs may not be sufficiently defined. In addition, the Service's existing internal controls may not be sufficient to insure that a taxpayer will be properly and honestly informed each time he requests the above information.

The Service generally rejects proposals for notifying taxpayers of reasons for audit selection on the ground that it is costly and difficult to provide. There is also some fear that, in those cases where returns are selected because information from third parties is involved, the informers' names will be divulged. Neither of these arguments is compelling. The Service now accumulates much of the data which would explain the selection. Additional expense could perhaps be obviated by merely permitting the taxpayer to see the relevant portions of his own tax file which has been prepared by the examining officer. As to the second objection, the taxpayer need not be informed of the identity of the informer. Indeed, a statement that the audit was initiated on information brought to the attention of the Service from sources outside the Service should be satisfactory. Further, in suspected fraud cases, the suspicion of fraud need not be disclosed. Obviously, management and 

Internal Audit would be required to police the use of such description to ascertain that improper return selection was not occurring in this category. 

(2) Audit. 

audit.

Improper conduct may also be manifested from the Because a Revenue Agent has greater latitude than a Tax Auditor in regard to the manner in which he conducts an audit, such conduct is more likely to occur in a field audit. Letters from taxpayers and

taxpayer representatives indicate that such improper actions are likely to arise when an agent requires excessive documentation, keeps the case open longer than necessary, or makes unjustified assessments. 227/ Further, the Service's examining officers have broad-reaching administrative summons powers. Such power runs not only against the taxpayer, but against any third parties as well. Thus, information may be requested from banks, customers, suppliers, or creditors, and if it is not voluntarily supplied, a summons may issue. Many taxpayers believe such requests and summonses are destructive of business and social relations. Further, the request may raise questions in the community's mind and certainly identifies the taxpayer as a target of Service investigation. 

The Service cautions that the power to issue summonses should be used sparingly and only when all other avenues for obtaining the necessary 228/ information have been exhausted.

An agent must also receive approval 229/ prior to issuing a summons, and such review may provide some protection from patently obvious abuse. A discussion of some aspects of the summons power will be found in Chaper 4 of this report. 

There appears to be little, if any, systemic protection against keeping a case open for an inordinate period of time, exacting overly burdensome proof, or making unjustified assessments.

There is no protection because a single case has little or no significance in regard to the annual Audit Plan. An agent may be asked to justify his keeping a 230/ case in inventory for an extraordinary period of time. 

However, that task is not difficult. Further, a taxpayer has little effective means of voicing a complaint. He may complain to the agent's Group Manager,

but there is little reason to believe that the Group Manager will take any action against his employee, primarily because he is likely to believe his agent. Further, discipline will consume efforts which could otherwise be expended to "make the Plan." It may also result in future personnel problems which will render "making the Plan" difficult. Finally, unjustified assessments are almost impossible to detect. Even if an assessment is reversed by the District Conference or other appeal procedures, the result will not reflect on the agent who made the original assessment, and, as will be discussed in the following section, it is unlikely that an agent's work will be reviewed. Further, even if an erroneous assessment is determined, even a mediocre agent can camouflage it well enough to make it appear nothing more than an error in judgment. 

(3) Effects of Improper Audits. 

The burdens of an audit can be substantial and those of an unwarranted or overly intensive audit are all the more onerous. 

Economic costs are one such burden. The taxpayer may well be required to hire professional assistance to aid him through his ordeal. His own bookkeeping records and staff will be interfered with during the examination, thus costing him lost time and inconvenience. If a taxpayer is an individual, he may lose wages due to time away from work. In either case an excessive request for documentation can compound this cost dramatically. 

Further, if a taxpayer fears improper conduct, he may refrain from arguing his case to the fullest extent possible. Hence, such fears may in practice prevent proper presentation of a case to an examining

officer. Finally, if our correspondence is any indication, the emotional costs of a regular audit can be severe and are exacerbated when harassment is suspected. 

It is apparent that condoning an agent's deviant behavior will have a deleterious effect on the operation of the entire staff. However, of more immediate impact are the economic and psychological costs borne by the taxpayer. One has to keep in mind that there are at the very least thousands of unexamined returns having equal or greater potential for tax change than the one subject to improper examination. Further, the emotional and economic costs of an audit are borne by the taxpayer under scrutiny, not the taxpaying public as a whole. This method of cost allocation might be justifiable if every individual whose return has equal potential for tax change had the same probability of being selected. It is impossible to justify such cost allocation when one return has a substantially greater chance to face audit, based on improper conduct of Service personnel, than a return with similar characteristics. f. 

The Review Function. 

(1) The Group Manager. 

"[The Group Manager's]. . .authority is defined throughout the Internal Revenue Manual. It is further spelled out in documents issued by managers in [their] .region and district. Unless otherwise stated in established procedures, [they are]. . .typically authorized to: (a) Assign and direct activities for each of [their]. . .employees. (b) Survey excessive workloads.

(c) Plan and direct examinations and other group activities. (d) Control the scope of investigations and examinations. (e) Instruct [their]. . .employees in the application of procedures and guidelines. (f) Approve administrative items such as travel vouchers, requests for returns, requests for supplies, and long distance telephone calls." 231/

Managers are promoted from the ranks of Revenue Agents. They are essentially technical people thrown into a situation in which technical knowledge is of only secondary importance to the knowledge of administrative procedure and to the ability to handle people. 

It is the Group Manager's job to see that the day-to-day operations of the Service are maintained. They are the first-level supervisors most responsible for transforming the Plan into actual fact. 232/ The Group Manager provides the final screening process prior to 233/ In accomplishing this a return's assignment to an agent for audit. task, he is looking for factors which may cause him to survey a return or which permit him to classify those returns in need of audit on the basis of the complexity and difficulty they present. 234/

On the other hand, a Group Manager is expected to assign work of greater difficulty than that normally assigned to a particular grade level in order 236/ to develop an employee's skills and enhance his career development.

Group Managers also have a major review function. They provide, essentially, the only review of an individual's performance and progress, and they provide the first level of review for an audited case. 237/ 

It is not intended that the cases be reviewed in depth. In fact, it is contemplated that the review function is fulfilled by a ". . .quick look through 238/ each examination report and case file." Our interviews indicated that, as a practical matter and as seemingly required by Service policy, the intensity of case reviews is commensurate with a given agent's judgment and 239/ experience, but it is almost never thorough.

If our review of the Service's Handbook for Audit Group Managers and our understanding derived from interviews are correct, the review process at this level is seen more as a tool for determining a general impression of each employee's capabilities and proficiency than for detecting errors on any given case. However, even to this extent we have been led to believe that the manager may not be able effectively to perform his review function. Crushing time pressures are placed on the Group 

Manager, and the flood of finished cases crossing his desk makes an adequate review of all or even a large percentage of cases virtually impossible. Further, we have been told that on-site visitation, which is a form of reviewing the employee's work habits, as prescribed by the 240/ Internal Revenue Manual, is largely ignored in some districts. 

Although we were impressed by the desire of most managers with whom we spoke to perform this important task, they all related the impossibility of finding enough time for it.

(2) Review of Group Manager's Performance. 

As stated before, Group Managers are responsible for making the audit process work. Thus, it seems quite reasonable to assume that they perceive their group's contribution to the accomplishment of the Service's goals of the utmost importance. Thus, a group's ability to produce closed cases with low no-change rates is perceived by all as a reflection of a manager's ability to select and assign returns effectively for audit and manage the time utilization of his group. He is told that his "principal" function is to "[o] perate your group efficiently and 241/ effectively to best accomplish its assigned tasks. . 

He also knows that his branch chief will monitor his group's accomplishments as a 242/ reflection of a manager's planning and managing ability, and as discussed at greater length earlier, these abilities are measured by Plan accomplishment.
