​III. THE SETTLEMENT PROCESS A. Description of Existing Settlement Procedure and Law. 

1. "Settlement" Defined.

As used herein, the term "settlement" shall encompass any kind of practical agreement reached between a taxpayer and the Internal Revenue Service which terminates a factual or legal dispute. However, it should be noted that the Service's concept of "settlement authority" is limited exclusively to those cases disposed of at the Appellate or District Conference level, based upon concessions dictated by the hazards of litigation. 2. 

The Audit. 

a. In General. 267/ Although a settlement might arise from a claim for refund, most follow an examination of the return by Audit Division personnel. 

While the audit process has previously been described in some detail, we will recapitulate those matters which directly pertain to subsequent settlement procedures. There are three types of audits: (1) office audits conducted by personal interview, (2) office audits conducted by correspondence, and (3) field audits conducted at the taxpayer's place of business. Office audits are performed by Tax Auditors and most field audits are performed by Revenue Agents. For purposes of the general discussion which follows, however, "examining officer" or "officer" will include all auditing personnel.

The possibility of a settlement first arises with the examining officer's tentative determination that a taxpayer has incorrectly reported his tax liability. The officer will inform the taxpayer of the proposed deficiency and usually discuss the facts and legal issues which have led to his 268/

conclusion. At this point the taxpayer or his representative may offer new facts, emphasize old ones, or suggest a different interpretation of the statute which would support the return as originally filed. 

If the taxpayer is sufficiently persuasive, a settlement will result and the taxpayer will receive written notification that his return is accepted as filed. If the taxpayer has not been sufficiently persuasive, a settlement at this level will result only if the taxpayer agrees to those changes proposed by the examining officer. In either case such an "agreed" case will be closed by the district office. 

However, in a significant number of cases, a basis for arriving at settlement cannot be agreed upon at this level, thus resulting in an 269/ "unagreed" case. The examining officer will then prepare a report, discussing those issues not resolved, which will became the foundation upon which the formal settlement process proceeds. 270/ Such an unagreed case will be closed at the district office when (1) the issues in dispute are resolved at the District Conference, the lowest appeals level, or (2) the time permitted for petition to the Tax Court has expired. 

b. The Examining Officer's Audit Determinations. 

The examining officer's primary purpose is to determine a taxpayer's liability. While he has some interest in discovering income not reported on the return, his major consideration will be to confirm the existence and the amount of each item thereon. In doing so, he will focus his attention on an examination of those books and records supporting, or showing as inaccurate any entry or omission of an entry on the taxpayer's return; however, this will not preclude his utilization of other, indirect methods to determine

3 the correct liability. Generally, he will reject a factual contention not supported by such an examination. 

The officer may also draw conclusions as to the verity of the items shown or determine "ultimate facts," i.e., subjective or intangible determinations based upon observable or finite matters. For example, the value of an item of property is a matter of opinion; however, for the purpose of audit 271/ determinations it is a fact, even though conclusionary. 

Such an issue may thus be resolved, but only when the taxpayer has carried his burden of proof to the examining officer's satisfaction; otherwise, the taxpayer must concede the issue or pursue an appeal. 

An officer may also apply relevant law to his determination of the facts. For example, he may decide whether compensation for personal services is reasonable (and thus deductible as provided by § 162 (a) (1) of the Code), or whether a payment should be considered as "alimony" (and thus deductible under § 215 of the Code).

If the dispute encompasses an issue of law, however, the examining officer is bound by the Service's position and can settle the case only on that basis. If, however, the issue is one on which the Service's position is not clear, the examining officer may seek technical advice from the national office.

There are many cases which entail various disputed issues of both a factual and legal nature. In addition, the merits of each issue may differ substantially. On reviewing the strengths, weaknesses, nature, and dollar magnitude of each issue involved, an officer may decide that proper settlement

can be effected through concessions of certain issues by both parties. 

Although the examining officer is instructed not to use this method of set- 272/ tlement (referred to as "issue trading" ) and to treat each issue independently, many dispositions at this level do not appear explainable on any other grounds. The officer's authority to settle is further restricted by the so- 273/ called "Prime Issues List.

Prime issues are identified by the national office as those presenting legal questions of major importance which have been inadequately tested in litigation. The officer is instructed to identify the existence of prime issues in discussions with the taxpayer, but he may 274/ not settle them.

The settlement authority of the officer is thus rather limited, although disputes are often resolved at his level. When agreement cannot be reached, however, the taxpayer may then pursue resolution through the various levels of administrative appeals available to him. The first step in this route is the District Conference. 

3. The District Conference. The District Conference is the first level of administrative appeal. Because the Conference staff is a functional branch of the Audit 

Division, each district office will have its own Conference staff. The Conference is composed of experienced examining officers who are detailed to 275/ the District Conference for approximately three years.

a. 

Procedures Following Office Audit of Individual's (Including Farming or Sole Proprietorship Business) Return. 

If the taxpayer and Tax Auditor fail to resolve their dif-

ferences at an office audit, either may request an immediate, informal con- 276 ference with the auditor's supervisor (Group Manager). This procedure allows the taxpayer an opportunity to resolve his case without the further in- 277/ convenience, expense, and delay of a formal District Conference.

Although the taxpayer's probable lack of preparation and/or representation at such a meeting is undoubtedly a practical deterrent, a large number of cases are 278/ nonetheless so resolved.

If an immediate conference is not requested, the taxpayer will receive a "15-day letter" from the District Director. This letter advises the taxpayer of the proposed adjustments and the alternative courses of action available to him for resolution of any disagreements. A copy of the auditor's report is included with the letter and explains the facts upon which such adjustments are proposed. The taxpayer may agree to the adjustments and sign a 

Form 870 which is also included with the 15-day letter; he may request a 

District Conference, usually by letter, within 15 days from the date of the District Director's letter; or he may ignore the 15-day letter in anticipation of a "30-day letter", which will permit him access to the Appellate Conference, or a "90-day letter", which will permit him petition to the Tax Court.

It should be noted that the taxpayer is free to bypass the District Conference, i.e., seek a conference with the Appellate Division, by awaiting issuance of the 30-day letter. However, the case will be reviewed by the district Audit Division prior to its being sent to the Appellate Division. If the issues involved lend themselves to easy resolution at the District Conference level, such will be suggested.

b. Procedures Following Correspondence Audits. 

If the taxpayer and auditor fail to agree after a "correspondence" audit, the taxpayer will receive a letter (combination 15-day and 30-day letter) along with two copies of the auditor's report. This report contains a "consent to findings" which, when signed, has the same effect as a 279/ signed Form 870. The letter advises the taxpayer that (1) he may agree to the auditor's determination, and sign and return one copy of the "consent"; (2) he may submit by telephone, mail, or interview additional evidence or information supporting his contentions within 15 days of the date of the letter; (3) he may request a District Conference within 15 days of the date of the letter; (4) he may file a protest and request an Appellate Conference within 30 days of the date of the letter; or (5) he may ignore the letter, in which event 280/ he will receive a 90-day letter.

C. 

Procedures Following Field Audit. 

When the taxpayer and Revenue Agent fail to settle a dispute in a field audit case, the agent will prepare a report explaining his pro- 281/ posed adjustments.

This report is given a technical and procedural review 282/

If the Review Staff concurs with the agent's findings, the District Director issues a 30-day letter with the agent's report enclosed. This letter advises the taxpayer of alternative courses of action. 

Specifically, he may: (a) Accept the findings in the report and sign a waiver of re- 283/ strictions on assessment (Form 870).

d. District Conferee Settlement Authority. 

The settlement authority of the District Conferee varies, depending upon whether the dispute involves disagreement over the facts, disagreement about the law, or a consideration of the hazards of litigation. 

The dollar amount in dispute for any one year is also a significant factor. 

The conferee has full All factual issues are open for discussion.

authority to weigh independently the merits of factual contentions and settle cases based upon his determination of their persuasiveness. However, where the facts are relatively clear and the dispute focuses on the applicable law or its application to the facts, the conferee is bound by the Service's position. 

If this position is not clear, either the taxpayer or the conferee may request 288/ technical advice from the national office. In cases involving less than $2,500 for any one year, when technical advice is requested and received, at the conferee's discretion the case may be disposed of by him or returned to 289, the examining officer for his disposition. If more than $2,500 is involved, the conferee must retain the case and dispose of it himself. In either case, Service personnel are bound by the position reflected in the technical advice 290/ received.

In cases involving more than $2,500 the conferee is confined solely 291/ to applying the applicable law to his perceptions of the facts of the case. 

If a single issue is in dispute, the conferee, in general, fully sustains either the taxpayer or the Service, unless the issue is one which is susceptible to a compromise (e.g., a valuation question where the opposing parties may have urged different values). On the other hand, if multiple issues are involved, an acceptable middle ground may be found by bargaining; some issues will be decided for, and others against, the taxpayer. 

In cases which involve less than $2,500 for a single year, the conferee may entertain a settlement based upon his estimation of the hazards 292/ of litigation, i.e., the government's chances of success if the case were litigated.

There are other restrictions on the settlement authority of the District Conferee. First, generally he will not settle the disputed tax of one year if another year's tax for the same taxpayer is pending before, or 293/ going to, the Appellate Division. 

Second, the District Conferee, like the examining officer, may not settle "prime issues, 294/ nor may he settle nuisance value cases. Third, the receipt of adverse technical advice on an issue from the national office may have an adverse practical effect on a conferee's willingness to settle a case for which he has settlement authority, although it does not have a binding effect on his ability to settle. 

The relatively restricted settlement authority at the District Conference level leads some tax practitioners, and perhaps some Service personnel, to question its efficacy. Certainly, the Conference is an opportunity to clear up facts and legal theories, although the results may differ from one 295/ district to another, as well as from one conferee to another. theless, many would agree that a case entailing major factual issues should 296/ Never This is so if only for the reason generally go to a District Conference. that by utilizing District Conference, even though appeal is eventually taken to the Appellate Conference, the taxpayer can have two chances at convincing the Service of the correctness of his viewpoint. On the other hand, when the issues are primarily legal ones, it may be preferable to seek Appellate con- 297/ sideration directly.

If a District Conference is initially chosen and the case remains in dispute after the Conference and any rehearings, the taxpayer is then entitled to seek an Appellate Conference. Since the multiple levels of appeal are not intended to allow the taxpayer a choice of settlements, the settlement offered

at the District Conference expires once recourse to Appellate is decided upon. 

The settlement proposal made at the District Conference is, however, included 299/ in the report that is forwarded to the Appellate Conferee.

298/ e. 

Review of Settlements. 

All cases which a District Conferee proposes to close are 300/ subject to final approval of the Chief of the District Conference.

However, under procedures recently established, the District Conferee's determination will not be reviewed by the district Review Staff in field or office audit 301/ cases.

An agreed case (i.e., one in which agreement has been reached between the conferee and the taxpayer) when closed at the District Conference will be reopened only if, upon approval of the Assistant Regional Commissioner (ARC) 302/ (Audit), it is determined that (1) there is evidence of fraud, collusion, or misrepresentation of a material fact; (2) the closing involved a clearly de- 303/ fined substantial error, based on established Service position; or (3) other circumstances in the case indicate that a failure to reopen would be a serious 304/ administrative amission. 305/ A closed District Conference case may also be reopened when (1) the 306/ (2) the year is affected by taxpayer files a claim, or sues, for a refund; 307/ correction of an error for a barred year; (3) a net operating loss is carried back to the closed year; or (4) there have been involuntary conversions and the taxpayer has not recomputed his tax liability pursuant to S 1033. These procedural rules do not, however, prevent reopening of a district office case to verify or adjust items reported on information returns, 308/ or to correct mathematical errors.

4. The Appellate Conference.

When the taxpayer fails to settle his case at the District Conference, he may proceed to the regional Appellate Division (hereinafter re- 312/ ferred to as "Appellate"). 313/ This division is a branch of the Regional Commissioner's office and, thus, is independent of the district office. 5. The Tax Court and Regional Counsel. 

During the 90-day period given the taxpayer to file a petition 325/ with the Tax Court, Appellate will not ordinarily grant another conference 326/ until the petition is filed and the government has answered. 

After a taxpayer files his petition in the Tax Court, authority to dispose of the case prior to actual litigation is shared by Appellate and Regional Counsel's 327/ office.

After the Tax Court convenes the session in which a case is scheduled 332/ for trial, or any pre-trial hearings, the Appellate Conferee relinquishes full jurisdiction over the case to Regional Counsel, who may settle, concede, or try it, as he deems advisable. If the case is settled, the taxpayer and the government stipulate the basis of their agreement in writing. This stipulation is filed with the Tax Court, which enters a decision in accordance 333/ therewith. 

6. Delay in Settling.

Apart from the obvious reasons of insufficient time for adequate preparation of a case or the pendency of an important decision on a relevant issue from another court, the advantages to delaying the settlement process and thereby delaying payment of taxes due are outweighed by its disadvantages. 

For the taxpayer, delay would involve the risks of loss of witnesses, fading memories, difficulties in locating relevant documents, and other evidentiary erosions of the taxpayer's case. Nevertheless, until recently, the 6 percent interest rate charged on tax deficiencies undoubtedly made delay by taxpayers in certain cases attractive. However, the new interest rate of 9 percent, with 334/ indexing adjustments geared to changes in the prime rate, should diminish that incentive.

B.

Settlement Results and Their Variations. 

1. Level of Settlement.

Taxpayers seem to fare better as they progress along the administrative settlement process. For example, in 1971 District Conferees 335/ settled for approximately 42 percent of the amount originally assessed. 

In that same year 19,743 disputes were settled by Appellate prior to resort to the Tax Court, at slightly more than 30 percent of the amount initially claimed 336/ Of 6,187 cases that were docketed in the Tax Court, the by the government. 

Service settled at slightly less than 32 percent of the asserted deficiencies. 

However, in cases actually tried by the Tax Court, the Service collected 41 percent of the claimed deficiencies. 337/ We think there are several reasons for this phenomenon. First, all appeal levels are instructed to settle cases if any reasonable basis therefor exists. Second, because each successive level of appeal receives a file containing a case's entire history, it has knowledge of any settlement offers rejected below. Thus, although its determinations should be independently made, the higher appeal level may reason that its settlement offer must be more favorable to the taxpayer than that offered below. The higher level may well be cognizant that the taxpayer's primary reason for appeal to it was to induce a more favorable offer, but the government nevertheless may make such an offer in order to facilitate settlement. Third, taxpayers may appeal fairly weak or thin issues to at least one appeal level and be unwilling or ill-prepared to carry through on all levels. When this happens, full concessions by taxpayers will increase the government's recovery ratios at the lower levels.

Also, as previously discussed, the standards of settlement differ at each level. Hazards of litigation may not be considered at the District 

Conference except in smaller cases. 338/ Thus, it may not concede issues based on the hazards even though it believes they will be lost by the Service. 

Prime issues also may not be settled at this level. Further, settlement of small cases contrary to a Service position is inhibited by a reporting pro- 339/ cedure requiring a full explanation for such activity.

340/ 

Finally, as later suggested, less adept counsel or taxpayers with no counsel at all may be more likely to settle at the district level. 341/ On the other hand, utilization of the hazards of litigation standard is not only available to the Appellate Division, but is believed by some to be its primary basis for settlement dispositions. Further, although there are constraints on Appellate's settling of prime issues contrary to Service 342 position, it may nonetheless do so. Finally, once Regional Counsel enters a case, the government's settlement decision will be made by a lawyer. Not unexpectedly, a lawyer who litigates will be more selective in choosing the cases which he will present to a court. 343/ There is another issue concerning settlement rates which we think is significant. Over the past 17 years settlements made by the Appellate Division 344/ have increasingly been at smaller percentages of the proposed deficiencies; presently they range from 30 to 40 percent. 345/ 

In other words, 60 to 70 percent of examining officers' initial recommendations of tax deficiencies are being rejected. Such a continuing low rate of sustension obviously raises questions concerning the validity and accuracy of either the officer's proposed assessments, or the settlements accorded by the Appellate Division, or both.

བྲ 1 The question of whether the low sustension rate is the result of overly zealous examining officers, excessively lenient Appellate Conferees, geographic variation, or some other undiscovered or overlooked factors has not been resolved. 

However, in an effort to discover reasons for this low recovery rate, the Service has recently instituted a nationwide Appellate 346/ Under this program, Appellate Conferees will prepare feedback system. a report, to be forwarded to the appropriate district office, on all cases where Appellate sustains less than 50 percent of the proposed deficiencies exceeding $100,000 and less than $2,500. 

2. Geographic Variations. 

There has been much discussion of statistics which seem to reveal a lack of uniformity in treatment of taxpayers from one part of the country to another, from the audit level through settlement at Appellate. 

The following examples document the extent to which the percentage of dollars recovered from proposed assessments at settlement varies from office to office. These figures raise the questions of whether uniformity may be expected and whether the Service has any programs or data by which uniformity may be measured.

The percentage of dollars of recommended assessments which survive the District Conference varies substantially from district to district. For example, in 1971 the Cincinnati District sustained only 19 percent of each dollar of assessments initially recommended, while the Newark District sustained 84 percent. In 1972 the Little Rock District sustained 24 percent, the lowest percentage; the Baltimore District sustained the highest, with 

74 percent. 347/

Similarly, in terms of the percentage of dollars of recommended assessments agreed upon after an Appellate Conference, the lowest recovery rate was in the Western Region (San Francisco) where only 16 percent of assessments over $1,000,000 was sustained in 1972. That same region, however, reported the highest recovery rate, i.e., 83 percent, in the $1,000 to $10,000 348/ assessment category in 1971. a.

Factors Affecting Uniformity Within and Among Districts and Regions.

Uniformity among districts can be affected by several factors. 

Recently recruited examining officers usually do not have a thorough knowledge of the law and Service positions and procedures. In addition, the capacities of examining officers' Group Managers undoubtedly will vary. Also, the degree 349/ to which different District Directors emphasize the informal conference will vary.

Sustension statistics can also be disproportionately affected by the effects of Service concession on one or two large-dollar cases. 

A related question is whether the use of production statistics and the pressures on district offices to make the Audit Plan impact upon the size of proposed deficiencies and the strength of the cases underlying the proposals.

Although the Service has no formal program to maintain uniformity in the disposition of similar substantive issues at the district level, there are numerous informal Service procedures adopted at the discretion of each 350/ District Director which are employed to encourage such uniformity. 

1. District Conferees prepare a feedback report to examining officers on every case heard.

This report, noting procedural lapses, issue-

RI treatment lapses, and other inconsistencies, will be discussed at group meetings with Group Managers and Branch Chiefs when the issues are of general significance. 

2. District Conferees will meet with groups of examining officers to discuss procedures and treatment of issues. 

3. Regional Analysts are responsible for monitoring District Conference activities within a district and among various districts. This program includes visits to each district, seminars with conferees, and coordination of information between districts. 

4. A Technical Review Institute is held annually, which most examining officers attend. This consists of a review of all new procedural developments, legislation, court decisions, and administrative rulings relating to the internal revenue laws which have arisen in the past year. is supplemented by the publication, four times a year, of the Review of Technical Developments which reviews thoroughly all these matters. It 

5. Examining officers receive weekly and bi-weekly Cumulative Bulletins and Tax Briefs (brief summaries of current developments in the tax law published by the national office Technical Division). 

6. The Internal Revenue Manual contains the Specialized Industries 

351/ and Audit Techniques Guidelines Handbook which provides techniques for uniform determinations within the same industry. 

7. The Manual also contains guidelines to ensure the uniform 352/ handling of those issues on which the Service's position is unclear. 

8. Regional Review Digests are distributed to all districts within a region, as well as to other regions. They discuss (1) procedural errors

made by examining officers, (2) frequent errors made by examining officers on technical issues, and (3) unique and significant issues encountered within the region. 

9. Regional Analysts visit each district in a region to review numerous cases at various stages of disposition to develop and encourage procedural uniformity. 

10. District Audit and Appellate managers will meet to discuss 353/ case development and treatment of issues within their regions. 

11. District Conference Chiefs from all the regions meet periodically to discuss the treatment of particular issues within their respective regions. 

12. There is currently underway a test of a new procedure for postreview of Appellate cases, the goal of which, if fully implemented, will be to assist in assuring a greater degree of national issue uniformity at the 

Appellate level. b.

Factors Affecting National Uniformity. 

The fact that our tax law is one unified "national" body of law is the most significant factor promoting national uniformity in the treatment of taxpayers. 354/ However, a number of other factors do exist which undoubtedly contribute to much uniform treatment. 

The Service conducts a national Technical Coordination Program involving the identification of unique issues and resulting in legislative recommendations and new procedural guidelines. This program is maintained in each district by a member of the district's Review Staff, whose title is that of Technical Coordinator. His duties are to collect ideas for legislation or new procedures from his office's personnel and transmit them to the national

office. As he is on the Review Staff, and thus responsible for looking at numerous cases, issues, and procedures, he is perhaps in the best position to became aware of such ideas. 

In addition, revenue rulings, regulations, and formal technical 355/ advices are issued by the national office and reflect the Service-wide position Further, prior to audit and/or appeal, on the laws addressed thereby. the taxpayer may also obtain an advance ruling from the national office to clarify certain legal issues. 356/ Finally, there is some degree of uniformity gained from the Service's refusal to decide certain issues which are in litigation or under consideration by Technical until a clear Service position has been established. 

Published actions on Tax Court decisions in the form of acquiescences and non-acquiescences and unpublished actions on decisions in other cases also contribute toward uniformity in a conferee's interpretation of specific areas 357/ of the law. The Uniform Issues List induces more uniform identification of issues by conferees. However, the availability of this information has, in the experience of same practitioners, prevented settlements except in accord with information on the settlement of similar issues in Appellate's data 358/ retrieval system. Also, the Internal Revenue Manual as it sets forth the 

Service's procedural requirements also seems to contribute toward more uniform treatment of taxpayers.

C. 

The Use of Statistics as a Guide to Geographic Uniformity. 

It is questionable whether variations in settlement percentages among various sections of the country are useful indices of uniform treatment of either taxpayers or the issues raised. This conclusion is based

on the fact that there are many factors affecting the size of proposed assessments.

For example, as mentioned earlier, a single large case involving a proposed deficiency of millions of dollars may have an extraordinary effect upon a district's recovery ratio. 

Whether such a case is settled at 0 percent or 100 percent, its sheer magnitude will exert inordinate weight on the camputation of percentages. Industry-wide audits and the resulting settlements also tend to compound the distortion, where the industry is located primarily in only a few districts.

Furthermore, statistics may well be skewed by factors that are unusual to a particular district in a particular year. For example, the 359/ The Narcotics Traffickers Program was centered in a few key districts. termination assessments made in conjunction with this program in many cases were based on limited factual information and are excessively large; thus, settlements may well be concluded for an extremely small percentage of the proposed assessments. Although such termination assessments will affect the statistics of only a few districts, this does not reflect a lack of geographical uniformity in treatment, since the termination assessment policy is generally the same throughout the Service.

Finally, the use of purely statistical data will reveal little about the substantive issues involved. Even when settlement data are campiled on an issue-by-issue basis, they provide no information on the strength or weakness of the particular cases decided. The variation in the hazards of litigation, from case to case, will largely undermine efforts toward uniform treatment, if uniformity is stated in terms of percentages of deficiencies recovered.

This discussion is not to suggest that the public should not have access to statistical data on settlements. Such data do little in themselves to reveal whether taxpayers receive equal treatment on substantive issues. 

But an analysis of the results reached in a representative sample of individually studied settlements, grouped by the substantive issues involved, could yield 360/ more meaningful insights into settlement variations. Such a study should focus on the most commonly controverted issues. It should analyze the recovery ratio (i.e., the ratio of the amount of deficiency agreed upon by the parties to the amount of the deficiency originally recommended by the examining officer), with reference to the factors of the amounts of tax involved, whether or not the taxpayers were represented, and patterns of geographic variation. 3.

Size Variations a.

Effects of Size Variations. 

The size of a particular case or issue (that is, the amount of the proposed assessment) is another factor affecting settlements. Size

is the "benefit" side of the cost-benefit relationship, which must be considered by the taxpayer when determining whether to settle a given case or pursue its appeal further. For the government, however, any cost-benefit analysis may be based on considerations other than the amount at issue in the particular case. A single case may have significance to the Service beyond the dollars involved, e.g., if a prime issue is involved. Also, government representatives are prohibited from considering the size of a case in their settlement deliberations, although size will affect the procedures by which settlements are reached. Thus, the size of a case may have less impact on the Service than it does on the taxpayer. 

In addition, while both Appellate and District Conferees are 361/ specifically forbidden to settle on the basis of "nuisance value," taxpayers are not similarly enjoined. Examining officers or conferees must be aware of this fact. 

b. Comments on Size of the Amount in Dispute. 

(1) 

Small-Dollar Assessments. 

Under District Conference procedures for cases involving 362/ proposed deficiencies of less than $2,500, the parties may settle on a basis reflecting litigation hazards. As a result, compromise settlements are likely to be more available to taxpayers at an earlier stage than in larger 363/ cases.

Such an opportunity undoubtedly will save taxpayers money.

364/ experiences However, as these procedures were only recently instituted, under them have not yet been adequately analyzed to confirm the statement. 

Professor Wright has argued forcefully that in those small-dollar cases where the taxpayer has the advantage in a legal argument, the Service 365/ This view is based on the premise that an should concede completely. appeal through a properly qualified representative would be prohibitively costly to the small taxpayer, and that he could not be expected to represent himself adequately.

An alternative technique of protecting the small taxpayer's economic interests during the settlement process would be a system of publicly funded tax advice. (2) 

Large-Dollar Assessments vs. Small-Dollar Assessments. 

The existence of special post-review procedures was 366/ noted above with respect to certain large settlements. 

In addition, § 6405 of the Code provides for review by the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue 367/ Taxation of refund cases involving more than $100,000. 

This extra layer of review would seem to increase the chances that any given settlement might be upset; however, there seems to be an absence of data reflecting how frequently the Joint Committee actually exercises the review powers granted it. 

There are data which reveal that, at the Appellate level, the government recovers a smaller percentage of the larger proposed assessments than of the smaller proposed assessments. 

In 1971 Appellate settled proposed deficiencies under $1,000 at 68 cents on the dollar. In 1972 it

settled the same class of proposed assessments at 67 cents on the dollar. 

However, as the amount of the proposed assessments rises, the percentage of recovery falls. Thus, in the $1,000-$10,000 category, the recovery rates were 

63 percent and 61 percent in 1971 and 1972, respectively; in the $10,000- $50,000 class, the rates were 50 percent and 53 percent; in the $50,000-$100,000 class, the rates were 44 percent in both years; in the $100,000-$500,000 class, the rates were 38 percent and 39 percent; in the $500,000-$1,000,000 class, the rates were 37 percent and 35 percent; and finally, in the over $1 million 368/ group the rates were 24 percent and 34 percent. Similarly, in the first half of fiscal 1973, in cases involving less than $1,000 the Service settled at a national average of 75 percent of claimed deficiencies. This number declined to 54 percent when the deficiencies sought were between $10,000 and $50,000, and further decayed to an average of 43 percent when the claimed de- 369/ ficiencies were above $500,000.

There are several probable causes for the occurrence of such a pattern. First, many small proposed assessments revolve around a single issue 370/ which must be decided on an all-or-nothing basis. Also, because smalldollar cases do not justify the same level of expertise as larger ones do, the taxpayer may be unrepresented or represented by an advocate unfamiliar with the law and settlement techniques. Thus, the taxpayer in a small-dollar case may be at a decided disadvantage.

Further, many large-dollar cases seem to present multiple and more sophisticated issues than small-dollar cases; such issues are more susceptible

to a trade as opposed to an unequivocal decision. Also, the more sophisticated issues lend themselves to numerous kinds of resolutions which, in 371/ effect, allow for a compromise on those issues. 

In addition, if a large sum of money is involved, substantial expense may be justified to pursue the case up the appeals ladder. Thus, the threat of a law suit becomes much more meaningful. Given that counsel in such cases are probably more prevalent and more skilled, a lower percentage settlement in favor of the taxpayer, based on the hazards of litigation, would seem justified. On the other hand, where a small amount is involved, the costs of representation will militate towards the taxpayer's acceptance of a settlement he might otherwise consider inadequate. 

Finally, we reiterate that the variations in percentages of recovery prove little about the substantive treatment of the issue. However, given the adversarial nature of the process, the more skilled advocates are more likely to represent large-dollar cases and to achieve more favorable results. 

Therefore, if all taxpayers were equally represented, we would expect the disparaties in settlement percentages to lessen, though not to disappear. 

4. Effect of Type of Taxpayer. 

Taxpayers come in many varieties as well as sizes individuals, corporations, exempt organizations, cooperatives, estates, trusts, and partnerships, to name the more significant ones. While at least to some extent different substantive rules will apply to these entities, there is no

evidence that the classification of a taxpayer has, in itself, any bearing on the settlement procedures. Each is subject to the same administrative procedures described above. 

5. Probability of Success in Litigation 60 

The Hazards of Litigation. 

Our previous discussion noted that the Appellate Division in all cases, and the District Conference in cases involving less than $2,500 for any one year, are empowered to consider hazards of litigation in arriving at 372/ settlement.

The estimate of the hazards of litigation is made by the conferee (with the advice and consent of Regional Counsel in docketed cases). 

Conferees are told, however, that their role is largely judicial and that a 373/ judicial attitude should be reflected.

Sim- Presumably, the conferee's evaluation will reflect insights gained from personal experience with the tax law. He will also be influenced by the Service's acquiescences or non-acquiescences in Tax Court decisions. ilarly, the Service's failure to take other actions (e.g., failure to appeal or apply for certiorari) may also be known to, and affect, the conferee. 

As a practical matter, mutual concession settlements hased on the hazards of litigation may be difficult to achieve. This standard envisions

374/ compromise by both parties. 

In many cases such compromise may present no difficulty, because multiple issues are involved or because there may be several theories which will support a settlement agreeable to all. For example, a payment made to a shareholder, characterized by the Service as a dividend, will be disallowed as a deduction to the corporation.. But then the Service may accept the corporation's contention that some of the payment is additional salary to the shareholder and some is additional rent on property leased to the corporation by the shareholder. Thus, part or all of the deduction may be allowed after all.

There are, however, cases in which the issue is not susceptible to such reasoned or rationalized results. For example, due to the intrinsic nature of the dependency exemption issue, only one of the opposing sides can prevail in litigation. The conferee and taxpayer may agree that the chances are even, and thus, under the concept of the hazards of litigation, a settlement at 50 percent should be reached. But such "split-issue" 375/ settlements are 376/ not favored by the Service and are made only when no other basis exists. 

It is, therefore, not surprising that Appellate Conferees in our discussions agreed that a propounded "theory" has a greater likelihood of occasioning settlement than an appraisal of the litigation hazards. Tax practitioners knowledgeable in the treatment of sophisticated and multiple issues may more easily and readily provide such a theory than the under-represented taxpayer in a single, all-or-nothing case. Hence, we surmise that a conferee, proficient in handling intricate and sophisticated issues, will be less inclined to settle split-issue cases and will await a full taxpayer

concession. This may reasonably occur once the taxpayer analyzes the cost benefits and finds his only alternative is time-consuming, expensive, and inconvenient litigation. 6. 

Representation as a Factor in Settlement Results. 

The quality of both the taxpayer's and the government's representation undoubtedly is a factor having substantial impact on the eventual outcome of settlement negotiations. As the quality of a taxpayer's representation may vary considerably, either his counsel or the government's representative may emerge as the better. Government counsel may have a consistent advantage in their day-to-day familiarity with the array of procedural options available to both parties. With regard to substantive factual and legal issues, however, neither side's counsel is consistently superior to the other.

How- 

In the settlement process, an unrepresented taxpayer is at a great 377/ disadvantage, which the Service has made sincere efforts to offset. ever, the very nature of the process is such that these efforts have not produced the desired result.

The law is exceedingly complex, 378/ even for taxpayers having relatively low incomes. This complexity is compounded by a confusing array of record-keeping requirements. Service personnel will invariably have a greater understanding than the taxpayer of both these systemic factors; yet they may be unable or unwilling to impart that understanding to him. The unassisted taxpayer thus finds himself entangled in a maze of rules, exceptions, and limitations through which he may never before have ventured. The resulting confusion probably cannot be overcome by even the most sympathetic and able 

Service personnel.

3791 At another point we have argued that, given the different expectations of the examining officer and the taxpayer, the audit is inherently an adversary proceeding. Since the taxpayer is likely to regard settlement procedures as a mere extension of that encounter, he is unlikely to believe that the Service has suddenly acquired a judicial nature. This may be so even where the settlement officer is kindly disposed toward the taxpayer. 

Because the taxpayer may be uncertain as to whether he should rely on the advice tendered by the settlement officer, he remains essentially without advice.

Also, the taxpayer's perception that the settlement process is adversary is undoubtedly fair in most cases. Settlement officers are drawn from the most qualified and experienced examining officers. They undoubtedly bring with them the predisposition (and sometimes a well-justified cynicism) that many returns are incorrectly prepared. That background would seem difficult to shed when thrust into the settlement process. despite the Service's best efforts, the settlement process retains much of the adversary atmosphere of the audit. Thus,

The record before a conferee also seems to militate against the unrepresented. The record will clearly show the evidence supporting the examining officer's findings and may also indicate evidence which the taxpayer does not have. The written record, then, is tilted against the taxpayer; this record may be overcome only if the taxpayer knows the nature of the

further evidence which will be required. If he does not, the conferee must supply that knowledge and give the taxpayer an opportunity to produce such evidence. A considerable investment in time will be required. Further, the conferee may assume that such an exploration will merely cover ground already traversed by the examining officer. Given the fact that conferees also have case-load inventories which must not became too large, there may be little disposition to undertake the necessary investigation. 

This disposition is probably reinforced by the fact that in many small cases of unrepresented taxpayers there is little merit to the case. The case is on appeal largely because the taxpayer does not understand some facet of the law. Thus, experience in handling such appeals may lead to an understandingly jaded view that few, if any, such appeals warrant the time and inconvenience necessary to a full explication of the facts. 

Furthermore, the mere fact that the Service side of the controversy is written would seem to give it undue weight. The taxpayer may be unable to make such a written presentation. Thus, his point of view may never be more fully laid out than in notes taken by the conferee at a meeting which by its very nature will not always be highly organized. 

As we noted above, split-issue settlements are not acceptable unless there is no other basis for settlement. The unrepresented taxpayer may not understand a split issue. Even if he does, he may not know that the 

Service is authorized to settle on that basis; given the institutional bias against them, settlement officers certainly are not encouraged to suggest such settlements. Thus, the all-or-nothing aspect of the settlement process may never be overcome, and a taxpayer may submit to a total recovery when

a knowledgeable representative would have insisted on a split-issue settlement.

Con- Another factor suggesting that representation is important may be inferred from the description of the process as one of settlements. troversies are settled, and settlement usually means bargaining. Bargaining, however, by unequals in knowledge of the law and procedures is hardly the kind of bargaining that leads to appropriate settlements. 

In addition, the intricacies of the settlement process itself sug- On first exposure, few taxpayers can gests a need for able representation. comprehend the differences and distinctions between 15-, 30-, and 90-day letters. Yet, same understanding of these terms and the various resting places along the settlement process would appear necessary for determining strategy. 

Also, there is almost no likelihood that the distinctions between District Conference, the Appellate Division, and Regional Counsel can be understood by the taxpayer. Further, even if they were understood, an untrained person may not be able to estimate where the best opportunities of settlement lie. All he may know is that the further one goes, the greater his inconvenience because more time is involved. Thus, the procedures themselves are designed for skilled advocates, and no amount of explanation by a settlement officer can impart the full understanding of the procedures and their implications. 

Nor will the uninitiated taxpayer know that to many well-represented taxpayers the settlement process is a game commenced when the return is filed in a belief that the likelihood of audit is great. Being unaware of this attitude, the uninitiated is unlikely to know that the settlement officer

may constantly be engaged in such a game and, thus, unwittingly be unable to change his attitude to accommodate the types of issues normally presented by the unrepresented taxpayer. 

Finally, a taxpayer who comes to the settlement process with so little knowledge of either the substantive law or procedural routes cannot come with a great deal of confidence. Thus, he is intimidated before the process begins. This feeling is undoubtedly heightened by the knowledge that he is contesting with his government which, since he is unaware of systemic pressures to the contrary, he thinks has unlimited resources. He is likely to be defensive, nervous, and confused. In those circumstances, his skills as an advocate are likely to be blunted. His defensive posture and lack of objectivity are also factors which may be conducive to an unpleasant attitude which will, on occasion, have a damaging effect on the outcome. 

In short, the taxpayer without representation is simply overmatched, and no amount of effort and care by the settlement officer can over- For these reasons, same have advocated an come all these disadvantages. 380/ office where taxpayers having disputes could obtain representation or advice.

7. 

Miscellaneous Factors. 

382/ The Service has suspended its special information reports on In the past the classification "sensitive" cases involving public figures. of a taxpayer's case as "sensitive" vastly increased the difficulties of negotiating a settlement.

Service personnel seemed unable to consider the hazards of litigation in a normal fashion. Further, a taxpayer whose case was so classified might submit to a settlement favoring the government because of his fear of the publicity resulting from litigation. 

While various political pressures may occasionally be exerted upon the Service, field personnel, including conferees, seem well-isolated from such influence. Another factor which may exist, but which seems very minor in proportion to the overall size of the enterprise, is corruption. Despite very 383/ recent newspaper reports to the contrary, our experiences, as well as those of persons at the tax bar, suggest that corruption in the Service's settlement process is minimal, or non-existent. 

Occasionally, administrative convenience has led to industrywide settlements. Presumably based on an unspecified "average" expected outcome of litigation, these settlements seem to injure some industry members and provide a windfall to others, when compared to settlements based on normal procedures. Of course, industry members who feel that they were less successful than warranted by their specific facts are free to litigate their own cases.

C. Conclusion. 

In conclusion, we repeat that the settlement procedures have worked well for those represented by skilled advocates. Not only do they work well, but there is much to be said for the view that they have been designed by and 384/ for those who act in a representative capacity. Thus, we should not be surprised that difficulties arise when the taxpayer is unskilled and unrepresented.

Further, since most of the outside influence in shaping these procedures has come from those in a representative capacity, we should not be unduly critical of the Service's failure to design procedures more to the advantage of the unrepresented. In fact, if tax controversies are best settled by adversaries, one can find little, if any, fault with current procedures. 

The difficulty, then, lies in the failure to have equal adversaries. 

Procedures can be devised for the handling of unrepresented taxpayers. Congress could well decide to provide accounting and legal expertise to those who are unable or unwilling to provide their own, but who question an examiner's findings.

IV. 

COMMENTS ON THE EFFECTS OF REPRESENTATION 

E: 

Nothing is as sure as death and taxes, and almost every segment of the population is affected by the latter. To the extent the audit and settlement systems work as tax law enforcement tools, rather than revenue collection tools, those taxpayers against whom the law is enforced should have at least some claim on the tax revenues which law enforcement is designed to maximize. However, the line between those who should receive assistance in the Audit and Settlement process at government expense and those who should not is difficult to draw, though the extremes on either side of the line are easily identified.

At one extreme are the corporate giants, which are primarily audited for the purpose of revenue production. At the other extreme are individual tax- 

Between these two groups are all payers with adjusted gross income of under $10,000, who are audited primarily for the purpose of tax law enforcement. other taxpayers, who are audited for a combination of these purposes, with one or the other of the purposes being predominant. 

For several reasons, few would argue that costs incurred by corporate giants for assistance in controversies about their taxes should be subsidized to a greater extent than the subsidy already provided by the tax deductibility of such costs. First, the large corporation is virtually certain that its return will be examined and that any tax change will be found. 

This is so, if for no other reason, because there are numerous transactions in which it will have been involved about which neither the facts nor the law are entirely clear. Given these circumstances the only situation in which a determination of no tax change is likely to result from an audit would be one in which the corporation had resolved each ambiguity in favor of the government, an unlikely Occurrence.

Further, the astute financial officer knows that, even as to clearly erroneous entries on the return, the examining officer will have great difficulty in ascertaining whether such inaccuracy is intentional, negligent, or without fault. Realizing the difficulty the Service is likely to have, it has even been suggested that some corporate officers are willing to make entries on their tax return which stretch the interpretation of the under- 385/ lying facts beyond credulity. The corporate officer also knows there is an elaborate appeals and settlement process through which disagreements with examining officers may be resolved. 

Experience has taught him that, because the Service is aware of all 386/ of these factors, it approaches an audit with a healthy cynicism, expecting that all questionable and ambiguous items will have been resolved in favor of the corporation. officer views the corporate taxpayer as a knowledgeable adversary and proceeds on this premise.

As we have detailed in another place, the examining With this attitude prevailing on the part of the government and the corporate taxpayer, both parties are likely to view the filing of the tax return as merely the beginning, rather than the consummation, of a long process through which the final tax liability is reached. Thus, the taxpayer is likely to view the preparation of the return as the foundation for antici- 387/ pated negotiations.

The gamesmanship involved in this process is based on cost effectiveness. 

As previously implied, corporate officers rarely if ever expect to prevail on every issue which can or will be raised on audit, though they do expect to prevail on some. In preparing a return, they must weigh the probability

that an examining officer will decide issues against the taxpayer, and the cost of appealing the anticipated adverse decisions, against the potential net gains to be realized from being sustained on these issues. Given that the potential tax savings riding on each issue are normally large and that the settlement process requires small additional costs over those already incurred in the preparation and inevitable examination of a return, the marginal cost of handling the settlement process may not be great in relation to the tax liability in dispute. The negotiation of these issues then is a highly cost efficient use of corporate resources; if at any point cost efficiency is lost, the corporation may withdraw from the game with whatever victories it may have achieved.

By the same token, the Service considers that the costs of examining one of these corporate returns and finally settling the issues arising therefrom are low relative to the increases in revenue potentially generated. 

Because there is a high ratio of revenue to cost, and because most large corporate audits result in the assessment of substantial tax deficiencies, it appears that they are conducted for the dual purposes of law enforcement and revenue raising but with emphasis on the latter. 

At the other end of the spectrum is the individual taxpayer having less than $10,000 adjusted gross income and who files his return claiming only the standard deduction. His return is simple, and because he is not likely otherwise to keep extensive books and records, the machinery employed by the taxpayer to determine his income is employed primarily for tax purposes. 

Issues open to question or discussion on any one return will be few in number, and many of them will be all-or-nothing type issues. It is true

that legal and factual ambiguities in these returns may have been resolved by the taxpayer in his favor. Nevertheless, two things are certain: (1) not every return will be examined, and (2) a substantial percentage of 388/ those returns audited will not result in additional revenue for the Service. 

These things do not mean the examination will be without rewards to the Service. 

The aggregates of proposed deficiencies will exceed costs by a large margin and thus this part of the audit program will be cost-efficient to the Service. 

However, there are other income classes where the no-change rate is lower and where the cost-benefit ratio for the Service is greater. The decision to audit low-income returns can be attributed not so much to the desire to raise revenue as to the Service's desire to maintain a "presence," i.e., the credible threat that a return in any income category may be audited. these returns, individual taxpayers are audited primarily for the effect such will have on the voluntary compliance of other taxpayers rather than the enforcement of the tax laws against the particular individual under audit. For

While the audit and settlement of low income returns is cost efficient to the Service, there is substantial doubt that the same holds true for the taxpayer. For example, if we assume a sustension rate of 70 percent on an average deficiency of $150, the average benefit to a taxpayer of contesting the matter is but $45. While such an average may indicate that, on the whole, appeal of such cases is not justified, the average is made up of a number of individuals who owe no deficiency at all. However, without representation and advice, the unrepresented taxpayer cannot appropriately estimate the merits of his case.

Furthermore, the $45 average benefit from appeal may well be less than the cost of getting commercial or professional assistance to pursue the appeal.

This kind of cost-benefit analysis must indicate to the taxpayer that appeal is at least a questionable avenue. He also knows his return is not likely much, if any, more inaccurate than his neighbor's whose return was not subjected to audit. Thus, from the taxpayer's viewpoint he is simply a victim of the enforcement system; he is no more, and many times less, "guilty" than other taxpayers who do not fall into the enforcement net. 

In general where society has been concerned with law enforcement, there have been increasing efforts to provide assistance to those against whom the law is being enforced. Taxpayer assistance in the Audits and Settlements appeals processes probably should be provided primarily in classes of cases where revenue raising is subordinated to the enforcement mission, rather than in cases where the primary objective is to raise additional revenue. 

While we believe that the foregoing discusses some of the issues bearing on the definition of those who qualify for public assistance, we realize that it is imprecise. However, a workable line might be drawn by the Congress or the Service with these thoughts in mind. Until the question is more exhaustively approached, we suggest that taxpayers subjected to office and correspondence audits, not involving issues relating to business or substantial investment income, should be accorded assistance. Perhaps an adjusted gross income level could be applied in conjunction with the suggested criteria.

8/ For example, Commissioner Donald C. The Service's measure is amazingly precise and mechanistic. The degree of voluntary compliance is stated as: "1

taxes reported on all returns filed taxes reported on all returns filed plus proposed assessments after audit of TCMP quality A slight variation of this formula is a numerator of taxes reported on all returns which are audited over a denominator of taxes on all such returns plus recommended assessments. 

9/ Both 'voluntary' and 'compliance' are highly agreeable terms. Voluntary suggests lack of coercion, but may also indicate an eagerness or willingness which may not exist where over 80 percent of all individual income taxes are paid through involuntary wage withholding. A large part of the balance may be paid because penalties and possibly incarceration will follow if not paid. Is conduct designed to avoid such consequences voluntary? Compliance is also an agreeable state, but it undoubtedly means different things to different persons. See supra note 8. To others it may mean an effort to the best of one's ability to compute the proper tax. Or, perhaps it means a return indicating the least possible tax after resolving all doubtful questions of fact and law against the government. Perhaps the converse where all doubtful questions of fact and law are resolved against the taxpayer is compliance. What of unintentional errors? What of carelessness? The term thus allows the perceiver of it to conjure up his own definition, and since both voluntary and compliance are agreeable words, the perceiver's image is likely to be agreeable.

38/ TCMP results and inferences therefrom reflect the compliance charac teristics of each income class on a national basis. Though the ideal would be to develop data particularized to the smallest meaningful geographical unit, we are told that the cost of such data accumulation would be great. Consequently, returns selected for audit under a DIF formula, which in turn relies on TCMP data, are manually reviewed to determine their audit potential in light of regional and district peculiarities. 

The size of each sample is determined by a statistics committee under the auspices of the Assistant Commissioner (Planning and Research), well as others throughout the Service, including Audit. The Audit staff engaged in the sample selection has no line authority over the agents who perform the audits, but it does monitor the quality of the audits, which by their nature are substantially more intensive than an ordinary audit.

140/ The Internal Revenue Code restricts the Service to one necessary inspection of the taxpayer's books (an audit is not necessarily an inspection of books and records) for any one given taxable year, unless the taxpayer is notified of the need to make an additional examination. 

IRC, S 7605 (b). The sole purpose of this section is not to limit repeated audits, but rather, to shift the discretion for their pursuit from field to higher management personnel. U. S. v. Powell, 379 U.S. 48, 54-55 (1964). Case law indicates that this provision is not much of a legal impediment to re-opening. See, e.g., U. S. v. Dawson, 400 F.2d 194 (2d 

Cir. 1968); Cole v. U. S., 342 F.2d 5 (2d Cir. 1965), cert. denied, 387 

U.S. 941; Donaldson v. U. S., 400 U.S. 517 (1971); Hinchcliff v. Clarke, 371 F.2d 697 (6th Cir. 1962); Harris v. U. S., 413 F.2d 316 (9th Cir. 

1968); U. S. v. Gross, 416 F.2d 1205 (8th Cir. 1969); U. S. v. Bank of

Commerce, 405 F.2d 931 (3rd Cir. 1969); Narragansett Wire Co. v. 

Commissioner, 32 T. C. Memo 643 (1972); Adams v. Commissioner, 26 T.C. 

Memo 1098 (1967); Geurkink v. U. S., 354 F.2d 629 (7th Cir. 1965); U. s. v. Pledger, 409 F.2d 1335 (5th Cir. 1969); McDonnell v. Commissioner, 6 B.T.A. 685 (1927); U. S. v. Giordano, 419 F.2d 564 (8th Cir. 1969);

U. S. v. Bell, 448 F.2d 40 (9th Cir. 1971); U. S. v. Delva, 73-1 T.C. 

9390 (1973); U. S. v. Nashban, 73-2 OCH U.S.T.C. 1 9567 (1973).

However, Service policy is not to re-open a case to make an unfavorable adjustment unless (1) there is evidence of fraud, malfeasance, collusion, concealment, or misrepresentation of a material fact; or (2) the prior closing involved a clearly defined substantial error based on an established Service position existing at the time of the previous examination; or (3) other circumstances exist which indicate failure to re-open would be a serious administrative omission. Rev. Proc. 74-5, 1974-1 Cum. Bull. 416. These criteria are expanded in the Internal Revenue Manual where the 

Service defines "serious administrative amission" as follows: "Serious Administrative Omission 

This criteria covers situations in which failure to reopen closed cases could: (a) Result in serious criticism of the Service's administration of the tax laws. (b) Establish a precedent that would seriously hamper subsequent attempt by the Service to take corrective action. (c) Result in inconsistent treatment of similarly situated taxpayers who have relatively free access to knowledge as to how the Service treated items on other taxpayers' returns." 

Int. Rev. Manual, S 4023.5(1).

267/ When an agreement results in an assessment of tax deficiency, the settlement document reflecting such accession will be either Form 870 or 

Form 870-AD.

By signing Form 870, the taxpayer waives certain restrictions on the assessment and collection of a tax deficiency by the Service. It is utilized at the district office level, as well as the Appellate level in those cases where only the taxpayer makes a concession. Thus, it concludes a case only in the practical sense of providing a plateau for consideration of further possible alternative action by either party. Professor 

Chammie describes its background and use as follows: "Under section 6212 of the Code the Service is required to send the taxpayer a written notice of deficiency (90-day letter). Section 6213 prohibits the assessment or collection of the deficiency for

90 days during which time the taxpayer may file a petition with the Tax Court for redetermination of the deficiency which action further stays assessment and collection. However, under section 6213 (d) the taxpayer may waive his right to a deficiency notice and consequent immunity from assessment collection during the 90-day period. Thus, if the taxpayer executes Form 870: (1) the Service may assess and collect the deficiency at once without sending the statutory notice (90-day letter), and (2) the taxpayer is precluded from litigating the proposed deficiency in the Tax Court. The waiver stops the running of interest 30 days after it is signed if the Service does not serve notice and demand for payment within that period. It does not prevent the taxpayer from filing a claim for refund after payment of the tax, nor from litigating in the District Court or the Court of Claims if the claim is denied. versely, the waiver does not prevent further assessment of deficiencies by the Service." 

J. Chommie, Federal Income Taxation 889 (1973).

Con- Form 870-AD is an agreement between the taxpayer and the Appellate Division, and is generally one on which mutual concessions are made. 

Thus, it imparts a much more final resolution than Form 870. It is described by Professor Chommie as follows: 

"The Service views Form 870-AD as an offer of settlement from the taxpayer. It regards its acceptance as precluding a subsequent claim for refund by the taxpayer because of the rights given up by the Service, especially when a claim is filed too late for the Service to retaliate with a deficiency. However, although the cases are by no means consistent, the majority of the courts have not regarded a Form 870-AD as a final determination, and either party may disregard the attempt to preclude the filing of a refund claim or the assertion of a deficiency. 

These courts, taking their lead from the Supreme

Court, view sections 7121 (closing agreements) and 7122 (offers in compromise) as providing the exclusive means of settling tax disputes by contract. 

Section 7121, for example, authorizes the Service to enter into a final closing agreement regarding

specific items or a specific tax liability. Such agreements bind both the taxpayer and the Revenue Service as to the items covered in the agreement in the absence of fraud, malfeasance, or mutual mistake.

Thus, a taxpayer may not thereafter bring a suit for a refund as to items contained therein nor may the Service assert a deficiency thereon. 

Id. at 893. not on all. "Occasionally agreement can be reached on some issues but .Under these circumstances a partial agreement. . . [must] .be used. . .limiting the pledges against reopening to the settled issues." Int. Rev. Manual, SS 8821 (1) and (2), MT 8800-16 (2-23-73).

Further, ". . .where settlement is reached but the taxpayer wishes to reserve his right to one or more issues and no weight was given to the reserved issue in the settlement [,]. . . [i]f a Form 870-AD is used it is essential that the agreement reflect the complete and exact understanding of the parties." Id. at § 8822 (1) & (2).

If you want to pay now, make your check or money order payable to the Internal Revenue Service and send it with your signed request for correction. 

If you do not agree, please give your reasons on the back of this letter. Also attach any other explanatory material which you may wish to present and send all of this information to the address shown above. If the explanation is satisfactory, your return will be accepted without change. If the explanation is not satisfactory, you will be advised by letter of the proposed tax change and of your appeal rights. 

We would like to complete the processing of your return as soon as possible, so please let us hear from you within the next 15 days. 

A self-addressed envelope is enclosed for your convenience. The copy of this letter is for your records. 

Thank you for your cooperation.

Dear Taxpayer:

We are examining your Federal income tax return for the above year(s) and find we need additional information to verify your correct tax. We have, therefore, scheduled the above appointment for you. If you filed a joint return, either husband or wife may keep the appointment.

We would appreciate your bringing to our office the records you used as a basis for the items checked at the end of this letter so we can discuss them with you. 

The enclosed Information Guides will help you decide what records to bring. 

It will save you time if you keep together the records related to each item. 

Please bring this letter also.

Taxpayers are required by law to substantiate all information reported on their returns when requested. If you do not keep this appointment and do not arrange another, we will have to proceed on the basis of the information we have. 

About the examination and your appeal rights-- We realize some taxpayers may be concerned about an examination of their tax returns. We hope we can relieve any concern you may have by briefly explaining why we examine, what our procedures are, and what your appeal rights are if you do not agree with the results. 

We examine returns to verify income, exemptions, and deductions. This does not always result in more tax due, nor does the selection of your return for examination imply dishonesty or suspicion of criminal liability. In many cases, the taxpayer's return is accepted as filed or he gets a refund. We are required to collect only the correct tax-no more and no less. But if taxpayers do not substantiate items when requested, we have to act on available information that may be incomplete. That is why your cooperation is so important. 

We will go over your return and records and then explain any proposals to change your tax liability. We want you to understand fully any recommended increase 12 721

or decrease in your tax, so please don't hesitate to ask questions about anything not clear to you.

If changes are recommended and you agree with the proposals, we will ask you to sign an agreement form. By signing, you will indicate your agreement to the amount shown on the form as additional tax you owe or as a refund due you and simplify closing your case.

Most people agree with our proposals, and we believe this is because they find our examiners to be fair. But you don't have to agree. If you choose, we can easily arrange for you to have your case given further consideration. You need only tell the examiner you want to discuss the issue informally with a supervisor, and a conference will be arranged immediately. If this discussion does not result in agreement, you may take your case to a conferee for still further consideration. In addition to these District office appeal rights, you may request the Service's Appellate Division, which is separate from the District office, to consider your case. We will be glad to explain this procedure and also how to appeal outside the Service to the courts.

We will also be happy to furnish you a copy of our Publication 556, Audit of Returns, Appeal Rights and Claims for Refund, which explains in detail our procedures covering examinations of tax returns and appeal rights. You can get a copy of this publication by writing us for it or by asking for it when you come to our office. 

Your appointment is the next step. We will consider the appointment confirmed if we do not hear from you at least seven days before the scheduled date. We will make our examination as pleasant and brief as possible and will welcome any questions you raise. 

Please contact us if you have any questions. Thank you for your cooperation.
