CHAPTER COLLECTION OF DELINQUENT TAXES INTRODUCTION 

The collection of taxes is a sine qua non of a nation's existence. 

Without revenues, it could not amass the manpower or resources necessary to shield itself from famine, pestilence, ignorance, or other dangers both natural and man-made. Being so essential, our tax-gathering mechanism invites close scrutiny. 

The Internal Revenue Service which is that mechanism, performs a task of stupendous scale it collected over $250 billion in fiscal 1974 from over 100 million taxpayers to which the public is uniquely sensitized. 

Given the speed and impersonality which this mission requires, the number of complaints voiced is remarkably few. The number of valid complaints is fewer still.

This report focuses on what in percentages is a small problem, but which in absolute numbers is large: that of taxpayers who fail to pay their taxes when they become due. In 1973, the Internal Revenue Service had an inventory of several million delinquent accounts amounting to more than $3.1 billion. Experience suggests that the Service eventually will collect the great bulk of these delinquent taxes. For example, in 1973 the six-year statute of limitations on collection action ran on only $83 million in delinquent tax accounts. If we assume that all those accounts arose in 1967, we find that the Service permitted less than .05 percent of assessments to go stale and that all but 2.5 percent of the delinquent accounts were collected. 

Such success, even when measured by this overly simplified technique, would (211)

be the envy of any commercial collection service. 

This success seems due to many factors. Primarily, many delinquent taxpayers sincerely want to liquidate their debts; the Service's procedures for encouraging voluntary compliance may be very effective; and the Service uses its Congressionally endowed, and very potent, forcible collection tools when the tax debtor is perceived to be unreasonably balky. 

Although it conferred drastic collection powers upon the Service, Congress has done little to guide their use, and the manner in which they are exercised is sometimes troublesome. We have for the most part limited our study of such facets of the delinquent tax collection process wherein real or imagined problems exist. As a result, much of what follows is critical in tone. One should not infer from the tone, however, that the Service does a "bad" job in collecting taxes forcibly or otherwise. Rather, the problems discussed are difficult to resolve, and we have attempted to examine the factors which raise difficulties. 

Many of the problems considered arise from the immense discretion with which Collection officials are endowed. This discretion is not always uniformly exercised. The unevenness is not surprising, for the Service is caught in a cross-fire. On the one side, it has a Congressional mandate to collect taxes, forcibly if need be. That is hardly a mission calculated to win friends, but the Service also has a need to accomplish its task without injury or damage to anyone. These goals may be mutually inconsistent. 

For Revenue Officers they are often irreconcilable. The forcible powers are necessary, however, and as a general proposition the uneven usage of the powers is preferable to any Congressional diminution of them. But a greater effort

should be made to channel the exercise of this potent authority. 

Finally, the report examines the agency's objectives and its evaluation process, both of which seem relevant in light of the considerable discretion granted to Collection officials to choose collection methods. 

The report is again critical, particularly in considering the evaluation process. While top management has attempted to install a subjective evaluation system, there is strong evidence that it is unworkable for, if not unwanted by, many line management personnel. Much of this seems due to the nature of the Collection official's job, which lends itself to easy quantification and thus to non-subjective evaluation. It is unclear whether an alternative system of subjective evaluation may be devised, however, and development of such a system would probably necessitate the appropriation of additional resources by Congress. It should be borne in mind, however, that subjective may be no better than objective evaluation because, in effect, a subjective evaluation is the same as discretionary evaluation.

The drastic powers vested in the Service for the collection of delinquent taxes and the general misunderstanding of those powers by the public have combined to nurture many "horror stories" in which delinquent taxpayers are alleged to have been unjustly harassed or injured. Having no powers to subpoena records or to swear witnesses, and not having access to tax return information, we have not investigated the alleged abuses which came to our attention. We have, rather, reviewed the Service's tax collection procedures with, among other things, an eye to whether such "horror stories" have possible foundation.

The procedures discussed are those existing as of May 1, 1975.

A. 

I. THE COLLECTION PROCESS Structure of the Collection Division. 

Very generally, the Internal Revenue Service is partitioned along functional lines. One such function is collection of delinquent accounts and securing of delinquent returns. As will be seen, however, same offices which are responsible for these duties also carry on several other broad functions which are intertwined with collection activities. Viewed vertically, the division of functional responsibility for the collection effort is fourtiered: authority filters down from the national to the regional to the district and Service Center levels. Each of these tiers will be discussed in turn. 

1. National Office. 

As the chief executive of the Service, the Commissioner has ultimate responsibility for its policies and operations. His principal assistant in matters pertaining to the collection of delinquent taxes and securing of delinquent tax returns is the Assistant Commissioner (Accounts, Collection and Taxpayer Service) or (ACTS), who has line responsibility for 1/ ACTS national office personnel, the National Computer Center, and the 2/ 3/ National Data Center. He has functional responsibility for all other 

ACTS missions, which include data processing, collection and processing of tax and information returns, handling of remittances, and rendering assistance to taxpayers. He has two advisory groups. The Program Planning and 

Review Staff provides a continuing evaluation and overview of ACTS programs through analytic and statistical appraisals and is concerned with budgetary and policy matters, resource allocations, and long-range objectives.

The balance of the ACTS national office staff is split along the line of its general functions into three divisions: Accounts and Data Processing, Taxpayer Service, and Collection. The last of these coordinates the IRS collection effort. General functional responsibility for development of nationwide programs to encourage the timely filing of returns and payment of tax is vested in.its Director. Implementation of these programs is, however, the prerogative of the Commissioner and, eventually, others at the local level in the chain of command. 4/ Distinct program management responsibilities for the Division's functional supervision are in turn held by each of the Collection Division's three branches. Each branch participates in the development of policies and procedures for inclusion in the Collection portion of the Internal Revenue Manual, the principal guidebook for Collection employees. The Operations 

Branch exercises functional supervision of the collection of unpaid accounts, acceptance of some offers in compromise, and investigation of the nature and causes of tax delinquencies. The Technical Branch provides guidance and support for collection programs. The Management Resources and 

Analysis Branch collects and analyzes quantifiable data relating to collection activities. It also exercises a wide-ranging authority over work planning and control within the Collection Division and serves as liaison to other divisions in outlining informational and training needs of the Collection Division.

2. Regional Offices. 

The seven regional offices across the country 5/ are headed by Regional Commissioners whose responsibility is to see that the policies and programs enunciated by the national office are effectuated in the districts comprising the region. The Regional Commissioners may establish standards and procedures within their own regions to implement the directives of the national office. They have command authority over the District Directors to assure that efforts are properly directed toward accomplishing national program objectives. 

The Regional Commissioner's chief advisors are six Assistant

Regional Commissioners (ARC's). The ARC (ACTS) exercises functional authority over, and evaluates programs for, the collection of delinquent accounts and securing of delinquent returns, as well as data processing, revenue accounting, and taxpayer service activities. He is assisted in these tasks by a staff of analysts who gather and analyze information for his benefit. 

The ARC (ACTS), in turn, keeps the Regional Commissioner advised on the status of ACTS programs and recommends adjustments he perceives to be necessary for heightening performance. In addition, the regional office serves as the primary source of empirical data on which the national office staff may judge the efficacy of programs to collect delinquent taxes and secure delinquent tax returns. 

3. The District Offices. 

The United States is partitioned into 58 revenue districts; another, the Office of International Operations, handles internal revenue

matters outside the United States. Each revenue district is headed by a 

District Director, who is responsible for audit, intelligence, taxpayer service, administration, and collection activities within the district. 

The district's organization is along these functional lines, with a chief being in charge of each division. While some districts combine responsibility for collection and taxpayer service in one division, they are now separate in the large districts. The district Collection Division is com prised of an Office Branch, Field Branches, and Special Procedures Branch, each of which is supervised by a Branch Chief who reports to the Division Chief. 

a. Office Branch. 

Delinquent accounts and returns requiring a district's attention are referred to it by a Service Center in the form of a Taxpayer 6/ 

Delinquent Account (TDA) or Taxpayer Delinquent Investigation (TDI). 

After receipt in a district office, the TDA or TDI is screened by the Office Branch, which tries to secure tax-payment or return-filing by telephone, office interviews, correspondence, or limited personal contact with taxpayers, and, for TDA's, by possibly filing liens or serving levies. It receives, accounts for, and forwards to the Service Center remittances and returns obtained by the district office.

The Office Branch is composed of Analysis, Contact, and Computer 

Services Sections.

Each is under the direction of a supervisor who reports to the Branch Chief. The Analysis Section is staffed by Processing Clerks 

(GS-3, $6,764-$8,789) and Processing Reviewers (GS-4 and GS-5, $7,596- $11,047) and Research and Adjustment Examiners (GS-4 through GS-7, $7,596-

$13,679), who initially handle incoming cases by correspondence, research, and the imposition of liens and levies. The Contact Section is staffed with 

Office Collection Representatives (GS-4 through GS-7, $7,596-$13,679) who handle taxpayer telephone calls and interviews as well as certain correspondence or lien cases requiring the touch of more experienced personnel. 

In large districts, the Contact Section may be split into an Interview Section, containing Office Collection Representatives, and a Revenue Representative Section composed of Revenue Representatives (GS-4 through GS-6, $7,596-$12,317) who combine the duties of Office Collection Representatives with field work such as filing of liens, assisting Revenue Officers in making seizures, contacting taxpayers on small dollar cases, and attempting to locate taxpayers who have moved. The Computer Services Section provides data input to and retrieval from the Integrated Data Retrieval System 7/ (IDRS) concerning the status of delinquent accounts and returns being processed by the District Office. It is staffed by Remote Terminal Operators (GS-4, $7,596-$9,873) and Remittance Clerks (GS-5, $8,500-$10,764) and clerical support personnel. In small districts, the Analysis and Camputer Services Sections are combined. 

A few Districts do not have an Office Branch. Its functions are instead performed by an Office Group folded into a Field Branch. The organization and staffing of such groups is similar to that of an Office Branch. 

If not satisfactorily concluded, the TDA or TDI is referred to the 

Field Branch.

b. Field Branch. 

The Field Branch is divided into groups of Revenue Of ficers (RO's), and in some cases Office Groups, covering certain geographic areas or case types. Each Revenue Officer Group is under the guidance of a 

Group Manager. While the journeyman level is GS-9 ($12,841-$16,693), Revenue Officers range in grade from GS-5 ($8,500-$11,047) to GS-12 ($17,463- $23,998). There is budget authorization for 55 percent of Revenue Officer positions to be staffed at the GS-11 and GS-12 levels. 

The purpose of the Field Branch is to handle those cases which present practical, procedural, or legal complexity. Line personnel in this branch, known as Revenue Officers, are endowed with enormous powers. All those given to Processing Reviewers, Office Collection Representatives, and Revenue Representatives are conferred on Revenue Officers, along with powers to seize and sell assets, to assess certain penalties, to recommend jeopardy assessments and various lawsuits, and to perform other functions too extensive to list. The more complicated lien-filing questions, as well as issues involving the subordination and discharge of Federal tax liens, are also examined by Revenue Officers for recommendation to the Special Procedures Staff,

In addition, Field Branch personnel also render determinations on taxpayer 8/ offers in compromise. Same of these functions require substantial expertise or experience and therefore are assigned to specific individuals who handle them on a district or office-wide basis. This is especially true of offers in compromise and cases involving very large liabilities.

c. Special Procedures Staff. 

The Special Procedures Staff furnishes technical assis- It reviews seizures and sales, tance to the other segments of Collection. accounts reported as not collectible, and actions on offers in compromise based on inability to pay. It processes and evaluates recommendations on civil suits, applications for discharge, subordination, or release of Federal tax liens, and certain penalty and transferee assessments. Advice is also rendered on suitability of escrow arrangements and sufficiency of collateral to ensure collection of the revenue. Finally, the Special Procedures Staff has responsibility for processing civil suits against the District Director and filing proofs of claim in matters of decedents' or insolvent estates. 4.

The Service Centers. 

9/ There are ten Service Centers located around the nation to perform data processing work for the regions and districts. Each of the 

Service Centers is headed by a Director, who reports to the Regional Com- 10/ missioner having jurisdiction over the districts served by the Center. 

Service Centers are data processing centers which account for returns, information documents, and payments of all kinds. Data collated by a Service Center are transferred to computer tapes which are then sent to Martinsburg, West Virginia, where the National Computer Center (NCC) 11/ maintains the "Master Files." On the basis of new data put into the 

Master Files, new tapes are made concerning accounts which are expected to produce problems. These new tapes are returned to the Service Centers and

update the files of the Integrated Data Retrieval System (IDRS). 

The Service Center also conducts initial attempts to resolve delinquent accounts through correspondence with the taxpayer. It processes taxpayer responses, which may be in the form of payments; or mail or telephone inquiries; or requests for abatement of the tax, interest, or penalties. 

It also verifies and puts into IDRS information arriving from district offices regarding accounts being worked in the field.

B. The Collection of Delinquent Individual Income Taxes (IMF Procedures). 

We turn now to the collection of delinquent individual income taxes. Business accounts, such as withheld Social Security and employee income taxes, are dealt with later. 

Most individual income tax returns are filed between January and April 15 of each year. In 1973 there were 77,726,625 such returns filed. 

Some 2,960,303 of these showed an unpaid balance due, and an additional 1,634,382 revealed a balance due after some form of review by the Service 12/ 

There were then 4,594,685 (such as the computer's mathematical check). returns which indicated further action for full payment. This further action is described below. 1.

Returns Processing. 

The Service prefers that returns be filed with Service Centers and provides a pre-addressed envelope for mailing the Form 1040 to the proper Service Center. The Service Center has its so-called "peak filing season" during February, March, and April when tens (and sometimes hundreds) of 13/ thousands of these returns arrive each day. Without regard to the number pouring in, the Service Centers are allotted no more than 16 working days to transcribe data from returns to the magnetic tapes used to update the National Computer Center's Master Files. This makes it necessary for the 

Service Centers nearly to double their staffing with seasonal employees during the first four months of the year.

Returns processing is commenced by segregating incoming envelopes by district into trays holding several hundred envelopes apiece. The envelopes

are then put through a device which slits them lengthwise. After reloading onto the tray, the envelopes are stored in great metal racks in order of the date received. There they remain until moved to a clerk's desk where their contents are removed and sorted, stapled together, and placed in stacks, e.g., 1040's with payment, 1040's without payment, Form 941's with payment, Form 941's without payment, and so on. Periodically these stacks of each classification are collected and measured by weight into "batches" consisting of several score returns. Each batch is numbered. Several batches make up a "block" which is also numbered and given a set of prepunched computer cards. 

These are then detached at various points in the processing to enable management to monitor progress of the batches through the "pipeline." 

Returns are then examined, batch by batch, to ascertain whether they have been signed and are legibly completed and whether accompanying checks are signed and can be properly credited to the taxpayer's account. 

Even though there is no Social Security number, the return will be processed; if there is also an amount due, a request for the Social Security information will be sent along with the bill. In the absence of a signature the return is treated as filed, if an attached check is signed by the party or parties who filed the return, on the theory that the return has been constructively signed. But if there is no check, the return is sent back for signature without further processing. 

The Social Security number (or Employer Identification Number, or other identifying data) on the return, the balance shown as due, and payment, if any, are transcribed to computer tape through the Direct Data Entry System

(DDES), a computer keyboard. To minimize the chances of error, the same information is entered again by a different transcriber, and the computer compares the second transcription to the first. If the information is thus verified, the information is transferred to tape bound for the NCC. 

Payments are double checked to ensure that they balance; then they are forwarded to banks for deposit and collection. National office guidelines require that payments be forwarded for deposit within seven working days of receipt.

After returns with payments have gone through the balancing process, they are now reunited with the flow of non-remittance returns. They are then examined for prima facie errors in arithmetic and preparation, e.g., use of the wrong tax tables or claims of pets as dependents. The returns are "coded and edited" by an examiner and assigned a Document Locator Number (DIN) by which they can be readily found. The coded material is transcribed and entered into a computer which checks the arithmetic. If there is inaccuracy, the document becomes an "error register return" which drops out of the pipeline process and is shunted to the Input Perfection Branch. Errors in the return (or in processing, if the error originated in the Service Center) are there resolved through validity checks, and the correction (if any) goes anto tape bound for the National Computer Center for posting to the Master File. If the mistake or amission is such that data cannot be entered, the taxpayer is notified by mail and requested to assist in resolving the problem. 

The Input Perfection Branch also handles remittances or returns which are "unpostable," that is, they cannot be identified for crediting to any account.

Each day's Service Center transactions are placed on magnetic tapes and mailed to Martinsburg for addition to the Master Files. Returns are verified against a tape of Social Security numbers, and return data credited to a given number are placed on the Master File with return information for that number from previous years. All accounts in the Master 

File are thus updated, and new modules are created if necessary. From 14/ this updated Master File, a new tape is made for each Service Center, reflecting new assessments, credits, tax return corrections, and other relevant information concerning taxpayers in that Service Center's assigned geographical area. New tapes are sent to Service Centers at the end of each week. The procedure of sending tapes to the NCC, updating the Master 

File, and returning new tapes covers five to nine working days. The whole process, from the time the return arrived at the Service Center to receipt of the updated tape, has taken from 16 to 25 working days. 

Such information on the NCC tapes which relates to accounts of taxpayers expected to have reason to contact the Service is relayed back to the Service Center computers. Most of these potentially active accounts will represent receivables and suspected non-filers, though same reflect credits for taxpayers whom IRS cannot locate to refund tax overpayments. 

During the course of the year, taxpayer account information, such as the collection of delinquent taxes, will flow from the IDRS networks to the NCC. Many accounts will be resolved and thus removed from IDRS. The histories of these accounts remain in the NCC, however, which continues reporting new problem accounts to the Service Centers as its computer becomes aware of them. 77-842 O 76 16

2. Notices to Pay the Tax. 

a. The Schedule of Notices. 

Once it has its weekly update from the NCC, the Service Center computer prints out notices to be mailed to those taxpayers whose accounts now show a balance due. Depending upon the type of account, dollar criteria, and background of the taxpayer, as many as four different notices may be mailed over a period of weeks. amounts 

When printed, the taxpayer's initial notice is postdated by approximately one week to permit some -- mostly those reflecting large dollar to be screened at the Service Center for error in the data processing routine, programming, or printing. Once past this review, the notices are deposited in the mail. In 1973 initial notices concerning $1,629,663,658 16/ of delinquent taxes were mailed to same 3,861,855 individual taxpayers.

17/ In routine matters, the first notice alerts the taxpayer to the existence of a balance due on his account, plus interest and penalties, if any, and advises the taxpayer to return the notice with proper information if his records are at variance with those of the Service. The notice requests payment by a date stated in the notice if there is in fact a balance due. 

A window envelope is provided in order that the taxpayer's response (which he is requested to write on a duplicate of the notice provided for that purpose) will be directed to the Service Center.

If the taxpayer does not respond, or if for some reason further 18/ notices to him are not halted despite a response, a second notice is sent after five more weeks. This notice reminds the taxpayer of the first notice, advises that he "should pay [the tax] within 10 days of the date of 15/

19/ this letter to avoid additional interest and penalty charges," and lists the accrued interest and late payment penalties. He is directed to make payment to the Service Center. Enclosed with the notice is a stuffer 20/ which notifies the taxpayer how to obtain an IRS publication explaining the Service's procedures and taxpayer rights with respect to unpaid taxes.

21/ Still a third notice follows after another three weeks if the account has not been satisfied and the delinquency exceeds a threshold minimum dollar amount or "tolerance level." Delinquencies below this amount are "deferred" for later action that is discussed elsewhere in this report. If issued, the third notice reminds the taxpayer, "the tax is overdue and you should pay it within the next 10 days to avoid additional interest and penalty charges, and enforced collection action." There is a warning that the liability may be collected through imposition of liens, levies, and seizures of the taxpayer's assets. Again, payment is to be directed to the Service Center.

Eleven weeks after the first notice (and up to 17 weeks after the return arrived at the Service Center), the taxpayer who has been silent re- 22/ This warns the taxpayer that payceives a "Final Notice Before Seizure. ment must be made quickly, "[o] therwise, 10 days after the date of this letter and with no further notice to you, any salary or wages due you will be levied upon by serving a notice of levy on your employer. Bank accounts, receivables, commissions or other income, property or rights to property belonging to you may also be seized."

The recipient is urged to respond to the appropriate local office, the address of which is provided in the letter. All four notices have been generated by computer.

If a balance-due condition exists on the account three weeks after the mailing of the fourth and final notice to the taxpayer, a Taxpayer Delinquent Account will be printed by the Service Center computer and mailed The TDA serves as a memo to the district office to the field office. 23/ that the case is now its responsibility.

In 1973 same 853,359 TDA's were 24/ issued on individual tax liabilities totalling $856,384,832.

b. 

Comments on Notices to Pay Taxes. 

(1) Taxpayer Response. 

Obviously, not all delinquent taxpayers receive four notices. Full payment may be made in response to an early notice and the account module will be removed from IDRS, which generates the notices. other cases, the taxpayer may contact the Service Center or a local office, claiming to have made full payment. The account can be "frozen" (i.e., further notices to the taxpayer are halted) while Service personnel test the 25/ taxpayer's assertion. Such research usually consists of an interrogation of the Service Center computer to ascertain whether payment has been posted to the system. If the taxpayer's assertion cannot be verified with a "pay- 26/ ment tracer," or if the claimed credit will not extinguish his liability, a TDA is generated without further notice to the taxpayer. It will reflect that the account had previously been "frozen," and from this it may be inferred by a Collection employee that the taxpayer previously contacted IRS. 

Also, the taxpayer may respond to the third or earlier notice by payment to the Service Center. If for some reason there is delay in posting, 27/ the TDA may be issued and followed by levy despite previous payment.

But they i.e., sent

Such occurrences appear to be rare, because the length of time between issuance of a non-final notice and the TDA is usually substantial. do occur, probably most generally where the TDA is "accelerated, to the local office after fewer notices than in the routine case. discuss "accelerated" accounts later in this report. (2) Taxpayer Unresponsiveness. 

We will

Some taxpayers appear indifferent to the notices. 

Some discard the missives without opening them. Others may, however, read them and do nothing, perhaps through fear, ignorance, or impecuniousness. 

Whatever, upon arrival of the fourth notice, a naive taxpayer will expect the Service to act forcibly in ten days. Yet, in the routine case, no collection action will be taken for several weeks, if ever. The TDA will not be issued for three weeks from the time of the last notice, and the local office will probably require at least a week or ten days to get to the TDA. 

It may or may not take forcible action to collect the unpaid balance. 

Failure by the Service to act on its warnings seems to cause two problems, particularly among individual income taxpayers who are generally 28/ viewed by IRS line personnel as being unsophisticated about the tax law. 

First, it may create an indifference to subsequent threats even when made by telephone or by personal contact. Second, when the eleventh day after the final notice passes, the taxpayer may believe the levy period has passed. 

When levy then occurs, say two months later, the taxpayer may be surprised 29/ and angry and may believe that he has been treated unjustly. Incorrect though the taxpayer's belief may be the Service will have unnecessarily 30/

aggravated a sensitized situation. This has serious implications for a taxing system which depends on voluntary compliance with the laws. 

(3) Repeater Delinquents. 

The Service views "repeaters," i.e., those who have previously been delinquent, less sympathetically than those who are first timers. Obviously, the repeater is no longer unaware of the length of the tax collection process and may be inclined to put off payment for as long as the system allows. Thus, the possibility of using different notices for repeaters is under consideration by the Service. First time delinquents could receive more gently worded reminders, while repeaters would receive more harshly worded ones, or fewer of them. 

(4) Two Views of Notices. 

The general efficacy of notices in producing fullpaid accounts is sometimes less than crystal clear, although each notice does produce a new crop of payments. Notices are generally effective in resolving accounts which show a balance due resulting from adjustment at the Service Center. During 1973, for example, over 86 percent of such cases in- 31/ volving Form 1040's were settled as a result of one notice. The Service was evidently unsuccessful, as a general rule, in precipitating payments through notices when the 1040 contained an admission of a balance due, however. 

While the Service possesses some helpful statistics on the effect of computer-generated notices for years prior to 1975, ACTS management is hopeful that programming difficulties have been sufficiently overcame to allow compilation of more accurate data this year. Even after complete tabulations are

developed, however, it seems likely that there will be healthy disagreement within the Service over the optimum number of notices to be sent on delinquent accounts. Some, especially data processing experts, would prefer to have more. Cost of collection by notice is low and thus viewed favorably. Another opinion, held principally by officials on the Collection side of ACTS, is that four notices encourage indifference in payment habits and detract from voluntary compliance with the requirements of law. The mailing of four notices in the routine Individual Master File (IMF) account appears to be a compromise between these two points of view. However, we do not know if some other scheme would be more or less effective, whether in terms of cost of collection or of voluntary compliance with the payment requirements of the law. 

Pending availability of better statistical data, IRS is still looking to see whether other notice routines can produce more responsiveness from taxpayers. The Collection Division has scheduled a test for the spring of 1975 in which certain district offices will telephone taxpayers at the time of the third notice to request payment or other resolution of the account. It is hoped that the telephone calls will create more and earlier resolutions of balance-due accounts by impressing upon taxpayers the gravity of the situation. The test procedures may certainly be expected to notify those taxpayers who erroneously throw out unopened IRS notices as "junk" mail or as something to be feared. 

3. The Office Branch. 

Unless directed to the contrary, the Service Center computer 32/ for any delinquency will automatically print a Taxpayer Delinquent Account

above the tolerance level. Just as with the mailing of notices, the issuance of the TDA is an automatic result of the time elapsing without payment since initial processing. Since that processing has been more or less as returns 33/ 34/ are received, April 15, and since most returns are received and processed prior to 35/ the 17 to 20 week lag between return filing and TDA issuance ends in July, August, and September when the system literally gushes cases to the district offices. While the number of Service Center processing personnel is adjusted to handle the workflow of the peak filing season, little fluctuation occurs elsewhere. District Collection employees are thus swamped with work at midsummer and autumn, though the introduction of the IDRS system has significantly reduced the "high tide" and, with it, the Service's need for part-time personnel.

Shipments of TDA's arrive from the Service Center once each week by mail in "batches" of several hundred accounts. The TDA's are reviewed for "assignment codes" printed on the TDA form by IDRS. As a result of the taxpayer contacts and levies, a number of accounts may be satisfied. Payments and other adjustments are put directly into IDRS from remote terminals situated at the local office. The documents and receipts which substantiate the inputted data are subsequently forwarded to the Service Center for verification. Those IDA's which are "closed" (IRS jargon for an account which has been satisfied by full payment) are retired to a closed file, which serves as a limited information source on the taxpayer's assets or income streams which may be subject to levy. After being kept for up to two years in the local office, closed TDA's are disposed of or are shipped to Federal Records Centers for storage. 

Those accounts which are not resolved are reviewed at regular intervals by the Processing Reviewer in the hope that the balance due may be collected. The Internal Revenue Manual directs that accounts be reexamined 50/ between 15 to 18 calendar days of the initial review. At that time, in the absence of taxpayer response to written communication from the local office, or if the taxpayer has failed to make good on promises to pay, levy 51/ on liquid assets should be made. A final check with IDRS is to be made through the remote terminal before garnishment: the computer gives the exact balance due on the account (including interest and penalty accruals) so that the levy amount is accurate. Thus, failure to interrogate IDRS might result in levy after the delinquency has been paid. While access to IDRS is limited by occasional breakdowns in the sys- 53/ tem and pressure of workloads, "double collection" of accounts are nonetheless probably rare.

The routine individual account is subjected to two more reviews at 15to 18-day intervals, and those cases which are not yet unraveled are 54/ generally directed by the Manual to be referred to Revenue Officers. 

Transfer to the Field Branch is unnecessary, however, if the matter is simply taking an unusual amount of time to resolve and collection is not jeopardized 55/ by failure to assign the account. It is thus not unusual for the Office 

Branch to retain cases well beyond the two-month period specified in the Manual. Delay in transfer to the Field Branch may occur, for example, when response to a query to the Social Security Administration for a record to a taxpayer's employer is being awaited. Some Office Branches routinely keep relatively low-dollar cases in their own inventories, transferring them to the Field Branch only in special circumstances. 

This procedure is more likely to be followed in large districts which possess Revenue Representatives authorized to do necessary field investigation work which would otherwise have to be performed by a Revenue Officer.

During the fiscal year 1974, Office Branch efforts accounted for 56/ 52 percent of all Taxpayer Delinquent Account dispositions. These were mostly small, simple cases requiring little expertise relative to the majority of cases worked by Revenue Officers. An unwritten, but oft-expressed,

57/ desire at all supervisory levels of the collection function is to close 60 This would reduce the percent of all TDA issuances in the Office Branch. flow of paper going to the Field Branch, enabling Revenue Officers to concentrate their efforts on large liability cases. In addition, closure by the Office Branch tends to reduce the cost of collecting the additional accounts since Office Branch employees are paid much less than Revenue Officers. 

The Collection Division hopes to attain this goal through implementation of improved training and recruiting of personnel, as well as more effective use of IDRS. Installation of IDRS was completed only in late 1973, and the full potentialities of the system are still being unfolded while programming and hardware kinks are straightened. 

4. The Field Branch. 

Those accounts which are beyond resolution by the Office Branch or which are coded by IDRS for immediate referral to a Revenue Officer (RO) are transferred to the Field Branch. As various leads may have been explored before the case arrives on the desk of the Revenue Officer, there is room on the TDA to note the actions by code and date. Separate sheets may also be attached to apprise the Field Branch of what has occurred prior to referral, as well as financial statements and correspondence from the taxpayer. 

Some accounts are not processed by the Office Branch in any way, but are referred directly to the Field Branch upon receipt from the Service Center. These generally present problems requiring considerable field work or special expertise of some kind; for example, insolvent and decedent's estates, penalty assessments against responsible corporate officers for 58/ 59/

60/ suspected nar- 62/ failure to withhold and pay over employee income taxes, 61/ cotics traffickers, and the interest equalization tax. In same districts cases involving taxpayers who have remitted two or more dishonored checks, accumulated large withholding tax liabilities, or refused to pay taxes as a means of protest may be referred directly to Revenue Officers or handled for a brief period only in the Office Branch before referral. 

Upon leaving the Office Branch, Taxpayer Delinquent Accounts are routed to Revenue Officer Group Managers. Some TDA's are coded by IDRS for assignment to specific RO's who are handling other accounts relating to the same taxpayers, but the Group Managers have authority to refer the remaining cases to any member of their groups. IDA's not previously destined for a specific officer are assigned predicted numeric difficulty indicators of "1", "2", or "3" by IDRS on the basis of delinquency size and (sometimes) the nature of the taxpayer to denote that an RO of GS-12, GS-11 or lower rating should initially receive the case. This grade determination is the 63/ primary consideration in assigning the account, and to the extent possible, work predicted as "1" or "2", that is, the most challenging, is given to the most experienced Revenue Officers, while other cases are assigned to RO's whose grade levels are GS-9 or below. Because the case assignment guide preprinted by IDRS is only an estimation of the level of difficulty, Group Managers are instructed to watch progress on cases to ensure that difficulty of the case is commensurate with their subordinates' grade levels by re- 64/ viewing the entire caseload of their groups at least once each year. 

If it is determined that 25 percent of an RO's inventory consists of cases

above or below his difficulty level, the Group Manager is charged with re- 65/ assigning the mismatched work. Some deliberate assignment of higherdifficulty cases is permitted, however, to avoid delay in handling the account, to allow for the geographical location of the taxpayer, or to allow 66/ "developmental" work for Revenue Officers.

Revenue Officers possess the broadest range of authority and discretion among line Collection employees, perhaps in the entire Federal bureaucracy. Possessing all powers enjoyed by Office Branch to collect or abate delinquent accounts, Revenue Officers also have authority to seize and sell property, impose and enforce major penalties for failure to comply with the revenue laws, and recommend compromises of accounts for less than the balance due. Revenue Officers also make the initial recommendation of whether to relieve property from the impact of the Federal tax liens and whether to protect the government's interests by lawsuit or jeopardy assessment. As the following discussion will more fully make clear, the discretion entrusted to Revenue Officers not only covers a broad range of actions, but is sometimes only superficially structured and lightly reviewed. 

These factors make for a great potential for abuse of Revenue Officer powers. 

The Revenue Officer also possesses the fullest range of investigative tools 

far more than available to private bill collectors. One of these is the administrative summons power, by which the RO can compel 67/ taxpayers to open up their books and records to inspection when the taxpayers will not voluntarily do so. 

There are the taxpayer's tax returns, which may be requisitioned from the Service Center or Federal Records Center

68/ for examination; data on levy sources may also sometimes be available from 

IDRS as well. If criminal activity is suspected, the account may be 69/ referred to the Service's Intelligence Division. Nearly every asset the taxpayer owns may be seized by the Revenue Officer with little notice and no prior judicial inquiry into either the validity of the debt 72/ or the existence of reasonable cause for the seizure.

71/ 70/ 

The Federal statu tory protections of property against attachment for debt do not prevail 73/ against the summary collection process of the tax collector. Nor, as a general rule, may the courts enjoin it. 74/ There being an array of collection tools from which to choose and few hard criteria to guide the choice made, Revenue Officers, as well as Revenue Representatives and Interviewers, indicate that their impression of the taxpayer is the single most important factor in determining the course of collection efforts to be taken. Collection personnel often begin with only a TDA, which says nothing about the taxpayer's personal situation (such as the number of his dependents or his income level) to suggest whether the cause of his delinquency is coincident to personal economic misfortune, error in return preparation, or other mitigating circumstances. Indeed, a 

TDA provides nothing more than data from the tax return, the status of the account, and a little of its history. Summary collection action does not fit all taxpayers, say Revenue Officers, a fact which puts a premium on their impressions of the taxpayer.

II. COLLECTION DEVICES 

To this point, we have observed the evolution of a delinquency in tax (whether imposed on taxable income as reported by the individual or as determined by audit) to a Taxpayer Delinquent Account. We have seen that, in the usual case, the Service Center mails to the taxpayer several notices of the balance due. When response from the taxpayer does not resolve the matter, the account is sent as a TDA to one of the 58 district offices or the Office of International Operations. The amount due is then either abated, determined to be uncollectible, or collected in some way by Office Branch personnel or by a Revenue Officer in the Field Branch.

The activities of the Office Branch we observed to be somewhat limited and ministerial. They may be inadequate to resolve the case. If that is so, the matter is referred to a Revenue Officer, who exercises the full range of collection powers. It is to the description of these powers and discussion of their use that we now turn. 77-842 O 76 17

Summary Collection Procedures. 

Pending an adjudicatory hearing,

The Congress has endowed the Internal Revenue Service with formidable power to act summarily to collect or protect the public revenues. 75/ the Service may lien and distrain all property and rights to property belonging to the taxpayer. The exercise of such powers raises a plethora of legal issues, some of which may rise to constitutional significance. 

However, this discussion of summary collection procedures will be confined to a narrow spectrum. Drastic as the summary collection may be and sensitive though the taxpayer may be to its imposition, Congress has provided little direction for when summary powers may or may not be used. The courts have had little to add. Resulting from the legislative and judicial abstention is a large and shapeless body of discretionary authority. We thus will focus on the form which Internal Revenue has imparted to it in the Internal Revenue Manual and the problems posed by the policy decisions made. 

We will also draw on our interviews with Internal Revenue Service personnel and those internal reports and statistical compilations to which the agency granted us access. 

1. Liens. 

a. Statutory Framework. 

Section 6321 of the Internal Revenue Code creates a lien in favor of the United States when a tax liability is assessed against the taxpayer and he "neglects or refuses to pay...after demand." The lien

continues until the liability is satisfied or becomes unenforcible because 76/ It attaches to "all property and rights to property, of lapse of time.

77/ whether real or personal," belonging to the taxpayer, including assets 78/ acquired by the taxpayer after the lien originally arose.

80/ Despite its broad applicability to the taxpayer's property, the lien is not valid as against any purchaser, holder of a security interest, mechanics lienor, or judgment lien creditor until notice of the lien has 79/ been filed. Some other interests have been specifically recognized and protected despite the filing of a lien. There is a long-standing exception for good-faith purchasers of securities and motor vehicles. A filed lien may also be invalid against interests of certain good-faith purchasers of tangible personal property at retail or in a casual sale, property subject to certain possessory liens, real property tax and special assess- 82/ 83/ ment liens, mechanics liens in respect of residential property, cer- 85/ 81/ tain attorney's liens, certain insurance contracts, certain passbook 86/ loans, 84/ 87/ and certain commercial transaction financing agreements. 

The lien must be recorded in the place prescribed by the law of 88/ the state where the property subject to the lien is situated.

Real 89/ property is situated at its physical location. The situs of personal property is, however, deemed to be the residence of the taxpayer at the 90/ time of the filing.

If the taxpayer resides outside of the United 91/ States, he is deemed to be a resident of the District of Columbia. 

The Service is also authorized to diminish the applicability or priority of its encumbrances.

It may release all the taxpayer's property

92/ from the lien 93/ or discharge only some of it under certain circumstances.

94/ The Service may also subordinate its prior tax lien to a junior claim or certify non-attachment of the lien to property of a person other than 95/ the taxpayer. Service. b. Perfecting and Preserving the Government's Claim 

(1) Filing the Notice of Lien. 

The lien is created when the taxpayer, upon demand by the Service, neglects or refuses to pay the tax. The impact of the creation of the lien may not, however, be felt by the taxpayer until the lien is filed by the However, neither the Code nor the regulations indicates when a lien should be filed. The regulations merely prescribe the form of notice and deem it 96/ acceptable as to form or content despite any contrary provision of state law. 

The Internal Revenue Manual does address the timing problem. It notes that the filing of a Federal tax lien may adversely affect the taxpayer's ability to generate money with which to pay the tax. Filing of the lien provides public notice of the taxpayer's economic woes. As a result, 97/ the collection effort might be substantially impeded. 

For this reason, the Internal Revenue Manual directs that a notice of lien "should not" be filed until "reasonable efforts" have been undertaken to contact the taxpayer personally and afford him opportunity to make 98/ payment of the delinquency. If no payment is made, the lien may be filed if"it appears that collection (of the particular account) might be jeopardized" 99/ by failure to do so. 

No definition of "reasonable efforts" or "jeopardy"

is provided. Our analysis of the Manual requires the conclusion that, beyond those specific situations for which it advises whether to file or not to file a lien, it offers minimal guidance for lien filing in other cases. 

Collection personnel are advised that the government's interest should be protected. This could be interpreted as a general admonition to assure that lien filings cover property the value of which is sufficient to secure the amount of the taxpayer's liabilities. Since the general guidance is punctuated with cautionary language, however, the objective is not so simply defined. Moreover, there is no way to measure the degree of consistency in lien filing practice throughout the nation. Summary statistics of actions taken, however, suggest that practices are at least divergent. 

During the fiscal year ending June 1974, 345,630 notices of lien were filed 113/ by the Service. Among the seven regions, among which the number of delinquent accounts is fairly evenly distributed, the number of liens filed 114/ ranged from 38,515 in the Central Region to 66,912 in the Western Region. 

While one would not expect the number to be uniform, such substantial unevenness does raise the question whether more criteria are desirable.

2. Levy on Assets Not in the Hands of the Taxpayer. 

The Internal Revenue Code authorizes distraint in respect of "any tax" if "any person liable" therefor "neglects or refuses to pay the 175/ same" within ten days after receiving "notice and demand." "[A] 11 property and rights to property belonging to" the taxpayer, with certain 176/ limited exceptions, may be taken to satisfy the tax debt. whether the assets are in the hands of the taxpayer or of others. directly against the taxpayer are referred to as seizures by the Service 

Distraints imposed and usually concern nonliquid property which must be sold if not released or redeemed. The Service uses the term levy to refer to distraints upon assets (usually liquid) held by third parties. There is little, if any legal difference between levies and seizures, which are created by the same language in § 6331 (a) of the Code. There are, however, different problems occasioned by the two, so they are discussed separately. We now turn 177/ to levies, which are almost universally limited to attachment of such liquid assets as salary and wages, bank, savings and brokerage accounts, and receivables. Our discussion will be confined accordingly. 

Prerequisities to Levy.

As prerequisities to levy, the Code requires only that there be (1) a tax due, (2) notice thereof to the taxpayer, (3) demand therefor to the taxpayer, and (4) failure to pay the tax within ten days of

178/ notice and demand.

A judgment or court order is not required. Also, the levy may be made without prior warning to the taxpayer, except that 179/ written notice must be given of intention to levy on salary or wages. 

The notice must be sent by mail to the taxpayer's last known address, left at his dwelling or usual place of business, or given to him personally, at 180/ least ten days before the levy. There is no requirement, however, that notice be given before any levy but the first: subsequent levies may be 181/ made without warning until the liability is fully paid.

182/ The Internal Revenue Manual gives somewhat more liberal instructions with regard to notice than does the Code. Collection personnel are directed that taxpayers "should be informed specifically of the contemplated action. 

This language, while precatory, extends to matters other than salary garnish- 183/ ments.

The Manual requires written notification in wage attachment cases, 184/ but allows verbal warning in other cases. However, the Manual does not require a description of the specific levy action being contemplated as to 185/ do so might well result in an attempt by the taxpayer to frustrate the levy. 

The notice contemplated by the Manual will, in the case of most delinquent taxpayers, be the "Final Notice Before Seizure" mailed by the Service Center to the Taxpayer after three prior notices. No additional notice is required from the local office "unless there is evidence, such as undelivered mail, that the taxpayer did not receive the 'final' notice." 186/ 187/ In such a case, the employee handling the delinquent account is to make a "reasonable effort" to contact the taxpayer by mail addressed to his residence 188/ or, if that is impossible, in care of his employer.

Release of the Levy.

The Code authorizes the release of levy when its imposition was wrongful or its release will facilitate collection of the liability. 225/ The regulations vest this authority in the District Director, delegation to journeyman Revenue Officers is authorized by the Manual. 224/ but re- 226/ Unlike the Federal tax lien, a levy has no prospective effect, but reaches only property or property rights presently owing or belonging to the 227/ taxpayer. Successive levies are required to garnish property acquired subsequent to the levy. The release of levy, then, affects only property or obligations held at the time distraint was imposed. Release does not prevent the same property from being subjected to subsequent levy for the 228/ same obligation, provided that the statute of limitations and claims of third parties do not intervene.

The Code authorizes the Secretary or his delegate to promulgate regulations delineating the situations in which release of a property im- 229/ posed levy is deemed to "facilitate collection of the tax.

The purpose might be to allow collection which is faster and cheaper than would be accomplished through summary action. For example, a levy on wages gives the Service the entire paycheck up to the amount of the indebtedness, but might also result in the discharge of the employee, and thus delay further liquidation of the tax delinquency. 

This might present the sort of situation which the release powers are intended to ameliorate, but there is nothing in writing which so informs Collection personnel. Indeed, the contrary intent may be supposed: there is a pervasive belief among Internal Revenue management and some line personnel that use of the levy power generally both collects delinquent taxes in the fastest way and encourages payment of current taxes when due. While the rationale supporting the latter half of this philosophy has not been empirically substantiated, it does militate against releases of levy. Further,

It is, however, difficult to comprehend the legality of a levy imposed to collect a nonexistent tax. Section 6331 requires that for a levy to be "lawful", the person in respect of whom the levy is imposed must be "liable to pay any tax." If the levy is not lawful, surely collection is illegal, and the limited prohibition of the regulations to refunds by District Directors does not apply. 

3. Seizure and Sale. a. The Seizure Power.

In Internal Revenue's lexicon, "levy" generally refers to attachment of assets from an employer, broker, bank or other third party. 

These assets are usually money or other liquid properties. The term "seizure" indicates the taking of assets (usually non-liquid) directly from the taxpayer, followed by application of proceeds from sale or redemption of the property to the liquidation of the tax liability. Seizures and levies are really the same thing, being created by S 6331 (a) of the Code though only the term "levy" is used therein, it is defined by $ 6331 (b) to include "the power of distraint and seizure by any means."

As in the case of a levy, then, the only prerequisites for seizure are the passage of ten day's time from service of a notice and demand to the debtor for payment of taxes due and his "neglect or refusal" so to 241/ pay within that time.

The regulations do not add any further considerations. Because the statute says only that "it shall be lawful" for summary collection activities to be undertaken after passage of the ten-day period, but does not require their use, considerable discretion accrues. 

Moreover, seizure may be made of "all property and rights to property (except that which is exempt under section 6334) belonging to" the 242/ taxpayer. Seizure may be used to collect taxes, interests, additional amounts, additions to tax and assessable penalties, together with costs or 243/ expenses which may be incurred in addition to the seizure action. œssive seizures may be imposed "as often as necessary." 244/ Suc- Any person in possession of seized property or rights to property belonging to the taxpayer must deliver them up, or discharge obligations to, 245/ the tax collector. 246/ the taxpayer.

In so doing, one is saved harmless from claims of 

Failure to comply with the seizure may result in personal liability on the part of the garnishee for a sum equal to the value of (1) the lesser of the taxpayer's property held by the garnishee, or the tax due 247/ plus (2) a 50 percent penalty. In aid of its seizure powers, the Service may require that "any person having control of any books or records" relating to the taxpayer's property rights make them available for inspection. 248/ 249/ The general power of distraint is vested in the District Director, but the authority to seize is usually redelegated as far down as journeymen 250/ 

Revenue Officers. 

While the Internal Revenue Manual allows the Revenue

251/ Officer to seize property without first consulting his Group Manager, many Revenue Officers whom we interviewed did review seizure cases with 252/ their supervisors for prior approval.

b. 

The Decision to Seize Property. 

The law and regulations, by specifying solely when summary procedures may not be used, block out a massive area of discretion for the agency's use. We therefore inquired of Revenue Officers what guidelines they used in making seizures and sales. All of them responded that they looked only to the Internal Revenue Manual. Yet, few rules beyond procedural prerequisites have been promulgated in the Manual to condition the exercise of the power granted by the statute. 253/ As a policy matter, assets of going businesses are to be seized only after thorough examination of all "opposing considerations" including foreclosure of the Federal tax lien through lawsuit. Revenue Officers whom we interviewed agreed that putting a firm out of business by seizing and selling its assets constitutes an extreme measure which should be resorted to only after all other attempts to resolve the matter have failed and if the business is not "viable," i.e., it continues to pile up tax in- 254/ debtedness. This determination of "viability" is a subjective, prognosticative, difficult one, for which the Manual is surprisingly devoid of guidance. The majority of Revenue Officers seemed to take a bottomline approach: that is, if the business is meeting its current withholding and other tax liabilities, it generally will be permitted to remain in business. 

The difficult problem seems to be in the rapidity with which the delinquency

must be paid. We have received several complaints of seizures allegedly made or threatened even though the business was meeting its current withholding obligations and was liquidating a past delinquency in steps agreed to by the Revenue Officer. If the business is seized and sold, the amount of employee income and Social Security taxes withheld and still unpaid can be assessed against the corporate officers or limited partners responsible 255/ therefor as a means of alternative collection. 

There are likewise few criteria given in the Manual to govern seizures of property from individual taxpayers. Public records "should" be examined to determine the existence of unsatisfied prior liens, which "should" enter into consideration of whether the interest of the government 256/ is sufficient to make seizure and sale of the property "worthwhile." 

What is "worthwhile" is apparently a matter of judgment. In addition, seizures 257/ are not to be made in cases of "undue hardships, though no line personnel could define the term for us. There are no specific criteria for houses, cars, and the like. The Manual does not require that seizures of property of individual taxpayers be a matter of last resort, as with business accounts. 

The difference may result from the greater likelihood of publicity in the news 258/ media and harm to innocent third-parties, such as employees, which may be caused by the seizure of a business.

4. Use of Summary Powers to Secure Endangered Taxes. 

396/ annually.

As a general rule, the Federal income tax is imposed once Computed on income derived over a period of 12 months, the 397/ tax is to be paid each year by the same date. If assessment or collection of the tax is in some way endangered, however, the Internal Revenue Code permits the Secretary or his delegate to compute the income tax and If voluntary payment is not immediate, 398/ declare it payable forthwith. 399/ it may be thereupon compelled, resulting in what has been rightly called 400/ "the Sovereign's stranglehold. 

Taxpayers left to wrestle in its grip are at a stark disadvantage: they may be rendered "indigent overnight," but the government's position has been protected. 401/ The problem areas presented by these emergency procedures, which are called "jeopardy" and "termination" assessments, are inter-functional in nature. Although usually growing out of the audit process, these assessments impact on the taxpayer when the Service takes his property to satisfy the alleged tax. Therefore, they are discussed in the context of summary collection procedures.

a.

Overview: Routine Assessment Procedure. 

(1) The General Rule. 

Taxpayer returns are received by the Internal Revenue Service Centers around the country. There the returns are registered by document locator number and inspected for prima facie errors in arithmetic and form and for proper execution. If all is well, the admitted liability of the taxpayer is entered with his name, an identifying number, the taxable period, and the type of tax, on an assessment list. The summary form of this document, styled an "Assessment Certificate," when signed by an assessment officer constitutes "assessment" for purposes of the Internal Revenue 402/ Code.

In effect, assessment is nothing more than formal declaration of the tax liability, making the taxpayer a debtor. The assessment may include an amount of tax in excess of that shown on the return if the under- 403/ statement was due to mathematical error by the taxpayer.

404/ Supplemental assessment may be made if it is determined that the 405/ initial assessment is incomplete or incorrect.

A subsequent audit of the return, or the original inspection itself, may reveal that there has been an understatement resulting from some non-arithmetic irregularity. In this case a Report of Examination and an agreement form are forwarded to the taxpayer. An additional assessment is made if the taxpayer agrees. If there is no accord or if there is no response from the taxpayer, a "30-day letter" is sent. This advises the taxpayer that he may request a conference with the district office or the Appellate Division of the Regional Commissioner's office (a "written

protest" form is included for these purposes) or he can execute the consent to the proposed adjustment. If there still is no agreement or response, one last step remains to be taken before assessment and collection. 

Generally, if the taxpayer has understated an income tax (or estate or gift tax, or excise tax on a private foundation), there exists a "deficiency" in the tax as defined by $ 6211(a) of the Code. Under $ 6213(a), before the 

Service may assess an alleged delinquency, a statutory notice of deficiency (also known as a "90-day letter") must be sent by certified or registered 406/ 407/ 

No collection action mail to the taxpayer at his last known address. may be undertaken for 90 days following mailing of the statutory notice, 408/ during which time the taxpayer may file a petition with the Tax Court. 

If he does so, he need not pay the tax, nor may the Service assess the tax, 409/ until the Tax Court has redetermined the deficiency. 

The amount of tax determined by the court may be assessed upon the lapse of time for perfecting an appeal or upon the failure to file a bond in timely fashion with the appeal. 

Should the taxpayer fail to petition the Tax Court within the 90-day 411/ 413/ period, however, access to that forum is closed.

The tax may thereupon 412/ be assessed, and it must be paid within ten days of notice and demand. 

If full payment does not occur, forcible collection action such as seizure of assets and imposition of liens may follow. It may be noted that penalties, interest, and additions to the tax are generally treated as tax for purposes of assessment and collection and, therefore, are subject to the foregoing 414/ rules. 410/ (2) "Immediate Assessments".

Despite the general rule just set out, the Code provides

that assessment of income taxes may be made prior to, or wholly without, 415/ the issuance of a statutory notice in several situations. 

Among these, "immediate" assessment, (i.e., without prior notice) may be made of: (a) income taxes owed by one whose taxable year is terminated (a termination assessment), 416/ and (b) taxes whose collection is found by the District 

Director to be in jeopardy (a jeopardy assessment). 417/

Jeopardy and termination assessments are the most significant exceptions to the general rule of notice before assessment, and are the ones which we discuss.

The absence of notice is important because the Tax Court's juris- 418/ diction is based on a statutory notice of deficiency.

Thus, judicial 419/ 

Yet, payment redetermination of the tax is afforded only after payment. following one of these assessments may be rendered difficult, if not impossible, because assets may be seized; some courts believe that neither the 420/ amount of, nor the justification for, the assessment is reviewable. 

These powers do, then, possess "atomic potentialities in the hand of the tax 421/ gatherer, "1 and we turn to them. b. Jeopardy Assessments. 

(1) Assessment and Collection Procedures. 

Generally speaking, an income tax may not be collected until it is assessed. As noted above in routine assessments, there is a considerable period between notice of a proposed assessment and final assessment. This lapse of time may permit a taxpayer to place assets beyond the reach of the tax collector. Thus, if Service personnel believe that collection

of a tax would be "jeopardized by delay" in utilizing normal collection 423/ procedures, the tax may be immediately assessed without prior opportunity for adversary hearing. 422/ and collected,

Since the assessment is likely to be made in emergency conditions, there is rarely reliable information on which to judge the size of the assessment. Further, since such assessments are made to secure collection of any tax which could conceivably be due, they are often on the high side, even arbitrarily and excessively so. In one instance the Service assessed tax of $1,718,238 and penalties totalling $1,552,767 against a taxpayer whose net worth was conceded to be $38,819. In another instance "every bit" 424/ 425/ of the taxpayer's property was seized. 

The average jeopardy assessment 426/ has in recent years amounted to well over $200,000, and the tendency to 427/ The overassess has created evident concern within IRS's management. taxpayer may thus have an immense indebtedness imposed upon him without any prior opportunity to contest the rationale or size of the assessment. 429/ Even more devastating than the assessment, however, is the immediate right of forcible collection which arises upon delivery of the notice and 428/ demand for payment.

While notice and demand for payment are necessary, they constitute a mere formality. Once it has been decided that collection of the tax is endangered, the Service need not allow any time for the tax- 430/ payer to produce the money.

In fact, the Internal Revenue Manual, which constitutes the procedural Bible for Collection employees, suggests that 

Revenue Officers work in teams: others would seize the assets. two would deliver notice and demand, while 431/

There is same nominal protection.

Collection of all or part of 432/ but the jeopardy assessment may be stayed by the filing of a bond, collection is immediate and, as we have seen, the assessment frequently exceeds the taxpayer's net worth. 433/ with which to obtain a bond. 

He is, thus, left without collateral The bond provision has been dismissed 434/ as a "mockery" by one court.

Furthermore, there is no provision in the Code or in the Internal Revenue Manual for return of the taxpayer's property in order that a bond may be obtained. Property has been returned in rare 435/ instances, but most Revenue Officers whom we asked indicated that they would not return property to taxpayers under any circumstances until the tax was paid because disappearance of the taxpayer or the assets might result. 

But, it would seem that the interests of the government are protected when a bond in the amount of the assessment or the anticipated net proceeds from the forced sale of the seized property (whichever is less) are given in 436/ exchange for its return. This can be accomplished through simple escrow proceedings: IRS can turn the property over to an escrowee for release to the taxpayer upon delivery of the bond in a specified sum from a reputable surety.

Pending the filing of a petition with the Tax Court, or a decision by it, the government may dispose of the seized property only if (1) the owner gives his consent, (2) the property will rot, or (3) conservation and 437/ management costs will greatly diminish net proceeds. 

No such protection is provided if the door to the Tax Court is closed, however. Then, the only remedy is to pay the tax and file for a refund in the district court or the

438/ 

Court of Claims.

Since normally all assets will have been seized, the taxpayer will have no capacity to pay the tax, and payment will result only upon liquidation of the seized assets and application of the net proceeds 439/ to the tax deficiency.

The amount of the assessment may be abated if it is found to be 440/ jeopardy exists. 441/ excessive, and it may be withdrawn altogether if it is decided that no The frequency or extent of abatement is not known to the Service, however, and the likelihood that some of the taxpayer's property will be thereby returned to him appears highly unlikely since the original assessment probably exceeded his net worth anyway. 

With all of his property thus pinned by the Sovereign's stranglehold, the taxpayer may find it impossible to retain accountants and attorneys to represent him. While indigency may prevent an adequate defense, the government has no obligation to provide the taxpayer with an attorney or 442/ accountant in a civil case.

Neither must the Service make advance release of funds to him to defend criminal charges to which the assessment is related, though there have been instances in which the courts or the District Director 444/ has returned funds for defense of criminal, and even civil, tax matters. 

In the absence of such a grant, however, the taxpayer may be compelled by lack of resources to settle the assessment disadvantageously. 

The jeopardy assessment may be of such magnitude as to force the 445/ 446/ taxpayer out of his home and destroy his business, not to mention his reputation. It may strip the taxpayer of all means of supporting himself 443/ or his family. 447/

(2) 

Determination of Jeopardy and Deficiency.

The Internal Revenue Code allows jeopardy assessment to be made if the Secretary or his delegate "believes" that assessment 448/ 

Despite the or collection of the tax will be "jeopardized by delay.' havoc which can be wrought by jeopardy assessments, however, that is the sole criterion provided by the Code for its use. The regulations add 449/ nothing. Conversely, the assessment may be abated only if "jeopardy no longer exists. 450/ to define "jeopardy."

Again, the underlying regulation suggests nothing 451/ The Collection employee who desires to determine whether taxes are jeopardized receives somewhat more guidance from the Internal Revenue Manual. Both auditors and Collection officers are advised that these three fact patterns constitute jeopardy: (a) The taxpayer is or appears to be designing quickly to depart from the United States or to conceal himself. (b) The taxpayer is or appears to be designing quickly to place his property beyond the reach of the government either by removing it from the United States, or by concealing it, or by transferring it to other people, or by dissipating it. (c) The taxpayer's financial solvency is or appears to be imperiled (other than by accruals of taxes and penalties and interest thereon). 

Most jeopardy assessments are initiated in connection with the 453/ examination of returns: Collection employees, on the other hand, do not encounter taxpayers until after the assessment. Perhaps for this reason 

Revenue Agents are the Manual provides additional instructions to auditors. advised, in unfortunate language, that "certain conditions and circumstances can properly be considered as establishing prima facie cases in which jeopardy 452/

assessments should be made." 454/ 

These "prima facie cases" include "operators in the criminal field" or in "other activities generally regarded as illegal," gamblers and bookies, "border hoppers", and persons who are 455/ These financially embarrassed or habitually indisposed to pay taxes. classifications lack specificity and seem to create a reservoir of discretion which is undesirably large. In addition, we have received several complaints alleging threats by zealous auditors to impose jeopardy assessment if the taxpayer refuses to execute an extension of the statute of limitations for assessment. However, we have no evidence that the threats are often carried out. 456/ Surely, the government's interests would be preserved by sending the taxpayer a notice of deficiency, which tolls the statute of limitations under § 6213 (a) of the Code. 

Once the existence of jeopardy has been determined, however, the amount of the deficiency must rapidly be discerned in order to guard against the perceived threat to the revenues. According to the Manual, Revenue Agents are to take care to avoid "arbitrary and excessive" assessments, but at the same time they "should be limited to amounts which reasonably can be expected 457/ to protect the Government." The risk of error is great: the assessment usually is calculated in haste with incomplete information and without adversary hearing. Perhaps, because of the exigencies of the situation, there is almost nothing to structure the amount of the assessment, other than the substantive tax law and the broad concept of protecting the fisc. 

The magnitude of the assessment is, otherwise, confined only by the Tax 458/ Court redetermination of the deficiency.
