cases has frequently been in favor of preserving the position of the government, causing drastic results. 459/ 460/ in which a

The best-known example is Pizzarello v. U. S., jeopardy assessment was levied for unpaid wagering taxes. assessed a $282,440.70

The Service by taking the gross wagers accepted by the assessee during a three-day period and extrapolating that over a five-year span, exclusive of Sundays. But, there was no evidence in testimony or affidavits to support the conclusion that Mr. Pizzarello had been taking wagers for any more than three days or that the three-day activity was representative of the rest of the five-year period. The Second Circuit, therefore, held that the assessment was "excessive, arbitrary, and without factual foundation. 11 461/ No statistics are available from the Internal Revenue Service to indicate the percentage or amount of jeopardy assessments upheld on judicial review. 

(3) Administrative Review. 

The Revenue Agent does not act alone in forging the jeopardy assessment. Proposed jeopardy assessments undergo review by the 463/ 462/ 

Chiefs of the Audit and Collection Divisions. 

In Rev. Proc. 60-4, the Service announced that no jeopardy assessment would take effect without 464/ prior, personal approval of the District Director. The Revenue Procedure also specified formal post-review of assessments by the regional and national offices of IRS. Under current practice, the regional office having jurisdiction over the district reviews the file on a priority basis to determine the reasonableness of the assessment and existence of any procedural or

technical errors. 465/ Each twentieth jeopardy assessment file (determined chronologically) is then forwarded to the Audit Division, national office, for further examination of whether Service policy and Manual procedure were 466/ observed.

Prior approval must be obtained from the Director, Audit Division, national office, if the taxpayer does not fit within the three broad jeopardy 467/ criteria enumerated earlier. The same is true if the assessment "might cause serious inconvenience to the general public," or if "a high degree of public interest is involved" and the District Director concludes that ap- 468/ proval by the national office is in the "best interests of the Service. 

This procedure might be taken as a backhand instance of requiring national office approval of action taken in "significant" cases 470/ 469/ something which the Service has always officially denied. However, cases which might be considered "significant" are much the same as those for which approval is required. 471/ (4) Judicial Review.

Section 7421 (a) of the Internal Revenue Code sweepingly 

472/ limits the power of courts to conduct speedy review of the Service's use of jeopardy assessments.

With narrow exceptions this so-called "anti-injunction act" provides that "no suite for the purpose of restraining the assessment or collection of any tax shall be maintained in any court by any person. . . . 

The exceptions ensure that the taxpayer shall have the full benefit of his access (if any) to the Tax Court in which he may litigate the assessment without first paying it.

The manifest policy of the Act, the essence of which has been on

473/ the books since 1867, is to permit orderly collection of revenues by 474/ the government without interference from the judiciary. 

While its earlier opinions sometimes indicated a disbelief in the plain language of 475/ the Act, 476/ the Supreme Court gravitated finally and unanimously to nearliteral reading 95 years later in Enochs v. Williams Packing and Nav. Co. 

Despite the seemingly flat prohibition of § 7421 (a) against injunctive relief, the Court ruled to permit it if a two-pronged test was met. Logically enough, the Court first ruled that the elements for equitable relief must be present. But, it added a second prong which impales most taxpayer hopes for injunctive relief. Only if it is "apparent that, under the most liberal view of the law and facts, the United States cannot 477/ establish its claim" may an injunction issue. The Court opined that a collateral purpose of the statute was to relegate taxpayers not petitioning the Tax Court (where proposed assessments may be litigated without payment) to paying the tax and suing for refund. At the same time, however, the bar of $ 7421 (a) assumed the existence of a bona fide effort on the part of the Service to collect a tax, not merely to make an exaction "in the guise of a 478/ tax."

The Supreme Court, therefore, made it clear that the trial judge's factual evaluation must be limited to evidence in the hands of the Service by the time of trial. It further implied that these facts need only be 479/ enough to support a good faith belief that the taxes are owing. 

Not surprisingly, inability to demonstrate "certainty of success on the merits" 480/ has stymied nearly all taxpayers who have tried to sur-

E 3 mount $ 7421 (a). The few injunctions obtained by taxpayers since Williams 

Packing have mostly been based on the government's alleged failure to comply 481/ with statutory requisites for jeopardy assessments, and it has been suggested by some commentators that the Service should be compelled to comply with its 482/ formal administrative practices as well. Taxpayers have found it difficult to derail jeopardy assessments on factual, rather than technical, grounds. 483/ An exception is Pizzarello v. U. S., in which the Service obtained its evidence solely through an illegal arrest of the taxpayer, an alleged gambler. The evidence being inadmissible, the government plainly could not prevail. Equitable jurisdiction probably existed, and thus, the second portion of the Williams Packing test was met because (1) the threatened loss of his legitimate business would have done the taxpayer irreparable harm, and (2) he had no remedy at law because prosecution of a refund claim would have necessitated his taking the stand and waiving his 484/ Fifth Amendment protections. Mr. Pizzarello's situation was an unusual one, however, and it is doubtful that the decision is of great pertinence to one not accused of a criminal offense. 485/ A similar result was obtained in Anderson v. Richardson. 

The taxpayer was detained for traffic offense by plainclothesmen, repeatedly questioned by them and by Internal Revenue agents without benefit of the Miranda warnings. Searches of his person and automobile turned up $7,900 in cash which Mr. Anderson claimed was part of the proceeds of sale of a small business. Mr. Anderson testified without contradiction that unbeknownst to him, all of this liquid assets were seized on the day of his

arrest and that he was left nothing with which to feed or provide for his family. The following business day the taxpayer, his accountant, and his attorney met with Service agents who assured that all his returns and work papers were in good order and that no tax liens were outstanding. Only later were the Service's actions discovered. At trial, the IRS spokesman conceded that "he saw no way the IRS could succeed on this jeopardy assess- 486/ 487/ ment." 

Terming the facts "odious"," the court ordered the seized property returned and denied the government's motion for stay of that order. 

Not all taxpayers are so fortunate to receive a concession of error as did Mr. Anderson, however, and the quantum of proof in injunction proceedings under § 7421 has remained in some doubt. It has been held that conclusory protestations of good faith by the government are not enough to establish that, under the most liberal view of the law and facts, it could possibly 488/ prevail on the merits.

Thus, if there is no proof introduced by the 489/ government to support the assessment, it may be enjoined.

It also seems 490/ the clear that the taxpayer must have the opportunity to show that under no circumstances will the government prove its case. In Lucia v. U. S., taxpayer claimed that a gambling excise tax assessment imposed upon him was arbitrary and excessive, but the trial court dismissed the case for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction without hearing testimony. In reversing, the 

Fifth Circuit held that "the taxpayer, Lucia, will have to prove his case upon remand, and the extent of our holding goes no further than to give him 491/ that opportunity." The burden of proof thus was placed on the taxpayer.

492/ The emphasis was different in Shapiro v. Secretary of State. 

The taxpayer, an Israeli citizen under indictment in his homeland for securities fraud, was subjected to a jeopardy assessment one business day before he was to leave the United States to face trial. He brought suit to compel release of the funds, which were needed for bond to prevent his incarceration in Israel and to prevent extradition until the tax matter was resolved. The government moved to dismiss for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction and resisted answering the taxpayer's interrogatories concerning the nature of the assessment. after the assessment, when the notice of deficiency was served on taxpayer's counsel, that the IRS suspected Mr. Shapiro of being a narcotics peddler and 493/ that the assessment was based on unexplained bank deposits made by him. 

It was not revealed until more than two weeks The same afternoon the Service's motion to dismiss was granted for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. But the Circuit Court, citing Pizzarello and Lucia, reversed and remanded the case for a review of the government's basis for assessment. It was emphasized that the IRS would have to make some kind of showing to support its action, even though the district court would not be bound to require the quantum of proof demanded by the Second and Fifth Circuits. "But at the very least the District Court must obtain same evidence by which to judge whether the asserted deficiency was a tax or was so arbitrary and excessive as to be 'an exaction in the guise of a tax.' While it is not probable that the Government created the deficiency out of whole cloth, it is equally true that. [the Government's] burden. . . [to show good faith] is not met by mere protestations of good faith and conclusory statements of plaintiff's tax liability. The District Court should therefore inquire as to whether

there are any facts which good faith may be inferred. . . [O]n remand the District Judge should examine the facts on which the Government bases its claim against Shapiro and determine its jurisdiction on the basis of these facts. 

494/ The Circuit panel further suggested that in camera examination of the evidence would be appropriate to protect the identity of informers and the sensitive nature of the case. 

Alleging that Shapiro conflicted with Lucia, the government applied for certiorari, which was granted on February 19, 1975. Lucia had only given the taxpayer the opportunity to "prove his case" that the assessment 495/ was plainly wrong. On the other hand, Shapiro required the Service to come forth with facts; this, the government alleges, will invert the burden 496/ of proof, which normally rests on the taxpayer. 

The government may be creating a distinction without a difference. 

While it is true that the Commissioner's determination of a deficiency is 497/ presumptively correct, a presumption is not itself evidence and disappears when evidence is introduced which rebuts it. 498/ 

In any event, the

Williams Packing decision requires that the Service's chance of sustaining the tax be judged "on the basis of the information available to it at the 499/ time of suit."

But, Williams Packing also said that no more than good faith would be required, and the Service apparently argues that it need only make conclusory allegations of good faith and the amount of tax liabiity. 

This is hard to comprehend because there cannot be a finding that the Service acted in good faith without a look at the evidence on which the act is based. 500/ 501/

1 The government need only show that it has some chance of winning on the merits; this is a long way from proving the assessment. 

The Shapiro, Pizzarello, and Lucia decisions all focused on the equity prong of the Williams Packing test. Since the irreparable injury of incarceration without bond would not be avoided by Mr. Shapiro through refund suit or Tax Court proceedings, the Circuit Court found that he met 502/ the first prong of the Williams Packing test. However, the taxpayer in 

Lucia was remanded to the district court to prove that levy during the 503/ pendency of a refund suit would be financially ruinous to him.

504/ Pizzarello was remanded for a similar purpose. The only completely successful taxpayer since Williams Packing was the plaintiff in Anderson v. Richardson.

Furthermore, a number of cases have held that the lack of statutory guidelines to test the District Director's findings precludes judicial re- 505/ view of his determination that jeopardy exists. 

Nonetheless, if there are no facts to support a belief that jeopardy exists, it is hard to understand why a court would not at least treat the exercise of jeopardy assess- 506/ ment powers as an abuse of that discretion. 

But, some courts, including some of those which adopt the view that the Service's discretion is not reviewable, will at least inquire whether a determination of jeopardy was, 507/ in fact, made since "belief" is required by the statute. 

That so few cases have reviewed the Commissioner's exercise of discretion is unfortunate. If there is insufficient evidence to support the exercise of discretion, it should be reversed or enjoined as an abuse of

discretion. Moreover, the prayer for relief from the rigors of of jeopardy assessment must be to the officials who imposed it. The absence of third party review of such drastic action is likely to contravene the sense of justice held by many. This may damage their willingness to co- 508/ operate with the tax laws. Because there are so few jeopardy assessments, would not seem that measurable damage to the public fisc would result from allowing judicial inquiry into the existence of jeopardy before imposing 509/ the assessment. 

c. Termination of Taxable Year. 

it (1) 

Assessment and Collection Procedure. 

Additional power for dealing with jeopardized taxes is provided by $ 6851 of the Code. Although $ 6851 stands consecutively with § 6861 in subchapter A of Chapter 70, labeled "Jeopardy," 510/ and applies to nearly identical factual patterns, a subtle distinction in wording between the two sections has permitted the tax collector on occasion to argue successfully that the so-called "termination assessment" of § 6851 is a power entirely distinct from jeopardy assessment. As will be seen, a result of adopting this construction is that the taxpayer's rights, so severely limited by jeopardy assessments, are even more constrained by termination assessments. 

Under $ 6851 (a) (1), if the District Director 511/ "finds" that "...a taxpayer designs quickly to depart from the

United States or to remove his property therefrom, or to conceal himself or his property therein, or to do any other act tending to prejudice or to render wholly or partly ineffectual proceedings to collect the income tax for the current or the preceding taxable year unless

such proceedings be brought without delay, then he may declare the taxpayer's tax year to be at an end. The District 

Director accelerates the due date of the income tax for the current and preceding years by declaring the tax to be immediately due and payable. 

No purpose is served by accelerating the due date of a tax wich is already owing; thus, the Service utilizes the termination assessment only if the time fixed by law for filing the return has not arrived, whereas a jeopardy 512/ assessment will be utilized if it has. Because the tax is perceived to be in jeopardy, it may be immediately and forcibly collected after presentment of notice and demand. 

The termination assessment section also differs from its neighbors in that its scope is much narrower: $ 6851 applies only to income taxes, while SS 6861 and 6862, combined, cover all taxes. 

Once the decision is made to close the taxable year, the IRS will prepare a substitute return for the taxpayer (under authority of § 6020 (b) (1) of the Code) in which he will receive credit for the full personal exemp- 513/ tion without proration for the short taxable year. The tax having been determined, its assessment is requested and verified by telephone contact 21 ​514/ with the Service Center.

With the assessment number in hand, the local office is prepared to begin collection efforts. 515/ A notice of the District Director's finding that the tax is jeopardized and demand for immediate pay- 516/ ment, signed by him, are given to the taxpayer. 

Under $ 6851 (a) (1), the 517/ tax "thereupon becomes immediately due and payable.

11 As is the case with proceedings under § 6861, the taxpayer whose

taxable year is closed may furnish a bond and thereby prevent proceedings 518/ Here again, however, seizure of the taxpayer's to collect the tax. assets may be so quick and extensive as to leave the choice illusory. 519/ A taxpayer has only one taxable year in a 12-month period. 

The terminated taxable year may be reopened, extended, and again closed by the Secretary or his delegate under authority of § 6851 (b) any time the taxpayer is found to have received income in the taxable year subsequent to the closing. It is automatically reopened when the taxpayer files a 520/ "true and accurate" return for the full 12 months.

The taxpayer whose year has been terminated must still comply with the requirement of $ 6012 that he file an income tax return for the full year, 521/ even though § 443 (a) (3) requires him to file one for the foreshortened taxable period as well. 

There is no clear statutory statement of authority to assess a tax after terminating the year. Unlike $ 6861 (a), which does contain assessment authority, S 6851 makes no mention of assessments. 

It provides only that upon demand by the District Director, the tax becomes immediately due and payable. As we shall later discover, there has been considerable, furious 522/ litigation over this question. Its resolution has a serious impact on taxpayer rights.

The cases have never questioned, or for that matter discussed, the existence of assessment authority where the year has been terminated. 

Such power is probably assumed to exist because $ 6851 (a) (1) allows the District Director to declare the tax immediately owing, and assessment is a sine qua non to a tax liability which the District Director declares due. 523/

ער Since the termination provision does not itself contain assessment authority, Congréss must be assumed, sub silentio, to have intended authority to assess since without assessment the tax is not due. The question is, therefore, not whether assessment authority exists, but whence it comes. itself,

The Service once insisted that this power was contained in § 6851 524/ but now contends that it derives from the general assessment 525/ authority provided in § 6201 (a) (1) of the Code.

526/ that it is found in $ 6861 (a), Taxpayers have urged which is the only section in the Code expressly dealing with assessment in the jeopardy context. The distinction is vital to the taxpayer because § 6861 requires (and § 6201 does not) that a notice of deficiency be sent to the taxpayer within 60 days of assessment. 

Hence, if the Service may properly rely on $ 6201, it need not give a notice of deficiency. If there is no notice of deficiency, the Tax 527/ Court does not have jurisdiction. If the Tax Court may not hear the case, judicial review may be had only through suit for refund, which probably 528/ may be prosecuted only after all the assessment is paid. Given the facts that the assessment is often in excess of the taxpayer's net worth and that forced sales rarely produce revenue equal to the market value of the object sold, the taxpayer may be left without means to pay the assessment and without access to any court. Moreover, even the very narrow exceptions to § 7421 (a), which generally prohibits suits to restrain or enjoin collection of any tax, do not apply unless a notice of deficiency has been issued. 

Taken together, all of these rules, which are founded on the lack of a notice of deficiency, may result in confiscation and liquidation of the 43

taxpayer's assets without possibility of judicial review prior to the forced sale required for "collection." And, if the liquidation does not yield sufficient monies to pay the entire tax, suit for refund may perhaps 529/ not be instituted. Thus, judicial review after collection may be denied unless the assets are sufficient to pay the entire tax. 

In contrast, if a notice must be issued, the taxpayer obtains access to the Tax Court, and he need not pay the assessment to obtain judicial review. Further, the Service cannot sell the seized property absent special 530/ circumstances and, thus, cannot compound the harm from seizure by following it with sale of unique or irreplaceable property. 

The Service has never demonstrated the injury which would result from the mailing of a notice of deficiency in a termination case -- a fact 531/ but has argued only that has not been lost on several puzzled courts on semantic grounds that no deficiency notice is required. (2) Determination of Jeopardy and Deficiency.

The termination statute, $ 6851, does little more than the jeopardy assessment statute to define the factual situations justifying use of the extraordinary power that is created. However, broad examples are given: one's tax year may be terminated if the taxpayer is found to menace collection of the income tax by sequestration of self or 532/ assets or "any other act." The regulations add nothing to this, saying only that the District Director may close the taxable year on "evidence satisfactory to him" of a taxpayer who "designs by immediate departure from 533/ the United States, or otherwise, to avoid the payment of income tax.

'

1 Again accorded a good deal of leeway by the statute, the Service has taken much the same course as with jeopardy assessments. Audit (but not Collection) employees are given a listing of "prima facie cases" in which it might "properly be considered" that termination assessments "should 534/ be made.

These are generally verbatim restatements of those justifying jeopardy assessments, except that no mention is made of taxpayers whose economic well-being is threatened by lawsuit or business failure. The amissions reflect the emphasis of the $ 6851 regulations on an "act" by the taxpayer to jeopardize the taxes, as opposed to the mere existence of a jeopardy condition from any cause, which arguably is contemplated by $ 6861. 

Again, the "prima facie cases" are described so vaguely that grave potential for abuse lurks within their hazy parameters. For example, the 

Manual directs that termination assessments "should be made" if the individual "frequently wager [s] large amounts" or possesses "a background and history of activity in illegal enterprises such as. .narcotics." 535/ led to the unfortunate chain of events in Willits v. Richardson, This may have 536/ in which the taxpayer was arrested for speeding, carrying a concealed pistol, and possessing narcotic drugs. A search of Mrs. Willits's purse revealed four barbiturate tablets (which she claimed were prescribed by her doctor), $4,400 in cash, and some jewelry. Within 24 hours of the arrest, the Internal 

Revenue Service, which had been alerted to the case, imposed a $25,549 termination assessment on supposed cocaine sales of $240,000. "Virtually all" 537/ of Mrs. Willits's property was seized.

The three criminal charges were

never prosecuted.

Reversing the dismissal by the district court (which 538/ admitted it was "revolted" by IRS's actions), the Fifth Circuit characterized the "gossamer basis" on which the assessment had been made as being "1 .scanty and largely inaccurate information which, at best, amounted to nothing more than a vague suspicion that she must have come by her jewelry and cash by improper means since she admitted that she gambled for a living and was being kept by a man who police believed was dealing in narcotics." 539/ Willits dramatizes not only the danger implicit in relying on "prima facie cases" as justification for terminating a taxable year, but the use of the Internal Revenue Service as a "law enforcement" agency. The case grew out of the Narcotics Traffickers Program (NTP) which the Service developed to "disrupt the distribution of narcotics through the enforcement 540/ of all available tax statutes.

By using termination and jeopardy assessments, the Service aimed to take drug cash out of the hands of suspected narcotics traffickers as quickly as possible, thereby depriving them of the 541/ ability to do business.

One district undertook to make termination assessments within two hours of arrest of a person suspected of dealing in 542/ narcotics.

Another, as a matter of policy, denied suspected narcotics 543/ traffickers a deduction for the cost of contraband allegedly sold.

Finally, a June 1974 Internal Audit Division study of the Narcotics Traf fickers Program as conducted in six districts concluded: "Generally, all six. . terminate the tax years of narcotics law violators on the basis that the taxpayer's illegal narcotics involvement constitutes a "prima facie" case in which termination assessments should be made. . . .With few

exceptions, there is no other hard evidence that income taxes are due or that the collection of such taxes are in jeopardy in these cases. 544/ "1 Since emphasis was not on protection or collection of the tax, but upon sequestration of funds believed to be related to the drug market, the audit process was reduced to an absurdity. Our interviews with Internal 

Revenue personnel indicate that the purpose of the audit in such cases is to discover the suspect's properties so that the "tax" bill is large enough to cover them all. By late 1974 NTP assessments totalled $223 million, but collections were only $34.5 million. The cases are replete with assessments just sufficient to cover the property seized in police raids; 

Hardly any 545/ 547/ 546/ some others, however, are so large as to strain credulity. recently reported cases have featured a termination assessment amounting to less than the value of seized property. A notable example of the usual 548/ audit tactic is Rinieri v. Scanlon, involving a French citizen who was arrested at Kennedy Airport as he was about to leave the country with $247,500. The Service terminated his tax year, and assessment was challenged in the following examination of the agent: "Q. To be very blunt about it, isn't it the fact that you were just merely told to write a report that would come out with an income tax of approximately $247,500 so that the government would have a basis of seizing this money, isn't that the blunt fact? "A. That would be part of it. My position is to protect the government. "Q. I want an answer, yes or no, Mr. Vita. Isn't that the blunt fact? "A. Yes." 549/

One would never guess from that exchange that official Internal 550/ Revenue policy requires that termination assessments be reasonable in amount. 

Our interviews indicated them to be usually the product of guesswork. The 

Revenue Agent will rely on a single performance by an entertainer or period of surveillance by law enforcement officials, then extrapolate from the known facts to obtain "income" for the entire terminated year. The national office claims to have disapproved calculations of this kind and to have urged that assessments instead be limited to the performance or period of surveillance. 

In the routine audit case the Revenue Agent provides the taxpayer with a Report of Examination, explaining how the deficiency in tax was determined. The reasonableness of a termination assessment is at least impugned by the practice of Revenue Agents not to provide such reports to termination 551/ In one such case the Fifth Circuit was struck by the "total --the word is total--lack of any basis for computing the quick terminated 552/ tax." assessees.

Plainly, it may be questioned whether the Service is sincere in an attempt to collect a "tax." 

Fortunately, this same

In fact, the Service has used termination assessments as a means of summary, extra-judicial punishment of suspected narcotics traffickers. 

Neither the statute nor the agency was established for such a purpose, as 553/ courts have repeatedly reminded the Service. view of the Service has been taken by its incumbent Commissioner, and the number and amount of termination assessments have declined. Further, the 

Commissioner has reminded the public and the Service that it is not a general law enforcement agency. In his speech before the American Bar

Association in August 1974, Commissioner Alexander agreed that the use of the taxing statutes as instruments of morality might affect the integrity of administration of revenue laws generally and the impartiality of the Service particularly. Therefore, he said, the Service has ...changed the criteria for IRS involvement in anti-narcotics. . .activities. Today, such activities must satisfy the revenue and professional criteria which have long been established within the IRS as guides for channeling resources. . [A]n excessive emphasis on drug dealers. .in my view would seem inappropriate from the standpoint of a fair and impartial administration of the nation's revenue laws. . [T]he overall · · emphasis of our criminal enforcement program has been shifted away from special enforcement programs such as Narcotics Traffickers. . .toward the taxpaying public in general."554/

Though there have been no formal changes in NTP procedure published in the Internal Revenue Manual, the national office did publish a reminder to field personnel that there must be some assurance that an income tax will be due and that it is in jeopardy before termination of the tax year is 555/ effected. It is our understanding that Revenue Agents now rely on the 

Drug Enforcement Administration to seize cash found in the possession of the suspected narcotics peddler as evidence of the crime. This permits the agent time to determine the probability of compliance of a potential assessee with the tax law. By means of personal interview with the suspect, an examination of his filing history, including tax returns, and evaluation of the taxpayer's living situation, the Revenue Agent may also approximate the amount of income and the extent to which it has been unreported. The trend appears to be in the direction of fewer termination assessments, though we cannot say whether 556/ they are smaller.

(3) 

Administrative Review.

The Internal Revenue Manual requires personal approval of termination assessments by the District Director (or acting District 557/ Director), who must sign the notice of termination and demand for tax which is delivered to the taxpayer. If the case is one which does not involve sequestration of self or assets by the taxpayer, or his pending insolvency, prior approval of the Director, Audit Division, national office, 558/ must also be obtained.

The file is post-reviewed by the Assistant Regional Commissioner (Audit) on a priority basis to ensure that no procedural or technical errors 559/ exist.

Each tenth case is then examined by the national office Audit 560/ 

Division for deviation from Service policy or Manual procedures. 

The efficacy of this internal review is at least questionable in view of several egregious cases which have come before the courts. Management examination of termination assessments failed to prevent such flimsy 561/ assessments as those in Willits and Pizzarello, for example. It is true that these were emergency assessments, made within hours of the discovery of the "jeopardy" and after hurried consultations between the auditor, his chief, and the District Director. But, neither did the Service provide subsequent review or investigation of the assessments sufficient to strengthen their basis or correct their magnitude. The Service, then, further blinded itself to the facts by instructing the Revenue Agents not to provide the taxpayers or their representatives with reports explaining the termination action;

nor were they given opportunity to test the assessments by the adversary 562/ proceedings of the District Conference.

These amissions would seem at least inconsistent with Commissioner Alexander's recent pronouncement that the Service is endeavoring to treat all taxpayers alike. IRS argues that it is not collecting a tax, but making a provisional seizure to ensure subsequent collection. Its justification for denying a conference, therefore, may be that one would not be timely until the full taxable year has ended. This prospect is not calming to the taxpayer who is meanwhile subject to financial ruin from an assessment which exceeds his net worth. 

The stage is set for further monitoring after assessment by inputting a command to the Service Center and National Computer Center computers not to process the taxpayer's year-end return. It is, instead, routed to the Audit or Intelligence Division of the local office which initiated the 563/ termination proceedings. 

(4) Judicial Review. 

(a) The Deficiency Notice Issue. 

Consistent with its practice of not permitting adversary proceedings on the administrative level, IRS has strained to prevent, or at least limit, judicial review of termination assessments. 

For this, as with defense of jeopardy assessments, it has relied on $ 7421 of the Code, known as the "Anti-Injunction Act." But the Service's results here have been mixed due to the exception in § 7421 that an injunction will be issued in cases where the Service has neglected to send a notice of delinquency to the taxpayer in conjunction with the assessment.

Assessment authority for § 6851 is unclear. The circuits which have considered the question mostly agree that the power derives either 565/ from the general assessment provision of § 6201 or from § 6861, the jeopardy 564/ assessment statute. But, they are split on the choice between the two. 

The Supreme Court decided in late 1974 to resolve the issue, perhaps motivated by the generous, but cacophonous, authority that has accumulated in the last six years (much of it generated by the Narcotics Traffickers 566/ Program).

The pebble which dislodged this circuit-splitting landslide is 567/ Schreck v. U. S., an exhaustive 1969 opinion in the District of Maryland. 

Holding that a taxpayer subjected to § 6851 termination proceedings was entitled to a deficiency notice under § 6861, the court ruled that because none had been given him, he was not only entitled to enjoin assessment and collection under $ 7421, but also was entitled to a return of the seized 568/ property. The court, candidly admitting that the issue was not free from doubt, rested its holding on Congressional intent that it discerned implicit in the structure of the Code, if not in § 6851 itself. Income taxpayers are generally entitled to be heard by the Tax Court, and the court could discern no reason why Congress would want to exclude termination assessees. 

Indeed, a review of the legislative history does not reveal that Congress ever considered the question; the Tax Court did not exist when the predecessor of 570/ 

S 6851 was enacted. 569/ The Service has pointed out that $ 6861 authorizes immediate assessment of a "deficiency," while $ 6851 refers only to termination of the taxable

1 year to protect collection of the "income tax." While agreeing that $ 6211(a) defines "deficiency" generally as the excess of the correct amount of tax over that tax "shown on the return," when no return was filed by the taxpayer, the court found the argument contradictory to the government's own regulations. Treas. Reg., § 301.6211(a) provides: "If no return is made. .for the purpose of the definition [of "deficiency"] 'the amount shown as the tax by the taxpayer upon his return' shall be considered as zero. Accordingly, in any such case, if no deficiencies with respect to such tax have been assessed, or collected without assessment, and no rebates with respect to the tax have been made, the deficiency is the amount of the tax imposed by [the income, estate, and gift tax laws]. 571/ There being a deficiency, the Service was obligated to issue a notice thereof. 

But, in Lisner v. McCanless 572/ the Service took the additional step of filing a short-year return on behalf of the taxpayer under authority of SS 443 (a) (3) and 6020 (b) (1) of the Code. It contended that no deficiency existed because there was no difference between the amount of tax due and the amount shown as tax on the return. That argument was rejected because the taxpayer was never given the opportunity to file a return himselfhis first notice of the termination was the seizure of his assets. which held On the other side of the semantic argument are two circuits which have recognized the distinction between jeopardy and termination taxpayers. 573/ The first was the Seventh Circuit in Williamson v. U. S., that because the taxpayer had not filed a return at the time of assessment, there was no "deficiency" and, hence, no notice of one was required. For

this conclusion the Seventh Circuit relied on dicta in a Board of Tax 574/ 

Appeals case and the Service's argument that § 6851 contained its own assessment authority. IRS has since abandoned this position, and one Indiana district court felt itself, therefore, not bound to follow 575/ circuit precedent.

Second Circuit in Irving v. Gray, 576/ The cryptic logic of Williamson was, however, adopted by the which involved Howard Hughes' bogus biographer. But, the court found alternative assessment authority for termination in $ 6201 (a) (1). The Irving panel further held that the legal remedy of a refund suit was adequate, and in doing so, backed itself into a rather questionable 577/ construction of Flora v. United States. In that case the Supreme Court examined 28 U.S.C. § 1346 (a) (1), which gives the district courts and the 

Court of Claims jurisdiction over "any civil action against the United States for refund of any tax" [emphasis supplied]. The Supreme Court concluded that $ 1346 (a) (1) "requires full payment of the assessment before an income tax 578/ refund suit can be maintained.

[emphasis supplied] The Second Circuit distinguished Flora because that case involved a deficiency assessment and reasoned further that because no "deficiency" had been asserted against Mr. 

Irving, he therefore had no Flora "assessment" to pay before suing for refund. 

Having adopted the faulty Williamson view that there is no "imposed tax" in a § 6851 proceeding, but only a sort of security for eventual collection of one, the termination assessment was not a 28 U.S.C. S 1346 (a) (1) "tax" to be paid in full before suit. On the contrary, the tax would be determined only when the taxpayer files a full-year return; if there is an overpayment shown, the

return operates as claim for refund. If no action is taken by the Service within six months, said the Irving panel, the refund suit may be commenced 5797 because the tax has been paid. To support this conclusion, however, the court cited § 6532 (a) and 7422 (a), which bar suits for refund until six months after claim therefor is filed, but do not say whether they may be brought thereafter. Instead, the jurisdictional statute is 28 U.S.C. § 1346 (a) (1) which, according to the Supreme Court, requires payment of the "assessment. 

The Second Circuit held to its position in Laing v. U.S., 580/ in January 1975 was argued before the Supreme Court in tandem with Hall 581/ which v. U.S., a progeny of the countervailing view represented by the Fifth and Sixth Circuits. 582/ In Clark v. Campbell, the Fifth Circuit found that a termination assessment was indeed an "assessment" within the meaning of Flora and must be fully paid before suit is brought. Therefore, the district court did not present a means of rapid review. Neither was it as effective, since only by sale and application of proceeds is there "payment, and sale might be blocked by forfeiture proceedings or "payment" by applica- 583/ tion of the proceeds to other liabilities of the taxpayer. 

The Sixth Circuit, on the other hand, was concerned with problems of procedural due process under the Fourteenth Amendment. Only if the taxpayer is given access to the Tax Court is the government prohibited from selling seized property prior to impartial judicial review of the alleged 584/ deficiency in tax. The Sixth Circuit pointed out that to deny the terminated taxpayer access to the Tax Court was to permit sale of seized property before the taxpayer had an opportunity to be heard. Pre-judicial

sale has occurred in a number of the decided cases, 585/ and the Sixth 586/ Circuit thought it raised a serious Constitutional problem. 

The Supreme Court has already sharply limited the prejudgment 587/ remedies of private creditors. Fuentes v. Shevin prohibited prejudgment repossession of household effects from a delinquent installment debtor. That case was recently followed by North Georgia Finishing, Inc. v. Di-Chem, 588/ Inc., which struck down pre-judicial attachment of a corporation's cammercial account. Both cases ruled that "[a]ny significant taking of property 589/ by the State is within the purview of the Due Process Clause." The decision in North Georgia Finishing was announced the day after oral argument in Hall and Laing.

However, there may be additional considerations affecting the Constitutionality of a governmental seizure of property. In Phillips v. 590/ Commissioner, the Supreme Court recognized and settled the Constitutional right of the United States to collect its revenues by summary administrative process. Although the taxpayer had, in fact, been accorded the right to take the matter to the Tax Court, he had chosen not to. He, instead, attempted to impose an onus on the Commissioner to obtain judicial approval of the assessment before attempted collection. The Supreme Court ruled that due process was afforded by the option accorded the taxpayer to seek de novo prepayment review by the Tax Court, and that opportunity having passed, prejudicial seizure was therefore justified by "the need of the government promptly 591/ to secure its revenues.

"

Phillips seems to take a much more unsympathetic view toward property rights than is represented by Fuentes v. Shevin or North Georgia 592/ Finishing, but Phillips was cited with approval in Fuentes (which did not approve prejudgment seizure) for the proposition that the need of the sovereign promptly to collect taxes could be one of those "truly unusual" situations in which summary seizure of property was Constitutionally per- 593/ missible. The determination of that, Mr. Justice Harlan wrote, rests an the necessity of resort to seizure to secure an important governmental or public interest, existence of a "special need for very prompt action," and the responsibility of an agent of the sovereign to determine necessity and 594/ justification for the seizure under the guidance of narrowly drawn laws. 

Aside from the questions of whether the few termination cases each year constitute a vital part of the government's revenues or whether the statute is fatally over-broad, it would seem desirable to provide some kind of rapid judicial inquiry before the taxpayer can be injured. In so doing the Service might assist the cause of voluntary compliance. For purely pragmatic reasons, if not out of a sincere desire to give the taxpayer every benefit of the doubt, the Service should conform to the notion, commonly held by the public, that "the coercive power of government should not be applied until an impartial judge has confirmed that the proposed 595/ action is lawful." The Supreme Court has long held that a "root requirement" of procedural due process is the right to reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard. In addition to striking down statutes providing for summary prejudgment wage attachment and replevin of goods, it 596/ has voided laws providing for prejudgment revocation of driver's licenses 597/

598/ and termination of welfare benefits because "significant" property deprivations occurred before the hearings took place. However, the applicability of this rule to jeopardy and termination assessments is at least doubtful. 

First, the collection of taxes is an "important public interest" which may Perhaps more significantly (in view of vitiate the right to hearing. 599/ the lesser rights accorded to private creditors) the Supreme Court has said that even though the seizure is to benefit a private litigant and "no more than private gain is directly at stake," seizure may be carried out if there 600/ is "immediate danger that a debtor will destroy or conceal disputed goods Moreover, prejudgment seizure in the jeopardy situation is explicitly permitted by the Internal Revenue Code even if the assessee is 601/ eligible for a hearing before the Tax Court.

Because the Service is so well protected, its resistance to sending out a notice of deficiency is puzzling. The agency incurs no harm in so doing, but the taxpayer faces (1) sale of his property, which may include unique or irreplaceable items, and (2) the Flora rule, which demands full payment of the assessment before suit for refund. The second requirement may be insurmountable, given the tendency of the Service to overassess and to conduct forced sales which bring less than market prices.

Indeed, the more grave Constitutional issue does not arise from the seizure and sale of property prior to judicial access, but from the interplay of the Flora rule and the denial of a ticket to the Tax Court, which may prevent a hearing altogether. The issue may be avoided in two ways by the 

Supreme Court: (1) resolution of the close semantic issue in favor of receipt

of a deficiency notice by the termination assessee or (2) reinterpretation of Flora along the lines of the Second Circuit's Irving opinion, thus allowing suit for refund based on the filing of a short-year return without reference to whether the assessment has been paid. (b) 

Review of the Director's Finding. 

The jurisdictional prerequisite for imposition of a termination assessment is the District Director's finding that the taxpayer plans to frustrate collection of an income tax not yet due and payable. Most courts will look to see whether such a finding was actually made; 603/ however, many will not review the factual sufficiency of the finding. 

This refusal seems difficult to justify because a finding which lacks eviden- 604/ tiary support is "arbitrary and baseless," and some courts have therefore 605/ voided such assessments. d. 

Lessons of Jeopardy and Termination Proceedings.

Same incidents of jeopardy and termination assessments 602/ vividly illustrate the negative side of overzealous employment of summary collection powers by the Internal Revenue Service. Staggering overassessments and simultaneous forcible collection can impact with nuclear suddenness on the taxpayer's life and livelihood. The spontaneous assessment may well mean the ruin of credit and standing in the community and, for the self-employed, the collapse of a lifetime of endeavor. 

The Service's self-image as a police agency has intensified the problem. Traditionally, it has sought only to "enforce" the revenue laws. 

However, this mentally prepared the Service to assert as extra-judicial punishment termination assessments based on suspected gains from the marketing of

contraband, despite the dismissal of criminal charges against the assessee or the failure to prosecute him. It is true that the United States' burden of proof is more onerous when it seeks criminal sanctions than when it seeks tax revenues. But, the fact is that the termination provisions of the Internal Revenue Code have been utilized not to collect taxes, but to clamp a suspected capillary of drug cash off from the arterial flow of narcotics traffic. determined.

In many cases termination and jeopardy assessments have amounted to punishment without trial. They have reached persons whose guilt was never 

But, even if the assessee committed the alleged offense, the use of termination and jeopardy assessments as a means of extra-judicial punishment is wrong because these powers were given to the Service to collect taxes. Presumably, that means the collection of taxes reasonably believed to be due.

The frequent lack of such belief, or any grounds to support it, may account for the Service's policy of refusing to reveal to terminated taxpayers how, or even why, the assessments are imposed. It might also provide the rationale for the Service's resistance to releasing seized property, even in return for adequate surety. Finally, it may help explain the Service's fiercely litigious refusal to give notices of deficiency to terminated taxpayers. That issue has been joined in about 200 cases and presented in 606/ most circuit courts and the Supreme Court, even though its importance to the Service's effective administration of the Internal Revenue Code has never been demonstrated.

It is illuminating to contrast this fervor with ex-

Commissioner Thrower's objection to public interest litigation against the Service to affect substantive law: "These kinds of cases, arising outside the ordinary course, cutting across established procedures and consuming time and energy far beyond the average tax case, could be seriously disruptive of orderly administration. Unless such litigation fills great needs, it ought not to be encouraged either by the courts or the Congress. "It is in the public interest that the world's most efficient and fairly operated revenue system be protected from the possibility of extensive and significant interruptions and diversions." 607/ 

However, very few public interest lawsuits have been directed at the Cammissioner, while the expenditure of manpower on the deficiency notice question has been staggering.

At the very least, the Service's use of jeopardy powers may be interpreted as a vigorous effort to promote "voluntary compliance" with the Internal Revenue Code. But, if we are to give credence to the courts and the Internal Audit Division, which have found little or no legal basis for same assessments, the motivation is deeper than that. And if misused, the powers could inspire the reverse of voluntary compliance by fostering enmity toward the tax collector. Our communications from taxpayers indicate that non-compliance has been engendered at least as often as compliance. 

Thus, Commissioner Alexander deserves praise for urging that the use of jeopardy powers be restricted to situations where a tax is endangered. 

If these weapons may be utilized against drug pushers for no other reason than their status as such, what is to prevent their use against others, except public outrage? Non-revenue use is a misuse, and abuse of the Service's powers surely will weaken confidence in the system as the public becomes aware of such misuse.

Stated another way, employment of revenue-raising powers for other purposes is illegal, or at least unjust. Either breeds contempt by the public; this is true even when the end to which the agency acts is "good," i.e., stripping suspected narcotics traffickers of their possessions. 

5. Other Problems of Summary Collection Action. 

a. 

Judicial Review of Revenue Officer Discretion. 

The forcible collection of delinquent taxes can result in drastic consequences and injury to the delinquent taxpayer. But he is unlikely to obtain redress of real or imagined grievances in an action seeking either legal or equitable remedies.

The "Anti-injunction Act," S 7421 of the Code, has thwarted nearly all taxpayer attempts to restrain the forcible collection of taxes. Not only is the plaintiff required to meet the classic requirements for equitable relief, but he must also demonstrate that under no circumstances could the government ulti- 608/ mately prevail on the merits of the case. 

While taxpayers from time to time meet one or the other of these tests, it is rare that a court will intervene absent failure by the Service to provide the taxpayer with a notice of deficiency 609/ (in which case § 7421 by its terms does not apply). 

Prior equitable restraint of collection action thus almost never occurs. The action not restrained may, however, damage both personal and property rights of the taxpayer; but a suit for money damages against the United States will also fail. While the United States waived its sovereign immunity to such 610/ an action in the Federal Tort Claims Act, "[a]ny claim arising in respect of the assessment or collection of any tax." the waiver does not extend to 611/ The taxpayer's relief, if any, thus must be obtained from the Collection officer.

2 1 612/ But the individual may interpose the doctrine of official immunity, which shields government officials from liability for tort damages arising from acts of discretionary character falling within "the outer perimeter of [his] line of duty. 

As traced by the cases, the arc of this "outer perimeter" is at least hyperbolic. The official immunity decisions often refer to the rule laid down by Judge Hand: "What is meant by saying that the officer must be acting within his power cannot be more than that the occasion must be such as would have justified the act, if he had been using his power for any of the purposes on whose account it was vested in him." 613/ 

More recently, the Second Circuit has defined the phrase to mean that the of- 614/ ficial "must have been acting in his role as a government officer." act is within the hyperbola, its good faith is apparently irrelevant. 616/ does it matter that the act was erroneous. 

Indeed, the doctrine of official immunity may be applicable even to alleged violations of constitutional rights. 615/ If the Neither 617/ For the immunity doctrine to come into play, however, the act complained of must be discretionary in nature in addition to being "official." Although the line between acts which are discretionary (and thus protected) and those which are ministerial (thus not protected) may not always be clear, Revenue Officers have immense discretion at every turn. Even if his act was determined to be in a gray area, however, the Revenue Officer would be protected by the policy approach adopted by some courts, which weigh the nature of the duties of the immunity claimant and the interests of government in the one balance scale against the nature and extent of the injury to the plaintiff in the other. 618/ 

The importance of the revenue collection process to government and the sensitized reaction of many taxpayers to that process cannot be doubted.

An instructive opinion in the workings of the official immunity 619/ doctrine is Jackson v. Wise, in which a tax return preparer sought damages from three officials of the Service who allegedly violated his Fourth Amendment rights by authorizing a warrantless search and seizure of his books and records. The court first found that the Service's mandate to oversee the smooth operation of the revenue collection system endowed it with special powers to intrude, in a limited way, into the private lives of citizens because their tax returns are prepared in secrecy. Thus the search and the seizure of returns was within the scope of defendant's authority. 

So was their publicizing of plaintiff's arrest and conviction for causing a false income statement to be filed, because of the benefits to tax law 620/ enforcement.

Secondly, the court considered whether these acts were "discretionary.' The publicizing plainly was, particularly in view of the public nature of the information published. The decision to search without 621/ a warrant was not discretionary, however. 

However, the Jackson opinion considered a separate defense of good faith and reasonable belief as to the conduct to which immunity did not attach. Recognition of this independent defense was based on the proposition that public servants who must act in difficult situations are entitled to protection for good faith actions. claimed by plaintiff were not of great moment, the search had been conducted in a reasonable manner, and because a supporting opinion had been received from counsel, the defense of good faith and reasonable belief was sustained." 

Because the constitutional injuries 622/

49 Officers and employees of the Internal Revenue Service have been 623/ highly successful in asserting the official immunity defense, however. 

Jackson is the only case finding the defense inapplicable. Indeed, the courts have made the policy decision that this is not a great price to pay for the efficient running of the tax collection system. b. 

Seizures of Businesses.

The delinquent accounts of business taxpayers present problems which are often different from those involving individuals. First, an individual may have an easy levy source such as wages. Compared to seizures, the imposition of a levy is quick and simple, and the proceeds will be liquid sums directly applicable to the tax. A seizure and sale is complex and time-consuming and may draw attention away from other cases in inventory. 

Second, the effect of a levy is noncontinuing. The taxpayer and the family will be deprived of sustenance, perhaps for only a week's time, until the next paycheck (which under Service policy will not be levied) arrives. A seizure, however, may destroy the business (foreclosing collection of the tax therefrom) and disrupt the lives of its employees. Finally, in some cases, the withheld taxes may not have been applied to personal expenditures but may represent, in effect, the government's contribution to the capital of the business without which goods and services necessary to the business may not be acquired.

This different set of problems causes Revenue Officers, in their terminology, to attempt to determine whether the business is "viable." The proper definition of this term was not immediately apparent in our interviews

of the officers. Does it mean that assets may be sold or mortgaged to raise the funds necessary to liquidate the delinquency? Or does it mean that profit prospects (resulting from sales or reduced costs) are such as to indicate that the delinquency will be paid? Does it mean that the business need only stay "current" in its withholding payments, thus preventing increase of the liability but perhaps not reducing it? 

While most Revenue Officers seem to agree that this last definition of "viability" is the most accurate, that course may commit the government to a long-term business risk requiring constant monitoring. If so, when, if ever, should the exposure of the government's "share" of the capital (i.e., the tax dollars which were plowed into the enterprise) to business risks expire? On the other hand, viability may merely mean that on balance the chances of being paid are not worsened by the failure to seize. But, whichever, of these is meant is not designated by the Code, regulations, or the Internal Revenue Manual. There was, then, a facts-and-circumstances approach; obviously, given the several possible definitions of "viability," the facts and circumstances differed with each. 

Furthermore, there is little in Revenue Officer training to suggest that Revenue Officers are adequately trained to make such prognosticative economic determinations. Undoubtedly, experience is helpful; but there is little else which serves as a guide to "viability" of a business. Clearly, however, a new and small business seems to be regarded as less viable than an old or large one. Though the Service has no data on the makeup of the delinquent tax paying public, it does have figures which show a comparatively 624/ high delinquent return rate among small businesses.

1 In comparison to the highly subjective and difficult considerations presented by the business seizure, levy on assets of an individual taxpayer does not present a viability problem. Unless he quits or is discharged because a levy was effected, his capacity for paying taxes is likely to be unchanged. He remains "viable" with or without the seizure. 

There are additional factors which must be considered by the Revenue Officer looking at a business delinquency. Without seizure there may be no grounds on which to demonstrate that the delinquency is uncollectible and, hence, no grounds on which to suspend collection efforts. Also, forcible action is often viewed as exhibiting a firm collection posture which is believed by many Revenue Officers to be a positive assist up the career ladder.

On the other hand, seizure may result in the closure of the particular business with serious disruptions to the lives of many employees. 

Thus, the effect on the larger community of employees is generally considered as a restraint on seizure power. Certainly disruption to them resulting from seizure may be less than would occur if the business were allowed to continue for a period before financial collapse sets in from pressures exerted by non-tax creditors. Yet, the effect on third persons is considered and, we suggest, in many cases without the kind of information or prudent analysis which seems called for. Seizures sometimes seem to be delayed on the theory that, while no one knows about the future, the impact of a seizure on today's job is certain.

The intensity of these considerations may be equated with the size of the business. Seizures of a large business may cause many inconveniences and immediate distruptions of employees. A large business is also much more visible to the community and the media. Thus, size has a restraining influence. It is Internal Revenue Service policy to seize and sell a going business only after thorough consideration of all counter- 625/ vailing considerations and attempt to secure voluntary payment. countervailing considerations seem to intensify as an organization affects greater numbers of the public. The Internal Revenue Manual provides: "When it is determined that levy action is required, consideration should also be given to the possible sensitive nature of the case. It may be that the action will directly affect innocent third parties. 

For example, the seizure of a going business will affect the taxpayer's employees. . ."626/

The The larger the business, the more sensitive the case and the more reluctance 

Revenue Officers believe that "firmness" is not too to use seizure powers. important here. We learned of cases in which seizures were not made only because of the taxpayer's size. We were told that one such taxpayer is a hospital which ran up a delinquency exceeding $1 million. Adequate alternative health services were available had the hospital been closed, but after lengthy negotiations, the account was compromised for about two-thirds of the total amount owing. The uncollected amount was expunged. 

We doubt that size should be equated with virtue where collection of delinquent taxes is involved, except to the extent that forcible collection would result in long-term damage to the local economy. A large bakery in 

Manhattan, for example, should not be treated any differently from a twoman operation: its closure would create same economic dislocation in the

community because of unemployment of workers and less business for some suppliers, but the effect is a temporary one and may be less severe than awaiting a future date. Also, other bakeries will experience a rise in demand for their products, making it necessary to hire new employees and increase purchases of supplies.

In short, the government does not have an obligation to subsidize businesses so inefficient that they cannot pay taxes. The Internal Revenue 

Service recognizes this fact, but we are concerned that its significance may be obfuscated by issues of "sensitivity." 

C. Property Exempt from Levy. 

(1) 

Statutory Allowances.

All property and rights to property held by the taxpayer are subject to levy except to the extent it is exempted by § 6334 of the Code. While the intent of any exemption law must surely be to preserve the debtor and his family from destitution, the allowances of § 6334 are remarkably scroogian and haphazard. Section 6334 627/ 629/ overrides every other provision of Federal law, including the protections 628/ 630/ of bankruptcy, unless expressly excepted. The tax gatherer's reach extends to property exempted by more generous state laws even though it 631/ is state law from which the taxpayer's property rights derive. 

The present law exempts $500 in fuel, firearms, furniture, personal effects, livestock, poultry, and "provisions" to the taxpayer if he is the 633/ "head of a family", but not if he lives alone. While the bachelor thus gets no food, he and every other taxpayer is allowed any "necessary" clothing

634/ and school books and $250 worth of books and tools used in his business. 

State and Federal unemployment benefits are exempt, but not welfare. 636/ 637/ 638/ The statute protects some military pensions, but not others; rail- 639/ road retirement benefits, 640/ but not old age security benefits; Workmen's 641/ 

Compensation awards, but not Social Security disability. 642/ Unopened mail is also excluded from levy. Finally, certain savings (not exceeding $10,000), deposited with the United States by armed forces personnel and 643/ public health officers permanently stationed overseas, are also exempt.

Administrative Exemptions. 

(2) (a) 

Exemptions for Wages and Periodic Income. 

Existing Practice. 

(i) The minimal exemptions accorded by the statute leave the Service with a drastic residue of levy power. The Congress may have desired merely to facilitate collection of the tax; but punishment, and thus discouragement, of tax delinquencies may have been intended. The committee reports do not reveal what was intended. Section 6334 (c) merely declares that no property other than that which is specifically enumerated is exempt, "[n]otwithstanding any other law of the United States." However, strict application of the jigsaw logic featured in the statutory scheme has been rejected by the agency. 651/ To exempt property from levy is one thing, but to refrain from applying the levy power is another. While Congress forbade the Service to apply the levy to certain items, neither did it compel the powers to be used. 

The distinction has not been lost on the Service, which has in practical effect 652/ created additional classes of exempt property.

Welfare and Manpower 653/ 

Development Training Act grants are not levied upon, nor are certain military dependents' allotments.

Although no rationale is stated in the 654/

Manual for the latter practice, the welfare and MDTA exemptions are grounded on a conclusive presumption that "undue hardship" would result from levy 655/ thereon.

This reasoning is based on (1) the nature of the payments and (2) the conflict with another governmental objective which would result from levy. Hence, another means to liquidate the account will be sought and, if none exists, the case is reported uncollectible if voluntary payment is not made. 

Most levies

These administrative exemptions are consistent with the Service's express policy of abstaining from use of the levy power in any case when 656/ "undue hardship" to the taxpayer would otherwise result. are likely to visit some hardship on the taxpayer. But neither the writers of the Internal Revenue Manual nor Revenue Officers are able to define 657/ As though to clarify matters somewhat sort of hardship is "undue". what, the Manual lists several kinds of income which are generally not to 658/ be garnished.

Only in "flagrant" cases will Social Security, Medicare, 660/ death benefits, or assorted forms of public-benefit income be attached. 

Even though the case be "flagrant", levy is permissible only if there is otherwise no (undefined) "undue hardship." It was thus not surprising to discover that nearly all Revenue Officers interviewed by us believed that 661/ usage of levy powers varies substantially among their colleagues.

659/ Apart from exempting certain income items, the Service has officially eschewed garnishment of successive paychecks. As an administrative 662/ 663/ convenience, it confines levies to take-home pay. 

Aside from limiting the effect of levies, the Service's policy is also to release levies if it

'664/ appears that the tax is not owed. 

Finally, if levy may cause undue hardship, the Service may allow installment payments or write off the account as uncollectible. 665/ We have little information on the extent to which these policies are followed. Although hundreds of thousands of levies are made each year, the quantity of complaints is small. The number never voiced because of ignorance, fear, or simple resignation will never be known. But, the 667/ Service asserts that errors are nearly nonexistent.

666/ It does appear reasonable to assume that the levies made nearly always fit within the spacious confines of the law. Nonetheless, our interviews with line Collection personnel confirm that the imposition of wage levies is the single most powerful magnet for taxpayer complaints concerning 668/ the Service's collection activities. It is also a subject for criticism by the news media. Some hostility is no doubt engendered by the curious status of Internal Revenue as the one Federal agency which takes from each of us, but confers few tangible benefits aside from tax refunds. But it is far more significant that few outside the Service seem to comprehend the very drastic nature of the levy powers. On the contrary, the Service often is equated in the public eye with private collection agencies; thus, for example, many seem to resent the Service's garnishment of entire paychecks without prior judicial approval, a practice which is far beyond the powers 669/ of a private creditor. 

Another argument for limiting the levy powers comes from the practice of imposing a great many levies "blind" (i.e., without prior personal contact with the taxpayer).

Without personal contact to warn the taxpayer of the 670/

gravity of the situation, the levy may to him be startling as well as drastic. This may be true even though the average individual delinquent taxpayer receives four notices that the tax is owing. As previosuly discussed, 671/ while the levy thus cannot be said to be entirely unheralded, there is some doubt that these notices are effective at least with respec: to taxpayers who have not previously been through the collection process. Fear, sloth, inadvertence, and illiteracy make it doubtful that all notices are read. Those who do read the notices may be lulled by the repeated unfulfilled warnings to pay within ten days. They are not made aware of how little of their property is exempt from levy unless the information is requested. When ten days have passed from delivery of the final notice and demand, the local office is authorized to levy immediately. But levy almost never occurs at the termination of the tenday period. More likely, levy occurs several weeks after the running of the ten-day period and seventeen weeks or more after the mailing of the first notice. It often comes without a new warning. The effect may be real hardship to a wage earner, who in losing his entire take-home pay may temporarily be worse off than if he had been receiving some public dole exempt from levy. He cannot be blamed for considering the result to be extreme, if not unjust. If he feels unfairly treated, it seems doubtful that the levy will encourage voluntary compliance by him with the tax laws. 

Some Proposals for Change. (ii) The exemption statutes have recently come under considerable criticism for their failure to allow some minimum level of sustenance to the wage earner. The Tax Section of the American Bar 

Association has proposed an exemption of $100 per week, net of taxes withheld
