Pending action of some kind by the Congress, should Internal Revenue devise a more restrained use of levies? The agency has considered the matter of across-the-board wage exemptions of various kinds. One such review of the question took place during 1961 when the then Chicago Region proposed to exclude from the initial levy, on a test basis, a flat $25 for a 674/ single taxpayer and $40 for a person with dependents. The proposal was eventually withdrawn on the objection of the national office that § 6334 of the Code compelled the taking of all take-home pay up to the amount of 6757 delinquency. This rationale of inclusio unius est exclusio alterius. has apparently been abandoned, but the test proposed by the Chicago office was never undertaken.

Indeed, the Service has found other grounds upon which to continue to resist suggestions that it restrict levies, on either a percentage or a dollar basis, to less than the net paycheck. In response to an inquiry from Senator Montoya eliciting its view of the ABA recommendation, the Service argued that (1) its existing procedures adequately protected taxpayers, and (2) "any set exclusion from levy would considerably hamper our efforts to collect from elusive and chronically delinquent taxpayers. "1 676/

Collection Division management believes that the four written 678/ notices (including the "Final Notice Before Seizure") adequately alert the taxpayer to the possible consequences of failure to contact the Service before levy occurs. As we have seen, this is a doubtful proposition for those who do not or cannot read them. Even those who do, however, are not thereby advised that their entire paychecks may be taken. Indeed, the reasonable belief of those who have experienced levy only by commercial creditors is that the garnishment will reach about one-quarter of the pay- 677/ check, allowing a minimum level of subsistence. They may not realize the completeness of the Service's power to tie up wages even when they read its pamphlet explaining taxpayer rights in the collection process. 

To demonstrate that taxpayers are adequately protected from deprivation of life's essentials, the Service also pointed out to Senator Montoya that it generally (1) levies only on alternate paychecks, (2) limits the garnishments to "take home" pay, (3) releases the levy if there is reasonable doubt as to the existence of a liability and (4) makes alternate 679/ arrangements if there is "undue hardship or loss, i.e., financial loss. 

The first three arguments are less than convincing. If a taxpayer does not expect the loss of his entire paycheck, he may have few reserves with which to buy food or medical supplies until he is next paid if it is a bona fide financial hardship which caused the tax delinquency in the first place. The limitation of garnishment to take-home pay is immaterial to the wage earner, who was not going to have the withheld funds anyway. The levy may lead to loss of employment, making it necessary for the State to support the taxpayer or his family through public assistance and, ironically giving the taxpayer

the benefit of an administrative levy exemption. Finally, while levy is released if there is doubt as to the existence of the liability, this does not protect the taxpayer against whom a wage levy is proper under the 680/ statute.

The Service's fourth argument is that as a matter of administrative practice it accedes to taxpayer pleas of undue hardship, thus effecting a minimum subsistence exemption. However, no definition of "undue hardship" is given in the Manual's instructions on use of levies. The Collection Officers interviewed by us were similarly unable to define the term and, moreover, differed significantly on the nature and quantum of proof required for a showing of hardship. Our interviewees agreed that some officers were substantially quicker to use levies than others, and that taxpayers could be treated quite differently depending upon which Collection Officer was assigned to the case.

In addition to these systemic objections, the Service has insisted that a set levy exclusion would hamper the collection process. In 1971, the then Commissioner, Randolph W. Thrower wrote, in response to the ABA proposal, "[f]urther dilution of the levy process could only benefit the intentional 681/ evader. That is unquestionable, but additional statutory exemptions will similarly help those wage earners who do not evade their tax obligations. 

Revenue Officers generally indicated to us a willingness to levy more quickly where an incorrigible was concerned, but agreed that if assets could be found, the only issue was whether "undue hardship" would result from levy. What hardship was "undue" admittedly varied from person to person. Of course, the identification of the evader is likewise a highly subjective process.

Finally, Commissioner Thrower opposed a minimum subsistence levy exemption because "feasibility studies have consistenly indicated that any "1 682/ That type of levy exclusion would be impractical and unworkable. conclusion was based not on usage of such an exemption but on the conclusions of an in-house study group of five district directors convened to review the Service's levy practices. That group concluded, among other things, that the imposition of new Federal levy exclusions would impose a difficult burden on employers who in some cases are faced with complex state exclusion 683/ requirements. This was thought to be true even if the Service did nothing more than track the exclusions permitted under the various state laws, in which case the Service might not appear to be treating taxpayers 684/ evenhandedly. Even if some nationwide exclusions were to be adopted, it was believed that there could be no agreement on what exclusion would be reasonable and that hardship to taxpayers from levies would continue to occur. Finally, it was noted that additional exclusions would necessitate use of more manpower and levies to liquidate delinquent accounts, meaning that accounts would remain in inventory longer, swelling the Service's caseload. 

Although it is true that additional levy exclusions might mean greater problems of record keeping for employers, their burden is already substantial. However, under the present system some employees are driven to quit their jobs by the specter of losses of entire paychecks. With a minimum subsistence exclusion, some of these employees may feel able to carry on, thus reducing the burden on the employer to find and train new employees. 

Some hardship will continue to result but may be expected to be less frequent and less severe.

1 1. 

While the minimum subsistence exemption may also increase the Service's workload, the amount of the increase is surely relative to the type of exclusion. A small dollar exclusion such as that proposed by the 

Chicago Region ($25 or $40 exempted from the first levy only) may not raise inventory much. The increase might also be affected by the number and kind of taxpayers who qualify for the exclusion. One might apply it to all delinquents, or to those for whom TDA's have been issued not more than twice, or to individuals, but not employers. 686/ However, 685/ The applicability of a wage exclusion would seem to be as important as its amount. It might be determined by the purpose of the levy. 

According to many Revenue Officers, the message from management is to the effect that "[f]irm enforcement [i.e., use of levies] fosters compliance, and that the fostering of compliance is the agency's goal. nobody knows whether levies do increase compliance, and the proposition is at least questionable in view of the very large number of "repeater" delinquents. 

However, the habitual or willful delinquent is not a sympathetic figure. 

Further, if a delinquent taxpayer has once been subjected to the full brunt of a levy, he should know enough to contact the Service to work out a voluntary payment arrangement if he is beset with financial hardship not of his own making.

A subsidiary purpose of having a "blind" wage levy against a taxpayer who has not responded to notices should be to persuade him to contact the Service and arrange voluntary liquidation of the remaining delinquency. 

From the Service's point of view, the success of further wage levies depends upon (1) further expenditure of manpower; (2) cooperation by the employer in 687/

not prepaying the salary of the employee since a subsequent levy reaches only the salary owing at the moment of attachment; and (3) continuation of the employment relationship. These problems are avoided by some kind of voluntary arrangement which can be tailored to the individual case. 

Therefore, it seems to us that the Service should allow a minimm subsistence exemption to a taxpayer being subjected to levy for the first time. Such an exemption might be modelled along the lines of the general 688/ Federal wage exemption statute presently in force (which would foist no new accounting procedures on the employer) or be a flat dollar exclusion such as that proposed by the ABA. We suggest that the exclusion apply only to the first levy, and that no other levies be made against the taxpayer in the next few weeks unless the revenues will otherwise be jeopardized. The exemption might vary according to the number of dependents claimed by the taxpayer on his return.

In sending the required written notice of wage levy to the taxpayer, the Service might include a warning that subsequent levies on the entire paycheck will follow if no voluntary arrangement to pay the tax is made. While some taxpayers may abscond before the second levy is made (whether or not they contact the Service), the voluntary payment of taxes by the great majority of citizens makes it likely that any first time delinquent taxpayer is a member of that majority. While he may not be, we believe that to give him the benefit of the doubt on the first levy will not occasion great loss of revenue and may generate goodwill for the Internal Revenue and possibly also ease some of its burdens.

(b) 

Exempt Assets. 

(i) 

Current Practice. 

There are very few seizures relative to the number of lien filings or wage levies. 

Seizures are imposed to well under one 689/ percent of taxpayer delinquent accounts and, while they are normally thought of as distraints upon tangible assets, many are solely upon such liquid assets as the contents of a cash register. These have much the same effect as a levy. The Service does not know the nature of seizures which are imposed in any given year, however, which may range from seizures of the contents of cash registers to the padlocking of businesses. This discussion will focus upon nonliquid assets. 

Because seizures are rare, one may argue that taxpayers' assets are substantially exempt from levy. However, this might be of little comfort to one who is subjected to seizure and sale of his assets. The restraint shown by Revenue officers in making seizures is the result of several factors.

One is the general rule that levy action will be avoided if undue hardship will result. The determination of hardship seems somehow more tangible when a valuable, nonliquid asset is involved. In the case of individual delinquent taxpayers, these are frequently automobiles and homes. 

Seizures and sale of an automobile might deprive the taxpayer of any means of getting to work, thus costing him his job and making collection of the tax much less likely. Forced sale of a home might constitute a deprivation of investment disproportionate to the delinquency.

All of the Revenue Officers whom we interviewed mentioned the hardship consideration, but none could define the term. However, all considered a seizure to be a last resort. This attitute seemed genuine but was, by their admission, largely a recognition of the difficulties involved in seizing property and selling it. The procedure is complex and time-consuming; it involves much accounting, planning and general paperwork. For all the difficulties encountered, the tax delinquency will be reduced only by the application of sale proceeds in excess of expenses 690/ of sale and administration and satisfaction of prior claims.

691/ By contrast, the notice of levy procedure against liquid assets held by a third party is very simple, and the dollars which are produced are fully applied to the tax liability, without deduction for expenses. 

This has the result of liquidating liabilities and thus "closing" cases which many Revenue Officers believe beneficially affects their evaluation by management.

A seizure and sale, on the other hand, entails a large investment of time and effort but may not result in a case closure. 

As a practical matter, then, non-liquid assets in the hands of the taxpayer are virtually exempt from levy. Thus, it is not surprising that while the Service has established several exemptions for types of income, it has no policy excluding classes of nonliquid assets from distraint. It has 692/ not, for example, adopted such state law exemptions as homesteads.

(ii) 

Proposals for Change. 

While the establishment of exemptions from seizure in specific pecuniary terms has the laudable effect of clearly

circumscribing exercise of the Service's seizure authority, the dollar limitations have not been adjusted since 1954 to reflect changes in the cost of living. The protections of § 6334 (a), expressed monetarily, are 693/ less than 25 percent of what its predecessor allowed in 1866. Not only has the exclusion of only $500 for provisions, furniture, and fuel become restrictive, it also lacks any flexibility to accommodate the differing needs of particular families. The $250 exclusion for tools and books used in the taxpayer's trade takes no realistic account of the varying requirements of any profession. 

Valuation of used personal effects is a peculiarly difficult problem. The Manual's sole instructions on appraisals directs that "inven- 694/ tory" values be used. Adequate though that may be for business seizures, it holds little or no pertinence for seizures of personal assets, with respect to which a better approach would be a listing of basic household furnishings to be exempted without regard to their value. For example, one bed, chair, and lamp per person, a refrigerator, table, and couch, per household and enough fuel to heat the living unit would appear to be appropriate minimal exemptions from personal asset seizure, since IRS rarely takes such things anyway. 

Alternatively, the Service might adopt as exemptions the state law restrictions on assets which are subject to attachment. However, since state law provisions vary widely, it may be argued that they would not be suitable for any effort to give equal treatment on a nationwide basis to similarly situated taxpayers. Sensitivity to, and a sense of urgency about, the need for reform in the area of asset exemption are dulled by the rarity of seizures

and the lack of data on the Service's practice when seizure does occur. d. Costs of Seizure and Sale.

The Internal Revenue Code prescribes that proceeds of seizure and sale are to be applied first against the cost of the seizure and 695/ Put sale proceedings before being used to diminish the tax liability. another way, only the net proceeds of sale may be applied in diminution of the tax debt. The statute thus establishes priorities but leaves to the secretary or his delegate the determiniation of the expenses which are to 696/ The regulations promulgated pursuant to this authority permit the District Director to assess the costs of sale and the expenses be allowed. of presale protection and preservation of the property against the delinquent taxpayers. Allowable expenses do not, however, include salary and overhead 697/ of the Service.

This order of priorities is a time-honored principle of creditor's rights: the debtor, who by failing to meet his obligations makes it necessary for his creditor to incur costs to obtain involuntary payment through the courts, should bear these costs. But the relationship of government and taxpayer differs greatly from that of commerical creditor and debtor. Unlike a commerical creditor, who is required by due process to seek prior judicial 693/ approval of any forcible collection action, the government may exercise its distraint powers without even a hearing. And, as we have seen, the powers of the tax collector to distrain property summarily are affected by the garnishment exemptions of neither state nor Federal law applicable to 700/ commercial creditors. 699/ Furthermore, the Internal Revenue Service sees its mission as not only collecting the tax but also encouraging future compliance 701/ with the law.

Given the special features of the relationship between the Service and the delinquent taxpayer, the allocation of sale proceeds first to expenses bears some re-examination. A review of the Service's Internal Audit 

Division into 289 sales of seized property of individual and business taxpayers in seven districts for the seven-month period ended January 31, 1972, revealed that the net proceeds (proceeds after deduction of costs pursuant to § 6342 in 42 (14.5 percent) of them did not exceed the cost, salary and 702/ overhead allocable to the proceeding. Salary and overhead exceed net proceeds in 90 percent of sales in which the net proceeds were less than $100 and 40 percent of those yielding less than $400. Ninety-five of the sales (30.4 percent) had net proceeds of less than $400. We have no other facts on these sales from Internal Audit which are relevant to our immediate consideration.

This low yield of some sales suggests a number of negative possibilities. The Revenue Officer may have erred in judging the amount to be realized. Or the restraint that a seizure and sale should not result in undue hardship was not adequately heeded. Or perhaps that term is so elusive that definition is impossible and hence varies substantially from officer to officer. But whatever the reason, one wonders whether "undue" hardship resulted where sales proceeds were low. On the other hand, the paucity of proceeds in some cases suggests that Revenue Officers exercised their powers with restraint.

What may be a desirable rule, though nothing similar to it has been adopted by the Service, is that seizure and sale not be undertaken unless

the proceeds thereof are expected by the Revenue Officer to equal the salary and overhead to be invested. Though salary and overhead do not reduce the proceeds of sale applicable to the tax debt, it seems that the Service should not, as a rule, spend more than the amount expected to be collected. Internal Audit found little to justify so doing and questioned whether compliance with the tax laws is promoted by such 703/ sales.

The Collection Division response to the Internal Audit findings pointed out that considerations must be discarded in the seizure and sale of a delinquent business which may be the only means by which it may 704/ be prevented from "pyramiding" liabilities. In other words it may be necessary to close down a business through seizure and sale procedures to terminate a spiral of unpaid credits against employee income tax liabilities regardless of the costs of the proceeding. And because the officers of the corporate taxpayer responsible may remain personally 705/ liable to satisfy the unpaid withholding obligations, the Service need not commit itself to keeping the business in operation in the hope that the business will ultimately become solvent enough to make payment of the liability. Moreover, there may be some additional, unquantifiable benefit from the seizure such as encouragement to other taxpayers to meet their tax obligations. 

Thus, the Collection Division argued that the need to halt pyramiding, the prospect of payment from a corporate officer, and the need to maintain a firm enforcement image overcame considerations of undue hardship. While the pyramiding point is obviously a valid one, there apparently was little

mot to suggest it was the major determinant or that an effort to keep the business current had been made. As to the other factors, Internal Audit 

Et seemingly questioned whether they could outweigh the hardship. ei B. 12 F 3 Moreover, the Collection Division's response was limited to pyramiding argument is not relevant. seizures of business assets; as to seizures of assets of individuals, the 

The question then becomes whether any other benefit accrues from use of the seizure and sale powers to collect just a few tax dollars from non-business taxpayers. Internal 

Audit suggested that benefits to the Service from seizure and sale of low-value personal property are questionable. Certainly the slight (if any) diminution of their tax liability makes clear that the taxpayers are not benefitted. The Internal Audit study thus raises the question whether the Service should ignore economics in seizures and sales in cases involving individual taxpayers, even where habitual delinquents are concerned. The Service may accomplish little by the action. 

Moreover, if the taxpayer is a "resister" (one who actually avoids paying the tax), an inefficient expenditure of time and effort by the Service may be precisely what he desires. The use of seizure and sale powers against personal assets should be limited to substantially revenue-producing situations unless it is necessary to prevent an employer from "pyramiding" liabilities. 

The recommendation of the Internal Audit Division was that this might be brought about through closer supervisory review. The Manual calls for a pre-seizure conference by the Revenue Officer with his Group Manager and for review of the case file by the Special Procedures Staff after the sale has been completed by the Revenue Officer. However, there is evidence

706/ that pre-seizure conference does not occur in a significant number of cases. 

The review of the Special Procedures Staffs was not directed to quality but rather to whether all the necessary forms were received from Revenue Officers and in some cases whether they were properly prepared. While the Internal 

Audit evaluation was prepared over two years ago, we are not aware that practices have changed. There is still no requirement that the Group 

Manager review, much less approve, a proposed seizure and sale of assets. 

A requirement of supervisory approval would be desirable as a potential check on unwise seizures. The Revenue Officer may be expected to have acquired familiarity with the taxpayer's circumstances, and presumably would base, thereon, his decision to seize. The Group Manager will form some opinion about the judgment of the Revenue Officer. His opinion may lead him to scrutinize the facts developed by some more closely than those developed by others. promoted out of the ranks of Revenue Officers, they should have technical skill and experience to enable them to give adequate review.

In addition to closer management involvement, the organization might emphasize cost considerations in seizing property of individual taxpayers. As previously suggested, a possible rule is to impose seizures only if the gross proceeds of sale can reasonably be anticipated to exceed expenses of sale, salaries, and overhead, and the sum of prior encumbrances. 

Moreover, the regulations requiring sale proceeds to be applied first to the expenses of the proceedings might be revised to eliminate or minimize chargeable expenses. The underlying statute § 6342 seems to permit amendment by the Secretary,

ויו 41 

Supervisory review, clearer guidelines, and diminution of chargeable expenses might discourage some sales whose "profitability" is difficult to prognosticate. Whatever deterrent effect there may be to the seizure, it would be lost if not made (though the extent of the loss is dubious); collection of some small amounts of revenue would be delayed. 

But these drawbacks seem marginal. As opposed to selling distrained property at a low net yield (which could be expressed as a minimum dollar figure), it could instead be released to the nonbusiness taxpayer. Release does not require the payment of any part of the tax nor does it prevent future seizure by Internal Revenue. And while § 6335 (d) of the Code states that sale shall be within a specified time after giving public notice, this does not foreclose the authority of the Service to release property. A decision to release the property may be made on the ground that eventual collection of the liability may be aided thereby. 

Finally, the use of seizure and sale powers to produce minimal amounts of revenue may be diminished if there is clarification of the purposes to be accomplished by their use. We now turn to that issue. 

The Purpose of Summary Collection Action. 

e.

The Code and Regulations fail to suggest when the Service's drastic powers created should be used. They direct only when the powers may not be used. Legislative history does not indicate that 

Congress has considered the purpose of these drastic instruments; hence, considerable discretion is reposed in the Service. 

The Internal Revenue Manual provides few rules. Levy will some-times be made automatically in the absence of any response from the taxpayer

707/ Seizure to notice and demand for payment of the delinquency, for example. 708/ may be made if that will be "worthwhile.

There are generally no concrete guidelines. In fact, the absence of a particular set of criteria in the Manual may manifest significant organizational confusion over the purpose of summary action. We do not know whether the confusion has always existed or whether it merely reflects the lack of written guidance, but exist it does.

Nowhere is the uncertainty more evident than in the area of seizures of nonliquid personal assets from taxpayers. The review by Internal Audit 709/ of seizure and sale activities previously discussed revealed facts 710/ tending to support this analysis, as did our own interviews. For example, the Internal Audit study concluded that twenty-six of seventy seizures in one district were made before the taxpayer's equity in the property was determined; in another three, seizures were made despite a known lack of 711/ equity in the property. In fourteen of the twenty-nine instances the property was returned to the taxpayer without securing either payment of the tax or an agreement to pay. Finally, there was wide disparity in the methods of setting the "minimum bid price" (below which the property will not be sold at auction), which may substantially affect the amount received on 712/ sale.

Internal Audit concluded that these results indicated a lack of management involvement. 714/ ing. 713/ The Collection Division acquiesced in this find- On a policy level, Internal Audit took the view that seizure of property having little equity or value may create the appearance of taxpayer harassment, and it questioned whether seizure and sale of low value property 715/ fosters voluntary compliance with the tax law.

The Collection Division's response, as we saw, was limited to a defense of its business seizure practices. 716/ 

The Collection 

Division also made the general observation that to impose a seizure, "[t]he prime factors to be considered [by the Revenue Officer] are compliance and enforcement." 717/ This statement does not reflect anything to be found in agency publications such as training materials or the Internal Revenue Manual. 

However, nearly all Revenue Officers interviewed by us believe that management desires expeditious use of "firm enforcement" collection methods--use of liens, levies, and seizures-to collect the tax speedily and to encourage compliance with the tax laws. Management and line personnel agree that as a rule summary methods will tend to collect the tax more quickly than voluntary means. But line personnel often allow considerations of taxpayer hardship to prevent or delay "enforcement".

The element of encouraging "compliance" is more puzzling. While this aim has been adopted wholeheartedly by Service management, nobody has ever quantified the effect of liens and levies either upon the taxpaying public or upon the delinquents themselves. One desirable effect would be to reduce the inclination of a repeater delinquent to again ignore his tax debt. 

But the extent to which considerations of encouraging compliance should govern a particular case is not touched upon in the Manual and is a matter or uncertainty among Revenue Officers.

Many Revenue Officers interviewed by us believe that a significant issue in their evaluation by management and promotions is based on their usage of the summary collection powers. Until early 1975, the raw number of

liens, levies, and seizures made by each district was reported to the district by the national office. Nothing else about these activitiesthe collections produced by sales, reasons for use, releases, and redemptions of property--was reported. This is not to suggest that the agency should be keeping more statistics, but that it seems to be measuring the wrong thing. If the numbers of liens, levies, and seizures are what is measured, then leins, levies, and seizures are what the national office will get. If quality indicators are measured, more quality may be achieved. It is only natural for the human mind to conclude that what is measured is what is wanted. We were told, by line personnel, of several cases in which Revenue 

Officers seized businesses comprised of a number of items, such as washing machines in a laundromat, and claimed a seizure for each machine, although only one seizure (the laudromat) could be claimed under proper reporting. 

On one of these occasions, so we were told, the officer reported upwards of twenty seizures, which resulted in a commendatory letter from the national office.

However, experienced managers in the national office stated that such a letter would not have been issued. 

The emphasis on numbers gives rise to more serious possibilities of abuse, such as the instances reported by Internal Audit of seizures of property in which the taxpayer was known to possess no equity. In each case the property was returned without payment of the tax. Such action exposes the Service to suggestions that it is misusing its powers and thus may tend to diminish voluntary compliance by the public--a damaging result for our self-assessment system of taxation.

reż sin 30 57 Lacking guidance, Revenue Officers vary in their criteria for seizure of assets of individual taxpayers. Some told us that they will seize only when they expect to make forced sale of the seized assets. Others claimed to seize only when it was anticipated that the taxpayer would redeem the property. A few mentioned making seizures to impress the tax- 

E payer with the serious consequences of not meeting his tax obligation. So long as the Internal Revenue Service fails to delineate clear purposes for the use of summary powers, we believe that these divergent criteria will continue to exist. The variations in practice may lead to the appearance of arbitrariness and caprice in some actions, thus undermining the taxpaying public's confidence in (and compliance with) the taxing system.

B. 

Alternatives to Forcible Collection and Immediate Voluntary Satisfaction of the Delinquency. 

1. Accounts "Deferred" from Immediate Action. a. Generally.

We have seen that forcible action to collect a delinquent account usually will not be initiated until several notices and demands for to individual taxpayers; three are sent to businesses. payment have been sent to the taxpayer. Four such notices are normally sent 718/ 719/ 

In 1973 at least one notice was mailed in regard to some 7,380,000 individual and business accounts. However, only 2,746,216 of these were sent to district offices in 720/ the form of TDA's for further collection efforts. 

Thus, about 4.5 million delinquent accounts were not assigned to local offices as TDA's. While this was usually because the accounts had been fully paid, some 817,125 of them 721/ were not.

Nonetheless, issuance of TDA's on these accounts was "suppressed" because they involved only small balances due. This procedure, re- 722/ ferred to as "deferral" of accounts by "dollar tolerance," enables the Service to concentrate its limited manpower on larger delinquencies, and it was made possible by the computerized processing of delinquent accounts. 

There is a substantial expenditure of Service Center computer time and manpower in the issuance of TDA's. Similarly, the local offices make heavy investments in managing the TDA's and, of course, in carrying on further collection efforts. Thus, by deferring these small accounts, both the Service Center and local offices are able to concentrate their finite resources on the larger cases, which by themselves appear sufficiently numerous to keep all personnel busily employed. On the other hand, by keeping the "deferred

H. 3 account" in the Master Files, the account is not lost and may be paid or finally become sufficiently large (through accrual of interest and penalties or addition of new delinquencies) to be generated as a TDA. If 817,125 accounts deferred in 1973 had instead been sent to local offices for collection, they would have swelled the number of 1973 TDA issuances by about 30 percent. 

In terms of dollars, however, the cases deferred in 1973, even when added to previously deferred accounts, totalled slightly more than $50 million, or about 1 percent of the Service's total dollar inventory of uncollected taxes. 

The deferral of small accounts allows a more intensive application of manpower to larger accounts. Although failure to make any personal or forcible collection effort may have a negative effect on compliance of taxpayers whose accounts were deferred, this negative effect is not quantifiable. If the account is ultimately collected, which is very likely, the government does have some recompense, in the form of accumulating interest and penalties, 723/ for the failure to pay the tax. Thus, while the adverse effects of deferring accounts is speculative, the manpower benefits are clear and governmental pecuniary loss is minimized. b. Procedure. 

While delinquent Individual Master File (IMF) taxpayers ordinarily receive four notices (and Business Master File (BMF) taxpayersthree), individuals whose unpaid balance is less than a minimum dollar amount 724/ receive only two notices (and BMF taxpayers-only one). No further notices and demands for payment are sent to IMF or BMF taxpayers so long as the balance 725/ due is under the minimum, though semi-annual reminders are sent to individuals to notify them of the amount of the unpaid obligation and of the accrual of 726/ penalties and interest.

There are three ways in which an account may be eliminated from deferred status. It may be paid voluntarily. It may be involuntarily cllected by deduction from a refund claimed by the taxpayer on a subsequent 727/ tax return. (This is referred to as "refund offset.") Or, if the accumulation of subsequent tax liabilities, penalties, and interest raises the balance due to the dollar tolerance level, the account will be generated to the district office as a TDA. 728/ The great majority of deferred cases leave deferral status quickly by one of these three methods. Most deferred accounts, particularly those of individual taxpayers, leave deferred status through offset of refunds which 729/ would otherwise be paid to the taxpayer. 

Refund offset occurs as a byproduct of returns processing. Initially, the return is received by the 

Service Center, and its data are transcribed to a computer tape which goes to the National Computer Center (NCC) for posting to the Master File. The 

NCC computer is programmed to reduce any refund claimed by the taxpayer to the extent of any liabilities outstanding against his account. The likelihood of collecting delinquencies by refund offset is substantial for individual accounts. During 1973, nearly 82 percent of Form 1040's filed sought refunds, the claimed overpayments normally being the result of overwithholding of income taxes by employers. Corporations are not subject to withholding and 731/ file relatively few returns claiming refunds. While few Business Master 

File deferred accounts are thus candidates for refund offset, about one-third 732/ of them are believed to be satisfied by voluntary payment.

730/

ily: BQUE the The the al Many other deferred BMF and IMF accounts are assigned as TDA's to district offices when accrued taxes (including delinquencies on later returns), penalties, and interest exceed the minimum dollar tolerance. In these instances no further demands and no "final notice before seizure" are mailed by the Ser- 733/ vice Center.

The debtor is instead personally contacted by the district office regarding the balance due. If this does not result in satisfaction of the account, the final notice is given and forcible collection efforts may follow.

When the taxpayer with an existing deferred account incurs a new liability, the notices and demands for payment sent to him are in the amount of the latest delinquency only and do not reflect the combined indebtedness. 

This results from a computer programming problem which the Service has been unable to resolve. However, once the computer assigns a TDA to the district office, it will include the previously deferred indebtednees. If the new delinquency is below the dollar tolerance, it will be deferred after two notices. If, when the new delinquency is combined with other deferred lia- 734/ bilities the total amount due is raised to the tolerance level, a TDA will be issued without the mailing of further notices or demands. 

Some accounts are not removed from deferred status by these methods, and eventually become barred by the statute of limitations forbidding for- 735/ cible collection of the account more than six years after assessment.

736/ In 1973, 101,759 deferred accounts totalling $1,715,560 became barred by the statute of limitations. The Service has not translated the numbers of accounts and dollars barred into the loss rate of deferred accounts, but

believes that the percentage is small. There is some support for that view in other figures which reveal that of the individual income tax accounts added to deferred inventory during 1972, about 18 percent had not left that 737/ status, through collection or otherwise, by mid-1974. Most of them do not languish at length, therefore, which suggests that few are not collected before the statute runs.

C. 

Small Accounts Not Deferred. 

Not all delinquent accounts are subject to deferral. An account is not deferred if the liability is that of an IRS employee, a taxpayer on whom a TDA is already outstanding, or a taxpayer who has been selected for "special handling" by a district office on the basis of a history of resisting payment or otherwise being habitually delinquent. Delinquent accounts of Internal Revenue employees are not deferred because they may be familiar with the tolerance level and, thus, may attempt to take advantage of it. (Failure of a Service employee to file his return or pay taxes is a basis for dismissal.) New delinquencies of taxpayers on whom a TDA is already outstanding are not deferred, doubtless because it is hardly more expensive to collect two delinquencies than it is to collect one. 

However, the exceptions from deferral of accounts of chronic delinquents present some difficult questions. These accounts are coded with a "Q" on the Integrated Data Retrieval System (IDRS) to denote that the taxpayer is a resister or a habitual delinquent. The Internal Revenue Manual allows Q-coding if, in the discretion of the local office, "expeditious 738/ issuance of the TDA's. . .is considered necessary. 

Presumably, &

hat coding would be based on same prior experience by the local office in collecting a delinquent account of that taxpayer. Thus, when a subsequent de- oft 739/ he balance due amounting to at least $25 olle ​linquency appears and the taxpayer does not respond to one notice of a on his Q-coded account, a IDA will be sent to the local office without further notice and demand. The case 740/ LI is then immediately assigned to a Revenue Officer for personal contact. 

Beyond the word "necessary," the Internal Revenue Manual says nothing to indicate when the account may be Q-coded by the local office. The decision so to code the account is thus entirely subjective. While the national office generally supposes that Q-coding is limited to those tax- 741/ payers with a history of being delinquent, any unpaid balance is sufficient to give one a "history" of delinquency. But, a history may not be necessary if one is a "tax resister" (the term "tax resister" is, however, not defined by the Manual or other national office criteria). Thus, tremendous latitude is given the local office; moreover, no instructions are given by the Manual regarding who should exercise it. 

As a general rule, the Service does not pursue small-dollar liabilities with its customary vigor. It refrains on grounds of economy and efficiency. At some point these considerations are cast aside, and a decision is made to pursue the account more aggressively despite the small balance due. This allows the Service to teach the "lesson" of forcible collection more quickly. This lesson is to be taught those who are habitually resisting, or merely insouciant about, their responsibilities under the tax The decision to defer small accounts was made largely as a matter of law.

economics, and the decision not to defer them should at least be based on same consideration shown to outweigh the economics. Yet, the criteria grant almost unfettered discretion for Q-coding. This unstructured authority may thus be used without any guidelines and may perhaps be used to teach a lesson. 

There is little to suggest that the lesson results in greater compliance thereafter. The Service, by deferring accounts, may have taught taxpayers not to pay -- a teaching which may have to be untaught. But in many cases, as with same who resisted paying telephone excise taxes, the expenditure of manpower by the government to collect such paltry sums may be precisely what is desired by resisters. If the Service spends more than the tax involved 742/ which is a likely prospect 

so much the better. 

The efforts of the Service to collect the small accounts of chronic delinquents seem to be an outgrowth of excessive concern about enforcement. 

To permit habitual delinquents and "resisters," whoever they may be, to es cape payment apparently is considered very harmful to the system. Yet, the definition of those persons is thrust into the hands of perhaps the rawest recruit Revenue Officer, who may have to psychoanalyze a taxpayer and base his actions on his perception of the intent with which he fails to make payment. He may not know whether the taxpayer was merely impecunious, intended to "beat the system" (in the case of a repeater delinquent), or intended to protest military action (in the case of non-payers of telephone taxes). 

Neither we nor the Service knows the number of Q-coded accounts. 

They may be few, but the possibility of retribution and of cost inefficiency is not lessened by anything in the national office's directives.

78 

d. Use of Tolerances to Control Workloads. 

Dollar tolerances were introduced in July 1967 to control the number of small accounts being assigned to the field for further collection efforts. Different tolerance levels were established for Individual and Business Master File accounts. The level applicable to IMF accounts has been increased repeatedly, so that while it is not a large sum, it is now four times what it was in 1967. 

The BMF tolerance has never been changed. A recent study by the 

Collection Division projected that 43 percent of all Business Master File delinquencies will be under $100 in 1975, but that these will represent about 

1 percent of BMF dollar liabilities. However, it is projected that only 

332,000 of the expected 823,030 accounts in this category will be deferred 743/ from TDA issuance under present criteria. Here again, however, the Service chooses to put aside considerations of cost-efficiency in favor of presenting a "firm enforcement" image to the businessman.

The establishment of TDA "issuance criteria;" such as the dollar tolerance level, is the only means available to Collection to limit the delinquent accounts workload of local offices. The existence of a tax delinquency is entirely within the control of the taxpayer and the circumstances which beset him. While the Service thus cannot control the number of delinquent taxpayers, it may decide which accounts have priority. For example, same delinquencies are assigned as TDA's after one notice to the taxpayer, and some after four. Importance may be attached to the nature of the case, as with employers who are delinquent in paying over withheld employee income

taxes. The Service has properly chosen to de-emphasize small-dollar cases, although this is not done because such cases do not have an importance of their own. Instead, the Service's limited resources necessitate the assignment of priorities. Rational as that may be, one is left with the uneasy feeling that Q-coding of small accounts is an undesirable exercise of discretion which should be channeled by more stringent guidelines, or eliminated. 

Installment Payments. 

2. a.

Policy of the Internal Revenue Service. 

The Internal Revenue Code charges the Secretary or his delegate with the responsibility of collecting delinquent taxes. 744/ Despite enumerating a number of methods by which these sums may be forcibly collected 745/ by the Internal Revenue Service, the Code is silent on payment of delinquent taxes in installments. This silence is read by the Service as denying taxpayers a right to pay delinquent taxes in installments, but as not precluding Service acceptance of "part payment agreement" when immediate payment in full would result in "undue hardship or loss" to delinquent tax- 746/ payers.

Installment payment of a tax delinquency being a privilege, Collection personnel are directed to request immediate satisfaction of the ac- 747/ count on their first contact with a delinquent taxpayer. If immediate payment in full is not made or assured, the taxpayer is requested to complete a financial statement listing assets, liabilities, income, and expenses. 

While such statements may identify assets amenable to one of the forcible collection procedures, they are also necessary to lay a basis for the installment payment privilege.

DE If the financial statement does not identify an asset or present income stream available for immediate payment, collection obviously cannot be immediately effectuated. The same is true if assets or income exist, but are outside the range of the lien or distraint powers: then there is little choice but to accept payment on the delinquent's terms. The most difficult question of whether the tax collector will exercise his discretion to allow deferred payment arises only when an asset or source of income vulnerable to forcible collection procedures does exist. Whether hardship or loss is "undue", then, should be determined by the impact on the taxpayer of applying this asset or source of income (in whole or in part) to the liquidation of the delinquent taxes. One would therefore suppose that instructions to revenue officials would detail at length the factors to be considered in determining whether forcible collection would result in undue loss or hardship. They do not.

Instead, directions contained in the Internal Revenue Manual, the guidebook used by Collection employees, center on a multitude of other problems surrounding the installment agreement. The device is to be used only 748/ "when no other alternative is available", which is hardly the same as undue hardship. Indeed, this criterion focuses on the Service's collection problem instead of the effect of forcible collection on the taxpayer. The agreement is to be drawn between the narrow confines of satisfying the tax 749/ liability at the earliest possible time and assuring that the taxpayer 750/ is capable of meeting its terms. 

Also, as noted below, any employer 751/ is to be involved if possible. 

The Service also passes judgment on the source of financial distress: having no sympathy for wastrels, it does not

752/ illness, casualty, or unemployment. extend the time for payment if there is no element of involuntariness from The taxpayer is required to eliminate 753/ expenditures which the Collection officer views as ill-advised.

Future delinquencies are avoided by the requirement that if too many dependents 754/ are claimed on the employee's W-4, a new one is to be executed and forwarded Some district offices go further than by the Service to the employer. that, requiring a new employee wage withholding schedule to cover all current tax liabilities accruing on all other sources of current income. Over the course of the year, there may be excess withholding which will be available . for "refund offset" against the delinquency, when the taxpayer files a return claiming a refund. 

In principle, the taxpayer who cannot, or might not, be immediately able to pay may be given a more lenient payment schedule. However, the conditions necessary to qualify for the privilege are not detailed by the Manual, while internal procedural matters are dealt with extensively. The decision to require immediate or installment payment, appears to be left to largely unguided Revenue Officer discretion. This inaction would appear of doubtful wisdom and, as we shall see, policy in most cases is determined by local supervisory personnel who have filled the gap in guidance with varying kinds of signals.

Even though we cannot say with certainty what the content of the signals is, it seems not to encourage so-called "part payments." During the year ending June 30, 1974, there were 2,409,167 TDA dispositions through the IDRS computer system. In the same period forcible collection action was

.H 755/ eli CO 11 stayed on 89,368 Taxpayer Delinquent Accounts through "part pay agreements. 

The ratio of part payments to total TDA's was thus 3.7 percent, a small quantity in a society where many debts are paid by installments. Although this figure did represent an increase over two years before, when there were only 48,000 756/ "part payment" accounts out of 2.6 million TDA's, one may safely draw the inference, we think, that for reasons hereinafter explored "part payments" are generally not viewed with favor and are rarely employed. b. Procedures. 

(1) Installment Payment Agreements. 

As noted above, the financial statement is cornerstone to the decision whether deferred payments will be permitted. The Manual recognizes this fact and underscores the need for complete and accurate in- 757/ formation. Yet, the practices related to us by field officers were not designed to meet this need. The taxpayer is usually requested to complete this document when being interviewed in an IRS office without adequate prior notice of the kind of information required. Thus, the statement is frequently imprecise and likely to permit an inaccurate determination - often on the high side 

of maximum payments consistent with financial capability. The high payments, so we were told by Revenue Officers, is often as much a result of the taxpayer's desire to pay the account rapidly as it is the Revenue Officer's to collect it rapidly. 

Armed with this inexact statement, the Service employee decides whether to institute an installment plan and, if so, the amount of installments. 

Guidelines on their computation encourage early payment by one party and exercise of realism by the other. Yet, the very process engenders inaccurate

financial data, and with it, the likelihood that at least one of these constraints will be violated. For example, in many agreements the payments required are more than what the financial statement shows as the excess of income over expenses. Still others give the taxpayer no leeway to accommodate unforeseen expenses. 758/ Nevertheless, the taxpayer executes a payment agreement, detailing the size and timing of the payments to be made and allowing for the accrual of interest and imposition of any penalties. There is an escalator clause to increase the amount of payments to IRS in the event other term obligations of the taxpayer are liquidated during the period covered by the agreement. 

As part of the standard agreement, the taxpayer consents to prepare updated financial statements so that the agreement may be "reevaluated" to determine 759/ whether the taxpayer is paying the maximum amount feasible for him. 

The taxpayer further signifies his understanding that in the event of his failure to comply with the terms and conditions of the agreement, forcible collection action on the entire debt may be undertaken without further notice to him.

The agreement, however, does not cover all the terms and conditions deemed pertinent by the Internal Revenue Service. To fill these gaps, the 

Collection employee is directed to inform the taxpayer verbally that if he 760/ is unable to make payment, the Collection office should be notified. 

There are at least seven other items and conditions that must be communicated by the IRS representative. They include such matters as warnings that nonreceipt of a reminder notice (which must be included with his payment so
