(2) Payroll Deduction Agreements. 

An alternative to an agreement under which the wageearning taxpayer voluntarily makes payments is one in which his employer makes the payments for him with amounts withheld from the employee's paycheck. The Manual states that such an arrangement is "desirable, if 774/ possible, and that, as a policy matter, they should be sought in every case in which the taxpayer is salaried. 775/ 

The obvious advantage of payroll deduction agreements is that they place the Service in the po-

sition of a preferred creditor: since the funds do not pass to the financially troubled taxpayer, the Service has greater assurance that payments will be made when due. The payroll deduction agreement is regarded by Collection 

Division management as an effective and cost-efficient means of collecting delinquent accounts and as a lesser burden on the taxpayer who, though he must limit his expenditures to his reduced income, need not endure the 776/ stress of paying the delinquency in one lump sum. But the attitudes of line personnel (and apparently of some local management) may not be the same. Payroll deduction agreements were seldom mentioned by our interviewees as a means of deferring payment of taxes unless we specifically asked. Some Revenue Officers expressed a liking for this arrangement, because employers are more reliable than taxpayers in making payments; others seemed ignorant of it; and still others lacked enthusiasm for it because of the burden of paperwork they perceived to be necessary. 

The criteria and procedures by which payroll deduction agreements are approved and managed are much the same as those underlying installment payment agreements generally. However, because it is necessary to secure the cooperation of the employer, a different standard form agreement is 777/ utilized. While the timing of deferred payments by the taxpayer is frequently made to coincide with receipt of paychecks, the employer is encouraged to forward sums to the Service on a monthly basis (even though withholding may be more frequent) so as to minimize the Service's administrative costs. Employer remittances are usually not monitored by computer, but are manually processed by the Office Branch at the district level. 778/

1: Fin The Manual contains no directions for action to be taken in the event of a default by the employer. Default by employers is infrequent, but interesting questions might be raised if, before remitting withheld funds to IRS, an employer became insolvent. Such occurrence is not foreign to IRS's experience when only current tax liabilities are involved, but there is no advice in the Manual regarding delinquent obligations from prior years. The IRS national office is considering the possibility of sending 779/ reminder notices to employers who miss payments.

780/ The swift and harsh reaction of same employers to withholding It might, therefore, be expected that in levies is commonly known. order to minimize adverse consequences to the taxpayer, the Service representative would be advised by his guidebook when and how to contact an employer in regard to payroll deduction agreements. The Manual, however, contains only the self-evident proposition that before payroll deduction terms are 781/ arranged, the cooperation of the employer should be assured.

This paucity of guidance suggests insensitivity by the Service to the risk that untimely employer contact by the employee's creditor will create considerable strain for the wage-earner. (3) 

An Experiment in Automatic Extensions of Time to Pay. 

In a test carried out at five Service Centers in 1974, almost two-thirds of taxpayers who, in response to IRS billings, requested up to 60 additional days to pay their tax obligations did so without further prodding from IRS. Not only were many delinquent accounts fully paid in this manner, but IRS realized substantial cost savings by suspending

issuance of further notices and by avoiding district office handling of The test was continued and expanded to all ten Service Centers the cases. in 1975.

The procedure will perhaps be formalized to allow, in certain circumstances, an automatic extension of time in which to pay delinquent taxes. Individual (not business) taxpayers who respond to notices of delinquent taxes from the Service Center with an indication that they will pay the full amount thereof within 60 days would be given the opportunity 782/ to do so if the balance due does not exceed $5,000. The taxpayer would be notified that his proposal had been accepted and would be advised of 783/ Further collection action would be the interest which would be due. suspended until three weeks after the due date of the final payment (to 784/ If the account is not liquidated insure that it is recorded if paid). by this time, a TDA would be generated to the field without further notice to the taxpayer and often with little or no delay beyond the time in which a TDA would have been issued had the taxpayer never responded to IRS notices. 

The Service is presently considering whether to allow still longer periods of time (up to the end of the tax year) upon request to taxpayers who have not previously been delinquent in meeting their tax obligations. C. 

Problem Areas. 

(1) Defaults.

As previously noted, 89,368 installment agreements were initiated on TDA's in 1974. The number of installment agreements which 785/ 

IRS counted as "defaulted" during fiscal 1974 reached 49,428. 

An account

"defaults" in the technical sense when the taxpayer falls sufficiently in arrears that a TDA is issued to the field. For all years the default rate 786/ on accounts monitored by IDRS has been measured at 42 percent nationwide. 

This percentage is distorted upwards by several factors, and thus make the fidelity of taxpayers to installment agreements appear worse than it is. 

IRS default statistics tabulate those accounts on which a IDA One re- is generated for failure to make timely payments. Line Collection Division personnel believe that IDRS programming limitations, not failure to pay, account for many "defaults", thus swelling the default rate. The computer's rigid requirements make it necessary for the taxpayer to remit to a special 787/ post office box the exact amount of the installment when due. sult of this, according to line employees, is that taxpayers prepay some or all of the remaining installments, only to be defaulted. The national office denies that this is possible, however. The computer will also default a taxpayer whose payment is, for some reason (e.g. credit to another taxpayer because of a misstated social security number) not credited to his account. 

Though there does not appear to be much information indicating the frequency of such errors, and so far as we can determine they are relatively rare in a percentage sense, the error base is substantial. Delays in mail delivery also result in untimely payment. Given the heavy workflow and numerous steps in processing, there are doubtless other impediments at the Service Center due to human mistake or mechanical failure.

The most frequent cause of retarded processing, however, is believed by IRS management and line personnel to be the behavior of the taxpayer.

The taxpayer may mail his payment late (or altogether neglect to make remittance). The payment, if made, may be unaccompanied by the payment reminder notice (without which proper crediting of the payment is sometimes impossible) or may not be enclosed in a special envelope which acts as a signal that its contents are to be given priority. These systemic problems and human errors distort the "default" statistics on installment payments. The percentage is skewed further by the practice of same Revenue 

Officers not to report deferred payment arrangements for input, after supervisory review, to IDRS. Rather, they handle these accounts themselves, providing a personal touch which they believe to result in a substantially lower rate of default. These Revenue Officers believe that the systemic problems and lack of human communication, inherent in IDRS monitoring, are dampers on taxpayer cooperation. Other Revenue Officers are subverting the policy of local-level management which in some offices discourages the use of installment agreements or will not approve them. Apparently, a substantial percentage of Revenue Officers are not submitting payment agreements to management for review or arranging for their input to IDRS. 

On the contrary, they are illicitly kept "in the desk" and payments are manually credited to the account.

In an attempt to remedy systemic problems, taxpayer oversights, and postal delays, the Collection Division is experimenting with test procedures in which taxpayers provide the IRS with postdated checks to meet all installments contemplated by a periodic payment agreement. The local 

Office Branch credits the accounts and deposits the checks as installments

3 5. become due, absent warning from the taxpayer that there are insufficient funds. The procedure is one which has worked well for private industry and for the Canadian counterpart of IRS, but for employee accountability reasons is not condoned by IRS outside of the test districts. However, preliminary results of the test have been favorable: only 20 percent of postdated checks were dishonored (2) Attitudes of Officers and Employees. 788/ Most Collection Division personnel express little sympathy for tax delinquents as a class. This attitude seems to be based on several factors. The vast majority of taxpayers satisfy their tax obligations in a timely manner. The delinquent portion of the citizenry thus is viewed as being unfair to those who have paid on time. Heightening the Revenue Officer's 789/ sense of inequity is the low interest rate applicable to tax delinlinquencies and the fact that many tax debtors would be summarily rejected by commercial lenders, even those making high risk loans. Moreover, the Revenue Officer is not usually assigned a TDA on an individual until the account is four or more months in default, a substantial number of these persons are repeatedly delinquent. The failure to satisfy the delinquency by the time the TDA is assigned to a Revenue Officer may easily be viewed as a failure to take tax obligations seriously. Line personnel may be slow to extend the privilege of installment arrangements. 

Obviously, the attitudes of line personnel toward periodic payments are also strongly affected by those of supervisors. In the offices we visited these were diverse, ranging from apparent neutrality to an announcement by one supervisor that installment payments would not be approved.

The prevailing management view is that "firm enforcement" (use of levies, liens, and seizures) is best if a taxpayer does not settle the account quickly There is a corresponding belief by some managers that deferred payment agree- 790/ ments are undesirable because their terms tend to be unrealistic. They add that many delinquent taxpayers do not take their obligations seriously and that delinquents are "rewarded" by low penalty and interest rates for not complying with the revenue laws. Most managers, according to line employees, rarely rejected a proposed installment agreement; but this seeming paradox comes about because few are suggested. 

Proposal of more deferred payment arrangements is deterred by management attitudes, which are revealed in several ways. For example, those offices which suppressed the extension of such agreements had imposed approval procedures including close questioning by the supervisor, which line personnel regarded as undesirably complex. Use of the device was constricted by restrictive criteria communicated by word of mouth. Frequent use of levies and seizures, the opposite of installment agreements, was praised by management, and Collection personnel believed by most to increase one's chances for raises and promotions. 

Management's dislike of installment agreements may be caused by statistical evaluation. The national office, in its formal evaluations of 791/ regional accomplishments, relies heavily on its numbers. Although it reviews a variety of statistical indicators of regional performance, such as repeater delinquents, large dollar accounts, and the like, the National Office puts prime emphasis on inventory levels and full-paid accounts. Use of installment payments, delays "closing" of cases, thus driving case inventory

levels upward. This result is viewed with no enthusiasm by the national office. The formal evaluations go only to the regional level, but somehow filter down to the line supervisor. What is measured is what is 

Intermediate managers will evaluate line managers according desired. to the way top management evaluates intermediate managers.

Line personnel are less preoccupied with numbers and have the conciliatory perspective arising from personal contacts with tax debtors. 

Thus, despite the attitudes communicated by their supervisors, the personal contact imbues them with some receptiveness toward installment payments which, for some Revenue Officers, changes their lack of sympathy for the taxpayer to ambivalence. At the same time, the vague and undefined concept of undue loss or hardship gives Collection officers considerable latitude in choosing whether to grant installment payment privileges. 

Thus, a substantial number of Revenue officers have formulated their own criteria for "hardship" in determining whether to allow deferral of payments. Same personally view the taxpayer's living situation and require documentary evidence of attempts to borrow the amount of the delinquency from financial institutions. 

One requires that homeowners attempt to obtain a second mortgage. Several do not accept time payment proposals by repeat delinquents (this would seem irrelevant to the question of hardship). 

Nearly all said they would not make such agreements spanning "too long" a period of time or in which installments were "too small." But almost none could specify what "too long" or "too small" meant: two said they would close cases as "uncollectible" if the delinquency could not be satisfied

within six months, though the Manual clearly contemplates payments spanning 792/ a year or more, while another named any payment under $25 as too small. 

Not a single line Collection Division employee who was asked could give any data on the cost of processing installment payments or state at what point 793/ it became economically impracticable to accept them. 

While the data is conflicting, we think one can generalize that We these fuzzy guidelines in the Manual and the equivocal guidance from management combine to depress the usage of installment payment agreements. tender this conclusion because so many Collection personnel make informal agreements which are kept in the desk and monitored by the officer. The principal reason for this procedure is either the desire by line personnel to avoid review by supervisors or the belief that continuing human contact is necessary. Our interviews strongly suggest that the former reason is the most important. Since "hardship" is not defined, the Collection officer assumes that the matter is committed to his discretion and that supervisory review often fails to take this intangible into account. Also, there is a natural tendency to resent intrusions into an area where discretion has been reposed in the officer.

In conclusion, we note that the Service seems much less likely to resort to deferred payment plans than do other tax-gathering agencies which came to our attention. For example, the Canadian counterpart of 

IRS automatically allows certain delinquents to satisfy their accounts 794/ with equal installment remittances. The State of California's Franchise 

Tax Board is believed to be more likely to allow "part payments" 

using

795/ basically the same "hardship" criteria as IRS 

than the Service.

OS R? d. Should There be a "Right" to Pay by Installments?

As we have seen, there is no provision of the Internal Revenue Code expressly allowing the payment of delinquent taxes by installments. The Service thus takes the view that such an arrangement is a privilege to be extended only in situations which, in the discretion of Collection employees, present "undue hardship." The term is only vaguely defined; our interviews and IRS's statistics suggest that the rule also is very unevenly applied because of different collection philosophies and, to some extent, of differing economic characteristics in various locals. 

The varying utilization of installment agreements is probably unavoidable given the present state of affairs, but would be narrowed significantly by structuring the discretion possessed by Collection employees. 

The problem of dissimilar access to deferred payment plans would be altogether eliminated if delinquent taxpayers were given license to pay tax debts in portions, regardless of whether they possess assets sufficient to pay the obligations in full without hardship. Such an administrative rule is employed by the Canadian equivilant of IRS. For example, if income taxes due the government are less than $5,000, it allows the taxpayer to make six equal monthly payments to liquidate the liability without forcible collection action being undertaken. 

It is possible that this rule contributes to a high incidence among Canadians of filing income tax returns without paying the tax. returns in 1973 made up 9.8 percent of all filings in Canada, well in excess 796/ of the United States rate of 5.7 percent. The incidence of balance-due Balance-due

returns would appear even more striking when it is considered that 86 percent of Canadian employment and individual income taxes are paid through withholding (compared to 82 percent in the United States). 

797/ 

However, among the delin- self-employed Canadians who are not subject to withholding quency rate in 1973 was 27 percent. 798/ These figures may suggest that the desirability of automatic installment payment arrangements for delinquent taxpayers is open to serious 799/ doubt. Yet, it should be noted that (1) Canada has no penalty for late payment to correspond to that imposed by our Code, and (2) interest charged on Canadian tax delinquencies in 1973 was only 6 percent." 800/ Given the imposition of a non-payment penalty and an interest rate more nearly 801/ comparable to the taxpayer's cost of borrowing money, the incidence of "borrowings" from the public coffers motivated by deferral of tax obligations could be substantially less than in Canada. While interest on delin- 802/ quent taxes is deductible to reach taxable income, the non-payment penalty is not. 803/ Unlikely though it is that capital-short, poor-risk business borrowers will be deterred from seizing the opportunity to pay by 804/ installments, it is questionable whether they would have not been delinquent in any event. 805/ The midpoint between automatically allowing taxpayers to pay delinquent taxes in installments and treating the deferral as a privilege is statutory creation of a taxpayer's right to pay by installments if undue hardship would otherwise result. The impact of such legislation can only be guessed, and would probably depend on the size and spacing of installments

Biz de and the definition to be given "undue hardship." But raising installment plans from the status of "privilege" to "right," conditioned only by the finding of hardship by the Revenue Officer, could result in Collection employees being more favorably disposed to their use. 

The earliest revenue acts scheduled payment of individual income 806/ taxes on an installment basis. The calendar-year taxpayer, instead of having to render the full amount of the tax by April 15, could pay at three-month intervals in four equal installments, the first being due on the date fixed by law for filing the return. The 1924 Revenue Act required 807/ the taxpayer to make an election to pay by installments. not accrue on the quarterly installments, except to the extent any of them became delinquent, in which case the entire amount of the balance could be 

Interest did 808/ accelerated by notice and demand from the Commissioner. Congress eliminated the choice for individuals to defer their income tax obligations 809/ in the Current Tax Payment Act of 1943. There is little in the legislative history to explain the repeal, but obviously the United States needed revenues to support a global war. Indeed, the same act which terminated installment payment of tax obligations introduced prepayment of those obli- 810/ gations in the form of the estimated tax.

Congress has left undisturbed 811/ the right of decedents' estates to defer payment of income taxes, 812/ has whittled that of corporations.

but Deferred payment of non-delinquent taxes, thus, has been accepted in limited situations as a matter of law. 

It would seem, moreover, that the United States is compensated for loss of use of tax revenues by the

813/ failure-to-pay penalty and by interest rates on underpayments. In the future the latter will be more nearly aligned with the prime market price 814/ of borrowing money. With this in mind, the Service should feel encouraged to liberalize its installment payment procedures at least so far as concerns smaller-than-average individual liabilities. Although a rise in the number of such agreements would allow case inventory levels to rise, the burden of managing heightened inventories might be more than offset by the benefits of freeing Collection employees for more vigorous pursuit of large-dollar liabilities. 

3. Accounts "Suspended" As Uncollectible.

Like any other creditor, the United States is not always able to collect its accounts receivable. In fact, during 1973, its agent, the Internal Revenue Service, "suspended" collection efforts on 313,884 delinquent accounts (representing $397,459,356 in unpaid, delinquent taxes) which were reported to be "uncollectible." 815/ During the same period, the Service's field offices received nearly three million delinquent accounts, The Service thus appears representing over five billion tax dollars. 816/ to write off accounts on a grand scale; but its immense influx of new accounts requires that same limit be placed on efforts to collect the old ones. Our purpose here is to examine the criteria and procedure utilized by the Service for reporting accounts uncollectible and to examine the fate of these accounts. 

As a threshold matter, it must be borne in mind that the reporting of an account as uncollectible does not forgive or abate the indebtedness.

It is, therefore, to be distinguished from taxpayer offers in compromise, which may result in forgiveness of a portion of a liability for taxes, penalties, and interest on the basis of doubt as to collectibility or 817/ liability.

Offers in compromise should be distinguished from the audit settlement process, which resolves proposed assessments solely on the basis of liability. Offers in compromise are infrequently tendered 818/ Thus, an offer in compromise, if accepted, exand rarely accepted. tinguishes the debt, 819/ but a suspension as an uncollectible does not. 

Since the debt continues, the potential revenue represented by an uncollectible account is not necessarily lost; the write-off merely "suspends" efforts by the district office to collect it. Collection activity may be deferred if the taxpayer or his assets cannot be located, if he has minimal income or assets for the support of himself and his family, or if the account is below a minimum dollar value or would otherwise be uneconomical to collect. Whether a case fits into any of these categories is determined largely by the exercise of broad discretion vested in the Collection employee. His decision is subject to review by line supervisors and technical staff, but because it is so based on subjective factors, it may be largely unreviewable. a. 

Determination of Uncollectibility. 

820/ Except for accounts worth over a specified amount, the national office has recently allowed district offices to decide whether the suspension of collection activity should be made by the Office Branch or by Revenue Officers. Most districts had previously

821/ The suspended reposed most of this authority in Revenue Officers. 

TDA will, thus, usually have been processed through the Office Branch, and except for field investigations, the Revenue Officer will merely duplicate the efforts of the Office Branch before writing off the account. These duplications are both uneconomical for the Service and frustrating to the Revenue Officer. However, his judgment in making the decision seems preferred. 

(1) Inability to Locate the Taxpayer or His Assets. 

The controlling consideration in reporting an account uncollectible is not whether the taxpayer can be found, but whether any of his assets can be located. 822/ If they cannot and the debtor remains sequestered, obviously there is little that the Service can do. The same is true if the taxpayer can be found, but not his assets. 

Now it is

The conclusion is obvious that further efforts are not justified because no assets of the debtor can be found; the point at which the conclusion is reached is not so obvious. Both the Manual and training booklets 823/ were, until recently, essentially silent on this point. provided that there must be a visit to the taxpayer's last known address and confirmation by the Post Office that he has moved without leaving a forwarding address before the Office Branch may report a case uncollectible 824/ for failure to locate the individual or his assets. 

Although the Form 53 825/ used to report accounts uncollectible contains a list of sources which the collector may indicate, by date, that he has checked, there is no direction to follow through on all these leads if no trace of assets can otherwise

I be found. The national office thus has generally abstained from the promulgation of firm guidelines. 826/ While one might expect local management to fill the void, our interviews with local line personnel indicated the contrary. The interviewees were nearly unanimous that there is little instruction from management on what is expected. Instead, Revenue Officers claim that their exercise of discretion is rarely, if ever, overturned on review. 

The infrequent reversals are normally based on a failure by the Revenue Officer to consider levying on assets known to be held by or for the debtor. 

In a review of 1,537 randomly selected accounts reported uncollectible in four districts, the Service's Internal Audit Division found, in nearly one case in fifteen, that "inadequate" investigation had been made. The inadequacies ranged from obtaining of inaccurate financial 827/ statements to failing to utilize information available on tax returns. 

Internal Audit concluded that proper investigation would have turned up the assets sufficient to pay the accounts. Another survey of uncollectible accounts, conducted by the Collection Division itself, uncovered same striking variations in the use of leads to find missing debtors and 828/ sequestered assets. (2) Collection Would Cause "Undue Hardship.' 11 If the taxpayer is located, the Collection employee 829/ 

If the debtor insists that is to request full payment at the outset. he is unable to pay and unable to borrow the amount due, the Collection officer prepares a statement of the taxpayer's income, assets, and liabili-

830 ties. 

Having obtained this information, he may then report the account uncollectible if he determines that payment of the delinquency would result in "undue hardship" to the taxpayer. 

We have seen this concept before. "Undue hardship" is a basis on which the officer may forbear forcibly collecting the tax, and may impel the officer to arrange payment of the tax in installments. The Internal Revenue 

Manual does not reveal the degree of "undue hardship" necessary to justify postponing hardship altogether, but it directs that "a determination should be made in each case as to whether levy would result in actual hardship as opposed to mere inconvenience." The line between inconvenience and 831/ hardship is not articulated, and neither term is defined. 

On the other hand, Revenue Officer training materials say that a determination of this sort of hardship must be based on the financial statement, with particular examination of the taxpayer's expenses for cer- 832/ tain "necessities." It inferentially suggests that any frills be discounted in determining whether the individual's cost of living precludes payment of his tax debt. Beyond this point, the Collection employee's dis- 833/ cretion is unstructured.

We believe that this lack of structure has contributed to the practice in some districts of requiring installment payment agreements from same taxpayers whose financial statements show expenses exceeding income. 

Revenue Officer training materials set forth limited criteria for determining "undue hardship" and the Manual can barely be said to have a standard at all. Collection employees indicated to us that reference is

res is a el: Res 2. ​S not made to training materials for any purpose. Any finding of uncollectibility of an account is based solely on the Manual and the officer's personal estimate of the taxpayer's financial situation. Our interviewees acknowledged receiving scarce feedback as a result of review of the writtenoff accounts. Since their discretion is basically untrammeled, we were not surprised that our interviewees enumerated varying standards of proof of hardship which related not to "hardship" but to ability to pay or borrow. 

Some insisted that an attempt to borrow the amount of indebtedness be made and that unsuccessful attempts be documented by letter or in some other manner. There was conflict on whether to require delinquents to make certain kinds of borrowings, such as second mortgages on residences and unsecured loans from finance companies, because of the steep expenses involved. Revenue 

Officers agreed that write-off practices varied widely as a result of the latitude permitted for the exercise of discretion. They did, however, seem bothered by the obvious inequality of treatment which results. 

(3) Small Accounts. 

At some point the cost of collection exceeds the amount to be collected. As a matter of policy, the Service allows accounts to be written-off when the account is under a certain dollar level and it is determined that probable collection costs are "out of proportion" to the 834/ eventual recovery.

On this basis, 60,518 small accounts were reported 835/ uncollectible during 1973.

The practice would seem to permit more economically rewarding utilization of manpower and resources than would result from pursuing these cases. These small accounts are also subject to refund offset. 836/

Cost considerations do seem to outweigh any undesirable impact on voluntary compliance with the revenue laws which might result from writing-off the account. 

Aside from setting a dollar criterion, the Internal Revenue Manual limits itself to warning that the tolerance write-off procedure should not be used automatically and that levy should be imposed if 837/ there is no hardship and the debt may be collected thereby. Our interviews with Collection employees led us to believe that the Manual's dictate is generally followed. 

(4) Other. 

Accounts may also go uncollected when the individual taxpayer dies or the corporation becomes insolvent, in which case there may be no assets to collect. The account will also be reported uncollectible upon the expiration of the statute of limitations for collection of the account. 838/ It is our impression that same accounts are reported uncollectible merely because they cannot be collected immediately. In one office we were told by its employees that if the account cannot be fully paid (by installments or otherwise) in less than seven months, it is generally written-off as uncollectible. Nearly all Collection employees indicated that if the balance can be paid only in installments and the schedule of payments is "too long" or their size "too small," the case would be written off. However, none 839/ would (or could) estimate what was too small or too long. 

We did not gain any clear impression of the motivation of local

1 offices to write-off accounts which the taxpayer is willing to liquidate by installments. Cost-benefit considerations might govern in same instances, yet no Revenue Officers knew the costs of processing installment payments. 

We were told by several line personnel that liberal write-off practices 840/ were encouraged by supervisors for so-called over-age accounts. This may derive from the perception, common to field offices, that regional and national management watch over-age inventory as an indicator of the promptness and "firmness" with which delinquent accounts are processed by the 841/ local office.

At least in those offices or groups where over-age inventory is high, therefore, the temptation to write-off some of these old cases may be considerable. Though uncollectible account reports are subject to review by the Special Procedures Staff, the discretion vested in the Revenue Officers to write-off accounts is substantial. b. Review of Accounts Reported Uncollectible.

Accounts are reported uncollectible on Form 53, which briefly states the identity and address of the taxpayer, the nature and amount of taxes and accruals, the efforts made to locate the taxpayer and his assets, and the reporting employee's recommendations as to the reasons for uncollectibility and timing of follow-up activity. Together with other documents which support the conclusion that the account should be 842/ written off.

The Form 53 is submitted to the Collection employee's 843/ supervisor for review.

For many accounts, review by the Group Manager is final, but the Special Procedures Branch of the district Collection Division has

responsibility to approve all reports of uncollectibility of accounts involving liabilities of at least $1,000, as well as to review five percent of all other uncollectible accounts. 844/ 

Confined to the case file before him, the reviewing official must determine whether the Form 53 and supporting documents have been properly prepared and sufficiently buttress the conclusion that the account is not collectible. 

The reviewer may, after consultation with the line employee, 846/ change the reason for reporting the case uncollectible or, with the concurrence of the employee's supervisor, alter the designation for follow-up activity. Either of these alterations will affect the 847/ 848/ 

The reviewer timing of future effort to collect the delinquencies. may also reverse the decision and send the case back for further investigation if he decides that there is a "reasonable possibility of 849/ collection." 845/ The account may also be returned if the reviewer feels 850/ he has insufficient data on which to base a decision. 

If the taxpayer has not been located, the Special Procedures Branch may send a letter (in a plain envelope without the telltale IRS indicia clause) to his last known address. 851/ 

If it is not returned as undeliverable, a second letter, certified with return receipt requested, is mailed; the return receipt may constitute a new lead to the taxpayer. 

The head of the Special Procedures staff has an additional responsibility with respect to uncollectible accounts generally. He must periodically review those Form 53's which were not immediately approved and advise 852/ line supervisors of trends and problems suggested by the rejections.

Judging from our interviews, this procedure, if used at all, does not result in guidance to line personnel. C. 

Subsequent Activity on Uncollectible Accounts. (1) Refund Offset.

As we have noted previously, the IRS National Computer Center has the capability to offset refunds claimed by a taxpayer against any balance due on his account. Businesses are seldom 853/ eligible for refunds, but most individual income tax returns claim refunds because of excess income tax withholding. About 82 percent of 854/ Form 1040's filed in 1973 showed overpayment of tax liability. 

Approximately 73,000 of those 63.5 million overpaid returns were filed by taxpayers whose accounts had previously been reported uncollectible. 

The refund offset program enabled the Service to apply $22 million in 855/ claimed refunds to offset tax delinquencies reported uncollectible. "Reissuance" of Uncollectible Accounts. (2) When an account is reported uncollectible (except by the "tolerance" method previously discussed), information called a "closing code" is recorded in the Master File at the National Computer Center to trigger "reissuance" or reassignment of the account to the district office as a TDA under certain circumstances. The reissued TDA indicates that the account was once suspended and the reason therefor. 

Reissuance occurs without new notices or demands being mailed to the taxpayer. The dollar tolerance level which defers issuance of TDA's on small liabilities does not prevent IDA reissuance; thus the Service again ignores cost benefits.

Selection of a closing code is primarily the responsibility of the persons writing off the account and is subject to the possible review just discussed. When the taxpayer cannot be located, the collector will usually input a code directing the computer to regurgitate the account 856/ when the taxpayer files another return showing an address. 

If cases are reported uncollectible on the basis of hardship, the Collection employee may choose a code triggering reissuance by the computer when the taxpayer reports, on a later return, an adjusted gross income which equals or The absence of criteria in the Manual to 857/ exceeds a certain amount. guide the selection of income level to trigger reissuance of the TDA raises 858/ substantial questions concerning the equality of treatment of taxpayers. 

However, the national office has preferred that the matter be left to unstructured Revenue Officer discretion. 859/ When a previously unlocated taxpayer files a sbbsequent return showing an address, a TDA is reassigned to the district in which the return was filed. Many of these accounts are small enough to have been deferred by a dollar tolerance because of intervening refund offset, but they are reissued anyway. The taxpayer frequently remains elusive, having used a fictitious residence address or one at which he is rarely found. This results in a manpower expenditure which is not only fruitless, but substantial as well. Since some field investigation is required, many of these accounts are processed in both the Office Branch and field branch before write-off.

An October 1974 study by the Collection Division of selected,

regenerated uncollectible accounts revealed that nearly half of them 860/ Those (about 14,000 accounts) were again reported uncollectible. taxpayers who initially could be "located," but not contacted, remained out of the Service's reach in the great majority of cases. Many accounts which were uncollectible on the basis of hardship remained so; to a major extent the hardship continued despite the taxpayer's increased income because real income had been eaten away by inflation. As a result of the study's findings, the Collection Division is considering whether (1) to establish a new closing code for taxpayers who cannot be contacted although their addresses have been located and (2) to change the computer program by raising, to reflect cost of living increases shown in general economic indicators, the adjusted gross income level which triggers reissuance of accounts written off for hardship. 

(3) Other Follow-Up. 

When reporting the uncollectible the Collection employee may designate some review or further action to be taken on the matter at a specific time, as well as on the occurrence of any of the events just discussed. Without reissuance of the TDA, the local office may re-file liens, take a new financial statement from the taxpayer, or attempt to secure a waiver of the statute of limitations. d. Attitudes of Line Employees and Management.

We have already seen that the Internal Revenue Manual contains few guidelines for reporting accounts uncollectible. Moreover, collection philosophies differ from employee to employee, district to

district, and even region to region. It is not surprising, therefore, that the efforts to find taxpayers or their assets or alternatives to reporting 861/ Economic and demographic diverthe account uncollectible also vary. sities may account for the attitudinal discrepancies, as well as for some 862/ statistical disparity. It is our impression that line personnel are generally more tenacious in seeking ways to obtain payment than management would prefer. The persistence of line personnel seems desirable for encouraging compliance with the law and preventing the taxpayer from "getting away" with anything. 

But, management's view is similarly commendable given the need to apply manpower to many priorities. We lack data sufficient to determine the overall effect of the tension between these points of view; we believe that this would be made clear only through a case-by-case study of write-off procedures. 

We were told repeatedly by Revenue Officers that once an account is suspended, serious collection efforts come to a close. This may be an outgrowth of the evident community of feeling among line personnel that an account should not be reported uncollectible unless there is no means of securing payment. The Revenue officer receiving a reissued account may assume that full diligence has already been applied. He may believe that further efforts by him will only duplicate those previously undertaken, at least if he perceives, after a cursory investigation, that the taxpayer's financial condition has not changed significantly. The Internal Revenue 

Service does not compile nationwide data on the fate of reactivated uncollectible

accounts; thus the accuracy of this common perception among Revenue 

Officers cannot be statistically supported. e. How Fair and Effective Are Write-Off Procedures?

While the subject of write-off procedures does not seem to provoke hot debate among IRS officers and employees, the variety of opinions which we encountered left us with no clear impression of their effectiveness. Such internal disagreement as we found was between line personnel, who thought some accounts were written off too early, and management people, who suspected it was not soon enough. 863/ The Service's assertion that closed TDA's are "tax return" information, required by law to remain confidential, precluded us from examining uncollectible account files to make our own determination of whether accounts are properly written off in a timely fashion. The only independent examination of uncollectible accounts has been made by the General Accounting Office. It found that "prescribed procedures were generally being followed" and that those procedures safeguarded the interests of the United States while ensuring fair treatment of taxpayers. After examining 426 delinquent accounts written off by four district offices, GAO had no adverse comments. Another review was performed in 1972 by the Internal 

Audit Division of the Service. In sampling about 1,500 cases reported uncollectible in six districts during 1971, it found an error rate of 6.6 percent. Some of these problems related to technical matters, such as a failure to input refund freeze codes to the computer. The report of the study called for more guidelines to help Revenue Officers decide when an

account suspended for hardship should again be investigated, as well as for closer review of accounts reported uncollectible. 864/ 

In spite of these recommendations, Collection Division management left the determination of when hardship accounts should be reopened to the judgment of Revenue 865/ Officers and regards increased review as impracticable. 

Any determination of the efficacy and fairness of write-off procedures by comparison with the practices and statistics of private collection agencies is unfeasible. Collectors in the private sector usually work on a contingent-fee basis for retailers who have screened their debtors ahead of time; smaller accounts are not worth the trouble of private collectors, while the element of customer relationships is another consideration. The United States cannot always pick and choose between debtors to whom it will "lend" and those to whom it will not. Same taxpayers who, because their taxes have not been withheld from income, have the option of paying or not paying, are unwilling or unable to pay; of 

106.3 million individual and business returns filed in 1973, taxes were not fully paid on 8.6 million (6.5 million of which were the result of 866/ "error" by the taxpayer). At the same time, the Service does not work on a contingent-fee basis, but rather, within the confines of a fixed budget. Furthermore, the Service must be concerned about the fostering of voluntary compliance with the revenue laws. 

A meaningful indicator of the Service's effectiveness in collecting accounts may be the amount of liabilities on which the statute of limitations expires. Suspending collection does not forgive the indebtedness, and new

attempts may be made to collect at a later date. But, once the limitations period has expired, there is no means of collecting an account except through unsolicited, voluntary payment. In the fiscal year ending 

June 1968, IRS issued about $2.09 billion in taxpayer delinquent accounts and suspended collection efforts on approximately $321 million 867/ of them.

Allowing six years for the running of the statute of limita- 868/ tions on collection, in calendar year 1973 $81.6 million in delinquent accounts which had been reported uncollectible became barred from collec- 869/ tion. However, this comparison is distorted because the Service may 870/ extend the statute of limitations by agreement with the taxpayer or 871/ 872/ create fresh limitations periods by transferee on penalty assessments. 1 Though the majority of dollars in accounts marked as uncollectible are eventually collected, the inventory of uncollectible accounts at the end of 1973 stood at $1.3 billion of the $3.1 billion in total outstanding 873/ delinquent accounts. The cost to the United States of not having these funds may be substantially offset by the imposition of penalties and interest. 

But, the magnitude of the sum should impel the Service to reconsider giving field personnel more guidance for writing off accounts. This is not to suggest that the Service does poorly in this regard (as we are unable to charac terize the efficacy of write-off procedures), but that it might do better as a result of experimentation.

The gossamer non-standards supplied by the Manual seem to us to engender an unnecessarily great potential for error. There is no indiction

therein, for example, at which point "inconvenience" shades into the sort of "hardship" which justifies writing off the account. At no point is the 

Revenue Officer assured that he has carried fruitless pursuit of the taxpayer and his assets far enough. It seems plausible that concrete guidelines will reduce the incidence of substandard judgment and inconsistency in treatment of taxpayers found by the Service's Internal Audit Division.

C. Employer Tax Delinquents. 

1. 

Overview of the Withholding System and Employer 

Tax Delinquencies. 

Businesses are subject to a panoply of Federal taxes and must file an equivalent variety of tax returns. Oddly enough, the most important of these returns, the Form 941, relates to taxes imposed partially on the business, but mostly on its employees. These taxes are income 874/ 875/ withheld by the employer taxes and Social Security contributions from the wages of its employees. The employer, who is constituted an agent of the United States for the collection, reporting and payment of these 876/ taxes, must also report and pay his own portion of Social Security contribu- 877/ 878/ tions as well as the Federal Unemployment Tax. 

The employee generally accounts for his income tax liability on an 879/ annual basis. 

The employer, on the other hand, files quarterly reports of taxes withheld and deposits such taxes as often as four times a 880/ month with commercial banks designated as Federal Depositories by the 881/ 

Secretary or his delegate.

This system is designed to produce the most expeditious deposit of a continuous stream of revenues to the credit of the United States in order that the Treasury can meet its day-to-day obligations without undue resort to borrowing. In addition, it helps assure that wage-earners will not became tax delinquents: amounts which they do not receive cannot be dissipated prior to the time that their income taxes are due to be paid.

The importance of the withholding system, while realized by only a few well initiated, cannot be overemphasized. During fiscal 1973, $145.2 billion of the government's entire revenue of $237.8 billion consisted of withheld taxes. 1930's. 882/ It is, thus, the primary means of revenue collection. 

Withholding was introduced with Social Security taxes in the 883/ When the Second World War brought the rapidly escalating tax rates of the 1940's, withholding was expanded to include income taxes on 884/ employees' wages.

The unprecedentedly high tax rates would otherwise have outstripped the foresight or willingness of many to save for a lump- 885/ sum payment.

If too much was withheld, as was often the case, the excess could be refunded when the income and taxes paid for the overwithheld year were reported. In 1943, the first year of income tax withholding, employees paid a somewhat reduced tax on income received in 1942 because taxes had not been withheld that year; however, the government also received taxes withheld from income earned in 1943. Thus, taxes due for 886/ two years were telescoped into one year. 

Having constituted employers as withholding agents, the government could not leave them with the funds, or the benefits might be lost. Congress did not delineate any plan under which collections were to be made, but delegated establishment of the payment scheme to Treasury Department regula- 887/ tion.

At first, employers were required to file quarterly returns, as they are today, but payments of withheld taxes ("Federal Tax Deposits" or FID's) for the first two months of each quarter were to be made to a Federal Reserve Bank (FRB). The FRB acknowledged these two FID's with receipts which the employer would attach to the quarterly return due during the month follow-

ing the end of the quarter.

Because a withheld-tax deposit for the last SLE month of the quarter could not be received and processed by the FRB in time to furnish a receipt for attachment with the quarterly return, the employer was expected to file this return with validated receipts for the first two months of the quarter and a check for the taxes withheld during the last month of the quarter. 

While this system accelerated receipts at a time of deficits and short revenues, the government decided that its time for borrowing, and hence payment of interest, could be diminished by shortening the time in which employers were permitted to retain withheld funds before payment to the government. Consequently, the time in which payment was due was accelerated by requiring larger employers to make Federal Tax Deposits within three banking days after the date that wages were paid, instead of some time during the month following the payment of wages. 888/ With the time for payment so shortened, the government might have required payment directly to the Service, rather than deposits to Federal Reserve Banks. However, fiscal personnel at Treasury were aware that payment to the Service might not result in as much acceleration as would be possible by continuing payments to the Federal Reserve Banks. 

For example, if checks were sent to the Internal Revenue Service, the transmittal time could run from one to three days. Processing by the Service would require another few days. The checks would then be deposited in a bank by the Service, and after a few additional days, the checks would be collected by the drawer bank. Advice of collection would then be forwar-

ded to the Service, at which time the funds would become available to the government. Thus, about 14 days would have elapsed from the time of payment to the Service to when the funds would be available to the government.

It was realized that this 14-day period could be reduced, if taxes were deposited by the employer directly with a commercial bank. 

The bank would wire notification of the FID to the Federal Reserve Bank and the funds would be thereupon available for expenditure by the govern- 889/ ment.

In shortening the collection process, this system accelerated the availability of funds to the government by ten days or more. 

Any delay in the collection of Federal Tax Deposits will increase the Treasury's need to borrow funds. On the other hand, any acceleration in collection increases Treasury's capacity either to repay former borrowings or to defer future borrowings. Wage withholding results in the collection of about $150 billion each year. Because of the immensity of this figure, a 10-day reduction in collection time saves the government as much as $250,000,000 a year (assuming a 6 percent interest rate). The prospect of achieving such savings motivated the Treasury to press commercial banks into service as depositories; in turn, the banks pay no interest on tax deposits.

The requirement that withheld taxes not be paid to the Internal Revenue Service has, however, separated the accounting for the funds from the processing of the quarterly return. So that withheld-tax deposits may be properly credited by the Service, the employer tenders a computer card,

890/ to the bank pre-inscribed by the Service with his name and address, with his deposit. A portion of the card is torn off along a perforation, stamped by the bank cashier, and retained in an interest-free demand account in the name of the Federal Reserve Bank. The cards are then forwarded to the FRB's branch for that geographic area where they are keypunched. Part of each card having been removed as a receipt for the employer, 891/ each is shorter than the standard computer card. Their size results in an unusually high "reject factor" by the data processing equipment; the rejected cards must be manually processed, thus slowing the payment accounting process. 

After keypunching, the cards are forwarded to the Office of the Treasurer of the United States in Washington, D. C. A specially designed card-reading device performs balancing operations and transcribes data for transfer to computer tapes bound for the National Computer Center (NCC) in Martinsburg, West Virginia, where the information on employer tax deposits is entered in the Business Master File (BMF). The normal time between payment and posting to the account in the BMF is six to eight weeks, but that period may be stretched to sixteen weeks by the data processing dfficulties in the payment accounting pipeline. In such cases, there is a substantial period during which the payment record is on the card, but not in the BMF. 

Employers report their withholding tax liabilities on Form 941, which must be filed by the last day of the month following the end of the calendar quarter. 892/ Because 941's are processed on an expedited basis, the regional Service Center will generally process the return and report the fact of filing, credits claimed, and all other relevant information to

the NCC within two weeks thereafter. Because Form 941 return-processing is wholly in the hands of the Service and receives high priority, it is often completed before the Federal Tax Deposits are processed by the Federal Reserve Bank and the Treasury Department and reported to the NCC. sequence, some employers claim FTD credits on their returns which are not reported to the NCC until well after the return is filed. 

Because of the delay in receiving credit information, the Service allows ten weeks from the scheduled time of the last deposit of the quarter for acknowledgement of the claimed FTD to arrive at the NCC. If at the end of that time all the credits claimed on the return have not been posted, as many as three notices may be mailed to the employer asking him to pay. 

But, if the balance due exceeds $500, a TDA is immediately sent to the 893/ district office.

These "accelerated" TDA's allow swift personal contact with delinquent employers. However, a 1974 Collection Division study showed ' that of all Form 941 TDA's issued in 1973, 28 percent, about 382,000, involved withheld taxes which already had been paid. This was thought to be due usually to the failure of tax-deposit credits to be timely posted to the 894/ 

Business Master File. 

The information delay also makes difficult the identification of an employer who has claimed non-existent credits. It is usually at least ten weeks after the end of the quarter, and after the employer's quarterly return is filed and processed, before the Service is able to detect his delinquency. Before being discovered, he may have accumulated half a year's withholding liabilities: the thirteen weeks of the quarter to which

3 non-payment relates and another ten weeks of new liabilities. 

At this writing, several proposals were being considered by the Service to reduce the time lag between the deposit of funds and credit thereof to the employer's BMF account. The proposal most likely to be adopted would require Federal Depository Banks to mail computer cards directly to the regional Service Center, where they could be transcribed to computer tapes bound for the National Computer Center. 

The troublesome practice of tearing off part of the card as a receipt for the employer would be terminated, the employer's check being regarded as a sufficient receipt. There is hope that the pipeline for crediting deposits will thus be shortened to two weeks from the time of deposit of withheld taxes. Cost savings of $13 to $14 million annually are anticipated. 

Quick identification of employer delinquents is vital for reasons that transcend cost savings. In times of high interest rates and a stagnant economy, United States money constitutes a ready source of cheap capital to unscrupulous or financially troubled employers. The penalty for failure to file a timely return is five percent per month, 895/ up to a maximum of 25 percent, but the costs of failure to pay have not always been great. There is a penalty of five percent of the underpayment for failure to make adequate deposits of withheld employee taxes, 896/ regardless of how late the payment is made. In addition, a monthly penalty of 0.5 percent is computed on the unpaid balance, to a maximum of 897/ 898/ 

25 percent. 

Finally, a mere six percent simple interest was

charged on underpayments until July 1975, when the rate rose to nine 899/ percent.

Interest on tax delinquencies is a business expense deductible for tax purposes, 900/ 901/ though penalties are not deductible.

Employers who may be most strongly tempted to utilize this source of capital are often those who are most likely to jeopardize the ultimate collection of the withheld amounts. If collection is not effected, the government is permanently damaged because sums withheld by employers are credited on employees' income tax returns and used in the computation of Social Se- 902/ curity benefits, whether or not remitted to the Treasury. 

Employers may be motivated not only by the comparative cost of borrowing in the marketplace, but also by sheer inability to do so. Thus, especially when money is tight, the government becomes an unwilling "lender" to the employers who "borrow" withheld taxes. The predictable result in 1973 was that employers filed 2.3 million balance-due quarterly withholding tax 903/ returns, 20 percent increase from the 1.9 million of the year before.

Over 180,000 more returns contained "errors" in arithmetic or preparation 904/ which, when corrected, resulted in tax owing to the government. 

Altogether, 15 percent of 1973 employer quarterly returns were not fully paid upon filing either because of "error" or an admitted balance due. 

While many of these balances were quickly satisfied in response to demands for payment, the Service assigned more than 1.5 million TDA's to local offices for collection of $2.5 billion in overdue withheld taxes. Some of these 

IDA's were issued without notice to the taxpayer and for taxes which had already been paid.

No accurate statistics exist of the number of repeater delinquents, but the consensus is that at least 50 percent of the employers on whom TDA's are The economic recession may issued have been delinquent in the past. 905/ have exacerbated the problem by crippling industries (such as transportation and construction) traditionally overpopulated with repeatedly delinquent employers. 2. 906/ 

Dealing with Employer Delinquencies. 

a. Office Branch Procedures. 

As a general rule, the Service seeks to close as many cases as possible in the Office Branch in order to (1) minimize collection costs by using Office Branch employees who are comparatively low-salaried; (2) avoid any duplication of efforts necessitated by transferring accounts to the Field Branch; and (3) maximize Revenue Officers' effectiveness by keeping their caseloads low.

TDA's coming from the Service Center are fist handled by the Office Branch, which in resolving delinquent accounts is substantially limited to telephoning and writing the employer about the account, filing liens, and serving notices of levy. It has no authorization to seize assets, which is restricted to Revenue Officers. By moving bank deposits around, an employer may frustrate levy attempts and pay only when threatened with seizure of his business by a Revenue Officer. Given the larger number of repeated delinquencies among employers, it is not long before the limited powers of the Office Branch became known to many delinquents. There is substantial belief that this knowledge emboldens the unscrupulous businessman to "borrow" at the Government's low interest and penalty rate until

approached by the Revenue Officer.

The issue of Office Branch handling of repeater employer delinquencies has engendered differences of opinion within every level of the Collection Division, as well as outside it. An Internal Audit Division review of accounts concerning repeat employer delinquencies concluded that failure of the Office Branch to make immediate referral of such cases to Revenue Officers weakened the overall effort to compel habitually delinquent employers to comply with payment requirements of the revenue laws.

Some offices continue to attempt resolution of most of these cases in the Office Branch, perhaps on the rationale that most employers will pay when told to do so and that seizures are infrequent anyway. 

Field Branch Procedures. 

b.

Revenue Officers must consider avenues foreclosed to the Office Branch, such as possible seizure and sale of the assets of the business. These problems are considered above under "Other Special Problems of Summary Collection." 

C. 

Civil and Criminal Penalties. 

(1) 

Special Accounting by the Employer. 

If an employer fails to collect, account for, or pay over withheld employee income or Social Security taxes, or fails to make deposit payments or file returns of the tax, $ 7512 of the Code provides that he may be required, by notice delivered "in hand" to him, to create a special bank account in trust for the United States for withheld taxes.

1 Deposits thereof to the special accounts must be made by the second banking day after withholding occurs, and are kept there until payment over to the 907/ 

United States.

Instead of quarterly returns, employers bound by the 908/ separate accounting provisions of § 7512 must file monthly returns 909/ and pay any balance due when the return is filed. 

With limited 910/ exceptions, any failure to do so (without regard to willfulness) renders the taxpayer liable to misdemeanor prosecution. 911/ 

Conviction carries with it a maximum sentence of imprisonment of one year and a fine of $5,000. 

In 1973 the General Accounting Office revealed that between 1958, 912/ when the separate accounting statutes were put on the books, and 1969 there had been only 56 prosecutions under § 7215. These resulted in 54 913/ convictions.

GAO concluded that the minimal number of cases which had been tried since the enactment of the statutes did not constitute a valid 914/ test of their deterrent capabilities. 

On April 3, 1973, four months before the GAO report was released,

IRS launched a "Trust Fund Prosecution Program" to intensify its utilization of the tools provided by the Code's separate accounting provisions. In the 

15 months that followed, there were 91 convictions and guilty pleas in $ 7215 915/ prosectutions - more than during the first 11 years combined. the same 15 months there were 1,680 orders to taxpayers to make separate accounting and monthly filings. 916/ In But despite the numerical advances engendered by the program, collection employees and management remain unconvinced of its efficacy.

Although many referrals for prosecution never get out of the Internal Revenue Service itself as a result of an in-house screening 917/ process, 919/ This officers and employees of the Collection Division perceive that the major problems of the program lie outside the organization. At all levels of the Collection Division there was agreement that the impact of the program would be much greater, but for the reluctance of the judiciary to act as "collec tion agents" and the preference of many United States Attorneys not to handle 918/ the cases at all.

The attorneys have bigger and more glamorous fish to fry. The judiciary's reluctance is manifested by light sentences for misdemeanor white-collar offenses (especially in metropolitan areas). result is galling to the Service because (1) whether or not the withheld funds are paid over, they must be credited to the employees' tax obligations, and (2) S 7512 denominates the withheld monies as "trust funds, thereby presumably holding the employer to the strictest integrity. A light sentence or insipid prosecution-- or no criminal proceedings at all are believed not to deter violations of the law but, perversely, to encourage them when it becomes known that there is no real penalty for failure to comply. 920/ Whether the lack of enthusiasm by prosecutors and judges will damper the Service's inclination to use the separate accounting provisions of the Code remains to be seen. 921/ One does hope that the Service will continue to work with both the U.S. Attorneys and the courts to obtain more vigorous enforcement of the separate accounting provisions, We suspect, as did Congress in passing the law, that same convictions would be preferable to not having a prosecution program.

Some delinquent employers claim false deposit credits on their returns in order to convey the false impression that all sums withheld have faithfully been paid over. Others claim only the insufficient credits to which they are actually entitled. Still other delinquent employers usually s? fail to make deposits, paying part or all taxes withheld when the return is filed. In any case these employers have not complied with the law -- not with fraudulent intent, in the usual case, but more probably as a desire to "borrow" 922/ capital which is too difficult or expensive to obtain by other means. 

Even if a fraudulent purpose existed, the requisite state of mind ติ 15 is stringently difficult to establish in either civil or criminal fraud JE 1 proceedings. 923/ Clear and convincing evidence of evil purpose and repeated, odious conduct are required.
