One other device is the "100 percent penalty," or the "responsible officer penalty." The term "penalty" is a misnomer, since the Service's practice is to employ the device not as a penalty, but as an alternative collection 933/ 934/ method.

This approach is supported by the cases. 

Section 6672 of the Code provides that an amount equal to the unpaid employee withheld tax may be assessed against persons reponsible to "collect, truthfully account for and pay over" such tax, who have willfully failed to do so. The amount of the responsible

the officer's liability, thus, is measured by employee income and social security 935/ as a taxes which are required to be withheld, but which are not paid over.

29 ​B. ofi As a practical matter, the responsible officer penalty is assessed only against officers of defunct corporations and against limited partners. Sole proprietors and general partners, being already liable for the tax debts of their ventures, are not assessed the "penalty.' There might be some deterrent value in the responsible officer penalty. 

Our distinct perception, however, is that many assessees of the penalty are unaware of it until the Service notifies them that it proposes to hold them liable for the withheld tax debt. There is no deterrent value in the existence of a penalty of which the officer has no knowledge. 

Plainly, the class of employers to be deterred consists of those who could make timely Federal Tax deposits but choose to prefer creditors other than the government. However, high delinquency rates strongly suggest that the Service's use of fraud, negligence, responsible officer, and perjury penalties have not discouraged many employer who willfully contravene withholding deposit laws. 

Civil money penalties do provide some deterrent effect, but do not render employer "borrowing" from the government economically unfeasible when commercial lending is costly or impossible. The threat of criminal sanctions, on the other hand, is puny. To deal with delinquent employers, the Internal Revenue Service has been compelled to develop special procedures, to which we now turn. 3.

Accelerated Handling of Employee Delinquencies. 

a. Federal Tax Deposit (FTD) Alerts.

Employers who have large payrolls rapidly accrue large withholding tax liabilities if they fail to make timely Federal Tax Deposits. The greater the

unpaid tax liability, the greater the collection headache for the Service, particularly if the employer is caught in a fiscal squeeze that makes it impossible to make up the delinquent taxes immediately. 

The National Computer Center computers have thus been programmed to generate an "FTD Alert" on certain employers for whom the Service has no record of deposits ten weeks after they are due. If the employer has been delinquent within the previous twelve months and the amount of his most recent quarterly withholding liability was $12,500 or more, an alert will be sent on computer tape to one of the ten regional Service Centers, which forwards it to the district office. A Revenue Officer is then assigned to contact the business. He will find out whether the deposit has been made, and if not, determine the reason and try to work out some means of bringing the deposits up to date. 936/ If the employer fails or refuses to cooperate, there is little the Revenue Officer can do. No summary collection action can be undertaken until and no assessment is possible until Form 941 However, the Revenue Officer can require the business to 938/ the liability is assessed, 937/ is filed. begin filing monthly returns instead of quarterly ones and put the firm on notice that it may be compelled to commence the separate accounting procedures of $ 7512. 939/ b. "Accelerated Issuance" Accounts.

A balance due may appear on the tax account of an employer when he files a return admitting nonpayment of taxes withheld or, if the return claims full payment of deposit liabilities, when no record of the payment is received within ten weeks of the time it was to have been made. Ordinarily,

B 1 if the employer has not already been the subject of an "ETD Alert", he receives three notices, which are mailed to him over a nine-week period, asking for resolution of the balance due, If receipt of the balance owing is not recorded by the Service Center in another two weeks, a Taxpayer Delinquent Account is generated to the appropriate district office for levy or 940/ other collection efforts. 

However, many BMF delinquent accounts are forwarded immediately to the local office as a Taxpayer Delinquent Account soon after or concurrently with the mailing of the first notice to the taxpayer. This is known as "acceleration," and occurs to TDA's coded "X", to denote that the NCC has no record of Federal Tax Deposits of $1000 or more claimed on the taxpayer's Form 941 or that the employer's return showed that large a balance due. As we have explained, it may take 16 weeks after the date of a deposit before the payment is posted to the NCC computer. Nonetheless, 941/ ten weeks after the due date for the last deposit in a quarter, if $1000 or more in deposit credits claimed on the return are not accounted for, a TDA therefore is assigned to the local office. (Of course, no waiting period is necessary if the return shows a balance due.) The "final notice before seizure," 942/ required before summary collection action is undertaken, is not sent to the taxpayer by the Service Center (which sends a single notice one week prior to issuing the TDA), but by the local office. If the matter is not resolved 943/ within ten days of the final notice, levy may be made automatically. 

Given the speed with which such "accelerated" accounts reach the field, the Office Branch is required to screen the accounts for late posting credits, which 944/ appear on IDRS before instituting levy action. 

If no levy source is

known, the account is referred to the Field Branch for assignment to a 

Revenue Officer. 945/ If the FTD is tardily posted, it is possible that summary collection action will be imposed against the employer even though he has made the deposit unless the Revenue Officer accepts his statement (if he is not in possession of a cancelled check or deposit receipt) that payment has been made. We do know of one circumstance in which forcible collection of such a nonexistent deposit liability occurred during the last year, but have no accurate estimate (nor does the Service) of the frequency with which this "double collection" 946/ It is known, however, that in 1973 about 382,000 941 TDA's were settled by "credit advice" (usually when the NCC received a deposit credit occurs. 947/ after issuance of the TDA).

This was an unusually high number, due to information-loading problems encountered during the phase-in of the IDRS computer system. These were all instances in which double collection was possible; given the few instances in which error is known to have occurred, one would have to conclude that the Service generally handled these accounts with a fair degree of care.

In addition to the X-coded employer withholding accounts, certain other Business Master File TDA's are also "accelerated." These TDA's are issued when there is an outstanding balance due on the employer's account ("A" coded) or a TDA has been oustanding on the account during the prior twelve months ("R" coded). "A" and "R" accounts will be accelerated even if the acount balance is under $1000: thus, even though the account does not qualify for acceleration 948/ through "x" coding, it may be accelerated on another basis. 

During 1973, "A"

coded TDA's 

some of which were for withholding tax liabilities and some not 949/ amounted to 393,600, or 24 percent of all Business Master File TDA's. "A", "R", and "x" accounts are accelerated to the local office because of the importance the Service attaches to withholding delinquencies. 

The revenue laws constitute the employer a trustee of withheld taxes--for the benefit of both the employee, from whose earnings taxes are withheld, and the government. 

Hence, accelerated accounts seemed to be most important to Revenue Officers whom we 950/ interviewed. C. 

Collecting Unpaid Returns Expeditionsly (CURE).

A third effort being made to deal with. burgeoning employer withholding delinquencies is focused on returns which show a balance due when filed. 

The Service, which shows no sign of ever running out of acronyms, has designated this program as CURE (Collecting Unpaid Returns Expeditiously). 

During the first steps of Service Center processing of quarterly Form 941 returns, those which show a failure to make withholding tax deposits are photocopied. The duplicates are mailed to local offices, where they are assigned to Revenue officers to contact the employer at his place of business. The Objective is to have a Revenue Officer on the employer's doorstep within five days after he mailed the return. If immediate payment is not made, the Revenue Officer may tender a written final demand for the taxes, which gives the employer ten days to pay before forcible collection action is taken. 

IRS management has determined that the CURE may be taken by any region in not more than two quarters of a calendar year, though it must do so in at

least one. The limitation of CURE is that it does not uncover those employers who have claimed fictitious deposits; hence, the Service worries that delinquent employers might feel driven to falsify their returns if it reacts so quickly on every filing of a balance due return. Claiming fictitious tax deposits is a felony offense, but the Service finds convictions hard to obtain. the CURE is not always administered, lest the patient develops an immunity. 

Making Deposit of Withheld Taxes with Revenue Officers. 

d. 951/ Therefore, Employers' Federal Tax Deposits are normally made to commercial banks designated by the Secretary or his delegate as Federal depositories. 

This creates some difficulties for the Service with habitually delinquent employers whose failure to make deposits does not trigger an FTD Alert. The delinquency usually does not became known until the quarterly return is filed, which means that the Service may have the tax obligations of an entire quarter or more to collect before it first becomes aware that deposits have not been made. 

Some Revenue Officers to whom we talked monitor the tax payments of habitually delinquent employers, even after delinquent accounts have been paid, by requiring them to furnish copies of FID receipts stamped by the depository bank, as well as duplicate Form 941 returns. It is our understanding that other 

Revenue Officers request the habitually delinquent employer to deposit withheld taxes with the district office, from which they are sent to the Service Center for crediting and finally to a depository bank for payment. Delivery of deposits or FTD receipts directly to the Revenue Officer is advantageous in several respects: (1) personal contact with the taxpayer enhances the likelihood that timely payment will be made by persuading the employer that the

Service is seriously concerned about his account; and (2) the Revenue Officer is immediately aware of failure to make timely payment. 

If deposits are to be delivered to the Revenue Officer, the cooperation of the employer is essential because Revenue Officers are not designated 952/ therefore, payments cannot be ordered to be made as Federal depositories; in that fashion. The 5 percent penalty for failure to pay over withheld taxes 953/ does not apply if payment is belatedly made to the Collection employee. 

However, the advantage of quickly identifying the delinquency may be worth surrendering the failure-to-pay penalty. 954% 

Because a Revenue Officer receives no statistical credit for monitoring FTD credits, he, thus, may not be motivated 955/ by the organization to do so, unless he is evaluated on such intangibles. 

Moreover, the Internal Revenue Manual makes no mention of this procedure. 

Because of all these factors, we believe this procedure is little used except if the Revenue Officer is holding an open TDA on the employer. 

While monies paid to the Revenue Officer would take more time to become available to the Treasury than would deposits with commercial banks, we believe that the delay is outweighed by faithful, timely payments by the 956/ employer who would otherwise be repeatedly delinquent.

The number of habitually and seriously delinquent employers who might be required to pay directly to the Service is a small portion of the taxpayer population. 

Although payment to the Service means delay in making the cash available to Treasury, the habitual delinquent might otherwise not pay until a TDA on his account is assigned to a Revenue Officer. Hence, in the case of habitually delinquent employers, an exception is warranted to the rule that withheld tax

deposits be made with banks. More efficient payment result when delinquencies are promptly detected. 4. 

Preventative Education of Employers. 

and collection willen Infant businesses are the most likely to fail to withhold and pay over employee income and Social Security taxes. Yet, the efforts by the 

Service to prevent delinquencies among them seem only marginal. 

When requests for an employer identification number are received by IRS, a set of pre-inscribed computer cards for tender of withheld tax deposits is mailed to the business, along with a circular explaining the obligation to withhold taxes and a flyer inviting the employer to request a personalized "Your Business Tax Kit " from Taxpayer Service Representatives at a local IRS office. The tax kit, which is delivered personally to the business upon request, consists of a set of tax forms and instructions for dealing with every Federal tax to be paid by the business. The tax kits are prepared only for those who request them, however, and the Service may not hear from businessmen who did not see the flyer or who do not have the education or sophistication to appreciate their tax withholding responsibilities. 

We have received a number of letters from employers who claimed not to realize their personal liability for payment of withheld taxes until receiving notice from the Service that it is considering assessment of a responsible officer penalty. These letters typically present an image of a small businessman innocently signing employee paychecks presented to him by an unscrupulous associate who has retained complete control of books and records. Only when IRS arrives does the 957/ signatory find that withheld taxes were never paid to the government. all representations in the letters may be true, of course, but they do have a Not

disconcerting similarity which led us to question whether the Service is making adequate efforts to alert neophyte businessmen to this responsibility. 

While it does not necessarily concern employers, the Service's experience with another tax involving businesses is also indicative of the problems faced in educating taxpayers. Not all of them are within the 

Service's control. For example, in 1956 Congress passed the Federal-Aid High- 958/ way Act, which imposed the Federal Highway Use Tax (HUT) on owners of certain trucks, truck-trailers, and buses using the public roadways. Nearly 

20 years later, many owners were not filing HUT returns, and the Service instituted a massive program to identify the non-filers. 

While it should be noted that the Federal-Aid Highway Act was passed as a temporary measure (it has been extended through 1977), the thrust of the Service's efforts have been on identifying those who are failing to file, instead of preventing the delinquencies from ever occuring. This could be done by placing informational flyers or decals in the vehicles before they are sold, but the proposal by IRS so to do was rejected by truck manufactures. Thus, the Service lost the opportunity to avert the disillusionment of those who have written to us protesting that even though they had never heard of the tax, the Service imposed penalties for failure to file returns and failure to pay the tax.

While the Service has not focused on preventative education, and sometimes has been prevented from so doing (as with HUT), it has attempted to resolve problems after they occurred. In Chicago, for example, the Service formed a task force to contend with the withholding tax liabilities accumulated

by approximately 125 new racial minority-owned construction firms after it was publicly revealed that many of them were in difficult straits with the tax collector. While the Service bent over backwards to keep all but two of these firms from amassing further liabilities or at least from being closed down by seizure action, our information is that in some instances the original delinquency was due to failure of the employer to comprehend, and plan for, his withholding obligations. Such lack of understanding might have been avoided through contacts by the Service when the taxpayers first received Small 959/ 

Business Administration grants. 

Such efforts by the Service are laudable (though resented by other ethnic groups), but they were designed to cope with delinquencies after they occurred and not before. 

In order for the Service to engage in such delinquency prevention activities, either an increase in manpower or a decrease in workloads may be required for Collection employees, many of whom feel there is too much to do already. While Revenue Officers are told that they should strive to spend 

70 percent of their time in the field, the consensus among those whom we interviewed was that 70 percent of their time was spent in the office filling out forms. 

This may not be a sincere estimate, since they did not generally feel the paper burden could be much reduced. The emphasis, they thought, should be on weeding out of small cases. 5.

Effectiveness of Employer Delinquency Collection and Prevention. 

Reduction of delinquencies depends on an interdependent array of factors, among which are public understanding of the filing and payment obligations which the law imposes on them, public confidence in the equity of

the tax laws, and the evenhandedness and efficiency with which the public perceives those laws to be administered. Swift, firm and fair collection of the tax is not an end in itself, for example, but only contributes to the greater purpose of fostering conditions that lead to voluntary compliance by the taxpaying public.

It cannot be said with certainty whether the Service could ever achieve this goal where the nation's businessmen are concerned. As a group, they are pragmatic and comparatively knowledgeable about the tax system. Examinations of the books of large corporations frequently result in huge tax adjustments, while small businesses are regarded by many as presenting perhaps the most serious problems in compliance with the substantive law. The problem on the Collection side, discussed at the beginning of this section, is more readily quantifiable: during 1973, businesses accounted for more than two TDA's out of every three, representing $4.17 billion of the $5.02 960/ billion in Taxpayer Delinquent Account issuances. 

The Service has no accurate means of ascertaining how many of these business accounts were generated by repeater delinquents. Neither does it know with certainty the present characteristics of the delinquent taxpayer population; for instance, the type, size, and longevity of the businesses involved, or the incidence of delinquencies resulting from economic reverses, ignorance, or calculated "borrowing." 

What the Internal Revenue Service does know is that the growth of Business Master File taxpayer delinquent accounts has not kept pace with the number of filings; BMF TDA's rose 17 percent in 1973, while filings increased by 961/ 

9.5 percent, but in 1974 the TDA figures dropped over 10 percent although 962/ filings rose by 4.4 percent.

It should be noted, however, that year-to-year

TDA statistical comparisons are inexact because of periodic changes in 963/ and alterations in IRS's criteria for issuing accounting techniques Taxpayer Delinquent Accounts.

Some were sent out in 1973 without first giving 964/ taxpayers nine weeks notice to pay, which had been the practice in 1972. 

Thus, it is not entirely helpful to compare the increase in delinquency rates to the increase in filings. The number and amount of delinquencies (not all of which become TDA's) might be a more reliable benchmark, but they are strongly affected by economic circumstances outside the Service's control. The rapid rise in business delinquencies is thought to have been largely due to the shortage of funds available from commercial lenders, high interest on available loans, and low penalty and interest rates charged by the Service on unpaid employee withholding and corporate income taxes. 

Instead of focusing on new delinquencies, therefore, one might instead look to the speed and cost of collecting the accounts. Such an inquiry is relevant because the additional revenue generated by penalty and interest accrued on delinquent balances is, in a real sense, depleted by the government's cost of collecting the accounts and of borrowing the amount of the delinquency in the public market. The result here is also unclear. Despite the multitude of statistics kept by the Service, the efficiency of collection programs is not known. About all that can be said is that most delinquent accounts are ultimately collected. For example, during 1973, the six-year statute of limitations on collection barred delinquent business accounts amount- 965/ ting to $54 million, a small figure when considering the hundreds of millions in business taxes which became due during 1967. 966/ 

But even that statistic is distorted by transferee, responsible officer, and multiple assess-

ments which have the effect of extending the statute of limitations, delaying and thus lowering 967/ the time by which some delinquencies become barred, the sum of taxes which are barred in a given year. 

Finally, one might consider that the burden on employers as collec- Remittances of income tion agents has expanded spectacularly in recent years. and Social Security taxes rose from $60.8 billion in fiscal 1966 to $145.2 billion in fiscal 1973. 968/ The total of trust fund TDA's issued during the 969/ same period rose from $454 million in fiscal 1966 to $2.

9 billion in 970/ calendar 1973.

Thus, the dollar amount of delinquencies has multiplied at about twice the rate of withholding obligations. This may, perhaps, be expected; as the sums to be withheld by employers have grown, so also has the temptation to "borrow" them.

In the opinion of some Revenue Officers whom we interviewed, the IRS business delinquency prevention effort is hampered by splintered management emphasis. The national, regional, and district offices each have their programs, such as CURE and separate accounting procedures previously discussed, which each desires to accent. The efforts are not always coordinated, and the result is that many local Collection officers feel unable to give any program the attention it merits.

Although it can be concluded that there are both strong points and shortcomings in the business delinquency collection effort, it may be impossible to assay the overall efficacy of the program. Even the Service cannot be (nor is it) entirely certain of its effectiveness in collecting delinquent business This is not just because of the unreliability of comparing statistics. 

The Service does not know what causes delinquencies (aside from adverse economic accounts.

conditions) and, thus, does not have clear notions of how to combat them. 

Until these concepts become clear, the efficacy of procedures for dealing with them will not be known.

​III. 

REVENUE OFFICER PERCEPTIONS A. Introduction 

The Internal Revenue Code and the Regulations thereunder allow the Revenue Officer to encumber and seize all property or rights to property belonging to the taxpayer, save the few items which are exempted from levy by S 6334 of the Code, to collect delinquent taxes. In creating these potent tools of collection, Congress did little to guide their use. However,

Our interviews with line Collection personnel indicate that, in seeking guidance, they look not to the Code and Regulations but to the Internal Revenue Manual. The Manual narrows discretion, as a general rule, chiefly by a process of elimination which leaves a large and essentially formless mass of discretion. Put another way, much attention has been given to telling the officer when he may not exercise his powers, but there is little to guide his actions within the scope of his freedom to act. same written and oral communications refer vaguely to encouragement of "compliance" with the law through "enforcement" of its provisions with the forcible collection tools. These terms may suggest a punitive theme, something more than collection of the tax, and indeed the consensus of Collection Division management is that a sizable majority of delinquent taxpayers have made a deliberate choice not to pay. Line Collection personnel whom we interviewed, however, would tend to agree that less than half of the delinquent taxpayer population is attempting to beat the system.

Be that as it may, there is nothing other than reference to "compliance" and "enforcement" which positively suggests the timing of distraint or lien-filling except in the context of jeopardy assessments. 

Instead, the Manual

is largely taken up with record-keeping instructions and mechanistic prerequisites. 

The Manual instructions for the filing of liens come nearest to providing the sort of guidance needed. The Revenue Officer to whom TDA's are assigned is directed by those instructions to determine within a specific time frame, whether or not to record the government's claim. He is at least invited to advise a supervisor of decisions not to file a lien to secure indebtedness exceeding a certain sum. Significantly, the filing of a lien is mandatory under same circumstances. Should any of them occur, the officer must reverse himself if he previously refrained from recording the lien. Beyond this, the lien instructions display a failing common to other Manual directions for exercise of summary collection powers.

They are not clear on what should govern the Revenue Officer's decision to record the Federal Tax lien. Moreover, while the Manual makes it plain that the Revenue Officer should attempt to extend the statute of limitations for collection if satisfaction of the liability is otherwise jeopardized by the passage of time, there are no directions whether to refile the lien in that event. 

Directions with respect to the serving of notices of levies on persons holding property or obligations of a taxpayer are quite brief. There is nothing to suggest what the timing of a levy should be. A laudable effort has been made to suggest when levy filing should not occur, however. Levies may not be imposed on successive paychecks, for example, and benefit income is also: largely immune from distraint. This has shrunken the large pool of discretion flowing from the statute and so far as we know, rules are followed to a large degree. But given the potentially severe impact of a levy, the substantial variances in levy practices disclosed by our interviews suggest that similarly situated taxpayers are treated very differently.

1 The same lack of guidance exists with respect to seizures of property from the taxpayer himself. The relative ease of serving notices of levy, the unpredictability of sale profits, and the paperwork entailed by seizure and sale combine to depress the number of seizures; there are still fewer sales, many items being returned to taxpayers. There is little to tell the Revenue Officer what the purpose of his action is, with the result that seizures are made for several reasons which are not altogether consistent. 

Cutting across the use of the seizure and levy powers against individual taxpayers is the concept of "undue hardship." Although the summary powers are not to be used if hardship to the taxpayer would be "undue," the Internal Revenue Manual contains no definition of the term and Collection personnel are uncertain of its scope. Collection personnel have a number of misgivings about entering into periodic payment agreements, and the uncertainty only dampens their use. Although our society widely accepts installment arrangements for payment of debts, some Revenue Officers do not believe that delinquent taxpayers are prepared to honor those relating to taxes. Moreover, nearly all believe that management discourages the use of periodic payments because they are not "firm enforcement" tools and do not close cases quickly enough. The result is that some accounts are reported to be uncollectible by Revenue Officers-an indication of the sort of latitude they have in writing off accounts. 

In the jeopardy and termination assessment areas, the Manual departs from form to set out affirmative instructions on "prima facie cases" in which use of the jeopardy powers is considered proper. This may have resulted in use of

the powers when there was nothing to suggest that the eventual collection of the tax was endangered. Indeed, some courts have voiced suspicion that the jeopardy powers have been used as an extrajudicial means of punishing suspected drug traffickers. This has occurred despite an extensive system of review established by the Service to ensure the reasonableness of such actions, again suggesting the confusion which has beset the agency over the purposes of the summary collection powers.

One concludes then that the power conferred by Congress is little fettered by Congressional action. Similarly, regulations do not greatly restrain the use of these powers. The Manual is somewhat more helpful, but it does not contain many precisely drawn job tasks. Rather it deals with the mechanics of taking action rather than with the considerations bearing on whether action should be taken. Put in other words, there have been few direct messages which give guidance to Revenue Officers as to the time and manner of exercising their discretion. 

We, therefore, thought it necessary to discuss with Revenue Officers the constraints and mandates they perceive.

A. Introduction. 

Endowed by the Internal Revenue Code with these forcible collection tools, Revenue Officers can be ranked among the most powerful of all. The utilization of these potent tools being largely unfettered by the statute, regulations, or any formal agency rulemaking, both the choice of the tool and the decision to exercise it are largely controlled by whim or judgment, depending upon one's point or view. The absence of any well-defined guidelines is critical because the use of summary collection actions may result in serious consequences to the taxpayer. 

While these actions may also be an effective means of collecting the tax, perhaps they are no more efficacious than methods less damaging to the taxpayer.

We found that the Internal Revenue Service, and more specifically, Collection Division personnel, were aware of these powers and their intrinsic potential for both collecting the tax and causing injury. Thus, we decided to interview a number of Collection Division personnel to discover whether the abundant discretion accompanying these powers might have been channeled by the Service through means other than formal rules. 

For example, the decision-maker may be sufficiently aware of, and committed to, agency goals to structure his conduct thereby. Discretion may also be patterned on objectives or strategies adopted by the agency to attain its goals. If neither of the foregoing are satisfactory, very specific job tasks might be drawn to limit the broad discretion not otherwise channeled. However, the Service has not generally drawn precise rules. 971/

Another effective and perhaps less direct means for structuring conduct is to reward (and thus encourage) certain kinds of conduct or to punish (and thus discourage) other kinds. 

Bearing on effectiveness of any of these techniques is the degree to which line personnel (those executing policy) understand and accept the policies rendered by management (the policymakers). Moreover, we believed that the attitudes of line personnel toward their immediate superiors, management in general, and taxpayers would be most relevant. 

Thus, one purpose of our interviews was to ascertain the perceptions of line personnel on these matters. Where perceptions and policies diverge and where they agree are discussed below. While we spoke with nearly fifty field Collection personnel in a number of offices, it may be argued that our conclusions do not represent the attitudes of Collection personnel nationwide. Although we recognize such a qualification, we have neither reason nor evidence to suggest that the opinions and attitudes expressed are not generally representative of Collection as a whole. several common threads of thought were almost universal among those interviewed. Also, it may be said that the geographic locus of our interviews 972/ was small, having been limited to the Mid-Atlantic Region. However, Furthermore, we found that many interviewed had migrated to this region from nearly every section of the country.
