B. Goals and Objectives. 

1. Formulation and Validity. 

Although "goals" and "objectives" are occasionally used interchangeably, the terms do connote different concepts. A "goal" is a broad statement of intent or purpose, while an "objective" is a performance statement (that is, strategy, action, or conduct) which is designed to reach 973/ the goal. a. Goals.

Without a goal there may be no principles by which to establish adequate priorities and strategies for organizational accomplish- Decision-makers may often decide questions on the basis ment of a task. of conflicting theories and thus pull in different directions without being 974/ aware of the differences. On the other hand, if a Revenue Officer properly understands the Service's goals, he may be expected to exercise his broad discretion consistent with his perceptions of them. If he does not understand them, he may vacillate, take inappropriate action, or generally exhibit confusion and inconsistency. The consequences may be damaging to the government and devastating to the taxpayer. 

Despite the need for Service goals, Congress has legislated very little with respect to them. Instead, it has charged the Secretary of the 

Treasury with responsibility for the administration and enforcement of the 975/ tax laws.

Although these duties are largely delegated to the Commissioner 976/ of Internal Revenue, either the Secretary or the Commissioner are empowered to issue such "directives, instructions, orders and rules" as are

977/ necessary. 

In the collection area Congress has merely decreed that 978/ the taxes be collected.

It granted formidable tools for this purpose, but gives no advice for choosing the means of collection to be employed in a particular case.

Neither the President nor the Treasury Department have filled the breach left by Congress in structuring goals. Nor has the judiciary, because the matter is outside its jurisdiction. By default, then, the agency and its Commissioner have been left to forage for themselves. 

One would not expect a Commissioner to be overly aggressive in 979/ establishing goals. First, he is serving a limited term, which consequently reduces his influence, and perhaps his interest, in the long-range direction of the agency. Having inherited a bureaucracy which will survive both him and succeeding Commissioners, he is encumbered by whatever longrange plans the bureaucracy has developed. These plans inevitably restrict his options, particularly in the budget area. Finally, after finding his way through the bureaucratic maze and learning what it does (which may take six months or more, depending upon his penchant for out-of-town speaking engagements and other public relations endeavors), a Commissioner 980/ may well focus only on specific projects and problem areas. these factors diminish his ability to direct attention to the Service's overall goals and consequent objectives and strategies. All of Given this lack of direction from the office of the Commissioner, the bureaucracy itself moved to fill the gap. It chose the promotion of "voluntary compliance" as the overall goal of the agency and apparently of the Collection Division

as well. 981/ While "voluntary compliance" is an agreeable term and a highly desirable condition, it is ambiguous and uncertain. Coupled with the doubt that the term may be defined is the lack of certainty about the reasons for compliance. It is not known why some people pay their taxes and others do not. Nor is it known which actions of the Service promote voluntary compliance. Because adequate objectives or strategies cannot be based on a gossamer goal, "voluntary compliance" cannot guide the conduct of Service personnel.

While there is little in the form of goals, either determined by the agency or as dictated from without, there are priorities or measurable accomplishments which are important to Congress and thus important to 982/ the Service. For example, from 1955 through the present 983/ the Service has annually provided tables showing delinquent taxes on which collection action has been suspended because they were determined uncollectible. In 1973, when the number and dollar value of delinquent accounts rose, Senator Proxmire stated that the increase ..raise[s] "I serious questions regarding the tax collecting performance of the Internal 984/ Revenue Service given existing statutory tools." Similar concerns surfaced just a few weeks ago when a Subcommittee of the House Ways and 985/ 

Means Committee held oversight hearings.

While there have been occasional questions about the use of 986/ forcible collection actions, interest in delinquent taxes has usually been directed toward the adequacy of collection efforts, and specifically toward the justification of expenditures on the basis of dollar-production

statistics. For instance, the Service responded to such a question at 

Congressional hearings by stating that "[t]he actual yield from the delinquent accounts collected in fiscal year 1973 was $2,457 million. The cost to collect this amount was $113 million, giving a yield cost ratio 987/ of 22.8 to 1." The message thus received was that taxes should be collected immediately, with the least possible cost. 

Obviously, collection of the tax is important. It constitutes But at least a major purpose of the Collection Division. Collection personnel have been provided with a group of strong tools to effect the purpose. whether they choose to use one of these tools or to employ some other means of collection is almost entirely within individual discretion. If the employee is guided toward securing the earliest possible collection and if he responds in a positive manner to this instruction, he will likely use one of these strong tools. Indeed, forcible action may be taken simply to demonstrate that every effort is being made to collect the tax, even when the Collection official knows that such action may not result in payment of the tax.

We conclude that the only strong guidance consistently given the Service by Congress over the years is that the tax should be collected quickly. 

The message falls on human ears which, predictably enough, translate it into the employment of those collection tools or techniques available, of which there is a wide variety. Thus, the tool employed by the Collection officer depends very little upon guidance from the Congress or management on overall goals. Because the goals charted by Congress and the Service

at -¿ The .A are either illusory or oriented toward more rapid collection, we turn to the Service objectives to determine whether different promulgations can be found. b. Objectives. 

(1) Objectives Stated by the Organization. 

Organizationally-defined objectives seem to 988/ In fall into two categories: those communicated to line personnel and those not communicated. Dissemination is made through training materials, which identify the primary purpose of Collection as the promotion of compliance and the securing of delinquent taxes and returns. addition to these overriding and general purposes, several functional abjectives are enumerated, such as "to locate taxpayers,. .to get information accurately, to talk with taxpayers and third parties [to] initiate 989/ various actions, [and to] process various forms. 

On a more abstract level there are five professional objectives: "(1) Enforcement of a firm collection policy (2) Protection of the rights of the government (3) Protection of the rights of the taxpayer (4) Utilization of [Revenue Officer and taxpayer] time and energy with maximum efficiency [and] (5) Education of the taxpayer to insure future voluntary compliance[.] 

We should not ask which of these objectives is the most important one: All are essential to the professional operation of the Service. All are of top priority." 990/

These objectives were the only ones communicated to line 991/ personnel. However, Service management perceived a need for further objectives, and thus, chose "to continue and improve the quality of 992/ [the Collection] program through:

"a. 

Strengthening public confidence in the Tax

Administration System by improving the image which the Service projects in the process of collecting delinquent accounts and securing delinquent returns. "b. Maintaining a balanced enforcement program and high level of voluntary compliance by closing, at a minimum, the same number of delinquent return investigations that will be issued during FY 1975. "c. Conducting an expanded Returns Compliance Program in order to...detect nonfilers." 993/ The primary objective was identified as "administering the tax laws in a firm impartial manner, using only that level of firmness needed to accomplish the task. 994/ [Emphasis added]. Because these were management objectives, they were not, as far as we could ascertain, communicated to line personnel, who, predictably, seemed unaware of them. 

(2) Objectives as Stated by Collection Personnel. 

During our interviews, we asked Collection personnel to enumerate the three most important objectives of their job. Most Offic 

Branch personnel (individuals who generally do not leave the office to effect collection) could not verbalize any objectives. Many did not seem to understand the question, despite our best efforts, and others admittedly had never given the question a thought. Many Revenue Officers (individuals who contact taxpayers in the field to effect collection and work on the

most difficult cases) could not verbalize three objectives. In both the 

Office Branch and the Field Branch, those who did articulate objectives most often mentioned "collecting the tax," "promoting voluntary compliance," and "educating the taxpayer," in that order. There were also scattered votes for firm enforcement, case closures, better public relations, maintenance of taxpayer goodwill, and taxpayer assistance. Almost all 

Revenue Officers mentioned "collecting the tax" as an objective. 

Probing further, we found that Revenue Officer conduct believed to promote "voluntary compliance" ran the gamut from immediate seizure to mere cajolery. "Collection of the tax," however, was more easily defined as the instigation of forcible collection action, if necessary. course, what constituted "necessity" varied form perosn to person. Means by which taxpayers could be educated were similarly diverse. of Almost no mention was made of the functional or professional objectives enumerated in the training materials. We also noted that management's objective of "collection of delinquent accounts" was almost universally translated into "collection of the tax." The phrases connote different actions: collection of "delinquent accounts" suggests a range of activities, such as securing a delinquent return or tracing a payment claimed by the taxpayer, but collection of "tax" suggests money in hand. 

Moreover, the phrases were given different emphasis. Management perceived the collection of delinquent accounts as one of several objectives, while line personnel saw collection of the tax as the major, and sometimes the only, objective.

C. The Evaluation Process. 

1. As Required by the Internal Revenue Manual. 

The divergence between the objectives expressed by management and those expressed by line personnel is heavily laden with significance. 

It is possible, however, that objectives not explicitly circulated among employees may be implicitly imparted through personnel evaluation. Thus, before discussing the discrepancies in expressed viewpoints, we turn to evaluation methods and criteria. a. 

Formal Evaluations. 

The Manual requires three "distinct but related evaluations" for Revenue Officer performance analysis. (1) The Civil Service Commission requires a supervisor 995/ to make an annual determination of whether an employee's overall performance has been satisfactory, outstanding, or unsatisfactory. A "satisfactory" 996/ Civil Service rating is a prerequisite to any salary increase. Revenue 

Officer promotions to GS-9 are automatic if the rating is satisfactory. (2) Promotions above GS-9 require a rating under the Servicewide promotion plan. This more extensive evaluation, which occurs only when promotion is requested, is based on a form listing ten items, each to be rated on a five-point numerical scale: job knowledge, utilization of time, job attitude, learning ability, dependability, initiative, judgment, communication, independence, and quality of work. Any rating other than "3" (denoting satisfactory work) must be supported by a written explanation. 

Apparently, an overall rating of "3" or better is necessary for promotion 997/ 998/

41 to grades above GS-9. Because GS-9 and GS-11 Revenue Officers are eligible for grade promotions annually, evaluation under this plan would 999/ be a yearly event for those who have applied for promotions.

(3) The third type of evaluation has been the 1000/ "workload review" which focuses on twenty items relating to specific 1001/ work issues, such as "financial statements are complete and current" These items are rated satisfactory or unsatisfactory by the group supervisor on the basis of his review of some or all of a Revenue Officer's work 1002/ accomplished since the last review. 1003/ This evaluation should be done at least annually and, according to Revenue Officers, typically occurs more frequently. The Manual states that this workload review will be the basis upon which the Civil Service and promotion-plan evaluations are made; therefore, the Group Manager "should" include his day-to-day observations of the employee and his work in this review and use them as a basis 1004/ for arriving at overall performance analysis. 

It should be noted that the Group Manager may gather data from a variety of optional sources in arriving at an overall performance analysis. One of the more common methods is the field visitation, in which a Group Manager accompanies a Revenue Officer for all or part of a 1005/ day on his visits to taxpayers in their homes or places of business. 

Other services include a review of the Revenue Officer's reports, workflow charts, activity reports, and closed cases. 

b. Other Requirements. 

1006/ There are a few other directions on the evaluation process found in organizational promulgations. Group Managers are given

Revenue Officers may be evaluated. the broad admonition to establish "performance standards" against which 1007/ The managers are also directed to inform their subordinates of the good and bad aspects of their per- 1008/ formance and to develop an action plan for any needed improvement.

C. The Use of Statistics. 

A more controversial issue involves the use of quotas or production statistics in evaluating Revenue Officer performance. 

Although quotas were uniformly used for evaluation purposes prior to 1961, the compilation of statistical information on individuals in the Collection 1009/ function has been forbidden by national office decree 1010/ on the one hand, on the other. The national office and more recently by union contract policy attempts to define statistics as a management tool for determining which "areas" need "attention" and for assuring proper manpower utilization. "[Statistics] shall not be used to evaluate an enforcement officer or to impose or suggest production quotas or goals...

Subject to this restriction, a manager may raise questions with an individual about the number of cases he has processed, the amount of time he has been spending on individual cases, or the kinds of results he has been obtaining." 1011/ 

This directive clearly rules out the use of production statistics as an evaluation tool. Effective use of time is, however, a discussable subject. 

The difficulty in distinguishing between these two approaches may explain some of the controversy surrounding quotas, norms, standards, and workload planning. We know that the use of quotas and norms is not allowed, but that the use of standards of production and workload planning, as discussed above, is permitted. The difficulty in drawing lines between the permissible and the impermissible arises from a number of factors.

First, management relies entirely upon statistics for inventory control and relies heavily upon them for workload planning. Presumably, the reliance is proper because, on a national level, the approximately 2-1/2 million Taxpayer Delinquent Accounts issued this year are very much like the 2-1/2 million TDA's issued last year. This sameness is perceived by people in local offices to be extrapolated to the current year's workload by the national and regional management to determine what accomplish- 1012/ ments may be anticipated.

Second, the incoming case level of the Collection Division in any office (including the national office) is dependent upon the number of taxpayers who have chosen not to, or who by necessity have been unable 1013/ to, pay their taxes. Local inventories may be somewhat controlled by shifting manpower or caseload on a local or regional basis to alleviate the situation. Another device which affects inventory is the dollar tolerance level for case issuance; however, a single tolerance level is established by the national office for nationwide application and is not adjusted to control local inventory. On the whole, however, inventory is difficult to control on a local basis, although there is a desire to keep it at a low level. 

The national office may reason that because of the similarity of case characteristics, the anticipation of certain levels of production by the local office is proper if not communicated to line personnel. They are not intended for use in individual evaluations, though many of these compilations require the reporting of case dispositions. Moreover,

the national office has informed line personnel, through training and memoranda, that quotas do not exist, although production standards may be discussed with them. The distinction between the two may lie in the manner in which they are utilized; i.e., quotas are mandatory, while production standards are precatory. However, the national office denies that workload accomplishment projections are made on any but a national basis, and that these are not reduced to standards or quotas for regions, districts or employees. It does appear that the development of production standards has been left to the Group Managers. However, they may lack the overall perspective for establishing production standards. Further, they are given no guidance by the Internal Revenue Manual. Although the similarities between TDA's on a national level may provide a basis for their categorization and classification into broad classes of complexity, no such broad range of information is available to Group Managers, who must allocate cases assigned to their groups. The national office has not formulated production standards for Revenue Officers, and the Group Manager has insufficient information with which to do so. As such standards are nonexistent, the Revenue Officer may (and often does) perceive that he is being prodded by his Group Manager to close more cases at such times when the supervisor raises the issue of effective time usage. 

This situation contrasts sharply with the utilization of production standards by the Audit Divison. In the Audit Division every return is initially classified by income level as presenting a known degree of difficulty. This initial classification is then questioned and

RE 1 CE perhaps modified, first by the Returns Program Manager and then by the Group Manager. After closure, the manager will again review the case to ascertain the correctness of the original determination. 

Based on such analysis, Audit Division personnel are expected to dispose of a specified number of cases for each work unit. If an individual fails to accomplish די- his part of the "Audit Plan," he may discuss with his supervisor whether he is receiving the "right kind" of returns for audit and thereby defend his use of time. In other words, there are production standards in Audit, and failure to dispose of the right number of cases is a matter of concern, investigation, and explanation.

The Collection Divison initially designates some accounts for handling by experienced personnel, the difficulty level being determined by the unpaid balance, initial assessment on the account, type of 1014/ entity involved, prior delinquency history and type of tax.

Cases not singled out for assignment to grade 11 or 12 Revenue Officers are grouped together for assignment. However, these do not seem to be the sort of easy handles, such as income levels, kinds of income or deductions, complexity of transactions, or similar factors, by which to determine the degree of difficulty presented by a particular account. Collection personnel undoubtedly embark upon assignments armed with less knowledge than Audit personnel, though the national office believes it adequate. However, data supplied to the officer or his manager seems insufficient to suggest how many manhours must be invested to obtain a specific number of TDA closures. The managers know how many are anticipated by the national office;

their subordinates do not.

1015/ Discussions between a Collection officer and his manager about effective time usage will consequently focus on inventory, a known quantity, rather than on production standards, which are either withheld or never formulated. 2. 

Revenue Officer Perceptions on Evaluation. a. 

Formal Evaluations. 

Nearly all Revenue Officers perceived the workload review to be the critical evaluation event. If the Revenue Officer has 1016/ handled his cases in a "proper" and "timely" manner and if his inventory has remained at an adequate level, he is given a satisfactory rating. Yet, the factors most determinative of his inventory, i.e., difficulty of cases and intake of new inventory, are not within his control. Nevertheless, the great majority of line personnel cited quantitative production indicators as an important, if not the most important, factor in performance evaluation. (The important quantity is the number of cases closed, not the number of dollars collected.) A large number of Revenue Officers also believed that frequent use of liens, levies, and seizures was desirable in demonstrating the ultimate effort to keep case inventories low.

Non-statistical evaluation was considered largely a question of compatibility with one's Group Manager or branch chief. Such evaluation is focused primarily upon technical job knowledge and the ability to work with the public. A few interviewees considered judgment and job attitude relevant factors to this evaluation; fewer still mentioned

5 f dependability, or the ability to work independently, or the effective use of time. None directly mentioned learning ability, initiative, communitcation, or quality of work. Thus, four of the ten items given on the Servicewide promotion plan evaluation form were not cited by anyone. b. Other Requirements. 

According to Revenue Officers, the other requirements of evaluation were not utilized. For example, it was reported that Group 

Managers do not reveal those performance standards which are considered acceptable, either in terms of acceptable quantum or quality of work. If the above speculations regarding the Service's failure to promulgate standards are accurate, this result is not surprising. 

Further, few Revenue Officers received any more than one field visitation per year. Many commented that they were rarely, if ever, told of good performance. Few had ever developed an action plan with the Group Manager for improving work quality. 

The Service's use of the numerical rating system was also a basis for comment. A few officers believed that the policy of rating them at "3" (satisfactory), unless another rating could be substantiated in writing, discouraged supervisors from giving poor ratings because of personal antagonisms that would ensue. However, most simply did not approve of the rating system. The common complaint was that a supervisor would not take the time necessary to substantiate a higher rating, even when deserved. Therefore, most officers considered the entire rating process meaningless since ratings other than "3" were rarely given.

C.

Use of Statistics. 

Revenue Officers believe that production statistics 1017/ are a significant factor in their evaluation, official decrees notwithstanding. Our analysis and application of general management theory support this conclusion. 

Management relies extensively on statistical data compiled by region, district, branch, and Revenue Officer group. At the group level, managers will announce group production statistics and compare 1018/ them to the quantitative records of other groups; this may put production pressure on all group members. Further, line personnel believe that managers keep individual statistics, either formally or informally; 1019/ there is no doubt that managers have the capability so to do. 

Audit discovered that some Group Managers were maintaining individual 1020/ production statistics as late as June 1974.

Internal Revenue Officers also receive other, more subtle, transmissions about production statistics.

Those who are not accomplishing the acceptable (though unannounced) level of production are made aware of this through repeated remarks by, or many talks with, Group Managers. Those who attain high production levels work with much less overt supervision. Also, seasoned Revenue Officers communicate the priority of statistics to recruits, 1021/ while the detailed time and workload reporting requirements also transmit a message. Finally, the emphasis in workload reviews is placed on rapid case closure, use of proper procedures, and thoroughness in case reporting. Consequently, there is a pervasive belief among Collection personnel

is bit 1 3 that those individuals who close a large number of cases and make frequent use of the "firm enforcement" tools--liens, levies and seizures--are pro- 1022/ moted more quickly than those who do not.

The officers' perception of the existence of mandatory standards of production, or at least pressures for case closure, seems accurate. 

Statistical information is collected, aggregated, and communicated by the national office to lower level management. This communication, made without any distinction between workload planning and production standards, occurs through the dissemination of a monthly "Box Score." This document, prepared monthly for each district and each region was until a recent reduction, a 10-column, 73-line sheet which generally detailed the number and amount of cases received and disposed of. There are also National 

Office Review Program (NORP) reports, heavily oriented towards statistics, in which the national office formally examines and comments upon a region's accomplishments. Although NORP reports are addressed to regional management only, there is an inescapable tendency on the part of some intermediate managers to stress those same factors to lower management. Thus, the ripple of statistical evaluation back down the chain of command gathers the momentum to reach the Revenue Officer.

Our interviews have led us to conclude that the degree to which the ripples of statistical evaluation are felt by Revenue Officers depends largely on their Group Managers. Some managers will exert substantial pressure on subordinates, even to the extent of "requiring" liens, levies, and seizures; others will not.

3. Lack of Quality Review. 

While Revenue Officers possess a number of tools which require the use of discretion, few believe that its exercise is reviewed. 

Moreover, none were aware of any disciplinary action having been taken against an officer as a result of taxpayer complaints regarding overly 1023/ zealous collection efforts, although nearly all knew a "butcher." 

The consensus among the Revenue Officers interviewed was that supervisors are far more concerned about "lenient" actions taken by their subordinates than "harsh" actions.

These perceptions are supported by a 1974 Internal Audit examination of evaluation practices in several districts. Internal Audit generally found poor review and follow-up procedures, including a number of instances where quality of performance was not even considered. was concluded that "top level field Collection Division managers were knowledgeable as to current trends relating to workload and accomplishments in the various program areas as shown by the statistical reporting system but had little information regarding the quality of the work performed by Revenue Officers. This, we believe, results in overemphasis on statistically measured achievements with an unfavorable effect on field collection activities." 1024/ 

4. The Role of the Group Manager. 

It

The Revenue Officer Group Managers are responsible for the overall performance of their groups and must evaluate each of their subordinate Revenue Officers. Thus, they are the critical, immediate representatives of higher-level Service management, responsible for interpreting and communicating procedures, objectives, and policies to line personnel.

Yet, the Group Managers are neither fish nor fowl: by Service definition they are not management, yet they are classified as managers in 1025/ the Service's contract with the National Treasury Employees Union. 

Thus, Group Manager input is seldom directly solicited by the national office, and they receive little opportunity to influence policy. Because 

Revenue Officers seem to understand this situation, they do not regard Group Managers as a part of management or as exerting much upward influence. 

Therefore, Officers do not hold them responsible for overall Service policy or procedures.

Further, Group Managers are likely to be ill-equipped to make As a general rule, they are a transition from line to management. promoted to their positions from the ranks of Revenue Officers, and thus, may be expected to retain line personnel's general uncertainty about goals and objectives. Because they are not "management," they are not privy to either the Service's overall objectives or the reasons for official policy, which thus cannot be communicated to their groups. However, they may be expected to urge upon their subordinates the priorities they perceive as emanating from higher-level management. 

Their overriding concern for case closures is, thus, only a reflection of their natural orientation: many are former Revenue Officers, most of wham believe that closure of a high number of cases and substantial use of summary collection devices are both desired by higher management and a requisite for promotion. Indeed, an evaluation based principally upon quality factors, the alternative to management by numbers, requires

skills and orientation often not acquired as a Revenue Officer certainly not perfected by Group Manager training. The Revenue Officer is told t that educating the taxpayer is of equal importance with closing cases, and that voluntary compliance by taxpayers is the goal of the Service.eu 

Group Managers, who are former Revenue Officers, are encouraged to review their subordinates' performances on the basis of quality rather than numbers. Nonetheless, meaningful subjective evaluation requires a belief that non-statistical factors are important, both to acceptable individual performance and to the Service. The pervasive concern of the Service appears to rest on numbers, rather than on quality factors. 

In defense of Group Managers, it should be noted that subjective review and evaluation of quality factors would be difficult, given their uncertainty about Service goals and objectives. For example, how would a supervisor justify a qualitative demerit when the action taken resulted in collection of the tax? In addition, the paperwork and other burdens imposed on a Group Manager would not seem to allow him the substantial time required for subjective evaluation of quality. 

Moreover, if production standards are unknown by the Group Manager, and they are, interpreting or inventing them without implying quotas may require skill beyond us all. Consequently, many Group Managers do not verbalize any standard of acceptable performance. Although we believe there is a difference between telling a Revenue Officer that his production is low and informing him that his work practices are inefficient (after statistical discrepancy or inconsistency has warned that something is amiss), many

1 Group Managers seem incapable of applying this distinction. The importance of such a distinction becomes clear when one considers that all occupations have both acceptable and nonacceptable levels of output. While the Group 

Manager may not be cognizant of the acceptable level for his subordinates, he does recognize that Revenue Officers' output is easily quantifiable and that such statistical data are important to management. Thus, he may interpret this importance as a requirement to utilize production quotas, although he is prohibited by Service policy from revealing them to his subordinates. 

The Service also denies their existence and refuses to verbalize any relevant standards of output. The manager may, however, doubt such a disclaimer and reward production. Certainly, however, such a process must render him uncomfortable. 

A variety of other special problems confront Group Managers. In the absense of sound criteria in the Manual for structuring discretionary use of the powers granted his Revenue Officers, it is difficult for the manager to evaluate their use of judgment. Given the emphasis on statistics, it is difficult for him to give a low rating to an officer who has "produced" or to down-grade an officer whose performance has been inferior although the group has performed well. Furthermore, the review process is timeconsuming and sometimes unpleasant. In addition to his inability to clarify Service policy for his subordinates the Group Manager is probably neither well trained nor inclined to evaluate these individuals subjectively, given his perception of the Service's reliance on production statistics.

D. 

Revenue Officer Attitudes Toward Management. 

Our interviews confirmed that there is a high degree of dissatisfaction among Revenue Officers with management (although Group Managers are amitted from this classification). These sentiments are based upon a variety of perceptions.

When Revenue Officers are inducted into the Service, they are repeatedly told that their position is a professional one and that they therefore must exhibit a professional attitude. While Revenue Officers desire such status, in their opinion the Service does not treat them accordingly. It is their feeling that they are the last among line personnel to be told of management imperatives; that policies and procedures are imposed on them without consultation; that because their comment on policy is not solicited, they are unable to influence any changes within the Service; and that management distrusts them, as evidenced by extensive accountability requirements and a general lack of facilities, equipment, support personnel, and direct access to those tools which would permit more efficient and effective utilization of their time, e.g., IDRS and micro- 1026/ film. 

Yet, they believe that they could contribute considerably to the more efficient functioning of the Service if their opinions were 1027/ solicited.

Furthermore, they were nearly unanimous in their belief that national office management had little conception of their problems and no interest in their ideas. 

They were also nettled by what they perceived as a practice by the Service of raising and lowering the entry level GS rating for Revenue

Officers to whatever the market would bear, i.e., sometimes it would be a 

GS-5 and sometimes a GS-7. Two individuals with the same credentials could, we were told, be a grade level apart during most of their careers, despite having entered the Service only six months apart. However, the national office advised us that these entry levels were not raised and lowered, but depended strictly on the education and prior work-related experience of the particular applicant. 

Revenue Officers also believed that they should have access to higher grade levels, given their responsibilities and discretionary powers. During our interviews we discovered that levels of Collection management believe low pay scales are at least partially responsible for the high rate of attrition among Revenue Officers in those geographic areas where more remunerative job opportunities are available. (The yearly attrition rate is seven percent nationwide.)

Finally, Revenue Officer attitudes varied from indifference to resentment on the frequent changes and conflicts in work priorities dictated by management at national, regional, and district levels. 

First, they may be exhorted to reduce the dollar amount of their inventory by concentrating their efforts on the larger cases. When that occurs, the unit number of accounts, overage cases, and delinquent returns investigations may increase. As a result of management's subsequent desire to lower unit inventories, the average dollar value of IDA's may then increase.

Thus, Revenue Officers feel they are continually kept off-balance if they

follow each new directive. As a consequence, many officers informed us that they did not respond to every such change in policy. 

Our review of NORP reports for the last several years suggests that this priority-shifting emanates from the national office. For example, one year these reports might criticize a region for doing something poorly, The next year the region may be criticized on other grounds, yet will receive no commendation for its successful treatment of the previous year's problem. In the following year the seesaw might tilt back to emphasis on the second problem. While same regional Collection officials expressed a 1028/ strong desire to achieve a balanced approach to collection efforts, this would be difficult to achieve under such circumstances. 

Among line personnel resentment fostered by this and other practices apparently leads to resistance to, or subversion of, changes dictated by higher-level management. For example, local management evidently decided that in some offices "too many" installment payment agreements were being defaulted and that the use of such installment agreements should be discontinued. Conflict initially arose over the definition of "too many," and was followed by disagreement over the reasons for default. It was discovered that same accounts had not, in fact, defaulted, but that same installment payments, though timely made, had not been posted by the Service to proper accounts. This was due both to 

Taxpayer and IRS errors. Also, line personnel within these offices believed that those accounts which were clearly defaulted resulted from an absense of periodic, personal Revenue Officer contact with the taxpayer.

This lack of contact is a result of the Service's practice to forward automatically an installment agreement to a distant Service Center for monitoring by computer. Thus, substantial controversy developed over the problem of defaulted payments. 

Management subsequently directed officers to cease utilization of such agreements. Revenue Officers responded by (1) ignoring the directive and continuing to refer installment payment agreements to their supervisors for approval; (2) following the directive; (3) writing off as uncollectible an account which previously would have been recommended for an installment payment agreement; or (4) initiating informal installment agreements and keeping them "in the desk" (i.e., in inventory as open cases) without reporting them for supervisory approval. 

Resistance to policies decreed by higher-level management was typified in another instance.

Revenue Officers are forbidden to accept 1029/ post-dated checks in payment of delinquencies. 

Recently, however, the Service decided to test an experimental procedure in several offices whereby post-dated checks would be accepted. Revenue Officers were apparantly confused by management's sudden change of heart. Also, problematical was the requirement that Revenue Officers forward all postdated checks to the Office Branch which would "close" the case when the checks were paid. Because Revenue Officers would not, therefore, receive credit for "closures" (the most important number in statistical evaluation), resistance was great. In fact, the experiment itself faltered until management changed its policy to permit officers to receive credit for 1030/ closures in transferring accounts to office branch.

E. Treatment of Taxpayers. 

Revenue Officers expressed generally benevolent attitudes 1031/ toward delinquent individual taxpayers. However, they took a dim view particularly those which are habitually of delinquent businesses, delinquent in paying taxes withheld from employees. Nearly all officers agreed that a taxpayer's behavior was an important element in determining what collection action would be taken. Thus, a courteous, pleasant taxpayer would more likely receive favorable treatment than one in a similar situation who is discourteous, hostile, or generally unpleasant.

F. Implications.

Without any guidelines to steer employee conduct, it is likely to be whimsical, inconsistent, unpredictable, and highly personal. Such guidelines are usually composed of comprehensible goals, a system of abjectives, or precisely-drawn job tasks. 

In aid of these, or even 1032/ in lieu of them, many organizations use employee evaluation as the "carrot-and-stick" to indicate those areas where conduct has been appropriate or deviant.

The Collection Division's goal of promoting voluntary compliance is meaningless in tempering employee behavior. Further, it has failed to create many precisely-drawn job tasks. In structuring employee behavior, Collection appears to rely on a system of (1) objectives and (2) evaluations. However, we found that those objectives known were differently perceived or considered unrealistic. In other words, the 

Service's stated objectives were, for the most part, in conflict with Revenue Officer perceptions of them. Where the two did not conflict, there often was a belief that the Service was unrealistic. Formal guidance from the Service was, therefore, left primarily to the evaluation process. However, this process is little understood by either Revenue 

Officers or Group Managers because management's use of numbers for planning purposes has not been effectively translated into comprehensible production standards. Because such standards do not exist, discussions of case closures and time utilization were interpreted as discussions of production quotas.

Thus, the Service's guide to appropriate behavior was generally perceived as case closure. As there are a variety of techniques by which to close cases, we found that the major constraint on choice was the ed officer's perception of, and ofttimes compassion for, the taxpayer. Hence, Collection personnel are guided by little more than a personal sense of justice (given the paucity and uncertainty about goals and objectives) and the need to close cases. 

One almost inescapable conclusion, unanimously supported by Revenue Officers, is that the above combination of pressures results in dissimilar treatment of similarly situated taxpayers. For example, some 

Revenue Officers admitted using summary collection action more readily when unit closure rates were low and consequently imposing levies prior to contacting the taxpayer. In situations where a business is delinquent in paying withheld employee taxes, one Revenue Officer might quickly seize and sell the business's assets; another might forestall immediate action in the belief that the business will pay its liabilities. Although both actions would probably be technically correct, the taxpayer would thus depend on happenstance. r's fate

While Service management has made efforts to prevent such disparities, line personnel doubt that uniform treatment exists and attribute this lack of uniformity to their own broad discretionary powers. 

Because this use of discretion receives little guidance from the Service and because it usually emanates from Revenue Officer's immediate imperative, we concur with line personnel.

Another consequence of uncertain objectives and interest in case closures is the firm conviction held by most Revenue Officers that performance evaluation is based on production of closed cases. However, most officers believe that statistics do not accurately measure the quality, nor recognize the difficulty, of their work, and they resent the perceived reliance on numbers. Because their perception conflicts with management's assertions that it does not evaluate by numbers, distrust of management also results. Revenue Officer resentment may lead to a subversion of policy in a desire to "get even," while distrust may lead to diffidence toward policy. An officer may reason that if managment is not candid about case closures, there is an equal chance that it will be insincere about other policy statements. 

However, the undesirable consequences fostered by a belief that numbers are important do not stop here. For example, the belief that unit closures are important may often cause Revenue Officers to close easy cases first. Since these cases tend to involve smaller liabilities, inventories of overage cases or large-dollar TDA's may increase, causing management to shift its emphasis to them for a time. As a result, unit inventory will swell and emphasis will again be shifted to reducing this. 

Thus, a self-generating cycle has been created. Emphasis on unit closure will also result in case closures at the sacrifice of collecting dollar liabilities.

Revenue Officers will report cases uncollectible in order to receive credit for closures even though they may believe that sufficient money would be forthcoming to justify the government's time investment if the matter were pursued.

The orientation toward management by numbers in evaluations also operates to the detraction of more subjective matters, such as uniformity of taxpayer treatment, quality of decision-making, and attitudes toward taxpayers. To the extent these elements are not reviewed, evaluation is not used to improve performance. The primary goals of evaluation are considered to be timely feedback on good and bad aspects of performance, the rewarding of good performance and the discouraging of bad, and the communicating of standards expected to be met. However, line personnel believe these factors are relatively unimportant. Thus, even when they are stressed by Group Managers, there is doubt about sincerity. Consequently, in many cases the evaluation process may not improve employee performance or develop personnel for positions of enlarged responsibility. 

There are, then, serious consequences to the present system of objectives and evaluation. While much of the foregoing appears to place the difficulties at management's doorstep, all of it does not belong there. It must be remembered that management responds to pressures. the one hand is a Congressional desire to collect taxes. Similarly, there is a generally held belief that it is unfair for the vast majority of taxpayers to comply while deviants circumvent the system. These considerations probably motivated Congress to fashion the powerful collection tools it did. But, Congress has also evinced a desire that these tools be used judiciously as they have the capability to destroy. 

Frequently trumpeting this viewpoint is the media (which sometimes acts

as though collection of delinquent taxes was somehow an evil), displaying cases where the injured taxpayer did not appear deserving of his fate. 

For various reasons the Service often does not respond with its side of the story. Service management is thus damned if it destroys taxpayers and damned if it does not collect the taxes. And, the utilization of these potentially devastating tools are believed essential to collecting taxes.

Not wishing to appear in the public eye overly fond of destroying taxpayers and mindful of the axiom that "you get what you measure," Internal Revenue management has attempted to steer a course between that Scylla and the Charybdis of failure to motivate employees to do their best. 

Thus, it authorizes use of statistics for overall management purposes, while forbidding their use in evaluating individual employees. Perhaps this effort may be a greater task than any individual, much less a bureaucracy composed of very diverse individuals, can accomplish. That the 

Service has been unable to draw a line between quotas and production standards should not be surprising. We are uncertain whether such a helpful distinction can be drawn and instituted. Perhaps, analysis of TDA's and workload planning would reveal characteristics with which to classify TDA's and thus establish work standards. If not, management should eliminate from the evaluation procedure references to production standards and realistically face the need for entirely subjective evaluation. other alternative, it seems to us, is to return to the quotas of the 1960's. 

There may also be other alternatives, but their development would, we believe, require considerable time and resources. Whether either the Congress, the public, or the Service is willing to expend such resources is unclear. One

The reporting of cases "significant to tax administration" is a hangover from the "sensitive case" reporting procedure, which was used to keep the National Office advised of matters which could be publicized by the media. In an IRS Manual Supplement, dated Nov. 13, 1974, the sensitive case procedure was suspended until "a modified and curtailed system has been developed and implemented. . . .[F] ield offices .[are to keep appropriate management levels advised of matters significant to tax administration." IRS Manual Supplement 48G-225, 51G-109, 5(17)G-125, 8(23)G-80, 956-53. This directive is ambiguous, but we have been told that it had virtually no effect on operating levels and that there is literally a logjam of sensitive material held at district levels. 

Indeed, the handling of sensitive cases in the Collection Division was revised and transmitted to the field under a date of issuance of December 18, 1974, more than a month after the sensitive case procedure was suspended. 

Int. Rev. Manual, § 5132, MT 5100-54 (12-18-74). The sensitive case" procedure was a formal reporting system by which the national office was kept informed of cases subject to publicity or inquiry by Members of Congress. 

Id. § 5132.1, MT 5100-54. The Service has maintained that the national office did not enter the decision-making process in these matters.

be 1 Hearings Before the Senate Subcomm, on the , U. S. Postal Service, and General Government Appropriations of the Comm. 

On Appropriations, Internal Revenue Service, Taxpayer Assistance and 

Compliance Programs, 93rd Cong., 2d Sess., at 789 (1974). Nonetheless,

It seems clear that the proposed action was, and still is, reviewed by the local office. This may be looked upon as not being evenhanded tax administration, since in the routine levy case there is no prior restraint by management. The more the proposed action is reviewed, the more chance that someone will veto it. Thus, Collection personnel are more cautious with a "significant" case than they would otherwise be, The opposing argument is that the prior restraint is desirable for the protection of the taxpaying public. For example, disruption of the financial affairs of a hospital might have adverse consequences to public health. Forcible collection of the debts of a radio station might adversely affect the Civil Defense communications network, The Service has adopted the latter line of reasoning. Thus, proposed action on "significant" cases is reported on an informal basis within the district level. Reporting by the district to the regional or national offices is apparently a matter of discretion. 

200/ Int. Rev. Manual § 5311:(10), MT 5300-44 (5-21-74) Id. at § 5132.1, 

MT 5100-54 (12-18-74) defines sensitive cases as those "which, if they became known, would be of considerable public interest, resulting in inquiries or criticism directed to the National Office, particularly by the mass media or Members of Congress." Examples are provided and include public figures, well-known or charitable organizations, and individuals whose prior dealings with the Service have been publicized. See also, id. 

S 4584.2: (2), MT 4500-136 (1-18-74) (banks, newspapers, insurance companies, and public transportation companies) and id. at § 5132.2: (1) (a), MT 5100-54 (12-18-74). ("The enforcement action to be taken in a particular case will affect a large number of people or will undoubtedly result in media coverage.")

455/ Id. at § 4584.5: (2) recognizes the following as "prima facie jeopardy cases: "(a) Cases involving well-known major operators in the criminal field, irrespective of present financial condition. 

This is due to the fact that these individuals by the very nature of their business activity are in such position that their financial condition could change at any time without warning. (b) Individuals generally known to frequently wager large amounts. In these cases the loss of a single bet might reduce the taxpayer to insolvency; this is especially true if his assets consist largely of cash. (c) Individuals engaged in taking wagers, irrespective of whether major, secondary, or minor operators. Although taxes in these cases might not be in jeopardy to the same extent as in cases under (b), nevertheless, a series of losses could absorb all of the taxpayer's assets. (a) Individuals engaged in other activities generally regarded as illegal where there are possibilities of large unexpected losses or interference with their business or activity by others of the criminal element such as hijackers, blackmailers, etc. (e) Individuals with a background and history of

activity in illegal enterprises such as gambling, bootlegging, narcotics, etc., who are presently engaged in so-called legitimate business ventures. Such individuals must be considered a poor risk by the very nature of their activities and probable associations with the racketeer elements. (f) Taxpayers engaged in legitimate business, but are consistently suffering business or personal losses. (g) Taxpayers against whom large damage suits are pending or against whom such suits are threatened. (h) Taxpayers who have a past record for resisting or avoiding payment of their taxes. (i) Taxpayers known or suspected of having plans for leaving the United States without making provisions for payment of their taxes, with particular attention being given to aliens generally considered as border hoppers. (j) Other taxpayers where the facts and circumstances indicate that the taxpayer's present financial condition or future possibilities are such as to make collection of the tax doubtful."

507/ See Sherman v. Nash, 488 F.2d 1081 (3rd Cir. 1973), which although subscribing to the rule that the courts lack jurisdiction to review the District Director's finding of jeopardy, held that the District Court had jurisdiction to entertain a complaint that a jeopardy assessment had been made solely to coerce plaintiff to appear before a grand jury and not to produce or protect tax revenues. Thus, though a finding of jeopardy cannot be reviewed, inquiry may be made to see whether, in fact, there was any such finding. To the same effect is U. S. v. Bonaguro, 294 F. Supp. 750 (E.D. N.Y. 1968), in which it was found that the assessment was not made because of jeopardy.

626/ Int. Rev. Manual, § 5311: (10), MT 5300-44 (5-21-74). Commissioner Alexander may have been expanding on this theme when he testified before a House subcommittee: "In the collection area, we want to be both vigorous and humane. We want to see to it that people pay their taxes. We want to use strong action only where really necessary to protect the interests of the United States and after taking into account the effect of that action, not only upon the entity that owes the

3 taxes but also upon the employees of that entity if that entity is a going business. We are trying to do that. "These two objectives are in conflict to some extent. A very strong collection policy--pay it now or we will close you down--would result in a higher percentage of collection returns to the Government than a stance which is more inclined toward taking the strong action, using the maximum weapons, only after we have exhausted all reasonable means of working with the delinquent taxpayer without putting that delinquent taxpayer out of business. We are trying as best we can to mesh these two goals because we think we do have a dual responsibility in this area."

precipitous decline of levies in recent years is partly due to changes in the substantive law which have reduced the tax burdens of many thousands of low-income individuals and exempted many thousands of others from filing returns

as well. At the same time, withholding rates have been sufficiently high that most individual taxpayers fully satisfy their tax liabilities in that manner. As a result, low-income taxpayers, who bore the brunt of much of the Service's levy power, no longer have tax liabilities at year's end. 

Several administrative changes have also helped. The Service has given the taxpayer more time to pay voluntarily by extending the amount of time between the mailing of a first notice to the taxpayer and issuance of a Taxpayer Delinquent Account (TDA) to the field Collection office. More nearly current information on the employers of delinquent taxpayers is received from the Social Security Administration, thus reducing the number of fruitless levies. 

Finally, the Service has raised the "dollar tolerance" level, thus delaying issuance to many whose balances fall below that level and collecting some by off-set against refunds claimed by the delinquent taxpayers on subsequent returns.

726/ The practice of sending reminder notices was initiated in the fall of 1974. It will certainly reduce the frustrations of taxpayers who wrote to us complaining that a refund expected on the filing of a return was reduced or entirely offset by some long-forgotten delinquency from a previous taxable year. At the very least, it is a step by IRS toward better public relations. 

The reminder notices are not sent to delinquent business taxpayers because their accounts are not frequently subject to refund offset. Further, the tolerance level for deferred business accounts is much lower than that for individual accounts. 

727/ The offset may only occur within the same Master File. That is, an unpaid balance due on the taxpayer's 1974 Form 1040, which would be entered on the Individual Master File, may be offset by an overpayment of tax indicated on the 1975 return. The taxpayer may also be filing business returns, data from which would appear on the Business Master File. Though IMF credits are not offset automatically against BMF delinquencies, or vice-versa, a code can be inputted to either Master File to prevent issuance of refunds until the other Master File is checked for outstanding liabilities. 817/ Offers in compromise are considered only as a last resort after all other possibilities have been explored. They are handled by a very few experienced Revenue Officers by means of an exhaustive review of the offerer's past and present financial circumstances, as well as his potential for future earnings or inheritances. A thorough investigation of the taxpayer's personal background is similarly required. While lump-sum payments are accepted, they are often tied to "collateral income agreements" which bind the taxpayer to remit from 20 to 50 percent of before-tax income over basic needs in liquidation of the difference between the

compromise payment and the original liability over a set period of years. 

Other collateral agreements reduce the basis of capital assets for purposes of reporting gain or loss on their subsequent sale or other disposition. 

Still others waive such tax benefits as net operating loss deductions, excess investment credits, and net capital loss deductions for certain Agreements accepted by the Revenue Officer are subject to intensive review which, if the amount being compromised exceeds $100,000, extends all the way to the national office. 

818/ During 1973, the IRS processed 3,211 offers to compromise a total of $115,910,000 in liabilities for $15,950,000. Some of these, 879 were accepted, representing payments of $4,693,000 in settlement of $47,868,000 in assessed taxes. IRS 1973 Camm'r. Ann. Rep., Table 13.

It is questionable whether the offer-in-compromise procedures are known to many taxpayers. For example, no mention of them appears in Publication 

586, the Service's explanation of the collection process which is published for the benefit of taxpayers. 

819/ The compromise agreement provides, however, that if there is a default by the taxpayer in any payment due under its terms, the Service may elect to pursue the entire liability without regard to the compromise.

832/ IRS Student Coursebook, Revenue Officer Training, Phase I, § 20.223, Training Doc. 2225-28 (7-73), directs: 

"Each expense item must be considered as to amount and also to its necessity. Expenses for luxuries should not be included in necessary living costs. 

Necessities include groceries, rent or house payment, utility expenses, drugs, clothing, customary educational expenses, hospitalization insurance, life insurance, automobile expenses, religious contributions and other like expenses. These are considered necessary only to the extent reasonable in each individual case. .No set dollar amounts can be set for these categories to cover all taxpayers. .You should not hesitate to require full payment if the financial information and verification through investigation reveals that the taxpayer is living above his means. 

To illustrate, there is no undue hardship if the taxpayer. . .enjoys special cuts of meat of the most expensive type as a regular diet, supplemented by cocktails."

840/ A delinquent account is "over-age" when it is in active inventory and was originally issued as a TDA prior to a date specified by the national office. The date is moved forward from time to time, but the general idea is to designate TDA's "over-age" if they were first issued more than one year from the present. Accounts can be written off and then regenerated as TDA's, but the date of first issuance controls. 

841/ The inference available to management is that the more overage cases in inventory, the more slowly (and less "firmly" and effectively) the local office is handling delinquent accounts. The inference can, of course, be confirmed only on a case-by-case review, but is regarded as very strong by local management, which often overemphasizes statistics. 855/ Uncollectible Accounts Recap. 

856/ The Service has experienced considerable difficulty with taxpayers who can be "located," but not contacted. Usually the addresses shown on their returns belong to relatives or friends and serve as mere mail drops. When reissued, these accounts almost always remain uncollectible because the debtor cannot be found. Considerable sentiment exists for developing a new closing code to limit successive attempts to close these cases. 

857/ By selecting any of 11 closing codes, the Collection employee may assure future TDA issuance if the taxpayer's adjusted gross income exceeds $4,000 through $14,000, in thousand-dollar increments. 

858/ After sampling 944 hardship cases written off by six districts during 1971, the Internal Audit Division concluded that concrete criteria were necessary because 96 cases were coded for income levels too high in relation to expenses revealed by financial statements. It was said, "...there are no definite guidelines for the coding of hardship write-off cases. . . [G]uidelines are necessary so that taxpayers in similar financial circumstances will be given uniform treatment. Taxpayers with similar financial conditions are not given uniform treatment when closing codes for different [income] levels are used. [Some] taxpayers. .escape the requirement to pay the amount that their income exceeds their expenses; accounts in deferred status must pay this amount at a miminum." 

IRS Internal Audit report, Coordinated Audit of Write-Off Activities, at 15 (1973). 

As we have seen, no such "requirement" is explicit in the Manual, which serves as the primary reference for Revenue Officers. Internal Audit recommended, however, that judgmental factors be reduced in hardship cases. Id. at 17. 859/ "We believe that closing code selection must be based on the Revenue Officer's judgment. Specific criteria would restrict the collection effort, and it could defeat the purpose of the closing codes entirely, by forcing the use of an unappropriate closing code. .The selection of [income levels for reissuance of accounts] must be based on the Revenue Officer's analysis of the taxpayer's financial situation. Strict criteria would eliminate the judgment of the Revenue Officer and would result in reissuance of accounts that will require further efforts only to again report [sic] them uncollectible."

IRS Internal Memorandum from Harold E. Snyder, Director, Collection Division, to

957/ One might question whether such a person is a "responsible" officer subject to the 100 percent penalty imposed by IRC, S 6672. The responsibility to identify the responsible person is in the hands of the Revenue Officer. By the time of assessment of the penalty, the corporation is often defunct. Hence, the Revenue 

Officer's motivation for imposing the penalty is heightened by the virtual certainty that if the tax is not collected from the corporate officers, it will not be collected. Further, the Revenue Officer may be motivated to place a maximum number of arrows in the government's quiver by assessing the penalty against as many officers as possible. For a more extensive discussion, see Civil Penalties, chapter 3, text accompanying nn. 180-185. Thus, it may be that Revenue Officers may assess the penalty somewhat liberally.

971/ "Though organizational leaders are quick to recognize the importance of involving their followers in system goals, they are slow to utilize the most natural devices available to them in the form of job rationale. . .The understanding of one's role and how it relates to other roles, is a good bridge to involvement in organizational goals. . .On the other hand, if the role incumbent receives information about job specifics without job understanding, it is difficult for him to see how his role is related to the organizational mission. "Withholding information on the rationale of the job not only is prejudicial to ideological commitment of the member, but it also means that the organization must bear down heavily on.. .specific instructions about the job. If a man does not understand fully why he should do a thing or how his job relates to the tasks of his fellow workers, then there must be sufficient redundancy in his task instructions so that he behaves automatically and reliably in role performance. 

Katz and Kahn, The Social Psychology of Organizations 241 (1966).

1012/ In the 1974 Taxpayer Assistance and Compliance Hearings, at 661, Assistant Commissioner (ACTS) Robert Terry testified: 

1013/ .we have a basic management problem of how much resources in terms of manhours do we need to do the job. So first we determine the workload to be accomplished, the total number of taxpayer delinquent accounts, taxpayer delinquent investigations to perform, et cetera. "We found the best way to identify both the workload, the number of units to be accomplished, and the manpower that is required to accomplish it, is to go to the district level. With 58 districts we do have quite a variation around the country. "So we have then first the workload identified, how many units can we expect as we project for the next fiscal year or the next period. Then we have to determine how many people, how many revenue officers will we need. То do that, each district looks at its past and current experience, total number of cases closed and hours expended to determine the norm for projecting their manpower requirements. "That is how we translate the number of units that have to be closed into the number of man-hours required, and in turn the various categories of people that will be needed to stay abreast of the incoming workload." "[From statistics prepared by the national office, the District Director].. .and other management personnel determine whether or not they are performing at the projected level and whether such actual performance is reasonable." "There is a significant distinction between audit and collection. The audit workload is a workload that is pre-determined by us and controlled by us, in terms of the number of cases we are going to audit in any given year. "In the collection area however, we are on the receiving end of an unknown workload that is generated as a result of external factors which impact on the taxpaying public. "Since we do not know nor can we control what kind of dimensions of collection workload will be received, we

attempt to make projections based upon factors that we do know about such as the economy, geographic variations, past experience, et cetera. These coupled with the kind of taxpayer delinquencies we are apt to be dealing with-for example, trust fund accounts--makes the time element in the collection area crucial. "We must know how much time it is taking us to dispose of the uncontrolled collection workload, so that, whether or not our own projections prove out we can adjust and siphon our manpower resources to the types of delinquencies with which we are being confronted as the year unfolds. And time provides us with the insight we require to make these program decisions." 

Id. at 669-670 (Testimony of Anita Alpern, Deputy Assistant Commissioner (Planning and Research)).
