Since there is then a lack of empirical data with respect to these penalties in the report which follows, we must assume that the practice of the Service is more or less accurately represented by decided court cases. 1

B. Fraud, Negligence, and Intentional Disregard of Rules and Regulations. 

1. Civil Fraud. 

a. Introduction. 

Section 6653 (b) of the Internal Revenue Code states that if any part of an underpayment of income tax is due to fraud, an amount equal to 50 percent of the underpayment shall be added to the 13/ tax. This penalty is a civil penalty and must be distinguished from the criminal penalty under $ 7201 for a willful attempt to evade taxes. 

The latter is considered a felony, conviction of which may lead to a fine, 14/ or imprisonment, or both. 

Both civil fraud and criminal tax evasion are intentional There are, however, actions and may thus appear indistinguishable. differences between the two which are discussed more fully later in this report. At this point we note only that there is a difference in the burden of proof and that assertion of one does not prevent assertion of the other. One may be guilty of criminal tax evasion under § 7201 and still later have the civil fraud penalty exacted. Indeed, even an acquittal of criminal tax evasion does not bar the collection of the 15/ 50 percent civil penalty under $ 6653 (b). 

The statute imposes the penalty for fraud, an apparently familiar concept of a knowingly false representation made with intent to induce reliance 16/ on the representation. Recklessness is deemed to be knowledge of falseness.

17/ The Internal Revenue Service appears to have adopted this definition by defining fraud as a knowingly false and material representation of fact with an intention 18/ that it be accepted as true.

If, as the Internal Revenue Manual states, civil tax fraud were a mere intentional misstatement, a taxpayer who knowingly pads his charitable contributions by even $5 would have committed fraud. 

Similarly, fraud would exist where tip or business income is knowingly underreported or where non-existent deductions are knowingly claimed. The Service, however, does not usually treat these cases 19/ as fraud cases; instead, they are often treated as negligence. 

Thus, notwithstanding the Manual's definition, the definition of tort fraud has not been carried over to the tax law. Rather, the construction placed by the Service on the concept of civil fraud is much narrower, and our common understanding of fraud does not help to define "fraud" for tax cases. Instead, the parameters of civil tax fraud may be fixed only by that definition, looking at the courts' treatment of it. b.

The Courts' View of Civil Fraud. 

20 tax fraud case.

M. Rea Gano is often cited as the paradigm civil 

In Gano the Board of Tax Appeals provided an apt description of the types of conduct which both the Service and the courts seem to consider necessary elements for a successful civil fraud case: "Isolated instances of discrepancy or occasional lapses from the rigid accountability contemplated

by the law might conceivably be overlooked, but where the whole fabric of petitioner's tax accounting is permeated with gross error, where elaborate artiface is employed to accomplish the ends sought, where the evidence adduced in explanation on different occasions varies so as to make it all unreliable, where sworn statements are proven by records to be false, and where the errors both of law and of fact all tend to accomplish a reduction of apparent tax liability, the situation goes beyond mere fortuitous coincidence, or unintentional error. 

It evidences a purpose to evade." 21/ 

Certainly, this language requires far more than mere knowing misrepre- Yet, civil tax fraud has been found with consistency only sentation. after proof akin to that described in Gano. 

The effect of such strong language may be more clearly seen 22/ in context of the following case. In Alfonso Castells the IRS asserted the civil fraud penalty against a waiter who had earnings of $2,490 from tips, but had reported only $865 of that income. The Tax 

Court judge rebuked the IRS in the following sharp terms: 60 "This seems to us another in the series of litigations which respondent's agents in a mistakenly zealous crusade have lost sight of the forest in their pre- Occupation with something that is not even a small tree more like a blade of grass. . .Either petitioner consistently understated his income from tips in the years before and after [1954] or he did not. 

If he did, no reason appears why respondent's agents .should construct their case on a single year. .it is

If he did not, and this we must assume, powerful affirmative evidence that the single amission in the year in dispute was not intentional. ..We regret the loss of time to all concerned in this proceeding, which could assuredly have been put to better use." 23/

3 Despite the Tax Court's assertion that fraud of a single year is proof of no fraud, the logic on which the assertion is based is not clear. 

However, the views expressed in this opinion are nearly uniformly shared by the courts: the scope of civil fraud is limited to egregious cases of highly culpable conduct.

The validity of this conclusion is illustrated by the factual situations in which fraud has been found. In the great majority of such cases the factual elements of the fraud have been remarkably similar. Income is usually omitted in a manner which reflects a repetitious pattern of evasion; namely, the income is concealed or 25/ The taxes evaded tend to 24/ understated in several different years.

26/ be relatively large in amount. Often there will be concealment such as hidden bank accounts, double sets of books, forgeries, giving false information to the accountant, lying to the Internal Revenue 27/ agent.

In some instances fraud arises where the taxpayer repeatedly 28/ fails to file a return. In sum, the message sent by the courts to the Service is unmistakably clear. The civil fraud penalty will be sustained only if the factual elements of the fraud are overwhelming. 

Burden of Proof in Civil Fraud. 

C. 

The judicial insistence on an overwhelming factual 29/ presentation may in part stem from the fact that the Service must carry the burden of proof in civil fraud cases. 30/ Furthermore, the Service's burden is heavier than the usual civil preponderance-of-the-evidence standard. 

Instead, the Service must prove civil tax fraud by clear and convincing

31/ evidence. 

The cases state that fraud: "...implies bad faith, intentional wrong-doing and a sinister motive. It is never imputed or presumed and the courts should not sustain findings of fraud upon circumstances which at the most create only suspicion." [footnotes amitted] 32/ Since a taxpayer will seldom admit that he knew his return was false or that he intended to deprive the government of the correct tax, the taxpayer's state of mind must usually be established by circumstantial evidence. This burden is easily met when an overwhelming factual case exists. For example, recurrence of the same pattern of evasion over a long period of time can hardly have been an accident. 

If the taxpayer funnels income from an undisclosed source into a secret bank account, he leaves no doubt of his intentions. Such "objective" 33/ evidence satisfies the clear and convincing criterion. 

However, the courts' desire for overwhelming proof appears based on more than an excess of care in seeing that the Service has carried its burden of proof by clear and convincing evidence, for example, where a taxpayer omits a large percentage of income from tips. 34/ Yet, courts have typically treated such cases as negligence, rather than fraud, cases. The reluctance to handle such cases as fraud appears to be founded on the belief that civil tax fraud involves something quite different from mere intentional inaccuracy in a tax return. Instead, our reading of the cases suggests that civil tax fraud is nearly equated to criminal tax evasion. This view of the cases is also reflected by Service policy, as indicated by a study done in 1974, when the Service found that in same districts 35/ the civil fraud penalty is rarely asserted in any non-criminal case.

d. Civil Fraud and Criminal Tax Evasion Compared. 

Before enactment of the 1954 Code, the civil penalty that is now imposed for fraudulent conduct was imposed for conduct This language was 36/ "false or fraudulent with intent to evade tax. very similar to the criminal statute which proscribes willful conduct 37/ "to evade" taxes. This similarity in language gave a good reason for similarity in construction. While the statute imposing civil penalties was changed in 1954, there is nothing in the legislative history to indicate that the change in language was intended to effect a change in the quality of the conduct subject to the penalty. Thus, the criminal evasion and civil fraud statutes have continued to develop together even though the language of the civil statute has been considerably changed. 

The parallelism of the two statutes is further reflected by the Manual which, after its initial bland reference to tort fraud, 38/ subsequently characterizes civil tax fraud as "tax evasion", a term 39/ which very often is used to connote the felonious criminal conduct handled in S 7201. Furthermore, the congruity of civil tax fraud and criminal tax evasion has been recognized by cases holding that a criminal conviction collaterally stops the taxpayer from denying that civil fraud was present. 

This result follows because § 7201 contains all the elements of fraud envisaged by S 6653 (b). 40/ Of course, this result does not necessarily answer the question whether civil fraud embodies fewer elements. 

The distinction between civil tax fraud and criminal tax evasion is quite blurred.

Criminal tax evasion is a felony offense that is

41/ against a petty cheater. prosecuted to punish highly culpable conduct and to generate maximum deterrence. A charge of criminal tax evasion is not typically brought 

Instead, the typical evasion prosecution in- 42/ volves large amounts of income and tax deficiencies, patterns of conduct stretching over several years, and particularly reprehensible forms of concealment. Also, it is used as an enforcement tool 43/ against racketeers and drug dealers. Apart from that aberration, it is generally accepted within the Service that the condemnation implicit in a conviction for tax evasion, carrying with it the threat of imprison- 44/ ment, is best reserved for the most flagrant cases of abuse of the tax laws. Since criminal tax evasion is applied in only flagrant cases and since there is a very close relation between the kind of conduct involved in civil tax fraud and criminal tax evasion, civil tax fraud cases also tend to be limited to taxpayers whose conduct is highly culpable. As Despite the factual similarities between litigated cases of civil tax fraud and criminal tax evasion, there are discernable differences. will be demonstrated in the next section, administrative practices have made a meaningful distinction between those cases handled only as involving civil fraud and those handled as criminal tax evasion as well as civil fraud. 

e. The Administrator's View of Civil Fraud. 

To appreciate fully the Service's use of the civil fraud penalty, it is necessary to describe the administrative path of a civil fraud case. 

Most civil fraud penalties (as well as negligence penalties) are assessed as the result of the audit of taxpayer's returns conducted by agents of the Audit Division (auditors).

1 At the first indication of fraud the auditor must refer the case to the Intelligence Division, the criminal investigation arm of the 45/ Service, which assumes control of the case and initiates an investigation of potential tax crimes. During investigation by Intelligence all work toward assessment of tax or a civil penalty ceases. The auditor may, and usually does, assist Intelligence in its investigation, however. After the termination of the criminal investigation, Intelligence decides either to prosecute the case criminally or to send it back to the Audit Division for assessment of tax and penalties, if any. A decision not to prosecute does not necessarily mean that the return in question is free of tax crimes. As will be discussed later a case may be returned to Audit for a variety of reasons. However, once returned, Audit is free to use its own criteria in determining whether further civil action to assess either taxes or penalties is warranted. 

If Intelligence decides to prosecute the case, all civil action by Audit remains suspended pending the outcome of the criminal proceeding. 

After considerable administrative review, criminal processing is continued by referring the case to the Tax Division of the Department of Justice. 

If the Department of Justice concurs in the decision to prosecute, it will forward the case to the appropriate United States Attorney for trial. The United States Attorney also has the opportunity to decline to prosecute, a right exercised infrequently. In any event, the case is either rejected for prosecution, settled, or tried. The criminal aspect is then a closed matter, and the case is returned to Audit to pursue civil assessments, including the civil fraud or negligence penalties.

With this bit of procedure, we return to the differences between civil fraud and criminal tax evasion. These differences are discussed in a 1968 IRS study of the civil penalty during a three-month period in 46/ 1965. The study revealed that 23 percent of the cases studied were recommended for criminal prosecution, but that only 14 percent were criminally prosecuted. 47/ Further analysis of this study shows that criminal prosecutions were restricted to the most flagrant cases of tax evasion. 

The likelihood of prosecution increased in direct proportion to the size of the deficiency, the amount of adjusted gross income, and the number of 48/ years involved.

In addition, there were many practical considerations which were used to explain the failure to prosecute each case criminally. 

For example, the case might lack sufficient deterrent value to justify the 49/ expenditure of resources necessary to obtain a conviction. Perhaps, the circumstances were not sufficiently egregious to persuade a jury, although they might persuade a Tax Court judge. There may be doubt whether the government's proof is beyond a reasonable doubt, while little question but that it looks clear and convincing. Or some procedural error, such as an unlawful search and seizure, might exist which would destroy the criminal prosecution, but might not be prejudicial in a civil matter. 

Thus, many cases of conduct sufficiently serious enough to warrant treatment as criminal evasion are dealt with only as civil fraud. 50/ In general, then, the difference between civil fraud and criminal tax evasion is one of degree. Though their fact patterns are similar,

those of criminal cases are more egregious. Further, the procedural burdens, such as burden of proof and the admissibility of evidence, are far heavier in criminal than in civil cases. 51/ 

f. The Failure to Use the Civil Fraud Penalty for Intentional Understatements of Tax. 

There are numerous cases of extreme taxpayer misbehavior where the Service has neither prosecuted for criminal tax evasion nor 52/ asserted the civil fraud penalty. Last year an internal review un covered substantial variation in the use of the civil penalty from district to district. The study focused on cases which were referred to the 

Intelligence Division as potential criminal matters, but which were then rejected because of insufficient prosecutorial resources or because the likelihood of conviction was too low. In the Wilmington district examining agents assessed the civil penalty in 77 percent of referrals. 

In the Cincinnati district they did so in 55 percent. But, the figure was only 36 percent in New Orleans, 20 percent in Philadelphia, and 6 percent in Dallas. To repeat, in each of these matters the signs of fraud were sufficient to persuade an auditor to refer the matter to 

Intelligence for investigation for criminal prosecution.

Numerous reasons were cited for the failure to assert the civil fraud penalty in the remaining cases. Examining agents often expressed the opinion that reviewers were a "bunch of give-away artists" and would set aside a severe penalty. This view was not supported by the facts: the Appellate Division upheld the fraud penalty in 67.9 percent of the cases appealed. Another significant reason for under-utilization of

the penalty was the pressure on examining agents to complete a large volume of agreed cases. Not only is the taxpayer unlikely to agree with an assertion of fraud, but the completion of the audit is delayed because the case must be referred to Intelligence at the first instance of fraud. While Intelligence has the file, the referring auditor cannot close it. Another deterrent to assertion of fraud was constraints against opening up the old returns needed to establish the pattern of conduct which the courts seem to require. Also, Intelligence Division rejection was wrongly interpreted by some auditors as a simultaneous rejection of 53/ the civil penalty. Poor training of agents in dealing with fraud was cited as another factor. Although unmentioned by the study, interviews with Service personnel reveal that some agents believe that Intelligence will reject cases not involving large dollar amounts and that many such cases probably are not referred despite definite indications of fraud. 

The aggressive use of civil fraud penalties in Wilmington and Cincinnati was attributed to strong administrative support for assertion of the penalties. Primary responsibility for under-use might then be laid to lack of enthusiasm on the part of management, which in turn may be an outgrowth of the belief that courts will limit the penalty to situations involving highly flagrant behavior. Our review of the cases suggests 53/ that, for the most part, this concern is well founded and helps to account for the fact that in some districts the civil fraud penalty is 54/ reserved for cases in which criminal fraud is likely to be present. 

As we have already seen, there is a multitude of cases involving seriously deviant behavior which would seem to amount to civil fraud,

at least under the common meaning of the term. They are not treated as fraud, however.

As discussed below, the Service has dealt with such cases with the only other tool available to it. 

2. Negligence

The Revenue Act of 1918 provided for the first time 55/ a penalty "if the understatement is due to negligence on the part of the taxpayer, but without intent to defraud...

I: 

This enactment is the predecessor of § 6653 (a) which still provides a 5 percent penalty for a negligent underpayment of taxes. 56/ The legislative history of the negligence statute failed to 57/ define the term "negligence". Consequently, the Internal Revenue 

Service has defined negligence in a manner consistent with its definition in tort law. "Negligence is the amission to do something which a reasonable man, guided by those considerations which ordinarily regulate the conduct of human affairs, would do, or doing something which a prudent and reasonable man would not do." 58/

The application of this familiar concept of negligence in its conventional usage to tax cases is illustrated by the following example. A corporation hired a new bookkeeper, and it failed not only to instruct her, but also to audit her work. When the corporation sold jewelry to related corporations at cost, the bookkeeper deducted the purchase price of the jewelry, but did not enter the offsetting sales. The negligence penalty was imposed on the theory that the corporation was careless by its failure to take 59/ precautions against such errors by a relatively unskilled employee. ?

Beyond such run-of-the-mill negligence cases, however, lies an entire body of cases which break sharply with the tort law analogue. 

In these cases the tax negligence statute has been applied to conduct far different from that considered negligence in tort law. Not only does tax negligence exclude some negligent conduct, but, more importantly, 60/ it includes same intentional conduct. This proposition can easily be verified by a look at the cases. In In a typical case of underreporting of tips, a group of waitresses kept no records of their tips. One waitress by a process of reconstruction based upon the hours worked reported that her tip income was $1,052.49. The Tax Court found the income to be $4,337.70. sustaining the penalty for negligence, the Court stated that "[p]etitioners have not even made a plausible argument to explain their fantastically low reporting of tip income. In no case did the amount reported by any petitioner approach the seven percent 'guesstimate' of tips made by some 61/ petitioners at trial.'

In a recent case concerning the underreporting of business income, a smuggling partnership reported net income of $24,000 and $41,000; but its true income, as reconstructed by the Tax Court, was $90,000 and $100,000. The partners took many inflated deductions. 

They deducted the purchase price of a plane by calling it maintenance 62/ expenses. The negligence penalty was upheld. 

In another case a taxpayer claimed deductions which he knew were not allowable, such as Social Security taxes, expenses of running

is for office, and tuition for his child at a private school. 

The taxpayer also arbitrarily increased other deductions, including his medical deductions. The Tax Court made the modest observation that "[a]t the 63/ very least, petitioner's conduct constitutes negligence. 

There are a limitless number of similar cases. 

Certainly, the conduct of the taxpayers in such cases is not simply negligent in the traditional meaning of the word. We would be naive not to assume that the taxpayers knew that their returns had false statements. However, as has been previously discussed, the courts have consistently refused to apply the fraud penalty to the above type of cases. Thus, the Service has applied the next best tool available the negligence penalty.

Consequently, a surprisingly broad range of conduct is covered by the negligence penalty. 

Intentional misstatements are often penalized with the same degree of harshness as is mere negligence. Such whimsical and unequal results are probably quite different from what Congress intended when it borrowed the familiar tort phrases for the tax statute. Thus, it can be said that the judicial and administrative constructions that have broadened the definition of negligence and narrowed the definition of fraud reflect a defect in the tax statutes as they are presently enforced. There is no penalty between the mild 5 percent penalty for negligence and the 50 percent penalty reserved for highly culpable conduct. However, an immense middle ground exists. There is an endless array of cases which involve reckless or intentional

overstatements of deductions or understatements of income where the inaccuracy fails to reach the level of quasi-criminality required to establish fraud. 

3. Intentional Disregard of Rules and Regulations. 

The Revenue Act of 1921 added the following provision to the negligence penalty. It stated that if any part of the deficiency was due to an "intentional disregard of authorized rules and regulations 64/ with knowledge thereof...", then the 5 percent penalty will be imposed. Today's negligence section, $ 6653 (a), still retains the above provision. Although the legislative history of the 1921 provision contained no explanation of the provision, one can presume that the addition was in response to the following problem. Early cases indicate that when a taxpayer felt that a regulation was invalid, the taxpayer 65/ would simply make out his return in disregard of the regulation. 

Since, in literal terms, the taxpayer did not commit a negligent act, it was feared that the negligence penalty would not be applicable. 

Therefore, the above amendment was added to insure that the negligence penalty would apply to any disregard of a regulation. ubrice Lac

the C. -H 19 M. 

Including the Excluded Middle. 

There are a number of different approaches that could be suggested for covering the excluded middle. 

1. Raising the Negligence Penalty. 

One approach would be simply to raise the negligence penalty to a substantial level, such as 25 percent. This would presumably provide a substantial deterrent to tax cheating. However, it is questionable whether such a heavy penalty is appropriate for simple negligence. By definition, negligence is unintentional conduct, an accident. A taxpayer is negligent when he has failed to take reasonable care in keeping records or in preparing his tax return. Such a taxpayer by our definition has not undertaken the economic calculation described above. Thus, it is doubtful that a heavy penalty is in order. 67/ 66/ The issue of whether a heavy penalty should apply to tax negligence is akin to the issue of the sufficiency of negligence for application of criminal sanctions. The propriety of such sanctions has long been debated. Although defended by same commentators, others take the view that such punishment is inappropriate. A careless person is far less blameworthy than the person who has intentionally or recklessly caused harm. 

The careless person is probably not in need of rehabilitation. Moreover, punishment for negligence probably generates much less deterrent force than punishment of recklessness or intentional conduct. Although the possibility of punishment may induce some careless persons to take greater care, it would usually have no effect on their behavior since they have neither in-

tended the result nor disregarded a known risk that the result would occur. 

Thus, the Model Penal Code defines criminal negligence as involving "substantial culpability. 

68/ This means, according to the Comment, that the jury must find fault and find it was substantial. Although expressing some doubts about the propriety of punishing negligence at all, the Comment acknowledges that some legislators are of the view that punishment of negligence can cause an actor to use additional care. Yet, the Comment points out that negligence should not be generally deemed sufficient as the mens 69/ rea required for specific crimes.

The arguments against criminal punishment for negligence seem applicable to heavy civil penalties as well. It is unlikely that tax negligence will be deterred since, by definition, the negligent taxpayer has made no economic analysis of the advantages of cheating. However, a relatively light penalty does seem appropriate. The primary justification for it is compensatory; the audit process is expensive, and it is not unreasonable to ask someone whose underpayment occurred through negligence to reimburse 70/ the Service for the transaction costs of rectifying the situation. 

Whether a figure of 5 percent of the deficiency is adequate for this purpose (or excessive) is beyond the scope of the present study and would require detailed cost accounting analyses by the Service. 

Another justification for a relatively light penalty on negligence is to express institutional disapproval of persons who are careless in preparing their tax returns. Certainly, someone who has negligently prepared his return is different from one who although taking reasonable care in pre-

paring his return still has a deficiency. It is not unwarranted to treat them differently. We are entitled to assert that reasonable care in preparing returns is desirable and carelessness is undesirable. It is equally ap- 71/ 

In sum, propriate to express that conviction through a token penalty. low penalty for negligence seems justified, but a heavy penalty of 25 percent seems excessive. 

2. A Sliding Scale.

A second possibility is to create a new penalty with a sliding 72/ percentage scale. Thus, the statute might provide a penalty from 5 percent to 25 percent for inaccurate tax returns. The 50 percent penalty would be retained for returns characterized by highly culpable tax evasion. 

The lowest penalty would be reserved for simple negligence. The percentage level for intermediate penalties would depend upon the degree of culpability. 

The 25 percent penalty would be utilized in cases of intentional inaccuracies, and the levels in-between could be used for grossly negligent and recklessly 73/ prepared returns. Presumably, the Tax Court would adjudicate the level of the penalty as well as the deficiency. It would have power to set the penalty at the level requested by the IRS, or at any lower level to 5 percent, or to remove it altogether.

This proposal would have the advantage of preserving a token penalty for relatively non-culpable negligence, while also imposing a rather stiff 25 percent penalty for purposeful cheating. The administrator and the 

Tax Court would develop expertise in setting an appropriate penalty between 5 percent and 25 percent if the conduct seemed less than intentional, but H.

more than merely careless. This approach would avoid difficult problems of statutory definition in creating a new fixed-level penalty between the existing 74/ ones. 

However, the sliding scale proposal suffers from one great shortcoming. The discretion it confers would be generally regarded as unacceptable. Abuses of discretion would be both difficult to police and inevitable. 

The result might be similar to the uneven standards of sentencing in criminal cases in which large and unjustified discrepancies exist from 75/ judge to judge and from district to district. The existence of sentencing disparities seems to defy reform, but that is hardly an argument for extending them to new domains. Even worse, the system might come to resemble the administrative remission of the draconian penalties and forfeitures provided under the customs law. 76/ Theoretically, some administrative abuses in a flexible statute could be rectified through the presence of appeal to the Tax Court. Through case-to-case adjudication the judges would gain experience and perhaps develop a consensus for the type of penalty that would be appropriate for different 77/ forms of cheating. But the expense of litigation would make this infeasible for many taxpayers. It also does not seem wise to swell Tax Court dockets simply to settle disputes over the proper level of penalties. Both IRS officials and private tax lawyers agreed; the great majority were opposed to 78/ a flexible penalty as conferring too much discretion on IRS employees. 

A Tax Court judge stated that the responsibility for setting the correct penalty level would be unwelcome and onerous. 

Writers in the administrative law field generally urge that discretion be narrowed whenever it is feasible

la 80/ 79/ to do so. 

Although flexible standards are in use in other nations, 57 ​ind there is little available information on how they function and what kinds of problems they have created. On balance, these problems appear more compelling than the advantages of the sliding scale. Thus, we have rejected a sliding scale penalty. 3.

A New 25 Percent Penalty. 

A third approach to the problem is the creation of a new intermediate penalty. This penalty would apply to conduct more culpable than negligence, but less culpable than quasi-criminal fraud. This proposal would have the advantage of preserving both the token but useful 5 percent penalty for negligence and the heavy 50 percent penalty for serious tax evasion. 

The new penalty would be sufficiently severe so that a taxpayer would have to weigh it in making plans to cheat. Consequently, it should considerably improve the deterrent force of the penalty structure. A fixed penalty avoids the perhaps excessive discretion accorded to the IRS and the Tax Court under 81/ the sliding scale proposal. structure. reasons.

This penalty would improve the IRS's administration of the penalty 82/ At present the fraud penalty is underutilized for a number of One reason is that all fraud cases must first be referred to Intelligence and small cases are often not referred at all since the examining GDO agent knows that there will be long delays and ultimately that they will be rejected. Further, same districts interpret a rejection by Intelligence as grounds for dropping the fraud penalty. These difficulties would be avoided 1 under a 25 percent penalty since such cases would not have to go to Intelligence first, and if they did, rejection by Intelligence would not suggest that a

83/ the ex- 25 percent penalty is inappropriate. Moreover, because the burden of proof under the proposed 25 percent penalty will be on the taxpayer, amining agent need not be so sophisticated. He need not spend as much time in gathering evidence, something now discouraged by the pressure on agents for production and closed cases. 

One problem with this approach is to define the conduct necessary to trigger the penalty. Formulation of a definition is difficult since it compels us to face the fact that the terms in § 6653 are now used in a way far different from their conventional meanings. The following is suggested: (a) The 5 percent penalty for negligence be retained, with 84/ same amendments to be noted; (b) The fraud penalty be redefined to cover "willful tax evasion"; 85/ and (c) A new penalty at a rate between the 5 percent negligence and the 50 percent tax evasion penalty (as defined in (b)) be established to apply to deficiencies occurring because of the intentional or reckless inaccuracies where the conduct did not amount to willful tax evasion. 86/ A draft of the proposed statute may be found in Appendix B. 

This scheme would have the advantage of making clear that the 50 percent penalty for civil fraud is to reach the same kind of conduct (except for the government's level of proof) as the criminal statute. The purpose is to clarify, not to change the law with respect to the 50 percent penalty. As we have seen, civil fraud cases generally show substantial culpability, such as patterned conduct, large amounts, devious methods of concealment, and the like. They are

B. 17 ? criminal cases in effect, some of which are not prosecuted for the variety 87/ of reasons discussed above. The confusing term "fraud" would be eliminated since its conventional definition clearly covers too broad a range of conduct to describe its function in our tax system. 

The new penalty would then clearly cover the excluded middle; that is, incorrect returns which are not proper for assertion of willful tax evasion (now the civil fraud penalty) but which also manifest conduct more egregious than ordinary carelessness. It would cover both intentionally inaccurate returns and those where the deficiency occurred because the taxpayer proceeded despite his lack of knowledge that the figures on the return were correct. 

One issue in discussing a new penalty is its level. A figure near twenty-five percent seems a reasonable choice. This figure lies about halfway 88/ between 5 percent and 50 percent. Historically, it has long been used as the maximum penalty level for long-term delinquencies in filing returns and 89/ in paying the tax. Of course, a highly culpable long-term delinquency in filing a return can be treated as civil fraud, attracting the 50 percent 90/ penalty under § 6653 (b). However, the typical delinquency case is not treated as fraud, and only the maximum 25 percent delinquency penalty is usually applied. It seems reasonable to treat intentional underpayment consistent with delinquencies. 

4. Additional Issues: Burden of Proof, Included Offenses, and 

Reliance on Preparers.

Another issue to discuss is the burden of proof required in asserting the new penalty. We believe that the taxpayer should have the burden of persuasion. 

After all, the facts concerning his state of mind 91/

are in his possession. Although the government has the burden of proof for establishing fraud, this reflects the quasi-criminal character of the 50 percent penalty. This proposal for the new 25 percent penalty has been specifically designed to avoid these quasi-criminal aspects. 

Placing the burden of proof on the taxpayer is, in fact, absolutely essential to cover the excluded middle. Many rather obvious cases of intentional cheating fail to be treated as fraud under present law solely because of the onerous burden of proof placed on the Service to establish the taxpayer's 92/ state of mind. However, in those cases it would be unlikely (though possible) that the taxpayer could convince the factfinder that the inaccuracy was merely an accident. Consequently, the 25 percent penalty would be applied. 

In the present statute, if the IRS pleads civil fraud but fails 93/ to plead negligence, the court has no power to impose the negligence penalty. 

As a result, some people think that the statute is defective because it seems to give the taxpayer the benefit of for what may be a pleading error by the government (or a tactical decision that pleading negligence in the alternative tends to weaken the fraud case). These arguments raise the question whether, given the statutory scheme if the new middle penalty is enacted, alternative pleading should be required for it, and second, whether alternative pleading should be continued for the negligence penalty. The new As to the new middle penalty, it should be pleaded in the alternative to the civil fraud penalty (to be denominated the willful tax evasion penalty). 

The civil fraud penalty operates with respect to intentional conduct. middle penalty will in many cases also operate on intentional conduct. Thus, the line between the two may in some cases be thin. However, there are also

differences - which might be obfuscated if separate pleading is not required. 

The burden of proof is on the government in a civil fraud case, but would be on the taxpayer in cases involving the proposed penalty. The standards of proof are also quite different. The government must prove its case in a clear and convincing fashion, while the taxpayer need only convince by a preponderance of the evidence. Additionally, if some separation is not required, the similarity of factual conduct might lead to the indiscriminate assertion of the civil fraud penalty in any case where the new middle penalty would apply.

Thus, alternative pleading seems necessary to keep the issues of proof separate. Further, even though there is much similarity between civil fraud and the new middle penalty, the separation resulting from alternative pleading will require the examining agent and pleading attorneys to focus on the differences involved. Also, by sharpening the nature and quantum of proof to be adduced by each party, the tendency toward indiscriminate assertion of the civil fraud penalty may be discouraged. Finally, since many cases pled in the alternative will require proof of intentional conduct, pleading of the middle penalty should not weaken the fraud case. 

Much of the same reasoning applies to the negligence penalty as an alternative to the fraud penalty. There are, however, fewer reasons for requiring that the negligence penalty be pleaded in the alternative to the new middle penalty proposed herein. The distinction between the penalty based on negligence and the proposed penalty based on intentional inaccuracy is more clear-cut and definable than the distinction between the proposed penalty based on intentional inaccuracy and the civil fraud penalty

which would also be based on intentional conduct. On the other hand, the burden of proof would be on the taxpayer in both the negligence and the intentional inaccuracy cases. Thus, the arguments for requiring alternative pleading of the negligence penalty are not so strong, but on balance there is no reason for not putting the taxpayer on notice of the possibility of a negligence penalty if the new middle penalty is asserted. 

One other problem in the penalty area is the defense that the error was made by the return preparer and thus should not be attributed to the taxpayer. Where all necessary information has been furnished to the preparer, taxpayers have successfully resisted the fraud penalty. The cases consistently point out that the mental element necessary to sustain the fraud 94/ penalty must be personal to the taxpayer. The negligence penalty cases are not so consistent. Many times the negligence of the preparer has been attributed 95/ to the taxpayer. However, the liability does not seem absolute; generally, the taxpayer has been personally negligent in failing to notice the preparer's error or in failing to create proper internal controls against the type of 96/ error that was made.

The same principles should be applicable under the new 25 percent penalty. The penalty should be asserted against a taxpayer by reason of an error made by the preparer only if (a) the taxpayer has intentionally or recklessly failed to keep proper records or failed to furnish all necessary information to the preparer, or (b) the taxpayer has intentionally or recklessly failed to discover and correct the preparer's error.

D. Corporate Officers. 

At present the civil penalties for negligence and fraud apply to corporations. The new penalty proposed above would similarly be applicable to corporations. 

The law today on the issue of whether the preparers of corporate returns are liable for inaccuracies is not the same with respect to civil and criminal penalties. Although a corporate officer is not usually subject to civil penalties, he can be convicted of criminal tax evasion when 97/ the tax evaded was a corporate tax. In fact, there are cases where the corporate officer was convicted of criminal evasion, while the corporation was acquitted. The corporate officer can be convicted of evasion- even 99/ when he has not personally benefitted from the evasion. This section will consider whether or not the current objections to treating civil and criminal penalties alike are valid. 98/ In most criminal cases it is usually claimed that a direct financial benefit results to the officer who commits the crime. Normally, the officer has either embezzled money or has benefitted by the increased value in his corporate stock. Since criminal sanctions are meaningless with respect to corporations, with the exception of minor fines, it is logical to apply the sanctions against the perpetrator and beneficiary of the crime. 

When a civil penalty is involved, a different situation is said to exist because there is now a meaningful penalty for the corporation. The corporation can pay the civil penalty, which is often a large sum, and the corporate officer involved, as well as all the stockholders, are correspondingly hurt by a decrease in the value of the corporate stock.

The above argument rests on the premise that the purpose of sanctions for tax crimes is punishment. When it is not possible to punish the corporation, an individual is punished. That argument, however, is based upon a false premise because deterrence, rather than punishment, is the motivation 100/ for the tax penal laws. Since deterrence, along with compensation, is also the major reason for civil penalties, that deterrence would probably be more effective when the penalty is imposed upon the officer involved, rather than upon the corporation. 

Another argument against applying civil penalties to corporate officers is that the penalty results in two penalties to the culpable officer when that officer is also a shareholder. However, this argument is in actuality a strong reason for applying the civil penalties to corporate officers. All shareholders suffer from a corporate penalty, and if no separate penalty is applied to the culpable officer, then that officer suffers only as a shareholder and not as the person responsible for the conduct. 

Finally, it is claimed that there is no reason to apply civil penalties against corporate officers when those culpable officers would not benefit materially from their wrongdoing. Presumably, only corporate officers who are shareholders benefit from their wrongdoing. However, this argument is not persuasive. Corporate officers do not aimlessly make intentional mistakes. Although a corporate officer who is not a shareholder does not benefit directly from lower corporate taxes, such an officer is benefitted indirectly when the corporation's profits increase. Not only does his position become more secure, but his chances for advancement are enhanced.

101/ The Previously, it was mentioned that an intentionally inaccurate return results from an economic calculation by the taxpayer. taxpayer weighs the tax savings against the losses that occur if the inaccuracy is detected. Since civil penalties do not currently apply against corporate officers, an economic calculation that results in deception by the officer may not be sufficiently deterred. In other words, the risk of loss to the corporation may not offset the potential benefit to the individual. By applying civil penalties to corporate officers, the deterrent factor in the above economic calculation will be much greater.

If there were a decision to apply civil penalties to corporate officers, there are other new issues that must be addressed. First, it may be difficult to determine the culpable officers and employees. Second, should the corporation and its officers be penalized at the same level? Finally, what type of administrative and judicial review should be available?

In an inaccurate return the culpable officers include at least the signer of the return, the preparer of the return, and the chief executive officer. Obviously, the signer and the preparer of the return are responsible for its contents. We also believe that the chief executive officer is responsible for any intentional inaccuracies. The chief executive will, thus, have a strong incentive to make certain that the return is accurate.

Many other people participate in the preparation of the return. They include the tax department personnel, a comptroller or other finance department

personnel, and outside tax advisors. 

If any of these people are responsible for the inaccuracy, they should then also be subject to the civil penalty. 

However, a preparer of an isolated part of the return, such as a schedule, would not be liable so long as that part is accurate. Clerical personnel who participate in the preparation of the return would not be subject to the penalty since they may be presumed sufficiently unfamiliar with the return information to know whether it is accurate. 

If previous recommendations in this report are adopted, the civil underpayment penalties will be three-tiered. Penalties will be assessed for either (1) fraudulent, (2) intentionally inaccurate, or (3) negligently prepared returns. Although deciding the level of any penalty is an arbitrary act, the penalty level applied to officers should be the same as that applied to the corporation. Hence, a negligence penalty would be imposed at the rate of 5 percent of the underpayment owing to the negligence. Because corporate liabilities may be huge relative to the wealth of individuals, the penalty to be imposed against an officer should perhaps have a maximum, say, not in excess of the maximum criminal penalty of $10,000. 

It should be noted that the penalty would not be deductible by the officer and that the corporation would be denied a deduction for any reimbursement of the penalty, whether through direct payment, increased compensation, or other subterfuge. The corporation could, however, deduct any reimbursement of legal costs to the officer. Similarly, if the officer includes such reimburse- 102/ ment in income, the officer will get a corresponding deduction.

"

As will be discussed in a later section, penalty assessments are often given haphazard administrative review, and in some instances there is no judicial review in the Tax Court prior to payment of the assessment. 

We recommend changes in these procedures, and the recommended procedures should be equally applicable to civil penalties for officers; that is, there should be judicial review before assessment or collection. 

One final cautionary point must be noted. Some people might argue that the penalty proposed herein could become a tool of abuse by the Service personnel. The threat of the penalty might coerce corporations into settling claims that ordinarily would be fought. Obviously, the potential for abuse exists. However, if the corporation is first subject to the penalty, then presumably someone must always be responsible for the wrongdoing and thus also subject to penalties.

E. The "Intentional Disregard" Penalty of $ 6653 (a). 

Section 6653 (a) now contains an anomalous provision which assesses a 5 percent penalty for "intentional disregard of rules and regulations (but without intent to defraud)." Neither the purpose nor the present function of this language is clear. Our earlier discussion suggested that its addition to the statute was due to a concern by IRS in the early 1920's that 103/ taxpayers disregarded regulations they felt invalid. 

At present this penalty is confusing and superfluous. If it is 104/ it is not necdesigned to reach garden-variety intentional cheating, essary under the present statute since the negligence penalty is routinely applied to such conduct. 105/ Certainly, it makes little sense to penalize both negligent and intentional cheating at the same level of 5 percent. 

If the intentional disregard penalty is intended to reach defects 106/ such as the failure to file returns, it is again superfluous. The delinquency penalty alone should be used for this purpose. It seems to serve no useful purpose to sometime place two penalties upon delinquent taxpayers, charging some of them 25 percent of the entire tax and others 30 percent. The statute should preclude the Service from applying the inaccuracy penalties solely because of a delinquency in filing unless the delinquency is to be treated as fraud. In such case the statute now prohibits the IRS from collecting both the delinquency and fraud penalties. 

If the intentional disregard penalty is intended to cover a failure to keep books and records required by the regulations, seems misdirected. Although it is reasonable to have a penalty directed 108/ 107/ it still

at a failure to keep records, it is unreasonable to tie the penalty to the tax deficiency. Instead, a penalty for failure to keep records could be related to the entire tax due (whether or not there is a deficiency) or it could be a set dollar amount. There is no reason to excuse a penalty from the taxpayer whose return has no deficiency; the damage to the government in extra audit costs is the same whether a deficiency is present or not. 

Most cases in which inadequate books and records exist will, of course, result in a deficiency. Unless the taxpayers are found to be without fault, that deficiency would seem to be based on conduct which is negligent, reckless, intentional, or quasi-criminal. Consequently, it would trigger the inaccuracy penalties of 5 percent, 25 percent, or 50 percent. No separate penalty for failure to keep records seems necessary. 

Finally, the intentional disregard penalty may be intended to penalize taxpayers who decline to follow a regulation on the ground that it is invalid.

Indeed, this may have been the original purpose of 110/ the intentional disregard penalty. But no penalty is necessary in this situation. If there is a bona fide dispute of law whether it concerns the validity of a regulation, a ruling, or any other position taken by the IRS penalty. 

the taxpayer should be allowed to assert his position without 111/ 

If the taxpayer's legal position is not maintained in good faith, however, or the point is not truly disputable (e.g., whether the proceeds of embezzlement are taxable), the inaccuracies produced by the taxpayer's position would seem to be covered by the existing penalty 112/ structure. 109/

F. 

The Deficiency On Which the Penalties for Incorrect Returns Are Computed.

1. Computing Penalties in Multiple Item Deficiencies. 

The inaccuracy penalties are presently computed on the entire deficiency if any part thereof is attributable to negligence or fraud. The result quite frequently is a disproportionate and completely unfair penalty. 

For example, a taxpayer might have fraudulently concealed a source of income and evaded taxes of $5,000 per year. But, he might also have a factory and claim excessive depreciation on machines, causing an additional deficiency of $80,000. This latter item could easily occur because of a goodfaith, but erroneous, use of the wrong method of depreciation or of excessively short useful lives. In such a case the statute requires a civil fraud penalty of $42,500, even though the fraud caused a deficiency of 113/ only $5,000.

If the $5,000 deficiency were attributable to negligence, the penalty would be $4,250 --more than 80 percent of the deficiency caused by negligence.

Sometimes, the present computing method discourages the IRS from seeking a fraud penalty where one should be asserted. According to some 

IRS personnel interviewed, agents would sometimes not assert the fraud penalty in cases (especially those of large corporations) where the deficiency was very large and only a small part was apparently owing to fraud. 

Thus, the method of computation may be contributing to underutilization of the civil fraud penalty. 

The existing method of computing penalties has been used for many years. Originally, the fraud penalties in the income tax were based

upon 100 percent of the entire tax, not just the deficiency. This may have occurred because (1) the fraud and failure-to-file penalties were together in the same statute, and (2) the failure-to-file penalty logically should be based on the entire tax due. 114/ In 1918 the penalty structure was overhauled, and the fraud penalty was substantially relaxed; perhaps this occurred because the needs for raising revenue diminished considerably after the end of World War I. The rates were generally lowered, and perhaps it was thought that the fraud problem would decrease. In any event, the fraud penalty was severed from the delin- 115/ quency penalty and, rather than being based on the entire tax, lowered to 50 percent of the entire deficiency. The negligence penalty, which was also enacted in 1918, adopted the same approach. It was certainly logical to apply the inaccuracy penalties to the deficiency, rather was I than to the whole tax. But apparently Congress failed to consider the logical next step of making these penalties apply only to the portion of the 116/ 

I deficiency attributable to the fraud or negligence.

The major defense of the existing statute lies in the argument I that it would be an administrative burden to differentiate the items making up the deficiency. But this is not persuasive. It seems a modest burden 

I to distinguish between the kind of extreme situations making up willful tax evasion, the less flagrant intentional inaccuracies, and the still less flagrant negligent inaccuracies, and non-negligent errors, and bona fide disputes of law. Just as each distinct item has to be separately stated and supported in the

deficiency notice, the examining agent should be able to make a judgment about the degree of culpability involved. 

Even if this does involve some additional burden, the present system, which can and often does create wildly arbitrary penalties, is simply not rationally acceptable. there is a further suggestion which would markedly decrease these administrative burdens. 

2. Single-Item Deficiencies and Burden of Proof. 

One problem with computing the penalty on only the fraudulent part of the deficiency arises where the taxpayer has previously been criminally convicted in a case based on indirect methods of proof. It seems that the present practice in criminal cases, based on the net worth theory, is to assert relatively conservative deficiencies. For example, frequently no estimate is made of the amount of income spent for personal consumption since it would be difficult to establish the figure beyond a reasonable doubt. However, in the civil proceeding the IRS asserts a larger deficiency which includes an estimate of personal consumption and other additional amounts not asserted in the criminal case. The criminal conviction serves as conclusive proof of fraud, and only the amount of the deficiency on which the penalty is based remains to be established. On that issue the taxpayer has the burden of proof. Under present law, of course, the proof of fraud as to part of the deficiency (established by the criminal conviction) causes the entire deficiency to be subject to the penalty. But under the revision proposed herein, only that part of the deficiency proved in the criminal proceeding would automatically be subject to the penalty.

Suppose, for example, a criminal conviction is based on the net worth method of proof and a claimed deficiency of $40,000. It is followed by a civil proceeding, based on a net worth increase of $100,000. The civil deficiency would under this proposal automatically be presumed fraudulent as to only $40,000; as to the other $60,000, fresh proof of fraud would be needed. Yet, it would be anomalous in such a case to have the fraud penalty apply to $40,000 and not the remaining $60,000 since the entire $100,000 of amitted income would generally be tainted by fraud. The figure was obtained by an indirect method based on consumption and increase in wealth and would ordinarily be indivisible as far as state of mind was concerned. 

One could, of course, put the IRS to the burden of proving that the additional $60,000 of deficiency was as fraudulent as the $40,000. 

But this would force the IRS to repeat the same proof in the civil case as it had previously furnished in the criminal case because the relevant indicia of fraud would be applicable to the entire deficiency. This would sacrifice the benefits obtained through the use of collateral estoppel in the civil case. Real judicial economies are obtained by not putting the government to a superfluous repetition of its proof of bad state of mind. It would, therefore, be a poor result to compel the government to prove fraud all over again in the civil case in order to collect the penalty on the additional $60,000 of deficiency. But it would generally be an illogical result to charge a penalty on the $40,000, but not the $60,000.

This problem may be handled by shifting the burden of persuasion to the taxpayer to disprove fraud once the IRS has established the presence 118/ of fraud as to any part of the deficiency. 

Thus, in the example given the criminal conviction would supply the proof of fraud as to $40,000 of the deficiency. The burden would then shift to the taxpayer to prove by a preponderance of the evidence that some or all of the remaining deficiency was not attributable to fraud. Ordinarily, the taxpayer could not sustain this burden since the entire deficiency would usually be characterized by a uniform state of mind.

Of course, the government might sustain its burden in some civil fraud cases by direct proof of fraud as to specific items. Under this proposal, the burden would shift to the taxpayer to disprove fraud as to remaining items. In the hypothetical case with which this section began -a $5,000 deficiency based on fraud and an $80,000 deficiency based on a goodfaith depreciation error the taxpayer should find such proof easy. Consequently, the basic purpose for the suggested proposal to avoid uncan- 

scionably harsh penalties in cases of multiple item deficiencies 

would still be attained. But anomalous results in single-item deficiencies, part of which were sustained in a previous criminal case, would be avoided. 

Furthermore, shifting the burden of persuasion to the taxpayer would alleviate the IRS's concern about administrative burdens which would arise if the fraud penalty applied only to those parts of the deficiency infected with fraud. The IRS would not have to sustain a heavy burden as to each item in the deficiency only as to one, just as it does now. 

---

665

The taxpayer, then, would have the onus to show that the remaining items were not subject to penalty. 

3. Penalties for Incorrect and Late Returns. 

Another difficulty with the base on which penalties are computed arises in cases where the return is filed late. The statute requires that the penalty be based upon the entire tax, not simply the deficiency, if the negligent or fraudulent return is filed even one day 119/ late.

The policy reason for this seemingly harsh result is that the taxpayer should not be allowed to make sport of the penalty by waiting to file a correct return after he discovers that he is under investigation. This makes some sense, but the statute reaches a result which is too severe when the late return is filed before the taxpayer has any reason to suspect that an investigation has begun. In such cases the inaccuracy penalty is compounded by a delinquency factor to a level which might be far more than a combination of the fraud and delin- 121/ quency penalties.

It may be argued that administration of a statute would be difficult where its application turns on whether the late filing occurs before or after the taxpayer learns of the investigation because this 122/ moment is difficult to define. 

That argument tends to overlook the files compiled by the Internal Revenue Service when it commences an investigation. The careful documentation and write-ups in Service files should reveal when there was contact by the Service with some source from which the taxpayer could have reasonably been expected to have 120/

learned of the investigation. If no such contact has been made, the 

Service would have no case for applying the penalty to the entire tax. 

Consequently, the statute should be amended. The penalties should be based only on the deficiency, if a return is filed late, unless the taxpayer believes, or had reason to believe, that the IRS had either selected his return for audit or had received information about him from a third party which could cause an audit to occur. 123/

G. Publicity of the Willful Evasion Penalty. 

The IRS publicizes criminal tax convictions, both those arising from guilty pleas and from guilty verdicts. Hopefully, the media will report the conviction, providing some data to the public about the defendant and the nature of his offense. Such publicity is absolutely essential if criminal tax law enforcement is to have a widespread deterrent effect. But, it would seem that the adverse publicity is also part of the punishment. To the affluent people typically convicted of tax crimes, the adverse publicity must often be as unwelcome as 124/ the criminal sanction imposed by the trial judge. 

However, imposition of the 50 percent penalty for fraud has not been publicized. If the taxpayer litigates the penalty, of course his name will appear in a reported case, but the general public would generally take no notice. If the taxpayer settles his case administratively, there is no publicity at all. The reason for secrecy of settlements, of course, is the statutory ban on disclosure of tax return data, 125/ except as authorized by the President. This statute and its problems are discussed in chapter 6 of this report. 126/ However, this policy does not apply in criminal cases. Obviously the return must be introduced in evidence. Still, the general public would ordinarily take no notice of the event if IRS did not affirmatively publicize the details of the fraud. The issue to be discussed here is whether the same policy should apply to the fraud penalty after liability for the penalty has been finally determined by settlement or litigation. 127/

As already noted, the cases arising under the fraud penalty 

This case selection makes are characterized by high culpability. 128/ the penalty quasi-criminal in nature. Indeed, it will not be sustained by the courts in the absence of powerful proof of wrongdoing. Consequently, it can be argued that the same publicity policies should apply Having committed such a serious to criminal and civil tax fraud. 129/ wrong against the fisc, the taxpayer should be treated as having given up the right to privacy with respect to such behavior. 

This policy should increase the deterrent effect of the civil fraud penalty. Releases to the media could indicate the amount, often many thousands of dollars, of the fraud penalty, clearly labelled as a civil penalty. To the extent that the existence of the penalty begins to sink into the public consciousness, taxpayers might revise the calculations on which they base their decisions to commit tax fraud. Moreover, the publicity is itself a severe sanction, one which to many people would be worse than any money penalty. The potency of publicity as a deterrent and as a sanction is strongly suggested by a 130/ 

Interviewers asked this question: survey commissioned by the IRS. 

What if the government did not take tax cheaters to court but only collected the taxes owed plus a fine of 50 percent of the taxes owed and did release information about these cases to the newspapers? 

Do you think that would result in more people attempting to cheat, fewer people attempting to cheat, or wouldn't that make any difference? More Fewer 12.7% 48.5%

To a follow-up question asking "why do you think so?", the following answers appeared:

Publicity alone would deter, scandal would hurt business, family, offend neighbors (no mention of fine) 34.2%

The surprisingly large number of respondents 

more than one-third 

who thought that cheating would be reduced by publicity alone, without mentioning the money penalty, is impressive. Thus, increased tax compliance seems likely to result from publicity of civil tax fraud sanctions.

One argument against this proposal is that publicity is all too potent as a sanction. Perhaps such a serious invasion of privacy

should occur only if the protections of the criminal law have been accorded to the taxpayer. 131/ This argument seems not persuasive. Certain protections are granted to criminal defendants because certain sanctions (such as imprisonment or expatriation) are involved, not because 132/ publicity may result. There seems to have been no issue raised about the publicity of non-tax civil money sanctions. The only reason it is raised in tax cases is because there is a prohibition against the disclosure of tax returns. While generally we advocate confidentiality of tax returns and tax return information in another chapter of this report, we think the breach of confidentiality appears justified where conduct of the civil fraud kind is present. 133/ Another argument against the proposal to publicize civil fraud dispositions is that there is a difference between fraud cases which are prosecuted criminally and those which are handled only civilly. 

As we have seen, there is a clear pattern of the most blatant cases being selected for prosecution, while those involving slightly less gross patterns of conduct are reserved for exclusively civil treatment. 

Such a difference could, arguably, support a difference in the policy toward publicity of the sanction. Again, this argument seems not persuasive. The fact remains that civil fraud cases are characterized by highly blameworthy conduct, much worse than garden-variety tax chiseling. 

Taxpayers who have engaged in such conduct have lost their right to privacy of tax data. The fact that there is a set of evasions which are even worse in nature does not suggest a different approach toward publicity.

In summary, there would appear to be advantages in publicizing the fraud penalty. It should appreciably affect the cheating equation of many taxpayers. The statute should, therefore, be amended to allow 134/ publicity when the 50 percent penalty has been imposed.

II. 

THE PENALTY FOR DELINQUENCY IN FILING RETURNS 

A return is "delinquent" if it is not filed when due. Under § 6651 (a) (1), a penalty is imposed for late filing only if there is tax due with the return. The amount of the penalty is five percent of the tax due (as computed in accordance with § 6651 (b) (1)) for each month or fraction thereof up to a maximum of 25 percent of the tax due. The penalty does not apply if the delinquency "is due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect." 

Thus, under this provision a penalty is imposed only if the return is not filed on time and if there is also tax due with the return. The conduct penalized thus is a combination of late filing and failure to pay tax due. 

The Amount of the Non-Filing Penalty. 

A.

The questions examined here are whether the non-filing penalty (a maximum of 25 percent) is proper in amount and whether the speed of escalation is appropriate. 

1. The Maximum Amount. 

Failure to file a return is unquestionably serious and may warrant a heavy penalty. Some commentators have argued that willful failure to file is as serious as fraudulent returns and urged that a criminal willful 135/ failure be raised from a misdemeanor to a felony. 

That suggestion has not been adopted but highly culpable instances of non-filing are sometimes prosecuted as felonious evasion of tax and may also be subject to the 50 per- 136/ cent civil fraud penalty. This treatment for very egregious cases would continue to be proper after redefining the civil fraud penalty to willful tax evasion as suggested above. 

Less egregious failures to file receive varying treatment. Some are

sufficiently willful to be prosecuted criminally as a misdemeanor. Others are not so serious, and no criminal action results. Both categories are subject to the civil penalty for failure to file the return unless the failure is due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect. This is our area of concern. The failure to file does not rise to a felonious evasion of taxes. It may be a misdemeanor, but it may not be criminal at all. the other hand, it is not excusable on reasonable grounds. On The question is whether the present maximum penalty of 25 percent is about right for such conduct. It seems so. The more egregious cases can be reached by the larger 50 percent penalty for civil fraud. The penalty here considered then applies to other unexcused failures to file whether intentional or merely negligent. Its maximum rate is about the same as that proposed above for the penalty for intentionally or recklessly inaccurate returns. Such a rate does not seem disproportionate, and a lesser rate might be considered too little for long term delinquencies. This last observation seems particularly true when one recalls that the penalty is computed by reference to the unpaid tax only and, for this reason, may not be nearly as large as would appear from the 25 percent rate. 

2. The Rate of Escalation. 

The question examined is whether, assuming that a maximum of 25 percent is proper, the penalty should be less steeply escalated. First, the penalty of five percent for the first month or fraction thereof seems about right, subject to remarks hereinafter made. It supplies an important incentive to get the return in on time. The existence of the penalty seems widely understood by the public who always queue to file returns on the afternoon and evening of April 15. The Postal Service publicizes the 

---

fact that post offices stay open late on the 15th to receive and postmark mail before the deadline. It always does a brisk business. 

The concern is that the non-filing penalty escalates too quickly. 

Five percent per month (or fraction thereof) after the first month is a 60 percent annual effective rate on the entire tax not paid when the return was due. We assume that a 60 percent annual rate of interest would be viewed as exorbitant by all. And the penalty provided in the very next subparagraph of the Code for failure to pay tax shown on the return is at the rate of only 0.5 percent per month--one tenth the rate of the $6651 (a) (1) penalty. 

Moreover, the rapid escalation of the penalty seems to create 137/ an undesired side effect. For the first five months after the due date, there would be intense pressure to rectify any discovered instances of nonfiling. But after the five months, there would be no additional pressure to do so, other than concern with civil fraud or criminal penalties. Would it not be better if the penalty kept on increasing, month by month, there would be an incentive to correct a non-filing as soon as possible? so that

The legislative history of § 6651 (a) (1) shows that the penalty has been steadily relaxed. Originally, it was 50 percent of the entire tax for 139/ even the shortest delinquencies.

Then in 1918 the maximum was reduced 140/ to 25 percent.

Finally, the 5 percent month-by-month escalation was added 141/ in 1935. The 1918 amendment placed the delinquency penalty at about the right level, as compared to the inaccuracy penalties, and the 1935 amendment 142/ distinguished between long and short-term delinquencies. 

We propose to build upon the 1935 amendment by slowing down the rate of accrual of the penalty. By doing so, the penalty would be less onerous for relatively short-term delinquencies and there would also be a longer period in which there is an incentive voluntarily to 138/

correct the delinquency. In the table below we set forth three different models to achieve these goals. Penalty for the 

1st Month
