In each of the above models the maximum penalty would remain at 25 percent, unless, of course, the IRS asserted the 50 percent penalty for fraud in lieu of the delinquency penalty. Given the slower rate of escalation and much longer period, the failure-to-pay penalty should 144/ also be exacted at the same time. 

Moreover, the present statute charges a full month's penalty for a delinquency of only a fraction of a month. It seems difficult to justify a result which treats a delinquency of one day the same as a delinquency of an entire month. Presumably, the argument in favor of charging a monthly penalty for a fraction of a month is administrative convenience. It obviously avoids the need for a mathematical proration. 

But such arguments seem not persuasive in the face of a statute which demands a capricious result. Someone must, in any event, make a calculation in which he measures the period of delinquency and calculates a given percentage of the tax. It is insignificant that an additional

proration on a daily basis would be needed. Indeed, interest is already computed on a daily basis. 145/ There is another difficulty with failure to prorate the penalty. 

Many failures to file result from mere procrastination. If the penalty is not prorated, once the date (or a monthly anniversary) for filing is missed, there is no incentive for tending to the matter until the follow- Proration might discourage such procrastination between ing month. monthly dates. 

Certainly, the present rate of escalation does not.

But these criticisms apply mainly to months after the month in which the return is due. The full 5 percent (or as in one model 

4 percent) penalty should apply to a delinquency of even a single day in the month in which the return is due. The present law provides a substantial incentive for getting a return in absolutely on time. It would not be wise to encourage a different way of thinking that the retur should go in somewhere around the due date if the taxpayer or practitioner is inclined to be dilatory.

Consequently, we would favor a statute which provides a 4 or 5 percent penalty for a delinquency of one month or fraction thereof, followed by a penalty of 1, 1 1/2, or 2 percent per month for each subsequent complete month of delinquency and scaled to the appropriate percentage for each day of delinquency for a period less than a full month.

Zeal for the proposal of a daily proration is far less in the case of a 1, 1 1/2, or 2 percent per month penalty than in the case of the

present law 5 percent per month.

It may well be that the problem is 

de minimis in the case of a penalty of a smaller monthly percent.

146/ But it is not de minimis in the case of a 5 percent monthly penalty. 

Therefore, one might view the proposal for a daily proration as a fallback position if the proposal to reduce the monthly penalty (for the months after the first month) from 5 percent to 1, 1 1/2, or 2 percent is rejected.

III. ADMINISTRATIVE AND JUDICIAL REVIEW OF THE NON-FILING, FAILURE TO PAY, AND RESPONSIBLE OFFICER PENALTIES A. Delinquent Returns and Failure-to-Pay Tax. 

147/ The failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties, among others, are generated by computer at IRS Service Centers. However, they are abated if the taxpayer establishes that the delinquency is "due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect." We turn now to the administration of these penalties and judicial review of reasonable cause determinations. The procedure is essentially the same for both penalties. We have traced through a delinquency in filing. Comments on the procedure are equally applicable to the failure-to-pay penalty. 

If an explanation for the delinquent filing accompanies the return, 148/ which is the procedure mandated by the regulations, the processing section at the Service Center deals with the problem. If no explanation accompanies the return (or the processing section fails to accept the explanation tendered with the return), the computer will send the taxpayer a bill for the penalty. This bill contains the telephone number of a local office with which the taxpayer can communicate concerning the bill. 

If the taxpayer calls the number given, he speaks to an employee who has access via a computer terminal to data concerning the taxpayer's account. If satisfied with the taxpayer's explanation, the employee has authority to abate the penalty. Alternatively, the taxpayer can write to the Service Center where Tax Examiners will consider his explanation and are authorized to abate the penalty. The personnel who pass on these

explanations accept the taxpayer's word concerning factual matters. If the facts asserted by the taxpayer fit the employee's conception of rea- 149/ sonable cause, the penalty is abated. Unless the return happens to be there is no occasion to investigate the audited at a later date, taxpayer's version of how the delinquency occurred. 

If the taxpayer fails to respond to the notice sent by the Service Center, three more letters are sent to him, demanding payment in increasingly urgent and threatening tones. Finally, the matter is termed a Tax Delinquency Account and referred to Collection personnel in the taxpayer's district. Personnel in Collection will generally contact the taxpayer and give him a final chance to explain the delinquency. If the explanation is not accepted by the Revenue Officer to whom the matter is assigned, there is a further chance to negotiate with his Group Manager. 

Then collection efforts begin.

At any point in this process the taxpayer can pay the penalty and then submit a claim for refund. The claim will be scrutinized by the same group of Tax Examiners at the Service Center who examine explanations submitted before payment of the penalty. If the claim for refund is rejected, the taxpayer can sue for a refund in the Federal district court or the Court of Claims. 

No doubt many of the explanations for delinquency submitted by taxpayers are accepted by the personnel responsible for considering them. 

But the noteworthy point is that if the explanation is rejected, the options open to the taxpayer are markedly different from those available in

connection with audits. If a deficiency is asserted after an audit (with or without inaccuracy penalties), an elaborate negotiating apparatus is open to the taxpayer before he has to pay the tax. He can negotiate with the Revenue Agent's group chief, a District Conferee, and finally the Appellate Division. If the matter is not disposed of through negotiation, he can file a Tax Court petition, still without paying the tax. During the pendency of litigation, he can negotiate further with the Regional Counsel. 

Finally, if the litigation is decided adversely to him, he must pay the 150/ tax.

By comparison, the administrative process available prior to paying a delinquency penalty is very sparse. The taxpayer has the opportunity to send a letter to a Tax Examiner at the Service Center or to speak over the telephone toll-free with a local employee. He can try to convince 151/ a Revenue Officer to whom his delinquent account has been assigned. 

In order to negotiate further with the IRS, he must pay the penalty and file a claim for refund. If it is denied, he can litigate in the district 152/ court or Court of Claims. 

The Tax Court is not open to him. 

Yet, failure to file cases may present many disputable issues of 153/ Late filing is excused if the taxpayer establishes that law and fact. his delinquency was "due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect. 

The test, then, is whether the taxpayer exercised ordinary business care 154/ and prudence. 

Needless to say, this sort of test does not lead to clear-cut and indisputable results in many cases. As in negligence cases of all sorts, litigation is often necessary to resolve what is reasonable.

Acceptable excuses include such relatively objective events as death or serious illness of the taxpayer or his family or destruction by fire 155/ of his place of business or records.

But how sick does one have to be on April 15? How about the taxpayer who suffers extreme mental depression around that time (whether or not attributable to his income tax problems)?

Suppose same books are destroyed by fire but enough are left to make reasonable estimates? 156/ Quite difficult cases are presented by the errors of tax advisers. 

The Tax Court seems to be clear that negligent failure by an accountant or attorney to file on time is not an excuse, but the point is not absolutely settled. Courts accept as an excuse good faith reliance on the opinion of a qualified tax practitioner that no return is due, 159/ 157/ 158/ but this test produces many disputes. And what of cases where the law is unclear about whether the taxpayer must file, and he has reasonable belief that he need not do so? 160/ Or, what of cases where the law is clear (although complex) and the taxpayer is ignorant, 161/ or what of 162/ If an cases where the taxpayer files on time, but on the wrong form? 

IRS employee erroneously advises the taxpayer that no return is due, this 163/ is an acceptable excuse, but will the taxpayer be believed if he 164/ pleads reliance on wrong oral advice?

The IRS policy is not to assert the penalty if a timely return is submitted without being signed, unless 165/ there is willful intent to disobey the law or gross negligence, 166/ but it seems that its discretion has sometimes been abused.

When one considers the mudiness of many reasonable cause determinations, the administrative and judicial review available to delinquent filers prior to payment begins to seem most inadequate. 

Can a taxpayer (especially an uneducated one) make a written presentation of his position which will satisfy a harassed Service Center Tax Examiner? 

If he writes only that he was sick, or that his accountant made the mistake, this will not be enough. But, perhaps he does not know to write more. 

The opportunity to make telephone contact with personnel at a local office is certainly helpful, but IRS telephone numbers are often busy. When the taxpayer finally gets through, it may prove to be difficult to communicate precisely over the telephone what his excuse was. The employee may seem abrupt and may not take the trouble to ask for additional, but necessary, details. Yet, in a face-to-face negotiating session with trained IRS review personnel, the excuse might well be accepted. If it is not, the available judicial review option to pay and sue for a refund is not adequate for most taxpayers. Aside from the hardship of having to pay the penalty before litigation, the formidable procedural problems of dealing with Federal district courts would require virtually all taxpayers to hire an attorney, which would hardly be practicable for cases involving a few thousand dollars of penalty or less. But if access to the Tax Court were allowed, the taxpayer could litigate before paying 167/ which may be of critical importance to his financial survival.

He would also have the benefit of the relatively simple procedures of the 

Here he can repre- 168/ Tax Court, especially the small tax case provisions. sent himself or have his accountant represent him.

What accounts for the fact that significant prepayment negotiating and litigating opportunities are denied to taxpayers in failure-to-file cases? Some insight into the reasons for not allowing the Tax Court to have jurisdiction over these taxes was furnished by a development occurring after the adoption of the 1954 Code. Several courts held that under the 169 1954 Code (unlike prior law) the Commissioner had to utilize a deficiency 170/ notice prior to assessing the delinquency penalty. 

This would have the effect of triggering Tax Court jurisdiction. But, in 1960 Congress acted to change the law, cutting off any need to use the deficiency notice 171/ procedure.

The legislative history of this change shows that the Internal Revenue Service was inconvenienced administratively by the need to furnish deficiency notices prior to asserting delinquency penalties. The IRS prefers to assess delinquency penalties as soon as late returns are filed. 

If the penalty had to be asserted by a deficiency notice, the IRS feared that it would be precluded from asserting any further deficiencies when it later audited the return. Thus, it felt that it would have to forego the immediate assertion of the delinquency penalty until it audited the 172/ return in question.

Although the IRS's concern on this point was warranted at the time of the amendment of § 6659 (b), the situation has now changed. By reason of an amendment to § 6212(c) in 1970, 173/ the IRS is no longer precluded from asserting a second deficiency as to the same tax year. 

Under the present statute, it is precluded only if the taxpayer files a Tax Court petition and

only then as to the act (or failure to act) to which the petition relates. 

Thus, the IRS would be precluded from a second deficiency notice only in respect to the late filing, not anything else on the return, and it would not be precluded at all if it determined that the late filing was 175/ fraudulent. 174/ Consequently, a reversal of the 1960 change in $ 6659 would not disrupt the audit process.

However, the real issue is whether the appellate processes of the IRS and the Tax Court should be opened up to pre-payment disputes concerning reasonable cause for late filing. At the time of the 1960 amendment to $ 6659, it was estimated that about one million delinquency and 176/ under-estimation penalties were asserted each year. 

No statistics are available on how many delinquency penalties presently are asserted, nor on how many of them would be disputed after the Service Center processing is completed. If a very large number of taxpayers asserted all their rights to negotiate with the IRS and then went to the Tax Court as a device to delay payment of the penalty, those institutions might be swamped. 

If many of the claims by taxpayers had no merit, there would be an unjustifiable diversion of resources from more worthy tax dispute settlement processes. 

The point is that nobody really knows. Many IRS personnel see no problem in placing delinquency matters within the same dispute-settlement process as other tax cases. They did not anticipate any undue administrative burden or that there would be a very large number of delinquent taxpayers who would pursue these rights. In light of the patent inadequacy of the

existing dispute-settlement system, $ 6659 should be amended to give delinquent taxpayers the right to deficiency letter procedures. If this creates unmanageable administrative problems, the law can always be changed again.

This analysis seems applicable to many other statutory penalties which contain a reasonable cause exception. These include the penalties 177/ for failure by an exempt organization to file a return, failure to 178/ deposit payroll taxes, and many others found in Appendix A. We have not dealt with these, however.

The Responsible Officer Penalty. 

Under $ 6672, the person responsible for withholding and paying over taxes may be subjected to a penalty if he willfully fails to do so. 

The penalty is equal to the amount of the taxes not so withheld and paid over.

Again there is little empirical data indicating the number of assess- 179/ ments made each year. 

However, as is described in the chapter concerning collections, there are many business delinquents each year, and, given the incidence of small incipient businesses which appear to fall delinquent, one would expect a substantial number of assessments each year. 

Other than the question of amount and non-payment, the only defenses to the assessment are that the assessee was not the person responsible for withholding and payment, or was not willful. That issue is largely a factual one requiring analysis of legal precedents and careful marshalling of facts. Yet this issue is tried on numerous occasions each year. For example, the index to the 1974 CCH Standard Federal Tax Reporter for S 6672, revealed at least 45 cases were decided in 1974. Thus, the crucial issue is frequently presented for court determination, but there is otherwise no data suggesting its importance. Hence, we turn to an analysis of the problem without further data.

In the garden-variety situation a corporation will fail to make payment of taxes (FICA and income taxes) withheld from an employee's wages. 

A Revenue Officer is sent to secure collection. We think his mental outlook is important and is likely to be shaped by two considerations. First, a belief commonly held by Collection personnel is that failure to pay over 180/ withheld taxes is the most serious of all non-payment violations.

and: tot 201 12 Second, a look at the history of these delinquent corporations and their officers frequently would reveal that one or the other has been in exactly this situation before, i.e., that either the corporation or its officers are repeat delinquents. Hence, there is little sympathy for them. In fact, Revenue Officers seem highly motivated when confronted with these accounts.

With this frame of mind the officer will make an effort to collect. If he finds the corporation without funds and otherwise fails to obtain the tax from it, the Revenue Officer is empowered to recommend assessments of a penalty equal to the withheld taxes against the corporate officers responsible for willfully failing to withhold to the Service. 

Since the corporation is without funds, we suspect that the Revenue Officer's motivation is heightened by the virtual certainty that if the tax is not collected from a corporate officer, it will not be collected at all. The corporate funds may have been diverted to the personal use of the officers against whom the penalty may be asserted. And, finally, the responsible officer may be one of several. Just which one is not clear, so it may be that any one corporate officer will prevail in court by demonstrating that he was not responsible for withholding and paying over. Therefore, the Revenue Officer may be inclined to assess the responsible officer penalty against as many candidates as he can muster. 

There are thus many cases involving multiple assessments of the penalty for a single failure to pay over. Multiple collections are very rare (if any occur at all) because as a practical matter, the Service will

181/ It does so on the settle for a single collection equal to the tax. theory that multiple collections for a single failure to pay would blunt the penalty's use as a collection tool. The Service fears that if it emphasized the penalty's penal nature over its compensatory purpose, the courts might be provoked to impose more stringent standards of proof. 

Once the assessments are proposed, the administrative review in such cases is slightly better than that for penalties for failure to file or to pay. Once the Revenue Officer has decided on one or several corporate officers as being subject to the penalty, an assessee may then request the Revenue Officer or his Group Manager, within the Collection Division, and finally a District Conferee to reconsider. Thereafter, 182/ there is a right to appeal the matter to the Appellate Division in the regional office. However, once that level has been reached and resolved unsatisfactorily to the corporate officer or officers, the penalty will be assessed. Because assessment is not preceded by deficiency procedures, the penalty is not subject to Tax Court review. Once assessed, the penalty may be collected after ten days' notice and demand. Hence, judicial review may be obtained only by paying the penalty, filing a 183/ claim for refund, and thereafter instituting suit. This procedure, except to the extent that administrative appeals are somewhat less haphazard, is then subject to the problem discussed with respect to the delinquency and failure-to-pay penalties: should the prepayment forum, the Tax Court, be open to the assessee? 

There appears to be no compelling reason to deny resort to Tax

689

Court litigation. It is highly unlikely that the Service will be inconvenienced if collection is postponed until the corporate officers Only in rare circumstances would delay have had a day in court. 184/ jeopardize eventual collection of the penalty, and in that event immediate 185/ collection may be had through jeopardy assessment. 

While Tax Court procedure is not available, an assessee may obtain judicial review of the penalty by paying it with respect to a single employee, then following the traditional claim for refund and suit route. This, however, does not assure restraint in collection from the other officers while one assessee litigates. They have only the mercy of a Revenue Officer to prevent collection. Some assessees might be somewhat insecure in those circumstances. There appears to be no good policy to support the present procedures or to cause this kind of insecurity. Thus, Tax Court proceedings should be available in this case.

C. Clarification of the Non-Filing Penalty. 

186/ 

The wording of § 6651(a) (1) 

is obscure. The penalty does not apply if the delinquency is "due to reasonable cause and not due to willful neglect." What is "willful neglect"? The two terms are contradictory. "Willful" seems to connote intentional conduct or a bad purpose. 

But "neglect" speaks of negligence, carelessness, accident.

Clearly, the exception is intended to apply if the taxpayer has not been negligent. This is made sufficiently clear by the phrase "reasonable cause." The confusing phrase about willful neglect should be dropped. 

Also, by way of clarification the IRS should amend the regulations relating to failure to file by listing the grounds which it finds to be reasonable cause. It has done so with respect to the failure-to-pay penalty. 

A list of acceptable excuses is contained already in the Internal Revenue 188/ 

Manual. 

Incorporation of this list in the regulations would make these 189/ standards considerably more accessible to tax professionals.

APPENDIX B PROPOSED STATUTORY LANGUAGE FOR SECTION 6653 

The following is suggested as new statutory language to replace present IRC, S 6653. 191/

SEC. 6653 UNDERPAYMENTS OF TAX 

(a) NEGLIGENCE.-If any part of an underpayment of any tax required to be shown on a return is due to negligence, there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 5% of such part of the underpayment. 192/ Negligence means failure to exercise reasonable care in keeping records or in preparing the return. 193/ 

(b) RECKLESS OR INTENTIONAL CONDUCT.--If any part of an underpayment of any tax required to be shown on a return is due to reckless or intentional conduct (but without willful tax evasion), there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 25% of such part of the underpayment. 194/ (1) This amount shall be in lieu of any amount determined under subsection (a). (2) Reckless conduct means that in keeping records or preparing the return, the taxpayer has consciously disregarded a substantial risk that an underpayment would occur. (3) Intentional conduct means that in keeping records or preparing the return, the taxpayer knew that an underpayment would occur or was substantially certain to occur. 

(c) WILLFUL TAX EVASION.-If any part of an underpayment of any tax required to be shown on a return is due to willful tax evasion, there shall be added to the tax an amount equal to 50% of such part of the underpayment. (1) This amount shall be in lieu of any amount determined under subsections (a) and (b). (2) Willful tax evasion has the same meaning as willful attempts to evade tax under section 7201. 195/

(d) DEFINITION OF UNDERPAYMENT. 196/--For purposes of this section, the term "underpayment" means the excess of the correct tax over the amount of tax shown upon the return if a return was made by the taxpayer. An amended return shall not be treated as a return for this purpose. 197/ This calculation shall be made without regard to any credit for an overpayment for any prior period and without regard to any adjustment under sections 6205 (a) and 6413 (a). However, for this purpose, the tax shown on the return shall be taken into account only if filed either (1) on or before the last date prescribed for filing such return, determined with regard to any extension of time for such filing, or (2) If the return is filed after such date, it is filed before the taxpayer believes, or has reason to believe, that his return has been selected for audit or that adverse information concerning his return has been reported to the Secretary or his delegate. 198/ 

(e) PREVENTION OF DUPLICATE PENALTIES.--In the event that a taxpayer fails to file a return within the time prescribed by law, or fails to pay a tax shown on the return, or underpays estimated tax, (1) Negligence, recklessness, and intentional conduct penalties precluded.--And if a penalty is assessed under a section specifically relating to such conduct, no penalty shall be assessed under subsections (a), (b), or (c) of this section by reason of such conduct. 199/ (2) Willful tax evasion penalty precludes other penalties.--And if a penalty is assessed under subsection (c) by reason of such conduct, no additional penalty shall be assessed under sections specifically relating to such conduct. 200/ (f) INNOCENT SPOUSE.--In case of a joint return under section 

6013, subsections (a), (b), and (c) shall not apply to the tax of a spouse unless the spouse engaged in the conduct described in those subsections. 201/ 

(g) LESSER INCLUDED PENALTIES.--A court which is adjudicating the taxpayer's liabilities for additions to tax described in subsections (b) or (c) shall have power to find the taxpayer liable for the penalty described in either subsections (a) or (b) if the Secretary or his delegate has determined that the taxpayer is liable for such penalty. 202/

(h) BURDEN OF PROOF.--In any proceeding in a court, including the Tax Court, to determine whether the taxpayer is liable for the penalties described in this section, the burden of persuasion to establish willful tax evasion, as described in subsection (c), shall be on the Secretary or his delegate. Such proof shall be by clear and convincing evidence. If the Secretary or his delegate proves that any part of the deficiency for any year or return is attributable to willful tax evasion, the burden of persuasion will shift to the taxpayer to establish the absence of willful tax evasion with respect to the remainder of the deficiency for such year or return. The burden of persuasion to establish the absence of negligence, described in subsection (a), or recklessness or intentional conduct, described in subsection (b), shall be on the taxpayer. 203/

1/ The penalties are listed in Appendix A. 

See infra note 190 for a discussion of the criteria for selecting these 64 penalties and excluding others.

An interesting article by Professor Charney of Vanderbilt School of Law has asserted that civil money penalties are criminal in nature. Consequently, he argues that a due process violation occurs if the penalized individual is not given the protections of a criminal trial. Charney, The 

Need for Constitutional Protection for Defendants in Civil Penalty Cases, 59 Cornell L. Q. 478 (1974). This issue is not addressed in this report. 

It seems clear that if Charney is correct, the entire tax penalty structure would crumble. It would not be possible, given the present or foreseeable resources available to the Federal courts, to collect the vast array of civil penalties by the criminal process. 

We feel that it is sufficient to collect money penalties through civil processes as long as the penalties are deemed to be civil. A "civil" penalty lacks the element of condemnation implicit in calling something "ariminal".

Consequently, it need not be collected through the rigorous processes of the criminal law. In any event the collectibility of civil penalties through civil processes is so well established that it is unlikely that Charney's argument will prevail in the foreseeable future. Helvering v. Mitchell, 303 U.S. 391 (1938), seems to be too solidly ensconced in our jurisprudence now to be dislodged. Therefore, our analysis proceeds with the assumption that civil money penalties are Constitutional.

37/ IRC, S 7201. An analysis of the legislative history of our present civil and criminal evasion statutes indicates an intertwined development. 

Although committee reports on these provisions are almost completely lacking, the language of the statutes and the timing of their enactment tend to show that criminal and civil fraud statutes were designed to penalize approximately the same kinds of conduct. For example, the present statutes can be traced back to the Act of 1864. Section 15 provided a fine and imprisonment in case of "any false or fraudulent list, [or] return. . .with intent to defeat or evade" tax. Using parallel language, S 14 of the same statute provided a 100 percent civil penalty "in case of the return of a false or fraudulent list or valuation. 

13 Stat. 223, 226-227. The 1894 Act retained these penalties and added an additional 100 percent civil penalty for a 'willfully false or fraudulent list or return. $ 29, 28 Stat. 509, 554. "1 11 11 The 1909 corporate tax was a veritable jumble of penalties. It preserved the two penalties from the 1864 statute. It changed the penalty added by the 1894 Act to cover "any return made with false or fraudulent intent."

It added a new criminal penalty in case of a "false or fraudulent return. .with intent to defeat or evade the assessment. And it added still another penalty of between $1,000 and $10,000, which might have been either civil or criminal, in case any corporation shall render a "false or fraudulent return. SS 5, 8, 36 Stat. 11, 116-117. Later statutes also contained a jumble of confusing civil and criminal penalties. The wording of the statutes varied, but yielded no clear pattern of different wording for civil and criminal penalties. See SS F, G, and I of the 1913 Revenue Act, 38 Stat. 114, 171; ch. 463, SS 9 (a), 14 (a) and (c), 16, 18 of the Revenue Act of 1916, 39 

Stat. 756, 763; and ch. 63, SS 1001 and 1004 of the Revenue Act of Oct. 3, 1917, 40 Stat. 300, 325. Finally, the Revenue Act of 1918 established the pattern of civil and criminal penalties of today's law. Ch. 18, SS 250 (b), 253, 40 Stat. 1057, 1082. A more detailed chronology of legislative history of the civil and criminal penalties is in the IRS Sanction Study, at 113120.

The 1974 Civil Fraud Study, at 19-20, acknowledged that the state of mind required to establish civil fraud and criminal tax evasion is the same, except for the different burden of proof in civil and criminal cases and the different "atmosphere" involved in the trials.

43/ Six hundred seventy such cases were studied, in which $9.1 million of civil fraud penalties were paid. Approximately 2,700 such cases occurred during 1965. Of the 670 cases 154 were recommended by the Intelligence 

Division as suitable for criminal prosecution, and 98 were actually prosecuted. 

The number of criminal cases seems low since according to the IRS 1965 Cam'r. Ann. Rep. 31, 1,393 cases were recommended for criminal prosecution in 1965. Thus, it is possible that the months studied were not representative. Furthermore, the above numbers are puzzling because the 1974 Civil 

Fraud Study, supra note 8, found that in most of the districts studied, the civil fraud penalty was not normally recommended in the cases rejected by Intelligence. In those districts nearly all the fraud cases were criminal in nature.

The 1968 study, IRS Sanction Study, at 144, broke down the civil fraud cases by the amounts of penalty asserted and by the number of years involved. 

This analysis indicated that the likelihood of prosecution increased very sharply as the size of the deficiency increased and as the number of years involved increased. Thus, for example, in false return cases there were 

511 cases altogether. Of these, 103 were recommended for prosecution (20 percent). But of the 143 civil fraud cases in which the civil penalty was under $1,000 (meaning that the deficiency was under $2,000), only 11 (or 7 percent) of the cases were recommended for prosecution. Where the penalty was between $5,000 and $7,500, however, there were 40 cases, 9 of which were recommended for prosecution (23 percent). Where the penalty was between $30,000 and $50,000, 14 of the 19 cases were recommended for prosecution (74 percent).

The same pattern occurred in the 159 cases relating to failure to file. Only 10 percent of the cases involving penalties under $1,000 were recommended for prosecution. Of the cases involving penalties between $3,000 and $5,000, 33 percent were recommended. Of those involving penalties in excess of $15,000, 62 percent were recommended for prosecution. 

Similarly, of 511 cases involving false returns, 59 involved only a single year. Of these, three were recommended for prosecution (4 percent). 

Of the 150 cases involving three years, 20 were recommended for prosecution (13 percent). But, of the 75 cases involving four years, 31 (39 percent) cases were recommended for prosecution. Of the 17 cases involving eight or more years, seven (or 41 percent) were recommended.

However, the pattern does not hold up very well for the failure-tofile cases. Of those involving two years, 33 percent were recommended for prosecution. Only 20 percent of those involving three years were recommended, but 48 percent of those involving four years were recommended. Only 13 percent of those involving five years were recommended, but 35 percent of those involving six years were recommended. The explanation for the relatively low correlation between number of years and likelihood of prosecution in the failure-to-file cases may lie in the fact that many failure-to-file cases involve organized crime figures where different prosecution policies are in effect.

Less complete data are provided by the 1968 IRS Sanction Study, at 142, on the amount of adjusted gross income of taxpayers involved in fraud cases. 

The figures relating to income are correlated only to the 154 cases in which criminal prosecution was recommended by the Intelligence Division. These show that 53 of the cases (34 percent) involved incomes of $30,000 and over. 

Forty of the cases (26 percent) involved incomes between $15,000 and $29,999. 

But, only five involved incomes under $3,000 (3 percent), and 13 involved incomes between $3,000 and $5,999 (8 percent), despite the vastly larger number of returns filed showing low incomes, rather than high incomes. 

49/ The resources expended are not only those of the Justice Department and IRS staff in prosecuting the case. The Service also perceives that prosecuting trivial criminal cases will lower its percentage of convictions, a highly relevant indicium for law enforcement agencies. Juries and judges are less likely to convict in such cases. Moreover, it is believed that judges tend to become impatient with the Service if a large number of trivial cases begin to clog the dockets. This has damaging consequences for the entire program of criminal tax law enforcement. See IRS Sanction Study, ch. 6.

81/ The deterrent factor supplied by the new penalty might discourage a particular form of cheating which is perceived by tax administrators to be quite significant. Larger corporations make deliberate and easily detected errors on their returns. These errors are immediately conceded when the return is audited. It is hoped that the Revenue Agent will be satisfied by detecting these errors and will not look so diligently for more subtle items. Also, this tactic conserves capital by deferring an appreciable part of the tax at the cost of only interest and (conceivably) the 5 percent negligence penalty. 

See Kiplinger Washington Letter, Sept. 6, 1974. This tactic is based entirely on rational economic analysis and the presence of a new penalty -if utilized for this purpose by examining agents could well be an effective deterrent.

86/ This approach avoids the use of the phrase "gross negligence. phrase has been generally condemned as excessively confusing. See Prosser, Torts 181-184 (4th ed. 1971); Elliott, Degrees of Negligence, 6 So. Cal. L.

Prosser, Torts 684 (4th ed. 1971). 11 33/ The statement in the text assumes that the 50 percent penalty for fraud is a given and will remain at that level. Of course, this need not be so. 

In the early versions of the income tax the penalty for fraud was 100 percent of the entire tax. The 1918 Act trimmed the penalty to 50 percent of the deficiency. Many other countries have higher penalties, although the scope of our research does not indicate whether they are combined with reasonably effective criminal enforcement. In light of the criminal sanction which is used, together with the civil penalty in the more serious evasion cases, the 

50 percent level seems about right.

Some consideration was given to raising the fraud penalty to rates much higher (ranging from 100 percent to 500 percent, for example) than the present 50 percent. Certainly, such a high penalty would have to be limited to fraud because such rates can be defended only as penal. However, most such cases would seem to be candidates for criminal evasion, and it seems doubtful that a court would impose such penalties without also finding criminality. 

Indeed, given the sentencing practices (see supra note 75) in criminal cases, a court might not impose a monetary penalty unless mandated by statute. On the other hand, if such a penalty necessarily followed a criminal conviction, a jury or court might be reluctant to find guilt.

Perhaps such a requirement would lead to earlier resolution of the disagreement by generating controversies at an earlier time. On balance, however, not every disagreement seems sufficiently serious to require disclosure. 

Differentiating between those which should be disclosed and those which need not is probably rationally impossible. The most obvious means is by the effect such item has on income or taxes. Yet, such a test stated as a percentage of gross, adjusted gross, or taxable income merely raises further complexity. If the rule were stated to require disclosure only when the item is "material", we enter an area where the term to be defined is probably too vague for imposition of a penalty, even though perhaps proper for ascertaining income. Hence, no such rule is proposed herein.

121/ For example, a fraudulent return declares that the tax due is $10,000. 

The correct tax would have been $14,000. The return has been filed six months before the taxpayer has any reason to suspect that he has been selected for audit. "Voluntary disclosure" is the name given to a policy that would prevent criminal prosecution if the taxpayer comes forward and admits his culpability (for example, by filing a non-fraudulent return or amended return) before he has reason to believe that a tax investigation has begun. 

Presently, the Service purports to adhere to a "discretionary voluntary disclosure" policy, but is not required either by statute or its regulations to do so. 

In administering the policy difficulties often arise in deciding whether the disclosure really is "voluntary" that is, whether the taxpayer had any reason to suspect that the law was starting to close in on him when he came forward. See IRS Sanction Study, at 46; letter from ABA to

Treasury, quoted in ABA Tax Section Bull. 32 (Oct. 1961). 

123/ A similar problem arises in cases of amended returns. Suppose an inaccurate return is filed on time. Later an amended return is filed which corrects the inaccuracy. The inaccuracy penalty is based on the deficiency which occurred in the original return. In other words, the additional tax paid with the amended return is not applied to reduce the deficiency and thus the base on which the penalty is computed. George M. Still, In., 19 

T.C. 1072 (1953), aff'd on other grounds, 218 F.2d 639 (2d Cir. 1955). See

Gelfand, Penalty Problems, 32 Taxes 289 (1954). However, we think this result is justifiable. Having filed an inaccurate return, the taxpayer should have to live with the penalty based on the original deficiency. This is not an instance in which a penalty for non-filing is piled arbitrarily atop an inaccuracy penalty, as is the problem discussed in the text. Instead, it represents a sensible decision not to allow removal of the penalty based upon a subsequent attempt to cure the inaccuracies. This problem presents issues similar to "voluntary disclosure." See supra note 122.

Still another related problem occurs in cases in which the original return is audited and a deficiency is asserted based on items not infected by fraud. The taxpayer pays the deficiency. Then the return is reaudited and fraud is asserted. Such a reaudit is permitted, even of the same items, in case of fraud. IRC, S 6212 (c). The taxpayer is not allowed to reduce

the deficiency (on which the penalty is computed) by the tax paid after the first audit. See Levinson v. Commissioner, 496 F.2d 651 (3rd Cir. 1974), cert. denied, 43 U.S.L.W. 3306 (U.S. Nov. 26, 1974) (No. 251); Gelfand, id. 

As contended by a dissenting opinion in Levinson, this result seems contrary to § 6211(a) (1) (B) which appears to permit a deficiency to be decreased by amounts previously assessed as deficiencies. From one point of view the result in Levinson seems appropriate as a matter of policy; the fraud penalty should not be less because the IRS made two audits rather than one. But from another point of view the result is not appropriate if different items on the return are dealt with in the two audits. We have contended that the fraud penalty should not apply to items of the deficiency which are not themselves fraudulent or negligent. See text supra at 3-38 & nn. 113-117. 

If the statute were amended as has been suggested, the problem in Levinson would not arise unless the deficiency in the first audit, because of information developed in the second audit, was subsequently found to be due in part to fraud. Such a case is Papa v. Commissioner, 464 F.2d 150 (2d Cir. 1972).

138/ By this analogy, however, we do not mean to suggest that the penalties for non-filing and for non-payment of tax shown on the return should be the There is a significant difference in the behavior associated with these two penalties which warrants different treatment. When a taxpayer files a return on time, without paying the tax due, he gains little respite from the hot breath of the tax collector. Very soon, he gets a bill for the unpaid tax and collection efforts soon follow. But by not filing a return at all, the taxpayer is left alone for a substantial time perhaps forever. At a minimum about six months will elapse before the computer alerts the IRS to the fact that a taxpayer in the Master File has failed to file. Then he will receive an inquiry, not a bill. And if the taxpayer has not previously filed, a much longer respite is likely. Consequently, the risks and losses to the government and the gains to the taxpayer are considerably greater in the case of non-filing as opposed to non-payment.
