CHAPTER THE IRS SUMMONS POWER 

I. 

INTRODUCTION 

The Internal Revenue Service may make very broad inquiry for the purpose of verifying any tax return and enforcing any Federal tax liability. 

To this end, it may summon a taxpayer, his employer, his accountant, his banker, or any other third party to produce such books, papers, records, or other data and to give such testimony, under oath, as may be relevant or material to any 1/ such inquiry.

The individual so summoned is often under the perceived threat of substantial civil and criminal penalties for failure to comply with the summons. 

In addition, rightly or wrongly, he may fear becoming the object of a yearly IRS 2/ audit or other harassment if he fails to cooperate.

The Service compiles no statistics about the issuance of summonses by its employees. It does not know how many summonses are issued, by whom, for what purposes.

It does not know the number of summonses with which taxpayers or other summoned parties do not voluntarily comply. The Service also lacks statistical records about the seeking of judicial enforcement of summons and the results thereof. Consequently, for lack of systematic, overall, empirical data. regarding the Service's use of the summons and its experience therewith, this report is confined to a discussion of principal Service guidelines and judicial opinions relative to certain key aspects of the summons power. (735)

A. 

Issuance of Summons. 

1. 

II. SUMMONS TO THE TAXPAYER Personnel Responsible for Issuance. 

The Commissioner of Internal Revenue has delegated throughout the Service his authority to issue summonses. Under his delegation order, most officials of the Service with responsibility for the examination of tax returns, the collection of taxes, or the investigation of any taxpayer's suspected failure 3/ to comply with the tax laws, have the authority to issue a summons. In addition, every Service official with authority to issue a summons is authorized to 4/ serve it on the person to whom it is addressed, and to apply to a U.S. district court judge or commissioner to seek enforcement of the summons whenever the person 5/ summoned neglects or refuses to obey the summons. Finally, any officer or employee of the Internal Revenue Service may be designated as the individual before whom a person shall appear in response to a summons, and any officer or employee so designated is authorized to take the summoned person's testimony under oath and 6/ to receive whatever data are produced in response to the summons. 

The Internal Revenue Manual contains guidance addressed to some, but not all, employees and officials of the Service regarding their exercise of authority to issue summonses. Service personnel in the Audit and Collection Divisions are directed to consider many factors before issuing a summons, including the possibility of securing the data by other means and from other sources, the significance of the information weighed against the effort to secure enforcement, and the amount 7/ of tax liability. 

A summons may be issued by a Revenue Agent if, in the course of his examination of a taxpayer's tax return and supporting books and records, he determines that he needs further information from the taxpayer or some other person. 

However, he is expected not to issue a summons if he suspects the taxpayer has

committed tax fraud. If fraud is suspected, the Revenue Agent should immediately refer the case to the Intelligence Division which will assign a Special Agent to 8/ investigate.

A Revenue Officer may issue a summons to discover income sources or assets of a taxpayer to apply against assessed liabilities. 

However, he is expected not to issue a summons when a criminal case is pending in the Intelligence Division without first obtaining approval from the office in charge of the case. 

As a member of the Intelligence Division, a Special Agent's function is 9/ to investigate possible criminal conduct. Thus, when a Special Agent has issued a summons, a taxpayer can infer that the Service suspects that there is a basis for criminal liability. The Special Agent appears to be no more constrained than a Revenue Agent or a Revenue Officer in issuing a summons, though the Service guidelines seek to give the Special Agent some responsibility to inform the tax- 10/ payer or other summoned party of his Constitutional rights. 2.

Service of the Summons. 

Any authorized Service employee may serve an administrative summons by delivering an attested copy into the hands of the summoned person or his authorized representative or by leading it at the individual's "last and usual place of abode." 

The summons must permit at least ten days from the date of the summons for the taxpayer's or third party's appearance, and it must identify a place for appearance which is "reasonable under the circumstances. 

12/ The ten-day response rule allows 11/ the summoned person and his counsel at least a minimum amount of time for preparation and investigation. Thus, "the date of the summons" has been interpreted as the date the summons is served; otherwise, delay in service would reduce the opportunity to 13/ assemble the requested material or to prepare objections to the summons. 

The interpretation of a reasonable place for the presentation of summoned documents or persons has been outlined by the Service. The IRS has announced that although it will consider the taxpayer's wishes, it expects

to conduct an examination at the taxpayer's place of business when that is the 14/ location of the relevant books and records. However, if a taxpayer attempts to impede an audit of his books and records by harassing the examining agent or by providing inadequate facilities for the examination, a summons may require that the audit occur at the local office even if 15/ hardship to the taxpayer results. A Service office near the taxpayer will usually be considered a reasonable place for an examination. 

3. Taxpayers' Rights and Responsibilities. 

If a summons requests a taxpayer to appear at the Service, he must do so. However, unless and until a summons is enforced by a court, a taxpayer may not be compelled by the Service to comply with its requests for testimony or records. Nevertheless, most individuals are likely to fear that their failure to supply the information sought by means of the summons will thereupon result in dire action by the Service. 

The taxpayer generally has no knowledge that he is not subject to penalty by the Service for failing to comply with the summons if he appears at the Service and presents good-faith objections to the production of evidence. He is not informed that a good-faith failure to produce the requested evidence may lead to nothing more onerous than a court hearing at which he may submit arguments on why the summons should not be enforced. Indeed, the summons form contains the following in terrorem statement: "Failure to comply with this summons will render you liable to proceedings in the district court of the United States or before a United States commissioner or magistrate to enforce obedience to the requirements of this summons, and to punish default or disobedience."16/

Not infrequently, a taxpayer may have legitimate reasons for not complying with a summons, but he may be unaware of his right to object and may, therefore, provide information or documents which he could rightfully withhold.

The withholding of information must be carefully structured.

In 17/ a landmark decision, Reisman v. Caplin, the Supreme Court generally validated the summons procedure, but described the means of testing a summons. The first step in testing the validity of a summons is to appear 18/ before an IRS official and assert "good-faith challenges to the summons. 

In making such appearance the summoned party may be accompanied by counsel 19/ or an authorized representative. Objections may be made orally or in writing, though the latter method may be advisable if no stenographic "1 20/ Appearance at the Service by the tax- 21/ record of the appearance is made. payer with good faith objections will prevent application of § 7210 which makes criminal a willful "neglect" to appear or to produce records. 

Similarly, it prevents contempt attachment under § 7604 (b), which the Supreme Court stated should be imposed only on "persons who were summoned 22/ and wholly made default or contumaciously refused to comply.' 

If the Service official rejects the challenge to the summons and the summoned party refuses to testify or to produce documents, the government must decide whether to seek judicial enforcement. Presumably, the summons should not have been issued if enforcement would not be sought. 

However, enforcement proceedings will result in substantial delay. Further, the Service must be represented by lawyers in the Department of Justice. 

They may apply a different standard from that applied by the Service. In addition, all the matters weighed when deciding first to issue the summons must be evaluated again. For these reasons, the decision will often be to 23/ forego enforcement, and the matter may thus end at that point. If there is a decision to enforce, then the matter moves to the Federal district court. 

Section 7604 (b) of the Code, by its terms, would appear to authorize the imposition of civil contempt punishment on a taxpayer or

other summoned party for failure to appear or to produce documents as specified in a summons. Our research, including inquiries to various knowledgeable officials at the Service, has revealed no instance where a civil contempt penalty has been imposed upon a person for failure to respond to the summons prior to being ordered to do so by a court, i.e., prior to the enforcement of the summons. As a practical matter, it is unlikely that the Service would ever seek to have a district court impose civil contempt punishment for a taxpayer's failure, through mere inaction, to respond to its issuance of a summons. The Service's interest lies in obtaining the testimony or records sought from the taxpayer, rather than in having the taxpayer punished for failing to obey the summons. ingly, the Service seeks a district court order under $ 7604 (a) of the Code to enforce the summons, rather than civil contempt punishment under $ 7604 (b). Moreover, it is doubtful that a court would deem it proper to impose a contempt penalty for a taxpayer's failure to respond to an IRS summons without having heard the taxpayer's objections and then ordering the taxpayer to respond, unless the circumstances of the taxpayer's initial failure to respond amounted to "contumacious refusal," e.g., if the taxpayer offered no explanation or justification whatsoever 23a/ for his default.

B. 

Enforcement Proceedings. 

1. 

Jurisdiction and Court Procedure. 

Accord- If enforcement of a summons is sought, the Code grants jurisdiction to the U. S. district court for the district in which the summoned 24/ person resides or may be found.

This court must permit "an adversary proceeding affording a judicial determination of the challenges to the summons 25/ and giving complete protection to the witness." 

If after a full hearing

the court orders compliance, a taxpayer's failure so to do may subject him to contempt proceedings. 26/ 

However, he may appeal the court's order. 

2. Appeals and Penalties. 

a. Appeals.

A district court's enforcement order may be appealed to 27/ 

To assure that the right to an appeal the appropriate Court of Appeals. is meaningful, a stay of execution of the enforcement order, while discretionary, should be granted in good-faith situations. 28/ 

An appeal without a request for a stay of execution, while not recommended procedure, may be deemed to include a request for stay of execution if the failure was not willful. 29/ If the order is complied with, the issue becomes moot 30/ and the appeals court will not act on the appeal.

b. Penalties. 

If the taxpayer (or other summoned person) fails to comply with a court order enforcing a summons after all his rights of court appeal 31/ have been exhausted, he may be held in civil contempt of court after a hearing at which he may raise any relevant issue except those which properly should have been presented earlier, at the enforcement hearing or on 32/ appeal therefrom.

A person found to be in civil contempt may be fined 33/ or imprisoned until he complies with the court's enforcement order. 

In addition to punishment for civil contempt, a person may, after trial, be criminally convicted for a willful failure to comply with a 34/ The penalty established by the Code may be either a fine, 35/ not to exceed $1,000, or imprisonment, not to exceed one year, or both.

36/ This penalty appears to have rarely been applied. summons.

Such are the procedures for issuing, enforcing, and challenging a summons. We turn now to the grounds on which these challenges may be made.

C. Certain Substantive Challenges to Enforcement of IRS Summonses. 

1. General. 

A summons will not be enforced if the material requested 371 is not sufficiently described or if the applicable procedures, such as valid service, have not been complied with. It also will not be enforced if the provisions of $ 7605 (regarding appropriate time and place) have 38/ not been satisfied, or if the purpose for which it is being used is improper. Further, a summons which is ambiguous, vague, or deficient on 39/ its face will not be enforced.

Improperly addressed summonses may be enforced if the intended 40/ recipient obtains clear and definite notice of the summons. The adequacy of notice and the question of whether the summoned person can or should reasonably comply with the summons must be decided on a factual 41/ basis. 

A summons will not be enforced if the witness can establish he is unable to comply with its demands. Witnesses have, for example, argued 42/ that summoned records were not in their possession. 

2. "Legitimate Purpose" Objections. a. General.

Section 7602 provides that "[f]or the purpose of ascertaining the correctness of any return, making a return where none has been made, determining the liability of any person for any internal revenue tax or the liability at law or in equity of any transferee or fiduciary of any person in respect of any internal revenue tax, or col- 43/ lecting any such liability. . 

Service personnel are authorized to

examine any taxpayer books and records, the taxpayer himself or certain other third parties. However, this access is not limitless. b. Alleged IRS Harassment.

A summons issued to harass a taxpayer or to force him to settle a collateral dispute will not be enforced. 

Harassment and the like are deemed to be improper purposes. The Supreme Court stated thus: "It is the court's process which is invoked to enforce the administrative summons and a court may not permit its process to be abused. Such an abuse would take place if the summons had been issued for an improper purpose, such as to harass the taxpayer or to put pressure on him to settle a collateral dispute, or for any other purpose reflecting on the good faith of the particular investigation." 44/

The courts are reluctant, however, to find a pattern of government harassment or bad faith, and the taxpayer has the burden of proof on this issue. c. 45/ 

Summonses Issued for Evidence of Criminal Tax Fraud or Evasion.

Taxpayers have strenuously and often objected to the use of the summons issued to obtain evidence of criminal tax fraud or evasion. They have alleged that Constitutional rights to be free of compelled self-incrimination and of illegal searches and seizures have been violated, that the summons was not authorized by $ 7602, and that the summons was issued in bad faith or for an improper purpose. 

The IRS, without question, uses its administrative summons power during criminal tax fraud investigations. Special Agents of the

Intelligence Division appear to be a major source of issued summonses. 

The Special Agent is charged with the duty of investigating for criminal tax fraud. The Handbook for Special Agents states clearly that a Special 

Agent's function is "to determine whether the person under investigation 46/ has committed a criminal violation." The function of the Intelligence 

Division is to enforce the tax laws "through the investigation of possible criminal violations of such laws and the recommendation (when warranted) of prosecution and/or assertion of the 50 percent civil fraud penalty." 

During a joint investigation with an auditing agent, the Special Agent is "responsible for the method of procedure and the conduct of the investiga- 48/ tion." 47/ Is the obtaining of evidence to establish a criminal tax law violation a proper use of the $ 7602 summons power? That question has rarely been faced by the courts because the Service has consistently asserted that the summons was motivated at least partially by civil tax investigation purposes. Thus, the Service position is that a dual purpose exists in the issuance of a summons by a Special Agent, either because he is acting in concert with an investigation of civil tax liability by an Audit Division examiner, or because even if acting alone, a Special Agent is also concerned with a civil liability (i.e., the 50 percent civil fraud penalty). The Service's view is also that any criminal case includes the possibility of civil liability and thus any summons issued is in part for a civil purpose. 49/ 

In 1971 in an opinion 50/ cases, consistent with many earlier lower court the Supreme Court approved the Service's use of an administrative

summons to obtain evidence from a taxpayer while investigating for violations of the criminal tax laws. 

In Donaldson the taxpayer argued that an administrative summons should not be enforced because it was being used "in aid of an investigation that had the potentiality of resulting in a recommendation for a criminal prosecution". 51/ The Supreme Court rejected the argument, stating: "Congress clearly has authorized the use of the summons in investigating what may prove to be criminal conduct. .There is no statutory suggestion for any meaningful line of distinction, for civil as compared with criminal purposes, at the point of a special agent's appearance. .To draw a line where a special agent appears would require the Service, in a situation of suspected but undetermined fraud, to forego either the use of the summons or the potentiality of an ultimate recommendation for prosecution. We refuse to draw that line and thus to stultify enforcement of federal law. "We hold that under $ 7602 an internal revenue summons may be issued in aid of an investigation if it is issued in good faith and prior to a recommendation for criminal prosecution. [emphasis added] 52/ This view was reaffirmed by the Supreme Court in 1973: "It is now undisputed that a special agent is authorized, pursuant to 26 U.S.C. § 7602, to issue an Internal Revenue summons in aid of a tax investigation with civil and possible criminal consequences." 53/ 

Does the underscored Donaldson holding mean, as the Service has argued, that the question of criminal purpose is to be decided in favor of the government if there has been no "recommendation for criminal prosecution?" Likely, the answer is that the holding has established a twopronged test: (1) the issuance of a summons must be made prior to recommendation for criminal prosecution and (2) the issuance of a summons must

be made in good faith. The test of good faith is not met if a summons is issued for no purpose other than obtaining evidence of criminal violation. 

To establish the Service's lack of "good faith" in issuing the summons, the burden is on the witness to show that it was issued solely for criminal purposes 54/ in violation of the legitimate-purpose doctrine set forth in Powell v. U.S. 

The post-Donaldson summons enforcement cases on the issue of criminal investigation motivation have generally been decided in favor of 55/ the government.

Some recent cases, however, have refused to enforce 56/ a summons in this context.

Donaldson did not decide the point at which a "recommendation" for criminal prosecution is deemed to occur. There is general agreement that a "recommendation" has occurred after referral of the case to the Justice Department; some courts believe that it should occur at an earlier 57/ time It is not clear whether a court would enforce a summons issued before a recommendation for criminal prosecution but where the enforcement 58/ proceedings occurred after the recommendation for prosecution.

59/ A recent district court decision in U.S. v. Friedman has criticized the entire situation and stated that it "invites hypocrisy and dissimulation on the part of Government investigators. . . In a provocative opinion, Judge Teitelbaum described the process and problems as follows: "1 "[T]he usual IRS investigation situation embodies a subtle paradox: the coexistence of two equally plausible enforcement options, epitomized in a statute which might easily lead the casual observer to leap to the conclusion that only one of those options, that of civil enforcement, is open to the government. Because the statute is at best poorly worded and impractical, it leads to two very unfortunate behavior 60/

patterns on the part of government officials who come before federal courts to have such summonses enforced. 

The first is an understandable inability on the part of IRS agents to explain what they are doing, an inability to articulate which, depending on one's point of view, may be seen as either pathetic or hypocritical. 

The second syndrome is far more irksome and occurs when, under the stress of questioning by the court or crossexamination by counsel, the government's inability to explain the § 7602 paradox turns into defensiveness and sometimes outright hostility on their part. "The present practice of the IRS seems to be that various members of the Intelligence Division are permitted to fill out and serve summons calling for various documents and files concerning certain taxpayers and serve them on third parties, in this case, banks, with very little supervision and with a great deal of discretion being placed in the hands of field agents. Indeed, it sometimes seems that a very broad use of summons is automatic. ...It seems to me that this statute invites hypocrisy and dissimulation on the part of Government investigators who are required to walk a verbal tightrope before a court which considers the propriety of such a summons and say that they are seeking both criminal and civil penalties at the same time when as a matter of fact they are taking full advantage of a lenient civil procedure for the obtaining of records when a criminal subpena might be more appropriate." 

Friedman was an unusual case in that the Special Agent testified that his sole purpose was the investigation of possible criminal tax law violation. The judge was troubled and, because of this testimony, he permitted the taxpayer to intervene in the third-party enforcement proceeding. The government later established to the judge's satisfaction that a dual-purpose joint investigation had been occurring. The summons was

enforced except for a demand to examine the taxpayer's safety deposit vault, which the judge considered to be solely motivated by criminal liability purpose. 

The Service's expressed view on the issue raised in Donaldson is that any information obtained "voluntarily" through the use of a summons may be used even though it is incriminatory. The Internal Revenue Manual, while noting that "the type of information sought through the issuance of a summons generally does not develop criminal case," stated: "Notwithstanding the privilege against selfincrimination, information or evidence furnished voluntarily by a person summoned may be used even though of an incriminatory nature. The mere fact that the person would not have appeared had it not been for the summons does not mean that this testimony or evidence was given under compulsion and is therefore inadmissible. Although the summoned person is required to appear, the question is whether it can be shown clearly that he was not thereafter compelled to testify as to incriminatory matters." 61/ If a person complies with a summons because he believes that failure to do so will result in the application of sanctions, then his compliance would seem to be compelled by his fear based on lack of knowledge. True voluntary compliance must be based on an adequate understanding of the underlying law. Although some taxpayers are aware of the law, many are not. In our view the Service has an obligation to inform every summoned person of his right to object to the summons. Only when a taxpayer is adequately informed can his compliance with a summons be fairly said to be voluntary. 

3. "Retevant or Material" to the Inquiry.

Even if a summons is issued with the proper procedures and

pursuant to a legitimate purpose, it may be used only to demand production of books and testimony "as may be relevant or material" to an authorized inquiry. The traditional complaint that a summons is not relevant or material to the Service inquiry is not often sustained by the courts when the witness is the taxpayer. Third-party witnesses have been somewhat more successful.

The test of materiality and relevancy has been characterized as analogous to that used in grand jury investigations and one which should be liberally 62/ construed.

Thus, a summons will be enforced if the information sought might 63/ throw light upon the correctness of the tax return. Probable cause for the investigation need not be established, and a mere showing that the ordinary statute of limitations has run will not render the material sought irrelevant 64/ or immaterial. 

Further, the Service is not required to show that the information sought will contradict a tax return.

Witnesses have objected to IRS summonses on the ground that they constitute "fishing expeditions" into their records. The Handbook for Special 

Agents comments as follows with respect to "fishing expeditions:" "The purpose of a summons is not limited to obtaining records of what the Government already knows, therefore the Government is permitted to indulge in some "fishing." The inquiry cannot amount to an inquisition or arbitrary inquiry on the part of the tax investigators. A reasonable basis for making the inquiry must exist. What is justifiable "fishing" will be determined from all the facts in each case including the end for which the information is sought. The investigation must not be an unreasonable burden on the third party whose records are sought." 65/

An Eight Circuit Court of Appeals panel, which included now Supreme Court Justice Blackmun, commented on the fishing expedition assertion thus: "Taxpayer in his brief characterized the Government's efforts as a "fishing expediton." If so, the 

Secretary or his delegate has been specifically licensed to fish by S 7602." 66/ 

Normally, most financial documents and testimony sought by the IRS are deemed relevant and material to its investigations. Witnesses can seldom convince a court that particular financial or conventional 67/ records and information are irrelevant or immaterial.

D. Summary. 

Because there are no substantial empirical data, it is difficult to measure the true impact of the current Service procedures relating to the issuance of summons. 

Nevertheless, the statement printed on the summons appears both uninformative and misleading. The statement does not make clear that only a court can enforce the summons. 

Further, it wrongly implies that the summoned party must appear and give testimony or produce documents or else penalties will follow. Such penalties may, however, he imposed only by a court, and only if there is a determination that failure to comply with the summons was not the result of good faith objections. 

It is also not clear that Service procedures are sufficiently monitored to forestall the issuance of the summons solely for criminal investigatory purposes. Indeed, it seems apparent that whenever a Special 

Agent is involved, the summons is in fact often issued for just such purposes. 

Perhaps, in accordance with the Donaldson decision, Special Agents should be permitted to issue summonses only for primarily civil investigatory purposes, and required to obtain court issued subpoenas or search warrants for investigations that are predominantly criminal in character. On the other hand, perhaps a clear and informative warning to the summoned party of his rights and a statement of his alternatives would provide sufficient protection of individual rights from the risk of abusive Service procedures.

III. 

THIRD PARTY SUMMONSES 

A. 

Summonses Issued to Third Parties. 

With respect to summonses issued to third parties in connection with the investigation of a taxpayer, the courts appear to be more sensitive to the burden that may be involved in providing the information than with respect to summonses issued to taxpayers. They require the IRS to make a strong showing of its need for the information. They also apply standards of specificity, relevance, and materiality which are more strict with respect to information summoned from a third party than for information summoned from taxpayers. The Second Circuit Court of Appeals has, in dictum, reflected the attitude of courts as follows: "This judicial protection against the sweeping or irrelevant order is particularly appropriate in matters where the demands for records is directed not to the taxpayer but to a third-party who may have had some dealing with the person under investigation." 68/

On occasion third parties have challenged summonses with same success on the grounds that compliance would be unduly burdensome, the requested material was not relevant or material to the inquiry, or the description of the requested material was indefinite. However, in such a case a court is more likely to modify, than to refuse, enforcement of 69/ the entire summons.

Third parties have also objected to enforcement of summonses on the grounds that compliance would be costly. Courts do not ordinarily recognize cost as a ground to refuse enforcement of the summons, but may permit a third party reasonable compensation, unless the expenses are 70/ incident to its business operations.

B. Taxpayer Rights to Intervene or Restrain Third Party Summonses. 

1. General 

The Internal Revenue Service uses its administrative summons power to demand records relating to a taxpayer from banks, employers, accountants, and others who have had dealings with the taxpayer. 

Although they or the taxpayer under investigation may have grounds to abject, many third parties readily comply with IRS summonses.

The Service, indeed, will issue a courtesy summons if a third party indicates 71/ he wishes it as evidence of the Service's request for information. In these situations the taxpayer who is the subject of the investigation may wish to obtain judicial restraint against third-party cooperation. In other cases the third party may contest the summons and the taxpayer may wish to intervene in the enforcement hearing. 

2. Notice to Taxpayer of Summons Served on Third Party. 

The threshold problem faced by a taxpayer in such situations is that of discovering whether a summons has been served on a third-party witness. The IRS is not required to give notice to the taxpayer under 72/ investigation that a summons has been served on a third-party witness. 

However, it would seem that notice should be given in order to make meaningful 73/ any right to intervene or apply for restraint.

The countervailing argument is that investigations would be unduly hampered if the taxpayer were to receive notice of a summons. Given the fact that a summons should be issued only when enforcement is anticipated if compliance is not had, each service of summons may potentially engender a 77-842 O-76-49

judicial proceeding. Since judicial proceedings may result, the party having the most at stake should be advised that the proceeding may occur. 

The individual, the investigation of whom is the cause of the issuance of the summonses on a third party has standing in this situation. He must, however, show adequate grounds to quash the summons. While such grounds are few, their paucity is no justification for denying a proper party access to a proceeding. Act. 74/ An analogous situation exists with respect to the Bank Secrecy A bill was introduced by Senator Cranston in the 93rd Congress which, among other provisions, would require that the government first serve a copy of an administrative summons on a bank's customer before serving it on the bank when the government is seeking the customer's financial records. Service on the customer would be in person or by certified mail, return receipt requested. The financial institution could not comply unless the customer consented or the bank was "served with a court order directing it to comply, issued after notice to and opportunity for the customer to challenge such subpoena or summons." 

3. Rights to restrain or Intervene.

Assuming the taxpayer learns of the matter, when is he entitled to intervene in an enforcement hearing and when is he entitled to judicial restraint of cooperation by a third party?

In Reisman v. Caplin, the Supreme Court seemed to indicate that a taxpayer or any affected person could be heard to challenge the enforcement of a third-party summons. 76/- 75/ Subsequently, intervention was often liberally granted.

77/ In 1971, however, the Supreme Court in Donaldson substantially restricted the situations in which courts may permit intervention or restraint. 

It held that a taxpayer has no absolute right to intervene or prevent third-party compliance. Rather, the taxpayer is required to show that he has a "significantly protectable interest" in the records being sought. 

It is now less than likely that a taxpayer will be permitted to restrain third-party compliance or intervene in a third-party summons enforcement proceeding. The taxpayer must establish that (1) he has a proprietary interest in the books or papers summoned, (2) the summons was issued for an improper purpose, (3) the material is protected by some form of privilege, 78/ or (4) the material is the work product of his attorney. Even then, permission to intervene or restrain is in the court's discretion and is seldom 79/ granted.

A taxpayer who either does not attempt to intervene or restrain or who fails in his attempt may assert his rights when the government 80/ subsequently attempts to use the material against him.

IV. 

"JOHN DOE" SUMMONSES 

The discussion to this point has generally involved summonses issued during the investigation of an identified taxpayer. A "John Doe" summons, in contrast, is a summons demanding records or testimony without stating the identity of the person under tax investigation. 

Analyzed as an aspect of relevance, burden, redundancy, legitimate purpose, or right of privacy, there has been recent concern with the issuance by the Service of broad "John Doe" summonses to financial institutions and other third parties.

Although the IRS is not required to have probable cause for an investigation, it usually exercises its summons power when it at least suspects a designated person may have tax liability. Is the use of the administrative summons on a "John Doe" basis proper? The answer the courts have given appears to be a qualified "yes" and depends upon the facts of each situation.

In U. S. v. Bisceglia, 81/ the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland received $40,000 in old "paper thin" $100 bills from a local Kentucky bank. 

This was unusual and it caused the IRS to suspect that the bills might relate to a transaction which had never been reported for tax purposes. 

The Service issued a "John Doe" summons to an officer of the Bank requesting extensive books and records which would disclose the identity of the depositor. 

The district court ordered the summons enforced, albeit in a narrowed scope. 

The Supreme Court upheld the decision of the district court (reversing the 

Circuit Court).

Reading the majority and concurring opinions together, we believe the Bisceglia decision is somewhat limited. It does not appear to justify wide-ranging "fishing expeditions" in the records of financial institutions and other large organizations in the hope that some unknown person might be shown to have done some unsuspected evil. Rather, it supports a limited search in a situation where a transaction reasonably indicates that a tax may be due. There is, however, same rather loose language in the majority opinion which might be viewed to mean that a § 7602 summons could 82/ support a general § 7601 inquiry. 

Subsequent cases may further define the balance between what is considered a right to be free from government "fishing expeditions" against the Service's right to conduct a legitimate investigation when there is some suspicion that a tax is due. 83/ In U. S. v. Humble Oil & Refining Co., the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals held that § 7602 summons power may not be used to enforce a "John Doe" summons issued to an oil company, seeking information for a general $ 7601 research project. It said: the summons power can be utilized only when IRS scrutiny of a taxpayer or a group thereof becomes particularized or focused. 84/ However, a recent district court decision permitted use of "John Doe" summonses issued to several financial institutions seeking the identity of Hartford Fire Insurance Company shareholders when the tax-free nature of the corporate reorganization with I.T.T. was being questioned. 85/

The court said that "The controlling factor. . . is that the taxpayers being investigated, if not identified, were at least easily identifiable. . and this identifying characteristic was set forth on the face of the summonses. " 86/ A number of recent decisions have involved "John Doe" summonses issued to: tax return preparers for the identity of large numbers of their clients and/or copies of the clients' returns. These cases resulted from undercover investigation of professional tax return preparers which often led to IRS suspicion that the preparers were erring in favor of taxpayers. 87/ The courts have been troubled by the broad summonses, but if the Service cannot otherwise reasonably obtain the information by 88/ other methods, they have generally ordered enforcement.

For example, in U. S. v. Theodore the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals said: the Internal Revenue Service is not to be given unrestricted license to rummage through the office files of an accountant in the hope of perchance discovering information that would result in increased tax liabilities for same as yet unidentified client. "We hold that (Sec. 7602). . . only allows IRS to summon information relating to the correctness of a particular return or to a particular person and does not authorize the use of openended John Doe summonses." 89/

Yet the court held that the IRS would be permitted to summon the names of all of the tax preparer's clients for those years if the IRS could establish there was no other reasonable means available to the IRS to compile the list. The Court would not require production of these clients' returns, however, since the Service could reasonably obtain 90/ the returns from its own files. 

The courts will likely enforce a "John Doe" summons if the

IRS is engaged in an investigation of a situation of suspected tax liability, whether or not the identity of the suspect is known. The extent of enforcement is determined by a somewhat vague standard of "reasonableness". On the other hand, though less than certain, it seems likely that the courts will refuse to enforce a "John Doe" summons to support only a generalized inquiry. 

In an attempt to balance these considerations administratively, the Commissioner of Internal Revenue has recently established guidelines 91/ for the issuance of John Doe summonses. 

To prevent the IRS from becoming involved in "fishing expeditions," they provide, generally, that issuance of summons can be accomplished only with approval of the Chief of the division of which the individual seeking its issuance is an employee. 

These administrative guidelines seem appropriate and may well have the desired salutary effect on the use of such summonses.

CHAPTER 4 THE IRS SUMMONS POWER FOOTNOTES 

1/ The statutory basis for the Internal Revenue Service's investigatory powers is set forth in SS 7601-7608 of the Internal Revenue Code (IRC). 

All these powers run to the Secretary of the Treasury "or his delegate." 

IRC S 7602, which provides the specific basis for the IRS summons power, reads, in pertinent parts as follows: "For the purpose of ascertaining the correctness of any return, making a return where none has been made, determining the liability of any person for any internal revenue tax or the liability at law or in equity of any transferee or fiduciary of any person in respect of any internal revenue tax, or collecting any such liability, the Secretary [of the Treasury] or his delegate is authorized. ** *** "(2) To summon the person liable for tax or required to perform the act, or any officer or employee of such person, or any person having possession, custody, or care of books of account containing entries relating to the business of the person liable for tax or required to perform the act, or any other person the Secretary or his delegate may deem proper, to appear before the Secretary or his delegate at a time and place named in the summons and to produce such books, papers, records, or other data, and to give such testimony, under oath, as may be relevant or material to such inquiry; . . 

The Secretary of the Treasury's delegation of the summons power to the 

Commissioner of Internal Revenue is contained in Treas. Reg. $ 301.7602-1 (b), which reads, in pertinent part, as follows: "(b) Summons. For the purposes described in paragraph (a) of this section, the Commissioner is authorized to summon the person liable for tax or required to perform the act, or any officer or employee of such person, or any person having possession, custody, or care of books of accounts containing entries relating to the business of the person liable for tax or required to perform the act, or any other person deemed proper, to appear before a designated officer or employee of the Internal Revenue Service at a time and place named in the summons and to produce such books, papers, records, or other data, and to give such testimony, under oath, as may be relevant or material to such inquiry. The Commissioner may designate any employee of the Internal Revenue Service as the individual before whom a person summoned pursuant to section. 7.7602 shall appear.

2/ The broad general grant of investigative power to the IRS has been criticized. Commentators have been concerned with the use and possible abuse of these powers. For example, see Kostelanetz and Bender, Criminal 

Aspects of Tax Fraud Cases, ALI-ABA (1968); Duke, Prosecutions for Attempts to Evade Income Tax: A Discordant View of a Procedural Hybrid, 76 Yale 

L. J. 1 (1966); Ritholz, The Commissioner's Inquisitorial Powers, 45

Taxes 782 (1967). The latter states at 782: "Draconianism is the succinct judicial description of the statutory schemes endowing the Commissioner with his inquisitorial powers. . . At least on the basis of the statutory language, summary powers of vast magnitude, far exceeding those of the FBI, Secret Service, CIA, Military Intelligence or of any Police Department in the land, are part of the arsenal of each one of the thousands of Revenue Agents and Special Agents employed by the Internal Revenue Service."

23/ Reasons for failure to enforce a summons are not always clear. The summons may have a technical defect on its face or perhaps a detail mentioned in the Manual has not been followed. In addition, enforcement requires the expenditure of additional time and effort to prepare the case for court. 

Enforcement is also delayed because the case must be turned over to the Department of Justice for court presentation. Further, it is not unlikely that Justice would react adversely to being inundated by Service requests for enforcement of a massive number of summonses. It should be noted, however, that a summons should not be issued unless

36/ The only reported case (in which a conviction was upheld) is U.S. v. 

Becker, 259 F.2d 869 (2d Cir. 1958), cert. denied, 358 U.S. 929 (1959). The

IRS informed us that it is aware of only three other convictions. It is not clear whether these criminal sanctions would be imposed upon a taxpayer who appears to raise good faith objections to the summons but who does not bring with him any summoned documents. The provision establishing these sanctions can be read to mean that they may be imposed if the summoned documents are not brought to the appearance, even though the taxpayer's intent, based on good faith objections, is not to turn them over. However, common sense suggests that bringing the documents, in such an instance, should not be necessary to preclude the imposition of criminal sanctions.

For a diff_sing point of view, see U. S. v. O'Conner, 118 F. Supp. 248, 251 (D.Mass. 1953), where the court stated:

"The Grand Jury [is]...the agency of compul sory disclosure. That is the inquisitorial body provided by our fundamental law to subpoena documents required in advance of a criminal trial, and in the preparation of an indictment or its particularization. . . "To encourage the use of administrative subpoenas as a device for compulsory disclosure of testimony to be used in presentments of criminal cases would diminish one of the fundamental guarantees of liberty. Moreover, it would sanction perversion of statutory power. The power under. . .[a predecessor of $ 7602] was granted for one purpose, and is now sought to be used in a direction entirely uncontemplated by the lawgivers."

CHAPTER TAXPAYER SERVICES AND COMPLAINTS I. TAXPAYER SERVICES 

The bewildering complexity of the nation's tax laws creates confusion and problems for individual taxpayers. In recognition of the difficulties faced by the taxpayer and the importance, in a tax system based on the principle of self-assessment, of inducing maximum taxpayer cooperation, the Internal Revenue Service has long undertaken to assist and advise the taxpayer in meeting his tax responsibilities. 

At the same time, the complexity of the laws has led to the emergence and growth of a taxpayer assistance industry to help the taxpayer determine how the law and its accompanying rulings are applicable to his individual return. 

It can be urged that, in principle, a taxpayer ought to be able to turn to his government and particularly to the IRS for such help rather than being forced to spend extra money for assistance in determining what taxes he should pay. The IRS, on the other hand, in determining how far it can go in providing assistance to individual taxpayers, is faced with the practical problem of the sheer numbers of taxpayers. Since agency budget and personnel are obviously limited, questions arise as to how much and what type of assistance the IRS reasonably can be expected to provide, and how well it can perform its assistance functions. A. 

Development of Taxpayer Service 

Internal Revenue Service assistance to individual taxpayers probably originated soon after the individual income tax was enacted in 1913. Until 

1952, the provision of such assistance was the responsibility of Internal Revenue Collectors whose primary duties were processing returns and collecting (779)

delinquent taxes. Over the years, the work of Collectors was augmented by Audit personnel, particularly during the tax return filing season. 

In 1952 taxpayer assistance was made the responsibility of the Audit Division where it remained until 1959. Having each had exclusive responsibility for taxpayer assistance, the Collection and Audit Divisions shared the responsibility from 1959 to 1963. This arrangement proved unsatisfactory, and in 1963 taxpayer assistance functions were consolidated within the Collection Division. A national office branch in the Collection Division developed, and in 1971 it became the Taxpayer Service Division under the 

Assistant Commissioner (Accounts, Collection and Taxpayer Service (ACTS)) 

in the national office. The purpose was to sever responsibility for taxpayer assistance from the Collection Division except at the Assistant Commissioner level. This purpose was fulfilled in 19 of the 58 district offices in July 1974. In the other 39 districts Taxpayer Service is a 1/ separate branch within the Collection and Taxpayer Service Division. 

As of July 21, 1975, however, divisional status for Taxpayer Service has 2/ been authorized for 24 additional districts.

A number of ways to assist taxpayers have developed. Originally it seems to have been largely by means of personal contact, starting at Collectors' offices, later at headquarters offices, and eventually at all offices, on a walk-in, first-come, first-served, basis. In the 1950's emphasis on the use of the telephone developed and has continued to the present for the reason that more people can thus be helped at less cost 3/ and inconvenience to both taxpayers and the Service. Service is now provided by means of a nationwide, toll-free telephone system, known as Centiphone. IRS has successfully encouraged telephone inquiries. In fiscal 1974 telephone contacts represented 72% of the Service's taxpayer 4/ assistance contacts.

Walk-in assistance is provided year-round in

district and local offices; in addition, satellite offices and mobile tax assistance units (taxmobiles) are used in some of the more remote areas during the filing season. Minor amounts of taxpayer assistance are provided in the Service Centers. 

There are now also many outreach programs designed to provide return preparation assistance or education about tax law and taxpayer responsibilities: the Volunteer Income Tax Assistance (V.I.T.A.) program, in which volunteers are trained to assist such groups as the Spanishspeaking, senior citizens, and low-income persons; special educational programs distributed to high schools and adult education classes; special training programs prepared for tax practitioners; efforts to inform new businesses of their tax responsibilities, and speeches before various civic groups for similar educational reasons. Some of these programs have been in existence for several years, for example, the V.I.T.A. program and the Understanding Taxes program designed for high school students. 

Special programs have been adopted, expanded, and refocused from year to year as new and changing needs were identified. 

It appears to be virtually impossible to determine accurately the number of personnel and dollars which the Internal Revenue Service has been devoting from year to year to the provision of assistance to taxpayers. This is understandable and derives ultimately from limitations in the Service's accounting systems. 

Accounting for personnel and expenditures is conducted primarily according to the Service's organizational structure rather than by function. (This is also true of planning and budgeting.) However, since personnel and dollars from several different divisions within the Service have been applied to taxpayer assistance, and because the patterns of such application have varied from year to year, often without any change in the structure of the Service's operations, accurate and consistent accounting

records are not available.

For example, there is substantial fluctuation during the year in the volume of taxpayer requests for assistance. Demand peaks during the tax return filing season leading to temporary assignment of personnel drawn from the Audit and Collection divisions to perform assistance functions of the Taxpayer Service Division. Conversely, slackening of demand for taxpayer assistance leads to temporary assignment of Taxpayer Service personnel to perform other functions. These shifts in function of personnel together with "overhead" time associated with taxpayer assistance functions, e.g., management, leave, and training, have not been accurately reflected in records of taxpayers assistance activities and its dollar costs. Another example of the difficulty in gauging accurately the amount of funds devoted to taxpayer assistance is the accounting treatment of the costs of preparing, printing, and distributing tax returns and other IRS forms, instructions, and taxpayer publications. Prior to Fiscal Year 

1974, they were not consolidated and accounted for as costs of the Taxpayer Service division. Furthermore, it is not possible accurately to allocate within totals of personnel and costs of Taxpayer Service amounts for direct taxpayer assistance, general taxpayer information programs, and programs of taxpayer education. However, it is reasonable to estimate the overall budget for providing taxpayer services at $100 million annually an enormous figure in the absolute, but not so significant when compared to the total $1.6 billion budget of the Internal Revenue Service. 

In terms of numbers of personnel assigned to Taxpayer Service, precise figures are also elusive. IRS has supplied an estimate of 2079 direct man-years, i.e., excluding overhead time, for Fiscal 1974;1 in 5/ recent Congressional testimony the Service stated that in Fiscal 1974 it had 1822 permanent Taxpayer Service Representatives (average) and over 1200 temporary workers. The corresponding figures for Fiscal 1975 are 2077 permanent

1 6/ and 600 temporary positions. 

Perhaps because of increased interest in recent years by the Congress in taxpayer assistance, the share of the IRS budget allotted to carry out this function has risen from 3.5 percent in the Fiscal Year ending 

June 30, 1973 to 6.4 percent in Fiscal Year 1975. In the same year, by comparison, 38.9 percent of the total IRS budget went for audits and 25 percent for data processing. 

The principal contact within the IRS for dealing with taxpayer requests is the Taxpayer Service Representative (TSR), whose exposure and training make him the most responsive person in the Service to taxpayer problems. Because of this exposure and their basically sympathetic approach to the taxpayer, Taxpayer Service Representatives are becoming a major public relations adjunct of the Internal Revenue Service. 

The TSR position has been upgraded recently by the Service, which now requires that a candidate have at least six semester hours of college level accounting and a college degree or equivalent work experience. Before 

June, 1975 TSR's needed only two years of education beyond high school, or two years work experience which demonstrated an aptitude for meeting and dealing with people, plus an ability to understand a body of rules and to apply them to specific cases. Upon entering the service, TSR's are required to undergo 11 weeks of training encompassing complex issues such as investment credits, and such technical matters as Automatic Data Processing and the Integrated Data Retrieval System (IDRS). Supplementing the permanent TSR's are temporary TSR's recruited for peak season work, who receive two weeks of classroom and one week of simulation training. 

Additionally, Audit and Collection Division personnel with varying qualifications are detailed-in during the peak filing season. These divisional employees for the most part are relatively new personnel, whose training

has been in their designated areas. For taxpayer service training, Revenue 

Officers, i.e., Collection personnel, are given a five-day course on tax law changes and new revenue rulings. Audit personnel receive only three days of refresher taxpayer service.

It is difficult to evaluate the adequacy of the qualifications and training of Taxpayer Service personnel. We note, however, that of TSR's recently surveyed, 18 percent had received no training in IDRS and another 22 percent characterized IDRS training as poor. These responses were in contrast to the over 90 percent who said that other areas of training were 7/ good or fair.

A major stumbling block in general evaluation is the lack of extensive data on the general type and level of complexity of taxpayer inquiries. 

Without such information it is impossible to determine the necessary extent of training. Obviously, if a significant percentage of taxpayer questions relate to the more complex areas of the law, still higher qualifications and more training for some fraction of Taxpayer Service personnel will be However, TSR work varies from the routine to the complex. Much of it is not unusually difficult and can be performed by relatively inexperienced and less trained employees. But, upon occasion TSR's necessary. face more complex questions. Thus, at least two different kinds of personnel are required. The Service has addressed this problem by adding an upgraded 

TSR position, Taxpayer Service Specialist (TSS). (TSS). The solution, however, requires an adequate referral system to channel taxpayer inquiries to the right TSR, TSS or Revenue Agent. This issue is discussed more fully later. 

B. Kinds of Assistance 

(1) tax The Service provides three basic kinds of assistance: return assistance and preparation; (2) resolution of problems stemming from 

IRS notices, communications, and failures to understand either, or from

દુ the IRS's bureaucratic structure; and (3) education of individuals or groups on their tax responsibilities. 

The Service has no information about the relative resources that it . devotes to providing these different types of assistance. 

Nevertheless, it can be speculated that the bulk of resources consumed by direct taxpayer contact are in the return assistance and preparation category, particularly since two-thirds of all taxpayer contacts occur during the peak filing season. To offset this lack of information, it is recommended that the Service compile data on all personnel and funds allocated for each type of taxpayer service performed. With such information the Service should be better able to plan its training and resource allocation in accordance with demonstrated taxpayer needs. 

Taxpayer assistance in substantive tax law is designed by the IRS to enable the taxpayer to prepare his own return through the ready availability of clear and comprehensive information. Taxpayer 

Service Representatives are present in local and district offices to provide personalized service in explaining the return forms, and in a limited number of cases, as a last resort, to prepare returns for taxpayers. 

At one point the Service considered providing taxpayers with a free-of-charge alternative to paid assistance from commercial and professional sources in the preparation of returns. It abandoned the idea because of the anticipated large number of taxpayers that would avail themselves of the free service. Yet, most taxpayers polled in a recent survey said they would prefer more IRS help in return preparation. Buttressing the taxpayer preference is the assertion of TSR's that they frequently have difficulty in promoting self help, implying that taxpayers regard return preparation as the most significant aid that could be provided by the 8/ Taxpayer Services Division.

77-842 O 76 51

Procedural assistance covers a wide range of activities, from the routine handling of requests for extension of return filing time to problems emanating from the Service's heavy reliance on computers in processing taxpayer returns. In one important respect this type of assistance is more significant to the taxpayer than is return preparation. 

No low-priced commercially available assistance can cope with the internal workings of misdirected or erroneous IRS computer notices. 

The need for procedural assistance may have increased in recent years as a result of the Service's near total automation of its operations. recognition of the vital role of the TSR as an intermediary between the IRS computer and the individual taxpayer, the Service is considering a proposal that TSR's become the primary problem solvers for taxpayers with 9/ IRS difficulties. Implementation of this proposal would help allay taxpayer frustrations in dealing with the IRS bureaucracy. 

TSR's are the most responsive employees of the IRS to taxpayer inquiries and problems. They have the ability to explain notices, to trace payments. and to initiate freezes on further notices in confused account situations. Thanks to their knowledge of computers and preferential access to the IDRS, they are capable of resolving taxpayer problems rapidly. There are, however, limits to the TSR's problem-solving capabilities. For example, a TSR cannot delay, stop or interfere with an audit, nor can he initiate a freeze on a tangled taxpayer account after it has been sent to a local office for collection. And he is not equipped to deal effectively with taxpayer complaints emanating from taxpayer contact with an auditor or collection agent. In most circumstances such complaints are ignored, leaving the taxpayer with little opportunity to air or redress his grievance.

The Taxpayer Contact Unit in Service Centers is also a critical

cog in resolving taxpayer post-return filing problems, many of which stem from confusion generated by computer-printed notices. In their capacity as a back-up resource for district office personnel, Service Center personnel handle all district office referrals, primarily from TSR's, although occasionally from Revenue Officers and Revenue Agents. They have the ability to unravel complicated account problems, solve complications arising from dual filing situations (e.g., married taxpayers filing separately, but one signed the other's return), perform the computation and assessment of penalties and interests (particularly in special situations such as the restricted interest computation involved in audits), and similarly complex situations which TSR's are generally unable to resolve. 

In addition, some types of adjustments and other problems can be resolved only by Service Center personnel.

The Service has attempted to standardize referral procedures for routine and "special" referrals to be used by district offices and Service Center personnel in facilitating efficient and effective responses to 10/ taxpayers. Correspondence inquiries to the Service Center are routed to appropriate personnel for response. 

The Taxpayer Contact Unit handles all walk-in and telephone inquiries at the Service Center. Although taxpayers are discouraged from visiting or calling the Service Center 

11/ because of "security problems, some taxpayers remember the days when considerably more taxpayer service was generated from the Service Center. 

Thus, they continue to rely on it, primarily by telephone contact and to a lesser extent by visiting the Service Center. Despite their proficiency in dealing with specific types of problems, there have been from time to time attempts to cut back on the number of employees in the Contact Unit. 

We believe that any such reduction would lower the quality of procedural aid unless satisfactory alternatives were developed.

C. Quality of Service 

The public measures the quality of service provided by the Taxpayer Services Division in terms of aid given in the preparation of tax returns rather than in procedural matters. Based on taxpayer polls of those who had used the Service, the overwhelming majority of respondents gave high 12/ marks to the quality of assistance received. In general, the taxpayer consumers found that the service was clear, complete, and courteous and stated that they would use it again. Whether this confidence is justified or not is open to some question. 

1. Walk-in Assistance 

In 1972 the Wall Street Journal submitted the same tax case 13/ to IRS offices in five cities across the country, and the Washington 14/ Star News sampled three IRS offices in the D.C. area. 

In 1973 the New 15/ York Post surveyed eight IRS offices in New York City, and in 1974 the Tax Reform Research Group submitted the same case to four IRS offices in Michigan, three in Colorado, three in Oregon, four in New Jersey, three 16/ 

Each survey in New York, four in Washington, D.C. and two in Indiana." found that results varied widely on the same tax facts. 

Although in no instance was the tax case extremely complicated, each survey case contained items that might classify it as more complex than the average 1040 return. For example, the Wall Street Journal case involved moving expenses and pension income; the Star News case had stock dividends and expenses for an office at home; the New York Post case contained home office expenses, as well as income from a divorced husband and child care expenses; and the Tax Reform Research Group had home office expenses, plus political contributions and unreimbursed employee expenses. 

Each survey disclosed a significant amount of error by 

IRS "assistors."

In most instances errors of substance were made in

1 areas where the law is most complex or acceptable treatment most uncertain. 

Since complexity and uncertainty exist in computing office-at-home expenses, much of the disparity in each case related to this deduction. 

Another error-prone area was the treatment of payments to a former spouse when the payments were not specified as child support or alimony. Errors were also made in electing either the credit or the deduction for political contributions and on deductions for child-care expenses. 

The surveys also disclosed some amount of procedural error. 

Some IRS assistors used the wrong income figure or tax table. In the Tax 

Reform survey two IRS offices substantially increased the tax liability by advising the use of the standard deduction. 

In terms of the kind of service given, few complaints were voiced in these surveys. In the 1974 survey waiting times were generally short, although the contrary was true in the earlier surveys. Several shoppers reported "sharing the expert" with other taxpayers, or that IRS employees refused to give substantive assistance and merely handed the inquirer the forms and publications. A more common occurrence was when the IRS assistors refused to sign the return they had prepared or had told the taxpayer what to put in each space. It also appears that about half of the assistors used reference materials, and less than half had calculators available. Finally, nearly all shoppers reported that they received friendly and courteous assistance. 2. 

Math Errors 

IRS Prepared Returns

Each Service Center tabulates the mathematical errors made on IRS-prepared and stamped returns. For the 1974 filing season the error rate reported by Service Centers was 2.8 percent on 580,000 IRS-prepared returns. 

The error rate in the seven regions ranged from a low of 2 percent in two regions, to a middle range of 3 percent in four regions, and to a high of

5 percent in one region.

The error rates varied tremendously from one week 17/ to the next, ranging from 1 percent to 7.3 percent over the season.

3. Telephone Assistance Surveys 

There have been few shopping surveys of telephone assistance.

Centiphone assistance. 

18/ Knight Newspapers conducted a limited survey in 1974 to test the level of Included in this test were six calls to a number of district offices in the Northeast. Six to eight questions were asked each assistor. According to the reporter, the questions ranged from "simple to fairly tricky." While one officer got them all correct and another got seven out of eight, overall, one-third of the answers were incorrect. Several times Service employees would ask the caller to wait while they conferred with a supervisor, and in these instances the answers were uniformly correct.

The IRS national office conducted its own survey of Centiphone 

Responsibility for sample testing assistance during the 1974 filing season. has since been delegated to the districts and will include year-round sampling. 

The 1974 survey was conducted over a period of 11 weeks. It contained both administrative and technical questions which were designed to become progressively more difficult, and totaled 920 calls. The table on the next page 20/ summarizes the results.

The lack of uniformity in performance is somewhat surprising. 

In our view none of the questions was difficult or complex, although a few would probably be uncommon. 21/ Only one question was addressed to the areas of common difficulty discovered in walk-in shopping surveys. Uneven but poor performance overall was registered in the area of probing adequately for additional facts. Few referrals and no call-backs were made in spite of an error rate as high as 40 percent in the first week and generally ranging from 10 to 30 percent. 19/

In addition to the national office survey, tests of telephone assistors' responses were made by the IRS Internal Audit personnel and by district and regional office personnel. The error rate for the questions asked by
