4. 

TSR Qualifications and Training 

Given the significant number of errors, one may ask if better qualified and trained personnel would reduce the rate of error. A recent survey of TSR's found that 37 percent had been TSR's one year or less, and 23/ 45 percent were at a grade level of GS-5 or lower. As to qualifications, the Service has at least achieved a professional series for new TSR's. In view of the complexity of the law and its explanation, this upgrading appears needed.

TSR training has not been extensive, although it, too, has been recently revised and upgraded. While new materials are now being developed for both pre- and post-filing training, we reviewed the current basic

(pre-filing training) TSR coursebooks. Generally, we thought substantive tax law was adequately treated. Close review was accorded areas of the law that had proven difficult for TSR's in the shopping surveys; all were treated accurately and clearly with one major exception-the deduction for office-in-home expenses. 

The treatment given this item readily explains the confusion 24/ among TSR's on this issue. The explanation begins with a description of the various burden-of-proof tests required by the IRS and discusses several Tax Court decisions that have rejected the IRS' view, holding that only the "ordinary and necessary" guidelines apply. It concludes that 

TSR's must present the IRS position. Following this is a description of the three methods of allocation--square feet, number of rooms, and space and time. The only guidance given the TSR is that "whatever method is used, it must clearly reflect income," and further, "any method which is 25/ reasonable under the circumstances will be acceptable. 

It may be unrealistic to expect TSR's to provide taxpayers a "right" answer on such a question as the deduction for office-in-home expenses, where the law is uncertain and the Tax Court and IRS are in disagreement. Perhaps a better approach in such a case would simply be to provide the taxpayer with printed material rather than personalized advice on the subject. At the least, a TSR should advise the taxpayer that the law is uncertain and that if the sum involved is sufficient he may find it worthwhile to seek professional assistance. 

One may not conclude that the TSR's problems are solely or even primarily ascribable to deficiencies in training materials. Errors, or at least differences, were found in shopping surveys even when training documents were accurate. Such errors may reflect lack of qualifications, lack of time spent in training, complexity in the law, lack of diligence

by the TSR, the presence of excessive workloads, or other problems. 

The disturbing factor is not that differences arise, but that not enough has been done by the Service to sample quality. Although the 

Manual directs district offices to do walk-in shopping surveys of their own offices, none of these results were made available to us and they are not available in the national office. Neither has the Service analyzed the data from Taxpayer Compliance Measurement Program (TCMP) audits for the purpose of sampling the quality of preparation of returns, whether prepared by the Service or by others. 

One way of dealing with the problem of incorrect responses to telephone inquiries, which would also provide a mechanism for reviewing quality in general, is the monitoring of calls by supervisory personnel. 

Centiphone offers this capability, but monitoring has not been uniformly used. At present it is a matter of local choice, although the 1975 program objectives list weekly monitoring as part of the district plan. 

The Manual also directs the use of sample telephone calls to test the quality of assistance and emphasizes quality review on a year-round basis. 

A recent review by the General Accounting Office of IRS' Centiphone monitoring program during the 1974 filing season concluded that district monitoring efforts were inadequate in coverage, were concentrated in the last six weeks in the filing period, and in two districts gave insufficient attention to the accuracy of the assistors' responses. also concluded that the program made inadequate provision for identifying and reporting deficiencies to agency management. 27/ GAO 26/ Compounding the problem of inadequate training is the enormous staffing crisis the Service faces during the filing season when demand

for services reaches a peak. To meet the increased workload, the Service has customarily tapped employees and former employees with varying levels of skills and experience and given them a little refresher training. 

Collection personnel, because of their orientation, have demonstrated too little sympathy for taxpayer problems and have had scant training in substantive law. As a result it would be preferable that they not be used at all in such sensitive taxpayer dealings. Audit personnel, on the other hand, represent a valuable asset in taxpayer services because they are among the most highly skilled and experienced personnel in the Service. 

However, as a matter of course they are not as likely as TSR's to advise the taxpayer in areas where substantial legal conflicts arise. 

The quality of taxpayer service would be upgraded significantly if there were a standard procedure for funnelling complicated questions to more experienced technicians. To achieve this desired improvement, expansion of the TSR workforce during the filing season should include as many personnel from the ranks of its most experienced and knowledgeable employees as possible.

The heavy use of the telephone in providing assistance to taxpayers, particularly those with complicated inquiries, raises questions about the quality of advice that can be given without visual aids or personal contact.

Another handicap to providing high grade and efficient service is the lack of an adequate number of adding machines and calculators. 

Surely, this deficiency could be easily remedied at small cost in the interest of assuring mathematical accuracy and conserving time. 

D. Risk of Error 

Although IRS advice, whether given over the telephone or face-to-face, frequently proves inaccurate, IRS has consistently refused to accept responsibility for errors in returns made in reliance on such advice or

even in returns prepared by its employees. If IRS advice is incorrect the taxpayer is held responsible and must pay any deficiency, interest or penalty assessed (although the penalty may be excused for reasonable cause). While this policy has been subjected to criticism, we believe that it is appropriate under the circumstances. 

First, communication between the taxpayer and the TSR may be difficult. A taxpayer may inadvertently omit or misstate facts, and the 

TSR may fail to discover such omissions or mistakes. Further, even if the facts are fully related, the TSR may unwittingly fail to assimilate them. As a consequence, there is a possibility that the advice is given on an incomplete or incorrect statement of facts. The ascertainment of accuracy of facts in all cases would probably be so burdensome that the entire system of advice-giving would collapse if complete assurance of accuracy were required. 

Second, since incorrect advice nearly always relates to completed transactions, the taxpayer may feel aggrieved when he subsequently learns that he must pay a deficiency, but he is not significantly worse off than if he had paid the correct tax in the first place (if we assume that IRS accepts his excuse as reasonable cause for not imposing a penalty). 

The general rule that the Government is not bound by the incorrect advice of its agents has been applied in far harsher circumstances than are present 28/ here.

Although the Service's position on incorrect advice is proper, the Service should make greater efforts to minimize undue reliance on the advice it gives. To this end, the Internal Revenue Service should adopt procedures designed to assure that any taxpayer who inquires for tax law advice from any employee of the IRS Taxpayer Service Division will be

informed that: (1) the answer to his inquiry is based on the facts understood by the employee and that such understanding may not be identical to, nor as comprehensive as, the taxpayer's; (2) the Service is not bound by the advice given by the employee and may assert a different position at some later date, for example, if the taxpayer's return is audited; (3) the advice given by the employee is based on the Service's interpretation of the tax laws and, if such be the case with respect to a particular inquiry, that there is authority for a different interpretation as to which the taxpayer should seek his own tax law advice; and (4) the taxpayer should preserve any records pertaining to the subject matter of the inquiry for at least three years following the time fixed by law for filing the tax return to which the inquiry pertains. 

The substance of the foregoing information should be incorporated in all writtn materials issued by the Service describing the availability of taxpayer services.

II.

TAXPAYER COMPLAINTS 

A. Background of the Problem. year.

About 80 million individual income tax returns were filed last 29/ To receive and process these returns and otherwise administer the law pursuant to which they are filed, the Internal Revenue Service 30/ Even in the best of possible worlds employes nearly 80,000 persons. the processing and settlement of 80,000,000 accounts would not be an easy task. But the tax world is not the best. Its substantive rules are complex, and the procedures governing the dealings between the agency and the taxpayer are little understood by the latter. Finally, the natural reluctance to pay taxes decrees from the outset that the relationship between agency and taxpayer will be an adversary one. There is little wonder, then, that taxpayers and Service employees often misunderstand each other and find their contact abrasive. This situation is exacerbated by the fact that the taxpayer's financial well-being may be imperiled. 

When one adds to these problems the public distrust of government in general and the immense discretion reposed in many Service employees, the potential for charge and countercharge is so great that some conflicts will undoubtedly occur. 

Some of these disputes involve only substantive and procedural issues affecting tax liability. But others, while aggravated by the financial aspect of the controversy, arise largely from a real or perceived lack of response or a real or perceived over-reaction to the situation by one of the parties. These conflicts may occasionally reach the courts, but more often do not. Because litigation costs will be prohibitive, the results may be meaningless, or for other reasons, taxpayers rarely sue the Internal Revenue Service concerning perceived procedural injustices. 

Furthermore, those dissuaded from judicial recourse but sufficiently

aroused to pursue the matter administratively often look in vain for an effective mechanism for processing their complaint. 

There are numerous complaints. There has been an outpouring of "horror" stories describing strained relations between the Internal Revenue Service and taxpayers. The media has reported on breaches of 31/ confidentiality of taxpayers' returns and the establishment of "stress 32/ seminars" to test a tax agent's resistance to liquor and sex. Members of Congress and public interest groups report incidents of double collection of tax and of threats of arbitrary assessments. 

In addition to these more visible cases, during the course of this study we received, directly from taxpayers, numerous complaints which cut across the entire breadth of the administrative process. They include objection to having an additional assessment on a tax return prepared by Service personnel; anger at a computer which spews out billings when a refund is due and expected; frustration when a seizure of a taxpayer's assets is being pursued without acknowledgment of the fact that the tax delinquency has been paid; and many other complaints over real or imagined injustices.

Of course, complaint alone does not establish the legitimacy of a grievance. Some complaints arise simply out of a misunderstanding of communications received from the Service; many result from a lack of knowledge of the substantive tax law provisions, and, of course, there are always those taxpayers who try to "beat the system." 

Without considerably greater resources and removal of legal impediments, we could not investigate these complaints in order to establish their validity. Nevertheless, we replied to all correspondents, had further correspondence with many, held extensive telephone conversations with others, and met with a few taxpayers or their representatives. We were also

informed of innumerable similar reports in the files of Congress and of public interest groups. 

Based on these contacts, we concluded that there were a considerable number of taxpayers who had perceived complaints against our revenueraising organization and were willing to inform us of them. Those who contacted us obviously constitute a statistically insignificant part of the taxpaying population. Furthermore, some complaints seemed to lack merit. We were, however, impressed with the distress and frustration, sincerely expressed, resulting from contact with an agency that many believed was not well attuned to their concerns. Many considered the 

Service an impenetrable monolithic organization which either responded defensively and abrasively or, more likely, not at all. Let us hasten to add that we also received same letters commending the Service and its discharge of its responsibilities. While we believe that the overwhelming majority of taxpayers fall somewhere between these two extremes, the issue of taxpayer complaints could not be ignored. Thus, as the study progressed, it became increasingly evident that in dealing with the problem of taxpayer relations it was important that the Service respond to taxpayer perceptions about the Service, even if those perceptions had little to validate them. 

There is little need to reiterate all that has been written with regard to the importance, in a democratic society, of a responsive government sensitive to the needs of its people. The government is strong when it has the confidence and support of its citizens. It can earn this support only when it provides recourse to the wronged and consideration for the distressed, even if not wronged. It is particularly in this process of raising revenue that the reasons for responsiveness are most compelling.

In its "Statement of Organization and Functions" published in the 

Federal Register of October 5, 1972 (37 F.R. 209601), the Internal Revenue Service describes its mission as follows: 

"The mission of the Service is to encourage and achieve the highest possible degree of voluntary compliance with the tax laws and regulations and to maintain the highest degree of public confidence in the integrity and efficiency of the Service. This includes communicating the requirements of the law to the public, determining the extent of compliance and causes of non-compliance, and doing all things needful to a proper enforcement of the law.' Since collection of the income tax depends on self-assessment by taxpayers, it is imperative that such persons believe the agency will perform its mission with some degree of fairness. We have seen the effect on tax collections in those foreign countries where public confidence has not been maintained. reluctance people have toward the payment of taxes by refusing to respond to those who find themselves in distress, real or only perceived. 

There is no need to intensify the natural As Mr. Justice Stewart noted in his remarks at the dedication of the new Courthouse of the United States Tax Court on November 22, 1974: "Federal tax law is complex, but there is surely no body of federal law that so immediately and so directly impinges upon the lives of so many American citizens. 

There is no branch of federal law of which so many Americans are so acutely and sometimes so painfully aware. There is certainly no area of federal law where expert and even handed administration is more vitally important." "We in the United States are proud of a federal tax system that largely depends upon voluntary self-assessment and self-administration. But that system could not begin to work unless there existed in the background a judicial system which had earned the confidence of the people for its fairness, its incorruptibility, and its competence."33/ 

Why, we might ask, put all the pressure on the judiciary? If the goal is the highest degree of compliance on the part of taxpayers,

the confidence and cooperativeness should be encouraged to the greatest extent by the tax collecting agency itself. 

Failure to provide recourse to the aggrieved and a responsive ear to those who experience despair and frustration in their dealings with the revenue raising process will only intensify the "turned-off" feeling noticeable in many parts of our society. Indeed, the Commissioner has acknowledged publicly that maintaining public confidence in the Internal 34/ 

Revenue Service was his "No. 1" task.

Acknowledging the desirability of maintaining taxpayer relations at the best possible level, both to preserve the integrity of the fisc and to preserve the dignity of the persons who provide it, we concluded that the Service should provide some kind of a response mechanism. 

We have, therefore, described the present system, or possibly non-system, and suggested a device which would provide the necessary response. 

Complaints Concerning the Tax Result. 

There is a category of complaints about which the Internal Revenue Service can do little more than it now does. Those complaints are directed at the complexity or alleged unfairness of the tax statute. Such complaints include dissatisfaction with the results of an audit, with a request for ruling, or with a request for a determination letter. The Service has provided mechanisms for the resolution of this kind of problem to the extent that it can resolve them. Thus, audit results may be appealed, and there are administrative and judicial procedures for deciding matters which deal with tax liability or interpretations of statute, regulations, rulings, and other announcements affecting a question of tax liability or of tax planning. While one may not always agree with the Service's position on these matters, there are remedies. In another part of this report we have

also suggested that taxpayers be provided assistance in pursuing at least some of these matters. The complaints for which a grievance procedure would be designed are not of this kind. 

C. Other Taxpayer Complaints. 

We move now to the second general category of complaint. For want of a better title we shall call these "taxpayer complaints." Our concern is with complaints arising from the Internal Revenue Service's conduct of its operations, that is to say, difficulties which taxpayers experience with IRS's practices, procedures, and personnel. For example, a notice of tax due may be misunderstood; a taxpayer may have received an unsatisfactory explanation of a communication; a tax may have been twice collected; a jeopardy assessment may have been threatened when no grounds therefor existed; a form may not be clear to a taxpayer; the right to appeal may not have been explained; a notice of tax due may not have been received; conflicting notices may have been received; account adjustments may not have reached a collection officer in time to prevent this action; a payment on an installment agreement may not have been properly posted to the account; the taxpayer may not understand collection procedures; the taxpayer may need assistance in preparing financial information; the taxpayer may believe that a levy will result in undue hardship; a taxpayer may believe an audit has been prolonged; or other circumstances may have resulted in the taxpayer thinking that the administrative processes, practices, or procedures have been improperly invoked. 

In these and other situations, the taxpayer may first appeal to Taxpayer Services for assistance. In many cases the matter will be resolved by Taxpayer Services. In some cases, particularly complaints 2191dem

regarding abusive personnel, the taxpayer may talk with appropriate supervisory personnel and resolve the issue. However, in some cases, the taxpayer will not be satisfied with the result reached by the first contact with the Service. In those circumstances, the taxpayer should be referred to the complaint specialist for further assistance and to log a complaint. 

1. Present System.

At present, an inquiring taxpayer will find no formal complaint process, though a fairly well-defined informal method for handling complaints has developed. Depending upon the subject matter, a complaint will generally be handled by the Audit, Collection, or Taxpayer Services Division. However, the Inspection Office will investigate any complaint that alleges "improper conduct and irregularities on the part of Service 35/ officials and employees. In the following sections we examine the entry of a complaint into the system and the response it will generate. 

Collection and Audit Divisions. a.

Since the Audit and Collection Divisions handle complaints in a similar manner, they will be discussed together. In theory, all complaints that relate to an audit are handled by the Audit Division and frequently include, among other grievances, complaints about the time and expense of an audit, repeated audits, and harassment by auditors. The 

Collection Division ordinarily handles only those complaints that concern 36/ delinquent accounts. They usually arise from a Collection officer's use of summary procedures, such as levy and seizure. A response to a taxpayer complaint involving both collection and audit issues will be handled by the division with which the major issues pertain, though secondary issues involving other divisions will be referred to those divisions

for guidance.

There are primarily two places where written taxpayer complaints enter the system, the national office and the district office. Complaints to third parties, for example, Congress, usually are referred to the national office but may on occasion be sent to the district office. Oral complaints are normally directed to the employee involved or his supervisor, and thus enter at the district office. 

(1) National Office. 

Taxpayer complaints sent to the national office are referred to the division to which the complaint pertains. Collection complaints go to the Operations Branch of the Collection Division. Audit complaints go to the Audit Division. Nearly all complaints are then sent to the appropriate district office for investigation. The district officer to whom the complaint is assigned will either respond to the complaint or report the results of his investigation to the national office in accordance with its instructions. The Internal Revenue Manual lists three types of situations where the national office should answer the complaint. 

These situations are: (1) The complaint or inquiry deals with a matter over which the district and regional offices have no control. (2) The reply is to be signed by the Commissioner or other national office official. (3) There is reason to believe that nothing short of a reply by the national office will satisfy the writer that his complaint has received proper attention. Many of the letters addressed to the President on internal revenue 37/ problems fall into this category.

A taxpayer who writes his Congressman or the President receives "preferential" treatment in the sense that the national office will usually respond to the complaint. Such a reply may be more speedily obtained, but it is doubtful that the result will be any different. 

Where the taxpayer charges that the district office has not responded to a complaint, the national office will refer a complaint to the 38/ appropriate regional office. The Regional Commissioner then decides whether to answer the complaint or to pass it back to the district office. 

The Manual warns that "taxpayers with valid complaints have reason to question the Service's integrity if their letters ultimately end up for reply with the very officials about whose actions they have complained. (2) 

District Office. 

(a) District Director.

A District Director may receive a complaint 39/ 40/ from the national office, regional office, through channels from below, or directly from the taxpayer. The manner in which the District Director will proceed is left to local practices of each office. Normally, the 

District Director will sign any responses to the taxpayer when the complaint is received by referral from the national office or when the complaint is addressed to him.

Seemingly because a group supervisor has easy access to his subordinates, a complaint requiring investigation will be sent to the supervisor of the allegedly offending employee. The division or branch chief might intercept the complaint and handle it if he desires. 

There is no established procedure to ascertain whether the complaint is valid or to fix responsibility for response to the taxpayer. Apparently, the more complex complaints are considered by the higher officials. event, the response procedure may be ad hoc, and both the procedure and 

In any substance of the response may result from a group discussion by the supervisor,

the branch chief, and perhaps the chief of the division.

(b) 

The Examining and Collection Officers. 

Most complaints entering the national office are in letter form. In contrast, most complaints entering at the bottom of If the the system are direct oral complaints against line personnel. taxpayer and the line personnel reach an impasse, the taxpayer is to be 41/ notified of his right to talk with the supervisor. Among the officers whom we interviewed none expressed any hesitancy in referring complaints to his supervisor. Normally, the supervisor will attempt to mediate differences between the taxpayer and the officer. There is no established procedure for further action if the taxpayer remains unsatisfied. The supervisor apparently will write a memo to the file concerning the complaint. 

Although the branch chief has access to the file, the procedure for review of such files seems to differ from office to office. Perhaps if the complaint raises a complex question or levels a serious charge against the agent, the supervisor will pass it up to his branch chief. A taxpayer can insure further action only by writing the district office, national office, or his Congressman.

The entry point of the complaint seems to have little effect on the outcome. The nature and identity of the respondent may differ, but most complaints are eventually dismissed because the officer will be found to have acted with appropriate discretion. 

The prevailing attitude of most Service personnel seems to be that complaints are inconvenient, but that they are to be expected, given the difficult nature of the job, attitudes of a few taxpayers, and the necessity on occasion of using discretionary tools. Thus, while taxpayers' complaints are not desired, they are also not necessarily looked upon with alarm.

(3) 

The Use of Inspection. 

A complaint involving the integrity of the examining or Collection officer (i.e., alleged bribery, acceptance of gratuities, and the like) is viewed differently by the Service from the complaints arising 42/ from use of discretion described above. The District Director usually makes the decision to notify the Regional Inspector, and his decision is based on his general appraisal of the validity and seriousness of the charges made.

Inspection compiles a factual report without recommendation and submits it to the appropriate District Director for the disciplinary action he deems appropriate. Normally, the District Director gives the report to the chief of the employee's division who then decides whether the case warrants disciplinary action and, if so, what the action should be. 

The District Director has the power to disagree and change the decision. 

b. Taxpayer Services Division. 

The Taxpayer Services Division usually handles a quite different kind of complaint. These complaints are ordinarily made in person or by telephone. They are generally not directed against identified Service personnel. Rather, such complaints generally involve systemic dysfunctions relating to some written communication which has or should have come from the Service. These include, for example, complaints over unexplained or erroneous bills, non-receipt of a refund, or an unintelligible notice of some sort. In responding to these complaints, the Taxpayer Service Representative has the power to freeze individual taxpayer accounts thus stopping further bills and notices until the taxpayer's inquiry has been acted upon, initiate payment tracers, and initiate 43/ account adjustment actions.

Under earlier procedures, complaints to be handled by Taxpayer Services which entered at the national office were routinely referred

44/ Today, however, most to the proper Service Center for response. routine complaints are referred to the district offices, while only the 45/ most complex and difficult complaints are sent to the Service Centers. 

However, perhaps the major difference in the "complaint system" between Taxpayer Services and Audit or Collection is in the attitude of the division to the complaint. Audit and Collection activities are adversary, and complaints arise in that context. This adversariness is usually absent in public contacts with personnel of the Taxpayer Services Division. Generally, the complaint is not personalized, but is more directed against the "system." Also, the responsibility of a TSR is to assist taxpayers, rather than to audit or to collect from them. These differences result in an atmosphere conducive to resolution of taxpayers' complaints.

C. Inspection.

The Office of Assistant Commissioner (Inspection) is the investigative arm for internal matters of the Service. One type of charge it investigates is that arising from "improper conduct and ir- 46/ The regularities on the part of Service officials and employees. authority of Inspection is limited to fact-finding on which it reports without recommendation to the officials responsible for taking appropriate action. 

In theory, Inspection is available to receive complaints from the public or Congress as well as referrals from Service personnel. However, even most sophisticated tax practitioners are wholly unaware of Inspection, and the public and Congress are even less aware. There is no Service publication that directs taxpayers to take their complaints to Inspection. 

Thus, in practice, nearly all investigations by Inspection arise from referrals from Service personnel. Routine cases are not referred to

Inspection, but integrity matters may be. 

Inspection will initiate a conduct investigation if: (1) the charge against the employee is specific; (2) the complaint is derived from a reliable source; (3) the employee is named; and (4) a violation of a law or a written behavioral rule is involved. If one or more of these factors is absent, but Inspection nevertheless thinks that the facts warrant an investigation, then an investigation will be commenced and classified 47/ as a special inquiry complaint.

An employee will always know of a conduct investigation but will not be told of a special inquiry investigation. He may, however, learn of the latter, and in some cases, the latter may become a conduct case. 

During the investigation of a conduct case, the employee is permitted to present his side of the story. Inspection then reports the facts of its investigation to the chief of the employee's operating division, who will determine whether discipline is called for and, if so, its severity. If the offense is criminal in nature, administrative discipline usually must await judicial resolution. If the chief of the employee's operating division finds that the employee is without blame or fault, then the employee will reveive a letter of clearance from his chief. Letters of clearance are not required if the employee subject to a special inquiry complaint is found without blame and has no knowledge that the investigation has taken 48/ place.

In 1974 personnel investigations resulted in 1,479 disciplinary actions. This figure comprises 331 separations, 115 suspensions from duty and pay, and 1,033 reprimands, warnings, or demotions. IRS figures do not break down these 1479 cases by source of the complaint, but Inspection has supplied such a breakdown for the 1367 conduct cases closed

in Fiscal 1974: 

During FY 74 Inspection closed 1,367 conduct cases of which 62% (849) resulted in disciplinary actions.

Of these 849 disciplinary cases, 26% (217) were based upon information received from sources outside the Service. While only four of these cases were reported directly by a taxpayer, 156 came from Federal sources including Congress, 19 from private citizens or organizations and 14 from anonymous informants. Obviously most of these sources were forwarding information which orginated from some kind of taxpayer complaint even though such complaints were not sent directly to the Service. 

Of the remaining 74% disciplinary cases during FY 74 (which were based upon information Inspection received from sources within the Service), 42% (355) came from IRS officials and employees. Again it would seem obvious that a significant number of these cases probably stemmed from some type of taxpayer complaint. 49/ While Inspection estimates that a significant proportion of its disciplinary cases were triggered by taxpayer complaints, it is hard to see anything "obvious" in this conclusion on the basis of the figures cited. 

What is clear is that very few cases resulted from direct communication between the taxpayer and Inspection. At any rate, it is simply not possible to tell from the figures at hand how many cases involving misconduct or abuse in relations with taxpayers are investigated by Inspection. 

2. Proposed System. 

The Internal Revenue Service is a vast agency, vested with great power, peopled with persons of different temperments and varying degrees of skill, attempting to administer a vitally important function within a highly complex substantive framework. However, the present system of handling non-substantive individual complaints is quite limited in scope and so ad hoc as to be not a system at all. The consequence is that taxpayers who are caught up with a problem have few places to go for assistance. 

In our judgment there is need for an organizational structure with the

function of receiving, evaluating, and responding to taxpayer complaints. 

The Service's duties might be more easily discharged, and both its image and public awareness of its problems would likely be enhanced by a responsive taxpayer complaint-handling device. We believe that a procedure can be created which will fit within the existing system and will not adversely affect the basic responsibility of the Service for collecting the revenue.

The collection responsibility is indeed a most crucial one and the Service's effectiveness in this role must not be undermined. Enough has been said about the impact on the rest of the citizenry of lost revenues from any source. Consequently, it is important that any device chosen not be one which lends itself to use by taxpayers in "beating the system." 

On the other hand, it is difficult to see how the effective collection of taxes can be undermined, indeed, how it cannot be enhanced by the presence of competent and understanding persons available to correct misunderstandings and unreasonable attitudes or to help avoid hardship. 

In the evaluation of a mechanism for the handling of taxpayer com- 50/ plaints, knowledgeable observers have asserted that the following characteristics are essential for effectiveness: (1) Independence (2) Expert within its sphere of competence (3) Widely available (4) Highly visible (5) Client-centered (6) Capability for developing general recommendations for the improvement of complaint-producing situations. 11 In keeping with the desired characteristics of competency in the subject

matter and the ability to affect policy for the improvement of complaintproducing situations, the proposed mechanism should be created within the structure of the Internal Revenue Service. We believe this can be accomplished without the sacrifice of an inordinate degree of independence, and this would avoid the greater proliferation of agency upon agency. 

In spite of some of its present deficiencies for the task, the Taxpayer Services Division appears to be the most appropriate unit within the Internal Revenue Service to undertake the function of handling taxpayer complaints. It has the greatest face-to-face contact with taxpayers and currently serves taxpayers in connection with matters which require personal assistance, such as in the preparation of returns and the correction of computer errors. Moreover, it is engaged in public information activities which are deemed essential for the publicity required by a complaint-handling mechanism. a. 

Elements of the New Structure. 

Whether the complaint resolution responsibility is placed in Taxpayer Services or in some other organizational unit, this responsibility should be exercised in accordance with the following principles. First, the line of bureaucratic responsibility must be one which permits the degree of independence that complaint personnel should have. Experience suggests that such personnel might not be able to perform effectively if they must report to the persons responsible for the action producing the complaint. There is no question but that the position of the complaint specialist (for want of a better term) would be a delicate one. Delicate in that often a response will be required to what is simply arbitrary and injudicious behavior on the part of a fellow employee. 

Delicate also in that the complaint specialist will have to distinguish between those complaints honestly motivated and those which will represent

an attempt at procrastination or disruption of the normal Service functions. Nevertheless, in order to be effective, the complaint specialist must be clothed with sufficient responsibility, authority, and independence to get to the heart of the matter and deal with it. 

Second, those entrusted with the complaint handling responsibility must be thoroughly familiar with the authority, organization and procedures of the Service. It is quite often the unusual matter which prompts a taxpayer complaint and, hence, would require a person with greater knowledge of the law and the procedural workings of the Service to cope adequately with the problem. Therefore, complaint specialists should be highly-trained, full-time professionals who would be fully knowledgeable and highly motivated to respond to the needs of the individual taxpayer who feels aggrieved. Preferably such persons would also have had considerable experience at the service centers and understand thoroughly the processing of returns, refunds, adjustments, and other items. They should also have familiarity with the Taxpayer Contact Units at service centers. Experience answering taxpayer inquiries in local officers would also be desirable. 

Third, the complaint response procedure should be designed and operated so as to provide adequate information to line management regarding the causes of complaints as well as the means of correction. 

It should also be designed to assure prompt response to the complaining taxpayer, so that he knows that his complaint has been acted on and what was its dispostion. 

One criticism of the present handling of complaints is that no official log is made of type and disposition. Management thus does not have the data necessary to take appropriate action as to the cause of problems. 

Further, the taxpayer has no evidence of the fact that his complaint has

been acted upon or of its disposition. Hence, every complaint referral to the specialist should be put in written form, signed by the taxpayer where appropriate, and logged with the disposition, for distribution to all 51/ interested parties. Telephone complainants should be sent appropriate forms to be completed, along with return envelopes, and the initial telephone contact should be logged and kept with the file when the written form was returned. 

Further, not only should the fact of a complaint and its disposition be logged, but also the promptness of the Service's response to the taxpayer should be recorded. If a matter is permitted to drag on, the taxpayer will think that the mechanism is nothing more than a placebo and a whitewash. He will, then think himself doubly aggrieved. Hence, every complaint should be included in a tickler system which would cause it to be reviewed after a definite time period at which time the complaint specialist should respond to the taxpayer on the progress of the investigation, if not the final resolution of the problem. If more information was required, the complaint specialist should ask the taxpayer to supply it. perhaps two weeks 

Finally, to be effective a complaint procedure must be highly visible. 

Complaint specialists should be physically located in Service offices and identified so that taxpayers are made easily aware of their presence. 

Information about the complaint process might appropriately be included in audit and collection notices and in the tax return packets mailed annually to taxpayers. Posters placed in local offices should explain the availability of complaint services. A taxpayer who makes a complaint should be given a written notice of the name of the specialist handling his case and where he can be reached. The notice should explain how the

investigation will be conducted and what actions may result. Also the fact that the specialist is not responsible to line management should be made clear.

D. 

Conclusion. 

In spite of the "horror stories" recounted, with the exception of a few aberrational incidents taxpayer complaints do not arise from a conscious or deliberate desire by the Service or its personnel to abuse their powers. Indeed, there is evidence that the Service is concerned with its relations with taxpayers and does take corrective measures within the context of its primary role of collecting revenues. In addition to task force studies intended to eliminate some of the problems mentioned, it has implemented some noteworthy responses. To mention a few, offices are now open on weekends and in the evenings during the filing season, special efforts are being made to assist the poor and elderly in tax 52/ matters, and a collection manual has been published in Spanish. 

Perhaps the major problem stems from the inherent nature of bureaucracy and its seeming inability to respond quickly to changing needs. This image perhaps could be improved by prompt institution of complaint procedures without prolonged deliberations over the need for such a system.
