CHAPTER CONFIDENTIALITY OF TAX RETURNS I. INTRODUCTION 

An individual income tax return may contain an immense amount of information about its filer. By the time he answers the first seven questions on the form, the taxpayer has identified himself and his address, social security number, marital status, and children or other dependents. By responding to the next eight questions, he exposes his entire gross income for the year, at least in summary form. Before he has completed the first half of the first page of Form 1040, he has revealed the skeletal outline of his personal and financial life. 

The more attachments he affixes, the more vulnerable he becomes. There is likely to be a W-2 form, through which others may discover vital facts about his employment. By reviewing Schedule A to Form 1040, a reader may learn whether the taxpayer or his family are under medical and psychiatric care. It also may reveal the filer's religious affiliation, the objects and degree of his eleemosynary inclinations, the sources of his borrowed money, his union membership, his political leanings, and many other facets of his personal and private life. 

A close reading of Schedule B in conjunction with proper financial publications may reveal an entire investment portfolio 

not just its general content, but the taxpayer's precise holdings. 

All of this information, and much more, may be necessary for a true and accurate tax return. The Service is empowered to require that any information relevant to the computation of taxable income be in- (827)

cluded on the return, and it does so. But whatever the nature of the information, failure to tender a proper return may result in a criminal fine and imprisonment and, if any tax is due, possibly civil money penalties. 

Furthermore, if any of his reporting is knowingly inaccurate, the tax- payer may also be prosecuted and imprisoned even though the inaccuracy may have had no effect on tax liability. This financial and highly personal information thus is collected, collated, and dispatched to the Internal Revenue Service on pain of substantial criminal and civil penalties. In many cases, the information would never be assembled were it not necessary to compute a Federal tax on income. The return on which the information appears is then delivered to an agency which has no congressional mandate, with respect to income taxes, other than the collection of revenue based on the information in the return. When putting income tax data in the Service's hands, the taxpayer probably has no thought about other uses of the information. 

One may hazard the guess that, if asked, a taxpayer would request that this information not be available to the public. His return may contain much that could be the source of neighborhood gossip and that could prove embarrassing to the taxpayer or others. There is also considerable information beneficial to commercial interests such as loan companies, life insurers, mailing list brokers, and many others. 

A political opponent might seize on a small segment of the return to embarrass and humiliate in the wider public arena. None of these uses has a particular benefit to the public. Many would represent substantial invasions into private lives. It is likely that there exists a

consensus that such information should not be made public, yet, the statute defines tax returns as public records. Further, the President could apparently open returns to public inspection and examination by an executive order. No President has done so, however. 

Since such information has not been generally available to the public, taxpayers seem to have assumed that tax returns are confidential documents. Indeed, public officials consistently refer to them as if they were locked away in the Internal Revenue Service's vaults. 

But, since the 1920's, this mythology has been less and less true. 

Around 1920, government officials discovered that the tax return contained considerable information. While not containing a complete personal profile even reflective of economic income, tax returns are (aside from the decennial census) perhaps the single best and most available source of information about our population in general and individuals in particular. Upon realizing this, government officials sought ways to inspect this material. The loosely drawn statute permitted such access merely by concurrence of the President and the Secretary of Treasury. The history hereinafter recounted is one of increasing availability to governmental agencies. Given the, prevalence of the belief that tax returns are confidential, distribution to governmental agencies seems anomalous. Most likely, it has been permitted because it has occurred without any public debate. 

While there may be some public benefit to non-tax governmental use, there are also drawbacks. If there is concern about using compelled

testimony for criminal investigation and prosecution, must not there be indignance at the thought that one must reveal certain information on a tax return or go to prison? Yet, revealing such information may itself result in imprisonment. 

While data should be available for program shaping and implementation, there are sources other than tax returns. Congress can, if it so desires, provide specifically for collecting of information for these purposes. Hence, there seems little reason to permit, almost sub silentio, access to information compiled for revenue purposes and which may, therefore, be inappropriate for other purposes. But even if the data are appropriate, the major justification offered for disclosure to other agencies is mere availability. 

However these considerations and others are answered, the most striking feature of present dissemination of tax information is the fact that it nearly all happens through regulations prepared only by the executive. Certainly where practice is based on unpublicized administrative decision that departs so significantly from commonly held belief, the practice is suspect. It cries out to be reexamined and thrust into the public arena.

There is another, somewhat separate, aspect to the tax return privacy question. There has been, during the last several years, evidence that unauthorized use of tax return data was being made, generally by White House personnel. The evidence relating to obtaining tax data through other than regular channels, surfacing

mainly during the proceedings relating to the impeachment of President 1/ Nixon, raises questions somewhat different from those raised by the plethora of regulations 2/ permitting access outside the Internal Revenue Service. Both, however, will be treated and discussed in this paper. 

Perhaps the largest user of tax return information for non- 3/ statistical purposes, the Department of Justice, systematically employs it in the investigation and development of criminal cases involving non-revenue offenses. A substantial portion of such data is simply "volunteered" to the Department of Justice by the Service, which views itself as having the duty to report the possible commission of nonrevenue related offense to a sister agency. Both Justice Department and 

United States Attorneys also frequently use both tax returns and tax information in preparation and litigation of civil cases to which the 

United States is a party.

Other Federal agencies, such as the Department of Commerce, receive "raw" tax data in the form of IRS computer tapes for use in a host of business and economic studies and analyses. The states, too, utilize Federal tax returns and tax return information in the administration of their revenue statutes. Committees of the Congress (not limited to those which write the tax laws) can, and do, frequently obtain tax return information. The White House, and other executive agencies, systematically receive so-called "tax check" reports on prospective appointees (and other persons) which contain information which is otherwise confidential.

The practice of using tax returns, and information obtained from tax returns, for non-revenue related purposes is a matter concerning which the public is only beginning to become aware. The notion that the tax return is a private and confidential document, used solely for tax administration, remains conventional wisdom. On the other hand, it is arguable that, in reality, tax return information is a generalized governmental asset. 

Perhaps, if the

While the prevailing opinion seems to be that tax return information should not be available for covert political purposes (as it allegedly was during the Nixon and Johnson presidencies), the extent, if any, to which such information should be available for legitimate and bona fide functions of the federal government is a question fraught with deep legal and philosophical issues. A strong case can be made "for the proposition that the tax return is an instrument for administering and enforcing 4/ the tax laws of the United States and nothing more. rules relating to the use of tax return information were being written on a clean slate, it would be feasible to limit the availability of such data to those charged with the responsibilities of tax administration. Certainly the opportunity for a successful invasion of the privacy of tax return information is increased when it escapes the grasp of the Internal Revenue Service. To same, however, certain non-revenue related uses of these data seem more meritorious than others. For example, some see little harm in the use by the Department of Commerce of computerized tax return information

1 to distill purely statistical data, but shudder at the thought of the Department of Justice "fishing" through individual tax returns to develop leads in non-tax criminal cases. On the contrary, others may consider it not only the right, but the duty, of the Justice Department to use all of the information which can be made available to it, including data obtained by a sister agency for another function, in its drive against organized crime. Considerations such as these raise complex and weighty policy questions. 

Legal issues abound also. For example, after the Watergate experience, many consider it highly important to place restrictions of same kind on the availability of tax return information to the President. 

Considering, however, the broad constitutional power which the President 5/ has over any officer of an Executive department, the viability of attempted restrictions on his access to data in the hands of Internal Revenue must be carefully examined. Moreover, the use of information obtained from tax returns, which taxpayers are required to file and prepare truthfully under penalty of law, must be balanced against the background of the Fifth Ammendment privilege against self-incrimination and restrictions upon the use of compelled information. 

This report endeavors to survey the subject of tax return confidentiality with primary emphasis on disclosures to establishments of the Federal government and to State tax officials. 

The discussion is limited to disclosures controlled by § 6103 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1954. Thus, we are confined primarily to information and returns of income tax, self-employment tax, estate and

gift taxes, interest equalization tax, manufacturer's excise tax and excises on certain facilities and services. 

This report will not relate to, nor discuss, those provisions of the law which govern the disclosure 6/ of IRS records other than those controlled by $ 6103.

14 

II. 

BACKGROUND OF CURRENT STATUTE 

A.

Legislative History of $ 6103 (a) 

1. Pre-1913 Developments. 

Quite surprisingly, the shape of the present tax return disclosure statute was cast long before the inception of the present income tax in 1913. 7/ The original income tax act (Act of Aug. 5, 1861, 12 Stat. 

292) was replaced before it went into effect by legislation which 

Congress enacted in 1862 (Act of July 1, 1862, 12 Stat. 432). The 

1862 legislation directed the assessors for each collection district to . .advertise all persons concerned of the time and place within said county when and where the lists, valuations, and enumerations made and taken within said county may be examined; and said lists shall remain open for examination for the space of fifteen days after notice shall have been given as aforesaid." (12 Stat. 432, 437).

Initially, at least, this provision was not interpreted as permitting open examination of tax information. Early in 1863, the Commissioner issued instruction that returns should be open only to Internal Revenue officials. 

The Secretary of the Treasury stated that this was done so that the income 8/ tax "might not be felt to be inquisitorial." However, the statute contained no prohibition of publicity (and, in fact, could be construed as requiring it). Newspapers strongly urged that they be allowed to print returns of 9/ income. The 1863 legislative recommendation of the Secretary of Treasury was to the contrary, requesting that the uncertainty surrounding the 1862 10/ legislation be removed by "express enactment" prohibiting disclosure.

Congress responded by making clear that disclosure was intended. 

The 1864 legislation provided that: "It shall be the duty of the assessor for each collection district, at the time fixed for hearing such appeal, as aforesaid, to submit the proceedings of the assessors and assistant assessors, and the annual lists taken and returned as aforesaid, to the inspection of any and all persons who may apply for that purpose. (Act of June 30, 1864, 13 Stat. 218, 228) (Emphasis Supplied). The same legislation, however, contained the progenitor of the present provisions imposing criminal penalties for the divulgence of confidential 11/ information by government employees. The 1864 legislation provided: "If any such official shall divulge to any party, or make known in any manner other than is provided in this Act, the operations, style of work, or apparatus of any manufacturer or producer visited by him in the discharge of his official duties, he shall be subject to the penalties prescribed in $ 36." (13 Stat. 218, 238).

In those more simple and naive days, the prohibition against revealing 11 "operation, style of work, or apparatus. . probably did not appear to include tax return information and thus was not contrary to the inspection required earlier in the statute. 

Not surprisingly, three weeks after enactment of the law, the Commissioner bowed to pressure and ordered that all "copies of all lists returned to the collector. .shall be open to the inspection of all persons who may apply to inspect the same.

12/ Being based on the statutory language previously quoted, this position was taken in the hope that "the amplest opportunity may be given for the detection of any fraudulent returns that may have been made." 13/

Subsequent editorial comment on the publicity of tax returns took some rather dramatic swings. On December 29, 1864, the New York 

Times lamented the lack of secrecy concerning tax returns, and contrasted it to the privacy shielding tax returns in England. "There ought to be a similar rule here" it noted, "and that there is not is another illustra- Ly tion of the hasty and slipshod way in which our system of taxation has 14/ been formed." a list of incomes.

The next day its editorial argued that: 

Then on January 30, 1865, the New York Tribune published "So long as an income tax shall be required and levied, we are satisfied that it About 18 months is best for all who are honestly concerned therein that there should be 15/ no restriction on giving publicity to the items. later, the New York Times converted to the Tribune's view and stated that 16/ only by making tax returns public could full tax returns be secured. 

The Times later opined that publicity prevented collusion between taxpayers and unfaithful collectors. An opposing note was struck by the 17/ Commercial and Financial Chronicle, which argued that publicity led to falsification of returns for purpose of ostentation and for securing credit. 

As the tax became more unpopular, the publicity feature of the law came in for more criticism. In July, 1869, the New York Times again reversed its field, noting that a properly organized revenue force could 19/ prevent evasion and thus obviate the nuisance of publicity. Shortly thereafter, it denounced the publicizing of returns as "offensive and 20/ objectionable. On April 5, 1870, a new Commissioner, Columbus Delano, 21/ forbade the assessors to furnish tax lists for publication. His decision was seconded by Congress when, the following July, legislation was passed 18/

halting the policy of making the tax lists public and explicitly prohibiting disclosure of returns. This legislation provided: .no collector, deputy collector, assessor or assistant assessor, shall permit to be published in any manner such income return, or any part thereof, except such general statistics, not specifying the names of individuals or firms, as he may make public, under such rules and regulations as the Commissioner of Internal Revenue shall pre scribe." (Act of July 14, 1870, 16 Stat. 256, 259). 22/

The income tax was itself abolished in 1872. 

There is one additional significant point that should be noted concerning the 1870 enactment.

While that legislation generally prevented disclosure, it was permitted, "under rules and regulations" prescribed by the Commissioner, for statistical uses in which the taxpayer was not identified. The allowance of same disclosure of tax returns pursuant to administrative order is, of course, a significant feature of present law.

In summary, the administrator initially opted to keep returns confidential. His later reversal of this policy, while not mandated by the 1864 legislation, certainly could be supported thereby. However, as the issues and implications became clearer, both the Commissioner and Congress cut down access to returns. By that time the invasion of privacy inherent in return publicity had became one of the central issues surrounding this early experiment with the income tax. The issue, of course, passed away when the tax did, but the furor surrounding publicity was one of the central causes of the early demise of the income tax as a reve- 23/ nue raising instrument.

With the re-enactment of an income tax in 1894, the publicity 24/ question was resurrected. 

This time Congress fashioned somewhat more 25/ elaborate anti-disclosure provisions. than it did in either 1864 or 1870. 

The prohibitions were that no Internal Revenue employee (a) divulge the operations, style of work, or similar confidential business data of any 26/ person visited by him in the discharge of his duties; (b) reveal the amount or source of income disclosed in any income tax return, or permit 27/ the return to be examined by any person "except as provided by law;

" 28/ or (c) print or publish an income tax return or part thereof. It also established penalties for violation of any of the above prohibitions. In 1895, the Supreme Court declared the tax unconstitutional in Pollock v.

29/ Farmers Loan and Trust Co.

, "and the cause of confidentiality received 30/ its ultimate victory, the burning of all tax returns."

It was not until the enactment of the Payne-Aldrich Tariff Act of 1909, which imposed a special excise tax on corporations, that the questions of return publicity was again introduced. Section 38 of that legislation dealt with the problem as follows: "Sixth. When the assessment shall be made, as provided in this section, the returns, together with any corrections thereof which may have been made by the Commissioner, shall be filed in the office of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue and shall constitute public records and be open to inspection as such. "Seventh. It shall be unlawful for any collector, deputy collector, agent, clerk, or other officer or employee of the United States to divulge or make known in any manner whatever not provided by law to any person any information obtained by him in the discharge of his official duty, or to divulge or make known in any manner not provided by law any

visions. document received, evidence taken, or report made under this section except upon the special direction of the President; and any offense against the foregoing provision shall be a misdemeanor and be punished by a fine not exceeding one thousand dollars, or by imprisonment not exceeding one year, or both, at the discretion of the court. (Emphasis Supplied.) 31/ The legislative history does little to illuminate these pro- 32/ Since, however, the Payne-Aldrich legislation did not provide any funds for the examination of returns filed pursuant to the Act, 33/ it became necessary (in 1910) to appropriate them. During the debate on the Appropriations Act of 1910, considerable light was shed upon the 34/ Congressional intention behind the 1909 legislation. (1) The prevailing opinion seems to have been that paragraph six of the 1909 legislation was intended to make tax returns "public records" 35/ open to everybody. It was believed by many that public inspection of corporate tax returns would be of great assistance in the supervision and control of corporate entities (of which there was considerable fear). (2) The contrary view, held by a minority, acknowledged that the 1909 legislation constituted tax returns as public documents. However, paragraph seven of the law made it a criminal offense for any government officer or employee to release material contained in these public documents without special instruction from the President. If, the argument proceeded, the public access granted by paragraph six had been entirely unfettered, paragraph seven would not have imposed criminal sanctions for divulging information without the President's consent. This illogical result was taken to mean that tax returns had not been opened to indiscriminate public 36/ 37/ inspection but only to persons having a proper interest in the returns.

(3) While there was thus disagreement over what was intended by the 1909 legislation, it was universally conceded that it altogether failed to open returns to the public. Some blamed this result on inadequate draftsmanship. Others thought the failure lay in lack of an appropriation to provide clerks to do the publicizing. (4) It was also agreed that paragraphs (6) and (7) of § 38 were inconsistent. Paragraph (6) seemed to provide that returns were fully public, but paragraph (7) imposed a penalty for the disclosure of any information obtained by a U.S. employee in the discharge of his duties. A majority concluded that another approach was necessary. An amendment to the provision in the 1910 Appropriations Act resulted. 

This legislation, which appropriated funds for the necessary classifying, indexing, and processing of corporate returns, also stated: "any and all such returns shall be open to inspection only upon the order of the President under rules and regulations to be prescribed by the Secretary of the Treasury and approved by the 

President.' 38/ 11 Debate surrounding the 1910 Act plainly indicates that Congress intended by the quoted provision to back away from the fully "public" treatment of 39/ corporate returns. Same Congressmen argued for full publicity and "against publicity only at the whim of the Administration" 41/ 40/ as provided by the bill. Congressman Payne stated, however, that returns would "be made public on the order of the President of the United States and only on the order of the President." The majority chose that approach "to make effective, in an intelligent way, the publicity feature of that law. 42/

Left standing was the notion of the 1909 Act that returns constitute "public records" open to public inspection. The 1910 effort to revise congressional intent merely added on the seemingly contradictory and confusing concept that these "public" records would be available only upon order of the President. But such was the law after the 1910 amendment. 

2. Revenue Act of 1913 and After. 

Even though the statute thus seemed to have two rather inconsistent threads, Congress surprisingly wove both of them into the 

Tariff Act of 1913. 

43/ In pertinent part, it provided: "G. (d) 1 When the assessment shall be made, as provided in this section, the returns, together with any corrections thereof which may have been made by the Commissioner, shall be filed in the office of the Commissioner of Internal Revenue and shall constitute public records and be open to inspection as such: Provided, That any and all such returns shall be open to inspection only upon the order of the President, under rules and regulations to be prescribed by the Secretary of the 

Treasury and approved by the President." 44/

The 1913 Congress thereby merged the mismatching philosophies emanating from the 1909 Act and the 1910 amendment. Although there has been, through the years, same change in language, the basic pattern 45/ adopted in 1913 remains today as a part of present law. 

The enactment of each revenue act subsequent to 1913 was (at least through 1934) accompanied by debate on the question of whether or 46/ not individual and corporate returns should be made fully public. TWO main arguments were proposed in favor of making tax returns public:

1 (1) publicity in the affairs of businesses generally is appropriate and would serve to end improper trade policies, business methods and 47/ conduct and (2) publicity would assure fuller and more accurate reporting by taxpayers. 1924. 49/ 48/ The proponents of full disclosure had a limited victory in The Revenue Act of 1924 provided that the Commissioner would "as soon as practicable in each year cause to be prepared and made available to public inspection. .lists containing the name and... address of each person making an income tax return. .together with the 50/ amount of income tax paid to such person.

"T 

The Revenue Act of 1926, however, removed the provision requiring that the amount of tax be made 51/ public (dashing the "direct mailers' delight"), leaving, simply, the requirement that a list be published containing the name and address of each person making an income tax return. 52/ In 1934 those favoring publicity 53/ obtained enactment of another form of limited disclosure. The Revenue Act of 1934 contained provision for the mandatory filing of a so-called "pink slip" with the taxpayer's 54/ return. The slip, to be filed with the return, was to set forth the taxpayer's gross income, total deductions, net income and tax payable. 55/ 56/ The slip was to be open to public inspection.

The resulting uproar 57/ caused repeal of the provision even before it took effect. Since 1934, there has been no substantial change in the statute respecting the disclosure of tax returns. The existing statute is, thus, very much the product of the 1909 and 1910 legislation, making venerable this oddity of "public" records open only under regulations or orders of the President.

Administrative Interpretation. 

During the first decade under the 1910 Act, access to corporate returns was allowed to government agencies upon written application to the Secretary of Treasury, signed by the head of the applicant agency, specifying the reasons for inspection. If the return were to be used in legal proceedings or might otherwise be made public, the Secretary could permit 58/ inspection only upon recommendation of the Attorney General. Thus, general access in the discretion of the Secretary of Treasury was limited to government agencies although the prior approval of the Attorney General was required if there was a possibility of publicity. There was, then, even in 1910 an embryonic notion that corporate tax returns constituted generalized government assets. 

In addition to allowing general access by government agencies to all corporate tax returns, the Regulations permitted the public to inspect the returns of corporations (1) whose stock was listed on an exchange or (2) whose stock was advertised or offered to the public. The carte blanche to inspect certain corporate returns seems to have been premised on the belief that all corporate returns could be made open to the public, but the Secretary and the President never did exercise that supposed authority in full.

The 1913 Act imposed an income tax upon individuals as well as corporations. While the 1913 Act perpetuated the confidentiality provisions, the discretion with respect to individual returns was exercised differently. 

Inspection was denied to anyone not an employee of the Treasury Department. 

Release of returns was allowed only in legal proceedings to which the United 59/ 

States was a party.

This disparity between corporations and individuals existed until 1920 when, without benefit of statutory change, the regulations were relaxed. 

Other government agencies were, at the Secretary's discretion, henceforth, permitted to inspect both corporate and in- 60/ dividual returns.

At the same time, however, the provision allowing deleted. the public to inspect returns of listed or publicly sold corporations was These amendments to the regulations marked the end of two significant features: (1) the almost complete prohibition against governmental inspection of individual returns, and (2) the unlimited public access to certain corporate returns. Thereafter, all returns would be a generalized government asset, and the public would be denied unrestricted access to any returns. 

In 1921, a new era began. From this time forward access to returns would be broadened. State tax officials and shareholders of 61/ In 1926, in an corporations were added to the inspecting class. amendment unclear in nature, there was deleted from the regulations the language which had required the Secretary to consider the reasons stated for inspection. However, the regulation did continue to provide that inspection by executive agencies would be allowed only in the Secretary's 62/ discretion.

This broadening of access for governmental agencies took a new turn in 1930. President Hoover approved a regulation authorizing 

Treasury to allow, upon such conditions as it would impose, the Department 63/ of Commerce to inspect returns upon request for statistical purposes.

This "blanket" authority differed from that which had gone before in that (1) Commerce was not required to name any taxpayer and (2) the grant of a request was founded on criteria established in the regulations, not on reasons stated in the application. The "catchall" regulations which had theretofore existed required specification of both the taxpayer and the reasons for inspection; Treasury, at least nominally, retained the discretion to deny such a request. The pattern of the "blanket" regulation, however, would thereafter be repeatedly copied. 

Regulations issued in 1931 again expanded access. These rules expressly permitted inspection by persons who had a material interest in the taxpayer, such as beneficiaries of estates and partners of a part- 64/ nership. 65/ In 1933, the group entitled to inspect tax returns was broadened again when President Roosevelt approved a regulation permitting a special In 1935, the President extended 66/ examination rights to another non-tax writing committee. 

These precedents were but the first drops of a gentle rain which nearly became a Senate Committee to examine returns. 67/ downpour.

A broad overhaul of the Regulations in 1938 68/ greatly facilitated the obtaining of returns for non-tax uses by United States attorneys and attorneys of the Department of Justice. 69/ Although the regulations provided that they were able to obtain returns "where necessary in the performance 70/ of [their] official duties," this broad language may have been somewhat constricted by a further provision.

It stated that if the purpose of

obtaining the return was for use before a grand jury, in litigation in which the United States was a party, or in preparation for either, 71/ the request for inspection was to be signed by the Attorney General, his assistant, or an Assistant Attorney General. "Neither the original nor a copy of the return" was to be supplied where the United States 72/ was not interested in the result. 

The 1938 language was very similar 73/ to that found in the regulations under the present statute. 

It is discussed in greater detail below because it appears to be a hybrid of the "catchall" and "blanket" regulations. 

Later in the same year the regulations were amended to permit any government agency to obtain tax return information for evidentiary use in proceedings, conducted by or before it, to which the United States 74/ 75/ was a party. This provision remains in the regulations today.

76/ Little changed with enactment of the 1939 Code. However, in 1941, we went to war. Soon thereafter, new as well as old federal agencies found the Commissioner and President sympathetically issuing regulations extending permission for inspection of returns or information taken therefrom. 77/ War's end saw no reduction in the number of federal 78/ agency requests for tax returns, however. 

In 1961, the first general regulations under § 6103 of the 1954 Code were promulgated. 79/ Most of the changes were by way of elaboration and were not substantive. For example, the provisions dealing with the inspection of returns by offices of the Department of Treasury other than the Internal Revenue Service was amended to require that the applications

for such use contain the name, address, taxable period involved and the 80/ 81/ reason for desiring inspection. The same kind of alteration was made to the provision dealing with the examination of returns by executive departments other than Treasury and to that dealing with inspection by United States Attorneys and the Attorneys of the Department of Justice. 

With respect to the use of returns in litigation there was the further elaboration that returns would be furnished only upon written application in all cases except tax matters, for which no written request was needed. 

The early 1970's saw three significant developments. First, The the filing of return requests (for non-tax litigation) by U. S.

attorneys 83/ was shifted to the National Office from the District Directors. same kind of centralized request procedure was required for requests by U. S. attorneys or by an attorney of the Department of Justice for use in 82/ either grand jury proceedings or litigation which did not involve revenue 84/ matters. Further, the regulations were amended to deny to Justice Department attorneys access to returns for purposes of examining prospective jurors (but the obtaining of information as to whether or not a prospective juror had been investigated by the Internal Revenue Service was specifically 85/ approved.)

A second development was the promulgation of another authorization 86/ for the Department of Agriculture, followed by amendment of the authority, 88/ and even later followed by rescission of the authority. These developments will be discussed later. Also, more detailed rules for White House access to tax returns were developed. 89/ These appear to be the first steps in reducing the use of tax return information. 87/

113 51 Finally, in 1972 the definition of "return" was broadened 90/ to engulf oral or written information related to the return, schedules, lists, "or other written statements filed on behalf of the taxpayer." 

It was provided that these internal documents relating to taxpayer's returns would be available "only in the discretion of the Secretary or the Commissioner or the delegate of either." The significance of this definitional change is discussed at a later point. 

In summary, although corporate returns were originally (in 1910) made available to the public, as well as to other government agencies, individual returns were cloistered within Treasury until 1920. In 1920, individual returns joined corporate returns as being generally available to federal agencies. Both were denied to the public. The 1930's saw a new technique of more general access being granted to specific agencies as well as to Congressional Committees. The 1940's, 1950's and 1960's were marked by almost unrestrained growth in the use of tax returns by government agencies. During this time tax returns became a generalized governmental asset. The public, however, was denied access. Finally, although the 1970's have not witnessed a significant reduction in tax return access, the expansion of access has at least been stemmed. 

This diverse history is, however, based on a statute which, in all significant respects, has been unchanged since 1910. Thus, the story is one of the exercise of discretion granted by a Congress unwilling to define precisely the policy to be followed. Having committed such discretion to the President, and an agency headed by his designee, Congress 77-842 O 76 - 55

should not be surprised that the power was exercised toward expanding the use of information garnered largely at taxpayer expense. Indeed, no political figure, as the President is, could be expected to resist agency arguments for more information on which to base important decisions, even though such information might not be necessary and might well be used for many purposes other than that ostensibly intended. 

As noted above, there are two methods by which an agency or department may obtain tax returns. The so-called catchall regulation permits an agency to have its executive head request inspection by an officer or employee in connection with a matter officially before the 91/ agency head.

The request must be in writing, signed by the agency head, set forth the name and address of the taxpayer, the type of tax, 92/ the periods covered by the return, and the reason for the inspection. 

Nominally, the Secretary or the Commissioner retain discretion to deny inspection. In fact, such discretion is rarely, if ever, exercised 93/ although the Commissioner may request clarification of the request or seek to limit inspection to the information clearly pertinent to the request. The Commissioner may also ask whether the desired information 94/ is otherwise available; if not, he will divulge it. 

The other route to tax returns is that offered by regulations, approved by the President, which usually confer "blanket" authority on 95/ the agency to inspect returns. They generally state the circumstances under which inspection will be permitted and generally do not impose the procedural requirements of naming a taxpayer, giving an address, stating

1 the type of tax, and stating the period. While the language of these regulations state that the Treasury "may" furnish the requested information, it is not believed that "may" is meant to confer discretion to refuse inspection. Rather it appears merely to authorize release. 

However, the Commissioner presumably may determine whether the request is within the scope of the regulations and refuse inspection if it is not. "Blanket" regulations appear designed for large volume users 96/ Such of tax returns who have generally defined reasons for their use. regulations obviate the inconvenience of making separate requests and stating reasons therefor. They also facilitate requests for classes or groups of tax returns because specific taxpayers need not be named. 

An agency having a "blanket" regulation may also request tax return information under the "catchall" regulation, § 301.6103(a)−1(f). 

For example, the Department of Health, Education and Welfare has "blanket" authority to inspect returns for purposes of administering Title II of 97/ the Social Security Act.

At the same time, the Secretary of HEW may 98/ request tax returns pursuant to the catchall regulation. Apparently, HEW has the right to inspect returns for administration of the Social Security laws under the "blanket" provision. If, however, an employee of 

HEW wishes to gain access to tax information in connection with some other matter "officially before him," inspection lies within the discretion of 99/ the Commissioner. Such requests, signed by the head of the department, stating a reason for the requested inspection, and specifying the taxpayer(s), 100/ are rarely denied by the Commissioner.

By and large, requests under the catchall provision are for investigative purposes. On the other hand, the majority of examinations of returns under the blanket regulations are for the purpose of gathering statistical data. Most of the blanket regulations, although not expressly limiting the use to statistical purposes, provide that the data obtained from the Internal Revenue Service is to "be held confidential except that it may be published or disclosed in statistical form provided such publication does not disclose, directly or indirectly, the name or address of any taxpayer." Only the regulation giving the Department of Health, 101/ Education and Welfare authority to examine returns seems to envision a clearly non-statistical use (i.e., administration of the social security laws). 10 The inspection of tax returns by Justice Department and United States attorneys is governed by a separate set of regulations. While it would apparently be appropriate for these attorneys to obtain tax returns (upon a request signed by the Attorney General) pursuant to the catchall 102/ regulation, they have their own special "investigative" regulations. 

These provide that a "return. . .shall be open to inspection by a United 

States attorney or by an attorney of the Department of Justice where 103/ necessary in the performance of his duties. 

The investigative provisions differ from the blanket regulations. 

Under the former the need for the return does not have to meet conditions specified in the regulations but must only be needed in connection with the performance of duties. Further, a request under this provision may be

signed by either the Attorney General, Deputy Attorney General or an Assistant Attorney General if the information is needed by a Justice Department attorney, or by the United States attorney if the return or copy is for him. The investigative provisions are also different because the attorney must state "the reason why inspection is desired. 

Other regulations authorizing access by employees of specific agencies 105/ either contain a statement of the reason for inspection or allow 104/ ready inference of the reason for which access is permitted. The "inves- 

3 tigative" regulations may appear to be more stringent but, as is hereinafter discussed, may in fact be less stringent than the blanket regulations. For example, while HEW "blanket" requests for tax information are limited to social security purposes, we will see that requests under the "investigative" regulations do not make precisely clear the reasons for which access is allowed. 

Another "investigative" provision provides that a United States attorney or an attorney of the Department of Justice may obtain tax returns "for official use in proceedings before a United States grand jury, or in litigation in any court, if the United States is interested in the result, 106/ or for use in preparation for such proceedings. While this regulation states that returns "may" be furnished in such circumstances, there is little indication that the Commissioner has any discretion in acting on upon him. 107/ a request under this provision. the Commissioner to make the returns available and not to confer discretion If the use of the tax returns is in grand jury proceedings or in litigation involving matters arising under the Internal Revenue laws or related statutes which were referred by the , the returns are available to the Department of Justice without written request.

139/ Two conclusions may be drawn from this cross section of requests. 

First, while the regulations are drafted so as to reserve the discretion to refuse inspection, it is not exercised as firmly as it might be. Second, the statement of "reasons" for inspection is largely a charade. The requester need only state that an investigation is proceeding and that the return is needed. A few requests for investigative purposes identify the event which prompted the asserted need for return information, but none indicate "why" the return is desired except in the most indefinite way. The reasons given reveal little about the need for the return or the use to which it will be put.

The real uses to which the various agencies put tax returns were more clearly suggested in a survey made in 1970 by the Commissioner of Internal Revenue at the behest of the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation. But, as will be seen later, the replies to this solicitation revealed only the use to which the agency typically put tax data. An allegation of the use is not an explanation of the need for the return. Furthermore, changing circumstances create new needs and new uses. Thus, the survey may not be regarded as an accurate indication of the current situation.

Since the Survey did not, and does not, adequately describe "why" tax returns are sought, and since individual requests do not do so either, such information is simply not available. 

2. Type of Material Obtained. 

The material delivered by the Service varies substantially depending on the agency's entitlement under the appropriate regulation or executive order. Entitlement is, of course, closely related to the Ser- 141/ vice's bifurcated definition of "return." A return is first said to include "information returns, schedules, lists, and other written statements filed by or on behalf of the taxpayer.. 142/ These include audit reports which have been furnished to the taxpayer, claims for refund and copies of certificates of over-assessment or notices of adjust- 143/ ment.

A Federal agency which is entitled, for example, to obtain tax returns under the "catchall" regulation (Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-1(f)) would 144/ obtain the data which is described in this category. The second grouping embraces, for the most part, material prepared inside the Internal Revenue Service, such as work papers of examiners, cover letters of reports in which opinions are expressed, reports of Special Agents, and 145/ inter-office communications. 

This material is not available as a matter of right (even if material in the first category is) but "only in the discretion of the Secretary or the Commissioner or the delegate or 146/ either."

In response to investigative requests, the Service will usually produce both the documents filed by the taxpayer and the material prepared inside the Service, including conference and revenue agent reports (except "information relating to informers' identities or other

similar confidential information"). 147/ However, scandalous matter which is not relevant to the case, work papers of examiners, cover letters of reports in which opinions are expressed, reports of Special Agents and inter-office communications may be obtained only with express authoriza- 148/ tion by the Assistant Commissioner (Compliance).

Some of the agencies for whom special executive orders have been issued giving them blanket authority do not get the "return" but only data taken from the return. For example, as well be discussed in more detail later, the Bureau of Census (a part of the Department of Commerce) frequently gets only entity data (name, address, and social security or employer identification number.) It may also obtain financial data in the form of computer tape which is limited to adjusted gross receipts, certain deductions, exemptions, and the like. Similarly, the 

Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, which obtains information for purposes of administering the social security laws, will obtain, on tape, 149/ data relating to the earned income of certain taxpayers. 

All requests by federal agencies must be made through the Na- 150/ tional Office. 

Consequently, the National Office is in a position to decide whether the associated material should be given over to the requesting agency. However, requests made by United States attorneys and attorneys of the Department of Justice for use in judicial or grand jury proceedings arising under the revenue laws are made not to the National 151/ Office but to the District Director.

3. Uses by Specific Agencies.

The discussion thus far indicates that a number of departments and agencies are consistent users of tax return information in large quantities. Included among these would most certainly be the Department of Justice, the various United States attorneys, the Department of Canmerce, the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, and the Securities and Exchange Commission. Because of the massive use of tax information by these agencies, the problems they raise will be discussed separately, on a department-by-department basis. 

In addition to the use of tax returns by these five offices, there has been use of such material, over the years, by more than two dozen other agencies and departments. Most of this use was pursuant to the catchall regulation making tax returns available to government agencies "in connection with a matter officially before" an employee of that agency. Considerable tax return data has also, of course, been made available to certain departments pursuant to executive orders bestowing "blanket" authority to examine tax returns. In any event, while the use of same departments or agencies may be small, it is nonetheless important to observe the grounds on which they have requisitioned tax return data. 

While the use of tax returns by any single department or agency to be discussed is not as large as any of the five departments or agencies mentioned above, these other parties still continue to use tax return data and the aggregate use by them is substantial. 

A rather thorough picture of the requests of federal departments

The objective of this solicitation was to obtain more accurate information from the agency with respect to the circumstances under which the department has requested, or is likely to 152/

D. Effect of Privacy Act of 1974. 

174/ 

The Privacy Act of 1974 

has a number of potential effects on the practice of making tax returns available to departments and agencies of the Executive Branch. This legislation was designed to protect the privacy of individuals identified in "information systems" maintained by Federal agencies through the regulation of the collection, maintenance, use, and dissemination of information by the agencies. The legislation asserts fundamental privacy rights, but at the same time recognizes a legitimate need of the Federal Government to collect, store, and exploit personal 175/ information in certain instances. Four aspects of the Privacy Act are relevant to the use of tax data by other Executive departments: (1) the requirement of consent before disclosure, (2) the identification of the person who may make the request for information when disclosure is permitted, (3) the imposition of record-keeping requirements on the disclosing agency, and (4) the requirement that notice be given of the uses. 

These aspects will be discussed in order. 

1. Requirement of Taxpayer Consent Before Disclosure.

Although subject to exceptions, the Privacy Act provides, in a key provision, that no agency of the Federal Government "shall disclose any record. .to another agency, except pursuant to a written request by, or with the prior written consent of, the individual to whom the record per- 176/ tains.

Since, in the disclosures previously discussed, the taxpayer is rarely, if ever, aware that the return or tax information has been transferred, this provision might be expected to hit directly at the Service's practices of divulging tax returns to other agencies and departments.

However, the provision requiring consent has eleven exceptions, two of 177/ 

Consent before 178/ or (2) "civil which are relevant to the disclosure of tax returns. disclosure is not required for either (1) "routine use" 179/ or criminal law enforcement activity.' 11 use."

A"routine use" is defined as "a use of such record for a purpose 180/ The which is compatible with the purpose for which it was collected. legislative history gives only scant evidence of the meaning of "routine The memorandum analyzing the compromise reached between the House and Senate versions states that the "definition should serve as a caution to agencies to think out in advance what uses they will make of infor- 181/ While the act "is not intended to impose undue burdens. mation. 

[upon] housekeeping measures," such as the transfer of information to the Treasury Department to complete payroll checks, it is "intended to discourage the unnecessary exchange of information ... [with] agencies [which] may not be. .sensitive to the collecting agency's reasons for using and 182/ interpreting the material." 

As previously discussed, the normal use of tax information by transferee agencies is in either the gathering of statistical data for non-revenue purposes or the investigation of offenses unrelated to tax administration. Although, giving ordinary words ordinary meaning, it would seem reasonable to conclude that the use of tax data for investigative or statistical purposes is not compatible with the purpose for which they were 183/ collected, the recently published Privacy Act Guidelines appear to take the position that use for both purposes should be described as routine.

Although there is clearly some support for this position in the legislative history, it is by no means clear that Congress intended "routine use" to be interpreted in this manner. 

The Privacy Act Guidelines state, at the outset, that "[o]ne of 184/ the primary objectives of the Act is to restrict the use of information to the purposes for which it was collected." After thus stating what appears to support a conclusion that statistical and investigative use of returns is non-routine, the Guidelines begin building a thesis that "routine use" encompasses any use that was properly being engaged in prior to the 1974 privacy legislation. The Guidelines view the "routine use" exception as constituting a recognition of "the practical limitations of restricting use of information to the explicit and expressed purpose for which it was 185/ collected. "

The "routine use" exception "recognizes that there are corollary purposes" which are "compatible" with the purposes for which the data has been collected which "are appropriate and necessary for the efficient conduct of government and in the best interest of both the indiv- 186/ idual and the public.

Although the Guidelines make an attempt to bless as "routine" any use which is "appropriate and necessary for the efficient conduct of government," the legislative history seems to refer to only two categories of use by other agencies as "routine." First, the transfer of data for "housekeeping" purposes is authorized. This would include the transfer of information "to the Treasury Department to complete payroll checks, the receipt of information by the Social Security Administration to complete quarterly posting of accounts, or such other house- 187/ keeping measures.

"1 The second category, referred to by

Congressman Moorhead in a statement on the House floor, is considerably broader. Lamenting that it would be an "impossible legislative task" to set forth all uses to which Federal records could be put, Congressman Moorhead noted that the legislation "gives each Federal agency the authority to set 188/ forth the 'routine' purposes for which the records are to be used. 

The law "is intended to prohibit gratuitous, ad hoc, disseminations for 189/ private or other irregular purposes.

"1 191/ Congressman Moorhead further stated that "[r]ather than attempting to specify each proper use of such records, the bill gives each Federal agency the authority to set forth the 'routine' purposes for which the 190/ records are to be used. 

Thus, it appears to be the position of the Guidelines that if the use is defined by the agency, and is pursuant to a regular practice, it will be treated as a "routine use. Although there may be something to support this interpretation, it does seem overly broad. The only examples cited by Congressman Moorhead of this type of use involve situations where data obtained by one agency is referred to another for the investigation or prosecution of an offense related to the purpose for 192/ which the data was collected. It is one thing to say that the disclosure of data for the investigation of offenses related to the purpose for which the data is collected is "routine" (i.e., a tax offense) and quite another to say that the disclosure of tax data for purposes of investigating a Title 18 criminal offense is "routine." If all the agency involved has to do to establish a use as routine is to regularize the practice, it hardly seems clear how the objective of restricting "the use of information to the purposes for which it was collected" is achieved.

The point of view that the use of tax data for statistical purposes outside the Internal Revenue Service is not a "routine use" is supported, certainly, by the fact that the Privacy Act specifically provides an exception to the general rule requiring consent before disclosure for disclosures "to the Bureau of the Census for purposes of planning or carrying out a census 193/ or survey" and "to a recipient who has provided the agency with advance adequate written assurance that the record will be used solely as a statistical research or reporting record, and the record is to be transferred in 194/ a form that is not individually identifiable." For what purpose would specific exceptions for these statistical uses be needed if the use was "routine"?

The scope of the "routine use" exception is, thus, far from clear. While there is something to support the apparent conclusion of the 

Privacy Act Guidelines, to-wit, the establishment of regular procedures will bless a use as "routine", the underlying philosophy of the entire legislation seems to indicate that a use must be related to the purpose for which the 195/ record is maintained if it is to be "routine".

196/ If "routine use" is to be construed more narrowly than is indicated by the Privacy Act Guidelines, tax information could still be transferred to other agencies, without the taxpayer's prior consent, pursuant to the exception for "civil or criminal law enforcement activity. exception provides that the data is to be disclosed "if the head of the agency or instrumentality has made a written request to the agency. "1 This .specifying the particular portion desired," thus apparently not covering the situation

in which the service "volunteers" the data without prior request. The legislative history and the Guidelines do little to define "civil or criminal law enforcement activity." For example, it is unclear whether the term "enforcement" should be construed to involve the imposition of some form of penalty. If it is so construed, use by many agencies may fall outside the term. 

For example, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation has requested and obtained tax return data in connection with its responsibility of overseeing the liquidation of a bank. It would seem that this use may not constitute "enforcement". Much of the use by other agencies would seem, however, to fall within the law enforcement exception. Such data would thus continue to be available to other agencies without the taxpayer's consent. 

Surely this result follows with respect to tax returns used in investigations by such agencies as the Department of Agriculture, Civil Aeronautics Board, Federal Communications Commission, and the Federal Home Loan Bank Board. 

More difficult are uses which are not strictly investigative in nature. For example, it could reasonably be asked whether the use by the Civil Service Commission of tax data for purposes of determining suitability for employment is for a law enforcement purpose. As another example, the Civil Service 

Commission has in the past (through its Bureau of Retirement, Insurance, and Occupational Health) requested tax information to determine whether an annuitant's annuity should be discontinued. If such use is not "routine" (and it appears that it may not be), the use must be discontinued unless prior consent is obtained or unless the use qualifies as "enforcement" (which it also may not be).

Further, it should be noted that the law enforcement exception is available only for a civil or criminal law enforcement activity "authorized by law". While it may be argued that the use of tax data in joint investigations is assuredly authorized (i.e., by the regulations under section 6103), problems with its authorization may exist if there are (as later discussion indicates there might be) Constitutional problems with the Transfer of 

Tax data. 

2. Source of the Request.

Under the present regulatory pattern, inspection under a regulation or executive order giving blanket authority to examine tax returns (e.g., to the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Federal Trade 

Commission) may be made by an employee duly authorized by the head of the examining agency. In the usual case there need not be a formal request by the head of the agency for "blanket" access, 197/ it being provided that "upon written notice by the Chairman [of the requesting agency] to the Secretary of the Treasury" an employee of Treasury "may furnish" the requesting agency with data. If the examination is made under the catchall regulation, Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a) -1 (f), the request must be made by the head of the department or agency. If the request is for investigative use by the Department of Justice or by the U. S. attorney (SS 301.6103 (a)-1(g) and (h)), the request must be made by the Attorney General, Deputy Attorney General, an Assistant Attorney General, or a U. S. attorney. 

Under the Privacy Act, records may be released for civil and criminal law enforcement activity without the consent of the subject of the records. The Privacy Act requires that "the head of the agency or

instrumentality. . . [makeja written request to the agency which maintains the record specifying the particular portion desired and the law enforcement 198/ activity for which the record is sought.

The question arises whether the requirement that the request be made by "the head of the agency or instrumentality" has the effect of altering the procedures in the regulations under § 6103 with respect to who may make the request. A bit of legislative history in the form of a statement by Congressman Moorhead makes it clear that the Privacy Act will have no effect in tightening procedures regarding the source of the request. Congressman Moorhead states: "Such duties [requesting data from another agency] may be delegated, like other duties, to other officials, when absolutely necessary but never below a section chief, 199/ and this is what is contemplated by section (b) (7).' 

3. Record-Keeping Requirement.

At the present time the record-keeping by the Internal Revenue Service with respect to the disclosure of tax returns to other agencies 200/ is not wholly formalized. It may not have made arrangements for retaining such records or for an adequate accounting to the individuals named in the records. The Privacy Act of 1974 imposes three record-keeping requirements 201/ "with respect to each system of records" under an agency's control. 

First, the agency must "keep an accurate accounting of. the date, nature and purpose of each disclosure of a record. . .to any agency. name of the. . .agency to whom the disclosure is made." .and the 202/ 

Second, it

must "retain the accounting. . .for at least five years or the life of the record, whichever is longer, after the disclosure for which the accounting 203/ is made." Third, except for disclosures made pursuant to the civil or criminal law enforcement exception, the agency must "make the accounting. . .available

204/ "1 to the individual named in the record at his request.

" 4. 

Requirement That Notice Be Given of Uses.

The Privacy Act also provides that each agency maintaining a system of records shall "publish in the Federal Register at least annually a notice of the existence and character of the system of records, which notice shall include. .each routine use of the records contained in the system, including the categories of users and the purpose of such use.

205/ The chief question with respect to this requirement is whether a practice is rendered (as seems to be indicated from a reading of the Privacy Act Guidelines) "routine" simply by announcing the practice and treating it established 206/ by the agency. The Privacy Act also apparently requires the Service to place on the return itself information concerning the "purposes for which the information is. . .to be used" and "the routine uses which may be made of 207/ the information.""

E. 

Use of Returns and Return Information for Statistical Purposes. 

One of the chief uses of tax return data by agencies other than the Internal Revenue Service is for statistical purposes. Agencies with a need for current and accurate data concerning income, business size, entity, and similar information have long known that the annual income tax return constitutes an enormously fertile source of information. 208/ 

1. Department of Agriculture. 41 The Department of Agriculture can obtain tax return information 209/ under the catchall regulation (Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a) -1 (f).

There are, however, difficulties if the data is desired for statistical uses. First, the request must be signed by the head of the department (i.e., the Secretary). 

Second is the cumbersome requirement that the request contain the name of the taxpayer. This requirement literally precludes acquisition of returns by classes or groups. Hence, when the Department of Agriculture decided it had need of a voluminous class of returns, it sought an executive order. 

The possibility of such an order was discussed as early as the Agriculture's formal request therefore was made latter part of 1968. on October 19, 1970. 210/ 211/ In the discussions which followed, prompted 212/ largely by the concerns of the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation and the Chief Counsel, the appropriateness of an unlimited right to tax return information by Agriculture was questioned. 

As a consequence, there was a decision to draft "restrictions" into the executive order on the use of the material obtained by the Department of Agriculture:

(1) only the returns of those persons with "farm operations" would be 213/ available; 214/ (2) data obtained by Agriculture by using the tax return data was to be treated as confidential; (3) Agriculture was required to set forth, in the requests, the names of its employees who would have access to the tax data; (4) Agriculture was to detail its procedures which would be designed to guarantee security of the data and the Service could deny access if these procedures were deemed inadequate; and (5) the request by Agriculture was required to set forth "the specific tax data needed and how such tax data relates to the statistical goals of the Department. 

Thereafter, on January 17, 1973, President Nixon issued Executive

Order 11697 pursuant to his authority under $ 6103 (a) of the Internal Revenue Code, providing "that income tax returns. .of persons having farm operations shall be open to inspection. . . (for the purpose of obtaining data about such persons' farm operations) by the Department of Agriculture as may be needed for statistical purposes only." 215/ It appears that there was, from the time the Internal Revenue Service first discussed the possibility of such an order with the Department of Agriculture, some concern about what the reaction to the order would be. 216/ Such concern was warranted. The "unexpected negative reaction" to his executive order prompted President Nixon, on March 27, to rescind it and to issue in its place Executive Order 11709 which approved regulations narrower than their predecessors. The key change limited "other data" which the Department of Agriculture could obtain to "type of farm activity, and one

20 or more measures of size of farm operations such as gross income from 217/ farming or gross sales from farm products." 

In subsequent Congressional hearings, Agriculture's need for tax 218/ return data of this nature was spelled out in great detail.

The Statis tical Reporting System (SRS) of the Department is responsible for a statistical program which tracks such matters as the number of farms, livestock, numbers by specie and class, the acreage yield and production of crops, prices paid and received by farmers, and farm labor and wage rates. SRS had been dependent 219/ on data collected in nonprobability mail surveys to make its crop and ​al 1} livestock estimates. To keep the survey sampling current, SRS checked its lists of farmers against the quinquennial Census of Agriculture. SRS maintained that while this methodology performed well when there was a high degree of similarity from one farm to the next, by 1961 it had become clear that rapid changes in the number and structure of the nation's farms had occurred. SRS therefore abandoned its mailing list of farm operations and turned to selecting sampling units by marking off areas of land on aerial photographs. Personal interviews were then undertaken to collect data from a true cross-section of farms. This program provided national estimates for major commodities with sampling errors of two percent. However, when (amidst considerable uproar) in 1967 SRS's national cattle estimates were revised by about two percent (to make them consistent with the results of the 1964 Census of Agriculture), the Department reduced its goal for sampling errors in major commodity estimates to one percent. Agriculture might then have met the goal by quadrupling the size of the sample. Instead, it developed a new technique, called multiple

frame sampling, which was said to reduce errors to one percent or less and to be comparable to a complete census. 220/ Indeed, SRS had run successful livestock samples using this technique. 

Multiple frame sampling, however, requires a complete set of mapping materials (which were already available) and "a virtually complete list of farm operator names and addresses with broad measures of size and 221/ type," which were not available to USDA except through great cost. 

Agriculture was aware, however, that the Census Bureau had a "virtually 222/ complete" list of farm operations compiled largely with income tax return data. Agriculture suggested a joint utilization of this material with the 

Census Bureau, but confidentiality restrictions on Census prohibited this 223/ approach. Agriculture finally sought to obtain the information directly from the Internal Revenue Service under authority of regulations approved by an Executive Order issued especially for that purpose "in the interest of good management and prudent stewardship of public funds to utilize for a public purpose and for the public good a list that is already available from administrative records. 224/ Despite this demonstration of need by Agriculture and the nar- 225/ rowing of the order, criticism continued almost unabated.

While a limitation of disclosure to names and addresses of those with farm income 226/ might have stilled the dispute, the threatened release of information on gross receipts or gross income (a size classifier) was apparently considered an unacceptable invasion of privacy. In addition, there was concern that

Agriculture's request was the beginning of a "raid" on the Internal Revenue Service. This belief was largely prompted by the revelation that the revised regulations which tightened the scope of access, use, and security 227/ were to be a model for subsequent regulations. 

The key objection, however, was raised in a letter from Congressman Moorhead to Agriculture Secretary Butz. Agriculture's use would not be identical to that of Census (which had been going on for years without 228/ criticism), the Congressman pointed out, because "Census does not operate 229/ programs which affect the livelihood of citizens as Agriculture does." 

In reply, Secretary Butz noted that the Department of Commerce (of which the Census Bureau is technically a part) also operates programs which depend heavily on Census data. He also attempted to equate SRS with Census, stating that the former serves only "as the general purpose statistical agency for the Department of Agriculture [and] does not operate programs but provides the basic agricultural statistics for agencies with program responsibilities. 

Although the Census Bureau is part of the Department of Commerce, it bears no relationship to the other functions of that Department. 

Functionally, it is the handmaiden of the entire Federal Government and of the public at large for the gathering of a broad range of informational 231/ and statistical data. The sole relationship of Census with Commerce seems to be its organizational placement. On the other hand, while 

SRS does have similar (though narrower) information gathering duties, it is not autonomous of its host agency. SRS gathers data 230/

for policy making by the agency of which it is a part, but Census data is available to all. Moreover, Census information identifies no one. The fear existed, however, that the SRS could or would make data on individuals available to Agriculture. Apparently, there would have been no objection to the obtaining of names and addresses of those with farm income, thereby 232/ permitting Agriculture to obtain further data by way of solicitation. 

A voluntary submission of data after solicitation was not objectionable. 

Multiple frame sampling, however, required a size classifier which was not 233/ available from a mere list of names and addresses. No compromise between these alternatives could be struck, and the second executive order was rescinded on March 21, 1974. 234/
