The Bureau is required by statute to conduct certain censuses and surveys, though it also conducts surveys which are merely authorized. 240/ 

The Bureau evaluated

In 1944, Census began to use tax return data. this use in 1950 and concluded it was very economical and accurate. Four types of census and survey activities performed by the Bureau utilize tax return data.

The first, the Economic Census, is conducted every five years, and covers manufacturing, mining, retail and wholesale trade, selected service 241/ industries, construction, and transportation. 

This census forms "the primary source of facts about the structure and functioning of the Nation's 77-842 O 76-57

economy" without which "the statistical framework needed by policymakers.

would be severly impaired." 242/ 

The results are also used in surveys conducted by other agencies (e.g., the Federal Reserve Board's Index of Industrial 

Production and the Bureau of Labor Statistics Index of Wholesale Prices). The return data utilized in the preparation of the Economic Census data is limited to name and address, EIN, entity type, business activity, number of employees, and payroll by quarter. On the basis of this information, business establishments falling within the six census groupings are identified and classified by group, size, and location. The tax data will reveal that some firms are outside the scope of the census. Thus, in preparing the 1972 

Economic Census, 6.5 million businesses were excluded because tax data demonstrated that they were not within the scope of the program. Another 3 million small firms were not required to file with Census, their tax return 243/ data being used in lieu of such reports.

The Bureau estimates that without the tax information to develop its "universe" for the purposes of this quinquennial Census, its cost would rise from its present level of $34 million to between $60 and $100 million. 244/ The Census of Agriculture, which is also quinquennial, provides data concerning farm size, tenure, form of organization, market value of 245/ products and type of farm. This data is widely used by the Congress and the Executive Branch for "legislative action, policy decisions, and program 246/ planning and execution."

Through the 1964 Census of Agriculture, data had been collected by field enumeration. In 1969, survey by mail was undertaken to increase identification and to decrease the costs and burdens

to farmers and the agency. Here again, tax records were essential for purposes of developing a "universe" subject to the Census. Size indicators derived from tax information enabled the Bureau to send abbreviated report forms to small farmers and thereby reduce the reporting burden for onehalf the Nation's farm operators. 

A third activity conducted by the Census is the compilation of Current Economic Indicators -- a broad series of weekly, monthly, quarterly, and annual sample surveys in trades and industries to measure current 247/ The monthly retail sales data, for performance and economic trends. example, is essential data in developing estimates of consumer expenditures, a major component of GNP. The Bureau is able to conduct these surveys by obtaining from the Internal Revenue Service complete and up-to-date lists of business employers, classified by size and industry. Tax records constitute the most reliable and current data concerning existing businesses, giving the Bureau capability to complete quickly special surveys designed to meet needs of policy makers. For example, when a shortage of cattle hides developed recently, the Census Bureau was able to determine rapidly 248/ the extent of the shortage, through a survey of producers, consumers, and stock pilers of this commodity based on a list compiled from tax data. 

Finally, the Bureau conducts a Survey of Minority Owned Business Enterprises, designed to develop reliable data concerning the extent and growth of minority participation in private enterprise. 249/ A number of other agencies of the Federal Government (i.e.

, Small Business Administration,

Department of Housing and Urban Development, Office of Economic Opportunity, Department of Labor, Economic Development Administration) underwrite the cost of the survey. Again, determination of the composition and size of the universe (from which a sample comprising abut 140,000 businesses is plucked) depends on tax data. 

The Census Bureau anticipates that significant problems will beset 250/ these programs if tax return information is withdrawn. For example, Census is presently able to exclude businesses from these surveys, and the lack of tax return data would cast reporting burdens on those businesses presently excluded. Secondly, the Census Bureau asserts that without tax data, it would have to generate census lists from sources which, lacking in classification information, are less refined. This would depress the quality of the samples. Third, the process would be materially delayed, thereby. limiting the survey's timeliness, which is one of its chief benefits. 251/ Aside from these four activities just discussed, the Bureau of Census engages in a Demographic Statistics Program to furnish population and per capita income estimates on which to base allocations of revenue 252/ sharing funds to units of local government. Tax information also allows the Census Bureau to obtain data concerning migratory pattems. For example, as is well known, the 1972 individual income tax return was revised to des- 253/ ignate the taxpayer's county of residence. By comparing (through Social 

Security numbers) the 1972 data with 1969 information, a residence migration matrix was developed for the 1969-1972 period. 254/

ww SL 5,3 The data obtained for this demographic work ties in closely with the general population census work. Also, the information received for this purpose is identifiable only by Social Security number, 255/ difficult the identification of any particular individual.

thus rendering The Bureau concedes that the Internal Revenue Service could develop the information required by the Demographic Statistics Program. 

However, Census has developed the necessary expertise, and argues that development of such capacity in the Internal Revenue Service would serve only to "duplicate and maintain in two separate agencies, similar statistical capabilities. . 256/ Several observations may be made concerning the use of tax data 257/ by Census. First, while organizationally a part of Commerce, Census has no program either to implement or to shape. It is a neutral and objective agency having no part in decisions affecting those whose tax returns are examined. Its sole function is statistical tabulation and analysis for use by the public and by policy makers in other agencies. Second, Congress has imposed upon Census the duty to perform most of the censuses and surveys in which tax information is employed. While its enabling legislation does not carry with it the specific authority to examine tax return data, Congress arguably intended Census to have any information which would maximize the quality and accuracy of its work. Indeed, Census itself is authorized to obtain information similar or identical to tax return data, through its own reporting requirements. Finally, an aura of confidentiality surrounds the tax data in the hands of Census. It cannot be divulged in any individually

258/ identifiable manner.

In conclusion, it appears that the use of tax data by Census, though not consistent with revenue administration, is a use which can be considered beneficial and is one which does not appear to have any undesirable side effects. b.

Bureau of Economic Analysis. 

The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) is like the Bureau of 259/ These

Census, a part of SESA. BEA is charged with clearly portraying the state of the U.S. economy -- a task accomplished through the preparation, development and interpretation of the National Economic Accounts. accounts, which are designed to provide a quantitative analysis of the economic health of the country, include the National Income and Products Accounts and the Balance of Payments Accounts. 

Like Census, BEA does not itself make economic or social policy but governmental policy at all levels is dependent on the "blocks of economic 260/ knowledge" which it produces, such as balance-of-payments and international investment analyses. The Council of Economic Advisors, the Federal Reserve 

Board, the Treasury Department, and the Office of Management and Budget use BEA-developed data in the formulation and execution of fiscal, financial, international, wage-price, and other economic policies. Considerable use is also made by Congress, state and local governments, businesses, labor, universities, and other groups. 

Compared to Census, its sister bureau, BEA uses a miniscule number 261/ 262/ BEA has many information sources, and it employs of tax returns. return data only in a limited way. BEA derives most of the tax information

cal material derived from tax returns. it needs from the Statistics of Income (SOI), an annual publication of statisti- Nonetheless, BEA asserts that it must make "selective use. .of information in the underlying tax records. 263/ For example, SOI will tabulate many retail sales on the installment method used by the retailer in computing taxes. However, if sales volume for economic purposes is to be stated accurately, such retail sales figures must be adjusted to an accrual basis in which sales and profit coincide with delivery. BEA also constructs a "bench mark" for its plant and equipment expenditures survey and uses tax return data for those industries which are not covered by the Economic Census. Another example of BEA use (similar to that made by Census) of tax material arises in connection with its enumeration, 264/ under the Foreign Investment Study Act of 1974, of U.S. private investment abroad. For this function BEA requires the names, addresses, and industry codes of all U.S. companies with more than ten percent foreign ownership and of all companies with overseas investments. 265/ Apart from these specific examples, BEA argues that it must have access to underlying tax returns to evaluate the impact on the SOI figures of such factors as mergers and acquisitions, changes in the tax law and interpretation, and accounting procedures used in tax computations. Thus, BEA is able to develop better estimating techniques to anticipate major differences between book and tax profits. Echoing Census, BEA argues that a denial of tax material". .would seriously imperil BEA's analytical capability and hence the reliability of the critical GNP and related data." Like Census also, BEA does not regard 266/

delegation of the preparation of this data to the IRS as a viable solution. 

Apparently, BEA concedes that the Internal Revenue Service could prepare tabulations of some items such as "book" versus "tax" income. It maintains, however, that in so doing the Service would have to analyze and explain a typical development in the data, tasks which BEA's seasoned economists do 267/ well.

The status and practices of BEA seem very similar to that of Census. An office of the government which has as its sole function (and sole reason for existence) the collection and analysis of statistical data, BEA has no policy making duties. The information it distills is made available in the manner of Census, in a statistical fashion only to policy making agencies and departments. Similar provisions relating to 268/ confidentiality also exist. BEA's use thus parallels that by Census even though some of the information obtained is for classes so small as to be identifiable to specific taxpayers. 3.

Other Agencies Using Tax Returns of Tax Return Information for Statistical Purposes.

Only a few other agencies or departments use tax return data in a manner which is similar to the Bureau of the Census and the Bureau of 

Economic Analysis. 

a. Federal Trade Commission.

Pursuant to a blanket regulation approved by a 1961 Executive Order, the Federal Trade Commission may inspect income tax returns "as an aide in executing the power conferred upon such Commission by the Federal 269/ Trade Commission Act of 1914 (38 Stat. 717)." 

Although the FTC can,

LCE 2. ​and does, obtain tax returns under the general regulation for investigative purposes, this blanket regulation is for statistical purposes in connection with its power "to gather and compile information concerning. the organization, business, conduct, practices and management of any corporation 270/ engaged in commerce,...

The press release which accompanied the 271/ 1961 Executive Order stated that the "inspection authorized will enable the Commission to obtain up-to-date information for use in its participation in the Industrial Financial Reports Program... [which] serves the needs of the business community and of government agencies for current and authoritative data on the financial operations of industrial corporations." 

The use of tax returns for statistical purposes is carried by two divisions of the Bureau of Economics of the FTC -- the Division of Financial Statistics and the Division of Industry Analysis. 

The Division of Financial Statistics (by far the larger user of the two) uses tax returns to obtain probability samples from which it produces quarterly financial statistics, published as the Quarterly Financial Report (QFR), for the Council of Economic Advisors, the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve Board, and others using economic data. 

The QFR is a part of the Industrial Financial Reports Program referred to 272/ in the 1961 press release. 

The access by the Division of Financial Statistics is substantial. 

In the first half of 1974, for example, it amounted to abstract sheets from 58,729 corporate income tax returns. The Division's requests for tax data seek returns in specific industries. Until 1972 it collected

data concerning manufacturing corporations only; it now obtains information on corporations engaged in mining and trade (both retail and wholesale) as well. The abstracts made available are limited to those corporate returns comprising the samplings on which the Statistics of Income is based. With respect to large corporations, the SOI sample may be 100 percent, although the samples of other classes of corporations will be less than that. On the basis of these samples, SOI sets out representative data concerning the income, deductions, and similar characteristics of all reporting corporations. In its arrangement with the Internal Revenue Service, the Division 273/ of Financial Statistics receives data concerning the corporations included in the SOI sample. This information is utilized not as the basis of the statistical data appearing in the Quarterly Financial Reports but rather as a classifier for purposes of soliciting information from the corporation sampled. The solicited information is received on a quarterly basis, thus rendering it more current than the SOI data. It is also more detailed, and forms the basis for the Quarterly Financial Report. In addition to not being individually identifiable, the information is protected by rules of which preclude its availability in a manner revealing the identity of any corporation, to any other part of the FTC, or to any confidentiality 274/ other agency or department.

Another FTC component, the Division of Industry Analysis, also requests tax data (under the "blanket" regulation) to assist in studies it is making. For example, in 1964 it requested the income tax returns of 

24 leading retail grocery corporations in connection with an analysis of

alt t! TE עם merger activity. In 1970 it utilized detailed tax return information of the advertising expenses of some 800 corporations in determining (as part of a larger study of the profit performance of large manufacturing corporations) 275/ the extent to which advertising costs are a determinant of profit rate. 

The use by the Division of Industry Analysis arises only infrequently and involves a small number of returns. During the years 1961-1970 it requested 276/ tax data on only four occasions. The Division of Industrial Analysis will generally seek tax data from specific returns, Although it does have "blanket" authority to examine tax returns, such authority is usually used to obtain returns by class, for statistical purposes, rather than by name. Hence, it is likely that requests for tax information by the Division of Industrial Analysis are made pursuant to the catchall regulation, The information obtained, however, is used not for investigative purposes (as are most requests under the regulation) but in analytical pursuits, The results of the division's studies, which are usually generated by the Commission or requested by a committee of the Congress, are published in a manner in which data concerning any taxpayer is not individually identifiable. 11 b. Recent Changes by Internal Revenue Service Regarding Disclosure for Statistical Purposes. 282/ Without any written announcement or change in regulations, the Service appears to have adopted new procedures which may reduce the avail-

$

Sz M. ability of tax data for statistical purposes. All requests by other agencies for income tax data are now apparently receiving the personal attention of the Commissioner, even though it has long been required that they be routed through his office. The Service apparently has concluded that income tax data should be available for statistical purposes only if (1) the data are absolutely essential and (2) no satisfactory substitute therefor can be found,

The effect of this new attitude was felt recently by the Census Bureau, which was unable to obtain, as it had in the past, data relating to income of farmers for preparation of the 1974 Census of Agriculture. 283/ In place of the specific income data, Census received a size code to be used as a size classifier. While Census was able to complete its work, it maintains that the resulting product is less refined and detailed than its predecessors because the size code is not as precise a size classifier as the specific income data. Thus, Census argues, it did not have sufficient information on which to decide whether field enumerations of non-respondents were warranted. Aside from this concrete manifestation of the Service's new "toughness", Census notes that negotiations with the Service over the nature of material to be disclosed is becoming increasingly difficult and 284/ slow.

The FTC has also encountered the new attitude. Its Division of 

Financial Statistics has become dissatisfied with the recently introduced panel of corporations to SOI statistics. Because this panel is substantially unchanged from year to year, FTC thought the quality of its Quarterly Financial Reports might be improved by gaining access to data on all

corporations contained in the Business Master File (BMF), The Internal Revenue Service has expressed a reluctance to change Past procedures on the ground, inter alia, of prospective legislative change in the area of return confidentiality.

Still another example of the new attitude apparently is manifested by the Service's reported attempt to persuade the Bureau of Economic Analysis that the Service should gather statistical data and perform requested analyses "in-house" (e.g., an explanation of why corporations engaging in a particular industry enjoyed a significant increase in profits). 

Aside from whether these additional burdens on gaining access to tax information for statistical purposes are desirable, they do raise new questions. First, the essentiality of the information presumably should have been considered when the orders allowing access were issued. But, because many of these regulations were promulgated when confidentiality was of less concern, it may not have been. Futhermore, essentiality may vary from time to time, and a periodic demonstration of need may thus be desirable. It would, however, seem to shift to the Internal Revenue Service the right, not granted (let alone mentioned) in the blanket regulations, to decide in each case the circumstances which will demonstrate essentiality. 

The lack of availability from other sources is a much different test, however, If the information sought is otherwise available, the Service's reluctance to disclose it must be based upon (1) the administrative burdens to the Service which would arise in disclosure, (2) the possibility that unauthorized information will be "leaked" in the disclosure, and (3) the desire to maintain a public image of reluctance to disclose the information.

​ཏྟཱ 

On the other side of the coin, the fact that the information is not otherwise available suggests that it would not be disclosed by the Service either. The concept of tax return confidentiality must apply equally to information which is otherwise available and to that which is not. Thus, the fact of unavailability from sources other than tax returns would seem to force a re-examination of the question whether the tax returns themselves should be divulged. At the very least, unavailability, standing alone, should not constitute an argument for disclosure. 

Whatever the proper resolution of these problems may be, the litmus tests of essentiality and alternative source seemingly are applied only to uses for statistical purposes and not to use for investigative purposes. 

5. Conclusion on Statistical Uses. 

Most statistical uses are for the purpose of compiling essential economic data by government agencies. The tax return information in many cases serves the purpose of identifying further sources of information. 

Not only is the anonymity of taxpayers In other instances, the return information is itself converted to statistical series made available to the public. In some cases the information could be directly compelled from the taxpayer. Also, most (but not all) information is transmitted by the Service in a form making identification of the taxpayer either impossible or difficult. preserved (and indeed required by law or agency rulemaking), the material is collated by instrumentalities having no power to shape or implement policies affecting those from whom the information was compelled by the revenue laws in the first place. The resulting analysis available to those who do steer the ship of state is both objective and generalized. Hence, this kind of disclosure would seen the least offensive of all.

F. 

Use of Returns and Return Information for Corroborative Purposes. 

Distinct from use for either investigative or statistical purposes is the employment of tax return data for corroborative purposes--to ascertain whether certain requirements or standards unrelated to revenue administration are met. Most of the non-statistical utilization of tax return data outside the Internal Revenue Service is in the nature of investigative use. 

Consumption of tax return data for corroborative purposes is infrequent. 

For example, the Civil Service Commissioner occasionally requests tax data to determine whether an annuitant's disability annuity should be discontinued due to the restoration of an "earning capacity fairly comparable" to the 285/ range of pay at the time of retirement. By far the most significant user of tax return data for corroborative purposes is, however, the Social 

Security Administration of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare. 

In 1955 President Eisenhower signed an executive order approving regulations providing that income tax returns "shall be open to inspection by the Department of Health, Education and Welfare as may be needed in its administration of the provisions of Title II of the Social Security Act.... 

Tax return information is used by the Social Security Administration (SSA) "in establishing entitlement to, and/or the amount of monthly benefits payable. 

SSA is normally able to obtain desired tax returns directly from the taxpayer, but it may have to be requested from the Internal Revenue Service. 

In many instances, SSA will be seeking to obtain evidence of earnings which for some reason have not been credited to an individual's Social Security record of. "the bona fides of a business structure or employment relation- 286/ 287/ 288/

289 ship. 13 The income tax return of either the insured or some other person is a useful source for obtaining evidence regarding entitlement 290/ questions. 

For example, an illegimate child of an insured individual will be eligible for benefits if the insured has made written acknowledge- 291/ ment of paternity.

The SSA regards a tax return of the insured, claim- Sp ing the illegitimate child as a dependent, as a sufficient acknowledgement 292/ for this purpose,

While enforcement of the Social Security laws may not be related to income tax administration in the strict sense, arguments. may be made in favor of disclosure to the Social Security Administration. Most obviously, there is an extremely close connection between income taxes and Social Security contributions. Since both are reported on forms attached to income tax returns, and since both are collected by the Internal Revenue Service, many taxpayers do not make a distinction between them. In many instances, also, the tax return needed by SSA is that of the claimant; the confidentiality laws exist to protect the taxpayer and thus should not preclude substantiation of his claim for Social Security benefits. Even if the return involved is not that of the claimant, questions relating to income often lie at the heart of matters of Social Security entitlement, making it essential for SSA to secure reliable reportage of source, amount, and timing of income received. 

The return may constitute the only source for that information. Finally, administrative rules prevent SSA employees from disclosing that data which 293/ is received from the Internal Revenue Service.

Use of Tax Return and Tax Return Information for Investigative Purposes. 

Aside from the statistical gathering just discussed, the largest use of tax data outside the Internal Revenue Service is for the purpose of investigating possible violations of law under the jurisdiction of other agencies. Disclosure of return information to attorneys of the Department of Justice and to United States attorneys is made pursuant to the Treasury regulation providing for use by the Department of Justice and U.S. attorneys (S 301.6103 (a) -1 (g)). Disclosure for investigative purposes is made also, to the Department of Agriculture, Civil Aeronautics Board, Federal Communications Commission, Federal Home Loan Bank Board, Department of Interior, Interstate Commerce Commission, Department of La bor, U.S. Postal Service, Securities and Exchange Commission, Small Busi ness Administration, and the Veterans Administration. Authority to reveal tax data to these agencies, predictably, comes from the "catchall" Regulation ($ 301.6103 (a) -1 (f)). Few of the agencies named are likely to make more than twenty requests annually, and their utilization of the confidential tax information obtained does not present issues notably distinct fram its exploration by the three largest users of such data. These are (a) lawyers of the Department of Justice, (b) United States attorneys, as distinct from the Department of Justice, and (c) the SEC, and we now discuss each of them in turn. 

1. Utilization by Specific Agencies a. Department of Justice.

The Department of Justice may receive return information

contained in investigative files made available by another Federal agency. 

It may obtain, on its own, returns for use in litigation (as hereinafter discussed). 297/ We will therefore focus on strike forces to illustrate all use of tax returns on criminal investigations. (1) Strike Forces.

The Strike Force has a number of antecedents. The concept is traceable to Thomas Dewey's Rackets Bureau in the New York 298/ County District Attorney's Office, which employed attorneys, investigators, and accountants having expertise in organized crime matters. In 

1954, the Department of Justice established an Organized Crime and Racketeering Section (OCR) to coordinate "generally enforcement activities 299/ directed against organized crime and racketeering." Its functions were "to accumulate and correlate data related to organized crime and racketeering, . . . initiate and supervise investigations, formulate general prospective policies and assist U. S. attorneys in preparing indictments and 300/ conducting trials in this field. By 1957, however, OCR had a staff of 

Following the meeting of organized crime figures in 301/ only 10 attorneys.

Appalachia, N.Y., the Department of Justice established its Special Group on Organized Crime. In September of 1960, the Federal Bureau of Investigation began supplying OCR with regular intelligence reports an Costa Nostra figures. At this time, however, there was virtually no intelligence recei- 302/ ved from other agencies by OCR, whose staff had grown to 17 attorneys. 

A major new approach was implemented, however, in 1961. Its chief feature was the involvement of a central office within the Department of Justice to administer the anti-crime fight along with field prosecution

15 11 offices "operating as close to the cooperating Federal, State, and local 303/ agencies as possible."

One of the recommended features of this new approach was an "easing of access to criminal intelligence" data. 304/ When Robert F. Kennedy took office as Attorney General he was faced with a history of independence and noncooperation among 27 separate 305/ intelligence agencies. It has been reported that Robert Kennedy saw 

Mortimer Caplin in December 1960 and asked his views on a close alliance between the Internal Revenue Service and the Department of Justice to fight organized crime. Caplin's appointment as Commissioner of Internal Revenue was announced January 24, 1961. Soon thereafter, the Internal Revenue Service detached a special organized crime group to work with the Department of Justice. 

The technique of the cooperative investigation approach was, bluntly put, "to circulate the list [of suspected racketeers] among twentyseven different investigative agencies and then to investigate these guys up 307/ to their eyeballs. The cooperation by same IRS personnel was at times reluctant, and there is some indication that Kennedy used a variety of tac- 308/ tics to insure Service cooperation. In 1968, President

Johnson promulgated an executive order creating the strike force as it is known today and designating the Attorney General "to facilitate and coordinate the criminal law enforcement activities and crime preven- 318/ Each tion program of all Federal departments and agencies... agency was "directed to cooperate with the Attorney General" and, "to the extent permitted by law and within the limits of available funds, furnish 319/ him such reports, information and assistance as he may request." is ample evidence that this order had a rejuvenating effect on the flagging efforts against organized crime. 320/ There The concept of the strike force is simple. It is an integrated investigation and prosecution program based on the pooling of criminal intelligence data among investigative agencies. 321/ The cooperative investigative approach takes advantage of the fact that "different responsibilities within the Federal agencies have produced investigators with special skills and talents" and that "expertise of these agents should be used by organizing them into investigative teams that work exclusively on organized crime 322/ matters.

" This combined intelligence system is the most, if not the 323/ only, essential feature of the strike force operation. This characteristic is critical to our study: the strike force has been inextricably tied to the use of tax returns for investigative purposes.

Upon the establishment of each new strike force unit, letters of request are sent to OCR and to the various Federal agencies asking that each assign supervisory personnel to the strike force. Although it has been 324/ noted that the "Department of Justice has no statutory power to compel assignment, and therefore depends upon cooperation, the Presidential or- 325/ 17 der requiring the cooperation of other executive agencies cast doubt upon the correctness of that statement. The assigned agents remain fully within the jurisdiction of their respective agencies. The Internal Revenue 

Service assigns its agents to a strike force for a two year period. 

The Detroit Strike Force, which became operational in 1968, is fairly typical in composition. It was initially composed of three representatives from the Internal Revenue Service, six attorneys from QCR, and one representative from each of the Secret Service, Bureau of Customs, Immigration and Naturalization Service, Department of Labor and the Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs. 

While the Federal Bureau of Investigation was not formally represented, it worked closely with the Strike 326/ Force.

The orientation (the beginning phase) of a strike force is in- 327/ volved chiefly with identification of groups to be investigated and consideration of the various statutes which may be employed as a potential 328/ basis for prosecution. As originally conceived, the pooling of information and the identification of potential targets was to be accomplished by the Department of Justice representatives. In operation, much or most of the data was volunteered, in accordance with the volunteering procedure

1 hereinafter discussed, from IRS files by the Service's Strike Force repre- 329/ sentatives.

The next stage has been described as that of intelligence gather- 330/ ing and investigation with emphasis on the inter-agency exchange of information. The grand jury stage, directed by the strike force attorney, follows. The association of the strike force attorney with the case at the investigative stage, and the familiarity he acquires with the evidence as a result, will presumably make him better able to present the complex evidence 332/ involved to the grand jury or court. 

The original supplement of the Internal Revenue Manual dealing with Internal Revenue Service participation in strike forces states that the "program was] designed to strike a blow at key members of the under- 333/ world." The activity of the Intelligence Division is divided generally into programs related to Taxpayers in General (TPG) and the Special Enforcement Program (SEP). The latter is subdivided into four categories, 341/ the most significant of which is the Strike Force Program. Strike

Statistical data nonetheless supports the claim that the results

obtained in the Strike Force Program are better than those which relate to TPG, the general Intelligence effort. Force cases, The disparity is not always this great, however. In fiscal

During fiscal 1973 and 1974 Strike Forces ob- 346/ tained convictions in 1,803 cases, of which 296 were for tax offenses. Since its inception, one of the difficulties in the Strike Force Program has been the relationship of the Strike Force attorney to the United States Attorneys. The presence of the generally autonomous Strike Force attorneys was resented by the U.S. attorneys, who "didn't want outsiders coming 347/ in and running their cases for them." Guidelines governing inter-relationships between Strike Forces and United States Attorneys' offices 348/ were established in 1970, presumably to reduce friction. The guidelines noted "that the government must present a unified front against organized crime and the necessity of complete cooperation must be recognized by all personnel in both the Strike Forces and the United States Attorneys' 349/ Offices." 350/ The Strike Force was made "responsible for supervising all federal investigations of organized crime matters. .. and for coordinating such investigations with state and local efforts against organized crime. 

Federal investigative agencies were instructed to refer organized crime 351/ cases directly to the Strike Force. United States Attorneys were to decide jurisdictional disputes, but the Chief of the Strike Force was pere 352/ mitted to appeal to the Criminal Division of the Department of Justice. 

Although the United States Attorney is to be kept fully advised of investigative operations, the chain of command runs "from the Attorney General to the Assistant Attorney General, Criminal Division, to the Chief of the Strike 353/ Force, to the investigating personnel assigned to the Strike Force.

" At

indictment hearings, the Chief of the Strike Force operates under the direc tion of the United States attorneys although "the matter shall be handled by attorneys assigned to the Strike Force unless the Chief of the Strike 354/ Force requests assignment to the United States Attorneys.' 

The guidelines, thus, made the "strike forces . . . basically independent from the 355/ local U.S. Attorney's office." Although this may have been intended to free "the young tigers from the political pressures which inevitably infect a U.S. attorney's office. . . the idea has never been very popular with U.S. 356/ attorneys around the country." 

The problem again came to the fore when a group of United States Attorneys, led by U.S. Attorney Richard Thornburgh of Pittsburgh (now the 

Assistant Attorney General in charge of the Criminal Division), recommended that Strike Forces be placed under the direct supervision of the United States Attorneys. In geographical areas where organized criminal activities were prominent, it was suggested that Strike Forces became "separately funded organized crime units within the U.S. Attorney's office, retaining the ti- 357/ tle of 'Strike Force' for public recognition purposes." In response, then 

Attorney General Saxbe named William M. Hoiles, his Administrative Assistant, to chair a committee to study the controversy. 

With respect to the rationale behind Strike Forces ("both stated and unstated, formal and informal"), the resulting Hoiles Report noted that an "early rationale for the strike force concept was the constant flux that 358/ characterizes many U.S. Attorneys' offices." It was found that the high turnover in personnel was due to the "lures of private practice" and "changes

in political administrations at the national level," which had been samewhat compensated for by the development in some offices of career staffs of "highly competent Assistant U.S. Attorneys. 

359/ Resolving a point vigorously contested by the United States Attorneys, the report next concluded that because organized crime activities are nationwide they "cannot be addressed by a single U.S. Attorney's office having limited territorial jurisdiction, but must be controlled from a 360/ centralized organizational location. 

A third rationale for the separate existence of Strike Forces found by the report was that the "fight against organized crime requires the cooperation and sustained effort of several agencies under one 'um- 361/ brella' organization, and the melding of legal and investigative efforts. 

Organized crime offenses frequently involve criminal statutes, particularly the revenue laws, administered by agencies other than the Department of Justice. For this part, the Strike Forces have made available to those agencies which themselves lack extensive investigative or prosecutorial resources the full weight of Federal authority in implementing and carrying 362/ forth their own enforcement responsibilities." 

The Hoiles Committee determined that U.S. Attorneys' offices could divert sufficient resources to meet this burden without detriment to other prosecutive responsibili- 363/ ties.

Strike Forces, thus, "permit the establishment of the independent, sustained, investigative capability necessary for adequate case development and unremitting effort against organized crime. while reducing 364/ "1 to a minimum the "bureaucratic jealousies and suspicions" that might otherwise exist. 365/

19 3667 It

The Hoiles report concluded that the basic concept and structure of the Strike Forces "were originally, and continue to be, sound. concluded that the weaknesses of the Strike Forces "are operational rather 367/ than structural."
