2. Problems with Disclosure and Use of Confidential Income

Tax Information for Investigative Purposes. 

We now turn to the legal administrative problems involved in using tax returns for investigative purposes. They are legion. a. 

Constitutional Problems. 

(1) The Fifth Amendment. 

By far the most serious problem involved in the use of income tax returns for non-tax investigations is the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination. The preparation and filing of truthful and accurate tax returns is compelled for reasons unrelated to criminal law. Subsequent exploitation of information in the returns for prosecutorial purposes in non-tax proceedings raises a difficult question of the scope of the privilege in a mandatory self-assessment 387/ taxation scheme. 

Until the recent Garner case, 328/ no court had squarely faced the issues surrounding introduction of tax information in non tax criminal 389/ prosecutions.

Garner was prosecuted for Federal gambling violations. 

The principal items of evidence were his tax returns, which revealed that almost all of his incane was derived from wagering. On first hearing, a 390/ divided Ninth Circuit panel overturned the conviction, concluding that the defendant faced a substantial hazard of self-incrimination as a result of the introduction into evidence of the tax returns. A rehearing en banc

392/ 73 followed, and the Ninth Circuit vacated the earlier opinion in a 7-5 decision. The majority concluded that the Fifth Amendment privilege should have been claimed at the time the return was filed. Having failed 391/ to do so, Garner could not do so at trial. Garner's petition to the 

United States Supreme Court for certiorari was granted on February 27, 1975. 

The variegated problems of the Garner situation and ramifications of the Ninth Circuit holding are discussed hereinafter. (a) Obligation to file returns--relation privilege against self-incrimination. 393/ In United States v. Sullivan, the taxpayer sought to justify his failure to file on the ground that a correct return would have revealed his illegal business and thus would have violated his privilege against giving compelled testimony against himself. Indicating that the taxpayer might have claimed the privilege on his return, the court did not excuse the failure to file. There is little reason to think that the Sullivan case would be decided differently today. To hold otherwise would impose the same intolerable burdens on tax administration since the law should apply to income derived from both legal and illegal sources. We note, however, that the level of confidentiality given tax data in 1927 (when Sullivan was decided) was far greater than it is today. The significantly more active market in tax return information lends weight to the assertion that filing tax returns confronts the taxpayer with sub- 394/ stantial hazards of self-incrimination" which did not exist half a century ago.

A significant corollary of Sullivan is that the privilege is not violated if the return is used in connection with a criminal tax prose- 395/ cution.

The offense in such a case would be a falsehood inherent in the return. Administration of the revenue laws would be impossible without adequate sanctions for failure to comply with them. Government could not exist. However, incrimination under the revenue laws by a deceptive statement on the tax return is far different from the non-tax incrimination which arises out of truthful information which the revenue laws compel. (b) At what point must privilege be claimed?

Although the possibility of incrimination does not void the obligation to file, neither should the obligation to file force the taxpayer to incriminate himself. The majority in Garner avoided the dilemma by concluding that the privilige should be claimed when the return is filed. The Court did not specifically hold that filing the 396/ return without asserting the privilege constituted a waiver, though it 397/ did say that the privilege could not be invoked "retrospectively. was thus unavailable to exclude the introduction at trial of answers previ- 398/ ously given.

It 

The Garner minority proposed a "use immunity" approach: since the taxpayer may not assert the privilege to avoid filing, his compelled re- 399/ turn and any evidence resulting therefrom should be excluded at trial. 

The time for objection was therefore at trial, because the objective of the Fifth Amendment is "to prevent the exercise of governmental power which might remove the prosecutorial burden from the government and place it on 400/ defendants.

" That purpose is "accomplished by the exclusion of evidence--

E! El answers which are or have been compelled out of the mouth of the person against whom they are sought to be used." 401/ (c) Application of privilege in the self-assessment context.

The application of the privilege against self-incrimination to regulatory self-disclosure inquiries has been the subject of several United States Supreme Court decisions. 402/ If the inquiries were designed to elicit information from a group "inherently suspect of criminal activities in "an area permeated with criminal statutes" (e.g., Communist Party members, gamblers, or owners of illegal firearms) and the government's prosecutorial motivation was high, the privilege has 403/ been held to be applicable. In such circumstances, "it can scarcely be denied that the obligation to [do the act or make the statement required] created 'real and appreciable', and not merely imaginary and un- In a second category of • · · substantial', hazards of self incrimination." 404/ cases concerning questions, neutral on their face, and put to the public at large, the Supreme Court has not permitted the privilege to excuse a re- 405/ fusal to answer.

If the privilege operated on Form 1040, the taxpayer 406/ would be the sole judge of his claim of privilege.

This consideration is dissipated when the questions are directed to a group "inherently suspect", concerning an area "permeated with criminal statutes", in which the Court "could be far more certain that the reason for the refusal to file or report 407/ was that the answers called for may have been incriminating.

The Garner majority reconciled this tension in favor of the government's need to know and against the privilege against self-incrimination, viewing the interrogatory of the individual income tax form as derived from a non-prosecutorial government interest and directed to the public at large (rather than to a specific, possible criminal group). In Califor- 408/ nia v. Byers, which the Garner majority found analogous, the defendant was prosecuted for refusal to comply with a California statute requiring those involved in automobile accidents to stop and give their names and addresses. The statute provided no immunity fram use of the information in a subsequent criminal prosecution. The California Supreme 

Court held that if Byers would incriminate himself by stopping and identifying himself, the privilege applied absent an immunity against use of in- 409/ formation so obtained. However, the four-Justice majority found the privilege inapplicable on two alternate grounds. First, taking into consideration the statute's non-criminal purpose (the promotion of personal financial responsibility for accidents), and the direction of the questions to the general public, the disclosures were not sufficiently "incriminating.' Second, the disclosures required were essentially non-testimonial: for the driver to stop was similar to standing in a line-up, and identification is "an essentially neutral act." The Garner minority similarly read Byers as being "controlled by Sullivan . . . since the non-criminal interests in obtaining a driver's identity outweigh the danger of incrimination drivers face as a class, the privilege cannot be asserted as a defense for failing to answer even if [the driver] faces a substantial risk of incrimination." Thus, the Ninth Circuit would unanimously agree that 411/ 410/

the privilege does not apply to permit a failure to answer "whenever the neutral interest is receiving the answers outweigh the dangers of incrim- 412/ ination posed to the class The disagreement lay in whether the • • privilege could thereafter be asserted to preclude the introduction of such compelled "neutral" answers into evidence in a criminal prosecution. 

The minority thought the privilege 'must be available to reconcile the requirement that regulatory inquiries be answered with the need 413/ for constitutional protection." Its "use immunity" approach seems a "rational accomodation between the imperatives of the privilege and the 414/ They legitimate demands of government to campel citizens to testify." will now presumably be balanced by the Supreme Court. If it were to adopt the view of the minority in Garner; the Fifth Amendment would quite probably constitute an insurmountable obstacle to the continuation of use of tax 415/ data by Strike Forces or other investigators. 

Such a solution is analogous to those in which the government confers a benefit on condition that the recipient surrender a constitutionally guaranteed right. In such instances, the doctrine of unconstitutional conditions will vitiate the condition. 416/ Similarly, the government presents taxpayers a Hobson's Choice, ie, the "benefit" of not being prosecuted for tax fraud if incriminating information is truthfully divulged. (d) Use Immunity as the Taxpayer's Remedy in a Compelled Information Situation. 

In Marchetti v. United States, the Supreme 

Court seriously considered restricting the use by Federal and State author-

417/ ities of information obtained from wagering tax returns. The court thought that to do so would preserve the delicate balance between the taxing powers of the government and the "constitutional restrictions which attend the exercise of those powers." If wagering tax information was inadmissible in criminal prosecutions, the defendant would be protected as 418/ if the privilege itself were applicable. 

But the court did not adopt this "use restriction" because it 419/ was "quite plain that Congress intended information obtained as a consequence of registration. .Itol be provided to interested prosecuting authorities." 

Consequently, "use restrictions would directly preclude effectuation of a significant element of Congress' purpose in adopting the wagering taxes." 

Instead, it invalidated the statutory framework. 420/ The question presented by Gamer is whether a "use immunity" similar to that considered in Marchetti would frustrate the purpose of the income tax laws requiring disclosure. That question should be answered in the negative. There is nothing to suggest that Congress intended income tax return information to be used for non-tax law enforcement purposes. Imposition of use restrictions thus would not frustrate any known Congressional purpose. Consequently, the judiciary could well forbid use of income tax data in non-tax criminal cases as the best means of "relieving the tension that exists between. . .the privilege and the strong governmental inter- 421/ ests in obtaining information, to say nothing of government's need for 422/ revenues.

A "use immunity" is a compromise 11 between complete protection and no protection, between the right to remain silent and the Government's right to compel incriminating information for valid Government purposes.

mission,

Exactly this approach was employed in Murphy v. Waterfront Cam- 423/ Incriminating information was demanded under circumstances which assured immunity from prosecution under State law. However, the defendant was prosecuted under Federal law. The Court held that neither the compelled information nor its fruits could be used in connection with a 424/ Federal prosecution. The Fifth Amendment did not, however, provide immunity from the Federal prosecution: it prohibited only the use of the compelled information therein. 425/ 427/ In situations such as Byers 428/ A "use immunity" of the sort approved in Murphy imposes a heavy burden on the prosecutor, who must demonstrate that the evidence he seeks 426/ to introduce was obtained independently of information which has became inadmissible due to use restrictions. "the police served both data-gathering and prosecutorial functions--hence the difficulty of proving that information compelled had not been used." 

Similarly, the prosecutorial access to tax records is such that a showing of "no taint" might be difficult. The significant question is whether the prosecution could show that the evidence offered was obtained independently from tax information submitted by the taxpayer to the Internal Revenue Service. Presumably, the prosecutor could show, even under the present practice, that the defendant's return had not been requested and that the evidence offered was therefore untainted. Considering the level of cooperation, however, between the Internal Revenue Service and other agencies, such assertion might meet with some skepticism from the bench, especially in cases 429/ brought by the Strike Force attorney.

He and his staff are regularly

consulting with Internal Revenue Service personnel, and the requisite independence may be impossible to show.

On the other hand, there would appear to be no difficulty (except 430/ for the negative effect on the Service's administration of the tax laws) with making available to the Department of Justice information obtained by the agent directly from third parties without the aid of any information supplied by the taxpayer in his return. However, the nature of the information involved and the tendency to comingle data in investigative files may render the prosecutor incapable of showing that the evidence offered was not from the taxpayer's return. The most obvious way of removing this proof problem is, of course, to stop the flow of all tax information gathered by 431/ the Internal Revenue Service to other agencies for investigative purposes. (e) Effect of Taxpayer's "Lack of Possession" of 

Incriminating Data. 

In Couch v. United States, 432/ the Supreme Court held that the privilege against self-incrimination did not apply to tax records in the possession of the defendant's accountant. The privilege was 433/ said to adhere "to the person, not to information that may incriminate him." 

Since the summons was directed to the taxpayer's accountant, there was no "[i]nquisitorial pressure coercion . . . compelling [the taxpayer], against her will, to utter self-condemning words or produce incriminating docue 434/ ments.

Couch poses the question whether the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination is applicable to incriminating information not

seized directly from the taxpayer by the investigator or prosecutor. 

Put another way, does the privilege attach to tax returns requisitioned from the Internal Revenue Service? Couch apparently does not establish 435/ "possession" as the litmus of Fifth Amendment applicability. The

Court instead seemed to rely on Couch's expectation that the accountant would not keep the information confidential but would comply with the 436/ duty to reveal the information in an honest and full return. the Court said, Couch was "seek[ing] extensions of constitutional protections against self-incrimination in the very situation where obligations of disclosure exist. 437/ Hence,

Unlike Couch's voluntary transfer of information to the accountant, the taxpayer's compelled disclosure to the Internal Revenue Service is probably made in the reasonable expectation that his return will be kept confidential. In Couch, there was "no semblance of govern- 438/ mental compulsion against the person of the accused" because the campulsion ran against the accountant, not Couch. The same can not be said of tax data, which is extracted under the compulsion of a legitimate governmental need and then made available to another agency for a purpose unconnected with that for which it was collected. While some have argued that Couch "repudiates the view that the Fifth Amendment privilege protects 439/ interests in privacy,' the repudiation may not attach where the personal 440/ 10 compulsions upon the accused [are] substantially intact. Surely, such language includes tax information compelled from a taxpayer for the purpose of tax administration. 441/

(£) The Volunteering of Tax Information. 

We noted earlier that many transfers of information to the Department of Justice (particularly to Strike Forces) are preceded by a communication from the Service identifying the taxpayer and stating that the Service has information concerning criminal activity by the taxpayer.

The fact that the Service "volunteers" the information should not change the analysis, but indeed make it apply a fortiori. Situations in which the Service induces the request fram Justice by identifying the target differ from those in which Justice identifies the target and requests information without knowing whether it is incriminating. Information volunteered by the Service will always relate to a specific, identifiable offense if some evidence of commission exists. Requests from Justice for tax data, unsuggested by IRS, constitute mere "fishing expeditions" in search of evidence to support a supposition of same yet unspecified offense. 

While the practice of volunteering tax data may at first blush seem less fishy, it is far more objectionable. On a practical level, the 

Internal Revenue Service may evolve into an all-purpose investigative body, 442/ sniffing out offenses of all kinds from compelled evidence. On the constitutional level, there is a far more insidious potential, if the information compelled from the taxpayer will be used against him. (2) The Right to be Let Alone and to be Secure in "Papers and Effects".

The dissemination of tax data given in confidence by the taxpayer raises the issues of infringement of the right to

privacy and the Fourth Amendment right of persons to be "secure in their persons, houses, papers and effects, against unreasonable searches and seizures." 443/ While the right of privacy is not explicit in the Constitution, the Supreme Court has consistently ruled that such a right is inherent in 444/ the document, particularly to protect individual pursuits. We are here concerned, however, with part of "the claim of individuals, groups or institutions to determine for themselves when, how and to what extent infor- 445/ mation about them is communicated to others. In the case of tax return data, the right of privacy might perhaps be said to be inherent, though unexpressed, in the Fourth Amendment. 446/ The question whether information is within Fourth Amendment protections has been held to hinge on a proprietary interest in the information, Thus, a depositor has been held to have no proprietary interest in his bank 447/ records. There are distinctions between records of voluntary bank deposits and compelled tax returns, however. The information contained in the return, and not the return itself, is the taxpayer's property, being an extension of his books and records which are protected by the Fourth Amendment. This apparent truism permits the avoidance of nice questions regarding ownership 448/ of tax returns and tax return information. 

Furthermore, the Fourth Amendment seems more concerned with privacy 449/ 450/ in the sense of control than ownership over information. In Katz v. U. S., the Supreme Court held that the electronic surveillance of a telephone booth 77-842 O 76 - 60

violated the Fourth Amendment and described the defendant's interest as 451/ the existence of "privacy upon which he justifiably relies.

" Ignoring 452/ the issue of proprietary interest in the telephone booth, the Court focused on the defendant's "constitutionally justified expectations of 453/ privacy." Subsequently, in U. S. v. White, the Supreme Court refused to give Fourth Amendment protection to statements made by the defendant to an accomplice who was outfitted with an electronic transmitter. The defendant could not, the Court held, justifiably expect "that a person with whom he is conversing will not then or later reveal the conversation 454/ to the police.' The cynosure of White was also control over information as the interest which is involved, however, and the relationship of accomplices is clearly distinguishable from that of a taxpayer to his govern- While those engaged in illegal activity may not justifiably rely upon the loyalty of their colleagues, taxpayers submitting data to an agency charged with revenue administration justifiably expect that the agency will use the information obtained only for the purpose for which it was intended. 

In determining whether expectations of privacy are "constitutionally justified," cases after Katz have examined the individual's degree of control over the information he gives. Tax returns are protected by a statute making tax returns confidential and punishing their dislosure by government employees. This creates control over the information and certainly justifies an expectation of privacy. 455/ Another Supreme Court case analogous to the collection and dissemination of tax returns for investigative purposes is Laird v. Tatum.

Plaintiffs there attacked the Constitutionality of the maintenance of a data collection and storage system by the Army to collect data on the membership, ideology, and practices of "activist groups." The data thus obtained was allegedly distributed to civilian officials in Federal, state, and local governments. Although the plaintiffs alleged that the collection and distribution of the information had a "chilling" effect on their exercise of Constitutional rights, the Supreme Court, in a 5-4 decision, found that without same showing of tangible injury, there could be no justifiable harm. The Court opined that "specific present objective 456/ harm or a threat of specific future harm" must be occasioned by the accumulation and circulation of data to afford justiciability. Importantly, the material collated by the Army was neither confidential nor compelled, as is tax return data; rather, its sources were public meetings and the media. 

Privacy and the Fourth Amendment were again considered by the 457/ Supreme Court in California Bankers Association v. Shultz, which held that the record-keeping and reporting provisions of the Bank Secrecy Act of 1974, which are designed to obtain financial information having "a high degree of usefulness in criminal, tax, or regulatory proceedings" did not violate the Fourth Amendment. The Act required banks to report currency transactions exceeding $10,000 and certain foreign commercial transactions. 

This information, said the Court, was so specific and limited and so related to the possibility of wrongdoing as to not infringe upon the Fourth Amendment. 458/

The limited information reported pursuant to the Bank Secrecy Act bears no similarity to that found on tax returns. The department or agency obtaining a tax return receives the broadest conceivable range of financial data, much of which has no particular connection to supposed misconduct. If the Internal Revenue Service were to turn over to investigative agencies limited information tentatively determined to have a relationship to illegal activity, it might came within the rule announced 459/ in California Bankers. The practice is, however, for the investigative agency to receive the entire return, frequently without any specific notion of what item on the return will be indicative of possible illegal conduct. 

The Constitutionality of such sweeping access to confidential financial information is questionable. 460/ 

Of course, the Fourth Amendment protects against "seizures."

While the filing of the return may not strictly be a seizure, the information is certainly coerced; any use of it for non-tax purposes might be said to raise the coercion to a seizure and thus illegal unless the investigative agency were able to obtain a search warrant by establishing probable cause, e.g., circumstances sufficient for the magistrate to determine that an offense has been committed and that the return is likely to contain data 461/ which will assist in the investigation. 

Aside from the privacy argument founded on Constitutional prin- 462/ ciples, one is also permitted by general policy considerations. Data obtained from the taxpayer by statutory mandate for a specific purpose 463/ should not be a "generalized govermental asset.

" Given the sanctity

which people attach to their income tax returns, it would seem to be sound governmental policy to cloak that return with privacy rather than open "endless doors for official access. fear of information systems and data banks 11 465/ 464/ The widespread is a compelling reason to insure that personal financial testimony compelled for the ostensible purpose of revenue administration, is not accessible by any other information system. 

(3) Discriminatory Enforcement of the Tax Laws. 

466 In Yick Wo. v. Hopkins, the Supreme Court recognized that consciously discriminatory enforcement of a statute, equal and fair on its face, may result in a denial of equal protection 467/ of the laws.

Selective enforcement occurs when there is an uneven allocation of investigative and prosecutorial resources against certain classes of putative violators based on religion, race, etc. But selective enforcement is condemned only if this uneven allocation 468/ is not reasonable in light of the statutory purposes. 

Unquestionably, the Internal Revenue Service now allocates proportionately greater resources to its Special Enforcement Programs, such as Strike Forces and Narcotics Traffickers, than it does to the public in general. The question to be answered, however, is whether there is evidence that this uneven allocation is reasonable considering the purpose of the tax criminal law. In other words, is there reason to believe that persons suspected of receiving income from organized crime activities are more likely to commit tax crimes? 469/ Available evidence shows that tax violations are more prevalent 470/ among this group than in others.

However, the ratio of investigations

and prosecutions of organized crime targets to investigations and prosecutions of other taxpayers may be disproportionately greater than the ratio of violations between the two groups. Potential tax violations in a self-assessment system run across the full spectrum of reporting tax- Yet there is a proportionately greater allocation of manpower to 471/ payers. such cases, but the percentage of completed cases resulting in prosecution in the special enforcement progran area is not that much greater than the percentage of prosecution cases produced by the general enforce- 472/ ment program. 

While these figures may not compel the conclusion that there is an unreasonable allocation of Intelligence resources to SEP, they do at least raise the possibility. b. Statutory Problems. 473/ While the legislative history of $ 6103 has been recounted in some detail, some repetition is necessary at this point. The antecedent of present $ 6103 seems to have been an ineffective attempt to reverse 1909 legislation which attempted to give corporate tax returns the status of public documents. The amendment perversely continued to denominate the returns "public records," though confidentiality was intended. The administrator relied on the intent. Corporate returns were opened to inspection by other agencies, but individual returns remained cloistered within the Service. The first breach of the confidentiality of individual returns was committed by 1914 regulations which made them available for use in litigation to which the United States was a party. General access by all agencies was permitted beginning in 1920.

1 There was then from the beginning the notion that returns were confidential. This idea undoubtedly drew upon the Civil War experience. 

However, by 1920, there had begun a process of administrative erosion of the confidentiality principle which was to turn tax returns into generalized government assets. Congress did not object, but it rejected efforts to open returns to further inspection by statute. Given this fact and the ·2 mythology that tax returns are fully confidential, there seems little to justify the exploitation of tax returns for investigative purposes, parti- 474/ cularly on a dragnet basis. As things now stand, the language of the statute is more consistent with mythology than practice. Certainly, also, there is no use which is more at war with confidentiality than is the investigative use. Disclosures which the Internal Revenue Code proclaims as confidential and compels on pain of prison are used to investigate possible reasons to imprison.

As previously noted, tax information is requested by Justice only after the Service suggests it do so. The Service circumvents the ban on 475/ disclosure contained in § 1905 of Title 18 with the dubious rationale 476/ that it does not apply to the "identity" of the person but only to the identity of trade secrets, formulas, and confidential information, While the Service's reading of § 1905 is strained at best, it argues in the alternative that disclosure of evidence of a crime cannot be an unauthorized disclosure. The latter argument is perhaps less labored than the first, 477/ but the Service can point to no statute authorizing such disclosure.

Statutory support for its inter-agency releases of confidential, incriminating information may be nonexistent. 

The cases seem not to have questioned the statutory authorization for such disclosure. Moreover, at least one court has held that the regulations promulgated to safeguard confidential tax data need 478/ a nontax not be scrupulously observed. In United States v. Tucker, criminal case, the defendant moved to suppress certain evidence on the ground the tax data was wrongfully supplied to the Department of Justice by the Internal Revenue Service. During the course of a tax investigation, IRS agents noted information indicating possible violations of Federal law relating to procuring loans for third parties from banking institutions. The Department of Justice was informed that the Internal 

Revenue Service possessed such information and that it would be forthcoming if requested. In its response to the Service, the Department of Justice set forth the name and address of the taxpayer and requested the information. The letter did not designate the kind of tax, the periods involved, and reasons for the request, all of which are required by the regulation (S 301.6103 (a) -1 (g)) under which disclosure was made. 

The court conceded the failure to observe the regulations. 

However, the obvious reason for the request was "further investigation." 

Hence, only the designation of kinds of tax and taxable periods were missing. These requirements, the court decided, "could not be literally complied with due to the unusual method by which the investigation arose. 

The court ruled that the "requirements were designed within the spirit 479/ 480/

of the statutes to prevent the Justice Department, or any other agency seeking such information, from engaging in a fishing expedition with respect to a particular taxpayer," and concluded that "expressly or by implication in the totality of the correspondence, [the request] fulfilled all the essential requirements. .. 481/ 

Thus, without ruling on the validity of the regulation prescribing the conditions of disclosure, the court sustained a disclosure made not in compliance with the regulations. It is, thus, difficult to obtain judicial assistance 482/ in obtaining compliance with their terms.

C. 

Administrative Problems - Imperilment of Internal Revenue Service Administrative Objectives. 

Ever since "tax problems got Al Capone" there has been a vague awareness in the public consciousness that the Internal Revenue Service, and the tax laws generally, were performing a function apart from the raising of revenue. Even more aware were law enforcement officers and public leaders, who "began to see in Internal Revenue a useful tool that they could apply not only to organized crime, but to other areas of criminal activity which were difficult to detect and to 483/ prosecute under traditional law enforcement methods. 

They did so utilize the Service, but without much thought about its effect on the agency's primary obligation. 484/ Recently, however, some serious thought has been given to In the impact of non-tax law enforcement on revenue administration. 

August of 1974, Commissioner Alexander noted that the Service's participation in the Strike Forces and information-gathering through the

485/ 486/ Special Service Staff were examples where tax administration had strayed from its proper path. The emphasis on nontax criminal enforcement could, in Commissioner Alexander's words, "be jeopardizing our traditional tax administration processes, both from the standpoint of the most effective use of our resources and from the standpoint of 487/ the public's faith in an impartial, non-political tax system. the Commissioner, of necessity, spoke in general terms, we now turn to a more detailed discussion of the jeopardy in which the Service's places its objectives by disclosing tax information for general investigative use. 11 While 

(1) Effect on Internal Revenue Service General Enforcement Program. 

The Intelligence Division of the Service has responsibility for discovering tax crimes. The Division has a goal of creating the "maximum positive impact on the compliance attitudes and practices of taxpayers. into two parts. 488/ 11 The Division has divided its program The Taxpayers in General (TPG) program is aimed at the public. 

One of the chief criteria for TPG case selection is the outlook for 489/ successful prosecution.

Another, however, is that they be cases of "significance" in which "prosecution may have a widespread deterrent or corrective effect." 490/ Intelligence personnel have been urged, therefore, to work "cases of significance, or high impact with less certainty of conviction. . .in preference to minor cases with more certainty 491/ of conviction!

The other hemisphere of the Intelligence effort is the Special Enforcement Program (SEP), which constitutes the Service's participation "in the federal effort against persons receiving income from illegal activities." 492/ "1 493/ 494/ In the fiscal year 1972, the Special Enforcement Program and the general program were said to be of equal importance but that "as first priority, we will fulfill our commitment to the enforcement of cases arising from...the Treasury Narcotics Program and the Strike Forces.

The following fiscal year, the Division said it would "give top priority to our participation in strike forces," in which "[o] ur objective is to participate with other federal agencies in concentrating our enforcement efforts on designated organized crime subjects in selected target cities." 

The latter objective is notable for its lack of relationship to tax administration, being simply to "participate" in a joint criminal investigation. The Intelligence Division's program letter for fiscal 1974, however, reversed the priorities, giving pre-eminence to the General Program. 

In addition, it was decided to limit direct investigative time allotted 496/ to SEP and information gathering to fiscal 1973 levels. These changes no doubt reflect the increasing concern, exemplified by Commissioner Alexander, over the role of the Service in criminal enforcement work generally. The Special Enforcement Program remains but with greater 497/ emphasis on tax law violations. 

The criminal enforcement program straddles TPG and SEP. 

Of course, only a small percentage of returns can be examined. Thus, a highly publicized program of criminal enforcement arguably might go a good distance 495/

toward encouraging the rank and file compliance on which hinges the entire self-assessment system of taxation. The question, however, is whether the operation of such a program, which has quite different 498/ objectives from those of the general program and which siphons off a good deal of manpower, runs at cross purposes with the Service's general enforcement objectives.

Perhaps the first step in answering this question is a determination of whether objectives of SEP generally, and of the Strike Force program specifically, serve to enhance the general enforcement program of the Service. There is grave doubt that the investigation, prosecution, and conviction of organized crime figures promote the objectives of the general program. The average taxpayer does not associate himself with the taxpayer in an organized crime criminal tax case. Not regarding themselves as part of the world of organized crime, general taxpayers whether or not committing tax crimes, probably do not view the Service's drive on organized crime as a threat. Indeed, they may be misled into believing that tax law prosecutions are more or less reserved for organized crime figures. This belief may be heightened by the imposition of severe sentences in organized crime tax cases, which the Service vigorously publicized. Possibly, then, the Special Enforcement Program is 499/ not having a "deterrent or corrective effect" on taxpayers generally. 

One argument suggested to counter this observation is that the public derives great satisfaction from seeing individuals involved in organized crime being called upon to bear their "share" of the tax burden and that, at least to this extent, SEP serves general Service objectives.

Since, however, the publicity normally focuses on the criminal penalty, the satisfaction probably derives more from knowing that a "criminal" has gone to jail. Further, the public concern about citizens who pay little or no tax seems more directed to legitimate "loopholes" and preferences than the tax evasion practiced by the criminal element. 500/ The argument is also made that the Service's image is enhanced by prosecuting known crime figures. The public believes, so the argument runs, that organized crime figures are not prosecuted for the non-tax crimes because there is graft, corruption, and political influence exercised on their behalf. Hence, prosecution of tax crimes suggests that the Service is the one fair and impartial agency to rise above these demeaning considerations. The hope is that this view of the 

Service carries over to its other activities. Even if we assume that the 

Service had been successful in achieving this image, recent publicity has tarnished it. Worse yet, the public has become so accustomed to the 

Service's investigation of non-tax crimes that it lumps the Service in with general law enforcement agencies. As a consequence of the Service's punitive image, even the suggestion of an audit results in causing fear and suspicion on the part of many taxpayers. Taxpayers in general apparently resent any kind of attention from the Service, which they regard as tantamount to an accusation of crime or at least dishonesty. 

One is therefore compelled to ask whether the mere existence of the SEP harms the general program. 

There are several features of the SEP which may be considered to have a detrimental effect on the General Program.

First, and quite obviously to the extent that Service personnel are assigned to work SEP cases, they will not be available for TPG, where deterrent objectives of the entire enforcement program are more fully served. Although Commissioner Alexander has placed, at a cost of causing considerable ire in the Department of Justice, a 15.7 percent limit on the Intelligence Division personnel assigned to strike forces, the level of the commitment of the Service to the Special Enforcement Program goes well beyond that. During fiscal year ending 1974 about 40 percent of Intelligence Division's manpower was assigned to 501/ SEP activities. Further, although Audit representatives have been removed from Strike Forces, considerable Audit Division time is committed 502/ to Strike Force activities since Audit Division personnel are regularly 503/ available therefor.

Second, it is appropriate to question whether SEP work affects the reputation of the Service for fair and impartial administration of the tax laws. The procedure in which the Service processes cases involving organized crime targets is distinctly different from TPG cases. 

One of the most significant is that a Strike Force criminal tax case cannot be "killed" (as can a TPG matter if the attorney thinks it is not a suitable case for prosecution) by the Service's Regional Counsel or Chief Counsel, but must be forwarded to the Department of Justice. Although, it is maintained that the Service's Counsel gives the case the same review for prosecution potential as any case, it can be questioned whether the mandatory forwarding requirement makes this

review anything but pro forma. 

Procedures thus are changed to the detriment of persons suspected of being engaged in organized crime. This 504/ deviation can hardly improve the image of equal and fair administration. 

Third, there is a belief by some that the criminal tax cases which are investigated by a Strike Force group tend to be dropped, at the indictment stage, in favor of Title 18 criminal cases. The Strike 

Force attorney, a delegate of the Department of Justice, controls the litigative functions of the Strike Force. He is anxious, generally speaking, to obtain convictions as rapidly as possible. While quite willing to do everything he can to push his cases to the head of the line for trial (something which can rebound to the Service's benefit if it is a tax case), his quest for a good record of convictions may often compel him to drop the Title 26 charges, which tend to be more complex and to take longer to try.

Fourth, a fully confidential system would presumably improve public compliance with the self reporting system. Although taxpayers do not now generally know the extent to which tax data is made available for investigative purposes, the extent to which they are becoming aware 505/ that tax information is shared must be increasing. If they were convinced the information was not shared in any way, and that the system had no leaks, most taxpayers would arguably be more inclined to report income truthfully. Put another way, if taxpayers knew that information reported on tax returns could be used only for tax purposes, there would be less reason to falsify a return where accurate information might lead to a non-tax investigation. 506/

(2) Advantages, if any, to Participation in

Strike Forces. 

In recent testimony before the Senate Finance Subcommittee on Administration of the Internal Revenue Code, the Department of Justice demonstrated a desire to retain its right to tax return information. Any cutback would be a matter of great concern 507/ to Justice. 508/ well, Although this sentiment has been evident elsewhere as there has never been any real articulation of the advantages which flow to the Department from joint investigations generally, and access to tax information specifically. An attempt to isolate the benefits uncovers three.

Obviously, Justice receives a good deal of data which it would These may be helpful in the investigation and not otherwise receive. 509/ prosecution of non-tax crimes unders its jurisdiction The second benefit to Justice is the use of investigators who are not on the Department's payroll. For Strike Forces alone, the Department has the services of the Strike Force liaison Officer (from the Intelligence Division), and of a considerable number of back-up Audit personnel with which to pursue investigative leads with tax overtones. The Audit personnel are over and above the limit placed on Intelligence Division manpower. Also if the investigative operation sours, as with Operation Leprechaun, for example, the Internal Revenue Service, not the Department of Justice suffers the adverse publicity. Finally, Service investigative personnel have available to them the administrative summons, which can be 510/ issued in a "John Doe" form and does not require the establishment

of probable cause. While there are restrictions on the extent to which this summons power can be used for purposes not connected with revenue administration, its availability in a joint investigation context does broaden the scope of information which may become available to a Strike 511/ 

Force unit.

The Service is also said to benefit. First, the Service gets "good tax cases.' The argument runs that the investigatory strength of the Strike Force unit uncovers potential tax targets, primarily with the aid of the Justice Department personnel. The resulting cases produce large proposed deficiencies. The cost of obtaining these higher deficiencies is the commitment of more manpower per case than to other Intelligence Division activity. But beyond the cost is the question 512/ whether "goodness" can be equated with the size of the deficiency. 

The answer is, obviously, that it is not. Revenue production should not be a consideration in a program of criminal enforcement. These investigations are not effective deterrents to potential tax law violations simply because they result in more revenue than do others. On the contrary, criminal tax cases coming from the Special Enforcement Programs probably do not further the objectives of the general enforcement program. Some of them may cause actual harm to those objectives. For example, in the 514/ the taxpayer reported wagering income on his tax return 

Di Varco case, 513/ as having been received from X corporation. Upon learning that the source of the income was incorrectly stated, the Service and the Department of Justice prosected Di Varco for having made a false statement on his return. 

Conviction followed. Though it may be argued that prosecution was necessary 77-842 O 7661

to insure accurate information regarding source of income, the selection of that type of case for enforcement purposes is likely to subject the Service to criticism and ridicule. 

A second alleged benefit of the Service's participation in Strike Force investigations is the supposed speedy and agressive prosecution of the criminal tax cases coming out of the Strike Force unit. 

This would give the Service faster disposition of a case than had it been handled by the United States attorney who, it is argued, has a much broader spectrum of responsibilities and is likely to have little trial experience and long term political ambitions. All these will persuade him to shy away form the complexities of a criminal tax case. On the other hand, the Strike Force attorney has no particular interest in obtaining criminal tax convictions in perference to non-tax criminal convictions. Certainly he is not imbued with the Service's concern for the establishment of a deterrent to tax crimes. His abiding concern is the establishment of a conviction record, and this creates the distinct possibility that the cases which he pursues will not be tax cases. 

In an effort to establish a strong conviction record, the Strike Force attomey may well drop the more complex criminal tax changes in order to concentrate on the more facile Title 18 cases. In so doing, he not only defeats the objectives of the Service's enforcement program but wastes much of the manpower the Service has devoted to the matter. 

In contrast, when the Service recommends prosecution of General Program cases, there is only a small chance that the case will be abandoned. 

Although the taxpayer is usually accorded a conference with the Department of

Justice, it rarely results in a decision not to proceed with the prose- 515/ cution.

When the indictment proceeds to the trial state, it will not be encumbered by non-tax counts and, hence, the temptation to surrender 516/ or bargain them away will not be present. 

It has also been asserted that the Internal Revenue Service obtains beneficial information from the Strike Force units. However, there is no evidence of a quid pro quo. There is not, as one might think would be implicit in a joint investigation, an exchange of information. The other agencies cooperating in the strike force activity (e.g., Postal Service, FBI, Department of Labor) are rarely, if ever, 517/ sources of information for the Service. 

The "information" which the Service receives is, therefore, whittled down to the identification of targets for potential tax cases which may very well not serve the 518/ ends of its enforcement program. 

A fourth argument is that organized crime operations are difficult to uncover, and their operations are quite sophisticated, thus making it difficult to investigate and prove criminal tax violations. 

Consequently, the joint investigation enables the Service to "handle" extremely difficult cases. It may be true that cases involving organized criminal interests are more difficult, but to accept the argument is to say that the Service's specially trained personnel are not capable of investigating complex cases. This is, quite obviously, something the 

Service would never admit to and, in any event, is not very likely true.

H. 

Use of Returns and Return Information by Department of Justice in 

Non-Tax Litigation. 

As previously noted, the Department of Justice may also obtain tax return information for use in litigation in any case in which the 519/ "United States is interested in the result." 

Of course, no request may be necessary because, prior to trial, the tax return information was used for investigation. In such cases, tax return information is usually not introduced into evidence at trial, but was used solely to develop leads to other evidentiary material. There are, however, a series of situations in which tax returns are used for litigation purposes, or purposes connected with that litigation, without any antecedent use for investigative purposes. 1. 

Returns of Prospective Jurors.

Examination of returns of prospective jurors has had a checkered history. When it commenced is unclear, but it first became generally known to the public following the trial of Frank Costello for income tax evasion. In that case the prosecutor requested an Internal 

Revenue agent to check the income tax returns of veniremen on the jury 520/ panel.

As a result, the prosecutor received notes concerning the prospective juror's occupation, amount and source of income, number of dependents, amount of taxes paid or refunds, and information regarding any unusual deduction. The stated purpose was "an effort to find out whether any of the prospective jurors had income tax troubles of their own 521/ or had other reasons to be unfavorably disposed to the Government.

On appeal from a conviction, the Court of Appeals found that the access was

in accord with the Treasury regulations, that the process did not result in a "specially conditioned" or "blue ribbon" panel, and that the resulting government advantage, if any, was not grounds for a new trial since "not all information properly available to the prosecution is equally available 522/ to the accused." The court in Costello did, however, focus on the question of whether the examination of returns produced a panel which was "specially conditioned" to convict, or to be biased against, the defendant. 

The court found that since the panel had no knowledge of the existence of the practice of examining returns, that no "conditioning" could have 524/ resulted. 

At most, "the practice led to challenges of jurors who might have been unduly biased in favor of the defendant" and since the "exercise of peremptory challenges is a rejective, rather than a selective, process. 525/ the appellant has no right to complaint.

' 523/ The Court of Appeals held that "[t]here would seem to be no good reason to believe that knowledge that jury service entails exposure of one's tax return to the scrutiny of a district attorney would deter a good citizen from service in the judicial establishment any more than the fierce publicity which beats upon the private affairs of the citizen appointed to high office in the executive department deters acceptance of such appointment." 

Yet, the government's brief opposing certiorari conceded that returns scanning, 527/ if known to veniremen, could lead citizens to want to avoid jury service. 

Thus, on June 27, 1958, the Tax Division of the Department of Justice directed 528/ United States Attorneys to cease scanning returns of prospective jurors. 

As a result of interest by the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue 526/

Taxation, the "scanning" of returns of prospective jurors was specifically prohibited in an amendment of the regulations. However, that same amendment blessed the practice (which may have sprung up as an alternative to scanning) of asking the Service to advise whether it had investigated any 529/ venireman.

If the response is affirmative, then bias toward the Service (or toward the United States, if the case involves matters other than taxes) is suspected. Such bias, so the argument runs, cannot be shown by the mere fact that investigation has occurred. Consequently, the United 

States Attorney then asks (apparently in contravention of the regulation 530/ against scanning) for the return itself and related documents under 531/ its investigative regulation. This information is then used on voir dire examination to direct inquiries concerning the nature of the investigation. These inquiries cannot be directed, the argument proceeds, unless the examining attorney has the prospective juror's entire tax file. For example, if the juror had forgotten about the investigation, his memory could be refreshed only if the examining attorney possessed further information concerning the investigation. If the juror is impeached, or bias is shown, then presumably the juror would be dismissed for cause and the United States would not be required to use one of its peremptory challenges. 

Laying aside the contravention of this procedure to the specific language of the regulations, the central inquiry must be concerning the 533/ wisdom of the policy which permits this access. At first blush, it might appear that such access is appropriate because it facilitates the discovery of bias against one of the litigants. Both sound judicial 532/

administration and the Constitutional requirement of a fair and impartial jury require an elimination of bias. There are, however, at least two strong arguments which can be lodged against the present practice. 

First, there is no prohibition against examining prospective jurors about their dealings, if relevant, with the Internal Revenue Service. If bias does exist, there is little likelihood that the investigation would have faded from the memory of the prospective juror. If this conclusion is accurate, then the invasion of the taxpayer's confidential return is for the single purpose of determining the veracity of a prospective juror on a narrow subject. Despite the Court's analogy in 

Costello to seekers of public office, there is a sharp distinction between a prospective Federal appointee and a venireman. In the former situation the individual involved has expressed an interest in the appointment. The bestowal of a benefit (i.e., the Federal position) is under active consideraion and a limited breach of the individual's privacy, as part of a check on his background, is at least quasi-consensual and perhaps not objectionable. 

The selection of jurors is not, however, comparable. It is a mandatory civic duty, and an individual cannot reasonably be considered to have agreed to the divulgence of personal tax information in connection with rendering this obligation. 

A second, and possibly even more significant, objection is the possible advantage to the United States resulting from information which is not available to the other party. Of course, as the court said

in Costello, not all information is equally available to both parties to a lawsuit. Further, the ends of justice are not served if any member of the jury is biased against either party, but as noted above, the discovery of bias seems not to depend on the tax information. Yet, the government obtains a great deal more information than is necessary to discover bias even if the government's argument were supportable. Rather, the government taps confidential information perhaps to structure a sociological profile of a jury and certainly to use its peremptory challenges more intelligently than the other party. These advantages could well be viewed as holding and hitting. Certainly, the defendant does not have available to him a comparable information source for the purpose of locating suspected progovernment bias. Counsel for the defendant is left only with his ingenuity and traditional voir dire examination in his quest to discern whether there 534/ is bias against his client. 

There seems little reason not to place the government on the same footing. 

2. Use of Non-Party Returns in Proceedings to Which United 

States is a Party.

The present regulations on the disclosure of tax returns provide that tax returns are available to United States Attorneys and Justice Department attorneys if the United States is "interested in the result of Federal judicial or grand jury proceedings.' 11 535/ 

The quoted language is so broad that one is hard put to imagine a situation where returns would be unavailable to the United States if it is a party to such proceedings. That is in stark contrast to the position of private litigants

who are given no privilege to examine tax data which the government has requested and received. Further, if the case is a tax case or involves "prosecution of claims and demands by, and offenses against, the United States," the return is available to the government's attorneys without so much as a written request. Consequently, there are no records regarding the volume of such requests. We surmise that such volume is not great. 

Nonetheless, such broad and trackless access raises the important policy question of whether and under what circumstances return confidentiality should be invaded by the United States to reduce its hazards of litigation. 

This issue is bound up in the Administration's bill regarding disclosure 536/ which proposes some drastic changes in existing pracof tax returns, tice and draws a distinction between tax and non-tax cases. 

In tax matters the Administration bill is exceptionally broader than the existing regulation, which is limited to Federal judicial and grand jury proceedings. The Administration proposals would govern disclosure in "a Federal or State judicial or administrative proceeding pertaining to tax administration before any Federal or State grand jury, 537/ court, department, or executive establishment. 

The term "tax administration" apparently refers to administration of both Federal and state laws. 

Tax returns of any taxpayer who is a party to such a proceeding "may be disclosed." The same is true for any other taxpayer who consents to the disclosure. 11 If a third party does not consent to the release of his return or return information, they nevertheless "may be disclosed," but only if 533/

the data "has or may have a bearing on the outcome of such proceedings" because (1) treatment of item as to a party to the proceedings may be determined, in whole or part, by reference to the treatment given the "item" in the return; (2) the return information may "relate to a transaction at issue in the proceedings;" or (3) the liability under the revenue laws for "any tax, penalty, interest, fine, forfeiture, or other imposition, or offense" which is the subject of the proceeding may be determined by reference to the infor- 539/ mation. 

The bill defines "disclosure" as "making known to any person in any manner whatever a return or return information. 540/ Hence, this data would be available to all litigants in a wide range of tax-related matters. 

Nonetheless, the purpose is to impose "strict conditions upon the use of 541/ third party returns," namely, that the returns must be transactionally related to a tax question at issue. For example, if the question before the court is whether X received income from Y, the latter's return would be obtainable for the purpose of showing that Y deducted the payment made 542/ to X. 

If the third party return is not transactionally related, but is desired only for comparability purposes, the Administration's bill would not allow the disclosure in the absence of consent by the third party. 

Thus, for example, the Administration's bill would not allow the disclosure of returns in an unreasonable compensation case to compare compensation

paid by the third party taxpayer. The underlying rationale is apparently that sound adminsitration of the tax law limits justifiable breaches of third party privacy to settings in which a direct transactional relationship between the third party and a litigant is material to the proceeding. Thus, disclosure would not be justified when there is no such connection and the third party's return is to be used only as an example of what other similarly situated taxpayers do. Even the invasion of confidentiality for the limited purpose permitted by the bill is of at least questionable wisdom if the third party is available to testify. 

But, if the third party does testify, the Administration's bill also provides that his tax returns will be available to all litigants to impeach him; if he does not testify, his return is available "to the extent necessary to impeach a witness. .as to a transaction with [the third party].' 543/ The implications of the impeachment provisions are astounding. 

Few litigants will feel adequately prepared for any kind of state or Federal tax proceeding without having critical opposition witnesses' tax returns on hand for impeachment possibilities. Information which a taxpayer has shared in supposed confidence with his government would be available to impeach him, if he testifies, or other witnesses if he does As to the taxpayer, the return would be exploited "against" him for embarrassment, contradiction, or impeachment. As to other witnesses, the return, though a sworn document, would be hearsay of the worst order because the witness may have had no control over the content of the not.

return. While invasions of tax return confidentiality to impeach, or otherwise embarrass, the taxpayer hardly seems justified, certainly the 544/ The use of a return to impeach other witnesses seems even less so. same is true even if the return is examined only to "check" the veracity of a witness.

When one considers the complex structure and multitudinous parties to transactions in which tax questions may arise, to say nothing of the vast number of cases lodged annually in the state and Federal judicial and administrative machineries, a blizzard of requests is possible. 

While these may be but "fishing expeditions," who is to say what the nets will yield? The government's trawling for Service investigation of veniremen has been conducted "in house" by the Service apparently without massive disclosure of confidential data. But the existence of impeaching material is often not known until testimony is given at trial and may involve subjective determinations arising out of careful scrutiny of available information. Hence, the fishing for impeachment materials must be accomplished before trial by the litigants themselves. To allow wholesale ramblings through tax returns by the government and private parties to discover impeaching material would render tax return "confidentiality" a sham. 

While the Service might conduct them upon request, an impossible administrative burden would result. Furthermore, private parties might not be able to specify the kind or nature of the material desired. Finally, they might not have much confidence in a search conducted by the adversary party. Thus, this provision would seem an administrative nightmare.

Given these problems, the breach of taxpayer confidentiality for impeachment purposes does not appear justified. There also seems little to be gained from such use. Hence, it does not seem appropriate to require that each person responding to a mandatory call to testify in a tax case bear the risk of having his tax return examined. Some comfort may be taken, however, from the provision of the Administration's bill that the Secretary may refuse to divulge tax returns or data if to do so 545/ would "seriously impair the administration of the Federal tax law." 

It may be that the Administration proposal would create just the situation described.

The intention to put the private litigant on the same footing as the government regarding access to tax returns in tax conflict resolution proceedings is laudable. But, the Administration opens up a Pandora's 

Box in permitting examination of non-party tax returns by all sides. The ideal of equalizing the resources available to the government and other litigants might instead be achieved by removing all availability of thirdparty tax returns. One can only speculate why this was not done. A reason may be found in the close relationship between the Service and the Justice Department, which represents the Service in trial and appellate litigation outside the Tax Court. This is a relationship which the Service may not wish to jeopardize, and Justice has traditionally been the heaviest user of tax return data for investigative purposes. One may speculate that the 

Administration provision was drafted in the form it was out of motivations to continue the harmony between these two agencies. That circumvented the problem, but the cost of so doing is potentially a much worse blow to tax

administration. Indeed, the real solution may be to discontinue Justice's representation of Internal Revenue, but that is an issue far beyond the scope of this report.

The Administration's bill also allows access to third party returns in proceedings before any Federal grand jury, court, department, agency, or executive establishment "pertaining to a specifically designated Federal statute (not involving tax administration)" to which the United States or one of its instrumentalities is a party. 546/ Again, the information may be allowed to any party, and for impeachment purposes to the same extent as in tax cases. However, the return of a non-consenting third party may otherwise be obtained only if the information may affect the outcome of the proceeding because (1) there was a transactional relationship between him and a party to the proceeding, or (2) the party to the proceeding is a successor in interest to the taxpayer. 

There is good reason to limit availability of tax return data in non-tax proceedings. Certainly, there is less reason to allow use where no question of tax administration is involved. Rather, in such cases, the tax return appears merely to be the quickest and easiest means of obtaining certain evidence. That hardly justifies the invasion of taxpayer confidentiality suggested by the bill. It will make the administrative burden to the Internal Revenue Service greater. 

Administration's proposal seems unsound.
