C. Basis for Request by Non-Tax Committees. 

During 1970, the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation surveyed the non-tax committees to obtain information from them regarding the reasons for requests to inspect income tax returns. Information concerning procedures designed to assure confidentiality was also sought. 

In general, the survey revealed that these committess used examination rights only sparingly and procedures had been adopted to protect the 553/ information obtained. 

The following responses received from the committees is useful in describing the kinds of situations in which Congressional committees request returns.

House Banking and Currency Committee 

"This Committee has requested the right to inspect income tax returns only once since Mr. Patman became Chairman of the 

Committee. This authority was not, however, utilized. Mr. 

Patman assures, however, that if such information is 'needed subsequently, you may rest assured that the information would be treated with the greatest degree of confidentiality and with the greatest safeguards. ""(Letter of Chairman Wright 

Patman to Chairman Mills, October 16, 1970)

House Government Operations Committee 

"No policy has been prescribed regarding security measures for income tax returns requested by the Committee on Government Operations. However, they are afforded adequate protection. 

Only those staff members, both professional and clerical, who

have a need to know are given access to the returns.

"1 

(Letter of Chairman Chet Holifield, Novermer 23, 1970) Returns have been requested by this Committee to assist in the investigations of Billy Sol Estes and of the FDA's efficiency in carrying out its responsibilities in the drug regulation area. 

House Committee on Internal Security 

"Committee Resolutions have been passed requesting. . .returns.. concerning the Students for a Democratic Society, the Black Panther Party, the New Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam, the Progressive Labor Party, and certain named officers in these groups. . .Each such resolution called for a complete investigation of the organization, including its sources of funds." Letter of Chairman Richard H. Ichord, October 29, 1970. 

Information from tax returns is retained (permanently) in a separate file system and is not generally available to staff members. 

House Committee on Public Works 

"Inspection of income tax returns has been done after careful consideration.

Information secured has been available only to investigative staff personnel and key Members on a need-to-know basis." 

(Letter of Chairman John A. Blatnik, May 7, 1971). 

After the Committee has used the material obtained, it is destroyed.

House Select Committee on Crime 

This Committee inspects tax returns to compare and corroborate information and data reflected in financial documents, records and materials produced pursuant to Committee subpcena. "All confidential information received by our investigative staff from tax returns. .is not kept in our general files, but rather is kept in a separate filing system maintained by our Chief This filing system has individual combina- Investigator. tion safe locks and the combination is known only by the Chief 

Investigator and Chief Counsel..." 

(Letter from Chairman 

Claude Pepper, October 16, 1970).

Senate Committee on Government Operations "This information sought in income tax returns is used by this Subcommittee staff primarily for investigation leads. This has been found to be helpful in past instances in locating sources of income, amount of income, additional addresses of the person filing the income tax return, and other factual data. 

During the current [91st] Congress, access has been requested to income tax returns only in connection with our investigation of riots, civil and criminal disorders, campus disturbances, and improprieties in the function of non-commissioned officers' clubs. In day-to-day operations, all material developed in investigations is indexed and filed as it is received. From that point forward access to the material is controlled according

to prescribed regulations which include limiting access to persons authorized by the Chairman to have such access." (Memorandum transmitted by letter of Senator John McClellan to 

Senator Long, November 9, 1970). All information obtained by the Committee is maintained in its files and is periodically relegated to storage from which it can be recalled if needed. 

Senate Committee on Rules and Administration In 1963 the Committee inspected income tax returns to inquire into the business interests of Senate employees or former employees. . .only specified people on the staff had access to the information. . . [which]. .was kept in a confidential safe." 

(Letter of Senator B. Everett Jordan, dated October ù, 1970). 

After the information was put to its intended use, it was destroyed.

D. 

Problems With Present Use of Tax Returns by Congressional Committees. 

1. No Procedure for Determining Whether Committee Staff Has

Adequate Prodedures for Insuring Confidentiality. 

While most congressional committees have some procedure to safeguard confidentiality of tax returns against improper disclosure, the Internal Revenue Service is not empowered to ascertain whether they are followed. Nor is it authorized to condition a grant of a request on adoption and implementation of such procedures. Presumably, however, such matters could be contained in executive orders granting access. 

2. Use of Returns for Investigative Purposes by Congressional 

Committee. 

Quite obviously the line between obtaining information for purposes of legislating and obtaining information for purely investigative purposes is thin. Yet it appears that some committees (for example, the 

Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations of the Senate Committee on Government Operations), plainly employ tax data for the purpose of developing investigative leads. To the extent that this information is forwarded by the committee to prosecutorial agencies, the practice of using income tax returns for investigative purposes would seem to be subject to the same objections as when such data is used by the Department of Justice for this purpose. 

3. Publication of Tax Return Information by Congressional 

Committees.

The regulation authorizing inspection of tax returns by committees other than those enumerated in IRC, § 6301 (d), Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-101 specifically provides that the information obtained by the committee "shall be held confidential."

The regulation further contains the following language:

"Provided, however, that any portion thereof relevant or pertinent to the purpose of the investigation may be submitted by the investigating committee to the appropriate house of the Congress." 554/ The Service reads this provision as permitting the committee to publish income tax return information in a committee report to the appropriate house. For example, a report of the House Committee on Internal Security, Anatomy of A Revolutionary Movement: Students for a Democratic Society, contains information taken from SDS's corporate income tax return for various taxable periods. Therefore, although the regulation provides that tax return information obtained by committees is to be held confidential, the possibility that the information may be made public through a report to a house of Congress 555/ leaves the way open for avoiding confidentiality. 

A more fundamental question can be raised as to whether, under any circumstances, the publication of tax retum information which indicates the identity of the taxpayer involved is necessary to the accomplishment of the legislative purpose. Certainly, in the area of tax legislation it is sufficient, for example, to point to the nature of the deficiency in present law, the number and type of taxpayers who benefit therefrom and how the benefit is obtained, without the necessity of identifying the taxpayers involved. 4. 

Use of Tax Returns for Legislative Purposes.

Particularly with respect to tax legislation, access to information derived from tax returns may be necessary. For example, the

studies on tax reform which were published in 1969 contained a large number of examples and other data taken from tax returns. However, none of it could be identified with particular taxpayers. Indeed, even with tax legislation, there seems no need to release tax information in identifiable form.

This conclusion seems equally appropriate where there is a substantive program to be framed. Aggregates and statistical information would seem not to raise problems. However, release of information which may be traced to a taxpayer who would be subject to the program would seem inappropriate. ง. 

REQUESTS FOR TAX DATA By The White House A. History of Requests by the White House. 

Since the emergence of the Internal Revenue Service from the old Bureau of Internal Revenue in the early 1950's, fully documented White House inspection of tax returns has occurred on several occasions. 

Internal Revenue records reveal no such requests during the eight years of the Eisenhower Administration (1953-1960). Within a few days after President Kennedy assumed office (on January 26, 1961), however, a Special Consultant to the President, Carmine S. Bellino, made oral requests to inspect returns and associated documents. These requests were honored and, on May 23, 1961, the practice was ratified by a memorandum from the 556/ 

Commissioner to the General Counsel of the Treasury. 

There are no records on the extent or on the occasion on which Mr. Bellino had such

access.

There apparently were no such requests during the Johnson Administration (1963-1968). 

It was agreed that each time In September 1969, requests by Clark R. Mollenhoff, Deputy 

Counsel to President Nixon, were regularized by an understanding between Mr. Mollenhoff and the Commissioner. 

Mr. Mollenhoff had occasion to inspect income tax returns or "associated documents," of one or more individuals or organizations, he would send a memo to the Commissioner listing them and "briefly setting forth the nature of the request." The Commissioner, in turn, would "infer in every case that the request is either at the direction of, or in the interest 557/ of, the President." During the period December 18, 1969, through 

April 14, 1970, Mr. Mollenhoff made seven requests to examine returns of nine taxpayers. 558/ Mr. Mollenhoff's activities soon became known to the press, and the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation held a hearing on April 14, 1970, to inquire into the general subject of availability of tax returns to the White House. The matter also was fully debated on the 559/ floor of the United States Senate. 

This debate recognized that the procedure worked out for Mollenhoff improved upon the "loose manner" in which tax returns had been examined by White House employees upon oral 560/ request. 

Written requests, however, did not answer all the criticism. 

For example, Senator Gore questioned the wisdom of the Commissioner's action "in supplying and in agreeing to supply Mr. Mollenhoff with tax returns and copies of tax returns without a direct communication from the President of the United States, either verbally or in writing." 561/ There was concern

about letting "a political operative in the White House. .have carte blanche access to income tax returns. 562/ Those who defended Mollenhoff's access replied, for example, that they had "every confidence" he acted in a 563/ "responsible fashion" and that it was not proper to "read into his actions a political motivation." Indeed, the hearings and the floor colloquy failed to reveal any "evidence that there was improper use made of tax returns under preceding administrations or the Nixon Administration . . 

But, the seed of doubt was planted. Many realized that the potential for abuse was present and that perhaps tighter rules were necessary. The con- troversy subsequently died out, however.

564/ Within a few years, access to tax returns by the White House had again become a matter of significant concern. It arose within the larger thicket of Watergate-related events with the charge that the Internal Revenue 565/ Service had been used for political purposes. It was alleged that, symptomatic of this misdirection of the agency, tax return information was improperly transmitted to the White House. While some of the instances in which tax data was transferred to the White House have been isolated (primarily in the voluminous amount of Watergate-connected testimony), same doubt persists that all has been revealed. Whether true or not, there was sufficient evidence of access for political purposes to prompt continuing 567/ concern about confidentiality of tax returns.

566/ White House access to tax returns was raised at President Ford's first news conference after he assumed the Presidency. At that time he 568/ announced a forthcoming executive order on the subject. 

Issued four

569/ days later, the order is notable in three respects: (1) returns "shall be delivered to or open to inspection by the President only upon written request signed by the President personally"; (2) any such request shall be addressed to the Secretary of the Treasury and shall state the name and address of the taxpayer, the kind of tax, and the taxable periods 570/ involved; and (3) language stating that the President "may designate by name an employee or employees of the White House Office who are authorized on behalf of the President to receive any such return. 

Commissioner Alexander stated on April 21, 1975: "Since I have been 

Commissioner of Internal Revenue i.e., since May 29, 1973 the White House has not asked me or to my knowledge, anyone else in the Internal Revenue for tax returns, and I surely do not expect President Ford to ask for tax returns." 571/

B. Authority of the President and White House Staff to Examine Tax Returns.

1. Statutory Authority. 

If the President and the White House staff must rely upon statutory authority to inspect income tax returns, they are remitted to the quixotic words in § 6103 that income tax returns "shall be open to inspection only upon order of the President and under the rules and regulations prescribed by the Secretary. 11 (emphasis added) Two questions seem to have arisen under this provision, both relating to whether the White House must follow the regulations in requesting tax information. 

The first controversy focuses on "and" in the phrase quoted: is it disjunctive or conjunctive? Put another way, do the presidential order and the rules and regulations prescribed by the Secretary and approved by the President constitute alternate routes to inspection or must they both be traversed? If the latter, then the only rules and regulations applicable 572/ are those of the catchall regulation, Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a) -1 (f). The answer is not clear cut, though past practice by the White House has been to ignore the rules and regulations. However, the statute does seem to intend to regularize access to tax returns, and the requirements of the regulations pursuant thereto do not seem burdensome. 

However, in 1970 the Chief Counsel opined that the President could simply order inspection and that the statute did not require White House observance of rules and regulations. The opinion states: "It is inconceivable that the President should be bound by such rules and regulations in prescribing the circumstances or manner in which returns are to be disclosed to a member of his staff for his use. Since

any such rules and regulations are subject to revision or modification by the Secretary at any time with the approval of the President, and the Secretary is the subordinate of the President appointed to serve at the pleasure of the President, it cannot be believed that he should be limited by the requirements of any such rules and regulations or that Congress so intended." 573/ 

The argument may prove too much, because although the President may be able to order his Secretary of Treasury to prepare regulations allowing Presidential access, he did not do so. The regulation-making process may also give the Secretary a chance to air his views on the manner of access. 

With 20-20 hindsight, one might well wonder if this view of the statute would have prevented the abuses which have been alleged. Moreover, the regulations regularize and publicize procedures spelled out in them. There is, then, some benefit to regulations, even though the right to access would not be denied.

Conversely, there are a number of difficulties in assuming that a Presidential request must run the gamut of the regulations. The arguably appropriate "catchall" regulation provides that requests for inspection made thereunder may be permitted "in the discretion of the Secretary of the Treasury or the Commissioner of Internal Revenue." In the Chief 

Counsel's view, such an interpretation would permit the Secretary or Commissioner to "frustrate a request of the President for returns the face of the fact that the statutory provision says that they should 574/ be open for inspection on his order." 

in Further, it is not entirely graceful to interpret the regulation's language that the request shall be transmitted by "the head of an executive department (other than the 

)," applying to the President.

The language seems to contemplate the President's cabinet rather than the President

himself. Both of these arguments, of course, overlook the possibility that none of the then existing regulations were drawn to permit White House access and that a properly drawn regulation would avoid the problems raised.

In retrospect, an opinion requiring promulgation and observance of rules and regulations would certainly have been preferable. However, the 1961 memorandum from the Commissioner and the 1970 opinion of the Chief Counsel both blessed ad hoc orders of the President, and this was reflected in practice. On balance, the desirability of regularization and publication of White House access would seem to warrant compliance with regulations. 

President Ford has taken this step, and we would hope that future legislative enactments will require it if any White House access is allowed. 

The second controversy revolves around the necessity of complying with regulations if the inspection is not performed personally by the President. Thus, even if we assume that the President may order ad hoc inspection, we must ask whether a subordinate may perform the inspection. 

This issue arose in 1970 when Mr. Mollenhoff's access was debated. The 575/ appropriate regulation certainly was not followed then nor by Mr. Bellino in 1961. One side argued that if an employee was to inspect 576/ returns, these regulations were to be followed." The other argued that such requirement would abridge the President's executive authority, because 577/ without assistants he is unable to see that the laws are executed. 

This side of the controversy was supported by three Chief Counsel's opinions. 

The first was issued in 1961 for Mr. Bellino. 578/ In 1962, another con- 579/ cluded that a subordinate could exercise Presidential powers.

Finally, the Warren Commission was viewed in 1964 as an extension of the President and given access to tax returns. 580/

Interestingly, the controversy seemed not to reach an intermediate position that the President personally must order inspection, but may also delegate the inspection. So far as is known, neither Mr. Bellino nor 

Mr. Mollenhoff had a Presidential order. They merely exercised the influence of the White House to obtain access to tax data without an order, rules, or regulations. There should not, however, be any doubt that the President may delegate inspection to a subordinate. 

2. Constitutional Authority.

While the present statute raises problems of interpretation, the Constitution may also be relevant to a consideration of whether curbs or prohibitions may be placed on White House access to tax returns. Certain constitutional provisions might support the view that access may not be impaired. 

Article II vests the executive power in the President. This power, so the argument runs, entitles the President to obtain for the purpose of executing the laws all information available to the government. Hence, it is argued, Congress cannot remove White House access under § 6103 of the revenue laws. But the Supreme Court has made it clear that the President's authority to execute the laws is limited to the laws enacted. He may not execute a power not granted. Justice Black's opinion for the Court in the steel mills case is particularly instructive: "In the framework of our Constitution, the President's power to see that the laws are faithfully executed refutes the idea that he is to be a lawmaker. The 

Constitution limits his functions in the law-making process to the recommending of laws and the vetoing of laws he thinks bad." 581/

582/ Furthermore, it remains to be demonstrated that the President's authority to "execute" the law would be inhibited by denying him access to tax returns." 

It appears that the known instances of transfer of tax return data to the White House have been for political, or politically-related, purposes. 

Certainly, nothing in any of the identified situations points to a use for 583/ a valid executive purpose.

584/ More possibly relevant language is to be found in section 2 of Article II: "the President. . .may require the opinion, in writing, of the principal officer of the Executive departments, upon any subject relating to duties of their respective offices. 

However, tax returns do not appear to be opinions of executive officers. Rather, they are statements compulsorily filed by taxpayers. Finally, section 3 of the same article provides that the President "shall take Care that the Law be faithfully executed." The argument may be made, therefore, that Congress cannot interfere with the crucial relationships between the President and his executive officers (in this case the Secretary of the Treasury or the Commissioner of Internal Revenue).

Once the duty to administer the revenue laws has been assigned by Congress to the Executive Branch, and once Congress has advised and consented to the selection of a Presidential delegate to perform this duty, it is arguable that Congress may be precluded from interfering with the President's ability to gather information from his delegate. 

Congress, however, is charged with making laws which the President shall execute.

While it presumably could not Constitutionally enact a

statute providing that the President could not have access to reports by the Commissioner affecting the internal administration of the Service, it might logically conclude that documents filed by legislative command be kept from the President, given the extreme likelihood of misuse for political purposes. 

Of course, in rare and exceptional circumstances the President may need access to tax returns or return information. For instance, to settle an allegation that a taxpayer was unfairly treated by an appointee, the President might desire tax returns to appraise himself of the facts upon which to make appropriate personnel decisions. Even in such instances, however, it is difficult to conjure a situation in which it would be necessary for the President to have the taxpayer's identity revealed to him. He should be able to render his executive responsibility on the basis of information in which the taxpayer remains anonymous. 77-842 O 76-63

C. Sensitive Cases.

The sensitive case reporting system, 585/ at least as it existed prior to its suspension on November 13, 1974, 586/ was fraught with extremely serious implications reaching beyond considerations of tax return confidentialty. 

A case was "sensitive" if the handling of the case was likely to result in publicity. This was usually dependent on the identity of the taxpayer. Thus, cases were "sensitive" if the taxpayer was a presidential appointee, Member of Congress, prominent state or local political figure, or well-known business, entertainment, or sports figures. Other cases might be sensitive because of the issues involved (e.g., deductions or credits for political contributions).

Once the case was identified as sensitive, a "sensitive case report" was prepared at the local level and disseminated, depending on the geographic sensitivity of the case, to the District 

Director, Regional Commissioner, or Commissioner. Afterwards, status reports (after a significant development in processing), transfer reports (upon transfer of the case from one department to another) and final reports (upon resolution of the matter or termination of sensitive status might also be prepared). The special report form disclosed the type and amount of tax involved. principal issues involved, and the reason for sensitivity. Elaborate procedures existed for expediting the reports to the interested administrative levels.

The asserted justification for the sensitive case procedure (which began in the late 1950's under Commissioner Dana Latham) was the need for management awareness of cases having potential for national or regional publicity. Whatever the soundness of this rationale the procedure had two distinctly harmful side effects. First, it allowed unnecessary (and in some cases unauthorized) dissemination of tax return information among Service personnel. Far worse than that, it also facilitated the distribution of tax return data outside the Service. There was a regular pattern of transferring sensitive case reports to 587/ the Secretary of the Treasury. Some information apparently went to the President as well. John J. Caulfield, a White House assistant, testified before the Senate Select Committee on Presidential Campaign Activities that he learned from a sensitive case report that an anonymous telephone call may have initiated an audit of Rev. Billy Graham. 588/ Roger Barth, a former assistant to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, revealed to the 

Committee that a sensitive case report involving the "Hughes

Project" was transferred to White House aide John Ehrlichman because it contained allegations "of possible wrongdoing by Mr. 

Rebozo and Mr. Nixon, the President's brother or brothers. 

Barth also testified that some sensitive case reports were funnelled 589/ to the White House on a continuing basis, including those concerning the President's osteopath, Dr. Ryland. 590/ 

The suspicion directed to the sensitive case reporting system resulted in a memorandum to Service personnel suspending it "until a modified and curtailed system" was developed.

It was added, however, that "[p] ending development and implementation of a new Reporting System, field offices should keep appropriate management levels advised of matters significant to tax administration." 

This language did not calm fears that the program is still operational. 

Complete elimination of the program seems appropriate. 

The forwarding of sensitive case reports by field personnel to the National Office in Washington, creates a pool of information 593/ with demonstrated potential for misuse. 

Commissioner Alexander has indicated that there is no need for him to know the status of a tax case involving, for example, a well known political figure. 594/ 591/ 592/

D. Proposals for restricting White House access to tax returns. 

The Watergate experience has made it clear that unfettered ability of White House employees to obtain tax return information presents distinct potential for abuse. Moreover there are few (if any) non-political reasons for such access: in 1970, a Presidential assistant conceded that White House examination of tax returns is "normally" to investigate prospective appointees and "sometimes" to 595/ investigate "impropriety in connection with government activity." 

If reform is to occur in this area, and it seems agreed that it should, 596/ the question is whether it should take the form of administrative change (such as that by President 597/ Ford) or alteration of the statute. Statutory change has the advantage of relative permanency. An executive order, on the other hand, is subject to modification. While it is hard to imagine a President having the temerity to alter the general flavor of President Ford's executive order in the next few years, a change could well be made once public consciousness has subsided. 

Relaxation of legislatively imposed standards would come far less easily and, presumably, attract public scrutiny. Whatever constitutional obstacles confront legislative restriction of presidential access to tax returns, they do not seem insurmountable. 

Such appears to be the view of the draftsmen of the revised version of the Administration's bill dealing with tax return confidentiality. The orignial simply provided that returns would be 598/ available "[u] pon order of the President", codifies the prerequisites contained in the Ford executive order. but the revision 599/

Thus, complete prohibition on the disclosure of tax returns and tax return information to the President or White House personnel might be appropriate. However, there remains the argument that access is necessary to investigate 600/ "impropriety in connection with government activities." 

Similarly, there is an argument that tax data is needed in connection with contemplated appointments by the President. However, a tightly 601/ controlled "tax check" mechanism, should provide sufficient information.

Statutory solutions falling short of a complete restriction would nonetheless constitute an improvement upon present law, but at least five safeguards seem necessary. First, the request for tax data should be made by the President personally. Second, the request should designate, by name the White House employee (s) to whom tax data may properly be furnished by the Service. Third, it should state (in a full and complete manner) why the tax return information is desired. Fourth, some impartial group should periodically review the instances in which the White House has requested tax return information. Fifth, some effort should be made to control dissemination of the data once it is obtained by the White House. To require the President to make the requests personally and to name the person examining the returns would render improper "an open ended arrangement [such as existed in the Bellino and Mollenhoff situations] with a political operative without direct orders from the President himself." 602/

If the reasons for the request were stated accurately, it would be unlikely that any President would attempt to obtain tax return data for political purposes. That possibility would be lessened further by outside monitoring of the volume of tax return information received by the White House and the justification therefor. 

Some of the proposals for reform contain one or more of the five elements referred to above. Both the Weicker-Litton 604/ bill 603/ and the revised Administration bill require that a written request for tax data be made by the President. personally. 

No proposal would require the President to name the individual authorized to examine the returns, though the Administration's bill authorizes the Secretary to furnish tax information "to such employee or employees of the White House Office as the President may designate by name in such request. might be construed as requiring the President to designate the 606/ persons authorized to examine, 605/ This but it seems preferrable just to say so. Curiously, none of the reform proposals require the 

President to state why the tax material is being requested. The amission may have been prompted by ill-founded concern that the that the Constitution requires that Presidential access be un- 607/ fettered. From the beginning, the regulations have generally required the requesting party to state why the return is desired.

None of the proposals would necessitate submission of data regarding White House requests to an outside monitoring party, but there is no reason information regarding White House requests (including the identity of those whose returns have been requested) should not be included in the semi-annual report submitted to the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation. In fact, the abuses in the area of 

White House access suggest that therein lies the greatest need for outside monitoring. Regarding the fifth element mentioned above, the revised version of the Administration's bill adopts the strong anti-disclosure feature contained in the Ford executive order to control dissemination of information reaching the White House. It provides that, unless the President otherwise directs in writing, the material will be seen by only the President and the person (or persons) named in the Executive order. This should have substantially reduced the potential for abuse. Another possible check the President's requesting of tax returns might result from a requirement that the taxpayer be informed of a Presidential request.

VI. 

TAX CHECK REPORTS ON PROSPECTIVE APPOINTEES AND OTHER PERSONS. 

A. History of "Tax Checks". 

In August 1961 President Kennedy wrote to Secretary Dillon stating that he desired a check of tax records "as a of prospective 608/ supplement to the character investigations" presidential appointees including "postmasters, judges, U. S. attorneys, employees at the White House and any other prospective" 609/ appointee.

The names, current address, and any other helpful information would be supplied by the FBI. 

Information discovered by the check is then sent to the FBI for inclusion in its preappointment investigative file. 610/ This procedure has been regularized into a so-called "type X" tax check and expanded to include a "type E" check which reaches nominees for Presidential 611/ "E" Awards." 

A type X or E check will summarize information (1) on whether the taxpayer has filed income tax returns for not more than the immediately three preceding years: (2) on unpaid taxes, and if so for what years but no amounts assessed or unpaid; (3) whether the taxpayer has been or is under investigation for possible criminal offenses under the tax laws, and the results of such investigation (but no details); (4) whether the taxpayer has been assessed any penalty for fraud or negligence (but no amounts or details); and (5) whether a notice of tax lien has been filed (which 612/ is a matter of public record.

A tax check is to be prepared within three work days after receipt of the request. If no record of a return is 613/ found, and unless the national office has forbidden field contact, the taxpayer will be contacted "as discreetly as possible," without any indication "that anything other than a routine check is being made." 614/ The purpose is to ascertain whether the return was filed in another district or if there are other reasons for the Service's failure to locate the file. If an audit appears desirable, special procedures exist for an audit of the returns 615/ within five working days of the receipt of the request. 

If the tax check is "negative" the Internal Revenue

Service informs the requesting party typically as follows: "Our records show that income tax returns were timely filed for the years 1972, 1973, and 1974. There is no record of unpaid taxes, liens, criminal tax investigations, or civil penalties for fraud or negligence. completes our report."

This If the tax check is "positive" (revealing, for example no returns or a pending intelligence investigation) the department 616/ requesting the "tax check" will be so advised.

The White House requests tax checks concerning all employees from gardners and maintenance men to Cabinet-level personnel.

Other departments of the executive branch will use tax checks for similar reasons but usually for only higher level positions.

For example, the Department of Justice requests tax checks for prospects for appointment as Assistant United States Attorneys or as United States Magistrates. Again as an example, the Department of Agriculture requests tax checks on individuals being considered for promotion to so-called "supergrade" positions. 

Treasury requests tax checks, for example, on individuals appointed to the various advisory panels created by the Commissioner of 

Internal Revenue. The Department of Commerce requests tax checks on the nominees for the Presidential "E" Awards. These cases are only examples, and tax checks are not limited to them. In all these situations, tax checks are considered to supplement investigations concerning the character, loyalty, suitability of employees or nominees.

C. Difficulties with Tax Checks. 

1. Statutory Authorization. 

Some of the information in a tax check is available to the public, e.g., whether a tax return has been filed or whether a lien has been filed or released. The balance of the material, however, is now defined as a part of a tax return subject to disclosure only 618/ under § 6103 of the Code. 

Thus, the tax check results in a disclosure of tax returns to an investigative agency, generally the FBI, upon its request but apparently on behalf of the agency for whom the investigation is made. While one may employ the fiction that such requests comply with appropriate regulations (generally, the "catchall" regulation), thay seem not to do so. Furthermore, as respects checks for the White House, the questions previously discussed are equally pertinent here and are not raised again. On the whole under the present statute and regulations the conclusion reached is that the procedure is at best questionable. 2.

The Privacy Act of 1974. 

Significant concerns arise as a result of the recently enacted Privacy Act of 1974. 619/ It provides that tax information will not be disclosed "to any person. . except pursuant to the prior written consent of, the individual to whom the record pertains. 620/ Some taxpayers are aware of a possible appointment and may even have signed authorization for a tax check. Others, however, are not aware of the possible appointment or the tax check. As to these individuals, obtaining a

"1 written consent would perhaps not be feasible. While the Privacy Act contains exceptions to the obtaining of prior written consent, none of them appear applicable unless it is concluded that tax checks are a "routine use". A routine use of a record is one "which is compatible with the pur- 621/ pose for which it was collected. Certainly, tax checks made for the purpose of avoiding Presidential embarrassment do not seem compatible with tax administration. There is little doubt, however, that, under the Privacy 

Act guideline, the position will be taken that the use of tax return data for tax check purposes. is a routine use. trouble. 

3. Policy Considerations.

Apparently there are two rationalizations for the tax check. 

The first is that tax information possibly has some relevance to competence or fitness for a public job. The second is that the President should not be embarrassed by appointing someone in, or who has been in, serious tax Both of these justifications overlook the fact that the prospective employee may be requested to furnish copies of his tax returns. Perhaps even taxpayer consent to the check would not be an objectionable course although the check then would be little more than a check on the taxpayer's veracity.

Obviously, the requiring of consent would change the present practice which operates surreptiously so that the taxpayer will not know that he is under consideration for appointment or employment. The need for such secrecy has not, however, been explained, and the need for tax infor-

mation before discussing the job with the prospective appointee is not inmediately apparent. On the present record, there is then little apparent reason to sanction surreptious tax checks. 

Also the secretive aspect of the tax check offers the potential for abuse. For example, the Watergate investigation revealed that on at least one occasion (i.e., with respect to Daniel Schorr, CES newscaster) the White House used the tax check machinery to obtain tax data regarding a political enemy. By simply adopting the pretense of considering a taxpayer for an appointment, the White House can tap a rich vein of personal and confidential infomation regarding that individual. Once obtained it can be misused to the individual's detriment. 622/ Furthemore, some of the information in a tax check response is likely to be misleading and damage or ruin a taxpayer's job prospects. 

While this result might le prevented by a full disclosure of the taxpayer's file, that procedure may not be followed. 

Even if it were, full disclosure is likely to result in the release of substantial infomation unrelated to the items which generated the need for full disclosure. 

Finally, what started as a device to investigate rerely a few appointees has spread to many levels of govertent eloy ant, de procedure seen to be another example of the axion that a re oval of the finger from the dike results in a flood of the lowlands. 

If some kind of tax check is to be continued, there is difficulty in separating legitimate tax checks from those which are not. fare ingrove-

ments could, however, be made to lessen the likelihood of abuse. First, the President could be required to designate the individuals who are authorized to receive investigative reports containing tax check material. A similar approach has been in the Ford executive order regarding White House 623/ inspection of tax returns generally. Second, information so received should then be made available only to the President or to those other in- 624/ dividuals whom the President designates in writing. Third, tax check information could not be received pursuant to an oral request but only in response to a written request that the information is needed for a nomination or appointment in connection with an investigation by the FBI or other 625/ appropriate agency. Surely, even with these improvements this procedure will be open to abuse, but the creation of a "paper trail" concerning the request would permit "rights [to] be better protected in the event 626/ that anyone should try to abuse this particular procedure.

VII. 

INSPECTION OF TAX RETURNS BY STATES AND LOCAL GOVERNMENTS 

Manner of Inspection.

Since 1935 the Code has allowed inspection of tax returns by state tax administrators designated in a written application by the gover- 627/ nor.

Returns may be so inspected only for state tax purposes or for the furnishing of information to local tax authorities. and copying of the returns in a secured area Eleven states have chosen to make this inspection by examination 628/ of the appropriate office 629/ 

of the Internal Revenue Service. 

Thirty-eight states satisfy their needs by obtaining magnetic 630/ tapes drawn from the Individual Masterfile (IMF). The IMF contains nearly all the information necessary to compute taxable income, It also contains information on the status of the taxpayer's accounts with the Government, but a taxpayer's "return" cannot be reproduced from information on the IMF. The delivery of data on tapes is generally preferred by the 

Service because the returns are not handled by non-Service personnel, Since a computer is necessary to convert a tape into generally readable form, information on a tape is not in a form readily usable by a wide group of 631/ people.

The remaining state, Nevada, has no authority to inspect tax returns. The statute (IRC, S 6103 (b)) provides that "[a]ll income returns ... shall be open to inspection by" state officials. Consequently, it would seem arguable that even if the Service terminated an agreement, the 77-842 O - 76-64

state could nonetheless obtain access to tax returns upon written application by the governor. While the Internal Revenue Service could balk at transferring the data, there is doubt that the Service could properly do So. 632/ All states, except Texas and Nevada, have entered into Agreements on Coordination of Tax Administration with the Federal Government. These agreements do not enlarge the inspection authority but do seek to spell out mutual obligations and usually require the state to make 633/ certain tax information available to the U.S. Government. 

Recently the form agreement (referred to colloquially as a "treaty") has been tightened 634/ up by imposing additional requirements on safeguarding tax information. 

It also provides that the agreement may be terminated or modified at the discretion of the Commissioner or of the governor on account of changes in either the Federal or State statutes and regulations or whenever in the administration of Federal or State tax laws that action seems appropriate. 

Despite the possibly doubtful legal effect of these agreements, they do seem to serve at least three objectives. First, the agreement may make the public aware that an exchange is taking place and thereby possibly improves the quality of self-assessment. Second, an agreement facilitiates the flow of data to the states by removing the need for gubernatorial requests. Third, the agreement is a representation that the state will adhere to certain standards regarding confidentiality. If the agreement is not observed on this point, the Service may then terminate it and remit the state to applications signed by the governor, probably much more cum- 635/

bersame that the method provided by the agreement. There is then an incentive to abide by the agreement. Absent such an agreement the only restriction on use of the data by the state is IRC, § 7213 (a) (2) rendering unauthorized disclosure illegal.

Procedures to Insure Confidentiality of Information Made 

Available to States.

The Service has obviously been concerned that releases to states be protected against disclosure. Internally, the Service has promulgated rules designated to assure confidentiality in the disclosure 636/ process.

The concern, however, is not with disclosure procedures but that confidence be maintained after information is in state hands. 

Three factors seem relevant. First, the form of the information 637/ . undoubtedly has a practical effect on improper disclosures.

638/ Data from IMF tapes seems less likely to be released improperly. Information gained through inspection and copying (eleven states obtain all information by this means) is in a form more readily disseminated. 

Second, the execution of an agreement with a state would seem to have practical value. The state agrees not to 639/ disclose information.

Also, the parties agree to review safe- 640/ guarding procedures whenever either so desires.

While termination is the only sanction for failure to safeguard, and while states may have a right to inspect even if the agreement is terminated, the governor should at least be concerned about his pledge and the other benefits of the agreement and thus encourage activity promoting confidentiality. 

Also, the state will agree to destroy returns after "they have served 642/ their purpose." 641/
