Third, § 7213 (a) (2) imposes a criminal penalty upon any state employee who permits the disclosure of income tax 643/ Although, 644/ information except in the manner authorized by law. there have been several prosecutions under this statute, there is some possible uncertainty concerning the applicability of the statute in situations where the information disclosed by the state employee may not, because it has at that time been incorporated into state tax information, be properly described as "information acquired by him through an inspection permitted. under § 6103 (a).. 645/ 

Texas

Thus, in situations where there is no agreement (and is at the present time the only such state), there is a criminal sanction but complete absence of any control by the Service over the state's practices regarding the maintenance of 646/ standards.

The objective should, of course, be the maintenance of standards which would prevent a potential criminal violation from occurring. If there is no agreement, the State receiving the data has not vouched that certain standards will be met. Nor will the Service have the right to inspect state practices regularly. 

Deficiencies in state practice, then, may not come to light.

C. 

Possible Changes in the Extent of Access by States. 

The threshold question is whether the making of returns available to states is appropriate. The Federal government may benefit 647/ tram better state compliance. Also, in some cases, state officials examine returns which are not examined by the Service, and these results are available to the Service. Both of these considerations seem stronger where the taxes at both levels are similar. Thus, if a taxpayer is required to report s tate income accurately, the effect should be beneficial at the Federal level as well. If the state (or local) tax is of a completely different nature (i.e., a local tax on intangibles), this benefit may not exist. However, even when there is no similarity between the taxes, compliance generally should be enhanced at both levels by increased awareness of cooperation between Federal and state tax author- 648/ ities.

Nevertheless, there have been suggestions that only those states which base their income tax on a percentage of Federal income tax should obtain tax information from the Federal government. adoption of such a proposal would, obviously, radically reduce the 649/ The availability of such material to states. A slightly less radical approach would be to require that there be some definitional relation between the state and the Federal income tax or a component thereof. If Federal income tax returns are used at the state (or local) level for the purpose of "administering" a state gambling tax, or even a state tax on gasoline or motor fuel, which provide criminal sanctions, the aura of using tax

returns for criminal investigative purposes arises. As discussed above, such use thus presents serious policy and, possibly, Constitutional problems.

Of course, any of these suggested changes would require legislation as the statute now provides that Federal returns may be • • "used for the administration of the tax laws [of a] state." In addition, there would be difficulty in deciding when the state tax was sufficiently similar. Finally, there would be serious practical problems in permitting a state to use Federal tax information only for administering some of the tax laws but not others. 

There are then benefits to both the states and Federal goverments. There may be an incriminatory aspect to the release of tax information to states. However, taxpayers likely are not surprised or do not consider releases improper where there is a high correlation in the taxing statutes. On the other hand, where there is little similarity of statute and where criminal sanctions may result, the disclosure has some flavor of a disclosure for criminal investigatory purposes. Also, taxpayers may benefit if errors favorable to the government are found by one government and reported to the other. 

Thus, a conclusion on the propriety of such exchanges is not easily reached. Despite the definitional problems, however, a limitation to use for highly co-ordinated related taxes seems appropriate. 

But whatever the limits on access, the Commissioner should have the power to review state practices on confidentiality safeguards

and to withdraw the authority to inspect Federal returns if the state's practices are found wanting. It should be made much clearer than it is, by amending the statute, possibly by amending the regulations, that the establishment of adequate procedures is a necessary prerequisite to obtaining tax material and that enforcement of such procedures gives the Service an unequivocal right to withhold tax data until any deficiency in state practice has been cured. 

One of the significant concerns regarding the present § 6103(b) is the improper use of tax return data for political purposes. While the chief potential for abuse has been at the local level, fear exists regarding the potential for political use by a Governor or other high 650/ level official, The Administration's bill on tax privacy takes what appears to be the appropriate step of removing the Governor fram 651/ the disclosure process. While this change may be largely procedural, it does remove the state's highest elected official from even nominal participation in the process and also seems appropriate.

D. Availability to Local Governments. 

As noted above, state officials may furnish tax data to local tax authorities. The statute is also clear that such information is to be used only for tax administration. However, once tax information reaches the local level, the potential for violation of confidentiality, or for misuse of the tax information, seems to rise. 

Certainly, the number of local governments potentially able to obtain Federal tax data makes exceedingly difficult, if not impossible, the monitoring of the local government confidentiality practices. Further, the organization and conduct of many local governments is such that the charge that Federal tax data will be misused (for political purposes, for example) is greater than at the more structured state government 652/ level. Also, that the local government may obtain considerably more information than that which it needs for its tax administration purposes, thus enlarging the scope of the violation of the taxpayer's 653/ privacy if the material is abused at the local level. For example, a county having a tax on interest and dividends could well receive data regarding the aggregate amount of the taxpayer's gross income and all of its components. 

All of these considerations prompt a belief that same change is dictated regarding local government access to Federal tax data. 

The scope of information given might be restricted, or same adequate monitor of local government safeguards should be erected. However,

these changes, which require legislative action, would impose a large burden on the Service because it would have to tailor the information and monitoring system to the needs of each locality. Considered in this manner, it appears that the other alternative, i.e., simply prohibiting local governments from obtaining Federal tax data, may 654/ well be the appropriate approach. While local tax administration may suffer, at least until alternative enforcement techniques are developted, the risk that tax return privacy will be violated, or that return information will be misused, seems too great to justify the continuation of present practice,

VIII. 

UNAUTHORIZED ACCESS TO RETURNS BY INTERNAL REVENUE SERVICE EMPLOYEES 

Although the primary focus of this paper has concerned the disclosure of income tax information outside the Internal Revenue Service, a taxpayer's right to confidentiality may be violated through an unauthorized examination by Service employees. Improper examination of tax returns by Service employees may be motivated by any number of reasons including political ones. During the Watergate investigation instances of employee access to tax returns solely for political purposes were uncovered. For example, Roger V. Barth, former Assistant to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue, testified that he "asked for Lawrence O'Brien's tax return and asked that they get them in a way that the agents working on the case in the field would not know 655/ that I had requested them."

Tax return information may exist in any number of forms. 

The returns are filed with Service Centers and are soon sent to Federal Records Centers for permanent storage. Data from returns is stored on master files consisting of magnetic tapes at the National Computer Center. 

Accounts likely to require attention are transcribed on magnetic tapes and returned to the Service Center to form the basis for IDRS (Integrated Data Retrieval System). There also exists a large number of other files on examinations and investigations, requests for technical advice, requests for filing, and other similar matters. 

Obviously, safeguarding each system may present a different set of problems.

A. Access to Return. 

Service employees make many legitimate requests for tax 656/ return information. About 18 million per year are made of the Federal 

Records Centers to which the returns are forwarded within a relatively short time following receipt (from 6-8 weeks to one year). Although there are many requisition forms, the most commonly used form for the return itself is the Form 2275, Records Requests, Charge and Recharge. 

Of the millions of requests which the Federal Records Centers process annually, in only about two-thirds is any permanent record of the request 657/ maintained.

If action is taken on the return (such as an examination or investigation), it is, when refiled, given a new document locator number (DIN), which causes it to be refiled in a different place. 

However, since both the original DLN and the new DLN would appear on the face of the return, there is a trail back to the original location of the return where the charge-out document (generally a Form 2275) will be found. If there is no action taken on the return, it is refiled in its original place and the charge-out document is destroyed. 

Consequently, there would, in a no-action situation, be no record of the return having been requested. Most of the abuse situations would be no-action cases where a photocopy is quickly made and the original returned to the file. The Service is reported to be developing a procedure whereby the requesting document would remain with the return as a permanent record indicating who pulled the return and for what 658/ purpose.

A complete discussion of all access procedures and requesting documents would have necessitated a study and report beyond scope. Hence, we chose to deal mainly with releases outside the Service. The Service has also indicated that it is studying unauthorized employee access. 

We note, however, that many of the political abuses obviously arose from improper (if not unauthorized) employee access. 

For our purposes, however, access to the return itself or to either of the major tape systems (Master Files or IDRS) is discussed.

This system was reviewed in 1969 by the Office of Records Management of the General Services Administration. It prepared a report en- 659/ titled "Tax Return Requisitioning in the Internal Revenue Service." 

This report, which is quite lengthy, technical and crammed with the language of the professional manager, is, for our purposes, significant because of what it amits rather than what it includes. 660/

The GSA report notes that all too frequently the Service's tax return requisition process would not "come with a hit. It noted that a return might either be: (1) in the files (in document locator number (DLN) sequence); (2) with a known user; (3) misfiled; or (4) missing.

According to GSA a few returns are misfiled. Many others were not where 661/ they should have been or even "with a known user." The GSA report notes that of the 18,000,000 requests, about 1,600,000 constituted "second and third requests from persons who did not get their returns the first time." 

While only 2.4 percent of the requisitions resulted in a finding that the return was missing, in a substantial portion of the 23.6 percent of the instances in which the return was reported as being charged to someone, the charge-out was unclear, thereby making it more appropriate to treat the 663/ return as "missing" until further investigation was made.

The GSA report 662/ noted that the "classic answer to situations of this kind is to enforce tight charge-out and recharging control"but lamented that "[t]his IRS has never been willing to do." 664/ In an attempt to attain certain goals in the requisitioning process, such as providing faster service to users and reducing the

second and third requests for returns to a more tolerable level, the GSA report made certain recommendations. For example, to remedy the "poor legibility and lack of essential information" it was recommended that a "Users' Guide" be adopted to establish clear communications between requisitioners and Returns Sections/FRC's (Federal Records Centers). Noting that there are over one hundred different docu- 665/ ments for use in requesting tax returns GSA recommended that the Service 666/ [e]xplore ways to limit and reduce [their] number." Further, the 

Service was exhorted to develop ways in which "information needs" of Service personnel could be satisfied without requisitioning returns. The 

Integrated Data Retrieval System (IDRS), which was then just getting under way was seen as a means to increasing "retrieval speeds and accuracy" and as "a long step forward". 667/ While the GSA report may have struck a major blow for an increase in managerial efficiency, it appears to have faced none of the issues which are of present concern. The objective in the late 

1960's was to develop a procedure capable of providing an accurate and fast means of locating tax returns; the GSA report gave little, if any, thought to the possibility that tax return privacy could be subverted 668 by an unauthorized employee's requisitioning of tax returns. 

Recent events have prompted the Service to examine its requisitioning procedures in light of these new considerations. Largely because these procedures are presently undergoing change, it is not possible to say with any certainty whether they are adequate to the task. Clearly,

it would appear to be appropriate to design a procedure of return requisition which would not unduly hamper the Service's administrative objectives. However, it does seem appropriate to develop a procedure which would possess three fundamental and very necessary features: (1) a mechanism which would permit only authorized employees to obtain access to the data (and which would ferret out unauthorized requests); (2) a proper definition and identification of authorized personnel; and (3) a procedure whereby a record of the request, including the identity of the requesting party, would exist in the event that it later was suspected that improper use of the tax material was made. We think that the recent attempts to shape a return requisitioning process have considered these attributes.

1009  

B. Access to Computers. 

While the procedures for access to the Master Files and IDRS are not identical, they have the same elements. The processes are 669/ quite elaborate in comparison with the almost casual way in which return documents are available to Service personnel. Perhaps, the difference in care results from the difference in nature of the material available if access is obtained. Thus, while requisitions for very large numbers of returns might not go unnoticed and bring scrutiny, once access to a tape system is gained, information concerning almost unlimited numbers of taxpayers is available. 

The requesting individual is required to submit information to a terminal operator who puts the information into the computer. 670/ The computer then prints the requested document. The employee using the terminal must "sign on" by feeding into the machine his name, SSN, employee number; and the password is a 4-letter, computer generated code which is changed quarterly (or more frequently if the IDRS Security Administrator sees fit). If the proper information is put into the computer, it is activated. The employee may enter one of about 125 different command codes such as, for example, a command that an adjustment be made, or that an abatement be made. Each employee is authorized to enter only certain designated command codes. For example, if an employee puts in an adjust command code, but his employee profile authorizes him only to obtain certain information from the system, the terminal will not function. If the employee persists, after three attempts

the machine will simply shut down by locking. Each such security lock is recorded for review by a security administrator assigned to the district. A permanent record (on magnetic tape) of all inputs into 

IDRS is presently being maintained. Certain IDRS tax modules (e.g., those belonging to celebrities and taxpayers in public life) are restricted 671/ and access thereto is limited to certain designated employees.

C. Conclusion: 

Although the internal procedures related to the use of hard copies of returns is somewhat casual, the tape system is fairly well guarded. Both are now undergoing study and change designed to render invasion of taxpayer confidentiality more difficult to effect and also more easy to detect. Improvement in this area can be obtained only with a good deal of experimentation. Hopefully, the Service will sustain its interest in this problem and improve procedures, particularly as regards tax returns.

IX. DEFINITION OF TAX RETURN FOR PURPOSES OF RESTRICTIONS ON DISCLOSURE 

A. Background of current Definition.

672/ Naturally the definition of that data which is subject to restrictions on disclosure is a key feature of any tax privacy scheme. Possibly because the word seems self-defining, the meaning of a "return" has not been addressed by the Congress. The early definition in regulations 673/ adopted the simplistic approach that a return was a return. Later the need for elaboration became apparent, and regulations in force prior to 1972 provided that a return consisted of taxpayer-supplied documents and also any other documents in the file which the Commissioner desired to 674/ include as a part of the return. 

This definitional problem may perhaps be better appreciated by considering the various kinds of documents in the file. The return and accompanying explanatory material are extracted under threat of prosecution for failure to file. If an examination or investigation has occurred, there may be considerable additional information received from the taxpayer either under the administrative summons process or on pain of a tax deficiency. 

This material seems sufficiently necessary to a full and complete return to be identified as a part of the return. In addition, however, there may be investigative information growing from information transmitted by the taxpayer. There may also be reports, primarily the Revenue Agent's Report (RAR) and the Special Agent's Report (SAR), deficiency letters, memoranda, and analyses of these documents. Also, in some cases there will be investigative material extracted from and submitted by third parties, including informer's

1 tips. This material may exist in situations in which the taxpayer has submitted a return and also when there is no return. 

There may also be, in separate administrative files, requests for rulings, changes of tax years, changes of accounting period, and similar items. There is, in short, almost no end to the variety of items which can be in a taxpayer's file, and some files will not contain a return form. 

The pre-1972 definition gave the Commissioner authority to include these other documents within the definition of a return so as to render them disclosable pursuant to a properly framed request by a department or agency. 

For example, in instances in which the Commissioner in his discretion chooses to treat the associated documents as part of the "return", the Service took the position "that disclosure need not be restricted to the information included or required by statute to be included on the return, but that the 675/ whole document may be exhibited." 

If the Commissioner chose not to treat the related material as a "return", it was not subject to the disclosure procedures under § 6103. 

Rather, regulations promulgated pursuant to 5 U.S.c. $ 301, the general "housekeeping" provision enabling the head of any executive agency to promulgate rules and regulations for the government of his department, would control requests for the disclosure of internal revenue records or information. Regulations under this provision to the Commissioner of Internal Revenue the authority to determine the 676/ appropriateness of disclosure and to establish relevant procedures. 

Thus, in a pre-1972 context the Service could either provide that the

associated material was controlled by $ 6103 or by the housekeeping rules (which were of its own making). Requests under the housekeeping regulation were subject to less control and supervision than those that would be made pursuant to the rules established under § 6103. Also, since there existed considerable uncertainty concerning exactly what documents contained "information included or required. . ..to be included in the return," there was considerable doubt regarding what documents were, without action by the Commissioner, the subject of S 6103. 

In 1972 the regulation was changed to read as follows (with the new language underlined): "(3) Terms used-(1) Return. For purposes of $ 6103 (a), the term 'return' includes (a) information returns, schedules, lists, and other written statements filed by or on behalf of the taxpayer with the Internal Revenue Service which are designed to be supplemental to or to become a part of the return, and, (b) other records, reports, information received orally or in writing, factual data, documents, papers, abstracts, memoranda, or evidence taken, or any portion thereof, relating to the items included under subdivision (a) of this subdivision. The items listed in (b) of this subdivision may be open to inspection in any case where inspection of the return is authorized by S 6103(a) and those regulations only in the discretion of the Secretary or the Commissioner or the delegate of either. The above rules and procedures also apply to any reproductions or recordings by whatever means made of any such documents or portion thereof." 677/

The change made in 1972 had the effect of reversing the approach prior to that time. Instead of providing that internal IRS documents could, in the 

Commissioner's discretion, be made a part of the return, it was provided that 678/ all such documents would be considered a part of the return. The obvious purpose of this definition is to cover so-called "associated documents"

with the mantle of § 6103. The Commissioner, however, has also attempted to retain discretion over the release of these "associated documents." 

Whether this effort to retain discretion will be successful must at least be questioned. He has defined them as a part of the return, and there are numerous regulations which require disclosure of returns. There is then at least an inconsistency between the mandatory disclosure of returns and this effort to retain discretion. A court might resolve this inconsistency in the 

Commissioner's favor by holding that, in effect, the 1972 change amended all of the mandatory disclosure regulations to provide that returns would be disclosed only at the Commissioner's discretion. But equally plausible is a holding that under a mandatory disclosure regulation the Commissioner must make available anything defined as a return. There is, then, reason to resolve this inconsistency.

While the Service and Treasury deny the charge, some observers believe that the reason for the 1972 change, which sweeps internal IRS documents into the definition of a return, was to prevent their disclosure under the 679/ 

Freedom of Information Act, originally enacted in 1967. The Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) provides that its provisions do not apply "to 680/ .specifically exempted from disclosure by statute!" matters that are.

Not only does the basic disclosure provision constitute a statutory bar for FOIA purposes but so, also, does § 7213, providing criminal penalties for unauthorized disclosure of tax information. 681/ The requests, under the FOIA, for access to private letter rulings gave the Service an opportunity to test the new definition.

The chief test came in the decision of the Court of Appeals for the District 682/ of Columbia in Tax Analysts and Advocates v. I.R.S.

As to whether a private 683/ ruling letter constituted a "return" as a document submitted by the taxpayer, the court concluded that since "they are issued at the request of the taxpayer" they are not returns and that "their attachment as a matter of convenience to the return does not make them supplemental to or. .a part of the return." A letter ruling concerning a transaction which is not executed would not be an associated document, within the other half of the "return" 684/ definition, "since it would not 'relate' to a filed return." Although letter rulings involving proposed, but subsequently executed, transactions seemed to the court to fall within the literal language of "return" as defined in the regulations, the court concluded that letter rulings generated by the voluntary request of a taxpayer for tax advice. . .are beyond the scope of that which the Congress sought to protect under $ 6103, that is, a" 'return' filed under compulsion of law containing information necessary to determine federal tax liability." On the other hand, the court in Tax Analysts held that technical advice memoranda (prepared in response to an inquiry by the District Director with respect to a return already filed) "deal directly with information contained in 'returns made with respect to taxes' and are a part of the process by which tax determinations are made and, thus, 'specifically exempted from disclosure by statute.'"

B. 

What Should Be The Scope of "Return" Definition. 

The effect of the Tax Analysts decision is to leave the "return" definition contained in the current regulations considerably weakened. The 

Court of Appeals seemed to have concluded that the administrative definition of "return", for purposes of § 6103, should include only documents "filed under compulsion of law containing information necessary to determine federal tax liability." Although it is not entirely free from doubt, it is arguable that the court's definition in Tax Analysts would bestow the mantle of "return" only on those documents which (1) are filed by the taxpayer under compulsion, or (2) contain information from the return filed 3 by the taxpayer and are a part of the process by which tax liability is E determined. A reasonable reading of the scope of this definition would exclude material prepared by the Service, such as the report of a Revenue Agent (RAR) : or Special Agent (SAR), which contains data from the return and which is part of the tax determination process.

From a policy standpoint personal and financial data, obtained by Service personnel from the taxpayer pursuant to the exercise of its administrative or investigative function, is just as deserving of protection from public scrutiny 685/ as is taxpayer-supplied data.

The more difficult question is whether the definition of a return contained in Tax Analysts should be broadened to include personal and financial data obtained from third parties. While the potential constitutional problems involved in the use of third-party-collected data for investigative purposes are of less force as respects this data, the concept of the fruit of the poisonous tree certainly

argues for such a definition.

On the other hand, the Service may, in same instances, have generated the information independently of taxpayer submitted data. It would not have been obtained, however, but for the tax laws. 

Thus, arguably even third party data relating to the taxpayer's personal income or financial status should be protected from disclosure in the same manner as are tax "returns" (a more narrowly construed). Since it appears that deletion of the personal and financial data from, for example, the RAR would render the document essentially meaningless, it would not seem that in camera production and deletion, an approach mentioned by the court in Tax Analysts, would be sufficient to render the document not a "return". 

At the same time it does not appear, as was evidently the objective of the 1972 regulation change, that "the basic policy of confidentiality should extend to every item in our computers, to every memorandum, report 686/ or document.

Such a definition may, however, be a reasonable starting point. But, as the decision in Tax Analysts shows, it would seem to be unreasonable, at least insofar as FOIA is concerned, to seek to place too much of the Service's internal material within the definition of "return". 

Perhaps the approach should be that presently taken by the regulations, and then, as has been suggested, "from this base. . .the exceptions should 687/ be clearly carved out." The basis for carving out should be a reasonable test such as that propounded in Tax Analysts. It is, quite obviously, difficult to state with the necessary precision those items (other than taxpayer-submitted documents) which should be protected. Some effort should be made (along the line, perhaps, although not with the same intent

​M ​688/ of the Administration's disclosure bill) to state those documents and material which should be subjected to protection. If such a comprehensive definition is not developed there may be administrative problems in combing the file to ascertain which bit of information is a return and which is not. 

Such a task would impose a considerable burden on the Service and would require considerable precision in definition. The more difficult question is, of course, whether the Service should be required to assume the burden of sanitizing the documents and whether, thereafter, they should be treated as neither "returns" nor otherwise subject to protection under 6103. 

Another possible, and entirely different approach, to this question is to provide that only taxpayer-submitted documents are protected by $ 6103 (or its successor) and leave to the developing of FOIA machinery the host of questions which deal with the availability of the wide variety of internal IRS material. Such a conclusion raises a number of difficult technical 

There would also be issues which courts may not find easy to resolve. considerable uncertainty for a period of time. For example, the Tax Analysts decision dealt with private letter rulings and technical advice memoranda (concluding that the former are, but that the latter are not, returns), and propounded a test suggesting that both RAR's and SAR's constitute documents 689/ exempt from disclosure under FOIA.

X. Conclusion. 

Despite the anomalous workings of the statute which defines tax returns as public records, in this century tax returns were initially treated as fully confidential. Undoubtedly, the Civil War experiment when returns were first fully public and then made confidential was instrumental in shaping this decision. The policy of confidentiality was fully debated by Congress and the press in the 1920's and early 1930's Congress opted to maintain confidentiality. 

Some European countries, notably Sweden and Norway, open some part 690/ or all of a taxpayer's return to public examination. Wisconsin has also experimented with returns as fully public documents. It has retreated 691/ from this position. The view that returns should be open to the public is supported by two considerations. First, there is the view that those paying taxes are members of a great partnership, and each "partner" has a right to know the other's income. Somewhat less idealistic is the notion that without publicity of tax returns, the government is a "blind man passing a Compliance would be enhanced if each citizen knew the details of others' returns.

Balanced against these considerations is the notion that tax returns contain a lot of private information which should not be available to one's friends and neighbors merely because the government has chosen to extract revenue through an income tax. There is also the likelihood that publication of returns would encourage the amission or falsifying of some kinds of information. Also, the Civil War experience revealed that antagonism to the tax itself arose from the fact that return information was freely available.

Further, the effect of turning one's neighbors and others into spies and informers may be undesirable and perhaps not even effective. Finally, at bottom, there is da undoubtedly some notion (and tradition) that information about one's personal ས་ EZ i and financial affairs should not be available to others without consent. 

The benefits of full publicity then are not great. A few tax cheaters might be apprehended, but the incidence and nature of tax cheating which would be detected seems small and not a compelling reason for public examination of returns. 

While public access to tax returns has generally been denied, governmental access has grown to the point that tax return information is available to nearly any governmental agency which desires it. This use of such information seems contrary to several fundamental precepts. 

First, the information is coerced from the taxpayer. In a sense it is the fruit of duress and has thus the trappings of unreasonable searches and seizures or self-incrimination. The very least, then, that the government can do is to confine its use of information, compiled for revenue purposes, to other uses which do not have a personalized adverse impact on the taxpayer. Second, the framers of our Constitution thought the gathering of personal information sufficiently sensitive to require a provision in the Constitution concerning the decennial census. Given this concern, one must doubt whether Congress should collect information for general government use other than through the census. 

Even if one concedes that Congress could enact a statute requiring the compilation and reporting of personal and financial information for general government use, it has not done so. Indeed, if it were to do so, one would expect considerable political and legal controversy to follow. 

Certainly such a statute would not go unnoticed.

But Congress has not attempted such legislation. Since it has not done so, should revenue-raising enactments be employed to achieve the same purpose? 

One would suppose the answer to be in the negative. That is, the revenueraising function should not be turned into a data bank for all governmental agencies. To do so avoids the political and legal debate which would attend a statute establishing such an information system. 

The use of tax return information for non-tax administration purposes has a very serious effect on the administration of the tax law. The tax administrator is primarily concerned about obtaining accurate and truthful tax returns. Yet, if citizens are told that the information on their tax returns would generally be available to other governmental agencies, there is likely to be a high degree of fudging and inaccurate returns simply because taxpayers do not want particular items of knowledge passed on to other governmental agencies. In some cases, this desire will be based on the possibility of prosecution based on that information. In others, it undoubtedly will be based on the thought that the more people that have access, the more likely that the information will became known to the public in general. other cases, it will be based on the notion that secrets told for the purpose of revenue raising should not be available for other purposes. 

The contrary argument seems based on the belief that once the government has forced compilation of personal and financial information and extracted the compilation, there are a number of beneficial uses to which such information may be put. In other words, because the information is available, there should be no constraints on its use. It should be available

3 for criminal prosecution of the preparer or others. It should be available to fashion legislation and administrative rules and remedies, to impeach witnesses, to select a particular kind of jury, to question grand jurors, and for a myriad of other uses. But only the government is allowed such access. The government may pick and choose those whose returns it will publicize and use for these various purposes. These then are the concerns and arguments. They are argued not to apply with equal force to corporate returns. That argument has some strength. It does not, however, respond properly to the tax administrator's concern about obtaining accurate returns. 

Furthermore, many corporations are in large measure merely individuals doing business under a different form. Thus, the revealing of information on corporate returns will in fact result in revealing information about individuals.

The line between these cases would be very difficult to draw. 

And that line would be even more difficult to place between individual returns and the partnership return or an individual return and a trust return. 

We have now traveled some of the many roads which some users of tax returns must follow. Generally speaking, the public is denied access to tax returns. On the other hand, returns have increasingly become available to government agencies. This practice has grown almost entirely by the joint order of the President and the Treasury or the Service. 

Arguably the public (and perhaps Congress) was misled by the mythology that returns were confidential. 

The present moment seems appropriate to question whether the myth should be fact. If it is not to be fact, then should not Congress so decide? Thus, administrative practice should largely be reversed, and the veil of confidentiality drawn around returns once again. 

If it is to be lifted, Congress should do so.

APPENDIX MAJOR CURRENT BILLS DEALING WITH TAX RETURN CONFIDENTIALITY 

A. Montoya Bill (S. 1511, 94th Cong., 1st Sess. (1975).

This bill would add to the present § 6103 a requirement that "no person and no agency of the Government of the United States, or of a State or political subdivision of a State, shall be permitted to inspect a return. . . unless...the Internal Revenue Service receives written consent from such "I taxpayer to such inspection. The consent requirement does not apply, however, to inspection by states and local governments, shareholders, the Joint Committee on Internal Revenue Taxation, or the Department of Justice or Internal Revenue Service in connection with tax matters. 

Returns may be available to the Department of Justice upon court order which can be issued if "there is probable cause to believe that information contained in the return. . .is necessary for the investigation. . .and that no alternative source of such information is reasonably available...."

1 

B. Administration's Bill (S. 4116, 93rd Cong., 2nd Sess. (1974)). 

This bill would, generally speaking, codify present practice, although it does, in a few areas, change present practice. It would, in other words, cement into this statute the practice that tax returns are a generalized government asset available to the Executive for numerous purposes. 

For example, it would deny access to local government tax officials and provide that access by non-tax writing committees of Congress must be authorized by a resolution of the whole house. With respect to White House access, the bill adopts the approach taken in the Executive Order, i.e., returns would be available only upon request of the President in writing. 

With respect to Strike Force use, the bill provides that only "return information" (documents other than those supplied by the taxpayer personally as part of the return) will be furnished and then only to the extent such return information contains data other than that furnished by the taxpayer. (This represents little change in present practice since the bulk of the data furnished Strike Forces consists of third party information.) would, as noted, also change considerably the availability of returns for litigation in impeaching witnesses. It

The bill corrects the present historical anomaly (pursuant to which it is stated that returns "shall constitute public records") by stating that returns shall be confidential except as otherwise provided in the statute. 

The bill seeks to have the statute spell out the instances in which tax returns are available outside the Service, leaving little (unlike present law) to the regulations. 77-842 O - 76 - 65

When the 1939

Code was adopted (Act of February 10, 1939, ch. 2, 53 Stat. 1, 29), both the 

1933-1938 and 1926 approaches, respectively, were adopted with § 55 (a)(1) of the 1939 Code providing that income tax returns were "open to public examination and inspection to such extent as shall be authorized. . .by the President" and § 55 (a) (2) of the 1939 Code providing that: "Returns. .upon which the tax has been determined. . .shall constitute public records; but,...they shall be open to inspection only upon order of the President and under rules and regulations prescribed by the Secretary and approved by the President."

This bifurcated approach continues today as IRC, S 6103 (a) (1) & (2). 

It is doubtful that there is any difference, in effect, between § 6103 (a) (1) and $ 6103 (a) (2). The regulations blur any distinction between them, providing only that "[T]he President is authorized by subsection (a) of § 6103 to open to public examination and inspection returns in respect of taxes. .

50/ Act of June 2, 1924, ch. 234, 43 Stat. 253, 293. The House-passed bill had adopted prior law with respect to inspection (only under the rules prescribed by the Secretary and approved by the President), whereas the Senate had voted, at the urging of Senator Norris, for full publicity.et During a threatened deadlock in the conference, Herbert Hoover, then Secretary of

Commerce, issued a statement that return publicity would do much harm to business (particularly small business where competitors would find out too much).

Hoover referred to the previous experiment with publicity during the Civil War income tax experiment and said it contributed to the industrial and financial chaos of the times. New York Times, May 17, 1924, at 1, col. 7.

The deadlock was broken, however, by the adoption of a compromise involving the making available of a list containing the name, address and income of the taxpayer. New York Times, May 22, 1924, at 1, col. 8. (Part of this campromise was the adoption of provisions providing for the availability of tax returns to the tax-writing committees of Congress and for the full publicity of tax details, in cases involving more than $10,000, in matters before the new Board of Tax Appeals. Act of June 2, 1924, id.) The limited publicity afforded by the making of the special list provided for in the 1924 legislation was not regarded as a victory by those who urged full publicity. Note comments of Senator Norris, 65 Cong. Rec. 9403-9409. 52/ Act of Feb. 26, 1926, ch. 27, 44 Stat. 9, 52. This amendment was accomplished by simply deleting from the statute the language "together with the amount of the income tax paid by such person. The surviving provision, providing that the Commissioner maintain for public inspection (in each district) lists containing the name and address of each person making an income tax return in such district, was eventually enacted as $ 55 (e) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1939, and IRC, § 6103 (£). 

In 1966 the provision was changed to authorize (in lieu of the directive regarding the maintenance of lists) the furnishing to an inquirer of the information as to whether or not a person has filed an income tax return.

Pub. L. No. 89-713, § 4, 80 Stat. 1109,

The change was adopted because of the difficulty of making microfilm (on which such data was to be maintained) available to the public and because of the undesirability of making the Social Security number of an individual (also the taxpayer identification number) generally available to the public. The availability of information relating to whether or not a person filed a return was, however, reaffirmed. S. Rep. No. 1625, 89th Cong., 2d Sess., 7-8 (1966). 53/ The publicity forces in Congress were unstinting in their efforts. 

In 1928 they had obtained Senate passage of a full publicity amendment. 

69 Cong. Bec. 9059-9064, 9069, 9073-9082. The 1928 Senate-passed amendment would have made returns "open to examination and inspection as other public records under the same rules and regulations as may govern the examination of public documents generally." During action on the conference report, Senator Couzens, ardently in favor of full publicity, made the point that "there is no provision for publishing the private affairs of individuals contained in this amendment" (69 Cong. Rec. 9850) and that they are simply "public records according to law" (69 Cong. Rec. 

9849). Even though newspaper publication was not anticipated, it was asked (by Senator Bruce) whether "the mere absence of newspaper publication would keep some fellow who really wanted, for selfish purposes, to know what the income of his business rival was, from going to the collector's office to gratify his desire?" 69 Cong. Rec. 9853. Senator

Smoot succeeded in getting a favorable vote on his motion that the Senate recede from its previously adopted full-publicity amendment. 

Cong. Rec. 9854. 

54/ Act of May 10, 1934, ch. 277, 48 Stat. 680, 698. The "pink slip" approach was conceived by Cong. Wright Patman who stated that secrecy of income tax returns placed the government in "the same position as a blind man passing around the hat," the "blind man does not know who contributes, or how much." 78 Cong. Rec. 2600. To protect against the disclosure of trade secrets, etc., and still permit availability of each taxpayer's "contribution," Patman proposed "a publicity sheet which could be detached and sent to a separate department and which would be subject to inspection of any citizen at any time. . .The sheet would contain limited by all essential information." 78 Cong. Rec. 2601. 55/ "Such statements [the "pink slips"] or copies thereof shall as soon as practicable be made available to public examination and inspection in such manner as the Commissioner, with the approval of the Secretary, may determine, in the office of the collector with which they are filed, for a period of not less than three years from the date they are

required to be filed." 

Act of May 10, 1934, ch. 277, 48 Stat. 680, 698.

T.D. 2016, Aug. 18, 1914. The regulations also stated that returns of individuals "are under no circumstances to be made public, except where such publicity shall result through the use of such returns in any legal proceedings in which the United States is a party. 

Despite the cloak of privacy which was to envelop individual returns, the 1914 regulations continued to provide that certain corporate returns (those of coporations the stock of which was traded on recognized exchanges and those whose stock was advertised in the press) would be open to inspection by any person. That returns were generally regarded as confidential, however, is made manifest by T.D. 1962, Mar. 

20, 1914, instructing Revenue Officers to "preserve as inviolably confidential all income-tax returns. Interestingly, the provision in the 1910 regulations providing that corporate returns could be made available to other departments of the government (upon submission of an application "setting out the reasons therefor") was not expanded to include returns of individuals under the 1914 regulations (at a time when the income tax applied to individuals as well). That this language was not inadvertent is indicated by the provision making 11 "all returns, whether of persons or of corporations" available for use "in any legal proceedings before any United States grand jury or in the trial of any cause to which both the United States and the person or corporation. . .rendering the return are parties either as plaintiff or defendant, and in the prosecution or defense or trial of which action, or proceeding before a grand jury, such return would constitute material evidence.

69/ There is a difference between United States attorneys and attorneys of the Department of Justice. United States attorneys are political appointees and are not members of the Department of Justice. Fish v. U.S. 36 F. 677 (D.C. N.Y. 1880). The President appoints one United States attorney for each judicial district for a term of four years. 28 U.S.C. S 541 (a) and (b). The President also has the power to remove United States attorneys. 28 U.S.C. § 541 (c). 

The duties of United States attorneys are enumerated in 28 U.S.c. § 547. Although the Attorney General does not have the authority to direct United States attorneys to institute suits, he may supervise all litigation. 28 U.S.C. § 519. United States v. 

San Jascinto Tin Co., 125 U.S. 273 (1888). Attorneys of the Department of Justice, however, are under control of the Attorney General and generally are employed by one of the functional divisions of the Department of Justice. These attorneys are usually considered to be more slanted toward a career in the Civil Service than United States attorneys.

92/ The purpose of these procedural requirements is not altogether clear.

Reg. $ 301.6103(a)-1 (f) (1961). By stating only that the return is requested "in connection with an official matter," the request simply states a conclusion and cannot be regarded as stating the reason why the return is desired. 

120/ Requested pursuant to Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-1 (f) (1961). The reason given appears to be more adequately stated than most requests for investigative use, but still seems to fall short of what might be thought a desirable explanation. 

121/ This request by the Federal Home Loan Bank Board, for purposes of investigating employees of an insured institution, does not set forth any of the information which is in the possession of the requesting agency which led it to believe that there may have been a violation of either fiduciary duty or criminal law. Given the conclusionary nature of the statement, the reason for inspection is little more than a statement that inspection is desirable to the requester. 

122/ Again, there is nothing more than a statement of need.

123/ Many of the requests by the Securities and Exchange Commission are as deficient in stating why the return is desired. 

124/ This request, too, states nothing about "why" the returns are desired. 

125/ The request, from the office of the Attorney General, stated: "I have been informed by...the Director, of Office of Watergate Special Prosecution Force, that the.. is of interest in connection with the matters he has under investigation. . .In order. . .to conduct and coordinate his investigations adequately. It cannot be said, in this instance, that the reason why inspection is desired is set forth in any sense. It is simply stated that the return is "of interest." Requests for the Watergate Special Prosecutor were made through the Attorney General, presumably under Treas. Reg., § 301.6103 (a)-1(g) (1961), on the notion that those requesting were attorneys of the Department of Justice. 

126/ For example, the Department of Justice's Anti-Trust Division requested returns for "investigation into whether [the taxpayer] should be prosecuted for violations of the Truth in Lending Act, 15 U.S.C. 1601 et.seq., aiding and abetting, 18 U.S.C. 2, and falsifying bank records, 18 U.S.C. 1005." However, this request does not state the facts, if any, which justify requesting the return. 

127/ E.g., "[t]hese returns are necessary for the defense of the Government's interest in this litigation. The action involves a suit. against the United States for injuries. . .sustained by working as a longshoreman upon a Government-owned vessel." 

128/ E.g., "[t]his Division is engaged in defending the interests of the 

United States in a complaint filed by the plaintiff for alleged personal injuries suffered by him. The income tax return information will be of assistance in the defense of this suit." This appears to be a request for use in litigation or for preparation for litigation. Treas. Reg. 

S 301.6103 (a)-1 (h) (1961). The question arises whether it is sufficient to simply state that the return "will be assistance in the defense of the

suit" or whether the Department of Justice should be required to describe the nature of the suit and how the return will be relevant and of assistance. Many of the requests by the Civil Division are honored on the basis of as minimal a showing of need as this: "This information is necessary in the defense of the above-captioned case [against the U.S.]." 129/ E.g., "[t]his Department is prosecuting a suit to recover for damages to. .which occurred while.. .was piloting the said vessel. 

The documents requested are needed in order to evaluate the ability of [this taxpayer] to pay any settlement or judgment." Although the reason for the request seems clear enough, it may properly be asked whether the reason offered is within the concept of use for litigation (or preparation for litigation). If it were not, the return would presumably still be available under Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a) -1 (g) (1961). Further, a return obtained under Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-1 (g) (1961), may be used later in litigation. Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-1 (h) (1961). 

130/ E.g., "[t]his Department is defending a lawsuit brought by. against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act. The requested tax returns are needed for the purpose of evaluating the damages sustained by. . .in the accident giving rise to the above suit." It may be asked whether making return information available to the Justice Department in such instances bestows upon it an unfair litigation advantage.

199/ Two other aspects of present practice are possibly affected by the language of the civil or criminal law enforcement exception. First, it is provided that the request specify the particular portion of the record desired. Does this prevent the requesting agency from obtaining the whole return? Such a result might be consistent with a notion that the requesting agency can get only that portion of the record which it needs and should not be able to obtain more than it needs. By requiring the agency to state what it needs, does the statute have the effect of imposing a probable cause requirement (i.e., the agency may not use the record to conduct a "fishing expedition," but must have a specific investigative objective in mind)? Second, the agency must state in the request the law enforcement activity for which the record is sought. 

Does this requirement have the effect of precluding broad-based investigations (i.e., the agency must state the offense for which the person is under investigation)? The Privacy Act Guidelines support this conclusion by noting that "[b]lanket requests for all records pertaining to an individual are not permitted." Privacy Act Guidelines, at 28955.

Further, although the Privacy Act Guidelines would seem to permit the volunteering of data regarding criminal offenses (by the Service to the Department of Justice), the Guidelines would permit this only when "such disclosure has been established in advance as a 'routine use' and that misconduct is related to the purposes for which the records are maintained. [Emphasis added] Privacy Act Guidelines, at 28955. 11 200/ The Disclosure Staff, however, presently maintains records which may come close to satisfying $ 552a (c) of the Privacy Act. 

It indexes requests under the name of the taxpayer and the requesting agency. It is doubtful, however, whether field offices (from which tax data may be requested in certain instances) maintain records which would comply with the Privacy Act. See generally Privacy Act Guidelines, at 28955-56.

No. 93-1416, 93rd Cong., 2d Sess. 14 (1973). Neither of the exceptions to the record-keeping requirement relating to records maintained by an agency "which performs as its principal function any activity pertaining to the enforcement of criminal laws" (5 U.S.c. § 552a (j)) or to a records system which is "[i]nvestigatory material compiled for law enforcement purposes" (5 U.S.C. § 552a (k)) has an application to the disclosure of tax returns to other agencies.

206/ To take the position that "routine use," as defined in the Privacy Act, blesses all existing disclosure practices followed by an agency would not only be tantamont to saying the Act has no restricting effect, but since there are eleven exceptions to the scope of the Act (5 U.S.C. § 552 (a) (b)), it would be the same as saying that it has the effect of broadening prior disclosure of tax returns, 207/ 5 U.S.C. § 552a (e) (3). 

208/ While income tax returns do contain enormous amounts of information which is useful for a number of purposes, it is not clear that all users of the information understand its limitations. For example, depreciation allowances rarely, if ever, reflect either economic depreciation or depreciation as generally recognized by the accounting professions. In some cases, the tax returns will contain a reconciliation of the tax depreciation to accounting depreciation, but the use of such reconciliation probably is uncommon. There are many other similar items. Indeed, due to the generally inaccurate, from an economic view, nature of tax information, use of it without adjustment may be an argument against making it available.

251/ The Census Bureau sets forth in its White Paper several alternative to its use of tax return data each, in its view, with serious disadvantages. 

Mailing lists, obtained by purchase from public and private sources, would not result in as complete a list (and an extensive field canvass would be necessary to determine the extent of error). Census could develop mailing lists by field enumeration -- an approach which would be both costly and inaccurate (e.g., many businesses are not recognizable as such causing a significant undercounting to result). Mandatory registration would require the cooperation of law enforcement agencies (since the Bureau has no enforcement powers) and would be allegedly destructive of the trust which now exists between the Bureau and respondents. Census also asserts that if it were given only a limited amount of tax information (i.e., name, address, business code), it would be required to obtain information from the 3 million firms excused from reporting in 1972 and that field enumeration would be required on non-respondents (since Census would possess no data concerning them). Another alternative would be for the Internal Revenue Service, acting in effect as a service agency for Census, to assume the function of gathering the data "in-house" and submitting it to Census. This is the approach taken in the Weicker-Litton bill (supra note 

236); while the Census Bureau would still be entitled to tax return data under the Adminstration's proposal (supra note 237), the in-house preparation of statistical material by the Internal Revenue Service is the approach adopted in that bill for other agencies which presently use tax data for statistical purposes. Census offers a number of reasons why in-house preparation of data for the Bureau would not be suitable. A great deal of the data Census obtains from smaller concerns is obtained by means of canvassing a smaller group. maintains that there would be no way to develop this sample scientifically (which involves relating Census data with IRS data) if the identity of the taxpayer, and certain data items, are not made available. (Furthermore, 13 

U.S.C. $9 prohibits making the Census data available to IRS for that purpose). 

Second, Census asserts that by not having an up-to-date Business Master File (BMF), it would not be able to respond as promptly as necessary for the purpose of producing current and accurate economic reports and forecasts. 

Third, difficulty is created by the fact that the two agencies collect data on a different basis--Census collects and tabulates its data on an establishment basis and IRS maintains its tax records on a legal entity basis. The 200,000 multi-establishment firms account for the major share of economic activity (e.g., they employ 75 percent of all persons engaged in manufacturing). Census must Census

EI be able to substitute Census establishment data for IRS legal entity data. do this IRS would have to identify the firms included in its tabulations (so that Census can weed out the duplications) or Census would have to disclose to IRS identifiable data which it is now prohibited from doing.

Until recently, when requesting tax returns under Treas. Reg. $ 301.6103 (a)-1 (g), (1961), Justice Department attorneys would simply request all available tax returns

for a particular taxpayer. Since the Internal Revenue Service begins the process of the destruction of returns in the seventh year, it made a regular practice of supplying the returns for the six years for which they were available. (In January 1971 the Service cut back on the number of returns made available to Justice by simply supplying it with the returns for the last three years.) This practice was in contravention of the regulation which requires that the return be requested by year, but it existed until 1975. 

When the old policy Prevailed, it was not possible to get a completely accurate count on the number of returns requested by Justice. For statistical purposes, the Disclosure Staff of the Internal Revenue Service would simply multiply the number of taxpayers by 6 (or by 3) to determine the number of returns requested. It was the uncertainty of this method which, in 

November 1974, prompted the Disclosure Staff to request the Department of 

Justice to comply with the regulation.

366/ Id. at 20. 367/ Id. at 21. In at least two instances the legality of the manner in which Strike Forces are operated has been questioned. In U. S. v. Williams, 16 Crim. L. Rep. 2223 (D.C. Mo. Nov. 15, 1974), the defendant moved to dismiss the indictment on the grounds, inter alia, that the Special United States Attorneys (attached to a Strike Force) who procured the indictment lacked authority to do so. The court, in granting a request requiring the United States to produce intra-departmental documents relating to the authority of the Special Attorneys to represent the United States and the relationship and division of authority between the Special Attorneys and the U. S. Attorney, was concerned about whether 25 U.S.C. § 515(a) intended to authorize the Attorney General to establish field offices of sections of the Department of Justice, to appoint Special Attorneys to staff those offices, and to attempt to vest those attorneys "with the identical general power to conduct legal proceedings, civil or

criminal, in connection with a group of selected statutes, which the duly authorized United States Attorneys are under duty and authorized by law to conduct.' The United States preferred to "suffer dismissal" of the criminal case rather than produce the documents requested. 11 U. S. 

v. Williams, 16 Crim. L. Rep. 2225 (D.C. Mo. Dec. 3, 1974). The U. S. 

District Court for the Western District of Missouri continues to dismiss Strike Force cases for the same reasons. U. S. v. Agrusa, 16 Crim. L. 

Rep. 2509 (D.C. Mo. Feb. 25, 1975).

In a second case, U. S. v. Crispino, 16 Crim. L. Rep. 2503 (D.C. S.D.N.Y. Feb. 13, 1975), the indictment was challenged on the grounds that the Strike Force attorney who presented the case to the grand jury was not authorized to present the case to that body. The question involved was whether the Special Attorney was "specifically directed" by the Attorney General (as required by 28 U.S.C. § 515 (a)) to handle the proceeding involved. The form letter appointing the Special 

Attorney (the result of a revision of the form made in 1972) directed him to conduct proceedings in connection with the "aforesaid cases" involving the violation of "federal criminal statutes." The court concluded, in dismissing the indictment that this did not constitute the specific direction required by the statute - "nowhere in the commission is there any attempt to give a description of the type of cases -- such as 'organized crime cases' or 'Land Division cases,' or 'tax fraud' cases, etc."

The intent of Congress in providing for the appointment of Special Attoneys was to make special counsel available for the prosecution of "particularly important" cases -- special situations "where the Attorney General concluded that the particular knowledge and skill of these special attorneys would be useful." The form of appointment used in Crispino made no attempt, the court held, to set forth circumstances justifying the appointment of special counsel or to limit the appearance of special counsel where "particular knowledge and skill" would be required. But, cf. 

U. S. v. Brown, 16 Crim. L. Rep. 2505 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 24, 1975), in which the U. S. District Court refused to dismiss the indictment, noting that 28 U.S.C. § 515(a) should be read "not as a limitation but as a broad grant authorizing commission as general as those questioned here" and observing that "no fundamental rights are at stake here that need be conserved in the constitutional interests of criminal targets." The court concluded that the "overriding purpose" of the statute "was to benefit and protect the public by expanding the prosecutorial capacity of the federal government.

405/ U. S. v. Sullivan, 274 U.S. 259 (1927); California v. Byers, 402 U.S. 424 (1971). In this context the so-called "required records" doctrine is also relevant. In Shapiro v. U. S., 355 U.S. 1 (1948), the Court held, in effect, that private records (kept pursuant to OPA regulations) were not within the reach of the privilege. The Court reasoned that as a result of the record-keeping requirement the private records became public records over which the individual record-keeper lost control. Reading this decision broadly, every transaction which could conceivably be regulated by the Congress is potentially beyond the scope of the privilege. The government has not, however, chosen to push the doctrine to the limit of its logiv. of its logiv. If it were applied, it would presumably permit the IRS to compel production of any tax records and use them for criminal prosecution or make them available to other agencies. It would also affect the rules controlling disclosure of tax data by stripping away any Constitutional argument against revealing such material. The Shapiro doctrine is, however, under attack and judicial contact with it has not resulted in its expansion. E.g., Marchetti, supra note 403, at 56-57. As Dean McKay states: "The required records doctrine is accordingly inconsistent with both major policy purposes of the privilege [against self-incrimination] : preservation of morality in government and preservation of individual privacy." Arguably, the Byers plurality was "balancing" the risks of incrimination and the government's need to know-- "allowing their concern for legitimate noncriminal governmental objectives to overflow into the definition of incriminating." The Supreme Court, 1970 Term, 85 Harv. L. Rev. 3, 274 (1971). The view has been expressed, however, that the plurality was not really "balancing," but simply concluding that the disclosures will not be incriminating unless the statutory scheme is directed at an "inherently suspect" group in an area "permeated with criminal statutes," thereby "virtually divorc ing fifth amendment protections from all situations where the government raises a colorable claim that it is not criminal-law motivated. Ibid. Justice 

Harlan, who supported the majority view in Byers, did, indeed, see a "balancing" approach as necessary when the government is pursuing legitimate regulatory interests. He saw the issue as follows: "Under what conditions, if any, does the fact that the government is pursuing goals other than the enforcement of the criminal law allow it to both demand and then prosecutorially use self-incriminating disclosures?" Id. at 276. In Byers, Mr. Justice Harlan developed an analytical framework for testing the relative importance of the personal and governmental interests. Although when applied to the facts in Byers the personal interests at stake were found to be weak, the same may not be true insofar as use of tax data for investigative purposes is concerned. Mr. Justice Harlan's first concern was the individual's personal interests, which would vary according to how explicitly incriminating the evidence was. As one commentator notes, the information disclosed under compulsion in Garner was far more explicitly incriminating than elicited by the motor vehicle statute in Byers." 86 Harv. L. Rev. 914 921 (1973). Second, Mr. Justice Harlan would look to the government's non-prosecutorial interest in the success of the regulatory or information-gathering scheme. the tax field, as in Byers, the government has a substantial non-criminal interest although honest and accurate reporting, being absolutely requisite of a selfassessment tax system, makes use immunity a more appropriate approach since it "fosters the confidence necessary to an efficient self-reporting scheme." 86 

Harv. L. Rev. 914,222 (1973). As a third point, Mr. Justice Harlan was concerned about the difficulty which the prosecutor might have in providing that the evidence offered was not related to the information gathered for a non-prosecutorial "1 In

purpose.

As later discussion will indicate, the proof of non-relation may be (and certainly could be) easier in the tax area than it was in Byers.

424/ In Murphy the Court adopted an "exclusionary rule" which prohibited the government "from making any. . .Use of compelled testimony and its fruits." 378 U.S. at 79, It would appear that the effect of a judicially imposed "exclusion" would be substantially the same as the grant of immunity, usually effected by the prosecutor pursuant to statutory authority. (For a listing of the Federal immunity statutes, see National Commission on Reform of Federal Criminal Laws, Working Papers, at 1444-1445 (1970).) Informal immunity (that given without direct statutory authority) has been "roughly divided into grants which are unintentional, being judicially imposed, and intentional, as a result of prosecutorial agreement. ... [The former] is frequently conferred as the result of the fact that exclusion of illegally seized evidence and the fruits thereof is the sanction for a violation by government agents of constitutional (and possibly certain procedural) rights." Id. at 1419. [Emphasis in original] A specific immunity statute, however, "reflects the importance of testimony, and the fact that many offenses are of such a character that the only persons capable of giving useful testimony are those implicated in the crime." Kastigar v U.S., 406 U.S. 441, 446 (1971). Insofar as the use of tax returns is concerned, it would seem that the "immunity" would be granted in the form of a restriction upon use (the Supreme Court in California v. Byers speaks of "use restriction"; e.g.,406 U.S. at 447. But, cf. Garner v. U. S., 501 F. 2d 236, 257, n. 26, which speaks of "use immunity".)

However, a situation could be imagined where a taxpayer would agree to make his return or tax records available for investigation of another party in return for a grant of "use immunity" by the prosecutor.

431/ In the event that the views of the Garner minority are not adopted, there are at least three methods of tighten up the present unrestricted flow of confidential tax information for investigative use. .One would be to amend the regulations authorizing investigative use. In U. S. v. Tucker, 316 F. Supp. 

Supp. 822 (D.C. Conn. 1970), the court stated that the spirit of § 6103 prohibited "fishing expeditions" for tax data relating to non-tax crimes. If this is so, the regulation under which tax material is made available to the Department of Justice should so state. At present they require only that the requesting agency declare "the reason why inspection is desired." Treas. Reg. $301.6103 (a)-1 (g) (1961). In practice, the Department of Justice will often make the conclusory assertion that the taxpayer is under investigation for possible violation of Title 18. An improvement could be made by providing the request contain considerably more detail. In investigations prompted by suspected criminal violations, the statement should contain a brief summary of the evidence that (a) there has been a criminal violation and (b) the taxpayer whose return is requested is connected with the alleged offense. It appears clear that, the present regulation is not sufficiently demanding and allows for the use of tax data in a search for evidence relating to the possible commission of offenses not associated with the revenue laws. No doubt the Department of Justice would urge that the requirement that it name the specific offense involved is too burdensome. At the very least, however, it should be required to state that "it is reasonable to believe that there has been a criminal violation." In this way, the Department of Justice or other investigating agency would be charged with the responsibility of developing, independent of the tax return data, evidence of criminal conduct. This might deter netting of tax returns in "fishing expeditions" for evidence relating to non-tax crimes. The better approach appears, however, to require that the requesting agency set out its evidence relating to the specific offense.

3 If it were required only to state that it had evidence that a crime was committed (without naming the specific offense), it could, upon obtaining the data, "fish for evidence relating to other offenses. 

Under a requirement that the department or agency set out the specific crime involved, it would seem that the evidence could be used for that purpose only. Thus, it might well be appropriate, in accord with the Federal exclusionary rule, to suppress the use of evidence obtained from tax data in a proceeding involving another crime. 

A second approach would be the enactment of legislation requiring a court order. To ensure that the party requesting tax data for investigative purposes has substantial evidence indicating the commission of a crime, the statute could be amended to allow release of tax data for an investigation purpose not associated with the administration of the revenue laws unless the requesting agency establishes the existence of probable cause. E.g., H.R, 18387, 91st Cong., 2nd Sess., at If a tax return is regarded as simply an extension of a taxpayer's own books and records, a requirement that a showing of probable cause be made is consistent with the Fourth Amendment rights generally accorded such records. A warrant would be necessary before a taxpayer's records could be examined in a matter not associated with the revenue laws, and it seems equally appropriate to provide such protection when the income tax return is involved. 

Finally, if the view of the Garner majority is adopted (i.e., the privilege to be properly invoked must be claimed at the time the return is filed), it should be required that taxpayers be informed of the availability of returns to investigative agencies. Most taxpayers believe that a return is a confidential document and is not used for purposes unrelated to revenue administration. To dispel this notion, taxpayers should be warned by a statement on the return that the information they disclose may be used against them. For example, the following would be appropriate: "This return may be used against you in any civil or criminal proceeding, whether or not related to the revenue laws." A strong argument can be made that without this type of statement the "taxpayer has a privilege of non-disclosure of some scope," which would be violated by making the return available for use in a non-tax investigation. See Mansfield, supra note 402, at 151, n. 86, making the point that the "privilege of non-disclosure" may be implied from the fact that an Internal Revenue Servie agent conducting a criminal investigation need not advise the suspect of his right to counsel and his privilege against self-incrimination. E.g., Cohen v. 

U. S., 405 F. 2d 34 (1968). And, it should be noted that the Service subsequently announced in a press release that, as a matter of policy persons suspected of tax fraud would be given Miranda-type warnings.

460/ There is also authority for the proposition that the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination limits the evidentiary items which may be searched for, or 'seized, incident to arrest or with a search warrant. Hill v. Philpott, 445 F.2d 144, 150 (7th Cir. 1971). Among them are tax returns. If they are, thus, protected from seizure upon an adequately grounded warrant, it would seem that they should clearly be protected from a warrantless search. See also Shaffer v. Wilson, F.2d, 75-1 U.S.T.C. 

87,279 (10th Cir. 1975); and VonderAHE v. Howland, 508 F.2d 364 (9th Cir. 1975), holding that although the search was unreasonable, a claim of Fifth Amendment violation was premature in absence of proceedings against taxpayer.

462/ There are several earlier cases which (without discussion of any Constitutional aspects) permit the evidentiary use of tax material in non-tax prosecutions. E.g., Lewy v. U.S., 29 F.2d 462 (7th Cir. 1928), cert. denied, 279 U.S. 850 (mail fraud); U. S. v. Rollnick, 91 F.2d 911 (2d Cir. 1937) (mail fraud); Shushan v. U. S., 117 F.2d 110 (5th Cir.
